The pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L encoder ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) processes each camera independently, producing observation features z ctx z_{\mathrm{ctx}} from the most recent frames, and future targets z fut z_{\mathrm{fut}} representing the 32 frames ahead. We normalize and spatially reduce these feature grids before projecting them into the World DiT’s embedding space. They are the model’s only visual input and prediction target, so the model gets no separate RGB pathway. Future predictions are matched to targets directly in V-JEPA space and require no pixel reconstruction.

A frozen FLAN-T5-large encoder ( Chung et al., 2022 ) embeds the instruction ℓ \ell , and learned projections map proprioception s t s_{t} to additional tokens; together they form the conditioning sequence z cond z_{\mathrm{cond}} , which both DiTs read through cross-attention.

The model is made of two diffusion transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles & Xie, 2022 ) : a World DiT over observation and future-feature tokens and an Action DiT over the action chunk. Both are initialized from scratch with separate attention projections and feed-forward layers, so pretrained knowledge enters only through the visual and language encoders. Rotary visual positional encodings ( Su et al., 2021 ) preserve spatial and temporal information. The two DiTs interact at every layer, where action queries read the World DiT’s observation keys and values alongside its own. The attention mask keeps future information out of the action pathway: observation tokens attend only to observations, future tokens to observations and futures, and action tokens to observations and actions. Actions therefore never access future features directly, yet predictive supervision still shapes the observation representations they read through the shared World DiT parameters during training.

We train both DiTs with future and action-space flow matching ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) . For each training example, we independently sample timesteps τ f , τ a ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \tau_{f},\tau_{a}\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) and Gaussian noise ϵ f , ϵ a \epsilon_{f},\epsilon_{a} , forming the noisy inputs

At inference, we drop the future-feature tokens, initialize the action chunk from Gaussian noise, and integrate the action velocity field from τ a = 0 \tau_{a}=0 to τ a = 1 \tau_{a}=1 with Euler steps, holding the World DiT’s timestep conditioning at a fixed value τ ctx = 0 \tau_{\mathrm{ctx}}=0 (since we do not predict the futures anyway). Since observation tokens attend only to one another under fixed conditioning, their per-layer keys and values are computed once and cached, and only the Action DiT runs at each denoising step. Like most recent policies, we convert the predicted action tokens to the robot’s action space, execute the first k k actions of the chunk ( k = 10 k=10 on LIBERO and 24 on RoboTwin, as in Fast-WAM), and then predict a new chunk from the latest observations.

We test the design choices behind Section 5 with the small (S) policy unless stated otherwise. We ask, in turn, whether to predict future features, in which feature space, how to encode motion (Section 4.1 ), and then how to make the policy robust to observation changes (Section 4.2 ). The studies use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and clean-trained RoboTwin 2.0 ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) ; in-distribution (IID) evaluation refers to LIBERO or clean RoboTwin scenes, and out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation to LIBERO-Plus or randomized scenes. Figure 3 reports each choice’s gain in success in percentage points (hereafter, points), grouped into blocks A to F. Each block has its own reference recipe, so comparisons hold within a block; Table 6 lists baselines and evaluation budgets, and Appendix A documents the protocols.

We first test whether predicting future features benefits the policy, comparing joint action and future-feature prediction with action-only training (Figure 3 A). Future prediction raises RoboTwin success by 7.0 points in clean and 3.7 in randomized scenes. On LIBERO-Plus, it improves success for each of three training seeds, by 2.1 points on average, with every paired comparison significant ( p < 0.01 p<0.01 , McNemar; Appendix A.1 ).

We next ask in which space prediction should be learned, comparing frozen V-JEPA 2.1 features with latents of the VAE of Wan2.2 ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ) , the video model underlying Fast-WAM, Faster-WAM, and LeapBot-WA (Figure 3 B). Each policy learns action and future-feature prediction with the normalization and projections suited to its representation, so the comparison evaluates each representation together with its interface to the policy. V-JEPA improves success in all four evaluations of this pair: by 15.9 points in clean and 16.0 in randomized RoboTwin scenes, and by 6.0 on LIBERO-Plus and 2.0 on LIBERO. In randomized scenes, the Wan2.2 policy collapses and succeeds in only 1.0% of episodes, close to the video-generator WAMs in Table 2 . In two additional RoboTwin comparisons (Appendix A.1 ), clean success is comparable in one and favors Wan2.2 in the other, whereas randomized success, reported for the second, again strongly favors V-JEPA. These results echo those of LDA-1B, which similarly reports a large gain from replacing VAE latents with DINO features ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) .

Unlike LDA-1B’s DINO, which only encodes images, V-JEPA 2.1 can process videos, which raises the question of how the observations and future targets should be encoded. We tested three configurations. Static encodings treat every frame as an image: the observation is the current frame, and eight future targets, spaced four frames apart up to 32 frames ahead, are encoded separately. Tube encoding instead processes two-frame clips aligned with the encoder’s tubelets, ending at the current frame for the observation and at each target frame for the futures; the observation clip thus gives the policy a motion cue without access to future observations. Tube-motion keeps the tube observation but jointly encodes the 16 future frames, spaced two frames apart, so each of the eight future feature grids attends over the whole predicted horizon (Figure 2 , right). Relative to static encoding on RoboTwin (Figure 3 C), tube encoding raises clean success by 1.1 points and randomized success by 3.6, and tube-motion preserves the randomized gain ( + 3.7 +3.7 ) while raising the clean gain to 3.4; the final recipe therefore uses tube-motion.

Before entering the World DiT, the encoded feature grids are reduced spatially, either by averaging neighboring features (mean pooling) or by concatenating them into one token (patch grouping). We initially used mean pooling for its simplicity, since it can be applied once to the precomputed features. On RoboTwin, patch grouping improved randomized success, so the final RoboTwin recipe uses it; LIBERO did not benefit from it (89.35% against 94.05% with mean pooling), so we kept mean pooling there (Appendix A.1 ).

To reduce reliance on any single view, we drop eligible cameras during training, always retaining at least one view and removing the dropped cameras’ future targets from the loss (Figure 3 D). This is the condition dropout used to train classifier-free guidance ( Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) , although we sample without guidance. Dropping only the wrist cameras raises randomized RoboTwin success by 7.1 points, while clean success remains essentially unchanged. LIBERO benefits from this too: by allowing either camera to be dropped, we raise LIBERO-Plus success by 10.2 points, with large gains under camera-viewpoint and sensor-noise perturbations (Table 8 ), while in-distribution success slightly improves.

Dropping the proprioceptive conditioning with probability 0.1 during training, with the configuration otherwise unchanged, raises RoboTwin success by 3.8 points in clean and 4.2 in randomized scenes (Figure 3 E). The final recipe therefore uses both camera and proprioception dropout.

Finally, we combine image augmentation of the observations with LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) adaptation of the observation encoder; future targets are still computed from unmodified frames by the original encoder for training efficiency purposes (Appendix B ). Relative to a plain LIBERO policy (Figure 3 F), LoRA alone adds 1.4 points on LIBERO-Plus, augmentation alone 5.8, and both together 7.2, while in-distribution success remains unchanged. The combined recipe also improves RoboTwin, raising clean success by 5.7 points and randomized success by 16.0 (Appendix A.2 ).

These studies define the final recipe: joint action and future prediction in V-JEPA 2.1 tube-motion features, camera and proprioception dropout, and image augmentation with encoder LoRA. We train it at three sizes, S, B, and L (Table 9 ), which correspond to 0.10, 0.34, and 1.14 B trainable parameters respectively. Appendix B documents the remaining benchmark-specific settings.

We evaluate the final recipe against WAM and VLA policies that, like La-JEPA, use no embodied pretraining on robot data beyond the target demonstrations (Figure 1 , Tables 1 and 2 ), and against the closest latent world-action models (Table 3 ); we then compare computational cost and, on four physical tasks, real-robot success (Table 5 ). Both benchmarks test generalization beyond the training distribution. On RoboTwin, policies are trained on clean demonstrations only and evaluated in both clean scenes and randomized scenes, which add clutter, distractor objects, and new textures. On LIBERO, policies are trained on the four standard suites and evaluated both on them and on LIBERO-Plus, which perturbs them along seven axes such as camera viewpoint, lighting, and sensor noise. On RoboTwin, all three La-JEPA sizes outperform every baseline in both regimes, with the largest margin in randomized scenes (Table 2 ). On LIBERO-Plus, success increases with size. With the released instructions, L exceeds every baseline except NowWAM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , which deploys four times more parameters; with corrected instructions (Section 5.2 ), all three sizes exceed or match every re-evaluated baseline, and L leads NowWAM by 1.8 points. On LIBERO, where most methods are close to saturation, all three sizes come within 0.6 points of the best baseline.

RoboTwin success, in contrast, does not monotonically increase with size. We did not vary the relative size of the Action DiT, which matches the World DiT at every size, and we hypothesize that a larger action expert more easily overfits the action distribution, which is far simpler than the distribution of future features, even when regularized by the world loss. Faster-WAM, whose single-layer action expert generalizes well on LIBERO-Plus ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , is consistent with this hypothesis.

The released LIBERO-Plus evaluator corrupts the instructions of 8,493 of its 10,030 variants by appending the perturbation’s parameters (Table 4 ); Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026a ) noted this issue but substitutes BDDL annotations that paraphrase the training instructions for most variants, so that the language remains perturbed. We therefore also evaluate all open policies with corrected in-distribution instructions (Appendix B ). The corruption affects video-generator-based WAMs most strongly, obscuring their true robustness to several perturbations: with corrected instructions, Fast-WAM gains 19.3 points, LeapBot-WA 8.1, and Cosmos Policy 4.1, whereas image-generator-based WAMs and VLM-based policies change by at most 1.4 points and La-JEPA gains 3.9 to 6.3. With corrected instructions, every La-JEPA size exceeds every re-evaluated policy without embodied pretraining (Table 1 ), and L leads NowWAM by 1.8 points with four times fewer deployed parameters; it also exceeds the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and π \pi -JEPA-WAM (Table 14 ).

La-JEPA also outperforms the two closest JEPA-based world-action models on LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin 2.0, although both retain pretrained predictors (Table 3 ). LeapBot-WA, which also pretrains on robot data and deploys 10.4B parameters, falls below all three La-JEPA sizes on LIBERO-Plus with both the released and the corrected instructions (Table 14 in Appendix B ). JEPA-WAM, built on a pretrained Qwen2.5 model ( Qwen et al., 2024 ) , is exceeded on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus by all three La-JEPA sizes, S and B deploying fewer parameters. On RoboTwin, JEPA-WAM trains and evaluates on 20 of the 50 tasks, and on these tasks every La-JEPA size, trained on all 50, leads it by more than 15 points in clean and 9 points in randomized scenes. This subset is easier than the full benchmark, since per-task DP3 and ACT policies score about 20 points higher on it in clean scenes (Appendix B ); because it was chosen by JEPA-WAM and applies equally to both methods, we do not consider the comparison biased in our favor. Even when JEPA-WAM’s scores are extrapolated to all 50 tasks using this difficulty gap, every La-JEPA size remains ahead in both regimes. LDA-1B, pretrained on over 30k hours of human and robot data with a 4B vision-language model ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) , remains far below on both benchmarks ( Yan et al., 2026b ) .

La-JEPA updates 0.10 to 1.14 B parameters during training, far fewer than the video-generator and vision-language-action baselines (2.0 to 7.8 B; Tables 1 and 2 ) while showing lower replan latency at matched or better performance. We time complete policy calls, with ten denoising steps on one consumer GPU (Table 15 , Appendix C ). With optimized (compiled) builds, S and B run two to five times faster than Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM, and S with original-kernel CUDA graphs, which reproduce uncompiled actions bit-for-bit, remains 2.6 × \times faster than optimized Fast-WAM. Compiled builds do not significantly change closed-loop LIBERO success (Appendix C ), and the physical-robot policy runs compiled. Reducing inference to three denoising steps lowers latency further while keeping success within about one point (Appendix E.2 ), consistent with evidence that diffusion policies do not require many denoising steps ( Clémente et al., 2025 ) .

We train a La-JEPA B policy from scratch, with encoder LoRA but without image augmentation, on demonstrations of four Franka tabletop tasks (Figure 5 ; Appendix D ) and compare it with Fast-WAM, Faster-WAM, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026 ) in Table 5 . We start with a simple cube placement as control, then test on fruit picking which requires lifting a lid, setting it down, and choosing the correct fruit; Push T tests contact-heavy interactions; and our dish task requires placing two plates from a rack onto the table, then a spoon on the gray plate and a fork on the pink plate in one uninterrupted rollout, with interchangeable utensil positions that require distinguishing the utensils.

La-JEPA achieves the highest average success among policies without embodied pretraining and is comparable to the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , although its policy transformer is trained only on the target demonstrations. It is the most successful policy on Push T, whereas π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} leads on the long-horizon dish task. On successful trials, La-JEPA also completes every task faster than the other policies without embodied pretraining (Appendix D ), and faster than π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on fruit picking and Push T, though slower on the dish task. LingBot-VA rarely succeeds on Push T and dish manipulation and is several times slower than every other policy. LingBot-VA’s low success may reflect a need for more real-robot finetuning than the shared budget allowed (Appendix D ).

We aim to show the potential of compact world-action policies rather than to optimize them exhaustively: beyond the targeted design studies, we did not systematically search learning rates, weight decay, dropout rates, LoRA configurations, or the relative capacity of the World and Action DiTs. This lack of scale-specific tuning, together with limited target data, may contribute to the non-monotonic RoboTwin scaling; our experiments do not isolate these effects. We also recognize that many high-performing baselines have external supervision objectives and robot-specific architectures that we do not: while this work does outline the performance of a policy with a simple setup, we cannot be certain that our improvements would stack with other work’s policy upgrades.

Our policies learn from target demonstrations alone, so how La-JEPA scales with embodied pretraining remains open. Adapting the policy and its visual representation across embodiments and environments would also test whether data, rather than capacity, limits the larger models. We consider this the principal future direction of research that should come out of this paper. La-JEPA remains below the strongest embodied-pretrained methods on randomized RoboTwin scenes, and its real-robot average, although comparable to that of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , comes from four tasks on one robot setup and does not establish parity across broader manipulation demands. The richer supervision, synthetic data, and additional objectives used by some stronger baselines are natural extensions of La-JEPA that we have not tested.

We asked whether world-action policies must inherit the architecture of a generative backbone, and whether a compact transformer trained from scratch can compete with those that do. Trained in a pretrained JEPA feature space, La-JEPA reaches the strongest RoboTwin 2.0 clean and randomized results among policies without embodied pretraining, and the strongest LIBERO-Plus results once the benchmark’s corrupted instructions are corrected, while running up to 5 × \times faster than Fast-WAM. On four physical tasks, La-JEPA’s average success is comparable to that of the embodied-pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Through our study, we empirically validate the benefits of the V-JEPA latent space for control tasks, provide some guidance on the benefits of different robustness design improvements and find that heavy generative models are not a requirement for high-performing learned policies.

In this work, we used generative AI tools to implement methods, including the optimization of the training and dataloading pipeline which was particularly heavy, evaluation, and data-preprocessing code; to reformat datasets into precomputed feature stores (always through verifiable scripts); and to help design the infrastructure that enabled the interpretation of our large amount of results. We did not use generative AI tools to generate synthetic data, develop theoretical models, formulate or prove mathematical claims, or translate text; these uses are not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit parts of the paper, to write the code that generates figures and tables from recorded results, to search for and summarize related literature, and to format references. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: code was tested and validated against recorded outputs, reported numbers were traced to their evaluation records, figures and tables are generated by code from the underlying data directly, never by the AI tool itself, and references were checked against their arXiv entries. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

This work uses public simulation benchmarks and robot demonstrations collected by the authors through teleoperation; it involves no human-subject studies and releases no new dataset. We do not foresee harms specific to this work beyond those of robot learning in general.

Code for feature precomputation, training, and LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 evaluation, with the configurations of the final S, B, and L policies, is available at https://github.com/mt-clemente/lajepa . passages.section: A.1 Prediction Target and Feature Space
passages.location: A.1 Prediction Target and Feature Space
passages.text: These studies determine whether the policy should predict future features, in which representation, and how motion and spatial resolution enter the tokens (Section 4.1 ).

Joint action and future-feature prediction improves LIBERO-Plus success over action-only training for each of three training seeds, raising mean success from 74.35% to 76.47%, a gain of 2.12 points (Table 7 ). Figure 3 A shows this mean gain; its in-distribution bar uses the seed-42 pair at 150k updates, evaluated on 2,000 LIBERO episodes. Both objectives train on all 1,743 LIBERO episodes of the original pipeline for 150,000 updates with image augmentation and encoder LoRA, whereas the headline policies use the revised pipeline (Appendix B ), so these controls are not directly comparable to Table 1 . The action-only control omits future-feature supervision and computation while preserving the action pathway. For each objective and training seed, we select the checkpoint with the highest LIBERO success from the 30k, 60k, 90k, 120k, and 150k grid and evaluate it on all 10,030 LIBERO-Plus episodes with EMA weights, action-noise scale 1 redrawn at every replan, ten denoising steps, and ten-action execution chunks. Selection picks the same step for both objectives within each seed. Paired tests use identical task and evaluation-seed episodes for the two objectives.
Table 7: Predictive supervision across training seeds on LIBERO-Plus (success in %; per-seed exact McNemar tests).

On 5,000 episodes per regime, each policy on its own set of evaluation episodes, joint training achieves 80.16% clean and 39.02% randomized success, against 73.14% and 35.34% for action-only training. Both policies use the final augmentation recipe (Table 10 ), all 2,500 clean demonstrations, 150,000 training updates, and a global batch of 400, split into four data-parallel ranks of 100 for joint training and eight of 50 for action-only training; the action-only policy neither loads nor computes future targets. Selection on the 1,000-episode clean grid picks 150k for joint training and 120k for action-only training, with ties broken toward the later step.

Block B compares frozen, static V-JEPA 2.1 features with Wan2.2 VAE latents at 150k updates, with action and future-feature prediction on the 95% split. Within each benchmark, feature dimensions, normalization, and input and output projections remain representation-specific, so the comparison concerns the two representation systems rather than their pretraining objectives in isolation. On RoboTwin, both policies use 384-dimensional, 12-layer transformers with patch grouping for observations and future targets and are evaluated on 5,000-episode clean and randomized manifests with 24-action execution chunks. On LIBERO, both use the 768-dimensional, 12-layer B transformer with 2 × 2\times spatial mean pooling and 10-action execution chunks; LIBERO evaluation instead uses a 600-step budget per suite and 30 settling steps, and LIBERO-Plus evaluation uses action-noise scale 1. On LIBERO-Plus, V-JEPA succeeds in 5,773 episodes and Wan2.2 in 5,173. All evaluations use EMA weights, a single observation context, and 10 denoising steps.

Two further RoboTwin comparisons pool the future targets, each evaluated on 5,000 episodes per regime (clean only for the first). With full-data, static-feature training and patch-grouped observations, V-JEPA and Wan2.2 achieve 61.50% and 61.44% clean success at 150k. In the second, with 768-dimensional transformers, Wan2.2 leads on clean success (63.90% versus 61.12%), whereas V-JEPA leads on randomized success (15.00% versus 1.28%). V-JEPA’s advantage therefore holds in randomized scenes but not consistently in clean ones.

Block C compares three frozen-encoder policies with patch grouping, trained on the 95% split, that differ only in the encoding: static, tube, or tube-motion. Each regime uses 1,000 episodes on the same scenes, and randomized success is read at the checkpoint selected on clean episodes: 150k for static and tube-motion, and 120k for tube.

On RoboTwin, grouping neighboring features into one token by concatenation (patch grouping) instead of averaging them (mean pooling) changes clean success by + 0.3 +0.3 points and raises randomized success by 4.1 points. Both policies apply the reduction to two-frame observations and to motion-based future targets and are compared at 150k updates; each clean and randomized evaluation uses 1,000 episodes, 32 samples per pixel, rendering depth 8, OIDN denoising, and action noise fixed within each episode. The pooling policy uses the full training set and the patch-grouping policy the 95% split, and their target normalization and projections also differ, so the comparison does not isolate the reduction operator. By contrast, on LIBERO, in a one-variable comparison between stored-feature S policies with tube-motion encoding at 150k updates, evaluated identically on 2,000 episodes, mean pooling reaches 94.05% against 89.35% for patch grouping. The final recipe uses patch grouping on RoboTwin, reducing the head camera 2 × 2\times and the wrist cameras 4 × 4\times , and 2 × 2\times mean pooling on LIBERO (Appendix B ). Appendix E.3 reports a related sweep that pools only the future targets.

These studies target robustness to changes in the observations through camera and proprioception dropout, image augmentation, and encoder adaptation (Section 4.2 ). All LIBERO variants in blocks D and F train on the 95% split and are selected on LIBERO success: stored-feature policies with a frozen encoder at 90k updates, and online-encoder variants at 120k.

The LIBERO row of block D compares either-camera with wrist-only dropout in stored-feature policies. Allowing either camera to be dropped changes both camera eligibility and the expected number of missing streams, from 0.10 to 0.19 per example; at least one stream is always retained. Before training, we encode every demonstration once with the frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and store the resulting features. Stored-feature policies, used in most design studies, read both observations and future targets from these stores and never run the encoder during training. Encoder LoRA and image augmentation require encoding the observations at every training step, so the final policies encode their observation clips online but still read their future targets from the stores. Encoding the targets online as well would dominate the encoder cost of each step, since each camera’s targets span 16 frames, eight times as many encoder tokens as its two-frame observation clip. Targets from the adapting encoder also do not improve success (Appendix E.1 ), so the targets remain those of the frozen encoder.

The features are then reduced spatially before entering the World DiT. Mean pooling, the simplest reduction, averages each 2 × 2 2\times 2 neighborhood of a feature grid into one token. Because it can be applied once when the features are precomputed, it shrinks the stored features fourfold. Most of our development therefore used pre-pooled stores, which are much smaller and far easier to load during training than full-resolution V-JEPA features. Patch grouping instead concatenates neighboring features into one wider token, reducing the number of tokens without discarding any feature values, but the stored features keep their full size. Mean pooling suffices on LIBERO, whereas on RoboTwin the detail it averages away matters: patch grouping raises randomized success by 4.1 points (Appendix A.1 ), so the final RoboTwin recipe uses patch grouping.

On LIBERO, all three sizes train on all 1,777 demonstrations retained by the revised pipeline (Appendix B ) for 150,000 updates, and we report the final checkpoints’ performances averaged over three training seeds; L additionally uses full-depth LoRA. The final RoboTwin S, B, and L policies train on the 2,438 clean demonstrations retained by the revised pipeline (Appendix B ) with three training seeds each. For each seed, the checkpoint is selected among 90k, 120k, and 150k updates on a 1,000-episode clean grid disjoint from the evaluation episodes, which picks 150k for every seed except one L seed (120k); the selected policies are evaluated on 5,000 episodes per condition with action noise redrawn at every replan, and we report the mean over seeds.

LIBERO scores are success rates over the four standard suites. LIBERO-Plus scores are success rates over all 10,030 evaluation episodes of the seven perturbation categories, including background textures, weighting every episode rather than every category equally. Literature aggregates are recomputed from reported per-category rates when needed. La-JEPA’s headline LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluations use MuJoCo 3.3.2 and the upstream suite-specific step limits (220, 280, 300, and 520 steps, after 10 settling steps). The design studies, evaluation-setting sweeps, and compiled-build validation keep a flat budget in every suite, 700 steps except for the LIBERO pair of block B (600 steps after 30 settling steps; Appendix A.1 ), so each comparison is made within one protocol. RoboTwin policies are trained on clean demonstrations and evaluated in clean and randomized scenes, and the mean of the two regimes is the leaderboard aggregate. La-JEPA’s RoboTwin policies are conditioned on each episode’s own RoboTwin instruction in both training and evaluation. JEPA-WAM reports 20 RoboTwin tasks, so Table 3 restricts our evaluations to the same tasks, using 2,000 episodes per condition and training seed. JEPA-WAM trains only on these 20 tasks, whereas our policies train on all 50. The subset is easier than the full benchmark: per-task DP3 and ACT policies reach 73.9% and 51.8% clean success on it ( Lin et al., 2026 ) , against 55.2% and 29.7% over all 50 tasks ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Projected to all 50 tasks, JEPA-WAM’s success is estimated at 65.5% clean and 25.0% randomized (see the full-suite estimate below), below every La-JEPA size in Table 2 . Methods pretrained on robot trajectories beyond the target demonstrations are outside the main comparison and are explicitly identified in the latent world-action model comparison, the leaderboard figure, and the physical-robot comparison.
Baseline scores come from the following sources.

Re-evaluations of released checkpoints: All LIBERO-Plus scores of StarVLA ( StarVLA Community, 2026 ) , JEPA-WAM, Fast-WAM, Cosmos Policy, ImageWAM, NowWAM, LeapBot-WA, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and π \pi -JEPA-WAM, with both the released and the corrected instructions (Section 5.2 and Appendix B ), and the LIBERO scores of StarVLA and NowWAM. For StarVLA, whose variant the Qwen-RobotManip report does not specify, we evaluate the released LIBERO checkpoint with a Qwen3-VL-4B backbone and a flow-matching action head; for LeapBot-WA, we evaluate its LIBERO-trained checkpoint, matching the zero-shot LIBERO-Plus transfer reported in its paper.

Training: Faster-WAM reports RoboTwin results only for training on clean and randomized demonstrations, so we train it on the clean demonstrations ourselves, adapting the open-source Fast-WAM code as described in the Faster-WAM paper.

Qwen-RobotManip report ( Yuan et al., 2026a ) : All Qwen-RobotManip-scratch scores and the RoboTwin scores of StarVLA, as well as the embodied-pretrained Qwen-RobotManip model in Figure 4 , taken from its clean-to-randomized comparison.

RoboTwin 2.0 leaderboard and report ( Chen et al., 2025 ) : Fast-WAM’s clean-trained RoboTwin scores and the embodied-pretrained policies added in Figure 4 come from the official leaderboard 1 1 1 https://robotwin-platform.github.io/leaderboard : 4D-WAM ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , GigaBrain-0.7 ( GigaBrain Team et al., 2026 ) , and OLA-Sem and OLA-Geo, which are leaderboard entries without an accompanying paper. The ACT and DP3 RoboTwin scores in Figure 6 come from the benchmark report.

Method papers: All other LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus scores, and JEPA-WAM’s 20-task RoboTwin scores, come from each method’s paper; in Figure 6 , SmolVLA’s LIBERO scores are those of its variants without robot pretraining ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) , and LDA-1B’s scores in Table 3 are those reported by Yan et al. (2026b) . Where a paper prints a category-averaged LIBERO-Plus score (Faster-WAM and MINT), we recompute the episode-weighted score from its per-category rates, so our values can differ from the printed averages.

LeapBot-WA’s clean-plus-randomized training regime is excluded from the RoboTwin comparison of Table 3 . In Figure 4 , the La-JEPA point is B, and the dashed contour fixes the arithmetic mean of clean and randomized success.

The headline policies use the data and evaluation pipelines below, with three training seeds per size. The design studies, representation diagnostics, evaluation-setting sweeps, adapted-target comparison, and compiled-build validation use the original version of these pipelines, with the same architecture, objective, and augmentation strengths; Tables 11 and 12 compare the two.

Simulator version: Demonstrations are rendered and all policies are evaluated with MuJoCo 3.3.2, the version used by the compared baselines; under newer releases such as 3.9.0, the bowl in the task “pick up the black bowl on the ramekin” is unseated at reset.
Demonstration filtering: Each demonstration’s recorded actions are replayed from its recorded initial state, and only demonstrations that end in task success are kept: 1,777 of the 2,000.
Proprioception alignment: Each frame is paired with the proprioceptive state at its own time step, as at evaluation.

Normalization: States and actions use per-channel 1st/99th-percentile scaling to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , as in OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) .
End-of-episode windows: Training windows extend to the end of each demonstration, and missing future targets are masked from the loss.
Training schedule: All sizes train on all retained demonstrations for 150,000 updates, and we report the final checkpoint averaged over the three seeds.
Evaluation protocol: Each episode takes 10 settling steps before the policy acts and is scored at the upstream per-suite step limits (220, 280, 300, and 520 steps).

The LIBERO training demonstrations store each task’s instruction in their metadata, identical to the instruction that standard LIBERO evaluation derives from the task’s file name. The released LIBERO-Plus evaluator derives the instruction from the variant’s file name instead, so every non-language variant receives the training instruction followed by the perturbation’s parameters. Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026a ) replaces it with the :language annotation of the variant’s BDDL file, falling back to the base task’s file for camera, robot-initial-state, and sensor-noise variants. These annotations are written independently of the training instructions: across the 8,493 non-language variants, only 2,351 match the training instruction exactly and 3,148 up to capitalization, so most variants still receive a paraphrase that the policy never saw during training. Our corrected text gives every non-language variant its base task’s training instruction verbatim. For the 1,537 language variants, whose paraphrases are the intended perturbation, the released and corrected texts are identical, and Flex- π \pi ’s annotations contain the same words but differ in capitalization for 1,209 of them. All re-evaluations share one protocol; NowWAM, Fast-WAM, and ImageWAM, whose released evaluations use longer step limits, are scored at the upstream per-suite limits like every other policy. Table 14 reports both evaluations. Because the corruption affects policies to different degrees, released-instruction scores partly rank policies by their sensitivity to corrupted text rather than by their robustness to the intended perturbation: correcting the instructions reverses the order of NowWAM and La-JEPA B and L, and of Cosmos Policy and La-JEPA S. With corrected instructions, S is on par with NowWAM, and L’s 1.8-point lead exceeds both its seed-to-seed standard deviation (0.3 points) and the binomial standard error of a single 10,030-episode evaluation (about 0.35 points).

Tables 15 and 5 time complete benchmark policy calls, not executed actions or control-loop cycles. Each timed call includes fresh instruction tokenization and encoding, input preparation, transfer, and host-side action output; loading, compilation, simulation, and transport are excluded. Text and vision encoders run on parallel streams where supported. Eager execution is uncompiled; original-kernel CUDA graphs reduce launch overhead without changing kernels; optimized builds also compile the computation. The head-to-head WAM rows use ten denoising steps and 32 predicted actions, whereas the three-step rows and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} (official JAX JIT, ten steps, native ten-action horizon) are separate operating points. Each method keeps its native inputs: La-JEPA uses two 256 × 256 256\times 256 cameras with two adjacent frames and FLAN-T5-large, timed in FP32 (our success evaluations use FP16), whereas in our setup Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM use two 224 × 224 224\times 224 single-frame cameras and BF16 UMT5-XXL ( Chung et al., 2023 ) . Action noise is pre-drawn and copied inside the timed call for La-JEPA, and drawn on the CPU inside the call for Fast-WAM. LingBot-VA is timed on the same device under the same protocol with its native implementation and appears, rounded to 10 ms, only in Table 5 .

For La-JEPA, original-kernel CUDA graphs reproduce eager actions bit-for-bit across 36 replays per model on 12 inputs that vary observations, instructions, and noise. Compilation is not bit-exact: the maximum ten-step action differences are 0.010, 0.021, and 0.009 for S, B, and L. Our simulation success rates use uncompiled execution, which the CUDA graphs reproduce exactly, whereas the physical-robot La-JEPA policy runs compiled. For Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM, original-kernel graphs exceed the available GPU memory in our implementation.

Using the original-pipeline checkpoints (Appendix B ), we evaluate the exact timed builds on 2,000 LIBERO episodes with a 700-step budget in every suite (Appendix B ), with action noise of scale 1 redrawn at every replan, and compare each with uncompiled execution of the same checkpoint using paired McNemar tests. Compiled ten-step builds reach 95.20%, 97.05%, and 96.25% for S, B, and L, against 94.30%, 97.35%, and 96.50% uncompiled ( p = 0.15 p=0.15 , 0.59 0.59 , and 0.69 0.69 ). In separate evaluation runs, ten-step CUDA-graph builds reach 94.70%, 97.00%, and 96.35% ( p = 0.55 p=0.55 , 0.50 0.50 , and 0.84 0.84 ), and the three-step B graph build 96.90% against 97.30% ( p = 0.45 p=0.45 ). None of the seven paired comparisons differs significantly. The timed L build applies LoRA to the final eight encoder blocks and is selected at 150k updates.

With serial rather than parallel text and vision encoding, optimized ten-step calls take 19, 26, and 61 ms for S, B, and L, against 92 ms for Fast-WAM and 54 ms for Faster-WAM, leaving the speedups essentially unchanged.

Table 16 lists the components behind the size columns. Trainable counts the weights updated on target demonstrations, including LoRA adapters. Deployed counts the policy and encoder parameter inventory, including frozen visual and language encoders; it is a size measure, not a measurement of memory use or operations per action. Deployed counts merge LoRA adapters into the encoder weights, adding no parameters, and count shared encoders once across cameras. Baseline counts use measured checkpoints or published inventories; where encoder-only counts are unavailable, we count full tokenizer inventories, including unused decoder weights, which conservatively overestimates executed parameters. Transformer initialization refers to the trained world-action predictor or VLA backbone: video or image generation, vision-language pretraining, or random initialization.

Table 16 refers to LIBERO configurations. RoboTwin’s token projections change La-JEPA’s sizes to 0.11/0.75 B (trainable/deployed) for S, 0.37/1.01 B for B, and 1.17/1.82 B for L (Table 2 ). Figure 6 complements Figure 1 by plotting success against trainable rather than deployed parameters.

This appendix describes the physical platform, the four tasks, demonstration collection, and the training and evaluation protocol behind Table 5 , and reports completion times.

A tabletop Franka Panda with a parallel gripper uses a wrist-mounted RealSense D405 camera and a fixed external RealSense D435 camera. A GPU workstation runs Linux with a real-time kernel. Policies receive both camera views, proprioception, and a task instruction, and execute end-effector deltas and gripper commands through Polymetis 2 2 2 https://facebookresearch.github.io/fairo/polymetis/ and the Franka Control Interface.

Cube placement uses a red wooden cube and a bowl. Fruit picking requires removing a bamboo steamer’s lid, setting it down, and then picking the correct fruit, a plum, from inside the steamer. Push T requires pushing a wooden T onto a T shape marked on the table. Dish manipulation requires placing both plates, then the spoon on the gray plate and the fork on the pink plate, in one uninterrupted rollout; plate locations are fixed, but the utensils’ starting positions are interchangeable. Every training demonstration and evaluation rollout contains the complete uninterrupted sequence of its task. Figure 5 shows the initial scene of each task from the external camera.

SpaceMouse teleoperation provides six-degree-of-freedom end-effector control through the same interface. We record camera observations, robot state, end-effector pose, and gripper state at 10 Hz, collecting 100 demonstrations per task (400 in total). Initial cube positions vary within 10 ​ cm × 10 ​ cm 10\,\mathrm{cm}\times 10\,\mathrm{cm} , and plum positions vary within the steamer; Push T and dish manipulation use smaller placement variations, including utensil rearrangements.

Policies train jointly on the four language-conditioned tasks using their respective recipes. Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM train for 30 epochs; La-JEPA trains its B policy transformer from scratch with encoder LoRA but without image augmentation. Table 5 reports counts over 20 rollouts per task, with explicit ten-rollout denominators for LingBot-VA’s dish result. Utensil 1 and Utensil 2 denote successful placement of the first and second utensils on plates, irrespective of utensil identity or order. Position additionally requires the correct spoon–gray and fork–pink assignments and success at all preceding stages; the two plate stages share one table column because their counts are identical. Average weights the four tasks equally, using Position for dish, in mean successes out of 20; LingBot-VA’s average is omitted because its dish result uses 10 trials rather than 20.

Table 17 reports the mean and standard deviation of completion time over successful trials. La-JEPA is the fastest policy without embodied pretraining on every task and the fastest overall on fruit picking and Push T, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is fastest on cube placement and dish manipulation. Our main hypothesis for LingBot-VA’s low Push T and dish success is that it requires substantially more real-robot finetuning than the other policies; independently of success, its completion times, three to eleven times longer than those of the other policies, make it impractical for closed-loop control on this platform. Its dish entry comes from its single successful trial.

This appendix collects results that inform but do not define the final recipe: adapted future targets, evaluation-time settings, future-only pooling, representation diagnostics, and per-task RoboTwin success.

On LIBERO with L, we replace the frozen future targets with targets from an EMA of the adapting encoder, keeping the clips, observation processing, and normalization statistics of the frozen-target policy and passing no gradients through the target path. The adapted-target policy, selected at 90k updates, achieves 81.65% on LIBERO-Plus, against 82.26% for the frozen-target policy at 120k, both trained with the original pipeline (Appendix B ) and at action-noise scale 1. Adapted targets do not improve success (paired McNemar p = 0.096 p=0.096 ), so the final recipe retains frozen targets.

At the 120k checkpoints of the original-pipeline policies (Appendix B ), we vary the execution chunk length, the number of denoising steps, and the action-noise scale for L and B, and test three-step inference for S (Table 19 ); the reference executes ten actions per replan with ten denoising steps and noise scale 1, and LIBERO runs use a 700-step budget in every suite (Appendix B ). Executing only five actions reduces LIBERO-Plus success by 3.29 points for L and 3.45 for B, whereas the number of denoising steps matters less: with three steps, B and L stay within one point of their ten-step references on both benchmarks, and S obtains 94.50% against 94.30% on LIBERO ( p = 0.81 p=0.81 , paired McNemar). Three-step calls take 23 ms for B and 39 ms for L with original-kernel CUDA graphs (Table 15 ), an operating point separate from the ten-step latency comparison. No tested noise scale gives a statistically supported aggregate improvement in the paired comparisons; the original L policy reaches 82.26% at the default scale 1 (Appendix B ), and the best single scale, 0.5, reaches 82.50%.

analysis.overview: La-JEPA在预训练V-JEPA 2.1特征上从零训练World/Action DiT，并沿用Fast-WAM的训练时未来监督、推理时只出动作及上下文KV缓存。可复用的是将控制器容量与生成骨干解耦的结构及其设计证据，不是取消视觉/语言预训练。S/B/L部署库存0.74/0.98/1.78B；纠正LIBERO-Plus混入的扰动文本后L达88.0%，RoboTwin随机场景B达35.4%。未来监督三种子消融平均+2.12个百分点较有辨别力，但多数其他设计比较混合管线/数据或只单种子。优化S完整查询17.78ms对Fast-WAM88.09ms约5倍，但eager和原核图结果不同。四任务实机仅70/80对π0.5的69/80；仓库目前空，作者结果未复现。

findings.title: 把策略容量从生成骨干解耦，仍保留预训练感知
findings.text: 本文不再将数十亿生成式VLM/视频DiT直接作为策略骨干，而是用预训练V-JEPA 2.1 ViT-L与冻结FLAN-T5-large，再从零初始化World/Action DiT。所谓无embodied pretraining指没有目标演示之外的机器人轨迹预训练，不是全模型从零、无互联网预训练或无需目标示范。目标是按控制需要选择容量，训练时未来监督、推理时不生成未来沿用Fast-WAM/Faster-WAM，不能将后者单独归为本篇原创。该结构为低部署库存策略提供路线选择，但还未验证大规模机器人预训练后的扩展性。

findings.title: 未来只作训练监督，推理缓存观察KV
findings.text: 每层action queries读取World DiT观察KV及自身action，观察token仅看观察、future token看观察与future、action看观察与action，互不把future直接送入动作。训练分别给动作/未来采样独立噪声与流时间，两项MSE等权；未来损失通过共享World参数塑造观察表示。按图2掩码，未来分支并非读取候选动作的在线rollout，所以不能把其成绩解读为行动条件仿真规划收益。推理删future token、固定World时间0，观察KV每层只算一次，Euler迭代只跑Action DiT；预测32动作，LIBERO执行10、RoboTwin24后重规划。

findings.title: 双帧观察与跨未来片段目标，正则化和特征预存构成实际配方
findings.text: 每相机独立编码，tube观察为当前及前一帧；tube-motion未来由每隔两帧的16帧联合编码成8个时间网格，覆盖32帧。它是训练目标的双向编码，非策略偷看未来。观察和未来用归一化与空间缩减，LIBERO均池化，RoboTwin拼接patch；各相机至少保留一路，文本/本体条件也dropout。最终观察增强并LoRA适配编码器，future仍来自未增强帧的冻结编码器预存特征，减少反复编码16未来帧的成本。150k更新、LIBERO batch128/RoboTwin400。没有报告完整预计算+训练墙钟或GPU小时，较少可训练参数不能直接换算训练费用降幅。

findings.title: 未来监督的收益有三训练种子对照，但不是88%主表的一次增量
findings.text: 表7在原数据/评测管线下，各训练种子比较joint与action-only，动作路径不变、后者不计算future。LIBERO-Plus均值74.35→76.47%，+2.12个百分点；各种子增1.67/1.37/3.33，配对McNemar p为2.3×10⁻⁴/0.002/2.2×10⁻¹²。两目标在各自种子选到同一步，按IID选择而非OOD挑点，较能区分未来监督贡献。RoboTwin另组joint80.16/39.02、action-only73.14/35.34（clean/random），但checkpoint不同、各自评估episode不同，不能当完全配对结果。大多数其他设计仅单训练run；这些旧管线控制不能与最终88.0%横向相减或叠加。

findings.title: JEPA对随机场景的优势比对干净场景更稳定
findings.text: 主特征对照在固定step与网络规模下，V-JEPA相对Wan2.2 VAE在RoboTwin clean/random约+15.9/+16.0点，LIBERO/Plus约+2/+6点；但特征维度、归一化、投影随表示而异，测的是整套representation system，不是纯预训练目标因果效应。附加对照一组clean61.50对61.44基本相同，另一组clean VAE63.90胜JEPA61.12，而random JEPA15.00胜VAE1.28，保留此反例。表21未来监督使有效rank48.41→137.70、clean62.8→66.5，却使5近邻动作readout R²0.7937→0.4315；动作可解码性并未解释控制增益，也不能由rank相关性证明泛化机制。

findings.title: 设计块各有参考，增强与token对照存在管线混杂
findings.text: 表6的A–F块只在块内比较，不是可相加收益清单。LIBERO相机dropout从仅腕到任一路也改了期望缺失流数0.10→0.19；增强/LoRA相对plain的+7.2点比较还改变在线编码和所选训练步。RoboTwin增强+LoRA的+16随机场景收益伴随2400→2500示范和评估实现变化；patch grouping相对均池化+4.1点也有full/95%数据、目标归一化与投影差异。表12最终新版管线将clean提高约5–8点、random降低约5–9点，平均变≤1点；不能混用旧44.7与新35.4作同一B模型的统一结论。保持目标冻结的对照未显著优于EMA目标（p=0.096），只能说未发现替换收益。

findings.title: 恢复非语言变体的原指令后重测，模型排序改变
findings.text: 表13/14：LIBERO-Plus从变体文件名生成指令，8493/10030非语言变体被附加view/light等扰动参数，变成双重扰动；这不是训练测试数据泄漏。纠正逐字恢复原训练指令，1537条本来要测语言改写的变体保持不变。Flex-π用BDDL注释仍常与原句不同，不等于同协议。作者同harness重测公开checkpoint：Fast-WAM51.5→70.8，Cosmos80.8→84.9，LaS80.0→86.3、B82.5→87.3、L84.1→88.0，NowWAM86.2不变；由此反转部分排序。主表未重测的corrected列留空，不能把88.0称赢过所有未有纠正分的模型。统一上游suite步限、episode加权；个别基线有无法实例化变体仅10029例，非全部严格同分母。

findings.title: RoboTwin容量不单调，35.4%随机成功仍有明显边界
findings.text: clean示范训练、三个seed、每条件各5000例：S/B/L clean85.5/86.2/86.0，random33.9/35.4/32.1，均值59.7/60.8/59.0；B最佳不是L。对照Qwen-RobotManip-scratch71.6/22.6、Fast-WAM77.8/1.9，显示该组非机器人预训练策略中较强，但并未达到稳健OOD成功，多任务如lift_pot随机仍接近0，且最强embodied-pretrained基线随机更高。JEPA-WAM仅训练20任务，La训练50而在其20任务子集比较；图中将其映射全50任务的65.5/25.0是7政策回归估计，含LaS/B，不是实际JEPA-WAM全量复测，不能同主表实测等权使用。

findings.title: 0.10B可训练与0.74B部署是不同成本口径
findings.text: 表16：LIBERO S/B/L训练约0.10/0.34/1.14B，部署0.74/0.98/1.78B，含V-JEPA0.305B和FLAN-T5-large0.341B，LoRA合并、跨相机编码器只计一次。RoboTwin投影不同，分别0.11/0.37/1.17B训练、0.75/1.01/1.82B部署。L1.78B对NowWAM7.1B约四分之一，但S对JEPA-WAM1.35B并非四倍小。部署库存是权重规模，不是峰值显存或每动作FLOPs；部分基线无encoder-only数而计入未执行decoder，可能高估其实际执行规模。编码器选择与架构容量同时变化，不能把所有成本差归为同等视觉/语言先验下控制DiT的独立收益。

findings.title: 约5倍依赖优化构建；25ms不是机器人控制周期
findings.text: 表15完整policy call，单消费GPU、batch1，20warmup后100次中位；含新文本tokenize/encode、准备/传输与host输出，排除加载/编译/模拟/机器人通信，论文未具体标明GPU型号。10去噪32动作优化S17.78ms、B25.16、L59.72，对Fast88.09/Faster50.96；S对Fast4.95×、B3.50×，L反而慢于Faster。eager S99.96/B98.21对Faster62.70也更慢；S原核图34.20对优化Fast仍2.58×。各方法保留原生分辨率/时序/文本编码器，La文本计时FP32而成功评估FP16，非相同输入/编码器隔离实验。原核图bit-exact，编译非bit-exact；原管线2000个LIBERO/700步对照无显著成功差，不等于所有新管线/OOD质量等效。3步B13.40ms是另一运行点，π0.5原生10动作也不能直接和32动作吞吐混算。

findings.title: 四任务实机70/80对69/80，不能据均值宣布普遍胜出
findings.text: Franka Panda双相机、SpaceMouse录400条示范（每任务100、10Hz），LaB+LoRA无图像增强，四任务每20次。完整得分用fruit/cube/PushT/dish正确Position：La19/20/15/16，合70/80=87.5%；π0.5为20/20/11/18，69/80=86.25%，只差一次成功，未给置信区间或更广实机范围。dish的utensil列仅阶段进展，最终Position要求两盘与正确餐具配对全部完成，不能平均阶段列当整任务成功。π0.5在dish更强18对16；成功试验条件下LaDish58.1s慢于π39.0s，且耗时不含失败，不能换成总吞吐优势。Fast/Faster各按自身recipe30epochs，LingBot dish仅10次、其调参需求未解决；结果非全模型充分等训练成本后的能力排序。

findings.title: 保留小规模设计和空仓库缺口，不把实现声明当已审计资源
findings.text: 多数设计单seed，优化未系统搜索LR、dropout、LoRA和World/Action相对容量，RoboTwin缩放非单调的成因未隔离；所有强结果限目标数据、这些模拟/四实机任务，尚无跨本体大规模机器人预训练检验。作者声明代码含预计算/训练/评估及S/B/L配置，但本轮访问github.com/mt-clemente/lajepa公开页明确显示仓库为空，未验证实现、权重或原始评估数据，不宣称已可复用代码。计时GPU具体型号、训练总GPU小时/显存等不足以独立复建成本。其主要贡献仍是紧凑控制DiT加预训练特征与有辨别力的设计研究，不应读成不需要预训练、无未来模型监督也同样好，或全面超过大基础策略。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：固定预算将容量由Action转到World，能否改善RoboTwin随机泛化？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在目标数据有限时，相同策略参数预算下缩小Action DiT并将容量分配给World DiT，可比等宽同深的扩模方式保留clean成功并提高随机场景泛化。仅公开仿真实验草案：固定新版RoboTwin2438 clean示范、V-JEPA/文本编码器与LoRA、观察增强/目标、150k更新和评估器，比较等宽B、World较宽/Action较窄、反向分配三组，投影参数也计入同约0.37B预算；另设无future监督控制以区分正则化和容量效果。因World处理future tokens，等参数不等FLOPs，先测预计算+训练FLOPs/GPU小时，另做等总训练算力的对照，分别报告，不能冒称同时已严格匹配。至少3个独立训练seed，checkpoint只由独立clean验证集选择，各5000个clean/random终测episode，按任务及训练seed报告区间；随机集只终测不作架构选择。记录同GPU精确型号、部署权重、显存和10步完整查询eager/图/编译时延，核动作差异与闭环成功，而非只测DiT。预注册clean非劣界和random改进门槛，并看每任务失败与dish等精确动作需求。若等参数或等训练算力条件下随机优势消失、只靠更久训练/挑OOD checkpoint，或clean与实际延迟明显恶化，则推翻容量重分配改善取舍的假设。实验未执行、未创建选题，未全面查新；待实现可核验后再复现，不宣称研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: 在JEPA特征上从零训练控制DiT，未来监督留在训练阶段
frontier_brief.change_type: 紧凑世界动作策略与评测纠正
frontier_brief.delta: 用V-JEPA 2.1表征代替生成VAE，随机初始化World/Action DiT；联合future/action流匹配，动作只读观察KV，推理删future并缓存观察，容量可独立于生成骨干选择。
frontier_brief.before: Fast-WAM/Faster-WAM虽已只在训练预测未来，仍部署大视频DiT及文本编码器；图像/语言生成骨干使控制器容量和部署成本难独立选择。
frontier_brief.after: S/B/L部署0.74/0.98/1.78B而非仅训练参数0.10/0.34/1.14B；纠正LIBERO-Plus指令后86.3/87.3/88.0%。优化S17.78ms对Fast88.09ms，但eager和图构建有不同取舍。
frontier_brief.relevance: 适合资源受限但已有目标示范的WAM方案选择：优先检查表示系统、训练时预测与容量分配，按完整policy call及部署库存评估；同时核数据/指令管线，不能照抄跨协议SOTA表。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者实验未复现；感知/文本仍预训练，许多设计对照含数据、接口或训练步混杂。RoboTwin随机B仅35.4%、L缩放不单调；实机70/80对π0.5的69/80不确证广泛胜出。GPU型号未明确，仓库当前为空，未核实现。
frontier_brief.question: 相同参数和另行匹配训练算力时，将容量从Action转向World能否改善随机泛化，而不损clean成功与真实延迟？

evidence.label: 训练时预测的辨别性对照
evidence.context: 表7，原数据/评测管线三训练seed，future对action-only平均+2.12pp、配对p均<0.01；两目标各seed选到同IID checkpoint，不与88.0%新版主表作直接相减。

evidence.label: 纠正语言后重测
evidence.context: 表14，8493非语言变体恢复原训练指令，1537语言变体保留原扰动；NowWAM86.2不变。统一步限/episode权重，仅实际重测模型有纠正分，不是训练泄漏或无条件所有基线SOTA。

evidence.label: RoboTwin与容量边界
evidence.context: 表2/12，新版管线、clean示范训练、三seed各5000例/条件；均值B60.8%高于L59.0%，不能假定大模型总更强。JEPA-WAM全50任务图点是回归估计。

evidence.label: 完整调用与实现依赖
evidence.context: 表15，10去噪步32动作、单消费GPU优化版；含编码/准备/host输出，排除编译/模拟/机器人通信，型号未明确。eager S99.96ms慢于Faster62.70ms，原核图S34.20ms；不能说所有构建均5倍。

evidence.label: 实机范围
evidence.context: 表5/17，Franka四任务各20次、共400示范，dish以正确餐具位置及前序全成功计。LaPushT更好但dish16/20低于π18/20，且成功条件dish58.1s慢于39.0s；不证明全面同等或超越。

mechanism.title: 固定预训练表示与可选控制容量
mechanism.text: V-JEPA和冻结FLAN-T5提供先验，两个控制DiT随机初始化。无额外机器人预训练不代表无感知预训练；库存应含两编码器。

mechanism.title: 训练未来、推理不读未来
mechanism.text: future/action独立流噪声，注意力掩码阻断future进动作；监督塑造共享World参数。推理KV缓存后只迭代Action，非候选行动条件的在线世界模拟。

mechanism.title: 配方与评测一起核对
mechanism.text: tube-motion、dropout、增强/LoRA和冻结future预存构成配方，A–F块参考不同。指令修复、示范过滤、状态对齐和模拟版本改变均可影响分数，不把混杂收益归于单模块。

attention.reason: 相对外围剪枝与单任务调参，直接重选表征、策略骨干及训练目标；有future目标对照，但跨架构成本和实机优势仍有限。

impact.comparison: 相对外围剪枝与单任务调参，直接重选表征、策略骨干及训练目标；有future目标对照，但跨架构成本和实机优势仍有限。

attention.headline: La-JEPA：让策略容量摆脱生成骨干的约束
attention.summary: 在预训练视觉表征上训练小型策略，把未来预测留在训练阶段；推理只生成动作，让策略容量可以独立选择。

passages.text: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On

passages.section: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
passages.location: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
passages.text: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.

passages.section: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
passages.location: Synthesizing Dexterous Robot Demonstrations from Human Videos via Virtual Try-On
passages.text: 1 KAIST 2 RLWRLD 3 Korea University

Robot foundation models trained on large-scale demonstrations have made substantial progress toward general-purpose robot control ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025 ) , while extending them to new tasks and environments still requires additional robot demonstrations ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . Collecting such demonstrations through teleoperation requires robot hardware, a teleoperation system, and substantial operator effort ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2024 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) . The burden is heaviest for dexterous hands, where operators must coordinate many degrees of freedom and fine-grained contacts through retargeting interfaces that are challenging to develop and operate ( Handa et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) .

Alternatively, human videos offer another way to demonstrate a new task. In particular, egocentric recordings of human object manipulation already exist at internet scale and far outnumber the demonstrations teleoperation can produce, ranging from in-the-wild collections to manually annotated corpora recorded for robot learning ( Goyal et al., 2017 ; Shan et al., 2020 ; Damen et al., 2022 ; Grauman et al., 2022 ; Grauman et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Hoque et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ) . They capture how people grasp and manipulate objects, including coordinated bimanual interaction, without a robot during collection. Recent works use these videos to learn transferable visual and behavioral knowledge ( Nair et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Dyna Robotics, 2026 ) , or convert them into robot data through retargeting ( Kareer et al., 2025 ) , rendering ( Lepert et al., 2025b ; Lepert et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , or generative translation ( Song et al., 2025 ; Ci et al., 2025 ) .

However, a human video is separated from a robot demonstration by a visual gap and an action gap, and both are severe for dexterous hands ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Punamiya et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . In terms of appearance, human videos show a human arm and hand, whereas the policy observes a robot at deployment. Prior work narrows this gap by masking the human arm or overlaying a rendered robot, and must apply the same edit to the robot’s camera stream during both training and deployment ( Kareer et al., 2025 ; Lepert et al., 2025b ; Lepert et al., 2025a ) . In terms of action, the reconstructed hand pose is itself imprecise, and no exact retargeting map takes it to robot joint commands, since human and robot hands differ in morphology and kinematics ( Handa et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Kong et al., 2026 ) . Even a perfect mapping would reproduce only the shape of the hand, not how firmly the robot must grip the object ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .

Our approach. We address these gaps by treating human-to-robot transfer as virtual try-on, which keeps the motion and changes the embodiment. RoboTryOn converts a human manipulation video into a paired robot demonstration with action labels. To this end, we first generate a target robot video performing the same task in the source scene and then predict the corresponding joint-space actions with an inverse dynamics model (IDM), rather than deriving robot actions directly from reconstructed hand motion. As in keyframe-based video virtual try-on ( Zuo et al., 2025 ) , we autoregressively translate selected human frames into robot keyframes, and synthesize the motion between consecutive keyframes under the guidance of the human hand skeleton flow. Our generative models learn this translation from robot videos through a shared arm mask and hand skeleton interface, allowing the same conditions to be extracted from human videos at inference without paired human and robot demonstrations. We then train a policy on the synthesized robot demonstrations, enabling the robot to learn new tasks with few or no teleoperated demonstrations.

Our experiments show that RoboTryOn consistently improves policy performance when task-specific robot demonstrations are limited or unavailable. In particular, averaged over two robot embodiments, RoboTryOn increases the success rate from 2.1% to 60.0% on out-of-domain tasks with goals, skills, and objects unseen in real robot demonstrations. It also achieves 45.9% on challenging bimanual tasks despite all teleoperated demonstrations containing only single-arm manipulation. Finally, training with demonstrations derived from human video matches the performance of training on teleoperated demonstrations alone while requiring approximately a third of the collection cost (see Figure 6 ).
We summarize our main contributions below:
We introduce RoboTryOn, which turns an egocentric human video into a robot demonstration the way virtual try-on swaps a garment, with generative models trained on robot data alone.
We show that our synthetic data bridge the visual and action gaps in human videos, removing the need for test-time visual editing and generating better action labels than retargeted actions.

Through experiments on two real robots with dexterous hands over diverse out-of-domain tasks, we demonstrate that our synthesized demonstrations enable learning tasks without teleoperated demonstrations and reduce data collection costs relative to teleoperation.

Learning from human videos. Human videos provide a scalable source of visual and behavioral knowledge for robot learning. Early work learns visual representations from human videos for downstream robot control ( Nair et al., 2022 ; Majumdar et al., 2023 ) , while recent approaches incorporate human videos into robot foundation model training to learn transferable visual and behavioral knowledge ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Dyna Robotics, 2026 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . Another line converts human demonstrations into robot training data through motion retargeting ( Kareer et al., 2025 ) , often combined with rendered robot observations ( Lepert et al., 2025b ; Lepert et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Approaches based on simulation further construct digital twins to generate robot observations and refine action trajectories ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .

Generative human-to-robot translation. Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled direct translation of human demonstrations into robot videos. Mitty ( Song et al., 2025 ) conditions generation on human videos and learns from paired human and robot data, including synthetically rendered pairs. H2R-Grounder ( Ci et al., 2025 ) removes the need for paired supervision by reconstructing robot videos from inpainted backgrounds and gripper pose cues. Our approach supports multiple dexterous embodiments through shared generative models and produces demonstrations with action labels for real-world policy learning.

Video synthesis and action labeling. Constructing robot demonstrations through video generation requires both temporally consistent synthesis and corresponding action labels. Video virtual try-on studies consistency when modifying a subject’s appearance ( Fang et al., 2024 ; Zuo et al., 2025 ) . In particular, DreamVVT generates keyframes and uses them to guide video synthesis. We adopt this decomposition for embodiment translation and, following prior work ( Baker et al., 2022 ; Du et al., 2023 ; Jang et al., 2025 ) , use IDMs to infer actions from the resulting videos.

Figure 1: RoboTryOn pipeline. (a) The image model sequentially translates keyframes of a human video into robot keyframes, the video model synthesizes the motion between them under the guidance of the hand skeleton flow, and the inverse dynamics model labels the actions. (b) The image model inpaints the masked human frame, using the previous robot keyframe as a reference. (c) The video model synthesizes the robot video, conditioned on the robot keyframes at their temporal positions and the skeleton flow.

Policy learning from demonstrations. We consider a teleoperated robot demonstration dataset 𝒟 = { 𝐗 ( i ) } i = 1 N {\mathcal{D}}=\{\mathbf{X}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{N} , where each demonstration 𝐗 ( i ) = ( ( 𝐨 t , 𝐪 t , 𝐚 t ) t = 1 T ( i ) , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{X}^{(i)}=\big(({\mathbf{o}}_{t},{\mathbf{q}}_{t},{\mathbf{a}}_{t})_{t=1}^{T^{(i)}},{\mathbf{c}}\big) contains a visual observation 𝐨 t {\mathbf{o}}_{t} , a proprioceptive state 𝐪 t {\mathbf{q}}_{t} , and a robot action 𝐚 t {\mathbf{a}}_{t} at each timestep t ∈ { 1 , … , T ( i ) } t\in\{1,\dots,T^{(i)}\} , together with a task instruction 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} . We mainly use vision-language-action models (VLAs) as our base policy π ω \pi_{\omega} , which predicts an action chunk 𝐀 t = 𝐚 t : t + H − 1 \mathbf{A}_{t}={\mathbf{a}}_{t:t+H-1} of horizon H H conditioned on ( 𝐨 t , 𝐪 t , 𝐜 ) ({\mathbf{o}}_{t},{\mathbf{q}}_{t},{\mathbf{c}}) .

Demonstrations from human video. RoboTryOn aims to augment 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} with demonstrations synthesized from human video to address the expensive cost of collecting real robot data. A human demonstration 𝐗 h = ( ( 𝐨 t h ) t = 1 T , 𝐜 ) \mathbf{X}^{h}=\big(({\mathbf{o}}^{h}_{t})_{t=1}^{T},{\mathbf{c}}\big) 1 1 1 For simplicity, we omit the demonstration index. contains egocentric observations 𝐨 t h {\mathbf{o}}^{h}_{t} and the instruction 𝐜 {\mathbf{c}} . Given 𝐗 h \mathbf{X}^{h} and a reference image of the target robot r r , RoboTryOn uses a three-stage pipeline to generate a robot demonstration 𝐗 ^ r = ( ( 𝐨 ^ t r , 𝐪 ^ t , 𝐚 ^ t ) t = 1 T , 𝐜 ) \hat{\mathbf{X}}^{r}=\big((\hat{\mathbf{o}}^{r}_{t},\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{t},\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{t})_{t=1}^{T},{\mathbf{c}}\big) that follows the human motion (see Figure 1 ). First, an image generation model f θ f_{\theta} translates selected human keyframes into robot keyframes ( Section 3.2 ). Next, a video generation model g ϕ g_{\phi} synthesizes the robot video between keyframes under the guidance of the hand skeleton ( Section 3.3 ). Finally, an inverse dynamics model h ψ h_{\psi} predicts the action labels 𝐚 ^ \hat{\mathbf{a}} from the synthesized video, and the states 𝐪 ^ \hat{\mathbf{q}} are then derived from the predicted actions ( Section 3.4 ). The resulting demonstrations form synthetic data 𝒟 ^ \hat{{\mathcal{D}}} , on which we train the policy π ω \pi_{\omega} alone or together with 𝒟 {\mathcal{D}} ( Section 3.5 ). We train the three models and the policy in the same way, as conditional flow-matching models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) . We provide the details of the flow matching process in Appendix E .

In this section, we describe how RoboTryOn selects keyframes from the human demonstration 𝐗 h \mathbf{X}^{h} and translates them into target robot keyframes. We first train the image generation model f θ f_{\theta} on robot demonstrations and apply it to the selected human keyframes at inference.

Keyframes. We select keyframes from the wrist trajectories of the reconstructed human hands ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . A frame is selected when the speed of both wrists reaches a local minimum, where the hands are unblurred, and a wrist has moved more than a threshold from its position in the previous keyframe. We also always include the first and last frames. The resulting keyframe indices form the set 𝒯 = { t 1 < ⋯ < t L } \mathcal{T}=\{t_{1}<\dots<t_{L}\} .

Conditioning. We condition f θ f_{\theta} on an arm and hand mask 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}_{t} and a hand skeleton 𝐒 t \mathbf{S}_{t} . As in virtual try-on methods ( Choi et al., 2021 ; Choi et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Lee and Kwak, 2025 ) , we enlarge and smooth 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}_{t} , so its outline does not reveal the embodiment it covers. The skeleton 𝐒 t \mathbf{S}_{t} is a 2D projection of hand keypoints obtained by forward kinematics for a robot or by retargeting the reconstructed hand for a human. We define a conditioning function Φ ⁡ ( 𝐨 , 𝐌 , 𝐒 ) ≔ ( ( 𝟏 − 𝐌 ) ⊙ 𝐨 ) ⊕ 𝐒 \Phi({\mathbf{o}};\mathbf{M},\mathbf{S})\coloneqq\big((\mathbf{1}-\mathbf{M})\odot{\mathbf{o}}\big)\oplus\mathbf{S} , which masks out the region 𝐌 \mathbf{M} of a frame 𝐨 {\mathbf{o}} and draws the skeleton 𝐒 \mathbf{S} over it. The same function gives the conditioned robot frame 𝐨 ~ t = Φ ⁡ ( 𝐨 t , 𝐌 t , 𝐒 t ) \tilde{\mathbf{o}}_{t}=\Phi({\mathbf{o}}_{t};\mathbf{M}_{t},\mathbf{S}_{t}) for training and the conditioned human frame 𝐨 ~ t h = Φ ⁡ ( 𝐨 t h , 𝐌 t h , 𝐒 t h ) \tilde{\mathbf{o}}^{h}_{t}=\Phi({\mathbf{o}}^{h}_{t};\mathbf{M}^{h}_{t},\mathbf{S}^{h}_{t}) for inference. To make the model robust to imperfect hand retargeting, we perturb and randomly drop the skeleton during training. The skeleton then provides only coarse guidance on hand position and motion, while detailed hand configuration comes from the learned prior over robot hands.

Model. The image generation model f θ f_{\theta} aims to translate a human keyframe into a robot keyframe as inpainting guided by a reference image: it fills the masked region 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}_{t} with the target robot in the pose specified by the skeleton 𝐒 t \mathbf{S}_{t} , using the reference image to determine its appearance (see Figure 1 (b)).

We train f θ f_{\theta} to generate a robot frame 𝐨 t {\mathbf{o}}_{t} from two conditions: the conditioned frame 𝐨 ~ t \tilde{\mathbf{o}}_{t} with its mask 𝐌 t \mathbf{M}_{t} , and a reference frame 𝐨 t ′ {\mathbf{o}}_{t^{\prime}} from the same episode at an earlier time t ′ < t t^{\prime}<t , which provides the appearance of the embodiment, the objects, and the background. With a pretrained image encoder ℰ img \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{img}} and 𝐳 = ℰ img ​ ( 𝐨 t ) \mathbf{z}=\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{img}}({\mathbf{o}}_{t}) , we train f θ f_{\theta} using the flow-matching objective with diffusion timestep τ \tau :

Can a policy learn tasks never demonstrated through teleoperation from human video alone, and does RoboTryOn outperform other retargeting or overlaying methods? ( Table 1 )
Does our synthesized data bridge the visual and action gaps between human videos and real robot data? ( Figures 3 , 4 and 5 )
Can synthesized data replace teleoperated demonstrations, and how does the success rate change with the amount of human video? ( Figure 6 )

Robots and tasks. We evaluate RoboTryOn on two bimanual robots with dexterous hands: an OpenArm with two 7-DoF arms and two 6-DoF Inspire RH56F1 hands, and an RB-Y1 with two 7-DoF arms and two 20-DoF WujiHand2 hands. Both are evaluated on eleven tabletop tasks (see Figure 2 ). There are four pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, i.e. , in-domain tasks, with 50 teleoperated demonstrations per robot and 50 human videos each: PnP Bottle , Doll , Box , and Ball . The other seven tasks, i.e. , out-of-domain tasks, have 50 human videos each and no robot demonstrations, and they introduce a single novel object task ( PnP Coffee Pot ), a single novel goal task ( PnP Bottle to Shelf ), two novel skill tasks ( Pouring , Brushing ), and three bimanual manipulation tasks ( Box Convey , Air Fryer , PnP Ball in Cup ), whereas the teleoperated tasks are all single-arm tasks. Further details on the robots and tasks are provided in Section C.1 .

Baselines. We compare with the two existing ways of turning human video into robot training data. Both retarget the reconstructed hand into actions and differ in how they handle the human in the image. EgoMimic ( Kareer et al., 2025 ) masks the arm out of the human frames, while Masquerade ( Lepert et al., 2025a ) inpaints the arm out, composites a rendering of the robot in the retargeted pose, and adds an auxiliary loss on future 2D robot keypoints. Following their protocols, both apply the same edit to the robot data and to the live camera image at test time, whereas RoboTryOn runs on the raw camera view (see details in Section B.3 ). All methods share the policy model, the teleoperated episodes, and the human videos, so they differ only in how the human video is converted.

Implementation details. For each robot, we fine-tune π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025 ) for the same number of training steps on 200 teleoperated episodes (50 per in-domain task), on 550 episodes synthesized by RoboTryOn from human videos (50 per task over all eleven tasks), or on all 750 together. We evaluate each policy over 28 trials per task with randomized object positions (see Section C.1 ). We train the image generation model, the video generation model, and the IDM on the teleoperated demonstrations of the four in-domain tasks and on additional robot videos, which enrich the embodiment prior of the models. The additional videos are not used to train any policy. We provide further details on the backbones and training in Section B.2.8 .

In-domain tasks. As shown in Table 1 , RoboTryOn improves the success rate over both baselines on the in-domain tasks of both robots. In particular, the success rate rises from 47.3% to 75.9% on the OpenArm and from 69.6% to 79.5% on the RB-Y1. This suggests that synthesized demonstrations add useful variation even to tasks with teleoperated demonstrations, as they cover more object placements and more varied arm and hand motions than the 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task.

Out-of-domain tasks. RoboTryOn yields the largest gains on the seven tasks without robot demonstrations, enabling the policy to learn these tasks, whereas both baselines largely fail with success rates below 10% (see Table 1 ). In particular, the success rate rises from 3.1% to 73.0% on the OpenArm and from 1.0% to 46.9% on the RB-Y1. Notably, the policy also learns the bimanual tasks, although every teleoperated demonstration uses a single arm. This demonstrates that RoboTryOn turns human videos into robot demonstrations from which a policy learns new objects, goals, skills, and bimanual coordination. Moreover, a single image model, video model, and IDM serve both robots despite their different kinematics, hands, and camera placements (see Figure 10 ). Additionally, we analyze why the baselines fail in Section 4.3 .

In this section, we analyze the quality of our synthesized data and the effects of human and translated robot data on policy learning, focusing on the amount of data, collection cost, and execution speed. Unless otherwise stated, we use π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} fine-tuned on the OpenArm in these experiments.

We first examine whether synthesized videos resemble real robot videos (see Figure 3 ). We encode the frames of raw, masked (EgoMimic), overlaid (Masquerade), and synthesized human videos with the visual encoder of the policy and compare their embeddings with those of real robot videos. Videos synthesized by RoboTryOn overlap with real robot videos in this embedding space, whereas raw, masked, and overlaid videos form separate clusters. Quantitatively, the Fréchet SigLIP distance ( Heusel et al., 2017 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ) to real robot videos agrees: RoboTryOn reduces it from 125.5 to 32.7, while overlay reduces it by about half and masking leaves it largely unchanged. This suggests that RoboTryOn closes the visual gap while the policy uses raw camera observations at test time. In contrast, both baselines narrow the gap only by applying the same masking or overlay to every camera observation during deployment.

Action gap. To evaluate action labels without ground truth robot actions, we replay them open loop in a simulated replica of each scene and measure task completion (see Figure 4 a). We compare the labels from our IDM with retargeted labels, which map the reconstructed human hand to the robot hand ( Qin et al., 2023 ) and solve for the arm by inverse kinematics. Replay succeeds in 69.7% of episodes with our labels and 34.8% with retargeted labels (see Figure 4 c), and the difference arises mainly during grasping: retargeted motions bring the robot hand near the object, but imprecise hand reconstruction and the difference in hand geometry prevent a secure grasp (see Figure 4 b). This suggests that labeling synthesized robot videos with the IDM yields more executable actions than retargeting, since RoboTryOn uses the reconstructed hand only to guide generation and the generated robot hand grasps the object as in the robot data.

We then examine how these labels affect policy learning by comparing the actions and the training gradients they induce (see Figure 5 ). Retargeted hand actions differ substantially from teleoperated actions (see Figure 5 a). At the pretrained weights of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we compute the gradient of the flow-matching loss on teleoperated in-domain data and on the data of each out-of-domain task. The cosine similarity between the two gradients measures how much the two sources agree on the update direction ( Appendix D ). Our data yields a cosine similarity of 0.53, compared with 0.17 and 0.14 for the baselines, and retargeted data yields slightly negative similarity within the action expert (see Figure 5 b). This suggests that retargeted labels steer the policy in a direction that conflicts with the teleoperated data, which may explain why the baselines gain little on out-of-domain tasks. Consistently, the baselines’ hand actions during robot execution stay close to the teleoperated distribution on in-domain tasks but diverge on out-of-domain tasks, whereas our policy stays close on both (see Figure 5 c).

Scaling and cost. To assess whether human videos are a cost-effective source of demonstrations, we vary the number of demonstrations per task on the four in-domain tasks and compare the success rate against collection cost in person-hours (see Figure 6 ). Recording a human video takes about a fifth of the time of a teleoperated episode (see Table 10 ). Notably, training with translated human videos alone matches the success rate obtained with 50 teleoperated demonstrations per task at about one third of the collection cost. This suggests that, although a translated human video yields a slightly lower success rate per demonstration than a teleoperated episode, it is more cost-effective in collection time. Moreover, augmenting the teleoperated dataset with an equal number of human videos increases the success rate from 47.3% to 71.4% and requires less than one additional hour of recording.
