Execution speed. Since human demonstrators move at roughly 1.25 × 1.25\times the speed of the teleoperated demonstrations, we examine how the speed of synthesized demonstrations affects the policy. Using the same keyframes, we retime the skeleton flow to the teleoperated speed ( 1 × 1\times ) or twice that speed ( 2 × 2\times ) before synthesis and compare with videos synthesized at the recorded speed (see Table 2 ). Matching the teleoperated speed improves the in-domain success rate from 75.9% to 85.7% while keeping the out-of-domain success rate similar. This suggests that the policy inherits the speed of its training demonstrations, as its task completion time follows the speed of the synthesized videos. However, training at 2 × 2\times produces the fastest policy at the cost of a lower success rate on both task groups.

We ablate the components of RoboTryOn and the policy backbone to verify that each component contributes to policy success and that the gains do not depend on a specific VLA. All ablations use the OpenArm, and per-task results are given in Tables 13 and 12 .

Pipeline components. As shown in Table 3(a) , removing any of the four components reduces the success rate on both task groups. Without the autoregressive reference, the robot appearance stays consistent but the scene changes across keyframes. Without subsequent keyframes, the video model is conditioned only on the first keyframe, so the motion is preserved but the objects and the scene deviate from the human video. Without the hand skeleton flow, the video model receives no motion guidance between keyframes, and the synthesized robot no longer follows the demonstrator, which causes the largest drop. This shows that each stage is needed to keep the synthesized demonstration faithful to the human video in scene, appearance, and motion. Interestingly, removing the wrist correction reduces the success rate more on out-of-domain tasks, since the policy relies more on generated action labels for tasks without teleoperated demonstrations, and many of their motions lie outside the training distribution of the IDM. We show failure cases of each variant in Section F.3 .

Policy backbone. To verify that the benefit of RoboTryOn is not specific to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we also fine-tune RLDX-1-Img ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , a VLA with a different architecture, on the same data (see Table 3(b) ). RoboTryOn consistently improves the success rate of RLDX-1-Img, from 53.6% to 60.7% on in-domain tasks and from 0.0% to 40.3% on out-of-domain tasks. This demonstrates that the demonstrations synthesized by RoboTryOn remain effective across policy architectures.

We presented RoboTryOn, which turns a human video into a robot demonstration the way virtual try-on changes the garment on a person: it keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the embodiment. RoboTryOn translates human keyframes into robot keyframes, synthesizes the robot video between them under the guidance of the hand skeleton, and labels its actions with an inverse dynamics model. On two real robots with dexterous hands, the synthesized demonstrations teach a policy seven tasks without any robot demonstration, including bimanual ones. Human video translated this way also matches the success rate of teleoperated demonstrations at about a third of their collection cost. We discuss limitations and future work in Appendix A .

passages.section: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work
passages.location: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work
passages.text: Limitations. Adding an embodiment still requires a few hours of teleoperated video of that robot, on any tasks, to teach the generative models and the inverse dynamics model what it looks like and how it moves. This cost is paid once per robot rather than once per task, but it is not zero. The actions are pseudo labels: the IDM reads the joints from pixels, and the hand reconstruction provides the wrist position. They cannot capture forces, and their precision is bounded by what stereo video and a hand reconstruction resolve, so tasks that depend on forces or on fine precision, such as tight insertion, are not yet labeled accurately enough. The wrist correction also relies on the head camera calibration. The human videos are recorded from the position of the robot’s head camera, and the teleoperated data keep the neck and the base of the robot fixed. Under this fixed viewpoint, RoboTryOn translates human videos into each embodiment reliably (see Figure 10 ). With a moving camera, as in in-the-wild egocentric videos, the input falls outside the training distribution of the video model and the IDM. In particular, the IDM always predicts fixed neck and base actions, since the neck and the base never move in its training data. The demonstrated motion must be one the robot can execute. The pipeline can retime the human video to the robot’s pace, but it cannot correct a motion toward a position beyond the reach of the robot arm or a grasp that the robot hand cannot form. Our evaluation covers tabletop manipulation on two robots. We also translate human videos into the GR-1, but could not evaluate policies on it without access to the physical robot. Finally, synthesis trades collection time for compute (see Table 10 ), which favors tasks that are expensive to teleoperate.

passages.section: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work
passages.location: Appendix A Limitations and Future Work
passages.text: Future work. The natural next step is scale: translating large egocentric corpora such as EgoDex into every embodiment we own, so that a robot’s training data grows with the supply of human video rather than with the supply of operators. Since the policy learns from pseudo labels, improving the accuracy of the IDM is another key direction. Policy rollouts on the robot are recorded with their executed actions, so they naturally become training data for the IDM, and the IDM can keep improving as the policy is deployed. Currently, the IDM and the hand reconstruction estimate actions separately, and we simply replace the wrist position predicted by the IDM with the reconstructed one. An IDM that takes the reconstructed wrist position as an additional input could combine the two estimates and predict more accurate actions.

π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is a mixture of transformers in which the action expert shares attention with the vision-language model, whereas RLDX-1-Img follows the design of GR00T N1 [ NVIDIA et al., 2025 ] , in which a separate action head is conditioned on vision-language features. Both π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and RLDX-1-Img are fully fine-tuned for 30k steps with a batch size of 64 on four H100 GPUs, with the same settings for every data mixture of Table 1 . π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is trained with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.95 \beta_{2}=0.95 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} , weight decay 0.01) at a learning rate of 2.5 × 10 − 5 2.5\times 10^{-5} with cosine decay to 2.5 × 10 − 6 2.5\times 10^{-6} , gradient clipping at norm 1.0, and an action chunk of 50 steps (2.5 s). States and actions are normalized by their 1st and 99th percentiles to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . RLDX-1-Img follows the configuration of its official repository: the vision-language backbone is frozen except for its top four language layers, the action expert is trained in full (2.4B of 6.9B parameters in total), the learning rate is 10 − 4 10^{-4} with cosine decay, and the action chunk is 16 steps (0.8 s), and the optimizer and the normalization are the same as for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .

Keyframes are selected from the 3D wrist trajectories of the reconstructed hands ( Section B.2.2 ), smoothed in time with a Gaussian of σ = 0.25 \sigma=0.25 s. A frame is a candidate when the larger of the two wrist speeds has a local minimum within ± 1 \pm 1 s: the hands are unblurred there, and a hand has typically arrived at a new location. The next keyframe is the first candidate at which a wrist has moved more than a threshold from its position in the previous keyframe. The threshold is set for each episode as the 30th percentile of the wrist displacements between all pairs of up to 400 frames sampled uniformly from the episode, where the displacement of a pair is the larger 3D movement of the wrists visible in both frames. Because the reconstruction is most reliable when a hand is slow and fully visible, this rule also tends to avoid frames in which a hand is undetected or detected with low confidence. The base video model supports clips of up to 20 seconds, but for the consistency of the synthesized video we cap the interval between consecutive keyframes at 145 frames, about 7.25 seconds at 20 Hz. When no candidate satisfies the rule within the cap, we take the frame with the largest displacement among those whose reconstruction confidence is at least the median of the interval, or the frame at the cap if no frame has a confidence. The first and last frames are always keyframes. Pick-and-place videos yield about four keyframes and the longer tasks six to seven.

Hand reconstruction. The human hands are reconstructed with HaWoR [ Zhang et al., 2025 ] from each view of the stereo camera. The depth of the wrist is corrected by triangulating the two views, and the left and right hand predictions of the two views complement each other, so that a hand that leaves the frame in one view and is misdetected there is recovered from the other view.

Keypoint set. Each hand is represented by 17 keypoints: four on the thumb, three on each of the other four fingers (the knuckle, the middle joint, and the tip), and the wrist. The skeleton connects the keypoints of each finger in sequence and connects the finger bases to one another and to the wrist. The same set is defined for the human hand, the Inspire RH56F1, the WujiHand2, and the GR-1 hand, so that hands with different degrees of freedom map to the same keypoints. For a robot the keypoints come from forward kinematics of the recorded joint state, projected into each camera view, and for a person they come from the reconstructed hand, retargeted to the target robot hand. Because the retargeting is imprecise, keypoints are perturbed and randomly dropped during training: each keypoint is displaced by up to half the length of the finger segment it belongs to, the whole skeleton is dropped with probability 0.2, and each keypoint is dropped independently with probability 0.2. The model thus learns to treat the skeleton as a coarse guide while its prior over robot hands, learned from the robot data, determines the configuration the generated hand takes. The retargeting error does not enter the action labels, which are read from the generated video by the IDM. The skeleton is rendered as its 2D projection, drawn over the frame for the image model and as a video of the same length for the video model.

Mask construction. The mask is shape-agnostic in the sense of virtual try-on: it is enlarged and smoothed so that the model cannot recover the original silhouette of the arm and hand it covers. For a robot frame the mask is built from a rendering of the robot from its URDF at the recorded joint state and a SAM3 segmentation of the robot, which are complementary, since neither alone covers the robot exactly. During training the mask is further deformed to random sizes and shapes so that the model is robust to its size and outline, and, with some probability and where the object is known, the region of the manipulated object is removed from the mask. At inference the mask of the human arm and hand comes from SAM3 alone, dilated so that the shape cannot be inferred, and the region of the manipulated object is always removed so that the object is preserved.

Reference sampling. The reference frame is sampled from the same episode two to five seconds before the target, since a closer frame would allow the model to copy the reference instead of learning to move the robot.
Stereo generation. Both views are generated as one token sequence with an additional rotary position dimension separating left and right tokens, and training mixes single-view and stereo examples.

Autoregressive inference. The denoised latent of 𝐨 ^ t j − 1 r \hat{\mathbf{o}}^{r}_{t_{j-1}} is reused directly as the reference tokens for 𝐨 ^ t j r \hat{\mathbf{o}}^{r}_{t_{j}} , without decoding and re-encoding.

First keyframe. The first keyframe has no previously translated keyframe to serve as reference, so its reference is a real frame of the target robot with everything but the robot masked out, which selects the embodiment. To train for this case, the reference is replaced by such a frame with probability 0.05 during training.

All videos and actions are recorded, synthesized, and labeled at 20 Hz. A demonstration is cut at keyframe times into clips of at most 145 frames ( Section B.2.1 ). Each clip is synthesized with the two to four keyframes that fall inside it, adjacent clips share the keyframe at their boundary, and the clips are concatenated in time. The rendered skeleton flow is encoded by the video VAE like the clip itself and attended to as in-context tokens. Demonstrations of 10–25 seconds are synthesized in this way ( Figure 14 ).

By default the human video is synthesized as recorded. For Table 2 each human video is divided by its action into phases, approaching the object, grasping it, lifting it, and placing it, into which the tasks without robot demonstrations divide as well. For each phase the skeleton flow is resampled in time so that its speed matches the mean action speed of the teleoperated episodes in that phase, at the chosen multiple, and the video is synthesized again from the same keyframes at their new temporal positions. Human demonstrators grasp and lift faster than the teleoperators in many episodes, so these are the phases the retiming changes most.

The IDM takes frames t t and t + 20 t{+}20 (1 s at 20 Hz) at 224 × \times 224, stereo for the OpenArm and RB-Y1 and monocular for the GR-1, and predicts a 20-step chunk of the full joint vector (28, 66, and 44 dimensions). Following the DreamGen IDM [ Jang et al., 2025 ] , the three embodiments share one model and are distinguished by an embodiment tag, and the action head is a flow-matching head on the Depth Anything V2 backbone. Of the 24 layers of its ViT, the first 11 are frozen and the rest are fine-tuned, and the Depth Anything head is not used. For labeling, the model is applied in a sliding window, overlapping predictions are averaged, and the sequence is smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter [ Savitzky and Golay, 1964 ] of polynomial order 2 over a window of 9 frames for the arm joints and 5 frames for the hand joints. The states 𝐪 ^ t \hat{\mathbf{q}}_{t} of a synthesized demonstration are derived from its action labels by the relation measured on the teleoperated data, where the recorded state lags the commanded action by four steps, so that 𝐪 ^ t = 𝐚 ^ t − 4 \hat{\mathbf{q}}_{t}=\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{t-4} .

The human wrist position is taken from the hand reconstruction of Section B.2.2 , in the camera frame, and transformed into the robot base frame with the head camera calibration, since the human video is recorded from the position of the robot’s head camera. The robot hand implied by the IDM’s joints is scaled, finger segment by finger segment, to the size of the reconstructed human hand, and the target wrist position is the one at which the end effector of the scaled hand coincides with the reconstructed wrist. Since the reconstruction is noisy, the target is taken only from segments with high reconstruction confidence and smoothed in time, so that the correction moves the arm gradually rather than snapping it to the reconstruction. The target orientation is the wrist orientation obtained by forward kinematics from the IDM’s arm joints, so that only the translation is corrected. The arm joints are then solved by inverse kinematics in MuJoCo, initialized from the IDM’s arm joints of the same frame, and the hand joints are left unchanged. The correction is applied to both arms for bimanual demonstrations. Section 4.4 ablates it.

Training corpus. All three models, the image model, the video model, and the IDM, are trained on the same corpus of teleoperated robot episodes: 3.79 hours (453 episodes) collected on the OpenArm with the Inspire RH56F1 hand, 2.53 hours (352 episodes) on the RB-Y1 with the WujiHand2, and 2.50 hours (1,180 clips) of the GR-1 taken from the public GR00T teleoperation dataset released with DreamDojo [ Gao et al., 2026 ] . The OpenArm and RB-Y1 recordings are stereo, whereas the GR-1 recordings are monocular, so the generative models learn stereo generation from the first two. The corpus consists of the teleoperated demonstrations of the four pick-and-place tasks used in Section 4 plus additional teleoperated recordings. The additional recordings are used only to train the three models above and play no part in training any VLA policy.

Training configuration. The image model f θ f_{\theta} is a fully fine-tuned FLUX.2 [klein] 9B Base [ Black Forest Labs, 2026 ] , the video model g ϕ g_{\phi} an in-context LoRA on LTX-2.5 [ Lightricks, 2026 , HaCohen et al., 2026 ] , and the IDM h ψ h_{\psi} a Depth Anything V2 backbone [ Yang et al., 2024 ] with the action head of the DreamGen IDM [ Jang et al., 2025 ] . Table 4 lists their training configuration, and all three are trained on the corpus of Section B.2.8 . The image model is trained with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 ) and a cosine learning rate schedule. Its input embedder does not accept the channel-wise concatenation of the conditioned frame with the noisy target, so the embedder is extended by zero-initialized input channels that are trained with the rest of the model. Training examples are stereo and single-view in a 3:1 ratio, and the GR-1 recordings are single-view only. The video model LoRA has rank 64 and is trained with AdamW ( β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 ) in two stages matching the two-stage inference of Section B.4 : 4k steps at 512 × \times 288 per view followed by 1k steps at 1024 × \times 576 per view.

Common setup. Both baselines are re-implemented on our hardware with the same backbone, teleoperated episodes, and human videos as RoboTryOn.

Retargeting. Both use the same pseudo actions: the 3D hand pose reconstructed with HaWoR is mapped to the robot hand by a geometric mapping of joint angles (finger flexion angles matched to the hand’s joint ranges, wrist pose transformed into the base frame with the head camera calibration) following AnyTeleop [ Qin et al., 2023 ] , and the arm joints are obtained by inverse kinematics in MuJoCo from the wrist pose.

EgoMimic. The human arm and hand are masked in every human frame. In the robot episodes the robot arm is masked from the recorded state, by projecting the URDF into the camera. At test time the mask is placed on the live image from the current robot state and the camera calibration. The masking follows the official implementation.

Masquerade. The human arm is inpainted out and a rendering of the robot from its URDF in the retargeted state is composited onto the frame. Robot episodes receive the same rendering from the recorded state, and at test time the rendering is composited onto the live image from the current state. The original uses E2FGVI [ Li et al., 2022 ] for the inpainting. We use ProPainter [ Zhou et al., 2023 ] , which leaves fewer artifacts on our videos. Following the original, the policy is trained with an auxiliary loss that predicts future 2D robot hand keypoints from the image features, with targets from the retargeted (human) or recorded (robot) state. The head, the prediction horizon, and the loss weight follow the official implementation. The original single-arm gripper pipeline is extended to both arms and to the dexterous hands of our robots.

Inference configuration and compute. Table 5 lists the inference configuration of every stage and its cost on a single H100. The video model runs in two stages: the first generates the clip at 512 × \times 288 per view with a distilled model in 8 sampling steps, and the second upsamples the result to 1024 × \times 576 per view and refines it in 3 steps. Both stages are conditioned on the same keyframes and skeleton flow, the second at the higher resolution, and both generate the two stereo views in one sequence. The image model generates each keyframe at 1024 × \times 576 per view in 30 sampling steps with a guidance scale of 3.5, and the keyframes of a demonstration are generated sequentially since each conditions on the previous one. The IDM predicts a 20-step action chunk from each 1 s window and is applied in a sliding window with a stride of one frame over the demonstration.

Table 6 breaks down the wall-clock time of the full pipeline for a typical 15 s demonstration (300 frames at 20 Hz, translated into one embodiment). Table 10 accounts for collection in person-hours and Appendix A notes the trade of collection time for compute.

Hardware setup. We use two humanoid robots, OpenArm and RB-Y1 ( Figure 7 b,c), in our real-world experiments. Both humanoids are equipped with two 7-DoF arms. Each arm of the OpenArm is equipped with a 6-DoF Inspire RH56F1 hand, and each arm of the RB-Y1 is equipped with a 20-DoF WujiHand2 hand. The head of each robot is mounted on a 2-DoF neck that supports pitch and yaw motions. A stereo camera is mounted on each neck, and its left and right egocentric views are used as visual inputs throughout all experiments.

Task details. All tasks are formulated as language-conditioned manipulation tasks. We evaluate eleven tasks in total ( Figure 2 ), comprising four in-domain pick-and-place (PnP) tasks and seven out-of-domain tasks. The in-domain tasks ( Figure 2 a) consist of PnP Bottle , PnP Doll , PnP Box , and PnP Ball , with 50 teleoperated demonstrations per robot embodiment and 50 human videos for each task. The human videos are recorded from the position of the robot’s head camera ( Figure 7 a). The seven out-of-domain tasks ( Figure 2 b) have 50 human videos each and no robot demonstrations: PnP Coffee Pot , PnP Bottle to Shelf , Pouring , Brushing , Box Convey , Air Fryer , and PnP Ball in Cup .

The four in-domain PnP tasks share the same task structure, where the robot grasps a designated object and places it into a white container ( Figure 7 d). PnP Coffee Pot follows the same pick-and-place structure with a novel coffee pot object. PnP Bottle to Shelf requires the robot to grasp a bottle and place it at a designated location on a shelf. Pouring requires the robot to grasp a bottle and pour its contents into a red cup. Brushing requires the robot to grasp a brush and wipe the area marked with black tape. Box Convey requires the robot to move a box to the right using both hands sequentially, with the left hand moving it first and the right hand moving it further. Air Fryer requires the robot to open an air fryer, grasp an apple-shaped object, place it inside, and close the door. Finally, PnP Ball in Cup requires the robot to lift an inverted cup with the left hand, grasp the ball with the right hand, and place it into the target container. Figure 7 e shows the objects introduced by the out-of-domain tasks.

We conduct 28 evaluation trials for each task. For single-arm tasks, a trial receives a score of 1 only when the task is successfully completed. For bimanual tasks, each hand contributes 0.5 to the score, yielding a maximum score of 1 when both required hand actions are successfully completed. The initial positions of the target objects are randomized within the workspace for each trial. For the PnP tasks, including PnP Bottle , PnP Doll , PnP Box , PnP Ball , PnP Coffee Pot , and PnP Bottle to Shelf , a trial is considered successful when the object is placed at the designated goal location. For Pouring , the trial is successful when the bottle is tilted over the target cup. For Brushing , success is determined by whether the brush reaches the designated region marked with black tape. For Box Convey , the trial is successful when the specified sequential manipulation with the left and right hands is correctly executed. For Air Fryer , success requires opening the air fryer, placing the apple-shaped object inside, and closing the door. For PnP Ball in Cup , success requires lifting the cup with the left hand, grasping the ball with the right hand, and placing the ball at the designated goal location.

Setup. We build a simulated counterpart of the OpenArm setup in Isaac Lab [ Mittal et al., 2023 ] . The simulated robot follows the real OpenArm: two 7-DoF arms with 6-DoF Inspire RH56F1 hands and a 2-DoF neck, fixed at the downward pitch measured on the real robot. The head camera is positioned to match the mounting configuration of the real stereo camera, ensuring that the simulated egocentric view shares the same viewpoint as the real one ( Figure 9 ).

Tasks. We simulate the three in-domain pick-and-place tasks that have simulation assets, PnP Bottle , PnP Ball , and PnP Box . PnP Doll is excluded because no simulation asset of the doll exists. For each human video, the objects are placed at the positions recorded in the corresponding real scene, measured with the depth sensor and the stereo views of the ZED 2i head camera and verified by overlaying the first frame of the video on the simulated scene. As in the real setup, the robot grasps the object and places it into the white container (see Figure 9 ).
Evaluation protocol. Each task is evaluated on 22 episodes (66 in total), one for each human video. An episode counts as a success when the object is picked up and placed in the container.

Visual gap analysis. From each corpus, 5,000 frames are sampled uniformly: the human videos, their EgoMimic and Masquerade edits, the RoboTryOn translations, and the teleoperated robot episodes. Each frame is encoded by the pretrained SigLIP vision tower [ Zhai et al., 2023 ] of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and its features are mean-pooled over image tokens. Action replay in simulation. We replay each set of action labels in the simulation environment of Section C.2 . For each human video, the labels are executed open loop from the same initial configuration, with the objects at their recorded positions, and each episode is evaluated as described there. Retargeting : the reconstructed hand [ Zhang et al., 2025 ] is mapped to the robot hand [ Qin et al., 2023 ] and the arm joints are solved by inverse kinematics from the wrist pose, the labels EgoMimic and Masquerade train on. RoboTryOn : the IDM labels of the synthesized video, with and without the wrist correction of Section 3.4 . Each labeling is replayed on the same 22 episodes of each task. On Bottle, Box, and Ball, RoboTryOn succeeds on 17, 14, and 15 of them, RoboTryOn without the wrist correction on 14, 16, and 12, and retargeting on 14, 7, and 2 ( Table 8 ).

Action distribution and co-training. Figure 5 uses right-hand actions at 20 Hz, every frame without subsampling. Panel (a) shows the thumb rotation, the opposition axis that turns the thumb toward the palm, and the mean flexion of the other four fingers. We normalize each joint so that the 1st and 99th percentiles of the three sources pooled map to − 1 -1 and 1 1 , compute histogram densities over 40 bins on [ − 1.15 , 1.15 ] [-1.15,1.15] , and plot them against the corresponding joint angle in radians. Panel (b) is measured at the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} base weights before fine-tuning, so the three methods start from the same weights and differ only in the data they produce. Each method keeps the normalization statistics of its own training setup. We take the gradient of the flow-matching training loss averaged over 896 teleoperated PnP frames, and over 880 frames of the method’s human data for each out-of-domain task. We split the episodes of each source into two halves, compute the cosine for the two resulting pairs, and average them. The bars average over the seven out-of-domain tasks. All params covers the 4.1B parameters of the model, and Action expert covers its 0.69B parameters together with the action and time projections. Gradients from two halves of the same source give a cosine of 0.96 to 0.97 for teleoperation and 0.78 to 0.95 for each task, so the differences in panel (b) are not measurement noise. Panel (c) uses every frame of the right-hand actions that the policy outputs during real robot rollouts, before filtering, in the units of panel (a). As the reference we sample 8,000 frames of teleoperated right-hand actions from the four PnP tasks. Following the k-NN precision of Kynkäänniemi et al. [2019] , each reference frame defines a ball whose radius is the distance to its fifth nearest reference frame, and a rollout frame counts as within the teleoperated distribution if it falls inside any ball. We compute this share for each policy and task and average it over the in-domain and over the out-of-domain tasks. Measured the same way, two halves of the teleoperated episodes give about 73 to 80%.

analysis.overview: RoboTryOn把固定机位人类视频先转成目标机器人关键帧，再以手骨架流插值为视频，由跨本体IDM补动作并用重建手腕平移作IK校正，形成可直接训练策略的演示。它改变的是新任务的采集与动作标注路线：有本体机器人先验时，可用人视频替代部分任务遥操作，部署直接用原始视图。两本体七个无任务级机器人演示任务上，加入合成数据的平均归一化得分约2.1%→60.0%，但双臂按每手半分，不能当整项任务完全成功率。生成器/IDM仍训练于8.82小时机器人语料，采集人时节省换来离线合成算力；精细接触、移动相机和不可达动作仍是边界。

findings.title: 减少新任务遥操作，仍需先学机器人本体先验
findings.text: 任务级瓶颈是高自由度手的视觉域差与动作域差：直接重定向手形未必能形成稳固抓握。本文不要求配对人/机器人演示，但图像模型、视频模型和IDM都先用机器人语料学外观与动作。语料为OpenArm 3.79小时453例、RB-Y1 2.53小时352例、GR-1公开遥操作2.50小时1180片段，合计8.82小时；额外机器人记录不直接进入VLA训练，却是合成管线的先验投入。四个PnP任务每本体200例遥操作还可用于策略。因此无新任务机器人演示与全流程无机器人数据不同；新本体仍需数小时录制，不能仅凭参考图迁移到从未见过的本体。

findings.title: 自回归关键帧锁场景，骨架流控制帧间运动
findings.text: HaWoR双目重建手部，用低腕速且足够位移选关键帧，首尾必选，间隔最多145帧约7.25秒。SAM3/URDF掩码膨胀平滑以隐藏本体轮廓，保留操作物体；17点手骨架为粗引导，训练加入关键点扰动及丢弃以避免依赖精确重定向。图像模型逐帧以先前生成关键帧为参考填入目标机器人，首帧用真实目标本体参考；视频模型以2–4关键帧和骨架流补全20Hz视频，邻接片段共享边界帧，可拼接10–25秒。式3.1–3.4及附录E使用条件flow matching，不是将人骨架直接作为执行动作。图像FLUX.2 [klein] 9B全量微调、LTX-2.5 rank64 LoRA，几何与接触可执行性没有形式保证。

findings.title: 动作由视频IDM标注，但腕平移仍借助手重建与IK
findings.text: 共享IDM带本体标签，以相隔20帧的一对224×224视图预测20步全关节位置动作，OpenArm/RB-Y1用双目，GR-1单目。采用Depth Anything V2-L的ViT特征及flow action head，前11层冻结，原深度输出头不用，不能写成直接输出深度图监督动作。滑窗步长1、重叠平均与Savitzky–Golay平滑；伪状态取动作滞后4步约0.2秒，不是实际机器人状态测量。IDM手关节保留，利用高置信度人腕三维位置、头相机标定和手指尺度匹配，IK仅修正腕平移，保留IDM腕朝向。故其改动是用生成手形的动作先验替代直接手关节重定向，再以几何补腕位，而非完全摆脱重建/校准或恢复接触力。

findings.title: 双臂按手计半分，倒水和刷擦也有明确代理判据
findings.text: 两本体各11个桌面任务：四PnP各有50条遥操作和50条人视频，七OOD各50条人视频、无该任务机器人演示。每策略每任务28次、物体初始位置随机。单臂二元评分，双臂每只手完成所需动作各0.5；因此表中SR及双臂平均值含部分完成，不能解释为整项双臂任务全成功比例。倒水判瓶倾斜到杯上方，刷擦判刷子到胶带区，不直接测倒入量或清洁质量。π0.5各数据组合均30k步、batch64、四H100，行动chunk50；比较改数据转换路径而非额外训练步。基线同策略/主训练集，但RoboTryOn的额外生成器先验并非零成本；Masquerade被作者重实现并由E2FGVI改为ProPainter、扩展为双臂灵巧手，不能当对原论文官方分数的直接替代。

findings.title: 60%来自混合训练，合成数据单独用于策略时为44.4%
findings.text: 目视表1/11：OpenArm七OOD平均从Teleop only的3.1到+RoboTryOn的73.0，RB-Y1从1.0到46.9，两本体等权约2.1→60.0；EgoMimic为5.1/5.1，Masquerade8.2/7.7。RoboTryOn-only策略OOD为48.5/40.3，跨本体约44.4，仍已利用训练生成器/IDM的机器人语料。主混合行每本体200真实+550合成共750例，合成覆盖11任务，不是凭没有新任务演示的Teleop策略直接零样本执行。域内主得分47.3→75.9、69.6→79.5。双臂混合平均63.1/28.6，跨本体约45.9且含半分；RB-Y1 Air Fryer全部方法0，OpenArm混合60.7。大幅增益支持新任务数据转换，但不能称所有任务/本体均学会、60%严格全任务成功或无额外人类任务演示。

findings.title: 消融显示骨架、后续关键帧与腕校正各有作用
findings.text: 表3/13均在OpenArm：完整域内/OOD75.9/73.0；去自回归参考68.8/66.3，去后续关键帧42.9/39.3，去骨架流42.0/21.4，去腕校正65.2/48.0。骨架流缺失的OOD下降最大，支持运动约束不能仅靠视觉真实感；腕位校正对OOD的25个百分点差说明生成动作先验仍需几何定位。但单消融不是组件间独立可加收益，未报告多训练seed/误差区间，也不能外推RB-Y1同量收益。RLDX-1-Img换骨干后域内53.6→60.7、OOD0→40.3，支持方法不只对π0.5有效；附录细节为训练2.4B/6.9B参数，不能照其概括句写成所有参数均解冻。

findings.title: 动作标签可执行性有仿真对照，但腕修正不是每任务都更好
findings.text: 图4/表8在Isaac Lab复刻OpenArm三PnP任务，物体从深度/双目测得初始位置并对首帧核准，每任务同22个视频、共66次开环回放，不通过策略闭环。直接重定向23/66=34.8%，IDM无腕校正42/66=63.6%，完整46/66=69.7%。完整Bottle/Box/Ball为17/14/15，无腕校正14/16/12：腕修正虽提高总平均，Box由16/22降至14/22，不能宣称逐任务必然改善。该对照支持比直接重定向更可执行的动作标签，不验证真实接触力、七OOD标签真值或全部实机可执行性。

findings.title: 约三分之一只比较采集人时，合成与本体训练另有成本
findings.text: 核图6/表9–10：四PnP独立成本实验各任务28次共112次，50遥操作/任务用5.26人时、53/112=47.3%；100人视频/任务用1.87人时、58/112=51.8%，人时为35.6%约三分之一，但未作非劣性/置信区间验证。不是同演示数比较：50人视频/任务0.93人时仅35.7%。成本模型为两人遥操作38例/人时、一人拍摄214例/人时；等量新增50人视频使混合达71.4%，采集多0.93人时。此实验只训练四PnP，与主表含七OOD的750例混合不能混用。表6一段15秒演示单H100各阶段134+173+150+150+22+66秒，按表值相加695秒约11.6分钟，是推算的离线处理时间，不是实时能力。预训练机器人语料、四H100/H200模型训练、算费与设备成本不在人时横轴，不能改写为总费用或从零建本体仅三分之一。

findings.title: 通过重定时改变策略速度，但存在质量代价
findings.text: 表2在OpenArm用同关键帧重采样骨架流再生成视频：原始人速度约1.25×，域内/OOD75.9/73.0、PnP均时11.9s；匹配遥操作1×后85.7/70.4、13.8s；2×后57.1/42.9、7.4s。遥操作基线47.3/3.1、14.2s。速度处理可调训练动作节奏，而不是让策略免费加速；未报告完成时长的失败/截尾口径和统计区间，不能把均时直接换成稳定吞吐倍数。分阶段调速还依赖任务动作阶段和遥操作阶段平均速度，非任意人视频自动可行性修复。

findings.title: 视觉嵌入更近与梯度更一致，是诊断而非物理正确性证明
findings.text: 图3/表7各抽5000帧，SigLIP特征至真实机器人域Fréchet距离：人125.5、遮罩129.0、覆盖渲染58.2、RoboTryOn32.7。真实参考仅四PnP，合成包含11任务，另有域内/七OOD分层26.6/41.9，UMAP仅可视化。图5在相同π0.5初始权重上算损失梯度，全部参数cosine为0.53对Masquerade0.17、EgoMimic0.14，动作expert0.51对−0.03/−0.05。每方法使用各自归一化统计，且是该初始化/数据采样的局部诊断，不能归为无混杂的因果机制或已证明融合梯度必然泛化。和遥操作手动作分布相近也不保证新技能成功，需与实机及标签回放证据合读。

findings.title: 固定相机与本体可达性限定复用，细接触是明确失败边界
findings.text: 人视频从机器人头相机位置拍，训练颈部与底座固定，IDM只预测固定颈/底座；移动视角的野外自我中心视频超出当前分布。依赖相机标定、双目与手重建精度，不能恢复力，也不能修复超出可达空间或手形能力的演示。图15有透明杯消失、手指穿把手、IDM闭手位置偏差；RB-Y1 Air Fryer0与未见细粒度插指抓握及长手指推走物体相联系。两本体桌面策略验证之外，GR-1仅生成视频，无该机策略执行证据。每任务28次且缺多seed统计，原始评分/训练材料本轮未审计；作者实验未复现，不能据生成样例推广任意本体、移动操作、紧配合插接或力控任务。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：同等新增本体先验预算下，接触多样性是否比追加PnP更有效？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在同等新增机器人先验采集与训练预算下，增加跨物体细粒度接触/抓握方式，比追加普通PnP更能降低IDM手关节标注错误并提高未见细接触任务的完整成功率。仅公开仿真研究草案：固定双臂灵巧手、相机、基础生成器/IDM、VLA初始化和人示范，选择公开可构建的把手插指/盖合等任务，按整物体与抓握类型划分训练和测试；全部测试任务的人视频相同，禁止用其机器人标签训练。新增本体先验分为相等例数/时长的通用PnP、接触多样抓握与无新增三组，模型大小、更新步数、合成次数与采样策略一致，并设仅几何校正对照；新增先验只更新生成器/IDM，不直接给下游策略目标任务机器人演示。至少3个独立训练seed、每任务50个配对初始场景，同时报告整任务二元成功、按手半分的原论文分数、接触前后关节/腕误差、穿透/物体消失率、不同抓握的失败分布，以及包含先验采集、训练、合成和人工筛查的总成本。用独立仿真关节与接触标签评估伪动作，标签只用于评估不泄入训练；若仿真有效，仍须另行验证真实双目与接触迁移，不能声称已解决实机问题。若效果仅来自更大更新量、测试抓握泄漏、视觉相似度提升而动作/完整成功不改善，或等总成本下不胜通用PnP，则推翻接触多样先验更具任务外价值的假设。实验未执行，未创建选题，未全面查新，不宣称研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: 先把人视频换成机器人视频，再用IDM与腕位校正补动作
frontier_brief.change_type: 新任务演示合成与动作标注
frontier_brief.delta: 自回归生成机器人关键帧，以手骨架流插值全视频，再用跨本体IDM标手关节动作、以重建腕平移作IK校正；策略训练用合成演示，部署直接看原始相机图像。
frontier_brief.before: 固定机位人视频经直接手重定向加遮罩/渲染，视觉与可执行抓握仍有差距；新任务灵巧手遥操作人时昂贵。
frontier_brief.after: 两本体七OOD任务加入合成数据，平均归一化得分约2.1%→60.0%；只用合成数据训练策略约44.4%。新任务不用机器人演示，但生成器/IDM已有8.82小时跨本体机器人先验。
frontier_brief.relevance: 适合已拥有本体先验与固定标定相机、需要扩充桌面灵巧手任务的采集决策；可降低任务级人时，需同时预算离线合成算力与精细接触验证。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者实验未复现；每任务28次，双臂每手完成各0.5，60%不是整项双臂任务完全成功率。基线为作者复现扩展，生成器有额外机器人先验；移动相机、力/紧插接不支持，RB-Y1 Air Fryer仍0%。GR-1仅视频展示。
frontier_brief.question: 等新增本体先验与总合成预算下，接触多样抓握能否比追加PnP改善未见精细任务的动作标注与完整成功率？

evidence.label: 任务级迁移
evidence.context: 表1/11，π0.5，同30k步，每任务28次；200遥操作+550合成/本体。七OOD各50人视频、无该任务机器人演示；双臂含按手半分，平均约60%。

evidence.label: 区分运动与定位贡献
evidence.context: 表3/13，OpenArm七OOD平均分，其他设置保持；支持运动条件与几何校正重要，未证明组件独立可加或对第二本体同幅有效。

evidence.label: 可执行标签对照
evidence.context: 表8，模拟OpenArm三PnP×22例；重定向对完整IDM标签，不是实机OOD回放。去腕校正63.6%，且Box腕修正反而16/22→14/22。

evidence.label: 人时与算力分开
evidence.context: 表9/10四PnP：50遥操作/任务47.3%对100人视频/任务51.8%，112试验；仅任务采集人时约三分之一。695秒由表6单H100各阶段相加，不含生成器训练、本体数据和算费。

evidence.label: 具名失败边界
evidence.context: 表11/附录F，插指抓把手超出标签精细度，WujiHand2长手指推物；生成还可出现透明杯消失/穿把手。不能由更真实画面推断接触正确。

mechanism.title: 共享机器人外观与动作先验
mechanism.text: 无配对人/机器人监督，先以机器人视频学习掩码与17点骨架接口。跨本体共享模型仍已见过相应机器人语料，参考图选择已有本体。

mechanism.title: 分离场景一致性与动作标注
mechanism.text: 前关键帧作自回归参考、后关键帧锁物体与场景、骨架流约束帧间运动；IDM从生成视图读动作，再校正腕平移，保留生成手形的抓握先验。

mechanism.title: 把新任务采集移到固定机位人视频
mechanism.text: 合成与真实演示可同格式训练，部署无需遮罩/覆盖编辑；伪状态为动作延迟构造，且无力标签。采集人时节省换来算力和校准需求。

attention.reason: 相对机器人示范的局部增广，跨本体视频生成与动作标注可能改变新任务采集路线；迁移有同训练步比较，不能忽略生成先验和分手计分。

impact.comparison: 相对机器人示范的局部增广，跨本体视频生成与动作标注可能改变新任务采集路线；迁移有同训练步比较，不能忽略生成先验和分手计分。

attention.headline: RoboTryOn：从人视频合成机器人演示与动作
attention.summary: 把人类示范视频中的人换成目标机器人，再推断动作标签，用于训练新任务策略；生成和动作标注模型的额外成本仍需核对。

passages.text: arXiv:2610.28480v1 [cs.RO] 20 Oct 2026 SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model Qiayuan Liao Yiyang Shao∗ Junfeng Long∗ Kevin Zakka Roberto Horowitz Pieter Abbeel† Koushil Sreenath† UC Berkeley https://supermimic.github.io > 1000×fewer GPU-h 128 L40 GPUs, 168 h [1] World-Model Rollout 1 H100 GPU, 3 h Figure 1: A learned differentiable world model trains a humanoid whole-body controller and reduces GPU-hours by more than 1000×versus cluster-scale model-free reinforcement learn- ing (§4.1). Left: the policy improves through imagined rollouts of the world model. Right: 128 L40

GPUs train for 168 h in SONIC [1], against one H100 for 3 h in this work. Abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many mo- tions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all mo- tions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, Su- perMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than 1000×and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline.

After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model’s prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion- tracking scaling laws. Keywords: Humanoid Robot, Whole-Body Control, Model-Based Reinforce- ment Learning 1 Introduction Humanoid robots hold the promise of operating in environments designed for people, but doing so requires whole-body controllers that span diverse human motion, from locomotion and dance to crouching and balance recovery. Physics-based motion imitation addresses this by training RL *Equal contribution. †Equal advising. 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin TX, USA.

policies to track reference motion clips [2] drawn from large motion-capture (mocap) datasets [1]. Existing systems scale this idea either by distilling many clip-specific experts into one controller [3] or by training a generalist policy over a large motion library [1]. In both cases, a more diverse motion library produces a more capable controller. But both also become computationally expensive as motion coverage grows: the state-of-the-art tracker SONIC [1], for example, trains for∼168 h on 128 GPUs, totaling roughly 21,000 GPU-hours. Although reference motions differ, they share the same humanoid hybrid rigid-body dynamics. Model-free RL fails to explicitly model this shared structure, instead repeatedly estimating action consequences from noisy simulator rollouts. Scaling to more motions therefore amounts to scaling up compute. SuperMimic addresses this inefficiency with a single learned, differentiable world model fit from logged simulator transitions. Backpropagation-through-time (BPTT) through short imagined roll- outs provides analytic policy gradients through the learned model, allowing one dynamics model to amortize learning across the entire mocap library. Because these gradients come from the learned model rather than from differentiating the simulator, SuperMimic remains compatible with rigid-

body simulators, including those with non-smooth contacts and non-differentiable implementations. On one GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the normalized return of SONIC’s released checkpoint within 3 h and reduces GPU-hours by more than 1000×(§4.1). On a 129,514-motion benchmark, Super- Mimic fails on 25 motions after 3 h on one GPU and on none after 9.8 h on two GPUs, against 179 for SONIC’s released checkpoint (Appendix F). Across a 264×increase in dataset length, the world model’s prediction error stays stable and SuperMimic’s compute to a fixed return grows slowly. The learned policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1. In a preliminary study of downstream interfaces, an RL-trained velocity encoder outperforms a distillation baseline. Contributions. • Model-based RL (MBRL) for deployable humanoid control. We demonstrate that BPTT through a learned, differentiable world model can train whole-body tracking policies in a set- ting long dominated by model-free proximal policy optimization (PPO) [4], and that the resulting controller transfers to a physical Unitree G1. • Compute is no longer the bottleneck to scaling. SuperMimic surpasses the return of SONIC, a

cluster-scale PPO pipeline, on a single GPU and reduces GPU-hours by more than 1000×(§4.1). Its training cost grows slowly as the motion library expands, making scaling humanoid whole- body control practical without huge GPU infrastructure. • An analysis of the ingredients behind the gains. We identify three world-model properties behind the compute reduction: prediction error that stays stable over a 264×increase in dataset length, rollouts more than 10×faster than the simulator, and analytic gradients, with which the policy reaches the best return of PPO on the world model with about 64×fewer imagined steps. • RL-trained downstream control beyond distillation. As a preliminary study, the same learned world model trains a downstream goal encoder on the interface’s own task reward. On velocity commands, the policy tracks more accurately with this encoder than with a distillation baseline. 2 Related Work Large-scale physics-based motion tracking. Physics-based motion imitation learns controllers that reproduce reference motions under contact-rich rigid-body dynamics. DeepMimic [2] demonstrated expressive character skills through model-free reinforcement learning, and PHC [11] extended this

paradigm to large motion sets with robust recovery. SONIC [1] further demonstrated that scaling motion data, policy capacity, and training compute produces generalist controllers that transfer to humanoid hardware. These results establish motion tracking as a practical route to broad whole- body behavior coverage. However, training these large-scale motion trackers requires extensive simulator rollouts and substantial computation. SuperMimic addresses this bottleneck by learning a differentiable dynamics model shared across all motions, so policy improvement can exploit analytic gradients rather than model-free rollout estimates. 2

The Mimic, Latent, and Downstream columns indicate the training strategy used at each stage. Task signal is what trains the downstream interface: its own task reward (RL) or a reference-tracking signal (Distill). Merged cells denote jointly trained stages, while adjacent unmerged cells indicate

sequential training, with each stage trained after freezing the previous one. SVG(0): stochastic value gradients; BC: offline behavior cloning on fixed expert rollouts, as opposed to DAgger’s student rollouts; CGD: classifier guidance diffusion; A2C: advantage actor–critic; DAg- ger: dataset aggregation. 1Behavior cloning with a one-step next-state consistency term through a frozen, learned dynamics model. 2Goal encoders train jointly with the tracker on the motion-tracking reward and latent-alignment losses; no task-specific reward. Learned differentiable dynamics for motion control. SuperTrack [12] optimizes motion-control policies through a learned differentiable surrogate of the simulator. ControlVAE [6] jointly learns a dynamics model, latent skill representation, and generative controller, while MoConVQ [13] extends learned-model training to discrete motion representations over tens of hours of data. SuperDyno [14] scales differentiable neural dynamics to tens of thousands of motion clips. These methods establish the effectiveness of learned dynamics and analytic policy gradients for scalable simulated-character control. SuperMimic extends this direction to single-GPU training of a large-scale humanoid tracker and to its sim-to-real deployment: its world model conditions on simulator context, while the de-

ployed actor uses noisy proprioceptive observations and a goal input (§3.2). We evaluate how model accuracy, rollout throughput, and differentiable policy updates contribute to training efficiency, and how prediction error behaves as motion coverage grows (§4.1–4.2), and demonstrate physical de- ployment of the resulting controller (§4.4). Model-based policy optimization and robot deployment. Dreamer [15] and DreamerV3 [16] learn latent dynamics for imagination-based actor–critic learning, while TD-MPC [17] combines short-horizon planning with terminal-value prediction. DayDreamer [18] demonstrates world-model learning directly on physical robots. SHAC [19] uses differentiable simulation for short-horizon actor–critic updates, motivating SuperMimic’s critic-bootstrapped objective. Analytic-gradient robot control can also combine a simplified differentiable surrogate with a high-fidelity forward simulator, as demonstrated for quadruped locomotion [20]. SuperMimic learns its surrogate from simulator transitions and backpropagates through short imagined rollouts, retaining compatibility with standard rigid-body simulators. RWM [21] and RWM-U [22] demonstrate that policies trained in learned neural simulators can trans-

fer to physical robots. Both optimize policies using PPO on imagined rollouts; RWM-U additionally uses uncertainty-penalized offline optimization. SuperMimic instead optimizes the policy by differ- entiating the return through its learned dynamics. RWM and RWM-U pretrain the world model on trajectories from other policies. In contrast, SuperMimic fits its world model during training on data its own policy collects. Reusable motion representations and downstream control. Reusable controllers connect mo- tion tracking to downstream goal interfaces (Table 1). NPMP [5] and PhysicsVAE [7] learn latent motor representations from expert behavior; PULSE [8] and LATENT [10] use learned motion rep- resentations for downstream reinforcement learning. It captures the shared humanoid dynamics in a differentiable world model and improves the policy through short imagined rollouts. Training alternates between

three phases in one loop (Figure 2). First, the current policy collects simulator transitions into a replay buffer. Second, we fit the differentiable world model to short replay windows. Third, the policy is improved by backpropagating an imagined return through the frozen world model, with each rollout seeded from a replay-buffer state in the Dyna style [23, 24]. The buffer, model, and policy are updated throughout training, so dynamics learning and control improve together rather than in separate stages (Algorithm A.1, Appendix D). Transitions from earlier policies remain valid for fitting the world model, because the dynamics do not depend on the policy that collected them. We denote the goal-conditioned partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) by M and use compact notation with state st, goal gt, and action at. State st gives the proprioceptive observation ot and the termination dt, which is 1 if st is terminal. Action at in state st yields the reward rt+1 and the next state st+1. The policy is deterministic, at = πθ(ot,gt), and at parameterizes a normalized joint setpoint; for motion tracking, gt is read from a reference motion. During data collection, the simulator executes the noisy action at + ϵt with action noise ϵt ∼ρϵ, and the replay buffer stores this executed noisy action. The noise widens the range of actions on

which the world model is fit; it serves only the model fit and is optional. Returns use a soft survival weight, c0 = 1 and ct+1 = ct(1−dt+1), giving J(θ) = E[ t≥0 γtctrt+1] with discount γ ∈[0,1). The simulator logs hard terminations, while the learned model predicts a termination probability ˆ dt ∈ [0,1], which keeps the survival weight differentiable in imagined rollouts. Throughout, a hat marks the world-model counterpart of a simulator quantity. We also factor the observation as 4

¯ ot = ot + ηt, with¯ ot the noise-free observation and known observation noise ηt ∼ρη sampled outside the world model. Appendix A gives the full spaces and reward. The default interface is full-reference motion tracking. Other goal interfaces, such as velocity, share the same learned dynamics and train jointly with motion tracking (Appendix B). 3.2 Learning a differentiable world model The simulator’s articulated multi-rigid-body dynamics are known, but the simulator need not provide gradients, so SuperMimic learns a differentiable surrogate to obtain policy gradients: it supplies the predictions and Jacobians for the BPTT update in §3.3. The resulting analytic policy gradient is the gradient of a surrogate for the expected return in simulation. Since the simulator’s randomness has known sources, the world model stays deterministic: it conditions on the per-episode sim context ξ (friction, calibration offsets, and torso center-of-mass) and predicts the noise-free observation¯

The critic Vψ estimates the return beyond step H, so the model must be accurate only within these H steps. This imagination horizon exceeds the k-step replay windows on which we fit the model (§3.2). In practice, the learned model remains stable over indefinitely long rollouts, because the k-step autoregressive fit trains it to correct its own prediction errors. The policy and critic updates together form a short-horizon actor–critic in the spirit of SHAC [19], which backpropagates through a differentiable simulator. SuperMimic replaces SHAC’s hard episode termination with the survival weightˆ ct, and its critic has no exponential-moving-average target network. Prior motion-tracking controllers trained with analytic gradients often omit a critic and optimize only the H-step reward sum [12, 6]. Without a critic, training can reach a similar nominal tracking return, but this unbootstrapped objective is more myopic. The critic matters after perturbations, where recovery or balance rewards can lie beyond the imagination window (§4.3). 4 Experimental Results We show that SuperMimic scales favorably relative to PPO pipelines, identify the world-model properties behind this scaling, demonstrate transfer on a real Unitree G1, and report a preliminary study of downstream goal interfaces. The simulator is MuJoCo Warp, a GPU implementation of MuJoCo [26]. All our reported costs are measured on NVIDIA H100 (80 GB SXM5) GPUs of Lambda on-demand instances. We ran several random seeds and found training very stable, which

we attribute to the dense reward that motion tracking gives at every step. The figures therefore do not report seed variation. Normalized return, return for short, is the undiscounted sum of the per-step reward over the full episode, divided by the largest value this sum can take. A policy that terminates early therefore scores low. 4.1 SuperMimic reaches SONIC-level tracking with far fewer GPU-hours We compare against SONIC, a published PPO pipeline trained on a 128-GPU cluster. Both methods build on the BeyondMimic motion-tracking formulation [3], making SONIC the closest available published comparison. Within 3 h on one GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the normalized return of the released SONIC checkpoint (Figure 3(a)). On a shared benchmark of 129,514 motions, it also fails on fewer motions than SONIC: 25 after 3 h on one GPU and 0 after 9.8 h on two GPUs, against 179 for SONIC’s released checkpoint (Appendix F). We state the 3 h conservatively: from then on, every checkpoint is ahead of SONIC by at least half of the gap between SONIC and SuperMimic’s best result, in both return and failed motions. SuperMimic thus uses more than 50×less wall-clock time and more than 1000×fewer GPU-hours than SONIC.

One model amortizes the motion library. In Figure 3(c), the world model’s 8-step prediction error stays between 0.007 and 0.011 as the dataset grows from 1 to 264 h. Every motion is executed by the same humanoid, so added clips supply more evidence about the shared body and contact dynamics rather than demanding new capacity. This is consistent with the slow growth of the compute needed to reach the target return (§4.1). Imagination accelerates rollouts. During policy optimization, rollout speed sets the update cost. Without the critic, training fails at H ≤16. With it, H=16 matches the critic-free H=32, and H=32 reaches a return of 0.82 fastest. Raising H from 64 to 128 nearly triples the time to that return and lowers the final return; H=128 is the longest horizon that fits on an H100. At matched return, the critic still changes behavior. Under 0.5–4 m/s velocity pushes while holding a static T-pose in simulation, the critic policy settles within 0.5–2.4 s.

The critic-free policy never settles: it keeps stumbling even at 0.5 m/s and falls at 4 m/s. 4.4 Real-robot transfer One general motion tracker deploys on a real Unitree G1 without per-motion tuning (Figure 6). The four motions cover locomotion (a skipping jump), contact-rich whole-body motion with the torso and limbs on the floor (a side roll), and acrobatics (a 90◦flip and an in-place 360◦flip). 4.5 Downstream tasks: RL encoder vs. distillation baseline SuperMimic trains downstream goal encoders jointly with the motion-tracking interface, sharing one decoder and world model (Appendix B). Our study of downstream interfaces is preliminary. We train one velocity encoder on a velocity-tracking reward through the world model. We compare it with a distillation baseline: a velocity encoder trained on the motion-tracking reward, with commands read from the reference motions. Figure 7 evaluates both on 672 step responses spanning the velocity space (Appendix G). The RL encoder has the lower steady-state error on 650 of them, and the distillation encoder on 15. Only the distillation encoder falls, on seven fast turns with almost no motion-library data.

5 Conclusion SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control. A single learned, differentiable world model captures the dynamics every motion shares, and backpropagation-through-time through it amortizes a whole dataset into one policy. The policy trains on a single GPU, surpasses the return of a policy trained on a 128-GPU cluster, and transfers to a real Unitree G1. We train the velocity encoder concurrently with the motion tracker, but the velocity-tracking reward updates only the velocity encoder and not the shared decoder (Appendix B). Concurrent training is therefore the same as training the velocity encoder after the motion tracker, and might not be necessary. Whether concurrent training helps once the velocity-tracking reward also updates the decoder is untested. • Simulator-only dynamics. The world model learns only from simulator transitions. Real-robot data could refine it, and its differentiability could support system identification.
• No terrain or object interaction. SuperMimic trains only on flat ground. Extending it to terrain and object interaction is ongoing work. 9

Return-based reset sampling. Simulator episodes reset to points of the motion library, favor- ing those where the policy currently earns low return. The motion timeline is divided into 1 s bins, and each bin b keeps a running estimate Gb of the discounted return from it, updated on the policy’s own rollouts. Resets mix three distributions: 50% uniform over bins, 40% from softmaxb(−25 Gb/Gmax), where Gmax is the largest attainable discounted return, and 10% in pro- portion to each bin’s past softmax weight, so a hard motion keeps some practice after it is learned. G Velocity-command task G.1 Training setup The velocity encoder of §4.5 maps the command (vx,vy,ωz) and a feature of the last 10 frames of oto the shared latent. Each encoder is trained from scratch in its own run, jointly with the motion-tracking interface, for 100,000 iterations. Both runs use a walking and running library filtered from LAFAN1 and BONES- SEED. Half of the 4096 simulator environments and half of each imagined batch use the velocity interface, so p(I) is uniform; unlike Algorithm A.1, which samples one interface per update, each imagined batch mixes both. Commands. The command gt = (vx,vy,ωz) stacks the target planar root velocity in the heading (yaw-only) frame and the target world-frame yaw rate. A reference command is the centered 25- frame mean of the reference root velocity in the reference’s heading frame. For the RL encoder,

each environment resamples its command source at every reset and every 250 control steps (5 s): with probability 0.5 it reads the command from the reference clip at every step, and otherwise it holds a command drawn uniformly from vx ∈[−1.5,2] m/s, vy ∈[−1.32,1.32] m/s and ωz ∈ [−3.35,3.35] rad/s, zeroed (standing) with probability 0.1. 18

Encoder. Velocity rollouts of the RL encoder use the velocity-tracking reward and a fall-only termination (Table A.6); those of the distillation baseline use the motion- tracking reward and termination of Appendix A. The relative steady-state error is the norm of the mean velocity error over the last 2 s, divided by the norm of the command, with the root velocity measured in the heading frame. The per-command value is the median over the trials that did not fall. analysis.overview: 把大规模全身动作跟踪从纯仿真采样的 PPO 更新，改为共享可微世界模型上的短时域解析梯度更新。价值在于训练预算和方法路线发生明显变化；作者结果仍需独立复现。
analysis.notice: 已完整读取 19 页提取文字，并目视核对第 7、8、18 页的图 3–5、表 A.8。未运行代码或真机复现；官网当前提供论文与演示，训练代码可用性仍需核实。

findings.title: 训练预算限制动作库扩展
findings.text: 既有路线以单动作专家蒸馏或大规模 model-free RL 训练通用跟踪器；不同动作共享的机体动力学没有被显式复用，扩展动作库伴随高采样成本。

findings.title: 在共同动力学上复用梯度
findings.text: 循环收集仿真转移、用 8 步自回归窗口拟合模型，再固定模型权重，通过 32 步想象轨迹反传策略梯度；critic 接续时域外价值。模型持续更新，梯度不穿过刚体仿真器。

findings.title: 受控对照支持训练方法收益
findings.text: LAFAN1 的 40 个动作、2.45 小时数据上，作者匹配观察、奖励、终止、随机化、网络规模与评测。单 GPU SuperMimic 在 1.2 小时达到 0.82；PPO-Sim 在 18 小时预算内未达到，1/4/8 GPU 最终为 0.60/0.70/0.72。图 5 的 PPO-WM 消融另支持解析梯度收益。

findings.title: 集群对照与训练集覆盖
findings.text: 作者报告 1 张 H100、3 小时完整训练循环超过 SONIC 已发布策略的归一化回报；对照训练预算为 128 张 L40、168 小时，硬件与数据量不同。129,514 个训练动作的失败数为 179→25，2 张 H100、9.8 小时为 0；真机展示一个通用策略执行四类动作。

findings.title: 覆盖结果不能代替泛化结论
findings.text: 失败数评测使用训练动作、确定性物理、固定摩擦且关闭随机化和观测噪声；终止口径取自 SuperMimic。训练限于平地，尚未覆盖地形和物体交互。主要图未提供种子方差，下游接口实验每种策略仅一个训练种子。

hypotheses.title: 先验证训练收益能否保留到新动作
hypotheses.text: 共享动力学的训练收益可能延伸到未见动作。固定 G1、GPU、数据时长和奖励，对比 PPO-Sim、世界模型上 PPO、BPTT+critic；按动作类别划分训练/留出集，记录达到目标回报的 GPU 小时、留出集失败率和模型误差。若预算收益只存在于训练动作，或留出失败率明显恶化，则推翻可迁移收益假设。

frontier_brief.title: SuperMimic：用可微世界模型把全身控制训练压到单卡 3 小时
frontier_brief.change_type: 训练路线变化 · 全身控制
frontier_brief.delta: 把策略更新移到共享的可微世界模型里：仿真采集、模型拟合与短轨迹反传交替进行，利用解析梯度降低训练预算。
frontier_brief.before: 通用动作跟踪主要依赖仿真中的 model-free PPO，或训练多个专家后蒸馏；扩展动作库需要大量采样。
frontier_brief.after: 同一动力学模型覆盖动作库，固定模型后反传 32 步想象回报，以 critic 接续远期价值；每轮继续更新模型。
frontier_brief.relevance: 为缺少大集群的实验室提供值得优先复现的全身控制训练路线；优先对照受控 PPO-Sim 实验，再判断是否迁移到自己的动作数据和算力条件。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者实验，未独立复现。H100 与 L40 对照硬件和数据量不同；零失败衡量训练动作覆盖。仍需仿真采样，地形与物体交互尚未验证。
frontier_brief.question: 在你的固定算力和留出动作集上，共享动力学加解析梯度还能保留多少训练预算收益？

evidence.context: 129,514 个训练动作；SONIC 发布策略、SuperMimic 单卡 3 小时、双卡 9.8 小时；表 A.8。衡量覆盖，不是留出集泛化。

mechanism.title: 共享动力学
mechanism.text: 由当前策略采集仿真转移，拟合包含随机化上下文的可微动力学。

mechanism.title: 解析策略梯度
mechanism.text: 通过固定权重的世界模型反传短时域回报，降低随机采样策略梯度的成本。

mechanism.title: critic 接续
mechanism.text: 用 critic 补足想象窗口外回报；图 4 对照显示它支持更短时域。

Failure Prediction and Classification in Vision-Language-Action Models via Calibrated Latent Probing
Michal P. Podolinsky 1 Yunhao Yang 1 Daniel Little 2 Hong Lu 2 Rohan Siva 1 Olin Goudey 2 Neel P. Bhatt 3 Matthias Scheutz 2 Ufuk Topcu 1

Figure 1: We introduce VLA-Tug , a probe on the VLA backbone embeddings that predicts failures and their mode. (a) A recurrent encoder maps the embedding into a latent failure space; a score head and a calibrated trigger raise the alarm, and a mode head then predicts the failure mode. (b) VLA-Tug alarms before the failure, allowing early stopping or intervention by an expert model.

Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) enable general-purpose embodied intelligence, but their performance is brittle under distribution shift, where unanticipated failures can damage equipment or endanger people. Deploying VLAs in real-world systems therefore requires a runtime monitor that is timely , calibrated , and informative while being efficient enough to run on the edge. Existing methods fail to fulfill these requirements. We present VLA-Tug , a lightweight probe over the latent layers of a VLA backbone that improves early failure detection and bounds the missed-detection and false-alarm rates, with minimal inference overhead. We show that supervising on the pre-failure segment of a trajectory increases early failure detection at matched false-positive rates by up to 30 % 30\% over the strongest learned baseline. Under shift to unseen tasks, the bounds on missed-detection and false-alarm rates remain valid in up to 86 % 86\% of runs, versus at most 21 % 21\% for baselines. Unlike existing methods, VLA-Tug predicts the failure mode to enable corrective actions, raising top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44 % 44\% over a majority baseline. VLA-Tug enables real-time monitoring where the well-timed and informative probe supports lightweight steering that improves task success. We release a dataset of 3,180 3{,}180 annotated manipulation episodes to support future work on latent failure detection in VLAs at vla-tug.github.io .

Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) ; Physical Intelligence et al. (2026) ; NVIDIA et al. (2025) are strong candidates for general-purpose embodied intelligence. By pairing a VLM backbone pre-trained on internet-scale data with an action expert fine-tuned on demonstration trajectories, they excel at complex dexterous tasks such as tightening screws or assembling cardboard boxes. Yet their performance is brittle and can degrade significantly under distribution shift, such as changes in lighting, novel textures, or rare object combinations Wang et al. (2026) ; Fei et al. (2025) . A VLA can therefore fail unexpectedly, especially as task and environment novelty increases, and such failures can be costly, damaging materials and robots, or outright dangerous to humans. This brittleness has slowed the adoption of VLAs in factories, homes, and public spaces.

Among multiple solutions, one solution that the robotics community is exploring is VLA steering. The idea of steering comes from research on LLMs, where activations are selectively modified to nudge a model towards a desired output Turner et al. (2024) . Steering VLAs is particularly interesting because it can unlock behaviors that cannot be reached through prompting alone Buurmeijer et al. (2026) ; Swann et al. (2026) . Various steering methods have recently been proposed ( Li et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2026 ; Swann et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ; Jeong et al., 2026 ; Li, 2025 ) , but they rarely use a calibrated probe to decide when to steer. Some steer continuously Li et al. (2026b) ; Liu et al. (2026a) ; Cui et al. (2026) , some rely on human-specified offline triggers Swann et al. (2026) ; Li (2025) , and others are gated by a one-sided calibrated trigger Tan et al. (2026) ; Jeong et al. (2026) . Overall, they lack an efficient and principled trigger that would make them deployable in real-world systems.

Research on failure detection for VLAs is becoming increasingly mainstream Gu et al. (2025) ; Agia et al. (2024) ; Ma et al. (2026) ; Huang et al. (2026) . In a nutshell, these methods compute a failure score from signals available in the VLA, often its latent variables Gu et al. (2025) or predicted actions Agia et al. (2024) ; Huang et al. (2026) ; Ma et al. (2026) , that encode how likely the policy is to fail at the current task. A detection threshold is then calibrated to give probabilistic guarantees on the detector’s performance Gu et al. (2025) . However, these guarantees often cover only the false-positive rate (FPR), i.e. the rate of successes misclassified as failures, and not a target true-positive rate (TPR), i.e. the rate of correctly classified failures, which is arguably even more important in safety-critical settings where a single failure could harm a person or damage costly equipment. These methods are also seldom evaluated systematically against ground-truth failure times, which we argue is crucial to assess whether they can prevent failures before they happen and thus enable VLA steering. Finally, they cannot predict failure modes (grasping, pushing, opening), so steering cannot be targeted towards the root cause and would require human interventions.

We argue that steering would be best supported by a probe that is (T.) timely , detecting failures before they occur; (I.) informative , outputting semantic information beyond a numerical score; (C.) calibrated , achieving the desired error rates; and (E.) efficient to train, calibrate, and deploy.

We address this with VLA-Tug 1 1 1 Like a tugboat beside the vessel it guides, the probe is small next to the policy it monitors and acts only when needed. , a well-behaved probe designed to support VLA steering in the real world. We train VLA-Tug on the latent layers of two VLAs Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) ; NVIDIA et al. (2025) using 228 distinct tasks in two simulation environments and 8 real-world tasks, and evaluate it against ground-truth failure times. We show that supervision should focus on the pre-failure part of the trajectory to improve early failure detection, and that calibrating the detection threshold to guarantee both TPR and FPR simultaneously yields guarantees that hold far more often, including on unseen tasks. Building on these findings, we propose a real-time architecture that incorporates VLA-Tug to autonomously support the detection and prevention of VLA failures. Our contributions are as follows:

VLA-Tug : A timely, informative, and efficient probe for early failure detection. On unseen tasks, our probe improves the area under the early-detection curve by up to 30 % 30\% over the strongest learned baseline. VLA-Tug also predicts the failure mode, raising the top-3 accuracy on unseen tasks by up to 44 % 44\% over a majority baseline, at under 1 1 ms per step.

Guarantees on false alarms and missed detections. We certify FPR and TPR early {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}} targets jointly; both held in every certified run, compared to 57 57 – 71 % 71\% of runs for baselines. Under distribution shift to unseen tasks, the false-alarm target still held in 40 40 – 86 % 86\% of certified runs, compared to 0 0 – 21 % 21\% for baselines.

A deployable failure-monitoring system. Through real-world experiments, we demonstrate that integrating the timely failure predictions and associated modes with steering strategies can lead to enhanced success rates.
An annotated VLA failure dataset. We release a dataset of ≈ \approx 289k policy-step VLA backbone embeddings from annotated 3,180 3{,}180 episodes of diverse tasks.

Existing methods can detect failures, but their alarms are not necessarily timely, informative, or sufficiently calibrated. Our method addresses these limitations through failure-aware representations, onset-based detection, and joint statistical guarantees.

Existing VLA failure detectors leverage different signals to identify potential failures, including external assessments from world models or LLM judges ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ) , action consistency across sampled or consecutive action chunks ( Agia et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , distributional deviations in policy inputs, outputs, or embeddings ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2025 ) , and internal policy representations ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Rajaprakash et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Chen, 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ; Francis-Meretzki et al., 2026 ) .

These approaches have three key limitations. (1) Detection performance is commonly evaluated at fixed time points using metrics such as AUROC or balanced accuracy ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , without explicitly measuring whether alarms precede the actual failure onset. Moreover, supervision ranges from episode-level failure labels assigned to all timesteps ( Gu et al., 2025 ) , to heuristic or human-refined timestep labels ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , to failure-free training ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , without explicitly accounting for the timing of failures. (2) Most detectors produce scalar risk scores without identifying the underlying failure modes. While semantic supervision and representation interpretability have been explored for embodied policies ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Swann et al., 2026 ; Buurmeijer et al., 2026 ) , they do not directly establish informative failure alarms. (3) Existing calibration methods typically control a single criterion. Conformal methods provide false-positive guarantees for sequential failure detection ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Rajaprakash et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ) , calibrate anomaly or failure scores ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) , or provide guarantees for one-shot policy compliance and embodied decision making ( Yang et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Bhatt et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025b ) . However, these guarantees do not jointly account for false alarms and timely failure detection.

We address these limitations by developing a failure detector that is timely, informative, and jointly calibrated . Following the internal-representation probing direction, we reuse the VLA’s latent representations and align them with failure-mode semantics, enabling the detector to identify both potential failures and their types. To evaluate timeliness, we measure detection relative to annotated failure onsets and investigate supervision strategies that explicitly account for when failures occur. To provide statistical guarantees, we adopt Learn-then-Test ( Angelopoulos et al., 2022 ) to jointly calibrate multiple detection criteria, including the false-positive rate (FPR) and early true-positive rate ( TPR early \mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}} ). Existing failure detectors primarily raise alarms without steering, while steering methods rely on predefined schedules or calibrated triggers. In contrast, to the best of our knowledge, VLA-Tug is the first framework to combine joint FPR and early-TPR calibration, failure-onset-aware evaluation, and failure-mode prediction for calibrated failure-triggered steering. In this section, we start by giving several broad definitions used to describe how failure detectors for VLAs function. Next, we give a mathematical formulation of our problem and then introduce how VLA-Tug addresses it.
To facilitate comparisons across methods, we give general definitions for the concepts of failure score, detection threshold, detection time, failure time, and failure mode.
Failure score. The score s t ∈ ℝ s_{t}\in\mathbb{R} , defined at every timestep t t , encodes the probe’s belief that the VLA is failing. It need not be a probability in the strict sense.
Detection threshold. The threshold h ⋆ h^{\star} over s t s_{t} separates failures from successes.
Detection time. The time t det = min ⁡ { t : s t ≥ h ⋆ } t_{\mathrm{det}}=\min\{t:s_{t}\geq h^{\star}\} is the first time the score crosses the threshold.

Failure time. The time t fail t_{\mathrm{fail}} , which we also call the failure onset, is when the policy makes an obvious mistake or its progress stalls to the point where an intervention, human or otherwise, is needed.
Failure mode. The label f mode f_{\mathrm{mode}} is a high-level semantic category assigned to each failure, such as grasping failure, placement failure, or no progress.

These definitions are general, and their exact form varies slightly across methods. The interpretation of s t s_{t} depends on the training strategy, but a higher score usually signals failure and a lower score success. The threshold h ⋆ h^{\star} may be fixed or vary with time, and it is often calibrated with probabilistic guarantees on a set of calibration rollouts 𝒟 cal {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}} . If s t < h ⋆ s_{t}<h^{\star} for all t t , the detection time t det t_{\mathrm{det}} is undefined, and the rollout raises no alarm. The failure time definition follows Gu et al. (2025) .

Consider a VLA policy 𝐟 VLA ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathbf{f}_{\text{VLA}}(\cdot) and a rollout τ i \tau_{i} of T T policy steps. At each policy step t ∈ { 1 , … , T } t\in\{1,\dots,T\} , 𝐟 VLA ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathbf{f}_{\text{VLA}}(\cdot) takes as input RGB observations 𝐨 t \mathbf{o}_{t} (agent and wrist cameras) and a natural language prompt 𝐩 \mathbf{p} , and produces a chunk of m m control actions 𝐚 t ; 0 : m − 1 \mathbf{a}_{t;0:m-1} . We denote the VLA’s internal embedding at step t t as 𝐞 t \mathbf{e}_{t} , so that τ i = { ( 𝐩 , 𝐨 t , 𝐞 t , 𝐚 t ; 0 : m − 1 ) } t = 1 T \tau_{i}=\{(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{o}_{t},\mathbf{e}_{t},\mathbf{a}_{t;0:m-1})\}_{t=1}^{T} . Each rollout has an episode-level label Y i ∈ { 0 , 1 } Y_{i}\in\{0,1\} , where Y i = 1 Y_{i}=1 marks a failure and Y i = 0 Y_{i}=0 a success. If Y i = 1 Y_{i}=1 , the rollout also has a failure time t fail {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t_{\mathrm{fail}}} and a failure mode f mode ∈ ℱ {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f_{\mathrm{mode}}}\in\mathcal{F} , where ℱ \mathcal{F} is a fixed taxonomy of failure modes.

Problem. Given a training set and a calibration set 𝒟 cal = { τ i } {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{cal}}}=\{\tau_{i}\} , and access to the internal embeddings 𝐞 t \mathbf{e}_{t} of 𝐟 VLA ​ ( ⋅ ) \mathbf{f}_{\text{VLA}}(\cdot) , predict an imminent task failure before it happens , i.e. t det ≤ t fail {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t_{\mathrm{det}}}\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t_{\mathrm{fail}}} where t det {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t_{\mathrm{det}}} is the detection time, and predict the failure mode f mode {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}f_{\mathrm{mode}}} in a manner that holds up empirically on tasks unseen during calibration.
We propose VLA-Tug , a probe that is trained and calibrated to detect failures before they happen. It is:
(T.) Timely. We propose a training and evaluation strategy that accounts for the failure time and improves early failure detection.

(C.) Calibrated. We introduce a risk formulation that jointly bounds the false-positive rate and the early miss rate 1 − TPR early 1-\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}} , and examine how well these targets hold on unseen tasks.
(I.) Informative. We design VLA-Tug to predict the failure mode, giving the semantic information needed to choose a corrective action.
(E.) Efficient. VLA-Tug adds minimal latency and parameters to the VLA, and is cheap to train and calibrate.
In this section we introduce VLA-Tug . In subsection 4.1 we present the probe and how we train it, and in subsection 4.2 we show how we calibrate its alarm threshold and what guarantees this gives.

passages.section: We train the probe to predict features that precede a failure.
passages.location: We train the probe to predict features that precede a failure.
passages.text: We hypothesize that training on post-failure embeddings teaches the probe what already failed trajectories look like, not what trajectories about to fail look like. If so, to predict failures the probe must be trained on the embeddings e t e_{t} before the failure time t fail t_{\mathrm{fail}} ( pre-onset supervision), rather than after it Ma et al. (2026) or at all times of failed rollouts Gu et al. (2025) . To test this, we compare four ways of labeling the embeddings of failed rollouts ( Figure 2 ; the mathematical formulation is in App. A.2 ). Successful rollouts are labeled 0 0 in all four. The window w w in onset and post-onset is the time span before t fail t_{\mathrm{fail}} that is labeled as failure. Pre-onset and onset truncate the rollout at the failure time, while post-onset and trajectory keep all steps. We exclude the steps after t fail t_{\mathrm{fail}} in the first two strategies instead of labeling them 0 0 : these embeddings already show a failed rollout, so labeling them as successes would give the probe contradicting training signals.

Where previous works only provided guarantees of false-positive rates (i.e. the rate of successful rollouts that were flagged as failures) ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Rajaprakash et al., 2026 ) , they did not provide guarantees on the false-negative rate (i.e. the rate of unsuccessful trajectories that were not flagged). In an effort to make these bounds interpretable to the practitioner, we compute the probability of failure given that a rollout was flagged.
