In this section, we answer five questions based on our problem formulation ( section 3 ): (Q1. Timeliness ) Does training on features that precede the failure onset improve early failure detection on unseen tasks ( subsection 6.1 )? (Q2. Calibration ) Can VLA-Tug jointly bound the FPR \mathrm{FPR} and TPR early {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}} , with bounds that hold on seen tasks and degrade gracefully on unseen tasks ( subsection 6.2 )? (Q3. Informativeness ) Can VLA-Tug predict the failure mode based on VLA backbone embeddings ( subsection 6.3 )? (Q4. Efficiency ) Are the cost and time of labeling, training, and inference appropriate for deployment in real-world systems ( subsection 6.4 )? (Q5. Steering ) Can VLA-Tug , as a timely, informative, calibrated, and efficient probe, support VLA steering ( subsection 6.5 )? We ablate our design choices in App. D.4 .

We evaluate VLA-Tug against a series of baselines using metrics that depend on the ground-truth failure time. Firstly, we describe how we split the data. Secondly, we review the baselines. Thirdly, we formally define our evaluation metrics. Lastly, we discuss the results.

For every run, we split the episodes as in Figure 4 . The training set fits the probe, the validation set selects the checkpoint, and the threshold is chosen on the calibration set. The calibration and held-out seen sets are exchangeable, and our guarantees apply to the held-out seen set. The unseen set, which the probe and the threshold never see, measures robustness to distribution shift. On LIBERO-X, the held-out tasks of the new-task and new-signature splits are the same for every seed, because they are defined by the semantic axis described in section 5 ; the seed changes only the shuffle of the seen episodes and the initialization. The new-skill folds and the LIBERO-10 seeds hold out different tasks.

Figure 4: Task- and episode-level data splits. Episodes from seen tasks are divided into training (65%), validation (15%), calibration (10%), and held-out seen (10%) sets. Unseen tasks form a separate evaluation set. Task-level proportions are schematic.
We consider the following baselines:
Embedding distance (Mahalanobis, Euclidean, PCA-KMeans). A step is scored by how much closer its backbone embedding is to failed than to successful training steps.
Action consistency (STAC, ActProbe, FailureSpot). Steps are scored based on the discrepancy between predicted and executed steps.
Latent (SAFE). A step is scored by a learned projection of its backbone embedding.

We evaluate VLA-Tug against three key metrics: TPR, TPR early {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}} , and FPR. Existing works often evaluate their methods against AUROC ( Gu et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) without accounting for the true failure times, making it hard to distinguish timely detections. The TPR \mathrm{TPR} and FPR \mathrm{FPR} follow their standard definitions. The TPR early {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}}} is the rate of failures detected before the failure time, i.e. t det ≤ t fail {\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t_{\mathrm{det}}}\leq{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}t_{\mathrm{fail}}} . We additionally define AUROC early \mathrm{AUROC}_{\mathrm{early}} as the area under the TPR early \mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}} - FPR \mathrm{FPR} curve. We compute it on the support FPR ∈ [ 0 , 0.4 ] \mathrm{FPR}\in[0,0.4] , normalized by its width 0.4 0.4 (reported in %), since a detector that raises false alarms on more than 40 % 40\% of successful rollouts is impractical to deploy. We formally define these metrics in App. C.1 .

We ask whether training on features that precede the failure onset improves early failure detection on unseen tasks. Our hypothesis is that it does: post-failure features only describe failures the probe has already seen, so training on them keeps it from learning a general notion of what leads to a failure, while features before the onset carry the cues that come before one. We compare VLA-Tug against the baselines in Table 3 and Figure 5 . On unseen tasks, our domain of interest, VLA-Tug is the best method in four of six settings: LIBERO-10 with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , new-signature , new-skill , and the real robot. Against SAFE-LSTM, the strongest learned baseline, its margin grows from − 𝟏 % \mathbf{-1\%} on new-task to + 𝟏𝟒 % \mathbf{+14\%} on new-signature and + 𝟑𝟎 % \mathbf{+30\%} on new-skill . On the real robot, the lead is small, and VLA-Tug does not lead on LIBERO-10 with GR00T. On seen tasks, the results are mixed. We ablate the label in App. D.4 : replacing the pre-onset label with the other variants lowers early detection on LIBERO-X.

Yes: for most unseen settings. Training on features that precede the failure onset lets VLA-Tug raise the alarm at or before the failure onset more often than the baselines, and on LIBERO-X the gap widens as the test tasks move away from the training tasks.

We validate the theoretical results from section 4 on seen tasks and examine how they hold under distribution shift on unseen tasks. We calibrate our probe with Learn-then-Test (LTT, δ = 0.1 \delta=0.1 ) at seven false-positive-rate (FPR) targets ( 10 10 to 50 % 50\% ), each certified together with a TPR early target, on the 14 LIBERO-X runs ( 3 3 new-task seeds, 3 3 new-signature seeds, and 8 8 new-skill folds). We compare against max conformal (MC) Agia et al. (2024) and functional conformal (FC) Gu et al. (2025) calibration (the complete table is in App. D.1 ). We draw three conclusions:

LTT bounds the TPR early \mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}} together with the FPR, which hold in all certified runs on seen tasks and in 40 40 – 86 % 86\% (FPR) and 57 57 – 90 % 90\% (TPR early) of runs on unseen tasks ; baselines give no guarantee on the TPR.

LTT states upfront whether the system can support the required guarantee whereas existing methods can give a false sense of safety. LTT abstains on 4 4 to 7 7 of the 14 14 runs, depending on the target ( FPR targets of 15 15 – 50 % 50\% ), which tells us before deployment that the model cannot support the requested rates. MC always returns a threshold, but it meets the FPR target in only 57 57 – 71 % 71\% of runs on seen tasks and in at most 21 % 21\% on unseen tasks.

Our LTT targets give a lower bound on the positive predictive value (PPV), the probability that an alarm is a true failure. It is 58 58 – 71 % 71\% across the FPR targets of the full table and holds in every certified run on seen tasks and in 70 70 – 100 % 100\% of runs on unseen tasks. Methods without a TPR guarantee cannot give it, and it tells the practitioner what an alarm means.

On unseen tasks, the guarantees hold only empirically, since new samples are not exchangeable with the calibration set, which applies to all three methods. The shares above are trends over 14 runs, not precise rates.

Yes: the rates we calibrate for are the rates we get on seen tasks. Under distribution shift, they hold in far more runs than with MC and FC, and when a target cannot be supported, LTT abstains instead of silently missing it. Together with the PPV bound, this makes VLA-Tug easier to integrate into real-world systems.

Here we focus on failure mode prediction, a crucial element to enable failure prevention through steering. Failure modes are strongly imbalanced, so we report balanced accuracy, the mean over classes of the share of their failures predicted correctly. Since existing baselines do not predict failure modes, we compare against a majority baseline and focus on LIBERO-X.

On LIBERO-X, the probe improves top-1 accuracy over the majority baseline by up to 149 % 149\% on seen and 79 % 79\% on unseen tasks, and top-3 accuracy by a smaller but consistent margin on both. On the real robot, it improves top-1 by 171 % 171\% and 8 % 8\% on seen and unseen tasks, respectively, and stays well above the baseline in top-3 on both.

The practical consequence is that the probe narrows a failure down to three candidate classes, which are more likely than the majority baseline to include the true one. Different failure modes carry different risks, so a practitioner can use these candidates to select the level of response, for example responding to the riskiest of the three predicted classes (a stop, a retry, or a handover to a human) instead of applying the same intervention to every failure.
Yes: backbone embeddings carry enough information to predict the failure class above a majority baseline, which lets a practitioner match the response to the predicted risk.

Any real-world system must balance performance ((T.) Timeliness, (C.) Calibration, (I.) Informativeness) with the cost of building and running it ((E.) Efficiency). We first evaluate the cost of labeling the dataset, then of training the probe, calibrating it, and running it at inference time.

Labeling costs about one cent per failed episode (under $50 for all annotations, including queries not used in this paper). Labels are therefore cheap, and practitioners will often already have unlabeled rollouts from system deployment.

VLA-Tug trains in 6.8 6.8 s on one RTX 4090, against 43.5 43.5 s for SAFE-LSTM, and holds 6.6 6.6 M parameters ( 26.5 26.5 MB), about 0.2 % 0.2\% of the VLA. It is therefore cheap enough to retrain whenever the policy or the task set changes, or to train online as new rollouts are produced.
Calibrating takes under 2 2 ms per target pair on a CPU, so VLA-Tug can be re-calibrated if system requirements change, or online along with the probe.

The VLA outputs a chunk of m m actions per call ( 8 8 at 20 20 Hz on LIBERO-X), so a policy step lasts 400 400 ms, and the probe reads the embedding of each call. It adds 0.12 0.12 ms per step on the GPU ( 0.2 % 0.2\% of the 54 54 ms GR00T policy call) and 0.9 0.9 ms on four CPU threads, so its score is available before the chunk is executed and its latency is not observable: the step period is about 7 × 7\times the combined VLA and probe time in simulation and about 2 × 2\times on the real robot on our GPU.

Faster baselines offer diminishing benefit, since the policy frequency bounds how fast a detector needs to be, while slower ones such as k-NN and STAC add noticeable latency to every step. VLA-Tug costs about the same as the cheapest learned baselines and far less than k-NN and STAC, while providing improved informativeness and timeliness on most unseen settings, which makes it a practical option for real-world deployment.
Yes: labeling, training, calibrating, and running the probe introduce minimal cost, and on a GPU the probe adds under 1 % 1\% to the policy call and fits within the step period.

We demonstrate how the four properties of VLA-Tug : (T.) timeliness, (C.) calibration, (I.) informativeness, and (E.) efficiency, can jointly support failure prevention through VLA steering. Our goal is to illustrate how an effective failure predictor can provide the signals needed to guide interventions rather than develop a steering method itself. We consider a steering architecture in which an expert model (e.g. a VLM) can invoke failure-recovery tools in response to the probe’s predictions. For our experiments, we implement these tools using failure-mode-specific heuristics in simulation and demonstrate corresponding interventions on a real robot.

For example, in the simulated rollout shown in Figure 6(a) , the task is “place the largest bowl inside the left compartment of the bowl drainer.” The probe raises an alarm before the bowl is mistakenly placed in the compartment on the right. After steering the end-effector towards the left side, the policy is resumed and the rollout succeeds. Without intervention, the bowl would be placed on the right side and the rollout fails.

Our real-world experiments similarly demonstrate that the joint properties of VLA-Tug help in steering a VLA away from failure. Figure 6(b) illustrates this with the “put the mushroom on the plate” task. Without VLA-Tug , the gripper misses the mushroom and hits the table. With it turned on, however, the probe predicts the imminent grasp failure (which would likely happen), and corrective action is taken. In the example, the corrective action is to pause the VLA, let an expert model shift trajectory to a successful one, and resume the VLA.

Such a strategy is possible with a failure detector like VLA-Tug , which anticipates the failure before it happens, rather than after it is too late. Our approach is agnostic towards the steering architecture. We leave exploration of robust steering strategies for future work. Nevertheless, these examples demonstrate the applicability of VLA-Tug to be utilized in safe and principled robotic systems.

Answer to Q5. Steering. Yes: Our proof-of-concept demonstrations show how VLA-Tug can provide the timing and failure mode information needed for targeted interventions during VLA execution. Timeliness creates an opportunity to intervene, calibration controls when interventions are triggered, informativeness guides which intervention is applied, and efficiency allows the probe to operate alongside the VLA.

We introduced VLA-Tug , a lightweight probe on the latent layers of a VLA that is timely , calibrated , informative , and efficient , making it well suited for real-world deployment. It is timely : supervising on the pre-failure part of the trajectory drives early detection, and the probe’s performance compared to the strongest learned baseline increases as the shift from the training tasks increases. It is calibrated : calibrating the FPR and the TPR early \mathrm{TPR}_{\mathrm{early}} jointly provides guarantees that hold in far more runs than the baselines under shift. It is informative : beyond a failure score, it names the likely failure mode. It is efficient : the probe adds under 1% to the cost of a policy call. Our steering demonstrations, in simulation and on a real robot, show that VLA-Tug can inform targeted interventions, and we release 3,180 annotated episodes to support further work on latent failure detection.

First, our calibration guarantees rely on exchangeability between the calibration and test episodes, which weakens as the distribution shift grows. Empirically, we observe that the degradation is gradual. Second, we do not analyze the choice of source backbone embedding systematically. Third, the steering component, in which an expert model intervenes on a predicted failure, is heuristic and not evaluated in the scope of this work.

Looking forward, first, we will adapt the probe and its calibration guarantees online, which our preliminary experiments suggest is computationally feasible. Second, we will maintain and extend our embedding dataset with additional backbones and action-expert layers to determine which layers contain the most generalizable failure prediction signal. Third, we will explore agentic frameworks as the expert model in our setup, combining fast and local inference of a VLA with general-purpose intervention and steering from a cloud-based LLM, triggered by a principled detector such as VLA-Tug .

At every policy step we average the backbone tokens of the agent camera, of the wrist camera, and of the (unpadded) language prompt, and concatenate the three means into e t ∈ ℝ 6144 e_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{6144} . No other feature of the backbone is used. All models in this paper read this vector, the baselines included.

A single-layer LSTM with 256 hidden units reads e 1 : t e_{1:t} . Three heads read its state, each an MLP with one hidden layer of 64 ReLU units: the failure score head (one sigmoid output), the failure mode head (logits over the 10 modes), and the semantic head (a 64-dimensional vector).

The target space of the semantic head is a PCA of the CLIP text embeddings of the timeline phrases ( clip-vit-base-patch32 ), reduced to 64 dimensions with a PCA fitted on the training split only. The loss is InfoNCE with temperature 0.07: the normalized output of a step must pick the target of the step’s phrase among the targets of all phrases of the training split. A step whose phrase is not among them is left out of this term. At inference the head is only a 64-dimensional MLP output; no CLIP encoder runs.

ℒ score \mathcal{L}_{\text{score}} is a binary cross-entropy over the steps that are not excluded, weighted by the ratio of negative to positive steps of the training set. ℒ mode \mathcal{L}_{\text{mode}} is a cross-entropy with class weights that balance the modes, on the positive steps of failed rollouts. Both auxiliary terms have weight 1. Early stopping follows ℒ score \mathcal{L}_{\text{score}} on the validation episodes only, so the auxiliary heads never choose the checkpoint.

We label each rollout with Gemini ( gemini-3.5-flash ) from its video, in three passes. A coarse pass over the whole video of a failed rollout returns the failure mode and a failure time; a second pass on a slowed clip around that time refines the failure time to a single frame; and a third pass on the same video session gives the timeline : a short keyword phrase (2–6 words, e.g. “reaching for mug”) for each 3-second window, which provides the targets of the semantic head. The failure time t fail t_{\mathrm{fail}} is the earliest point at which the mistake responsible for the failure becomes apparent. Following Gu et al. (2025) , if there is no single mistake but a human operator would take over (for example when the robot is stuck), we use that time, and if the robot behaves plausibly but is too slow, the failure time is the end of the rollout.

The failure mode is one of 10 classes: wrong_object (acts on an object or control other than the one the task specifies); wrong_target (right object, wrong destination); grasp_failure (never acquires the correct object securely); object_displacement (knocks over, pushes away, or drops an object); placement_or_insertion_failure (right object and target, wrong final pose); open_close_failure (right container, but not the required open or closed state); press_failure (right button or knob, but no effect); stuck_or_no_progress (looping, oscillating, hovering, or freezing); timeout_or_insufficient_progress (purposeful but too slow, no identifiable mistake); and other . The full definitions and the prompts are on the project page, vla-tug.github.io , and on the card of each dataset.

The failure modes are strongly imbalanced, so we report a balanced accuracy: the mean over classes of the share of their failures predicted correctly. We merge the two smallest classes repeatedly, once per dataset, until every class holds at least 5% of the failures. The rule uses label frequencies only. The mode head is not retrained: a merged class gets the sum of the probabilities of its modes. The accuracy is computed on the predictions pooled over the splits of a setting, since a split has few failures of a rare class. We exclude LIBERO-10: it has too few failures for a per-class accuracy, since even after merging its smallest classes hold only 6 to 16 failures, so one failure changes a class’s accuracy by several points.

A failed episode is predicted at an anchor step: the class with the highest mean probability over the 2.4 s window before the anchor and the anchor itself (the top three classes for top-3). The anchor is either the probe’s first alarm (max-conformal at α = 0.2 \alpha=0.2 ; episodes without an alarm are not scored) or the true failure time, which is an upper bound that a deployed system can reach. The baselines predict the most common training classes (always) or guess uniformly among the training classes.

Table 8: Balanced top-1 and top-3 failure-mode accuracy (%), pooled over the splits of each kind. Shaded rows: our probe, by label variant; the oracle rows use the true failure time and are an upper bound. Best in bold, second best in italics, among the other rows.
This section gives the details behind subsection 6.4 .

At each policy step the VLA receives the camera images and the prompt and produces a chunk of m m actions ( m = 8 m=8 on LIBERO-X, 5 5 for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on LIBERO-10, 6 6 on the real robot), which the robot executes at its control rate ( 20 20 Hz in simulation, 50 50 Hz on the real robot). A policy step therefore lasts m m divided by the control rate: 400 400 ms on LIBERO-X, 250 250 ms for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and 120 120 ms on the real robot. The probe reads the embedding of each call and must return its score well within one step.

All times are measured on one RTX 4090 and 32 CPU threads. The fit time is the training time of the probe or the SAFE models, or the time to fit the statistics of the distance baselines. The state is what a fitted method must keep to score a new episode: the weights, the stored training steps of the k-NN, or the statistics of the distance baselines. The latency is the online latency: the time to turn one new policy step into a score, one embedding at a time and with the recurrent state of the previous step, after a warm-up and with the device synchronized, as the median over up to 2,000 steps. The CPU is timed with four threads. Online latency is the one that matters for deployment.

The k-NN baseline has to keep every training step and compare each new step with all of them, so its cost grows with the training set; Mahalanobis keeps two 6144 × 6144 6144\times 6144 matrices. STAC needs the K = 10 K=10 plans of the policy at every call, which no other method needs, so its latency is its scoring time plus the time to sample them.

On the GPU the LSTM takes most of the time; the mode head and the CLIP head add little, and on the CPU they add nothing measurable. The probe is not the fastest online method (SAFE-LSTM and the MLP detectors are faster), but it is far below the duration of a policy step.

Per target pair, max-conformal takes 0.1 0.1 ms, functional conformal 0.7 0.7 ms, and LTT 1.3 1.3 ms on a CPU. The calibration sets hold 158 158 to 209 209 labeled episodes, of which 92 92 to 120 120 are failures.
We ablate the supervision strategy, the auxiliary heads, and the failure time used for evaluation.

Table 9 compares our pre-onset label (every step before the failure time is positive) with the window before the onset only, every step of the failed rollout, and the window before the onset together with all steps after it. The pre-onset label is the best, or within the spread across splits, in nearly every setting. On LIBERO-X the alternatives lose 24 % 24\% to 50 % 50\% of the detection area on average, and are lower on every kind of held-out split, seen and unseen; labeling the steps after the onset as positive is worst. On LIBERO-10 the differences are smaller ( − 1 % -1\% to − 14 % -14\% on average), within the spread across splits for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and clear on seen tasks with GR00T.

We include the mode and CLIP heads because their labels already exist for every failure. We find no consistent benefit from either on detection ( Table 9 ): removing the heads changes the area by less than the spread across splits in most settings. For mode prediction ( Table 10 ), the CLIP head changes top-1 accuracy by less than one point on average, while training the mode head jointly with the failure score adds three to four points over a mode-only probe. The CLIP alignment might help some subpopulations and hurt others, which we leave to future work.

Moving the failure time later makes the metric easier, since more alarms then count as early, so we check how much our results depend on it. We score the saved scores again with the failure time of every failed episode moved 1 1 and 2 2 s later, with the same thresholds and without retraining ( Table 11 ). Every method gains, but late detectors gain more than VLA-Tug , which already alarms early: on unseen LIBERO-X VLA-Tug gains 2.1 2.1 to 2.4 2.4 points of area over 2 2 s and SAFE-LSTM 3.5 3.5 to 4.0 4.0 . On LIBERO-X our rank among the methods does not change, and our margins hold, so these results do not depend on the exact failure time. On the real robot, where our lead is a single point, SAFE-LSTM overtakes VLA-Tug at 1 1 s for the same reason.

Table 9: Ablations of our probe in the simulated settings: area under TPR early vs. FPR up to 40% (in %), mean ± \pm standard deviation over the splits, and in brackets the change relative to our probe (shaded). Best in bold, second best in italics, within each block.

Table 10: What the CLIP head and the score term add to failure-mode prediction: top-1 and top-3 accuracy (in %), mean ± \pm standard deviation over the splits. Our probe is shaded. Best in bold, second best in italics, per column and anchor.
Table 11: Early-detection area (in %) on the unseen episodes when the failure time is moved later by 0, 1, and 2 s; nothing is retrained. Ours is shaded. Best in bold, second best in italics.

VLA-Tug encodes the VLA backbone embedding of each step with an LSTM into a latent state, which three MLP heads read: the failure score, the failure mode, and a CLIP embedding. The following figures show four of these spaces in two dimensions: the backbone embedding itself (the input), the LSTM state, and the hidden layers of the failure score head and of the failure mode head. Each is projected onto its first two principal components, fitted on the pre-failure steps of the training episodes only, and drawn for the training episodes and for the unseen tasks of the LIBERO-X new-task split. The points are the steps up to the failure of failed episodes and all steps of successful episodes; the ellipses are the 1 ​ σ 1\sigma ellipses of a Gaussian fitted to each class, drawn over the points. The classes are the outcome (success in blue, failure in red) or the failure mode. The mode head is trained on failures only and has only a mode plot.
Figure 8: VLA backbone embedding, by outcome.
Figure 9: VLA backbone embedding, by failure mode.
Figure 10: Probe LSTM state, by outcome.
Figure 11: Probe LSTM state, by failure mode.
Figure 12: Failure score head layer, by outcome.
Figure 13: Failure score head layer, by failure mode.
Figure 14: Failure mode head layer, by failure mode (failures only).

To see how an episode moves through these spaces, Figure 15 and Figure 16 follow one success and one failure step by step, for episodes of seen and of unseen tasks. Each panel shows one space in its first two principal components: (a) the VLA backbone embedding, (b) the probe’s LSTM state, and the hidden layers of (c) the failure score head and (d) the failure mode head. The points and ellipses are those of the episodes of the set shown (the training episodes, or the unseen tasks), grouped by outcome and failure mode, and the mode head is shown on failures only. The principal components are always those fitted on the training episodes. A trajectory starts at the ring; a failure is dashed and ends at the cross, at its failure step.

Figure 15: Seen tasks (training episodes). A success (green, “pick up the bowl on the plate and place it to the left of the bowl drainer”) and an object displacement failure (red, “place the striped book in the top region of the shelf”).
Figure 16: Unseen tasks. A success (green, “place the red bowl in the basket”) and a press failure (red, “turn on the flat stove”).

We use steering only to show how the signal of VLA-Tug could be used; the heuristics are simple and are not evaluated. When the score crosses the calibrated threshold, the policy is paused, an intervention chosen from the predicted failure mode is applied, and the policy resumes.

We implemented three heuristics for LIBERO-X. For a wrong-target or placement/insertion failure, the end effector is displaced by a small distance towards the destination. For a grasp failure, it is displaced laterally, perpendicular to its recent motion. For every other predicted mode, the policy replans from the current state. 17(a) shows the three on the task “place the white-yellow mug on top of the shelf”: after the alarm, the probe predicts the failure mode, the matching intervention is applied, and the policy resumes and succeeds, whereas without intervention the mug is placed on the table and the task fails.

In the task “put the mushroom on the plate”, the gripper misses the mushroom and hits the table without the probe; the probe predicts a grasp failure, and an expert would steer the wrist camera towards the grasp target and resume the policy. In the task “flip the basket upright”, we start with the basket standing on its tall end, outside the training demonstrations; an expert might move the gripper along the − z -z direction, so that the joint states are in the distribution of the flip motion, as the demonstrations are collected with the basket on its long side ( 17(b) ).

analysis.overview: 优先复用的改动是监督时间范围：失败episode只保留起点至失败时刻为正例，丢弃之后的损失，再用LTT同时认证episode误报与早期漏检。相同探针的标签消融支持这一选择；CLIP辅助头没有稳定检测增益。跨任务结果、可认证覆盖率与告警后的恢复能力必须分开：分布漂移下只有经验结果，steering仅为案例。
analysis.notice: 完整阅读196个提取片段，覆盖正文与附录A–E的方法、校准细节、数据与标注、实验、消融及定性案例。前四个片段是排版警告，不是研究证据。固定版本PDF共27页；目视核对物理页5、7、13、17、18、21的图2/4/7、公式1–6、标签定义和表3/6–11。未逐一检查其他图像、逐篇核查参考文献、重证LTT定理、执行源码或复现实验。表内数值来自作者；引文匹配只验证出处。

findings.title: 关键问题：检测最终失败，不等于来得及干预
findings.text: 论文把失败时刻定义为明显错误最早出现、或人会接管的时刻；指标要求首次告警t_det≤t_fail。这比只判断episode最终成败更接近干预需求，但允许等于失败时刻，没有要求留出停止、规划或恢复所需的非零提前量。FPR是成功episode中至少一次误报的比例，不是每个控制步的误报率。

findings.title: 探针输入和参数：复用骨干，不额外运行CLIP
findings.text: π0.5取归一化后的第18层，GR00T-N1.7取第16层；分别平均agent相机、腕部相机和未padding指令token，拼接为6144维。单层256隐藏单元LSTM接三个64隐藏ReLU的MLP，输出标量分数、10类模式及64维语义向量，共6.6M参数。语义目标由训练集短语的CLIP表示经训练集PCA降维，InfoNCE温度0.07；在线不运行CLIP编码器。论文未系统消融取哪一层。

findings.title: 监督增量：整段失败前缀为正，失败后不计损失
findings.text: pre-onset把最终失败轨迹从起点到t_fail的全部步标为1，之后排除损失；成功轨迹所有步标0。它不是只把紧邻失败的2.4秒标正，也不是把失败后标负。onset对照只在前窗标正、再早标0并丢弃失败后；post-onset从前窗起一直标正；trajectory将失败全轨迹标正。其作用是改变学习信号与序列截断，未做正例数量、长度等完全匹配的控制，不能只凭此证明探针学到因果先兆。

findings.title: 联合校准：接受合格阈值，否则拒绝认证
findings.text: 分数BCE加类别加权的模式交叉熵和CLIP对齐，辅助权重均为1；Adam学习率3e-4、batch32条轨迹，最多100epoch，以验证分数损失早停patience15。阈值用LTT同时检验FPR≤α和早期TPR≥β：181个sigmoid阈值、40个起点、δ=0.1，取已接受阈值中校准早期TPR最高者，无合格阈值则abstain。作者证书针对与校准数据可交换的episode；LTT是高概率认证，max-conformal的FPR界是边际保证，两者不能只凭某次拆分是否达标就视为同一种保证或定理失效。

findings.title: 最强消融：相同模型换标签，未见技能39.0对21.6
findings.text: 表9固定LSTM与模式/CLIP头，在LIBERO-X未见技能上，pre-onset早期面积39.0±7.0，trajectory21.6±3.9，onset25.5±9.0，post-onset17.0±3.4。前者比全轨迹正标签高17.4个百分点；这是监督策略控制，比跨探针基线更直接。优势不普遍：LIBERO-10/π0.5未见任务trajectory为52.0±14.9，pre-onset为47.9±20.9。所报误差是拆分标准差，不是配对差值置信区间。

findings.title: 主比较：30%是面积相对提升，真机仅高0.7点
findings.text: 表3/6的指标为FPR 0–0.4内早期TPR面积除以0.4，百分制，而非成功率或某一个工作点的TPR。LIBERO-X未见技能VLA-Tug39.0±7.0、SAFE-LSTM30.1±8.5，差8.9个百分点，约29.6%相对提升；未见任务40.2对40.4，未见签名47.0对41.2。真机25.8±11.6对25.1±18.8，仅差0.7点；LIBERO-10/GR00T本方法47.4，低于SAFE-LSTM51.2。因此不是所有底座、所有分布漂移均领先。主面积表VLA-Tug用MC，SAFE用FC，不应将整张主表当成全部已采用联合LTT。

findings.title: 认证覆盖率：20%误报目标下只认证7/14次
findings.text: 表7仅LIBERO-X的14次运行，α=20%、β=35%时，LTT只认证7/14次；这7次在留出seen集两指标均达标。到unseen集，FPR达标71%、早期TPR达标57%，分别约5/7和4/7，不是联合达标71%或57%，表中没有给二者交集。MC与FC此行各在全部14次中有21%的FPR达标，分母与认证子集不同。α=10%时LTT为0/14，不能将拒绝认证当作成功部署。真实机器人和LIBERO-10未展示可用的这类LTT证书，因校准样本太少。

findings.title: 摘要86%与PPV下界都需要条件
findings.text: 摘要把漂移下误报和漏检界概括为最高86%；表7的86%实际是某目标下FPR单列、且仅统计认证子集。表内α=15%时FC的unseen FPR达标率29%，故不能将“基线最多21%”推广到所有FC行。PPV公式下界为πβ/[πβ+(1−π)α]，需真实失败率π或有效下界；论文用校准集π估计，跨技能会漂移，不能直接给部署告警一个无条件正确概率。跨任务的达标份额只有经验含义，new-task/signature三个seed复用同一unseen任务集，也不是14个独立漂移环境。

findings.title: 辅助头消融：CLIP没有稳定带来检测提升
findings.text: 表9未见技能完整模型39.0±7.0，去掉两个辅助头43.6±11.5，仅模式头43.7±10.2；未见签名去头45.0±1.3对完整47.0±0.6。论文总结没有一致检测增益，不能把主要提升归因于CLIP语义对齐。模式头提供故障分类能力与检测收益应分别评估；表10显示CLIP对top-1平均改变量小于一点，联合分数训练较mode-only平均多3–4点，这不构成CLIP必需的证据。

findings.title: 模式分类：合并类别、只评已告警失败，非10类全覆盖
findings.text: 表8按数据集合并最小类直到每类占失败至少5%，输出概率相加但不重训；报告合并后类别平衡准确率。自己的告警以MC α=0.2触发，取告警前2.4秒加当前步的平均模式概率；未告警episode不计入该分类评价。未见技能top-3为56.3%，多数基线39.0%、均匀随机42.9%；约44%相对提升仅对应前一个弱基线。真机top-3为70.4%对多数32.6%，但随机已60%；top-1为21.7%对20.0%。表10是逐split均值，表8是汇总后统计，不能互换或把其中100%当作整体准确率；标为oracle的行也不是所有列都高于实际告警行。

findings.title: 数据：3180是发布的仿真episode，真机另外399条
findings.text: 两底座在原LIBERO/遮挡混合各500条，GR00T在LIBERO-X为2,180条，合计3,180条仿真数据；附录明确公开的是这些仿真embedding、标签、提示及split。Kinova Gen3真机另有399条评估轨迹、254失败，底座以8任务共510条示范微调。Gemini三遍视频标注失败类型、时刻和每3秒动作短语；t_fail是模型判读的可见错误/应接管点，未报告独立人工时刻一致性。本文使用现成文字材料，本轮没有调用该标注API。

findings.title: 标注敏感性：只向后挪时刻，真机排名会翻转
findings.text: 表11不重训、不重校准，仅把每次失败标签推迟1/2秒再评分。真机VLA-Tug从25.8到26.3/26.5，SAFE-LSTM从25.1到26.8/28.9，1秒时排名已反转；LIBERO-X各拆分排名相对稳定。向后移动必然放宽“早期”，不能替代双向标注噪声检验，也没测试必须提前一个控制块才能干预。真机40个拆分是8个留出任务×5seed，new-task/signature不同seed的unseen轨迹相同，误差须按层级理解。

findings.title: 成本：0.12ms只测4090上的探针每策略调用
findings.text: 作者在一张RTX4090报告探针拟合6.8秒、权重状态26.5MB，GPU在线中位0.12ms、四CPU线程0.94ms；同步后最多2,000步测量，不是端到端尾延迟或边缘设备实测。LIBERO-X每次VLA给8动作、20Hz消费，探针每400ms才有一个新embedding；真机6动作/50Hz为120ms。0.12ms是给定embedding后的分数延迟，低延迟不意味着50Hz监测动作中途风险；拟合秒数也不含数据采集、底座微调或embedding生成。LTT每目标对约1.3ms，但仍需158–209条带标签校准episode。

findings.title: 干预证据边界：恢复是启发式案例，没有成功率对照
findings.text: 论文展示触发后暂停策略、按模式小幅移动末端或重新规划，再恢复策略。仿真包括朝放置目标移动、抓取失败时横向移动；真机以蘑菇和篮子案例说明可能的专家修正。作者明确steering启发式未系统评价；没有恢复试验总数、干预成功率或对照区间，不能把告警检测改进写成已量化的任务成功率、安全性或自动专家系统提升。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：留出一个控制块的干预时间后，标签优势还在吗？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：pre-onset相对全轨迹标签的优势，在要求至少一个动作块提前量后仍能保留。固定GR00T与LIBERO-X数据、骨干层、LSTM、训练预算和任务拆分，比较pre-onset、trajectory、仅前窗三种监督；另做有/无CLIP控制。用独立验证集选模型，以seen校准集固定FPR≤20%目标，记录LTT认证率及拒绝次数。测试集失败时刻由两名不了解方法的标注者分别判读并保留分歧区间，不用unseen结果选阈值。分别计算t_det≤t_fail−τ的召回，τ取0、0.4、0.8、1.2秒，报告固定FPR的早期召回、lead-time分位数、无告警率、模式准确率与episode级误报，同时作时刻正负1秒扰动。以任务为单位bootstrap差值，区分同一unseen任务重复seed与独立任务。若0秒优势在0.4秒或更大提前量下消失、超过标注不确定性后无法区分，或认证覆盖率降到无可用阈值，就推翻“检测提升足以支持整块动作前干预”的解释；若只某技能失效则缩小适用范围。实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现空白。

frontier_brief.title: VLA-Tug：只用失败前缀监督，再联合校准误报与早期漏检
frontier_brief.change_type: 监测方法 · 监督与校准
frontier_brief.delta: 把失败轨迹的起点至失败时刻全部标正，丢弃失败后的损失；成功轨迹全标负。用骨干embedding上的LSTM读出分数与故障模式，再以LTT同时认证误报上限和早期检测下限，无合格阈值就拒绝认证。
frontier_brief.before: SAFE式trajectory标签将失败轨迹所有时刻标正，易混入已经失败的特征；单侧conformal只约束误报，不要求同时达到某个早期检出率。
frontier_brief.after: 将监督限制在失败前缀，以首次告警是否不晚于标注失败时刻评估；另外用带成功/失败标注的校准episode检验两项风险，并报告认证覆盖率。主要面积比较仍用MC，联合LTT单列评估。
frontier_brief.relevance: 做VLA失效监测时，先复现同探针的标签消融，再决定是否增加CLIP辅助头。部署决策应同时看可认证覆盖率、任务外漂移、动作块内观测盲区，以及能否给干预留出实际时间。
frontier_brief.caveat: 跨任务无形式保证；86%是部分目标下认证子集的FPR达标份额，不是双指标联合保证。真机检测只高0.7点且对时刻定义敏感，恢复仅有启发式案例。所有数值来自作者，未复现。
frontier_brief.question: 要求至少提前一个400ms动作块报警后，失败前缀监督还优于全轨迹标签吗？

evidence.label: 同模型、同头，仅换监督标签

passages.section: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
passages.location: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
passages.text: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner’s motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner’s motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world.

passages.section: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
passages.location: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
passages.text: Figure 1: Social Humanoid enables humanoids to perceive, anticipate, and respond to people with coordinated whole-body behavior. Examples include a hug (top) and a greeting followed by posing together for a photo (bottom). Given RGB-D video, our method reconstructs the observed human motion, then conditions on it to predict future human motion and a humanoid response. The generated motions are executed by a low-level tracking controller. Video results are available on our webpage: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/

passages.section: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
passages.location: Social Humanoid: Socially Responsive Human–Humanoid Interaction
passages.text: Keywords: Human-Humanoid Interaction, Motion Retargeting

Human interaction is the art of attunement, a continuous interplay of perception, anticipation, and response that enables seamless coordination. Whether synchronizing a high-five or collaborating on a shared task, people adjust effortlessly through gaze, posture, and timing, without words. This ability is a hallmark of social intelligence [ 56 , 18 , 21 ] , allowing humans to simultaneously anticipate and align with others in real time. In contrast, existing works train humanoids as solitary agents, leaving them unable to perceive social cues or respond to the people around them. As humanoids move out of labs and into homes, workplaces, and shared public spaces, they will need the same capacity to operate alongside and with people.

To address this, we formulate the problem of human-humanoid interaction, in which a humanoid must continuously generate and execute coordinated, socially responsive whole-body motion given observations of a human partner. We present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system with a high-level and a low-level policy. The high-level policy generates reactive humanoid motion from the observed partner’s motion and anticipates the partner’s motion, even when they are occluded or human input is missing, enabling continuous interaction. The low-level policy then executes the generated motion on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.

While recent advances in human motion generation [ 42 , 19 , 8 , 41 ] can synthesize realistic dyadic interactions offline, deploying this capability on physical humanoids introduces three challenges: First, a data gap : human-human interaction is captured at scale, but no dataset captures natural human-humanoid interaction and naively retargeting each partner independently destroys the contact, reach, and spatial structure that defines the interaction. Second, a representation gap : human and humanoid motion live in different spaces, which forces the generative model to learn the differences between the two embodiments instead of focusing on the interaction itself. This gap has been largely overlooked in prior work. Third, a generation gap : a natural approach is to generate the interaction with a human motion model and retarget to humanoid through optimization, but optimization-based retargeting is designed for clean, offline data and is brittle to noisy, discontinuous partner observations. A socially responsive humanoid needs a feed-forward model to generate humanoid motion directly.

Social Humanoid addresses these challenges with three contributions that build on one another. (i) For the data gap, we introduce a two-phase Adaptive-HHI Retargeting procedure that retargets one partner to the 29-DoF Unitree G1 and morphs the other’s body pose to preserve contact, reach, and relative scale. Applied to Chi3D [ 15 ] , Hi4D [ 62 ] , Harmony4D [ 33 ] , Inter-X [ 59 ] , and Embody3D [ 44 ] , it yields the HHI Benchmark, comprising 260 hours of dyadic and polyadic interactions paired with the G1. (ii) For the representation gap, our key insight is that a shared motion representation lets a single generative model reason jointly about both embodiments, which we instantiate with a shared-codebook VQ-VAE that tokenizes human and humanoid motion into a single discrete vocabulary. This vocabulary also supports real-time shadow teleoperation of the G1 without optimization-based retargeting (Sec. 5.2 ).. (iii) For the generation gap, our high-level policy is a Diffusion Forcing Transformer that autoregressively generates humanoid responses over this shared vocabulary; its diffusion-forcing objective is well-suited to imperfect, real-world input and supports fluid, long-horizon interaction. Paired with NVIDIA SONIC [ 39 ] as the low-level whole-body tracking controller, Social Humanoid demonstrates coordinated, interactive, and human-aligned behaviors in both simulation and real-world hardware experiments. Generation and execution run asynchronously, with a median end-to-end latency of 308 ms from camera frame to humanoid command.

Figure 2: Social Humanoid Architecture. From RGB-D observations of a human partner (red), we reconstruct the human pose and localize the body in 3D using depth and estimated gravity. Relative human and humanoid states are encoded through the VQ-VAE encoders E h \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{h}} and E r \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{r}} . The resulting latent motion tokens z ∗ z_{*} , relative pose transforms T ∗ T^{*} , and canonical motion transforms Δ ​ T ∗ \Delta T^{*} are concatenated and processed by the DFoT policy, then decoded via D h \mathrm{D}_{h} and D r \mathrm{D}_{r} to future human behavior (blue) and socially coordinated humanoid motion (purple). SONIC executes the motion in sim or the real-world, and the robot state is updated for closed-loop interaction.

Human Motion Generation. Large-scale motion datasets such as AMASS [ 40 ] have enabled major advances in generative human motion modeling. Early approaches relied on recurrent and convolutional architectures for motion prediction and synthesis [ 16 , 24 , 32 , 47 , 23 , 5 ] , followed by structured and probabilistic formulations for multimodal motion generation [ 2 , 65 , 70 ] . More recently, transformer-, VAE-, autoregressive-, and diffusion-based approaches have significantly improved long-horizon coherence, controllability, and diversity [ 12 , 22 , 1 , 29 , 67 , 68 ] .

Humanoid Motion Generation. Parallel progress in humanoid motion generation has combined reinforcement learning [ 64 , 63 ] , imitation learning and retargeting [ 10 , 38 , 66 ] , and generative motion priors [ 11 , 69 , 7 , 48 , 31 ] to produce increasingly natural humanoid behaviors. Recent systems further leverage monocular video reconstruction and diffusion-based policies for contextual and goal-aware control [ 3 , 35 ] , while optimization-based methods such as OmniRetarget [ 60 ] improve geometric and kinematic consistency during motion transfer. However, these approaches primarily focus on single-agent motion generation or independently retargeted trajectories, often failing to preserve the contact, reachability, and relative geometry required for socially coordinated human-humanoid interaction. In contrast, our interaction-aware adaptive retargeting sequentially optimizes humanoid retargeting and partner co-morphing to preserve socially meaningful interaction structure.

Dyadic Interaction and Human Motion Anticipation. Humans coordinate interactions by continuously anticipating others’ intentions through posture, timing, gaze, and motion cues [ 21 , 17 , 50 ] . Motivated by this, recent work has explored dyadic human interaction [ 45 , 14 , 58 , 49 , 28 , 30 , 8 , 55 , 20 ] , enabling realistic, coordinated behaviors between human partners. Complementary efforts study socially expressive and interaction-aware motion generation, including dance, social affordances, and language-conditioned interaction [ 36 , 52 , 42 , 51 , 13 ] . While these methods produce compelling human-human interactions, they do not address the embodiment mismatch, streaming perception, and control constraints required for deployment on physical humanoids.

Human-Humanoid Interaction and Embodied Control. Prior work on human-humanoid interaction has explored physical assistance and contact-rich behaviors such as standing support and hugging [ 34 , 6 ] , as well as compliant and safe humanoid control for close-proximity interaction [ 43 , 37 ] . Anticipating human intentions or trajectories has also been studied for cooperative robotics [ 27 ] , typically as auxiliary modules for timing or safety rather than as part of motion generation itself. Other recent approaches generate humanoid motion from high-level textual descriptions, including social interaction prompts [ 31 ] . Hierarchical control frameworks further demonstrate the benefits of decomposing high-level motion planning and low-level motor execution for robust robot behavior [ 4 ] . In contrast to prior work, Social Humanoid unifies predictive human motion understanding, cross-embodiment generative modeling, and embodied humanoid control into a single framework for socially coordinated human-humanoid interaction.

Enabling socially coordinated human-humanoid interaction requires not only realistic motion synthesis, but also the ability to react continuously to a human partner. We therefore train a generative model on human-humanoid interaction trajectories, enabling fast, reactive motion generation at inference time. The core of our Social Humanoid system is a high-level policy that predicts humanoid kinematic motion from observed human motion, which are subsequently executed by a low-level tracking policy; see Fig. 2 for an overview of the system. The construction of the interaction dataset via interaction-aware retargeting is described in Section 4 .

Formally, we adopt a canonical-frame motion representation rather than absolute world coordinates, inspired by MAGNet [ 41 ] . Human articulated motion is given by SMPL joint rotations in 6D form, 𝚯 h ∈ ℝ 21 × 6 \mathbf{\Theta}^{h}\in\mathbb{R}^{21\times 6} , and humanoid motion by the 29 29 actuated joint angles 𝚯 r ∈ ℝ 29 \mathbf{\Theta}^{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{29} . Root motion is encoded as a relative canonical transform between consecutive frames, Δ ​ 𝐓 can = [ Δ ​ 𝚽 ; Δ ​ 𝚪 ] \Delta\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{can}}=[\Delta\mathbf{\Phi};\,\Delta\mathbf{\Gamma}] , where Δ ​ 𝚽 ∈ ℝ 6 \Delta\mathbf{\Phi}\in\mathbb{R}^{6} is the relative root orientation (6D) and Δ ​ 𝚪 ∈ ℝ 3 \Delta\mathbf{\Gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} the relative root translation in the canonical frame. We additionally retain the absolute canonical-to-root transform 𝐓 can → root \mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{can}\to\mathrm{root}} and the cross-agent transform 𝐓 r → h \mathbf{T}^{r\to h} ( 𝐓 h → r \mathbf{T}^{h\to r} ) that places each agent in its partner’s canonical frame, both in ℝ 9 \mathbb{R}^{9} (6D rotation, 3D translation). The complete per-agent motion representations are given by

𝐦 r = [ Δ ​ 𝐓 can , r ; 𝐓 can → root , r ; 𝚯 r ; 𝐓 r → h ] , 𝐦 h = [ Δ ​ 𝐓 can , h ; 𝐓 can → root , h ; 𝚯 h ; 𝐓 h → r ] . \mathbf{m}^{r}=[\,\Delta\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{can},r};\,\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{can}\to\mathrm{root},r};\,\mathbf{\Theta}^{r};\,\mathbf{T}^{r\to h}\,],\hskip 8.03pt\mathbf{m}^{h}=[\,\Delta\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{can},h};\,\mathbf{T}^{\mathrm{can}\to\mathrm{root},h};\,\mathbf{\Theta}^{h};\,\mathbf{T}^{h\to r}\,]. (1)

Figure 3: Shared-Codebook VQ-VAE . Human and humanoid motion sequences are independently encoded into latent features and mapped to a shared vector-quantized codebook that learns a common motion vocabulary across embodiments. Embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct the respective motions, enabling aligned, transferable motion representations between humans and humanoids.

Generating motion for Social Humanoids requires efficient, streaming-based generation, which motivates us to compactly tokenize high-dimensional human and humanoid motion trajectories. Recognizing that human and humanoid motions may share a similar latent structure, we encode both trajectories into a unified discrete vocabulary using a shared-codebook VQ-VAE (Fig. 3 ). Crucially, this shared representation simplifies the training of the subsequent diffusion model (see Sec. 5 ), as the primary motion spaces of the human partner and the humanoid are inherently heterogeneous.

Embodiment-specific Encoders and Decoders. Human and robot motions lie in different feature spaces due to their differing dimensionalities and kinematic structures. We therefore use embodiment-specific encoders and decoders. Let 𝐱 t h = [ 𝐓 t can → root , h ; 𝚯 t h ] ∈ ℝ D h \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{h}}_{t}=[\mathbf{T}_{t}^{\mathrm{can}\to\mathrm{root},h};\,\mathbf{\Theta}_{t}^{h}]\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{h}}} and 𝐱 t r = [ 𝐓 t can → root , r ; 𝚯 t r ] ∈ ℝ D r \mathbf{x}^{\mathrm{r}}_{t}=[\mathbf{T}_{t}^{\mathrm{can}\to\mathrm{root},r};\,\mathbf{\Theta}_{t}^{r}]\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{\mathrm{r}}} denote the human and robot motion features at frame t t . The human and robot encoders, E h \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{h}} and E r \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{r}} , are 1D-convolutional networks with temporal downsampling by a factor of 4 4 and dilated ResNet-1D blocks, producing latent sequences 𝐯 h , 𝐯 r ∈ ℝ T z × d z \mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{h}},\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{z}\times d_{z}} .

These features are quantized into discrete sequences 𝐳 h , 𝐳 r \mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{h}},\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{r}} using a shared codebook. Finally, symmetric decoders, D h \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{h}} and D r \mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{r}} , upsample these quantized latents back to the original frame rate.

Shared Codebook. Both embodiments share a single EMA codebook, 𝒞 = { 𝐜 k } k = 1 K ⊂ ℝ d z \mathcal{C}=\{\mathbf{c}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} , defining a common discrete motion vocabulary. Given human and humanoid motions, the temporally downsampled continuous representations 𝐯 a \mathbf{v}^{a} produced by the encoders for agent a ∈ { h , r } a\in\{\mathrm{h},\mathrm{r}\} are quantized as:

𝐳 a = Quantize ⁡ ( 𝐯 a , 𝒞 ) , where 𝐳 t a = arg ⁡ min 𝐜 k ∈ 𝒞 ⁡ ‖ 𝐯 t a − 𝐜 k ‖ 2 . \mathbf{z}^{a}=\mathrm{Quantize}(\mathbf{v}^{a};\mathcal{C}),\qquad\text{where}\quad\mathbf{z}^{a}_{t}=\arg\min_{\mathbf{c}_{k}\in\mathcal{C}}\|\mathbf{v}^{a}_{t}-\mathbf{c}_{k}\|_{2}. (2)
The resulting discrete latents 𝐳 a \mathbf{z}^{a} are subsequently passed to their respective decoders.

However, a shared codebook alone cannot guarantee identical code assignments for paired frames. We thus introduce two alignment terms: (i) Continuous alignment directly minimizes the distance between encoder outputs, ℒ align = ‖ 𝐯 h − 𝐯 r ‖ 2 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\|\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{h}}-\mathbf{v}^{\mathrm{r}}\|_{2}^{2} , shaping a shared latent geometry. (ii) Discrete alignment applies a symmetric cross-entropy loss over the distance logits ℓ h , ℓ r ∈ ℝ K \ell^{\mathrm{h}},\ell^{\mathrm{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} with stop-gradient targets c h , c r c^{\mathrm{h}},c^{\mathrm{r}} , computed as ℒ agree = 1 2 ​ [ CE ⁡ ( ℓ h , c r ) + CE ⁡ ( ℓ r , c h ) ] \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{agree}}=\tfrac{1}{2}[\mathrm{CE}(\ell^{\mathrm{h}},c^{\mathrm{r}})+\mathrm{CE}(\ell^{\mathrm{r}},c^{\mathrm{h}})] . Together, these terms encourage cross-embodiment code prediction and tie the codebook to corresponding human–robot poses rather than letting each encoder claim separate regions of 𝒞 \mathcal{C} .

Training Objective. The complete objective combines per-embodiment reconstruction, the VQ commitment loss ℒ commit = ‖ 𝐯 − sg ⁡ ( 𝐳 ) ‖ 2 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{commit}}=\|\mathbf{v}-\mathrm{sg}(\mathbf{z})\|_{2}^{2} , and the two proposed alignment terms:

ℒ = ℒ rec + β ​ ℒ commit + λ a ​ l ​ i ​ g ​ n ​ ℒ align + λ a ​ g ​ r ​ e ​ e ​ ℒ agree . \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\beta\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{commit}}+\lambda_{align}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}+\lambda_{agree}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{agree}}. (3)

The codebook entries are the only shared parameters across the architecture; all other model weights remain strictly embodiment-specific. The shared codebook also enables human-to-humanoid motion translation in a single feed-forward pass ( E h → 𝒞 → D r E_{h}\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\rightarrow D_{r} ), supporting real-time shadow teleoperation of the G1 without optimization-based retargeting (Appendix 5.2 ).

To model human–humanoid interaction in the shared token space introduced above, we use a flexible sequence model based on Diffusion Forcing Transformer (DFoT) [ 9 , 54 ] . DFoT is a conditional generative model that integrates the denoising process of DDPMs [ 26 ] with the temporal strengths of transformers [ 57 ] . A core advantage of this design is its ability to learn non-Markovian temporal dependencies across entire sequences using adaptive noise levels.

Given the observed latent history { 𝐳 h , 𝐳 r } 1 : T c \{\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{h}},\mathbf{z}^{\mathrm{r}}\}_{1:T_{c}} , DFoT predicts the future latents { 𝐳 ^ h , 𝐳 ^ r } T c + 1 : T c + T f \{\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{\mathrm{h}},\hat{\mathbf{z}}^{\mathrm{r}}\}_{T_{c}+1:T_{c}+T_{f}} . During training, each future latent frame 𝐳 i a \mathbf{z}^{a}_{i} for agent a ∈ { h , r } a\in\{\mathrm{h},\mathrm{r}\} at timestep i i is noised independently according to its own frame- and agent-specific diffusion timestep t i a t^{a}_{i} , yielding 𝐳 i a ​ ( t i a ) = α ¯ t i a ​ 𝐳 i a + 1 − α ¯ t i a ​ ϵ i a , \mathbf{z}^{a}_{i}(t^{a}_{i})=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t^{a}_{i}}}\,\mathbf{z}^{a}_{i}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t^{a}_{i}}}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{a}_{i}, where 𝐳 i a \mathbf{z}^{a}_{i} is the clean latent, α ¯ \bar{\alpha} is the noise schedule, and ϵ i a ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \boldsymbol{\epsilon}^{a}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) . Crucially, human and robot frames are noised independently ( t i h ≠ t i r t^{\mathrm{h}}_{i}\neq t^{\mathrm{r}}_{i} ) to prevent shortcutting. Context frames 1 : T c 1{:}T_{c} remain clean ( t i a = 0 t^{a}_{i}=0 ) to preserve the history conditioning signal.

The network consists of transformer layers processing the noisy latents 𝐳 i a ​ ( t i a ) \mathbf{z}^{a}_{i}(t^{a}_{i}) combined with a sinusoidal embedding for noise-level, RoPE for temporal order, and a learned agent embedding. We train with a Smooth- L 1 L_{1} objective to recover clean latents, and during inference, the predicted future latents are passed to embodiment-specific decoders for motion reconstruction.

Sampling and Generation. Inference with DFoT uses autoregressive DDIM sampling [ 53 ] with η = 0 \eta=0 to generate coordinated human and humanoid motion. The denoising process is controlled by a sampling strategy matrix 𝐊 ∈ ℤ S × ( N × P ) \mathbf{K}\in\mathbb{Z}^{S\times(N\times P)} , which specifies per-token noise levels across denoising steps. Independent token-wise noise scheduling enables flexible generation over the agent–time grid, allowing the same model to perform tasks such as joint future generation, partner prediction, and partner inpainting through different sampling schedules without retraining.
Training Losses. We optimize Social Humanoid across three complementary spaces—latent, motion, and reconstruction—to balance diffusion accuracy with kinematic fidelity:

ℒ total = w latent ​ ℒ latent + w motion ​ ℒ motion + w recon ​ ℒ recon , \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=w_{\text{latent}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{latent}}+w_{\text{motion}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{motion}}+w_{\text{recon}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}, (4)

where w latent w_{\text{latent}} , w motion w_{\text{motion}} , and w recon w_{\text{recon}} are weighting coefficients. The latent denoising loss recovers clean latents via Smooth- L 1 L_{1} for human ( h h ) and robot ( r r ); the motion loss decodes predicted latents and applies Smooth- L 1 L_{1} in raw motion space against 𝐱 a \mathbf{x}^{a} from Eq. 1; the reconstruction loss enforces a robust bottleneck by passing ground-truth motion through a non-diffused autoencoding loop.

We deploy Social Humanoid on a Unitree G1 using the perception, generation, and control pipeline in Fig. 2 , with most computation offboard. A tripod-mounted ZED 2i stereo camera observes the human partner. We estimate the partner’s SMPL pose using Fast SAM 3D Body [ 61 ] and recover metric root position from stereo depth. AprilTags and onboard odometry localize the humanoid in the same gravity-aligned frame. We encode both agents’ states into the shared interaction representation for DFoT, which autoregressively generates humanoid motion conditioned on observed partner motion and recent humanoid history using 30-step DDIM sampling. NVIDIA SONIC [ 39 ] tracks the decoded motion at 50 Hz. Generation and execution run asynchronously, with 308 ms median latency from camera frame to executed humanoid command. See Appendix A.6 for details.

Social humanoid development is bottlenecked by a lack of human-humanoid interaction datasets. While human-human data is abundant, direct kinematic retargeting fails due to morphology gaps. To this end, we propose an interaction-preserving retargeting method maintaining contact locations, relative poses, and inter-person geometry.

Building on OmniRetarget [ 60 ] ’s Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) and interaction-mesh formulation [ 25 ] , we address a central challenge of dyadic retargeting: bridging the morphology gap without distorting the interaction. Retargeting the humanoid independently can place interaction points out of reach, while uniformly rescaling the pair would make the human partner unrealistically small, creating a mismatch between the people the humanoid interacts with at deployment. We use a two-pass pipeline that retargets the ego, then adapts the partner’s pose—not its scale—to the retargeted humanoid (Fig. 4 ).

Figure 4: Adaptive-HHI Retargeting. Our retargeting pipeline starts from two ground truth humans. In the first pass, we retarget the ego human (orange) to the humanoid using a contact-adaptive weight matrix to encourage body pose in regions close to the physical interaction to be preserved. In a second pass, we co-morph the partner’s pose towards more plausible interaction via a contact-gated morphing strategy driven by the amount of physical contact present in the interaction.

Pass I: Ego-to-humanoid Retargeting. Given an interaction between a source human (the ego) and a partner, this pass retargets the ego to the humanoid, leaving the partner unchanged. Following OmniRetarget [ 25 , 60 ] , we solve a per-frame SQP over the humanoid configuration that preserves the local shape of the ego’s interaction mesh, with Laplacian coordinates scaled to humanoid height, and keeps the humanoid’s wrist and elbow distances to the partner equal to the ego’s. Temporal smoothness and posture regularization complete the objective, subject to joint limits and foot-sticking constraints. Both the shape and distance terms emphasize the wrists, where most contact occurs. The full objective is given in Appendix A.3.1 and our contact-aware grounding in Appendix A.3.3 .

Pass II: Partner Co-Morphing. Pass I leaves the human partner unchanged, causing contact misalignment because the G1 is substantially shorter than the source human. For example, the partner’s hands may reach above the humanoid’s shoulders during hugs. Pass II adapts the partner’s pose to the retargeted humanoid. For all contacts, we apply arm-chain IK over the partner’s shoulder, elbow, and wrist during frames with humanoid arm contact, preserving the source ego–partner wrist and elbow offsets relative to the retargeted humanoid while respecting anatomical joint limits. For high-contact segments, we additionally solve a body-pose QP over key vertex clusters (wrists, chest, and neck), which additionally adjusts the partner’s hips, spine, and knees. This restores contact fidelity across large morphology gaps while preserving realistic human proportions.
We retarget each clip twice, swapping the ego and partner, so both interaction roles are represented in the dataset.

Metrics . We evaluate three tasks. For generative modeling, given the past and current human motion and the past humanoid motion, the high-level policy predicts the humanoid’s reactive motion, which we compare against the retargeted HHI data in terms of positional accuracy, motion dynamics, physical realism, and interaction coordination. For retargeting, we evaluate how faithfully a human–human interaction is transferred to the humanoid. Finally, we evaluate whether the low-level policy can execute the generated motions in simulation and on the real humanoid.

W-MPJPE is the mean per-joint 3D position error in the world frame. MPJVE is the mean per-joint velocity error, which captures temporal smoothness. Foot Skating (FS) is the skating contact ratio, measuring unrealistic foot sliding. Interpenetration (IP) is the penetration depth between human and humanoid body parts. Motion Interaction (MI) is the difference between the ground-truth and predicted correlations of human and humanoid joint positions. Fréchet Distance (FD) compares the distributions of real and generated motion to measure overall quality with respect to the training data. For retargeting, Pose distortion is the root-relative MPJPE (cm) between the humanoid links and the corresponding joints of the human, scaled to humanoid height. E wrist E_{\text{wrist}} (cm) is the mean absolute error between the humanoid–partner wrist distance and the demonstrated ego–partner wrist distance, where partner joints are taken at the homologous SMPL-X joint and the demonstration is scaled to humanoid height. Lower is better for all metrics except contact preservation and success rate.

Baselines . Evaluating socially responsive humanoid interaction is challenging because existing methods either synthesize human-human interactions offline or generate isolated humanoid behaviors without addressing executable cross-embodiment interaction generation. NN retrieves the training window with the lowest L2 distance between normalized partner joint positions in the canonical frame, and RS samples a window uniformly at random.

Sim and Real Humanoid Evaluation. Our retargeting pipeline and high-level policy do not model physics explicitly, so we test whether the generated humanoid motions are physically feasible by executing them with the low-level policy, both in simulation and on the real G1. In simulation, a rollout succeeds if the low-level policy tracks the generated motion without falling or other unsafe behavior; we evaluate 30 generated motions per scenario. On the real humanoid, a trial succeeds if the G1 executes the appropriate reaction and completes the interaction without falling or operator intervention; we run 30 trials per scenario across 4 participants. As Table 4 shows, the low-level policy reproduces nearly all generated motions in simulation (90–100% per scenario), and on the real G1 (Fig. 6 ) success matches simulation in every scenario.

Beyond interaction generation, the shared-codebook VQ-VAE supports shadow teleoperation, in which the humanoid reproduces the whole-body motion of a human operator. As in cross-embodiment translation (Appendix A.4.2 ), we encode the operator’s motion with the human encoder E h E_{h} , quantize it against the shared codebook 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and decode the resulting tokens with the humanoid decoder D r D_{r} . No humanoid motion is used as input, and no optimization-based retargeting is run.

Role of the shared codebook. Shadow teleoperation relies on human and humanoid poses mapping to the same codes, which is enforced by the alignment terms ℒ align \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} and ℒ agree \mathcal{L}_{\text{agree}} in Eq. 3 . Without them, the shared codebook reconstructs each embodiment well but translates poorly, with a human-to-humanoid MPJPE of 12.52 cm; with both terms, this error falls to 2.79 cm and code agreement between paired frames rises from 0.00 to 0.78 (Table A.5 ).

We present Social Humanoid, a system for generating and executing socially responsive whole-body motion on a Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner. It combines a two-phase Adaptive-HHI Retargeting procedure that produces paired human–humanoid data while preserving contact and scale, a shared-codebook VQ-VAE that maps both embodiments into a single discrete latent space, which also enables real-time shadow teleoperation, and a Diffusion Forcing Transformer that generates humanoid responses in this space, executed on the robot via SONIC. Together with the 260-hour HHI Benchmark, we show in simulation and on the real G1 that the system produces coordinated, human-aligned responses across a range of interaction types. We will release our data and code to support further work toward humanoids that coordinate physically with people.

Limitations and Future Work . First, we do not model hand articulation, facial expressions, or object pose, limiting dexterous, expressive, and object-centric interactions. Extending the shared codebook to fine-grained hand motion is a natural next step, while object interaction will likely require additional representation design. Second, we rely on SONIC and off-the-shelf human pose estimation, and inherit their failure modes in real-world deployment. Our system also tracks kinematic trajectories without modeling interaction forces, human comfort, or safety constraints during close contact, so safe deployment in unconstrained environments will require additional safety policies. Third, trackability and trial success measure execution, not social interaction quality; an HRI study is needed to assess the timeliness, naturalness, safety, and appropriateness of the humanoid’s responses. Fourth, we focus on dyadic human–humanoid interaction; extending to multiple humans, robots, or heterogeneous agents is an important direction for future work. Finally, when interacting with the robot, the lack of facial expressions or eye contact makes its behavior difficult to interpret, leading to awkward social interactions. An interesting direction for future work would be to enable more legible social interactions through facial expressions and eye contact.

Table A.1 summarizes our unified human-humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark, constructed by retargeting five popularly used human-human interaction mocap datasets to the Unitree G1 humanoid with our Adaptive-HHI pipeline (Sec. A.3 ). The source datasets span a diverse spectrum of close-range interactive behaviors — from contact-rich dyadic interactions (Chi3D [ 15 ] , Hi4D [ 62 ] ) and in-the-wild multi-person activities (Harmony4D [ 33 ] ) to large-scale captures of multi-person interactions (Inter-X [ 59 ] , Embody 3D [ 44 ] ). In this section, we compare Adaptive-HHI to existing retargeting methods and provide additional implementation details and hyperparameter configurations for our retargeting pipeline.

Table A.2 compares Adaptive-HHI to prior retargeting methods along four axes: hard kinematic feasibility, preservation of inter-agent interaction, partner co-morphing, and adaptive contact handling. Interaction meshes were introduced for close-interaction character animation [ 25 ] and later adapted to biped humanoids [ 46 ] , where Laplacian deformation preserves spatial relationships under hard joint constraints, but only for the robot’s own body parts; the demonstrated interactions are self-contacts, and no human partner enters the optimization. PHC [ 38 ] imitates single-agent motion through a simulated physics policy, so feasibility is implicit and retargeted references can still exhibit motion artifacts. GMR [ 66 ] solves per-frame IK with joint and velocity limits, but its soft keypoint-matching objectives admit foot skating and penetration, and it has no notion of a partner. VideoMimic [ 3 ] adds scene context but handles collision and contact through soft penalties that compete with its matching costs. OmniRetarget [ 60 ] formulates retargeting as an interaction-mesh-regularized SOCP with hard constraints and preserves robot–object–terrain relationships, yet the surrounding scene is a fixed input to the solve, not an optimization variable. This is the core limitation for human–humanoid interaction: when the partner cannot adapt, the robot must absorb the entire embodiment gap, and the interaction breaks. Adaptive-HHI keeps OmniRetarget’s SOCP base and adds (i) partner co-morphing, adapting the partner’s arm configuration to the retargeted humanoid on contact frames so the dyad deforms together, and (ii) wrist- and elbow-distance preservation with wrist-boosted Laplacian weights that concentrate on interaction-critical regions while preserving human-scale structure elsewhere. Adaptive-HHI is the only method that satisfies all four criteria for dyadic human–humanoid interaction.

We observed that pinning the feet to the floor on every frame fails during dynamic maneuvers such as high kicks and vertical jumps, and that the Laplacian term does not constrain global vertical positioning. We resolve this by introducing contact-aware grounding via three complementary terms: (1) velocity-based foot sticking , inherited from OmniRetarget , holds a foot’s horizontal position fixed only during stance intervals estimated from toe velocity; (2) per-frame ground shifting applies a smoothed correction to the robot base height, aligning with the floor during stance and tracking the source sole height during airborne phases, which we detect as runs of 3–30 frames with the sole more than 4 cm above a rolling-minimum floor estimate; and (3) ankle posture priors combine foot-keypoint downweighting with a diagonal ankle-pitch prior to suppress toe-down artifacts arising from human–humanoid foot mismatches.

Table A.4 lists the hyperparameters used throughout the retargeting pipeline. All values were kept constant across all five source datasets. The distance weights reflect the contact semantics of dyadic interaction: wrist terms receive the largest weights since wrist placement dominates contact in our data (high-fives, handshakes, pushes), and elbow terms anchor the upper-arm orientation. The grounding parameters operate at the temporal scale of flight phases (3–30 frames at 30 Hz), separating genuine jumps from foot roll and capture drift, and the small smoothing width ( σ = 1 \sigma=1 frame) removes solver jitter without attenuating fast maneuvers such as kicks.

To translate a human motion into humanoid motion, we encode it with the human encoder E h \mathrm{E}_{h} , quantize it against the shared codebook 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , and decode the resulting tokens with the humanoid decoder D r \mathrm{D}_{r} . No humanoid motion is used at inference, and no optimization-based retargeting is run. Translation is therefore a single feed-forward pass through the tokenizer. We evaluate it on held-out paired clips from the HHI benchmark, where the retargeted humanoid motion serves as ground truth for the translated output.

We train the shared-codebook VQ-VAE and DFoT models using the AdamW optimizer with an initial learning rate of 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , a weight decay of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , and a mini-batch size of 256. The learning rate is cosine-decayed to zero over the course of training. Both the Shared-Codebook VQ-VAE and DFoT architectures utilize GELU activations and LayerNorm layers in their feed-forward blocks, and the DFoT model relies on a standard post-norm Transformer encoder architecture.

For the DFoT, we adopt a discrete diffusion formulation with an x 0 x_{0} -prediction parameterization. During training, we sample a diffusion timestep t ∈ { 1 , … , 1000 } t\in\{1,\dots,1000\} independently for each agent token to prevent architectural shortcutting, training the network to reconstruct the corresponding clean motion token x 0 x_{0} . At inference time, we employ deterministic DDIM sampling over 30 steps. Unless otherwise stated, each VQ-VAE model is trained for 100,000 steps, and each DFoT model is trained for 300,000 steps. Final checkpoints are selected based on the lowest validation loss.

All training experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU with 48 GB of VRAM. Under the configuration detailed in Table A.6 , a full DFoT model convergence requires approximately 1 day of training time.

Shared-codebook VQ-VAE. Each agent’s motion is encoded by an embodiment-specific 1D convolutional encoder operating along the temporal axis with a compression factor of ω = 4 \omega{=}4 , mapping per-agent pose features of dimension D in D_{\text{in}} (with D h D_{h} for the human and D r D_{r} for the humanoid) into a shared latent space of dimension d vq = 512 d_{\text{vq}}{=}512 . Both embodiments quantize against a single codebook of K = 512 K{=}512 entries updated via exponential moving average, which encourages a common motion vocabulary across the human–humanoid embodiment gap; embodiment-specific decoders mirror their encoders to reconstruct each agent’s pose representation.

The high-level policy operates on unified motion tokens of dimension D m D_{\text{m}} , which augment the VQ latents with localized cross-agent transformations ( 4 × 9 × P 4\times 9\times P pairwise relative features). Per-token noise levels and agent identity are injected through sinusoidal and learned embeddings, respectively, concatenated with the motion tokens and projected to the model dimension d = 512 d{=}512 . Temporal position is encoded with RoPE, and the core consists of 6 Transformer blocks with 8 attention heads attending jointly over time and agents (sequence length T ′ × P T^{\prime}\times P ). A linear head maps back to D m D_{\text{m}} .

We implement a real-time system for Social Humanoid interaction. The system consists of a unified robot-human perception stack, followed by the high-level and low-level policies. This section describes the perception stack, system architecture, and the end-to-end latency.

We use an exoview ZED 2i camera to capture RGB+D at 1280x720 and 15 Hz (the capture rate is bandwidth-limited, see Sec. A.6.4 ). To estimate the gravity direction 𝐧 \mathbf{n} and camera-to-floor-distance d d , we capture 30 depth frames, apply per-pixel temporal median, and backproject to a point cloud in the camera optical frame. We fit a plane 𝐧 ⊤ ​ 𝐩 = d \mathbf{n}^{\top}\mathbf{p}=d with RANSAC under the constraints ‖ 𝐧 ‖ = 1 \|\mathbf{n}\|=1 and d > 0 d>0 , and refine the winning hypothesis via SVD on the inliers. To separate the ground plane from other flat surfaces, we: (i) enforce gravity direction 𝐧 ⊤ ​ 𝐩 ¯ > 0 \mathbf{n}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{p}}>0 for the inlier centroid 𝐩 ¯ \bar{\mathbf{p}} , (ii) use directionality heuristic requiring a normal that is sufficiently vertical, and (iii) require a minimum inlier count.
Table A.7: End-to-End Latency.
