Given per-frame RGB+D, we want to estimate the human’s SMPL pose and full SE(3) pelvis pose in a gravity-aligned, floor-origin camera frame C gcam C_{\text{gcam}} . We detect humans with YOLOv11 and pass each detection to Fast Sam 3D Body (FS3DB) [ 61 ] , which consists of an optimized MHR head and an MHR-to-SMPL regressor. Because the regressor is not trained to preserve global orientation, we recover orientation by using the Kabsch algorithm between corresponding regressed SMPL vertices and MHR vertices in the camera frame. To recover translation, we query a depth patch at selected vertices on the torso to get estimates for the pelvis depth. We perform outlier rejection using z z -buffer occlusion and MAD, aggregate the predictions by the detector’s confidence on the vertices, and then backproject the 2D pelvis using the camera intrinsics. A constant-velocity Kalman filter smooths the resulting trajectory against noisy depth. This yields T h → C cam T_{h\to C_{\text{cam}}} for every detected human, which we convert to T h → C gcam T_{h\to C_{\text{gcam}}} using ( 𝐧 , d ) (\mathbf{n},d) .

To maintain identities across frames, we construct and run a Kalman filter per tracked human. For each incoming frame, we KF-predict each active track and use the Hungarian algorithm on 3D Euclidian distance to assign each detected human to a track. Unassigned humans are allocated new tracks, and unassigned tracks retire after several consecutive misses. The robot maintains interaction with a single track determined on startup by the closest human. If no humans are visible, the high-level policy can switch from partner-conditioned prediction to joint prediction.

We place 8x8 inch AprilTags from the 36h11 family on the front and rear of the robot. During an initialization phase, we use the AprilTags to derive an estimate of the robot’s SE(3) pelvis pose T r 0 → C cam T_{r_{0}\to C_{\text{cam}}} and similarly use ( 𝐧 , d ) (\mathbf{n},d) to convert to T r 0 → C gcam T_{r_{0}\to C_{\text{gcam}}} . The robot is positioned so that at least one tag is unoccluded during calibration. At inference time, we use an onboard, proprioception-based state estimation available in the Unitree SDK. Because the estimator is with respect to some canonical frame determined on robot startup, we use the estimator to compute T r → r 0 T_{r\to r_{0}} , and compose it with the calibration estimate to get T r → C gcam T_{r\to C_{\text{gcam}}} . Empirically, the Unitree estimator is sufficiently stable for our interaction scenarios.

A laptop connected to the ZED 2i and the Unitree G1 performs time synchronization and publishes the RGB+D images and the robot estimation plus proprioception as a bundle at 15 Hz. Due to FS3DB’s compute requirements, we connect the laptop to a remote server using WiFi. We JPEG-compress the RGB stream and apply Zstd compression on the depth stream to maximize streaming rate. We run two instances of FS3DB with a global estimation coordinator at 15 Hz to tolerate variations in GPU load. The coordinator bundles the human and robot estimates and sends them to the high-level policy, which interpolates the incoming data to 30 Hz, performs inference, and emits chunks of 30 Hz robot motions at 7.5 Hz. Finally, SONIC interpolates the motions to 50 Hz and tracks them by providing desired DoF angles for a PD controller. We run inference on 2x NVIDIA 4090 GPUs for global human estimation, 1x NVIDIA 4090 GPU for the high-level policy, and 1x NVIDIA 4060 Mobile GPU for the low-level policy.

We support two optional improvements upon the existing system which tradeoff latency to improve motion generation quality and stability. After DFoT inference, we delay the emission of robot motion chunks by 1 chunk to improve decoded motion continuity. For robustness against deviations in network latency and other sources of variation, SONIC maintains a buffer of previous motion and delays execution by 100 ms.

We evaluate the end-to-end latency of our pipeline. In Table A.7 , we report the 50 and 95-percentile latencies ( n = 200 n=200 ), splitting the evaluation by stage. Stage 1: perception , which includes (i) fetch : retrieving the RGB+D image from the camera, (ii) sync : synchronization with robot estimation and construction of bundle, (iii) wire : network and blocking on input on the server-side, (iv) JPEG+zstd : compression encoding and decoding. Stage 2: human estimation, which bundles distributed coordination, FS3DB inference, and global estimation. Stage 3: high-level policy, which includes (i) interpolate : interpolation of SMPL from 15 → \to 30 Hz, (ii) VQ-VAE : encoding and decoding, (iii) DFoT : DFoT inference, (iv) postproc (optional): buffered decoding to improve motion continuity. Stage 4: low-level policy, which includes (i) SONIC : construction of observations, policy inference, sending commands to G1, (ii) wire : network transport back to laptop, (iii) wire buffer (optional): execution delay to improve tolerance to variation. We highlight optional components which tradeoff motion generation quality for latency. In reactive regimes, we achieve a median latency of 308ms.

We validate safety progressively, from simulation to a gantry-supported robot to gantryless deployment. SONIC holds a standing pose until a dedicated operator, separate from the person interacting with the robot, engages it, and then smoothly executes high-level policy (HLP) frames. We clamp the desired yaw change to 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} /s. SONIC smoothly returns to standing if consecutive HLP predictions differ by more than 0.7 ​ rad 0.7\,\text{rad} , or if the operator judges the behavior unsafe. Across five 60 s rollouts, we observed no unsafe generated behavior. Note that the low-level policy is neither force-adaptive nor force-compliant, so physical contact is not actively regulated.

analysis.overview: Social Humanoid的可复用选择是离线重定向时同时适配伙伴姿态、在分离的人/机器人编码器之间用共享码本加双重对齐，再让DFoT在联合时序中生成G1反应。最清楚的机制证据是同样共享码本下，加对齐使跨形态翻译12.52→2.79cm，而各自重建本来已较好。系统在六类互动上有真机执行，但轨迹指标、执行成功与社交质量不同；3张4090加4060Mobile的部署、308/541ms两种缓冲配置及无主动接触力调节必须一并考虑。
analysis.notice: 完整阅读120个原文提取片段，覆盖正文、方法、全部实验及附录A.1–A.6.6。固定版本PDF25页；目视核对物理页7/8/9/18/21/23/24的主表1–4、消融表A.3/A.5、配置A.6、延迟A.7与部署图。其他图像未逐张目视核查，未独立审计数据划分、源码、项目视频或复现作者实验。表1/2的部分指标未标单位，延迟total的分位估计方法和若干采样/训练细节留作缺口。

findings.title: 形态差异需要进入离线配对数据，而不是只在生成后修机器人
findings.text: 独立把一个人重定向为矮小G1会破坏双方接触和可达关系；统一缩小两个人又会改变真实人类尺度。该方法先改ego为29DoF G1，再在保留partner人体比例的前提下调整partner姿态，生成配对训练数据；高层直接生成人形机器人运动，SONIC负责跟踪。此处“社会响应”主要来自人体运动条件，不包括语言意图或情绪识别。

findings.title: 两遍重定向：腕肘距离约束后，按接触对伙伴做IK/QP
findings.text: Pass I逐帧SQP在关节限制、trust region和足部粘滞约束下，联合匹配按身高缩放的Laplacian局部形状、ego/机器人到partner的腕肘距离，另加时序平滑和姿态先验。Pass II在接触帧对partner肩肘腕做arm-chain IK，高接触段再对腕/胸/颈簇的body-pose QP调整髋、脊柱与膝；不是在线把现实伙伴强行变形。每clip交换角色处理两次。附录接触阈值源mesh5cm、腕/肘距离权重50/25，足部还有按支撑/腾空分段的高度修正。

findings.title: 接触消融：只加权重会增脚滑，距离保真组合才更稳
findings.text: CHI3D表A.3：OmniRetarget腕误差1.379±0.550cm、接触保留0.915±0.160、脚滑0.009±0.015；加接触自适应权重后0.976±0.534、0.933±0.131、0.014±0.018；完整接触/可达保真组合为0.501±0.290、0.936±0.119、0.0034±0.010，腕误差约降64%。这支持围绕互动距离设计目标，且提示简单加权的副作用。表中是clip均值±std而非配对置信区间，未单独隔离partner co-morphing每个子模块贡献。

findings.title: 三数据集重定向改善几何指标，RL执行成功不总有提升空间
findings.text: 表3相对OmniRetarget，CHI3D腕误差1.379→0.501cm、Hi4D1.729→0.804、Harmony4D2.981→1.909；对应接触保留0.915→0.936、0.827→0.881、0.676→0.775。Harmony4D下游RL成功81→97%，但CHI3D/Hi4D两者均100%，不能写为所有数据集执行率都提高。机器人没有真实参考mocap，pose distortion是对按G1身高缩放的源人示范进行比较，partner又被调整；几何吻合不是接触力或人类舒适度真值。

findings.title: 共享的是码本，跨形态编码器/解码器仍分开
findings.text: 人用21×6关节旋转，G1用29关节角；canonical根变换和跨agent相对位姿保留空间关系。各自1D Conv/ResNet时间压缩4倍，512维latent量化到同一个512-entry EMA码本，解码器也各自独立。除码本外并不共享tokenizer权重。连续对齐拉近配对encoder输出，离散对齐用距离logits的对称CE和stop-gradient目标约束码分配；仅共享参数表并不保证同姿态同码。

findings.title: 最强机制对照：自重建好不代表跨形态可用
findings.text: 表A.5固定共享码本，无对齐时人/机器人自重建3.665/2.809cm，但人→机器人12.520cm、FD0.2062、配对同码率0。双对齐后人→机器人2.793cm、FD0.0028、同码率0.780；自重建3.556/2.613cm，改变小得多。连续单独/离散单独翻译3.240/3.063cm、同码率0.508/0.634，双项最好。此为held-out HHI配对clip、root-relative MPJPE，机器人“真值”来自离线重定向；不等于现实接触定位误差。

findings.title: DFoT在人与机器人token上独立加噪，采样表控制补全方式
findings.text: 高层把VQ latent与跨agent相对变换一起输入6层、8头、宽512的Transformer，加agent embedding、逐token noise embedding及RoPE。训练future各frame/agent独立noise level，history保持干净，预测干净latent并辅以解码运动与自重建损失（权重1/0.5/0.5）；推理确定性DDIM30步。改变agent×time采样噪声表可做反应、共同预测或partner补全，不需为每种日程重训。没有单独遮挡长度/丢帧强度的定量扫参，不能把架构支持补全写成任意遮挡下稳定。

findings.title: 260小时来自重定向mocap，划分与泛化需按来源解释
findings.text: HHI把五个人–人mocap源重定向为人–G1并统一30FPS，表A.1约260小时，其中Embody3D220.97h、Inter-X37.50h，另外三源合计不足2h；不是260小时真实人机互动采集。作者给80/10/10划分，但未明确到可核查的subject/session/source-clip分组协议，交换双角色是否同组也需数据清单确认，不断言存在泄漏。VQ100k、DFoT300k steps、batch256，AdamW2e-4，单A6000 48GB上DFoT约1天；验证loss选checkpoint。没有同等长尾来源与未见参与者的全面分层统计。

findings.title: 高层预测更准，但检索的分布距离和脚接触仍更好
findings.text: 表1对R2R：W-MPJPE0.545→0.128、MPJVE0.019→0.007、IP0.088→0.051、MI0.088→0.002。NN的FD0.053优于本方法0.118，脚滑NN0.138、RS0.134也远低于本方法0.876；不能称所有物理/生成指标最佳。NN/RS重放训练运动，既可保持脚接触，又难对齐当前伙伴，因此需要同时看互动与分布指标。主表未为所有列标明单位，本卡不把0.128擅自转换成cm或与A.5的root-relative cm直接混比。

findings.title: 高层消融支持组合收益，未单独识别共享码本的因果贡献
findings.text: HHI-Chi3D表2：No VQ / Sep VQ /完整模型的FD0.253/0.181/0.072、W-MPJPE0.075/0.085/0.057、MPJVE0.007/0.007/0.005。完整模型脚滑0.845不如Sep0.833，MI0.019略差No VQ0.018。Sep同时改变“独立码本+无对齐”，故这一对照不能完全区分码本共享与显式alignment；A.5固定共享码本再去对齐更能解释迁移机制。表2是Chi3D子集，与表1全HHI不可当同一个测试统计相减。

findings.title: 六场景有真机执行，90–100%不是参与者研究结论
findings.text: 表4六场景（握手、挥手、击掌、拥抱、弯身、挽臂）sim与real均为100/100/90/100/100/100%。每场景sim30条生成motion，real总30次试验覆盖4位参与者，不是每人30次；真机成功定义适当反应并完成、无摔倒或操作员干预。表格未报告参与者分层、置信区间或独立多次训练；90%有限试验不等于普遍稳定性。执行与tracking指标不是及时性、自然度、舒适度或社会适宜性评估，作者明确需要HRI study。

findings.title: 部署频率分层：15Hz感知、7.5Hz运动块、50Hz底层
findings.text: 外置ZED2i RGB-D1280×720、15Hz；YOLO+FastSAM3DBody估计人体，用深度/MAD/Kabsch/Kalman恢复并跟踪全局姿态，AprilTag初始化机器人坐标后接Unitree本体状态估计。启动时只选最近的人作为单一伙伴，丢失时可切共同预测。WiFi向远程server传JPEG+zstd；两张4090做人体估计，一张4090跑高层，一张4060Mobile跑SONIC。高层输入插值到30Hz并以7.5Hz发30Hz运动块，SONIC插值50Hz再供PD；50Hz是跟踪频率，不能当相机到动作的新信息响应率或机载单GPU性能。

findings.title: 延迟308ms对应少缓冲配置，表中的max也非最坏时延保证
findings.text: A.7 n=200列total(min) p50/p95为308.1/376.2ms，total(max)541.1/609.2ms；增加一次chunk连续性缓冲约133ms与SONIC100ms后差233ms，因此min/max是可选缓冲组合的表述，不宜理解成观测最小/绝对最坏值。DFoT本身50.4/58.5ms只是子阶段，不能当端到端；高层103.2/118.2ms还含插值及VQ等。各主阶段p50和p95分别恰好相加等于total（本轮算术核查），但正文未明确联合端到端样本分位还是阶段分位加总；不能据此额外保证联合p95。也未给每项互动采用何种缓冲配置的配对成功率。

findings.title: 接触执行边界：运动学可跟踪，不是力顺应或开放环境安全证明
findings.text: 系统不建模手指、脸、物体位姿，也不建模互动接触力、人类舒适度或安全约束；依赖外部人体估计和SONIC。附录有独立操作员启用、yaw变化限45度/s、相邻HLP差超过0.7rad回站立及人工停止；5次60秒rollout未见不安全生成只是有限观察。低层明确非force-adaptive、非force-compliant，不能把拥抱成功率当已调节接触力的证据。多人数数据来源也不等于已部署多伙伴策略，当前仍双人互动。影子遥操作可Eh→码本→Dr单次前向，无在线优化，但精度参考仍来自重定向配对。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：给定共享码本后，对齐收益能否迁移到未见伙伴条件？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：配对显式对齐带来的收益不止是同一重定向轨迹上的姿态翻译，还能在未见伙伴姿态和感知缺失时改善互动响应。先在公开HHI内固定同一分组划分、重定向数据、512码本容量和训练步数，比较无对齐、连续单项、离散单项、双项四组，并分别用相同高层DFoT配置训练；分组按原始source clip和双角色副本绑定，若有subject/session标签再按其隔离。用held-out伙伴体型/接触动作及受控0/133/267ms丢帧测试，每组至少3训练seed；报告H→R root-relative MPJPE、同码率、反应时差、腕距离误差、脚滑、生成穿透及SONIC仿真跟踪失败率，分开给干净/扰动条件和各来源。保持动作块缓冲及底层相同，并单列端到端延迟；全部为离线/仿真验证，不安排真人接触实验。若双项只降低翻译误差却不能改善未见伙伴互动指标，或收益在source分组后消失，则推翻其可泛化到互动响应的解释；若脚滑明显恶化，也不能只凭位置精度宣称更优。该实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已证明机制或研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: Social Humanoid：共享动作码本加配对对齐，直接生成人机互动反应
frontier_brief.change_type: 人形控制 · 跨形态表示
frontier_brief.delta: 离线将ego重定向为G1并调整partner姿态保住互动几何；人/机器人独立tokenizer共享一个码本并显式对齐，再由DFoT联合生成运动、SONIC跟踪。
frontier_brief.before: 独立重定向会丢接触关系；仅把不同形态量化到同一词表，也可能各自重建良好却无法跨形态解码。
frontier_brief.after: 固定共享码本后，加入连续+离散配对对齐使H→R翻译MPJPE12.52→2.79cm、同码率0→0.78；高层直接输出G1运动，不必每次生成后再在线做优化重定向。
frontier_brief.relevance: 需要把人体互动mocap迁移到G1时，应把接触距离、partner适配和token对齐纳入数据/表示设计；用跨解码消融检验共享词表是否真正可迁移。

passages.section: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
passages.location: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
passages.text: Reliable robotic manipulation requires both semantic understanding and precise control in three-dimensional space. However, vision-language-action (VLA) foundations largely inherit visual representations from 2D vision-language pre-training, while spatial supervision is often introduced only during task-specific adaptation. Developing spatial understanding as a transferable foundation-model capability therefore calls for learning from broader robot experience. We present SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that scales implicit spatial alignment to continual pre-training and maintains it during downstream post-training. Initialized from a pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, SLA jointly optimizes action prediction and alignment between intermediate visual embeddings and spatial representations from a frozen 3D perception model. We curate and unify heterogeneous robot datasets to support spatial learning across diverse embodiments, tasks, and scenes. To accommodate this diversity, we introduce feature-dependent gates that adaptively aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. The teacher further exploits partially available depth and camera calibration alongside RGB observations, enabling effective use of heterogeneous geometric annotations. Probabilistic state dropout encourages reliance on visual cues and mitigates overfitting to demonstration trajectories. All auxiliary components are used only during training, allowing direct reuse of pretrained VLA weights and preserving the original inference architecture. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that SLA achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboDojo-Real, RoboTwin 2.0 under the Clean2Random setting, RoboCasa-Panda, and LIBERO-Plus, highlighting its strong generalization and downstream data efficiency. Across eight real-world deployment conditions, SLA further improves the average success rate over π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} by 24.0 percentage points.

passages.section: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
passages.location: SLA: Scaling Spatial-Language-Action Model via Continual Pre-training
passages.text: Figure 1 : SLA unifies heterogeneous robot data, aligns intermediate visual embeddings with frozen 3D features during training, and improves benchmark and real-world manipulation performance.

The development of robotic manipulation hinges on integrating semantic reasoning with accurate physical control in the 3D real world. Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Black et al., 2025 ; Intelligence, 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Team et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) , capable of instruction following and robotic action execution, have attracted significant attention. By combining the pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with action experts learning on diverse robot demonstrations, these models offer a promising foundation for general-purpose manipulation. However, successful manipulation requires not only recognizing objects and understanding instructions but also executing precise actions in the 3D physical world. Typical 2D VLA foundation models inherit knowledge from VLMs pretrained on 2D image–text pairs and learn robot control without explicitly incorporating 3D physical knowledge during pre-training. This limits their reliability in scenes that demand fine-grained spatial reasoning.

A direct approach to improving spatial understanding is to introduce 3D modalities during post-training on top of a pretrained 2D VLA foundation model. Several approaches ( Li et al., 2026a ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026c ) use depth maps or point clouds obtained from depth cameras or other 3D sensors, encode their geometric information, and feed it into the VLM backbone or action head. However, some limitations make it difficult to develop a universal and scalable 3D strategy for this paradigm: (1) Reliable 3D sensor data is hard to acquire, as measured depth maps and point clouds can be noisy or incomplete. (2) Robotic sensors vary in types, positions, and calibration status, which introduces substantial heterogeneity into the data. (3) Portions of existing large-scale robot datasets ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Brohan et al., 2022 ) do not include depth information, which limits the potential of scaling.

To address these questions, Spatial Forcing ( Li et al., 2025a ) has propose a implicit 3D representation alignment strategy to enbow 2D VLA with spatial intelligence without explicit demand of depth information. However, Spatial Forcing still concentrate on post-training, leaving spatial competence as a task-specific add-on and limiting the development of scalable 3D VLA foundation models with transferable spatial understanding.

Recently, continual pre-training has been widely adopted as a means of developing specific capabilities at scale while preserving the knowledge acquired during foundation model pre-training ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026b ) . Motivated by this approach, we propose to build on the strong 2D foundation model and develop spatial understanding through continual pre-training, laying the foundation for subsequent adaptation. We therefore propose SLA , a robotic foundation model with generalized spatial understanding capabilities developed through implicit representation alignment during both continual pre-training and post-training. Intuitively, action generation is conditioned on visual and linguistic representations, making the spatial content of visual tokens directly relevant to action. Higher-quality visual tokens that contain richer spatial information can facilitate generating more precise manipulation actions. Inspired by this, we align the intermediate visual embeddings of the VLA with external spatial representations extracted from a frozen 3D perception foundation model. This spatial alignment objective complements the standard action-learning objective, encouraging the policy to internalize geometric information in the representations used for action prediction. Crucially, this supervision requires no changes to the pretrained VLA architecture or the action-generation head. We can therefore initialize the policy directly from the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} foundation ( Intelligence, 2025 ) and continue training from its learned robotic knowledges. This architectural compatibility allows spatial supervision to shape the foundation model while retaining access to the general knowledge encoded in its pretrained weights.

Technically, to support continual pre-training across heterogeneous robot data, we combines a unified training corpus. We curate multiple large-scale public datasets covering diverse embodiments, tasks, scenes, and visual appearances, and unify their state and action annotations through consistent end-effector representations and coordinate conventions. This processing provides a common basis for learning how different robots act in space. The resulting visual diversity also makes a single manually chosen alignment layer restrictive: a certain intermediate visual layer of VLA models suited to one domain data may not be equally suitable for another. We therefore develop adaptive layer selection mechanism, using feature-dependent gates to aggregate visual embeddings from multiple VLA layers for spatial supervision. In addition, we adopt OmniVGGT ( Peng et al., 2025 ) as the external 3D perception foundation to exploit partially available camera calibrations and depth annotations alongside RGB images. We further introduce probabilistic state dropout during training to mitigate overfitting to demonstration trajectories and encourage the policy to make better use of visual cues, thereby improving generalization. After continual pre-training, we retain spatial alignment during post-training to adapt the resulting foundation model to specific down-streaming tasks. The teacher, alignment projector, and layer-selection gates are used only during training. At deployment, the policy retains its original inference architecture without requiring the external perception model, alignment projector, or layer-selection gates.

Extensive evaluations across three public simulation benchmarks, one public real-world benchmark, and eight real-world deployment conditions are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our SLA. On LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , it achieves an overall success rate of 87.4% under diverse observation, language, and scene perturbations, outperforming the compared baselines. On RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , training on clean demonstrations yields a 72.3% success rate in the Clean2Random setting and a 79.2% average across Clean2Clean and Clean2Random, demonstrating generalization beyond the training conditions. On RoboCasa-Panda ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) , SLA achieves 68.4% success with only 50 downstream demonstrations per task, exceeding compared policies trained with 300–3,000 demonstrations per task. On RoboDojo-Real ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , a single policy adapted across three embodiments achieves 33.9% overall success, compared with 12.8% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , supporting its applicability to real robot manipulation. Our eight deployment conditions further examine bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following. SLA achieves the highest success rate among the compared methods in every condition, averaging 83.8% and improving over π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} by 24.0 percentage points. Controlled data-scaling experiments further show that applying spatial alignment in both training stages outperforms either single-stage alternative at every tested data proportion. Together, these results support developing spatial understanding during continual pre-training and stengthen it during downstream adaptation.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
We introduce SLA, a robotic foundation model that implicitly enforces the integration of visual embeddings in VLAs with external spatial representations.
We extend SLA to continual pre-training on a carefully curated and unified corpus of public robot datasets, developing a spatially informed foundation model.

We apply SLA training principle during downstream post-training and demonstrate strong benchmark performance, together with bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following.

VLA foundation models learn generalist manipulation policies from large, diverse datasets and adapt them to downstream tasks. Cross-embodiment datasets ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Brohan et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2024 ; Allshire et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) have accelerated this development. OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2025 ) , RDT-1B ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and GR00T N1 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) learn language-conditioned action prediction from robot demonstrations, while GR-2 ( Cheang et al., 2024 ) combines large-scale video pre-training with policy learning on robot trajectories. To improve task understanding, RT-H ( Belkhale et al., 2024 ) and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Intelligence, 2025 ) adopt language-conditioned task hierarchies, whereas MolmoAct ( Lee et al., 2026 ) and MolmoAct2 ( Fang et al., 2026 ) incorporate action reasoning into robot control. RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and Xiaomi-Robotics-0 ( Cai et al., 2026b ) also co-train on robot and vision-language data to support semantic generalization and instruction following. The scarcity of teleoperated robot data has further motivated alternative sources of supervision. HumanScale ( Ma et al., 2026 ) investigates pre-training on egocentric human videos followed by adaptation with robot data. Separately, the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) ( Chi et al., 2024 ) enables portable demonstration collection using handheld grippers without requiring robots at collection sites. RDT2 ( Liu et al., 2026a ) and Xiaomi-Robotics-1 ( Team et al., 2026b ) exploit UMI data to expand training scale and coverage of environments and tasks. These advances support generalist action learning, but data scaling alone does not specify how geometric representations should be supervised during pre-training. Our complementary goal is to develop 3D spatial understanding in an existing VLA foundation model through spatially supervised continual pre-training.

Existing 3D VLA methods introduce geometry through explicit inputs, feature fusion, or representation supervision. PointVLA ( Li et al., 2026a ) and GeoVLA ( Sun et al., 2025 ) integrate point cloud features into action prediction. BridgeVLA ( Li et al., 2026c ) projects 3D observations into multi-view images; and FALCON ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) extracts geometric tokens from spatial foundation models for fusion within the action head. These approaches still require additional geometric input extraction at deployment. Another works use training-time supervision to encode spatial structure in internal policy representations. ROCKET ( Sun et al., 2026 ) explores multilayer spatial alignment, VEGA ( Wang et al., 2026a ) supervises visual encoder outputs, and Mind-VLA ( Ding et al., 2026 ) introduces instruction-aware alignment of target-object representations. Such approaches emphasize adding 3D capabilities during post-training on top of generic 2D VLA pre-training ( Intelligence, 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) , leaving spatial understanding as a supplementary capability rather than establishing a scalable 3D-aware foundation. Recent studies incorporate geometry into pre-training through egocentric spatial embeddings ( Qu et al., 2025 ) , egocentric 3D annotations ( Feng et al., 2026 ) , and object pose estimation ( Lin et al., 2026 ) . However, these 3D-aware pre-training efforts remain relatively limited in scale compared with large-scale 2D VLA pre-training. In contrast, we build on pretrained 2D VLA through continual pre-training to develop generalizable 3D-aware foundation models.

Continual pre-training extends the domain capabilities of existing foundation models through further large-scale pre-training, providing a basis for downstream adaptation. Early studies ( Lee et al., 2020 ; Alsentzer et al., 2019 ; Araci, 2019 ; Chalkidis et al., 2020 ; Gururangan et al., 2020 ) focus on adapting to domain-specific data distributions. Llemma ( Azerbayev et al., 2024 ) strengthens mathematical reasoning through continual pre-training on mathematical text and code. AgentFounder ( Su et al., 2026b ) uses diverse reasoning and action data to establish a foundation for agent capabilities before post-training. Recent efforts extend this paradigm to robotics: ET-VLA ( Li and Peng, 2025 ) uses synthetic data for continual pre-training to transfer existing VLAs to new embodiments, whereas AXIS ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) investigates how policy performance scales with data. These VLA efforts primarily focus on training data sources. In contrast, we use implicit spatial alignment framework during continual pre-training to develop generalizable 3D spatial understanding while preserving the pretrained VLA backbone architecture.

SLA aims to develop a scalable 3D VLA foundation model through continual pre-training. Starting from a pretrained 2D VLA backbone ( Intelligence, 2025 ) , we use external spatial representation supervision to shape its visual representations while retaining its backbone and action-generation architecture. Section 3.1 motivates this approach, Section 3.2 presents the model and training mechanisms, and Section 3.3 describes the continual-pre-training corpus and its unified processing.

VLA models are built upon pretrained VLMs and generate actions through specialized designs for action experts. A θ \theta -parameterized VLM model employs multiple causal attention layers in an auto-regressive manner to generate the next tokens, formed as 𝒙 t ∼ p θ ​ ( 𝒙 t ∣ 𝒙 < t ) , \bm{x}_{t}\sim p_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{t}\mid\bm{x}_{<t}), where { 𝒙 t } t = 1 T \{\bm{x}_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} denotes a sequence of tokens.

When adapted to VLA models, three modalities of information will be processed: vision, text, and action. The vision modality consists of multi-view images captured by robots, which are transformed into N N visual tokens { 𝒙 t 𝒱 } t = 1 N \{\bm{x}_{t}^{\mathcal{V}}\}_{t=1}^{N} through pretrained visual encoders such as DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2023 ) or SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) . The text modality consists of task instructions, which are converted into M M linguistic tokens { 𝒙 t ℒ } t = 1 M \{\bm{x}_{t}^{\mathcal{L}}\}_{t=1}^{M} by a text tokenizer. Then, the VLA models generate K K action tokens { 𝒙 t 𝒜 } t = 1 K \{\bm{x}_{t}^{\mathcal{A}}\}_{t=1}^{K} conditioned on the preceding visual and linguistic tokens:

𝒙 t 𝒜 ∼ p θ ​ ( 𝒙 t 𝒜 ∣ { 𝒙 i 𝒱 } i = 1 N , { 𝒙 j ℒ } j = 1 M , 𝒙 < t 𝒜 ) , \bm{x}_{t}^{\mathcal{A}}\sim p_{\theta}\big(\bm{x}_{t}^{\mathcal{A}}\mid\{\bm{x}_{i}^{\mathcal{V}}\}_{i=1}^{N},\{\bm{x}_{j}^{\mathcal{L}}\}_{j=1}^{M},\bm{x}_{<t}^{\mathcal{A}}\big), (1)
ℒ action = ℒ ⁡ [ 𝒢 ⁡ ( { 𝒙 t 𝒜 } t = 1 K ) , A g ​ t ] , \displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}=\mathcal{L}[\mathcal{G}(\{\bm{x}_{t}^{\mathcal{A}}\}_{t=1}^{K}),A_{gt}], (2)

where ℒ ⁡ [ ⋅ , ⋅ ] \mathcal{L}[\cdot,\cdot] denotes the training loss ( e.g. L1, L2, or cross-entropy loss), 𝒢 \mathcal{G} denotes the trainable action expert ( e.g. multi-layer MLP or flow-matching head ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) ). Equation 1 illustrates that the visual tokens as intermediate scene representations play a crucial role in generating action tokens and should be supervised properly.

Since VLA models must capture 3D information and reason about the relative positions between robots and objects to generate precise spatial movements, we hypothesize that the 3D information is implicitly embedded within the visual embeddings of VLAs. Such embeddings would allow action tokens to acquire 3D cues through the auto-regressive mechanism during inference.

To evaluate this hypothesis, we follow linear probing ( He et al., 2020 ; Wu et al., 2025a ) to conduct a lightweight depth probing experiment. Specifically, we freeze all the parameters of a VLA model ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and only train a DPT head ( Ranftl et al., 2021 ) to transform the visual embeddings of VLA to depth maps. This enables us to quantify the richness of spatial information embedded in the VLA representation space. As shown in Figure 2 , the probing results show that visual embeddings learned solely from 2D images do not produce meaningful spatial structures, suggesting a limited capacity of the model to encode 3D structure information without explicit spatial input or guidance.

Figure 2 : Depth probing of the visual embeddings of VLAs. Embeddings learned solely from 2D images without alignment do not produce meaningful spatial structures. The aligned embeddings inherently contain rich spatial information, leading to better performance in depth probing.

However, bridging this 3D physical gap through additional sensor inputs or depth-estimation modules would change the architecture of the original 2D VLA foundation model and may disrupt the general knowledge already acquired during its pre-training. We therefore seek a training strategy that reuses the existing VLA architecture and pretrained parameters to unlock its generalizable understanding of the 3D physical world through continual pre-training.

Our main philosophy is to employ external supervision signals to supervise the visual tokens 𝒙 𝒱 \bm{x}^{\mathcal{V}} . To provide the signals with rich spatial information, we first input a set of multi-view images ℐ \mathcal{I} into a frozen external 3D perception foundation model f 3 ​ D f^{\mathrm{3D}} , which outputs pixel-level 3D representations f 3 ​ D ​ ( ℐ ) f^{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{I}) for each image. Available geometric annotations like camera parameters and depth images are also provided to this external 3D foundation model, as described in Section 3.2.2 . Additionally, these spatial representations are augmented with positional embeddings E E to ensure that the supervised tokens preserve the critical spatial position order during supervised training. We extract the final-layer representations of f 3 ​ D ​ ( ℐ ) f^{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{I}) and bilinearly resample the feature grids with positional embeddings to the VLA token resolution, obtaining a spatial target 𝐲 i \mathbf{y}_{i} at each visual token location:
𝐲 = ℛ ⁡ [ f 3 ​ D ​ ( ℐ ) + E ] , \mathbf{y}=\mathcal{R}\!\left[f^{\mathrm{3D}}(\mathcal{I})+E\right], (3)

where ℛ ⁡ [ ⋅ ] \mathcal{R}\left[\cdot\right] denotes bilinear resampling to the VLA visual token resolution. For brevity, the available geometric annotations like camera parameters are implicit in ℐ \mathcal{I} .

To align the VLA’s per-pixel visual tokens with this external 3D perception foundation model, we first process each VLA visual token 𝒙 𝒱 \bm{x}^{\mathcal{V}} with layer normalization LN \mathrm{LN} followed by a two-layer MLP to ensure compatibility in feature dimension. Let 𝒙 𝒱 ( ℓ ) {}^{(\ell)}\bm{x}^{\mathcal{V}} denote the VLA visual tokens after attention layer ℓ \ell of the VLA’s vision-language backbone. The normalization and MLP parameters are shared across layers. As there are multiple causal attention layers in the VLA model, visual tokens can be obtained after different layers. We adaptively aggregate their projected features into 𝐳 \mathbf{z} :

𝐳 \displaystyle\mathbf{z} = ℱ ⁡ [ { 𝒙 𝒱 ( ℓ ) } ℓ = 1 L ] \displaystyle=\mathcal{F}\!\left[\left\{{}^{(\ell)}\bm{x}^{\mathcal{V}}\right\}_{\ell=1}^{L}\right] (4) = ∑ ℓ = 1 L 𝐠 ( ℓ ) ⊙ MLP ⁡ [ LN ⁡ ( 𝒙 𝒱 ( ℓ ) ) ] , \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}{}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{g}\odot\mathrm{MLP}\!\left[\mathrm{LN}\!\left({}^{(\ell)}\bm{x}^{\mathcal{V}}\right)\right],

where L L is the number of VLA attention layers, 𝐠 i ( ℓ ) {}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{g}_{i} is a token- and channel-wise gate, and ⊙ \odot denotes element-wise multiplication. This fusion operator ℱ ⁡ [ ⋅ ] \mathcal{F}\left[\cdot\right] denotes the adaptive layer selection strategy, which is detailed in Section 3.2.3 .
Then we employ a cosine similarity score to maximize the alignment between the visual tokens of the VLA and the external spatial representation signals. The alignment loss is
ℒ align = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N [ 1 − 𝒮 ⁡ ( 𝐳 i , 𝐲 i ) ] , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[1-\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{z}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i})\right], (5)

where 𝒮 ⁡ [ ⋅ , ⋅ ] \mathcal{S}\left[\cdot,\cdot\right] denotes cosine similarity and N N is the number of visual tokens across views. The target 𝐲 i \mathbf{y}_{i} corresponds to the same view and image location as visual token 𝐳 i \mathbf{z}_{i} . Gradients update the VLA, MLP projector, and aggregation gates, while the external 3D perception model f 3 ​ D f^{\mathrm{3D}} remains frozen.
The final training objective combines both the standard training loss for action generation and the 3D foundation model alignment loss with a weighting factor α \alpha :
ℒ = ℒ action + α ​ ℒ align , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}}, (6)

where α \alpha controls the spatial alignment strength. We instantiate SLA with the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy ( Intelligence, 2025 ) , whose action expert generates continuous action chunks through flow matching.

During inference, the VLA model trained in the SLA manner operates identically to the original VLA, introducing no additional structures or computational overhead. The frozen 3D foundation model, alignment projector, and adaptive layer gates are used only during training and are discarded at inference. Neither depth maps nor camera calibration are required as additional policy inputs for inference.

The external 3D perception foundation model f 3 ​ D f^{\mathrm{3D}} provides the spatial representations as alignment signals. Apart from RGB image observations, some source datasets provide calibrated camera parameters and depth images, while others provide only partial geometric annotations or none at all. Discarding these annotations would leave useful geometric constraints unused, whereas requiring complete annotations would exclude otherwise valuable demonstrations. Therefore, the external model should accommodate the uneven availability of geometric annotations across the continual-pre-training corpus.

We adopt OmniVGGT ( Peng et al., 2025 ) as the external spatial model. Built on VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , it alternates frame-wise and cross-view attention to integrate local structure with relationships across images. Its GeoAdapter encodes available camera intrinsics, extrinsics, and depth maps through separate camera and depth branches, using placeholder tokens when annotations are missing. Stochastic multimodal fusion exposes the model to different combinations of geometric inputs, including RGB-only observations. These mechanisms combine visual evidence and arbitrary available geometric constraints in a unified latent representation. We therefore argue that its backbone features contain sufficiently rich spatial information to serve as external supervision for the VLA’s visual tokens.

A heterogeneous pre-training corpus makes a fixed alignment layer a restrictive choice. Manually selecting a single layer requires separate training experiments, and a layer selected for one data domain need not offer the same balance of visual detail and task context in another. Differences in scenes, textures, and embodiments motivate a mechanism that can adapt the contribution of each layer to the observed visual content.

Inspired by Gated Attention ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) , we learn a feature-dependent gate for every visual token at every VLA transformer layer. Given the unprojected embedding 𝒙 𝒱 i ( ℓ ) {}^{(\ell)}\bm{x}_{i}^{\mathcal{V}} , the gate is
𝐠 i ( ℓ ) = σ ⁡ ( W g ​ 𝒙 𝒱 i ( ℓ ) + 𝐛 g ) , {}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{g}_{i}=\sigma\!\left(W_{g}\,{}^{(\ell)}\bm{x}_{i}^{\mathcal{V}}+\mathbf{b}_{g}\right), (7)

where W g W_{g} and 𝐛 g \mathbf{b}_{g} are the learnable weight matrix and bias vector of the gate, respectively, and σ \sigma is the element-wise sigmoid. These gate parameters are shared across layers. The fusion operator ℱ \mathcal{F} in Equation 4 uses these gates to weight the projected features and sums them across layers to obtain 𝐳 i \mathbf{z}_{i} .

Through this mechanism, multi-layer VLA visual tokens can be supervised simultaneously, allowing different visual cues like depth and channel informations contribute to a unified spatial representation. The gates belong exclusively to the auxiliary training branch and introduce no additional policy computation at deployment.

Spatial supervision is useful only when the policy learns to rely on visual evidence for control. Robot states provide precise proprioceptive information, but can become shortcuts: a policy may associate particular states with demonstrated trajectories instead of responding to visual changes in the scene ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . We apply state dropout to discourage this shortcut during both training stages. Independently for each training sample, we randomly omit the entire state-token segment during tokenization; the instruction and image tokens are retained. Together, our external spatial alignment and state dropout encourage the model to encode scene geometry and to use visual observations when generating actions. This dropout is disabled at inference when the normal state input is available.

The quality and diversity of training data are fundamental to the generalization ability of VLAs. To build a VLA model that generalizes well across embodiments, tasks, and environments, we carefully curate a large-scale corpus for continual pre-training. Furthermore, we apply a unified data curation and preprocessing pipeline to all sources to ensure consistent robot state and action annotations.
The six source datasets summarized in Table 1 collectively contain approximately 1.7 million episodes and 14,330 hours of demonstrations.

Different robot morphologies induce incompatible joint-state and joint-action spaces, making joint coordinates a difficult basis for shared control representations. We instead express action through end-effector (EEF) poses, which describe the spatial effect of an action independently of the number and arrangement of arm joints. We use absolute EEF states as observations and chunk-wise delta EEF actions as prediction targets.

We first express all poses in a consistent robot-centered EEF coordinate frame. We unified the coordinate origin to the arm base for single-arm robots and the midpoint between the two arm bases for bimanual robots. Besides, we unified its axes point to forward ( + x +x ), left ( + y +y ), and upward ( + z +z ). A rigid coordinate transformation maps each source data’s EEF positions and orientations into this convention. Thus, the numerical axes of the shared action representation have consistent physical meanings across embodiments.

Rotation format is equally important for consistent action targets. Common choices include Euler angles, continuous 6D representations, rotation vectors, and quaternions. Directly subtracting Euler angles as delta actions may convert a small physical rotation across an angular wrap boundary into a large numerical displacement. We observe such wrap-induced outliers in the pre-training action distributions shown in Figure 3 . Our controlled comparisons motivate representing orientation with rotation vectors while computing relative rotations through SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) composition.

A rotation vector has a unified physical meaning through its direction and magnitude, making it natural to normalize its three channels using a shared scale. However, our controlled experiments show that channel-wise normalization yields substantially better performance, and we therefore adopt this approach in our experiments.

Large numbers of similar trajectories can dominate a mixed training corpus without adding comparable behavioral diversity. This is particularly relevant to scripted simulation data, where repeated executions may follow highly regular motion patterns. We reduce such redundancy by subsampling complete episodes within tasks, preserving the original temporal sampling rate of every retained trajectory.

For example, for InternData-A1, we retain 3% of episodes for selected tasks with highly repetitive trajectories, and 10% for the other tasks. For the pre-training subsets of RoboCasa365, we retain 0.5% of the MimicGen episodes and 15% of the composite episodes. These source-dependent and task-dependent retention rates bring episode counts closer to a comparable order of magnitude, reducing the dominance of a small number of scenes or tasks.

We focus on manipulation with two-finger grippers and exclude dexterous-hand data and trajectories involving robot-base motion. We additionally use action statistics to identify and remove data with anomalous arm-motion speeds. Where existing annotations are available ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , we remove idle frames in which both the robot and the scene remain stationary. Together, these filters keep the corpus aligned with the intended control setting and reduce uninformative or inconsistent supervision.

We evaluate SLA through benchmark-specific post-training on three simulation benchmarks, one real-world benchmark, and plenty real-world deployments. These evaluations cover robustness to visual and language perturbations, manipulation under scene variation, and applicability across robot embodiments.

LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) tests robustness along seven perturbation dimensions: camera, robot, language, lighting, background, observation noise, and object layout. We post-train on the standard LIBERO demonstrations and evaluate the perturbed environments without additional training on LIBERO-Plus. Evaluation comprises 10,030 rollouts; the overall SR weights each dimension by its number of evaluation episodes.

RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025a ) contains 50 bimanual manipulation tasks. We jointly post-train on 50 clean demonstrations per task and evaluate each task for 100 trials in both the Clean2Clean and Clean2Random settings. Clean2Random introduces domain randomization to test generalization beyond the clean training conditions. We report the task-averaged SR for each setting and their equal-weight average.

RoboCasa-Panda ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) contains 24-task kitchen manipulation benchmark covering pick-and-place, articulated-object interaction, and appliance operation with a Panda robot. Our post-training uses 50 demonstrations per task. Each task is evaluated for 50 trials under each of three evaluation seeds, yielding 3,600 trials in total. Results are averaged over seeds and tasks.

RoboDojo-Real ( Chen et al., 2026b ) covers 18 tasks across ARX X5, Piper, and Piper X, with six tasks per embodiment. We jointly post-train a single model on demonstrations from all three embodiments. We report scores on a 0–100 scale to measure partial task progress and success rates to measure complete task success. Aggregation equally weights tasks within each embodiment and then the three embodiments.

Apart from these benchmark evaluation, we additionally conduct real-world deployment experiments under eight private deployment conditions A–H on a bimanual Piper platform and a single-arm Franka robot. Piper platform uses one main camera and two wrist cameras while Franka uses one main camera and one wrist camera. The type of All cameras is Realsense D435. For each method, we post-train one policy on 100 demonstrations of A and reuse it for A–C evaluation. For D, we jointly post-train on the 100 Piper demonstrations of A and 10 additional Franka demonstrations. For task E–H, one policy is post-trained on 100 demonstrations collected in the E scene configuration and evaluated across E–H. We report object-level successs rates over 50 evaluated object instances per method and condition. For A, B, and D, these instances come from 10 rollouts with five objects per rollout, and each object is scored separately. C and E–H each comprise 50 single-object rollouts. Success requires complete manipulation sequence for the evaluated object.
We initialize SLA from the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy ( Intelligence, 2025 ) to conduct continual pre-training, followed by post-training for specific tasks.

The continual pre-training runs for 36k optimizer steps with an effective global batch size of 4,608, obtained by accumulating gradients over two microsteps with a global batch size of 2,304 each. The learning rate warms up to 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} over the first 1k steps, follows cosine decay to 1 × 10 − 5 1\times 10^{-5} at step 30k, and remains constant thereafter. Continual pre-training takes approximately 110 hours on 48 NVIDIA H100 GPUs.

As for post-training, LIBERO-Plus takes 512 batch size and 30k steps, RoboTwin takes 256 batch size and 30k steps, RoboCasa-Panda takes 64 batch size and 60k steps, RoboDojo-Real takes 512 batch size and 40k steps, and all real-world deployment experiments take 64 batch size and 20k steps.

We compare against the methods listed in the benchmark tables. Spatial Forcing denotes our original method applied only during post-training from pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , without our continual pre-training stage.

A key question for continual pre-training is whether additional training data translate into better downstream performance. To examine this relationship, we sample demonstrations within each task of the full pre-training mixture to construct subsets containing 5%, 25%, 50%, and 100% of the original data. For each subset, we perform continual pre-training with and without SLA alignment to obtain separate checkpoints. We then independently enable or disable alignment during post-training to examine how spatial supervision in the two stages interacts, yielding the four configurations shown in Table 6 and Figure 4 .

We report RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Random SR averaged over all 50 tasks. With SLA alignment in both stages, SR increases from 49.2% at 5% data to 72.3% at full data, a gain of 23.1 percentage points. This configuration performs best at every tested proportion. Without alignment in either stage, SR changes from 43.8% to 48.2%, with a small decline between 25% and 50% data. Increasing data alone therefore provides a much smaller benefit in this comparison.

The two single-stage variants further clarify the role of spatial supervision. At full data, SLA alignment only during continual pre-training reaches 63.2%, compared with 57.1% when applied only during post-training. Applying alignment in both stages improves on these variants by 9.1 and 15.2 percentage points, respectively. Overall, the consistently stronger joint configuration supports using spatial supervision both to shape the pretrained representation and to guide its downstream adaptation.

A fixed alignment layer requires manual selection and may not suit different data domains. We therefore introduce the adaptive layer selection mechanism to learn each layer’s contribution to spatial supervision, as explained in Section 3.2.3 . Specifically, our PaliGemma VLM ( Beyer et al., 2024 ) has 18 transformer layers in its language backbone. We compare single-layer alignment at layers 1, 6, 12, and 18 with adaptive fusion across all 18 layers. In Table 7 , fixed-layer Clean2Random success rates range from 43.4% to 67.3%. Layer 12 performs best, while layer 18 drops to 64.6%, showing that deeper alignment is not necessarily better. Adaptive fusion achieves 72.3% Clean2Random success rates and 79.2% average success rates, exceeding layer 12 by 5.0 and 3.5 percentage points, respectively. This result supports learning the contributions of multiple layers instead of committing to a single layer depth. The improvement is consistent with the motivation for token- and channel-wise gating: allowing the spatial alignment signal to draw on features from different representation depths.
Table 8 : State dropout ablation. Experiments are conducted on RoboTwin to evaluate success rates (%, ↑ \uparrow ).

State dropout is intended to discourage shortcuts based on associations between robot states and demonstrated trajectories, encouraging the policy to encode scene geometry and use visual observations for action generation. To assess its effect on manipulation performance, we vary the state dropout probability during post-training, starting from the same continually pretrained checkpoint and evaluating all 50 RoboTwin tasks. As shown in Table 8 , 25% dropout achieves the best average SR of 79.2%, compared with 38.1% without dropout. It also yields the highest Clean2Clean and Clean2Random results. Larger dropout probabilities perform less well: even 75%, the next-best setting, reaches only 61.9% on average. The response is not monotonic, and removing state inputs from every training sample is also suboptimal. These observations favor partial state dropout, consistent with a balance between encouraging reliance on visual evidence and preserving access to proprioceptive information during training.

Because our action space is defined in terms of end-effector poses, the rotation representation determines how orientation changes are encoded as action targets. We compare four rotation representations during post-training from the same continually pretrained checkpoint on all 50 RoboTwin tasks. Table 9 shows that rotation vectors achieve the highest average SR of 79.2%, followed by quaternions at 74.3%, Euler angles at 65.5%, and Rot6D at 62.9%. All four variants compute relative rotations through SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) composition, following equation 10 . The comparison therefore isolates how the composed rotation is represented for learning; it does not compare composition with direct coordinate subtraction. The results identify rotation vectors as the most effective representation within this controlled post-training setting.

We design a diverse set of challenging real-world tasks to evaluate bimanual coordination, spatial and dynamic generalization, few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation, and instruction following. The training and evaluation protocols are specified in Section 4.1 .

For the produce tasks in Figure 5 , we post-train a single policy on 100 demonstrations of the base scene A and evaluates it in A–C. A (Base) Robot grasps five vegetables between both hands: the robot passes five objects between its arms and places them into a bowl, testing bimanual coordination. B (Position Generalization) Human throw fruit out, and robot picks it back up: we tests recovery after a person throws objects from the bowl onto the table, and the policy must retrieve them and repeat handover and placement. C (Dynamic) Human intentionally move fruit while robot pick it: we tests responsiveness to target motion during grasping, while still requiring subsequent handover and placement. D (Few-shot cross-embodiment) Another Robot grasps vegetables: To examine adaptation with limited target-robot data, we use a separate policy jointly post-trained on the 100 Piper demonstrations and 10 additional Franka demonstrations, and deploy it to a single Franka arm to place five objects into a basket.

For the tabletop tasks in Figure 6 , we post-train one policy on 100 demonstrations collected in the E scene configuration and evaluates it across E–H. E (Level 1) Grasp water bottle: we provide a reference for basic manipulation: the robot grasps a bottle and stably places it on the destination table. F (Level 2) Grasp watch from stationary table: we test adaptation to a different static table height by transferring a watch that is already represented in the training data. G (Level 3) Grasp watch from dynamic table: we further test responsiveness to changing target height as the supporting table rises and lowers during grasping, without additional table-motion demonstrations. H (Instruction-following) Grasp black tape: Finally, we retain the E table configuration and tests instruction following with objects absent from downstream training: the robot must select and transfer black tape as instructed while ignoring a carrot distractor.

Spatial Forcing applies spatial supervision only during post-training from π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , whereas SLA combines spatially supervised continual pre-training with downstream post-training. As shown in Table 11 , SLA achieves the highest success rate across all tasks while Spatial Forcing ranks second on most tasks, which supports the effectiveness of our approach. The task-specific discussion below examines several complementary capabilities of our model that are essential for real-world applications.

A: Bimanual coordination. The success rates are 74% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 84% for Spatial Forcing, and 94% for SLA, corresponding to gains of 10 and 20 percentage points over the base policy. These gains support the value of spatial supervision for the complete grasp–handover–placement sequence, with the full SLA recipe providing an additional benefit over post-training-only Spatial Forcing.

B: Recovery from positional changes. The success rates increase from 52% with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} to 66% with Spatial Forcing and 82% with SLA. Relative to A, the corresponding reductions are 22, 18, and 12 points. A smaller reduction for SLA indicates more robust reuse of the learned manipulation skill after object relocation. Because A and B share a trained policy, this comparison concerns generalization to the intervention rather than fitting additional recovery demonstrations.

C: Response to moving targets. The success rates are 42%, 58%, and 76% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , Spatial Forcing, and SLA, respectively, placing SLA 18 points above Spatial Forcing. This advantage is consistent with more effective use of current visual observations when the target moves during grasping, while retaining the ability to finish the subsequent handover and placement.

D: Adaptation with limited target-embodiment data. Under the training budget of 100 Piper and 10 Franka demonstrations, the success rates are 48% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 62% for Spatial Forcing, and 78% for SLA. Such a result supports the usefulness of spatial supervision when adapting manipulation across embodiments with limited target domain data. The 16-point margin over Spatial Forcing further favors the complete SLA recipe in this joint-training setting.

E: Execution in the training scene configuration. The success rates of 90%, 94%, and 98% means that both π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and our policies are near the upper end of the metric. The 4-point margin between SLA and Spatial Forcing corresponds to two additional successful object instances out of 50. Such closely spaced values would establish basic manipulation competence while leaving limited headroom for improvement, making the changed conditions in F–H more informative about generalization.

F: Adaptation to a different table height. The success rates of Spatial Forcing is 64%, below the 68% of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , while SLA reaches 84%. This result indicates that the benefits of post-training-only spatial supervision are not uniform across conditions. The 20-point margin over Spatial Forcing favors the complete recipe under the table height changes.

G: Manipulation during table motion. The success rates are 44% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 60% for Spatial Forcing, and 78% for SLA. Compared with F, the reductions are 24, 4, and 6 points, respectively. The result means that both spatially supervised policies retain more abilities of their static-condition performance, while SLA maintains the highest absolute success rate. This pattern supports spatial supervision under changing geometry and the additional benefit of the full recipe, suggesting that our methods has the powerful static-to-dynamic fitness.

H: Instruction-guided manipulation of an unseen object. The success rates are 60% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , 56% for Spatial Forcing, and 80% for SLA. A 24-point gain over Spatial Forcing supports the ability to follow the specified target while transferring grasp-and-place behavior to an object excluded from downstream training. This comparison attributes the gains of our method to language-following and geometric reasoning abilities.

Taken together, these results supports the significance of our SLA training approach across spatial perturbations, embodiment adaptation, and language-guided object manipulation. our SLAsupervision uses auxiliary components only during training, retaining the original policy backbone and action-generation architecture for deployment. This compatibility enables continued training without adding policy computation at inference.

In this work, we presented SLA, a Spatial-Language-Action Model that develops transferable spatial understanding through continual pre-training and downstream post-training. By aligning intermediate visual representations with a frozen 3D perception model, our approach integrates geometric supervision into action learning while directly reusing pretrained VLA weights. A unified robot-data corpus and adaptive layer selection support training across heterogeneous embodiments and scenes, while available depth and calibration annotations enrich the spatial supervision. The teacher and alignment modules are required only during training. Extensive evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on RoboDojo-Real, RoboTwin 2.0 under the Clean2Random setting, RoboCasa-Panda, and LIBERO-Plus, alongside improved spatial and dynamic generalization, downstream data efficiency, and few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation. Controlled experiments further show that applying spatial alignment during both training stages consistently outperforms either single-stage alternative across the tested data scales. These findings support developing spatial understanding during continual pre-training and reinforcing it during downstream adaptation, offering a practical path toward spatially informed robotic foundation models.

This section provides additional experimental results to complement the evaluations in the main paper. These results offer a more detailed view of the downstream performance of SLA following continual pre-training and task-specific post-training, illustrating its strengths and remaining challenges across manipulation tasks and evaluation settings.

passages.text: Table 12 reports the success rates of SLA on all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks. The policy is post-trained on clean demonstrations and evaluated for 100 trials per task in the Clean2Clean and Clean2Random settings, with the latter introducing domain randomization. Performance remains strong in both settings on several tasks: Grab Roller and Shake Bottle each achieve 100% success, while Adjust Bottle reaches 99%. Other tasks show larger gaps between the two settings. For example, success rates decrease from 96% to 40% on Place Cans Plasticbox and from 91% to 38% on Handover Block. Table 15 compares SLA with methods from the official RoboDojo-Sim leaderboard ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , which evaluates 42 base tasks across five capability dimensions; each Generalization task also has a randomized variant, giving 54 task configurations. A single policy is post-trained on the simulation demonstrations with the memory mechanism in appendix B ; for this benchmark, spatial alignment is applied only during continual pre-training. SLA obtains the highest average Score and SR among the compared methods, 16.4 and 12.0%, exceeding π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} by 5.0 points and 5.1 percentage points. The largest gain appears in Memory, where SLA reaches 26.2 and 25.8%, second only to SimpleMemVLA and well above the other methods, which reach at most 8.2 and 7.0%. Generalization achieves the highest Score of 15.3, whereas Long-Horizon remains below most baselines at 22.3 and 11.9%.

Table 16 details the results on all 54 configurations. The best result is obtained on cover_blocks, with a Score of 92.2 and 90% success, while stack_bowls, put_bottles_into_dustbin, build_tower, and match_and_pick_from_conveyor reach 65% to 70% success. Within Memory, however, swap_blocks, swap_T, press_by_number, and imitate_sorting_sequence have no successful episodes. Randomized layouts substantially reduce performance: success decreases from 70% to 10% on stack_bowls and from 45% to 15% on pour_liquid_into_cup. Several tasks also show partial progress without completion, such as organize_table with a Score of 41.2 and 0% success. In the Open dimension, general_pickup is the only task with non-zero success, and seven of the eight Open tasks are absent from the post-training demonstrations. These results indicate that randomized layouts, full multi-stage completion, and tasks without demonstrations remain the main challenges.

As illustrated in Section 4.3.4 , we utilize a memory mechanism for RoboDojo-Real post-training stage. Several recent VLA models incorporate memory through dedicated modules ( Shi et al., 2026b ; Shi et al., 2026a ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Sridhar et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Our memory mechanism instead supplies selected past frames of the main camera to the policy as additional image inputs, which are processed by the same vision-language backbone as the current views.

Let I k I_{k} denote the k k -th main-camera frame of the current episode, where k = 0 k=0 is the first frame, and let f f be the recording frequency of the embodiment ( f = 25 f=25 for Piper X and f = 30 f=30 for ARX X5 and Piper). When generating an action chunk at frame t t , the memory context consists of nine main-camera frames:

that is, the episode-initial frame followed by one frame per second over the preceding eight seconds, ordered from the oldest to the most recent. The initial frame records the scene layout before manipulation and remains available throughout the episode, while the recent frames capture short-term progress and motion that a single frame cannot convey. Within the first eight seconds of an episode, the missing recent frames are replaced by the initial frame. Memory frames are taken only from the main camera, while the wrist cameras contribute only their current frames.

Each memory frame is resized to the resolution of the current views and encoded by the same SigLIP encoder ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) into 256 visual tokens. Within the prefix, the image tokens are arranged in temporal order, namely the initial frame, the recent frames from the oldest to the most recent, and the three current views, followed by the language tokens. This order is conveyed only by the token positions, without additional temporal embeddings. Like the current-view tokens, the memory tokens interact with the other prefix tokens through full attention and are accessible to the action expert. The memory frames are excluded from the spatial alignment branch: they are not passed to OmniVGGT, and ℒ align \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{align}} in Equation 5 is computed only over the current-view tokens.

During post-training, the data loader retrieves the memory frames of each training sample according to Equation 11 .During deployment, an online buffer records the main-camera frame at the camera frequency, including the control steps at which no new action chunk is requested, and retains the initial frame together with the frames of the most recent eight seconds. Whenever a new action chunk is requested, the buffer assembles ℳ t \mathcal{M}_{t} following Equation 11 , so that the memory observed at inference matches the one constructed during training. The buffer is cleared at the start of each episode to prevent leakage across episodes.

analysis.overview: 值得复用的是把冻结3D教师的特征对齐从下游后训练移到持续预训练，并在后训练继续使用；用逐token、逐通道门控聚合多层特征，让异构数据共享空间监督。两阶段开关消融支持此训练选择，但state dropout、动作表示与数据处理也会显著改变成绩。RoboDojo还加入历史帧，不能把其全部收益或推理成本归于无额外开销的空间对齐。
analysis.notice: 完整阅读150个提取片段，包含正文方法、公式、实验及附录A全部结果和附录B记忆机制。固定版本PDF31页；目视核对物理页6、7、9、12、14–16、19、28、31的深度示例、对齐公式、表1–3/5–11/13–14及记忆定义。未逐一核查其他图像、逐篇核查参考文献、执行代码或复现实验。正文与附录的部分分机器人均值不一致，已保留原值，未擅自修正。

findings.title: 动机证据边界：深度示例不能证明所有2D VLA缺乏3D
findings.text: 作者沿用Spatial Forcing的训练时隐式空间监督，新增重点是让这一信号参与异构机器人数据的持续预训练。图2冻结VLA、训练DPT深度头并给出图像示例；正文称其为linear probing，但DPT头本身不应直接等同线性读出。未给完整深度误差、数据划分和跨底座统计，不能从这些定性图推导所有2D VLA没有空间信息，或证明空间表示是控制增益的唯一原因。

findings.title: 方法：冻结OmniVGGT，训练跨层聚合特征匹配
findings.text: 从π0.5初始化。冻结OmniVGGT读取多视角RGB及可用深度/内外参；缺失几何输入用教师的placeholder机制处理。教师末层特征加位置编码，再双线性重采样到VLA视觉token网格。VLA各层经共享LN和两层MLP投影，再由sigmoid门控按token与通道加权求和；不是只硬选一层，也不是跨层softmax。用同视角同位置的余弦距离对齐，加到原flow-matching动作损失。更新VLA、投影与门控，教师冻结；空间辅助分支在推理时丢弃。

findings.title: 状态丢弃：删整段state token，不改图像或指令
findings.text: 两训练阶段按样本随机省略整个state-token片段，保留图像和指令，以减少将本体状态与示范轨迹绑定的捷径。推理时关闭dropout并恢复正常state输入。它是训练配方的重要部分，不能把性能变化全部归因于3D教师；同一checkpoint的后训练概率扫描才是文中直接控制。

findings.title: 跨机器人动作接口：固定当前帧作整个chunk参考
findings.text: 状态用绝对EEF姿态，动作用chunk-wise delta EEF；单臂原点为臂基座，双臂为两基座中点，坐标前/左/上。每个动作t都相对当前姿态(p0,R0)，Δp_t=p_t−p0，ΔR_t=R_t R0^T，再取SO(3)对数为旋转向量，不相对前一个预测动作。作者采用逐通道归一化；这与统一坐标、相对旋转的计算方式是不同选择，复现时须分别保留。

findings.title: 核心控制：两阶段对齐72.3%，两阶段关闭48.2%
findings.text: 表6/图4在RoboTwin Clean2Random、全量处理后混合数据条件下：持续预训练/后训练都开对齐72.3%，仅预训练开63.2%，仅后训练开57.1%，两者都关48.2%。两阶段对齐相对各单阶段分别高9.1/15.2个百分点。数据占比5%→100%时，两阶段对齐49.2→72.3%，都关43.8→48.2%；中间无对齐曲线并非单调。此控制支持两阶段都用，不是拟合出的普适scaling law，正文没有充分交代各占比的独立训练重复与预算匹配，不补写统计显著或超加性协同。

findings.title: 门控消融：优于所测最好的单层，但没隔离动态权重
findings.text: 表7固定层1/6/12/18的Clean2Random为43.4/45.0/67.3/64.6%，18层全聚合自适应为72.3%，比最好单层12高5.0点；两设置平均为79.2对75.7%。因此更深并不必然更好。所测控制没有均匀多层平均、静态可学习层权重等对照，不能把多层信息、参数量和按内容动态选择的收益全部区分开。

findings.title: dropout消融：0%到25%的变化大于多数模块差距
findings.text: 表8从相同持续预训练checkpoint，仅改变后训练state dropout。0%时Clean2Clean/Clean2Random为55.5/20.7%，25%为86.0/72.3%，平均38.1→79.2%。50/75/100%时平均53.9/61.9/56.7%，不单调且全删状态不是最优。强烈说明配方对state输入处理敏感，但没做空间对齐×dropout的完整交叉实验，不能单独证明捷径被抑制的机制。

findings.title: 旋转消融：比较的是SO(3)合成之后如何编码
findings.text: 表9从同一持续预训练checkpoint后训练：旋转向量平均79.2%、四元数74.3%、Euler65.5%、Rot6D62.9%。全部先做SO(3)相对旋转合成，因此此表不是“Euler直接相减对矩阵合成”的消融；图3直接相减产生±2π离群值是另一组分布说明。79.2对74.3支持所测任务用旋转向量，不能推出对所有机器人或归一化都普适。

findings.title: 教师标定：额外3.2点来自作者另采的数据设置
findings.text: 表10在作者自采的50任务RoboTwin clean示范上，从相同checkpoint改变后训练空间监督：无对齐平均31.8%，VGGT42.5%，RGB-only OmniVGGT42.8%，加内外参OmniVGGT46.0%。标定额外+3.2点，RGB空间监督本身相对无对齐+11.0点；不能将46.0%与标准示范主实验79.2%拼成同条件结果。标定仅供训练教师，策略推理不必输入内外参；这张表没有独立量化深度标签的收益。

findings.title: 基准口径：大幅收益与小幅领先需要分别看
findings.text: RoboTwin用50任务各50条clean示范，每任务每设置100次，SLA Clean2Clean86.0%、Clean2Random72.3%，比π0.5的46.0%随机场景高26.3点；但clean仍低于ME-Dex89.6%。LIBERO-Plus共10,030次、按各扰动episode数加权，87.4%对π0.5的84.4%，对表内Qwen robot-only87.1%仅高0.3点。RoboCasa-Panda每任务50示范、24任务×3评估seed×50次=3,600次，68.4%对Spatial Forcing67.6%仅高0.8点。评估seed不是独立训练seed，文中未给足跨训练重复置信区间，榜单间总数据/计算量也不相等。

findings.title: 真机83.8%：物体级均值，A/B/D每条件仅10条rollout
findings.text: 表11 SLA八条件A–H为94/82/76/78/98/84/78/80%，算术均值83.75%（表记83.8%），π0.5为59.75%（表记59.8%），差24.0点。每条件各50个独立计分的物体实例，但A/B/D来自10条rollout、每条5物体，不能当50条独立整任务试验。A–C复用100条A示范训练的策略；D另用100 Piper+10 Franka联合训练，非零样本跨机器人；E–H复用100条E示范策略。H物体只排除于下游数据，未证明从未出现在底座预训练。E中98对Spatial Forcing94只多成功2物体，须保留有限样本边界。

findings.title: 数据与成本：170万是筛选前来源规模
findings.text: 表1的1,713.9K episode、14,330小时来自6个来源的筛选前统计，不是最终实际训练量。InternData特定任务只留3%或10%，RoboCasa365 MimicGen留0.5%、composite留15%，另删移动底座、灵巧手、异常速度及可识别静止片段；最终混合大小、各源占比和几何标注覆盖率未完整列出。作者声明排除导致下游泄漏的数据，本轮未独立审计去重。主要持续预训练36k步、有效batch4608，48张H100约110小时；约5280 GPU小时是卡数乘时间的核算，不是实测能耗。没有给对齐α数值、各对照总GPU预算和完整推理profile，不能称总数据或计算效率更优。

findings.title: 推理无空间分支，不代表RoboDojo没有额外视觉开销
findings.text: 空间教师、投影与门控在推理丢弃；但RoboDojo-Real另加9张历史主相机图：首帧加此前8秒每秒1帧，各经SigLIP产生256 token，即额外2,304视觉token。它们与当前三视图经full attention交互，按位置编码时序，无额外时间embedding；历史帧不进空间对齐。部署保留缓冲并逐episode清空。这保留网络骨干结构，却增加输入和视觉编码/注意力工作，文中未给其延迟或严格等历史输入的baseline控制，不能把RoboDojo收益全归于空间对齐或将整套方案概括成零推理成本。

findings.title: RoboDojo逐机器人均值冲突：整体一致不代表分项一致
findings.text: 表5 SLA的ARX X5为Score50.3/SR36.7%，表14为50.7/38.3%；Piper SR表5为55.0%、表14为53.3%；Piper X Score16.3对16.0。两表整体仍都记Score42.3/SR33.9%，本轮保留冲突、不改原文。整体33.9%对π0.5的12.8%还伴随SLA历史帧输入，缺少去记忆对照；不拿分项冲突数据给机器人表现作精细排名。

findings.title: 失败边界：布局与开放任务远未解决
findings.text: 附录RoboTwin Place Cans Plasticbox从clean96%降random40%，Handover Block91→38%。RoboDojo-Sim为另一个配置：带记忆、空间对齐仅用于持续预训练，平均SR12.0%、Score16.4，Open仅1.9%、Long-Horizon11.9%；它不是主文两阶段对齐的同一协议。54个配置中多项完全失败，stack_bowls随机化70→10%，7/8开放任务无下游示范。真机Piper X整体仅10%，说明更高汇总分并不等于稳健长程、开放任务或无示范迁移。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：空间对齐能否在控制state dropout之后仍独立改善泛化？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：正确对应的3D教师对齐在固定25% state dropout时仍提供独立的随机场景泛化收益。先从同一持续预训练checkpoint做RoboTwin后训练2×2对照：空间对齐开/关×state dropout 0%/25%；另在25% dropout加入教师空间位置错配的对齐控制，保留特征分布、投影/门控参数与相同损失权重。固定示范、旋转向量接口、归一化、训练步数和数据顺序，记录教师额外GPU时与显存；以验证任务选checkpoint，测试用相同clean/random场景seed，每组至少3个训练seed，并按任务聚类计算差值区间。主要指标为Clean2Random成功率、clean保留率及相机/布局扰动分项，另测有/无状态干扰时表现；不以深度示例替代动作指标。若25% dropout下正确对齐不优于无对齐，或位置错配对齐同样改善，便反对“对应的空间内容提供独立增益”的解释；若仅0%条件有效则结论缩小为与state使用方式的交互。实验尚未运行，尚未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: SLA：把空间特征对齐贯穿持续预训练与后训练
frontier_brief.change_type: 训练配方 · 空间监督扩展
frontier_brief.delta: 从π0.5继续训练，将冻结OmniVGGT的空间特征同时用于持续预训练与后训练。VLA全部18层的视觉token经共享投影和逐token、逐通道sigmoid门控聚合，用余弦距离匹配教师；教师可利用不完整的深度与标定信息。
frontier_brief.before: Spatial Forcing只在下游后训练做空间对齐；异构大规模数据通常缺少完整几何标签，单一固定层也可能不适合各场景。
frontier_brief.after: 在统一EEF接口的混合机器人数据上持续施加空间对齐，后训练继续保留；以可学习门控融合多层信息，并按样本丢弃整段state token来改变视觉与本体感觉的使用。空间分支仅训练时存在。
frontier_brief.relevance: 已有π0.5并准备做异构数据持续预训练时，值得先复现两阶段开关对照；同时核对state dropout和旋转接口，避免把整套配方收益只算给教师。若不做大规模CPT，可从固定checkpoint的对齐×dropout交叉实验起步。
frontier_brief.caveat: 源数据170万条是筛选前规模；主要CPT用48张H100约110小时，最终混合量、对齐α与多种子方差披露不足。RoboDojo额外历史图像增加输入开销，部分分机器人表格均值冲突；结果来自作者，未复现。
frontier_brief.question: 固定25% state dropout后，正确空间对应的教师特征还提供独立收益吗？

evidence.context: 表7，18层自适应融合对固定第12层，差5.0点；未比较均匀多层平均，尚不能隔离动态门控与多层信息的贡献。

mechanism.title: 教师吸收部分可用的几何约束
mechanism.text: OmniVGGT固定，RGB以外的深度和相机内外参有则用、缺则占位；末层空间特征加位置编码并重采样至当前视图token位置。

mechanism.title: 多层辅助分支持续对齐
mechanism.text: 18层视觉token经共享LN/MLP和内容相关sigmoid门控求和，与同视角同位置教师特征计算余弦损失；动作损失同时训练，后训练也保留对齐。

mechanism.title: 区分训练辅助与额外输入
mechanism.text: 门控、投影和3D教师推理时移除，正常state输入恢复；RoboDojo的9张历史图像是另一个保留在推理中的机制，成本应另算。

passages.section: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
passages.location: Radio-to-Pose Information for Gauge-Drift Correction in Cooperative Localization
passages.text: Cooperative localization uses odometry and inter-robot measurements to estimate the motion of a robot team. These measurements describe only relative geometry, but the team’s estimated position and orientation can drift together over time, i.e. , gauge drift . In this work, we study correction of this gauge drift using a radio attenuation map registered in the same world coordinate frame used for robot poses. Specifically, we propose Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI), an interface that converts power residuals and their pose derivatives into a Gaussian information matrix and vector pair. RPI builds on the insight that received power is sensitive to shared displacement in the world map. The pose estimator uses the interface together with odometry and inter-robot measurements to update poses and minimize uncertainty. We characterize the shared motions detectable from the map and observed links. For an uncertain shared map, RPI keeps correlations across robots and time and reproduces joint Gaussian pose estimates and covariances. Across 1000 1000 simulated Gaussian trials, RPI matches the results of joint estimation. Across 32 paired trials with a registered map, RPI reduces common-position RMSE from 0.542 0.542 m to 0.140 0.140 m in a 50 × 50 50\times 50 m arena compared with a baseline that uses radio only to weight relative measurements.

To carry out tasks such as exploration, mapping, and environmental monitoring, robot teams rely on coordinated motion and shared observations. When global positioning is unavailable, they can estimate motion through odometry and inter-robot measurements. These observations constrain relative geometry, but the estimated team can move away from its true location as a group. For example, translating every robot estimate by one meter leaves all pairwise distances unchanged. This shared error matters when robots must reach mapped destinations or report observations in world coordinates.

It is also important to precisely estimate uncertainty because the team can know its relative geometry while remaining uncertain about its position in the world. This ambiguity is called gauge freedom . Gauge freedom describes indistinguishable coordinate frames, which in the presence of motion or noise leads to gauge drift . Gauge drift describes the temporal growth of error or uncertainty in these shared-motion directions. Teams construct a reference frame from a prior over their initial poses, but subsequent noisy observations determine how well the team remains localized. For trajectories without a fixed point of reference, common translations and rotations maintain relative observations, but they do not provide useful information about global state.

A radio attenuation map aligned to the world frame can provide a reference because received power depends on both link length and the attenuation field. For example, in Fig. 1 , a common translation preserves separation and distance loss but changes link attenuation. Using a global attenuation map which captures knowledge of obstacles in the environment can help distinguish the team’s positions by using differences in the received power they observe.

Fig. 1: In the left map, when there is no registered attenuation map, equal-length links have identical distance-only predictions. In the right map, when a registered map is present, equal-length links have different power predictions. Colors indicate attenuation in dB/m.

We propose the Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI) interface which leverages this behavior. The RPI is an interface between two components: First, a radio module predicts received power from the current poses and attenuation map, then determines the power mismatch and pose sensitivity as an information matrix and vector. Second, a pose estimator uses this message to compute a correction and its uncertainty.
This paper describes three contributions:
We show that fixed weights on relative measurements add zero direct information about common motion. We characterize which shared motions the attenuation map and observed links can detect.
We propose the Radio-to-Pose Information (RPI) interface, which converts power residuals and pose sensitivity into an information matrix and vector for pose estimation.

We derive centroid covariance growth and a lower bound on mean-squared common-position error under stated motion and measurement assumptions. We evaluate agreement with joint estimation, drift correction, and sensitivity to map error.

Cooperative Localization. Relative measurements help robots estimate their positions with respect to one another, but they do not determine the position and orientation of the entire team in the world frame [ 1 , 2 ] . Gauge fixing chooses a coordinate frame for estimation [ 3 ] . Simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) adds persistent environmental features and loop closures, which can reduce trajectory drift [ 4 ] . However, a map built only from the robot’s own measurements defines position relative to the robot’s chosen coordinate frame rather than an externally registered world frame. Our comparison concerns a cooperative localizer that uses radio to set fixed weights on relative factors.

Radio and Field Maps. Radio tomography estimates spatial attenuation from power measurements and known link positions [ 5 ] . Radio SLAM jointly estimates motion and propagation structure using radio observations, including multipath information [ 6 , 7 ] . Its reference frame depends on the available anchors and priors. Known physical anchors can provide a reference [ 7 ] , but may not be available. Instead, this paper focuses on studying inter-robot links against a registered attenuation field. This follows the principle of localization against surveyed terrain or magnetic maps [ 8 , 9 ] .

Gaussian Fusion. Factor-graph smoothers combine measurement models and priors through local linearization [ 4 ] . Gaussian elimination provides a way to summarize part of this model for another estimator. Distributed smoothing must account for previously shared information when summaries are replaced [ 10 ] . Fusion with shared variables must also preserve the induced correlations or use an appropriate conservative approximation [ 11 , 12 ] . RPI applies these requirements to a radio module whose uncertain map is shared across robots and time. Equivalent radio factors in a factor-graph smoother give the same local Gaussian result when the models and linearizations agree.

In the cooperative localization problem, a robot team seeks to estimate each robot’s trajectory in a fixed world frame over an estimation window. Consider N N robots over a finite set of time steps 𝒯 = { t 0 , … , t w } \mathcal{T}=\{t_{0},\ldots,t_{w}\} , called the estimation window, where t 0 t_{0} and t w t_{w} are its first and last time steps. A constant field has zero spatial gradient, so the radio model cannot detect any shared translation or rotation. Uncertain field values reduce the information carried by these derivatives. Repeated map patterns can produce the same radio measurements at different team locations. However, the full rank of the shared-motion Jacobian ensures local distinguishability. This means that any small shared translation or rotation of the team changes at least one predicted radio measurement.

We design RPI using the insight that a radio map aligned to world coordinates can provide a reference for the team’s position. We treat the map’s position and orientation in world coordinates as known. This method accounts for Gaussian uncertainty in its attenuation values as we describe in § V-B . We introduce RPI to pass information from the radio module to the pose estimator, as Fig. 3 illustrates.
