In every task an actuator must bring a passive object to a target within a fixed number of steps. The reward is sparse and defined only on the final frame: the negative distance from the object’s centroid to its target. Each planner produces a single open-loop plan for the full horizon inside its world model; the plan is then executed in the task’s simulator from the same start state, and the simulator never enters planning.

Pushing. A rod pushes a rigid block toward a target on a tabletop. Targets typically require the rod to move around the block before pushing, so random rod motions rarely produce progress. Horizon 60 steps ( 3 × 3\times the model window), 50 scenarios, executed in ManiSkill.

Pile Manipulation. A paddle moves the centroid of a granular pile toward a target in the plane. World models are trained on 6,000 6{,}000 trajectories of 300 frames from a scripted policy that randomly pushes and presses the pile. Horizon 150 steps ( 7.5 × 7.5\times the model window), 50 scenarios, executed in Genesis.

Picking. A parallel-jaw gripper must grasp a tabletop object (milk carton, peanut-butter jar, soda can, pasta box, or water bottle) and carry it to a target 15 cm above and up to 15 cm to the side of its start (5 objects × \times 5 targets). Horizon 60 steps, executed with a floating Franka hand in Isaac Lab.
Figure 18 shows one scenario of each task and the executed plan found by LNO.

Figure 18 : Planning tasks. One scenario per task: the initial configuration with its target (top) and the outcome of the LNO plan executed open-loop in the simulator (bottom). The rod moves around the block before pushing it; the paddle sweeps part of the pile onto the target; the gripper grasps the jar before carrying it to the target.

Task progress is ( d 0 − d T ) / d 0 (d_{0}-d_{T})/d_{0} , where d 0 d_{0} and d T d_{T} are the object-to-target distances at the start and at the end of the executed episode; it is averaged over scenarios. The planning budget is the wall-clock time of the whole planning call on one L40S GPU. Each planner is run at a ladder of settings (Table 6 ), and the value reported at a task’s budget is linearly interpolated between the two settings that bracket it.

Each task uses a task-specific GPWM (100M parameters, 200k training steps) trained on that task’s data. During training, the actuator’s given motion is withheld in a random half of the windows and replaced by a learned token, so the model learns both to generate the actuator jointly with the scene and to follow a given actuator motion. Planning uses the same checkpoint in both modes: noise-space planners use the generative mode, and Action CEM uses the action-conditioned mode, in which the actuator’s motion is given as per-frame rigid displacements. Rollouts over the full horizon use the streaming sampler of Section 3.4 with 6 denoising steps.

Our PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) baseline is a deterministic, recurrent PTv3 dynamics model, obtained by adapting PointWorld to operate on complete 3D point clouds and to be applied recurrently (Appendix B.3 ). It is trained on the same data, for a number of action-conditioned training windows matched to GPWM’s, conditions on the actuator’s motion, and predicts the motion of the rest of the scene; longer horizons are rolled out by chaining 16-frame predictions, each starting from the previous prediction.

Noise CEM and both Action CEM variants use the same cross-entropy method ( CEM ) and differ only in what it searches over. Each round draws K K candidates from a Gaussian, rolls all of them out over the full horizon, and refits the Gaussian to the best eighth of the candidates. We use the elite-retention and variance-floor modifications of iCEM ( Pinneri et al., 2021 ) . The best-scoring candidate found over all rounds is the plan that is executed.

The CEM variable is the noise of GPWM’s sampler. We use a stochastic sampler, which draws fresh noise at every denoising step, so the searched noise is the initial draw together with these per-step draws. With a deterministic (ODE) sampler only the initial noise would remain, and noise-space planning applies to either. Every candidate is a complete generated trajectory, and the plan is its actuator motion.

Figure 19 : Guidance step with streaming lookahead. For a gradient step on noisy sample x t x_{t} , we get an estimate of the clean trajectory using streaming lookahead. Backpropagating through the lookahead allows guidance to optimize for long horizon tasks with sparse rewards only on the final frame.

LNO optimizes the same noise by gradient ascent on the reward, with the weights of GPWM frozen (Fig. 19 ). The streaming sampler strides the model window across the full horizon of T T frames, and the terminal reward r = − ∥ c ⁡ ( 𝐬 ^ T ) − g ∥ 2 r=-\lVert c(\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{T})-g\rVert_{2} on the predicted object centroid is backpropagated through every model call. LNO first draws a pool of at least 32 random samples and keeps the best P P ; each is then refined with I = 5 I=5 AdamW steps (learning rate 0.1, gradient clipping at 1.0, and a small penalty that keeps the noise statistically Gaussian). The member with the highest predicted reward is executed.

Both world models are searched in the same action space: the actuator’s per-frame motion along the degrees of freedom it uses in the training data. This is the rod’s planar translation for Pushing, the paddle’s translation and yaw for Pile Manipulation, and the hand’s 6-DoF motion plus gripper opening for Picking (the two fingers share one command). Candidates are sampled independently per frame, and to keep motions in distribution every step is clipped to the 99th percentile of the recorded steps, both during planning and at execution.

A planner can spend more time in several ways: more candidates per CEM round ( K K ), more CEM rounds ( R R ), more LNO members ( P P ), or more gradient steps per LNO member ( I I ). For each planner we sweep the setting that we found empirically to give the best performance for its planning time, and keep the others fixed (Table 6 ). Noise CEM and Action CEM with GPWM sweep K K , with R R fixed at three rounds, so the two search spaces are compared at identical settings. LNO sweeps P P with I = 5 I=5 ; for low planning budgets we also decrease the size of the initial screening pool. PointWorld sweeps R R .

Table 6 : Planner settings swept by each curve in Fig. 4 ; settings not listed are fixed. K K : CEM candidates per round; R R : CEM rounds; P P : LNO members refined with 5 gradient steps each. LNO’s smallest budgets decrease the screening pool and take no gradient steps.

Planner Pushing (100 s) Pile Manipulation (200 s) Picking (200 s) LNO pool 4–32; P P 1–48 pool 4–32; P P 1–6 pool 4–32; P P 1–12 Noise CEM K K 4–192 K K 4–64 K K 4–96 Action CEM (GPWM) K K 4–192 K K 4–64 K K 4–96 Action CEM (PointWorld) K = 64 K{=}64 , R R 3–48 K = 64 K{=}64 , R R 3–36 K = 64 K{=}64 , R R 3–15

For noise-space planning, the plan is the actuator motion that GPWM generates. At every frame we fit a rigid pose to the predicted actuator particles (Kabsch alignment to the actuator’s initial geometry), and the simulator tracks these poses open-loop: the rod and the paddle by pose control, and the Franka hand as a floating base together with its gripper opening. For action-space planning, with either world model, the planned per-frame actions are executed directly.

Table 7 compares each planner’s progress as predicted by its world model with the progress it achieves in simulation. Noise-space plans lose part of their predicted progress on Pushing and Picking but keep most of it, and on Pile Manipulation their predictions carry over almost exactly. Action-space plans predict progress on every task and achieve almost none, with the exception of PointWorld on Pile Manipulation. Figure 21 shows each planner’s predicted and simulated outcomes on Pile Manipulation.

Table 7 : Predicted and executed task progress (%), at each task’s planning budget: progress in the world model’s own rollout of the chosen plan → \rightarrow progress after open-loop execution in simulation.

Planner Pushing Pile Manipulation Picking LNO 89 → \rightarrow 57 27 → \rightarrow 23 89 → \rightarrow 56 Noise CEM 94 → \rightarrow 48 21 → \rightarrow 21 70 → \rightarrow 40 Action CEM (GPWM) 23 → \rightarrow 0 7 → \rightarrow 1 78 → \rightarrow 0 Action CEM (PointWorld) 37 → \rightarrow 1 29 → \rightarrow 19 98 → \rightarrow 0

Action-space search in either world model does not find the contact sequence these tasks require, and Table 7 shows that it fails differently on the two tasks. On Pushing, the search fails to find progress even inside the world models: its chosen plans are predicted to make only 23–37% progress, against 89–94% for noise-space plans. Under a sparse terminal reward, random per-frame motions that bump the block without pushing it toward the target give the search little to improve on, and the rod rarely moves around the block. On Picking, the search does find plans the world models rate highly (78–98% predicted progress), but none of that progress occurs in simulation. No progress is possible before a grasp, and a grasp is hard to discover in the high-dimensional space of hand and gripper motions. The search instead settles on plans whose predicted object motion comes from exploiting errors in the predicted dynamics. Noise-space plans in GPWM move the rod behind the block before pushing and grasp before lifting; these contact sequences come from the learned interaction prior, not from raw search over actions (Figs. 20 and 22 ). PointWorld’s predictions for its chosen Picking plans show the object rising to the target while the gripper stays 3–12 cm away from it (Fig. 23 ).

Figure 20 : Pushing. Executed plans at the 100 s budget on two scenarios. LNO in GPWM moves the rod around the block and pushes it onto the target. Action CEM, with GPWM or PointWorld, produces jittering rod motions that leave the block where it is.

Figure 21 : Pile Manipulation. Each planner’s predicted outcome and the outcome of executing the same plan in Genesis, at the 200 s budget. LNO’s predicted push carries over to the simulator almost unchanged.

Figure 22 : Picking. Executed plans at the 200 s budget for two objects. LNO in GPWM grasps and lifts each object to the target. Neither Action CEM plan establishes a grasp, and the objects are not lifted. The full Franka arm is rendered for visualization only; plans are executed with a floating hand.

Figure 23 : PointWorld’s predictions for its Picking plans. The predicted object rises to the target while the predicted gripper stays 3–12 cm away from it; executed in simulation, the same plans leave the object on the table (Fig. 22 , right).

passages.section: Appendix F Predictions from a Single Image
passages.location: Appendix F Predictions from a Single Image
passages.text: This section gives the details of the predictions from single images in Section 5.2 and more examples.

SAM 3 ( Carion et al., 2025 ) segments each object named in a text prompt, SAM 3D ( SAM 3D Team et al., 2025 ) reconstructs it as a mesh, and MoGe-2 ( Wang et al., 2025b ) estimates the metric depth and camera that place the meshes in the scene. Each object is represented by 1,024 particles sampled on its surface, as in the training data.

Each scene is rescaled so that its objects match the particle spacing of the training objects, by 1.7 times for the desk photograph, and times are reported at the original scale. Each object is assigned a material type and a Young’s modulus. The four given frames describe free fall from the chosen release pose.

Image pixels of moving objects are filled with LaMa ( Suvorov et al., 2022 ) . Each object mesh follows its predicted particles, every vertex moving with its four nearest particles, and is path traced with the camera of the image. Sand is drawn as grains, and sand particles that end below the table are drawn on its surface.
Figure 24 shows more drops from the desk photograph and from five generated images, two of them stylized images beyond the training data.

Figure 24 : More drops from images. Each row shows the input image with the simulated objects outlined, their particles at the last input frame, and three predicted frames. Row 1, the lemon from the desk photograph falls onto the toy car as an elastic, a plasticine, and a sand object, shown 1.53 s after release. Row 2, a plasticine ball lands on the pepper, rolls off and pushes it aside. Rows 3 to 7 use generated images. Row 3, an elastic gummy bear falls onto a plasticine donut on a dorm desk, flattens and slides off. It stays flattened, a limitation of the model for soft elastic objects. Row 4, an elastic gel cube falls onto a pile of Mars regolith simulated as sand and scatters it. Row 5, an elastic jelly cube falls onto sprinkles simulated as sand, and the gummy bear beside it slumps by 1.53 s, the same limitation. Row 6, in a claymation scene, a plasticine tomato lands on an elastic one, and the two topple and come to rest apart. Row 7, in a 1970s photograph, an elastic lemon lands on an elastic jelly mold and comes to rest on top. Rows 6 and 7 are stylized images beyond the training data. Young’s moduli are 10 kPa for the gummy bears, donut, gel cube, bread roll, jelly cube, and jelly mold, 1 MPa for the toy car and the block, and 100 kPa for all other objects. The car, pepper, block, and tennis ball are elastic. Times are at each scene’s original scale.

The model receives four frames of history, so editing them changes the predicted future. In Figure 25 a ball dropped onto a pepper comes to rest on top. We then rewrite only the ball’s four input frames so that it moves sideways at 9 cm/s from where it rests, and let the model continue. No actuator is modeled.

Figure 25 : Changing the observed history. Every row continues the same drop of the blue ball onto the pepper. In the top row the ball is released, lands, and rests on top at 0.35 s, when we freeze the scene. Without an edit it stays there. In each row below, only the ball’s four input frames at the freeze are rewritten so that it moves in the direction of the green arrow (the edited ball is drawn orange), and the model predicts the rest. Times are since the release at the original scale. The last column is 1.44 s after the freeze.
In Figure 26 , a sloth reconstructed from a photograph is dragged into a foam star. Every model receives the same initial scene and commanded drag, and the arrow shows the drag direction.

Figure 26 : Dragging a sloth into a foam star. A sloth reconstructed from a photograph is dragged into a foam star, and every model gets the same start and drag. The arrow shows the commanded drag. Objects are drawn with dense points that follow each model’s predicted particles.

passages.text: Figure 27 applies the Garment Folding specialist to garments from generated images. Each garment is segmented from a top-down image, represented as two cloth layers at the particle spacing of the training data, and placed on the most similar training garment, which sets its size and supplies the recorded gripper motion. The specialist predicts all frames from that motion, which moves the grasped edge 16 to 20 cm, so each garment ends in a partial fold.

analysis.overview: GPWM把动力学目标改成粒子位移与刚体位姿增量，结合对象内多分辨率压缩和逐帧噪声的流匹配，支持跨材料流式预测。对规划最值得复用的是联合生成执行器与物体轨迹后搜索噪声：同一任务检查点下比逐帧独立动作CEM更能发现接触序列，并减少模型预测进度在仿真执行中落空。但规划仍是任务专用模型、完整跟踪3D状态、单L40S上100–200秒的开环仿真；31%平均预测降幅取自每域较优版本，不代表单一统一模型的收益。

findings.title: 关键增量：把接触轨迹的生成分布变成规划搜索先验
findings.text: 相比先任意提出动作、再让动力学模型打分，GPWM让执行器和被动物体在同一几何变量中联合生成，再用末帧物体位置奖励优化噪声。这同时提供接触提案分布和动力学预测；因此同检查点的噪声/动作搜索对照比跨模型误差排名更能区分“模型更准”与“搜索分布更合适”。这里不声称所有动作优化都会失败。

findings.title: 柔性物体逐粒子位移，刚体由共享位姿增量保形
findings.text: 柔性/颗粒用帧间3D位移，刚体另设3维平移+6维旋转的9维增量pose token。刚体表面点由初始模板随位姿移动，不分别加独立噪声，因此形状保持来自表示约束，而非从粒子误差中自然学得。位移积分恢复绝对位置；条件包括已知材质、可用物性及执行器未来运动。要求粒子对应与对象归属已知。

findings.title: 对象内降采样保留几何身份，粗层处理对象间作用
findings.text: 四级U形网络在初始几何中按对象FPS固定anchor身份，PointNet++聚合与逆距离插值，每帧用当前噪声位移积分后的位置重算邻域；不是每步重新随机选粒子。全分辨率空间注意力限于同对象，粗层跨全场景，时间注意力窗内双向，pose token每级保留。1024点自由落体对象依次压到256/64/32，降采样8邻居、上采样3邻居，配3D RoPE、绝对高度和长跳接。粒子上限12000不等于证明任意密度、对象数都能无损扩展。

findings.title: 逐帧不同噪声与错位去噪，使固定窗可持续向前滚动
findings.text: 模型直接回归干净粒子/刚体增量，损失是两类端点平方误差，gamma=1，无额外物理损失。训练4帧历史+16帧未来，60%窗口各帧独立均匀噪声，40%沿时间线性递增；被动物体历史另加归一化std0.05抖动。推理先提交已去噪的近期帧，远期仍可修订，再右移窗口添新噪声。898帧衣物预测约为16帧的56倍，但不是一次并行预测898帧或物理守恒保证。附录表5另列Pick and Place最长921帧，故正文898不宜当全数据唯一最大时长。

findings.title: ParticleWorlds的25.5M按场景帧计数，物性与成功标签并不齐全
findings.text: 语料267864条可用训练episode、25463677场景帧，六域八来源；按各loader采样率计一次，含settling前缀，不因重叠窗口、粒子数或重复抽样倍增。MPM物性有记录，但衣物参数及部分刚体质量/摩擦随机化不作条件；衣物为数值筛查轨迹，不是验证成功的折叠。数据含脚本、RL推物及teacher技能，所以“无需目标专用策略/参考动作”指测试规划接口，不能解释成训练未见操作示例。

findings.title: 主表31%是各域取较优GPWM后的平均，不是Unified统一增益
findings.text: 表1依次为Free Fall/Dragging/Cloth/Pushing/Pick and Place/Hands：Specialist误差40.0/6.5/10.0/13.3/12.6/18.7，Unified41.5/6.1/10.8/18.0/11.1/22.6。最强既有基线53.0/7.8/10.6/23.9/34.1/24.8。每域取Specialist或Unified较好者，才得到约31%平均相对降幅；Unified仅五域胜既有基线，衣物10.8差于PointWorld10.6，也差于自家10.0。非衣物是被动物体粒子位置mm误差；衣物是对称Chamfer，不能把所有列当同一种逐点对应误差。各GPWM仅采一个未来，单参考轨迹误差不能完整评价生成分布。

findings.title: 统一模型的跨域收益伴随更大容量，未单独证明迁移因果
findings.text: Unified在Dragging6.1优于Specialist6.5、Pick and Place11.1优于12.6；但容量502.2M对103.1M，训练4张RTX PRO6000×600k迭代对每specialist2张×200k。统一按域等概率抽batch，平均每域约100k迭代；并非相同参数、总算力或域内更新数的纯数据混合消融。论文未提供足够逐组件消融来分离多分辨率、刚体保形、diffusion forcing与更大数据的各自贡献。

findings.title: 形状/对象数有外推，刚度测试仅区间内插值
findings.text: Free Fall训练1–4对象，测试5–7对象达7168点：specialist从已见形状37.5变为未见形状+更多对象45.2mm，PhysCtrl48.5→120.9。刚度已见10/100/1000kPa，未见30/300仍在区间内，specialist47.3→48.9；Unified54.5→53.1且未见值下不如PhysCtrl51.7。故证据支持specialist的形状/数量稳健性和刚度插值，不能写为所有模型都最优或已验证材料外推。测试物性作为输入提供，不是从视觉推断物性。

findings.title: 基线经同数据适配，但输入与结构仍不完全对等
findings.text: 作者在同episode/split上重训基线，PhysCtrl约100M、4历史/16未来，动作粒子聚类成区域条件，但无刚体pose接口；PointWorld约100M、voxel15mm改1mm、去颜色法线和sphere crop，仍只看1历史帧而GPWM看4帧。GNS仍为128维10次消息传递单步，PGND需改执行器、扩/缩网格并在拥挤场景冻结出界对象。结果衡量这些适配方案，不等于所有原模型在完全相同信息与容量下的最优上界。

findings.title: 规划模型半数窗口隐藏动作条件，让同权重支持两种搜索
findings.text: 规划每任务另训约100M、200k steps模型，不使用502M统一模型直接零样本完成全部任务。训练随机一半窗口把给定执行器运动换为learned token，学会联合生成；另一半学给定动作预测，推理两种模式共用同checkpoint。流式采样6步；Noise CEM搜索随机采样器的初始及每步新噪声，不只是一个初始latent。LNO也优化这一噪声，用末帧质心距离反传穿过所有窗口，常规每member5步AdamW、lr0.1、梯度裁剪1.0和高斯性惩罚；低预算可不做梯度。

findings.title: 同检查点规划对照支持接触先验，但指标是距离进度
findings.text: 图4在单L40S整次规划预算100秒Pushing、200秒Pile/Picking下，开环仿真执行的LNO/Noise CEM进度分别0.57/0.48、0.23/0.21、0.56/0.40。Pushing与Pile各50场景，Picking5物体×5目标共25；进度是(d0−dT)/d0，不是成功率。动作CEM是逐帧独立采样，逐步裁到训练步长99分位；与Noise CEM同3轮并扫相同候选数，但不含结构化/时序相关提案策略。因此结论局限于所测动作搜索；pile里PointWorld动作CEM可达0.19，噪声空间优势较小。预算数值来自曲线相邻设置插值，图未给置信区间。

findings.title: 预测对执行差距：抓取动作搜索在模型里高分，执行几乎不动
findings.text: 表7 Picking预测→仿真执行：LNO89→56%、Noise CEM70→40%、GPWM动作CEM78→0%、PointWorld动作CEM98→0%。Pushing分别89→57、94→48、23→0、37→1%；Pile27→23、21→21、7→1、29→19%。该对照比纯预测误差更直接支持动作优化利用模型错误的解释，但噪声搜索仍有33或46点等预测落差，未消除模型利用。目视发现图4 Picking的GPWM动作CEM终点−0.03，而表7记0；原文未解释是否截断/汇总差异，保留为缺口，只概括为无正进度。

findings.title: 完整状态、浮动执行器和长规划预算限制真机解释
findings.text: 预测默认完整时序跟踪粒子和对象身份，动作条件任务整个rollout知道未来执行器运动且评分不含执行器；不是从相机端到端闭环。规划只在ManiSkill/Genesis/Isaac Lab仿真开环执行，噪声计划从粒子Kabsch拟合位姿并追踪，抓取用floating Franka hand，渲染全臂不代表满足全臂IK/碰撞/扭矩约束。跨窗口反传随时长增成本，100–200秒不能当快速在线控制；未报告真机、闭环抗扰或边缘功耗。

findings.title: 图像重建演示提供几何入口，没有验证物理参数识别
findings.text: SAM3分割、SAM3D重建、MoGe2尺度/相机估计后，每对象采1024表面点，手工指定材质/刚度和释放姿态构造四帧历史；桌面图另缩放1.7倍匹配训练点距。部分示例来自生成图，渲染把桌面下sand画回表面，衣物也沿用相似训练衣物尺寸和记录的夹爪动作。没有对应真实动态轨迹定量真值，不能称实物物理验证；柔软elastic gummy bear持续扁平是附录明确反例。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：时序相关动作提案能否缩小噪声搜索优势？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：GPWM噪声搜索在Picking上的部分收益来自接触序列的时间相关先验，逐帧独立动作提案是其优势的重要对照条件。冻结同一任务GPWM检查点、场景/目标与6步采样器，在原有独立动作CEM之外加入仅用训练split拟合的低频样条动作CEM和时序相关动作CEM，对照Noise CEM；各组同时画相同候选模型调用数与相同L40S墙钟预算曲线，不只挑一个终点。保留相同每步幅度限制、控制器和仿真执行设置，在原25个Picking问题与独立目标集上至少3个搜索seed，报告执行距离进度、额外明确定义的抓取成功率、模型预测−执行差、非接触悬空率与总耗时。所有统计用配对场景区间，训练提案不看测试目标。若相关动作提案在两种预算匹配下仍不能提高执行进度或缩小预测−执行差，而Noise CEM优势稳定，则推翻“弱时间相关提案解释大部分优势”的假设；若缩小差距，则应将结论表述为所学接触先验相对原提案的收益。该实验尚未执行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已证实机制或研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: GPWM：联合生成执行器与物体轨迹，在噪声空间搜索接触计划
frontier_brief.change_type: 世界模型 · 生成式规划
frontier_brief.delta: 将3D粒子位移/刚体位姿的流式生成器同时训练为动作条件预测与执行器—物体联合生成；规划冻结同一检查点，以物体末帧奖励搜索生成噪声。
frontier_brief.before: 直接在逐帧独立执行器动作上做CEM，再用动作条件世界模型评估，容易遗漏先抓后提等接触序列，也可能找到只在模型预测里有效的动作。
frontier_brief.after: Noise CEM或LNO沿联合交互分布提出整段计划；同GPWM检查点的Picking在200秒L40S预算下，执行距离进度分别0.40/0.56，原动作CEM无正进度。
frontier_brief.relevance: 若准确的3D动力学模型在规划时被利用，先比较动作提案分布与预测−执行差，再决定是否需要更强预测器；联合执行器表示和同检查点双模式训练可复用。
frontier_brief.caveat: 全部是完整跟踪3D状态下的仿真；规划用任务专用约100M模型，100–200秒开环预算，Picking为浮动手而非全臂执行。31%预测降幅取各域较优版本，统一模型更大且衣物有反例。图4 Picking动作CEM−0.03与表7的0不一致。
frontier_brief.question: 加入匹配预算的时序相关动作提案后，噪声空间对执行进度和模型利用的优势还能保留多少？

evidence.label: 同检查点搜索空间
evidence.context: 5物体×5目标；单L40S整次规划200秒，曲线插值；指标是仿真开环距离进度，非成功率。动作提案逐帧独立。

evidence.label: 模型利用诊断
evidence.context: 表7同任务GPWM Picking；图4动作CEM标−0.03，与表7不一致，未擅自合并。噪声搜索仍有预测落差。

evidence.label: 优势较小的任务
evidence.context: 50场景、150步，单L40S200秒；最强动作基线是PointWorld，随机接触也可推动颗粒堆。

evidence.label: 统一预测的边界
evidence.context: 20条898帧held-out衣物轨迹，对称Chamfer(mm)；统一502.2M对specialist103.1M，其他域指标为逐点位置误差。

mechanism.title: 混合几何状态
mechanism.text: 柔性逐粒子增量，刚体共享pose增量保形；对象内压缩anchor、粗层跨对象交互，4帧历史/16帧生成窗。

mechanism.title: 流式逐帧去噪
mechanism.text: 逐帧噪声训练后，先提交近期、保留远期可修订状态，右移窗口持续生成；并非一次生成完整长轨迹。

mechanism.title: 同权重双模式
mechanism.text: 半数训练窗口隐藏动作条件，联合生成执行器与物体；噪声CEM或反传LNO从末帧物体奖励选计划，随后仿真开环执行。

attention.reason: 共享检查点的双模式与搜索空间对照值得复用，但完整跟踪状态、长时开环规划和浮动手限制部署范围。
attention.notice: 阅读优先级判断，不是科学质量定论。

impact.comparison: 共享检查点的双模式与搜索空间对照值得复用，但完整跟踪状态、长时开环规划和浮动手限制部署范围。

passages.section: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
passages.location: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
passages.text: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark’s success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark’s criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

passages.section: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
passages.location: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
passages.text: Keywords: embodied agent, self-improvement, robot policy evaluation

passages.section: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
passages.location: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
passages.text: Figure 1 : Learning the task or the verifier? (a) : in press_by_number, the criteria C orig C^{\text{orig}} verify a button protocol that the instruction does not state (highlighted). Without Criteria Exposure (w/o CE) the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded; with it (w/ CE) it also reads the criteria code, score and stages. Right of each setting: the test successes of its library on 20 layouts, judged by C orig C^{\text{orig}} and by the instruction-faithful criteria C faith C^{\text{faith}} . (b) : libraries learned under C orig C^{\text{orig}} on the 16 criteria-limited tasks, 320 test episodes each, with every episode judged by both criteria ( section 4.2.1 ). The lead of w/ CE under C orig C^{\text{orig}} , 51.6% against 27.8%, is gone under C faith C^{\text{faith}} (45.0% against 47.2%).

Agents that write code to control robots with multimodal language models complete many manipulation tasks zero-shot [ 19 , 15 , 12 , 29 ] , but preserve nothing from one episode to the next, which makes self-improvement across episodes a natural next step [ 28 , 31 , 36 ] . Such agents are developed and compared on embodied simulation benchmarks [ 9 , 20 , 22 ] originally built to evaluate end-to-end policies trained by imitating demonstrations, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 6 , 17 , 4 , 25 ] and world action models (WAMs) [ 26 ] . The actual success criteria of these benchmarks often ask for more than the instruction; in the press_by_number task of RoboDojo, for instance, the criteria require the blue button to be pressed exactly twice, between two groups of red presses, which the instruction never states ( figure 1 a). For policies trained by imitation, this gap is harmless, since their demonstrations already contain every detail the criteria verify: order, counts, end states, and the return of both arms. An agent that receives only the instruction, however, lacks this information. Existing self-improving methods therefore expose the criteria to the agent to different degrees, from rule descriptions [ 10 ] and published scoring tables [ 18 , 13 ] to numeric thresholds [ 14 ] , formal goal predicates [ 32 ] , and the source code of the verifier [ 3 ] . A robot in the real world, by contrast, receives only its instruction and, at most, a success judged by a human or a VLM. Our research question is: when a self-improving embodied agent is exposed to the success criteria, does the code it iteratively produces better perform the instructed task, or simply overfit to the verification criteria?

Studies of benchmark validity and of specification gaming show that criteria can demand more than the instruction states and that agents exploit a verifier they can inspect [ 16 , 40 , 37 ] , but we are not aware of work that measures how much of a reported gain in embodied self-improvement comes from reading the criteria, or whether it survives when the criteria change. We therefore compare two settings of one fixed self-improvement loop, in which a frozen coding agent acts and a learner agent turns its episodes into a library of skills and memory: with Criteria Exposure (w/ CE), the learner reads the criteria; without it (w/o CE), the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded. We ask three questions: on which tasks exposure raises the score; whether its lead survives a change of criteria, both of the criteria that judge the episodes and of the criteria the learner reads; and whether what it adds carries over to new tasks and to two further benchmarks, LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365. To change the criteria, we rewrite them for the RoboDojo tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction, so that they verify only what the instruction asks. On these tasks every episode is judged by both versions, and in a separate run the learner reads the rewritten criteria instead of the original ones.

Our experiments reveal three findings. First, under the original criteria, exposure helps only on tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction; when criteria and instruction agree, learning from success alone does just as well. Second, the score of exposure follows the criteria it read: when the same episodes are judged by instruction-faithful criteria, its advantage disappears, as the exposed libraries lose successes while the success-only libraries gain them ( figure 1 b); conversely, a library learned from the rewritten criteria scores far lower when judged by the original ones. Third, the lead of exposure does not reappear on new RoboDojo tasks, and across benchmarks neither the exposed nor the success-only library gives a clear gain over the empty library; only experience gathered within the target benchmark does.

Taken together, these results suggest a practical principle for evaluating embodied self-improvement: the learner should receive only the feedback a robot would receive in the real world, and the benchmark’s criteria should verify what the instruction says. A gain that holds when the criteria are changed but still agree with the instruction reflects what the agent has learned about the task. Seen this way, whether the learner reads the criteria is not an implementation detail of a self-improving agent but a choice about measurement, and it determines what a reported gain means.

Code-writing embodied agents and their benchmarks. Language models plan and act for robots by selecting skills [ 1 ] , writing policy code [ 19 ] , or composing value maps [ 15 ] ; recent agents close the loop with code replanning and thin tool layers [ 12 , 29 , 13 ] , and frontier models now control robots zero-shot. These agents are evaluated on benchmarks built for vision-language-action policies trained on demonstrations [ 6 , 17 , 4 , 25 ] : RoboDojo [ 9 ] , LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO [ 20 , 38 ] , RoboCasa365 [ 22 ] , and RoboTwin 2.0 [ 8 ] . These works score agents with criteria written for demonstration-trained policies; whether the criteria verify only what the instruction asks is rarely examined on its own, and we measure how this gap enters the score of a self-improving agent.

Self-improving agents and the feedback their learners see. In digital domains, programs are evolved against automatic evaluators [ 23 , 34 ] , agents reflect on textual feedback [ 28 , 36 ] , skills are verified in a game world [ 31 ] , and code is revised against tests [ 33 ] . Embodied systems differ in how much of the success criteria their learners or agents see. Some give only success or keep the grader isolated [ 27 , 21 ] ; others add rule descriptions with coarse feedback [ 10 ] , published scoring tables and partial numeric thresholds [ 18 , 13 , 14 ] , formal goal predicates [ 32 ] , or the source code of the verifier [ 3 ] . In RATs, the verifier reads goal predicates and ground truth while the policy writer’s side is filtered [ 35 ] . In these systems the amount of criteria information is mostly fixed by design rather than varied as an experimental factor. The closest comparison is an ablation of EmbodiedEvo between task descriptions alone and descriptions with the wiki, but both arms are judged by the original criteria [ 18 ] . We treat exposure as the variable and test what it gains under a second set of criteria.

Specification gaming and benchmark validity. Optimizing a proxy diverges from the intended objective [ 2 , 30 ] , with measurable effects of reward misspecification [ 24 ] . Language agents exploit tests and evaluators they can inspect [ 37 , 5 ] , and agentic benchmarks need checks of their own validity [ 16 , 40 ] . Where rule-based criteria are missing, success is judged by VLMs [ 11 ] or by autonomous real-world evaluation [ 39 ] . Building on these studies, we further show that on embodied benchmarks the act of reading the criteria turns the gap between criteria and instruction into score, and we measure this share with counterfactual criteria that score the same instructions.

This section describes the controlled study we use to analyze what a self-improving embodied agent learns from the success criteria. The study compares two settings of one loop, w/ CE and w/o CE, and answers three questions: where exposure raises the score under the original criteria, whether the advantage holds when the criteria change, and whether the library carries over to new tasks and benchmarks. We describe in turn the loop and its two settings, criteria-limited tasks, instruction-faithful criteria, and the evaluation protocol.

Figure 2 : Overview of the self-improvement loop. Left, learning: the actor (GPT-6 Astra, high reasoning effort) writes and executes Python cells that call the robot’s primitives on five development layouts, and sees the result of each cell. Between batches the learner (Claude Code with Opus 5.5, high reasoning effort) turns the evidence into one revision of the library ℒ k \mathcal{L}_{k} , whose skills are callable code that reports what it did and whose memory entries say when to apply what, with the evidence for it; a revision is usually tried first in verification rollouts, and the loop rolls back to the best revision so far when a batch falls clearly below it. Whether the learner also sees the success criteria is the one switch between the two settings, w/ CE and w/o CE (the switch under the learner). Right, evaluation: the final library ℒ K \mathcal{L}_{K} is frozen and read-only, and the same actor runs alone on layouts the loop never saw.

A task τ = ( I τ , D τ , C τ ) \tau=(I_{\tau},D_{\tau},C_{\tau}) has an instruction I τ I_{\tau} , a distribution of layouts D τ D_{\tau} and success criteria C τ C_{\tau} that judge each trajectory; some benchmarks also report a score and stages. The success the instruction asks for, S τ S_{\tau} , is defined by I τ I_{\tau} and cannot be computed directly. A frozen actor π \pi , GPT-6 Astra with high reasoning effort, acts through the primitives of PyRUA-Lean [ 29 ] . In each round a learner U U , Claude Code with Opus 5.5 and high reasoning effort, makes one revision of the library ℒ \mathcal{L} , a set of callable skills and memory entries, from the evidence E v ​ ( B ) E_{v}(B) of the last batch, and the revision is rolled back if the batch clearly regresses. Each task has its own library, learned over five rounds on five development layouts. Algorithm 1 and figure 2 summarize the loop for one task.

The loop runs in two settings. Without Criteria Exposure (w/o CE), the learner sees only whether each episode succeeded; the criteria code, the score and the stages are withheld. A robot in the real world has no criteria code and receives success from a human or a VLM, so this is the setting in simulation closest to the real world. With Criteria Exposure (w/ CE), the learner also reads the criteria code of the task and the score and stages of each episode, as systems that give the learner the source of the verifier do; the actor never reads them. The actor, the primitives, perception and benchmark scoring are frozen and only the library changes; the two settings share the loop and differ in what the learner reads, so differences between them reflect exposure rather than the loop itself.
Algorithm 1 Self-improvement loop

We call a task criteria-limited if C τ C_{\tau} disagrees with S τ S_{\tau} on some trajectories, either by rejecting a trajectory S τ S_{\tau} accepts or by accepting one S τ S_{\tau} rejects (criteria looser than the instruction); all other tasks are faithful . Such tasks appear in every benchmark we examined, RoboDojo, LIBERO [ 20 ] (whose instructions and goals LIBERO-PRO keeps), RoboCasa365 and RoboTwin 2.0 [ 8 ] , and their disagreements fall into a few kinds. The criteria may ask for more than the instruction states, such as an order, a count or an end state: in RoboDojo, press_by_number requires a button protocol its instruction never gives. They may be stricter than the instruction needs, such as an unstated tolerance for an object resting on another in LIBERO. They may contradict the instruction, as in a LIBERO task that asks to stack a bowl on the front bowl while its criteria require the back one. Or they may verify less than the instruction asks: in RoboTwin 2.0, shake_bottle_horizontally succeeds once the bottle is lifted.

We rewrite criteria and re-judge episodes on RoboDojo only. Its criteria report a score and stages besides success, so an exposed learner reads the most complete information there, and we compared the criteria of all of its tasks with their instructions; rewriting the criteria of other benchmarks and repeating these experiments on them is left to future work. We distinguish seven types: hidden rules, hard thresholds, timing and irreversible events, criteria defects, extra end states, loose criteria, and contradictions. In RoboDojo, after a manual review of every task, the 20 criteria-limited tasks have 26 variants, and hidden rules and hard thresholds are the most common types. Criteria-limited is defined with respect to the instruction the agent receives at reset; the RoboDojo website publishes part of these rules in its task descriptions and scoring tables.

For each criteria-limited task we rewrite only the criteria code, never the instruction, and leave the original repository untouched: hidden rules are removed or relaxed, defects fixed, hard thresholds relaxed to what still clearly satisfies the instruction, loose criteria tightened where the simulator state can detect the difference, and the return of both arms kept. The two criteria judged the same episodes independently, and every episode whose verdict flipped was checked by hand without finding a misjudgment by the new criteria. Each evaluation episode is then judged by both criteria, giving SR orig \text{SR}^{\text{orig}} and SR faith \text{SR}^{\text{faith}} . Since both criteria score the same instruction on the same episode, any difference between the two success rates comes from what the criteria verify, not from behavior. C faith C^{\text{faith}} is ours and serves as a proxy for S τ S_{\tau} ; we discuss this in section 5 .

To isolate the effect of exposure, the two settings of each comparison use the same actor, primitives, round budget and development layouts. The 25 learned tasks comprise 16 criteria-limited and 9 faithful tasks, grouped in advance by whether their criteria were rewritten; Appendix A.4 lists the tasks. Development uses layouts 0–4 of seed 1 and testing layouts 0–19 of seed 0. We report the success rate (SR) and compare settings layout by layout. All experiments use the same actor and learner. To reuse libraries, we distill the libraries of ten source tasks into one shared library and apply it to disjoint target tasks, in RoboDojo and on two further benchmarks with aligned primitives.

We use three simulated benchmarks with different roles. RoboDojo is the main benchmark: its rule-based criteria report a score and stages, and all three questions are answered on it. LIBERO-PRO is a single-arm tabletop benchmark where zero-shot success is already near the ceiling; it tests whether transfer still has room at high scores. RoboCasa365 has household kitchen scenes and the lowest zero-shot scores; it tests cross-benchmark experience and also hosts in-benchmark learning.
H1. Exposure raises the score only on tasks whose criteria ask for more than the instruction ( section 4.1 ).

H2. If exposure teaches the verifier rather than the task, its lead shrinks or reverses when the same episodes are judged by instruction-faithful criteria ( section 4.2.1 ), and each exposed library scores best under whichever criteria its learner read ( section 4.2.2 ).
H3. What exposure adds does not carry over to new tasks or benchmarks ( section 4.3 ).
We first judge the benchmark’s way, by the original criteria, which are also the criteria the exposed learner reads.

We learn one library per task and setting on the 25 learned tasks (16 criteria-limited, 9 faithful), over five rounds on five development layouts, and test each library on layouts 0–19 of seed 0 against the empty library. The two groups were fixed before any result was seen.

Tasks Empty library ℒ ∅ \mathcal{L}_{\varnothing} w/o CE w/ CE All (25) 24.6 47.8 (+23.2) 62.0 (+37.4) Criteria-limited (16) 8.4 27.8 (+19.4) 51.6 (+43.2) Faithful (9) 53.3 83.3 (+30.0) 80.6 (+27.3)

Figure 3 : Development success by round , on the 16 criteria-limited and the 9 faithful tasks. Dashed: w/ CE; solid: w/o CE; round 0 is the empty library. On criteria-limited tasks both settings start at 6% and part in round 1 (40% against 28%); after that the success-only learner barely moves and ends at 31%, against 55% with exposure. On faithful tasks the success-only learner is ahead through round 4 and both end above 90% (91% and 95%); its lead, at most 16 points, is close to the 14-point gap of round 0 (66% against 52%), where both run the same empty library.

Table 1 and figure 3 show three patterns. First, learning from success alone doubles success, from 24.6% to 47.8%, and reading the criteria adds another 14.2 points (62.0%). Second, this extra gain comes from the criteria-limited tasks: on faithful tasks the two settings are level (83.3% and 80.6%), while on criteria-limited tasks exposure leads, 51.6% against 27.8%. Third, among criteria-limited tasks the lead depends on whether an unstated rule shows in failed episodes: in build_tower the leftover blocks reveal it and both settings reach 20/20, whereas the button protocol of press_by_number, blue pressed twice and between the two red groups, never shows, and the success-only learner never finds it.

Exposure pays off only where the criteria ask for more than the instruction. Richer feedback is often assumed to make self-improvement better. Our results show a condition: when the criteria verify what the instruction says, success alone tells the learner what the task requires, and what remains, a reliable procedure, is learned equally well in both settings. Exposure helps only with rules that the instruction omits and that failures do not reveal.

The advantage of exposure measures the benchmark as much as the agent. Because it comes from what the instruction leaves out, the gain of exposure grows with the gap between a benchmark’s instructions and its criteria. Some of what the criteria reveal is legitimate task knowledge, but it belongs in the instruction: benchmarks that state in the instruction what their criteria verify (counts, order, end states, the reset of the arms) and release versioned criteria with a comparison against the instructions would let self-improvement be compared on the task alone.

passages.location: 4.2 Changing the Criteria: Task or Verifier?
passages.text: Section 4.1 judged with the criteria the exposed learner read. Changing them separates two explanations. If exposure teaches the task, its lead should survive under C faith C^{\text{faith}} ; if it teaches the verifier, the lead should shrink or reverse, and each library should score best under whichever criteria its learner read. We change the criteria used for judging and the criteria that are read.
We run the libraries of section 4.1.1 on the 16 learned criteria-limited tasks, all of which have rewritten criteria, 20 layouts each, and judge every episode by both criteria.

Figure 4 : The same episodes judged by the original and the instruction-faithful criteria. Libraries learned under C orig C^{\text{orig}} on the 16 criteria-limited tasks, 320 episodes per library. Light bars: judged by C orig C^{\text{orig}} ; solid bars: the same episodes judged by C faith C^{\text{faith}} ; arrows give the change in points.

Figure 5 : Each exposed library judged by the criteria it read and by the other. Both on the ten tasks of ℒ CE faith \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} , seed-0 test, 200 episodes per library. ℒ CE orig \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} : their episodes in figure 5 . ℒ CE faith \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} : its final library on the same layouts. Figure 5 shows the lead of exposure disappear. Under C orig C^{\text{orig}} the exposed library leads, 51.6% against 27.8%: paired by task and layout, it alone succeeds on 93 layouts and the success-only library alone on 17. Judged by C faith C^{\text{faith}} , the same episodes give 45.0% for the exposed library and 47.2% for the success-only one, a difference within noise (47 against 54 layouts); the gap shrinks by 25.9 points (95% bootstrap interval over tasks 4.7–54.4). The success-only library loses almost nothing: C faith C^{\text{faith}} accepts all but 2 of its 89 successes under C orig C^{\text{orig}} , and it gains where the original criteria demand an unstated protocol, as in press_by_number, swap_blocks and make_kong. The exposed library loses where it had learned that protocol, and on tasks whose criteria changes mostly fix defects or relax thresholds the two criteria give nearly the same scores.

passages.section: 4.2.2 Swapping the Criteria that Are Read
passages.location: 4.2.2 Swapping the Criteria that Are Read
passages.text: We then let the learner read C faith C^{\text{faith}} instead (ten tasks, five rounds) and compare the resulting library ℒ CE faith \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} with ℒ CE orig \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} on the same ten tasks, each judged by the criteria its learner read and by the other.

passages.section: 4.2.2 Swapping the Criteria that Are Read
passages.location: 4.2.2 Swapping the Criteria that Are Read
passages.text: Figure 5 shows that each exposed library does well only under the criteria it read: ℒ CE orig \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} falls from 57.0% to 45.0% under C faith C^{\text{faith}} , and ℒ CE faith \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} from 65.0% to 13.5% under C orig C^{\text{orig}} . The fall is steeper for ℒ CE faith \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} because the two directions differ: C faith C^{\text{faith}} mostly removes or relaxes the hidden rules and thresholds of C orig C^{\text{orig}} , so moving ℒ CE orig \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{orig}} to C faith C^{\text{faith}} loosens the verification, whereas moving ℒ CE faith \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}^{\text{faith}} to C orig C^{\text{orig}} adds back every rule the library never saw. The score follows the criteria that were read even where they are looser: having read C faith C^{\text{faith}} , the library no longer sets the bottle upright in pour_by_language, which C orig C^{\text{orig}} requires, and solves 19 of its 20 test layouts under C faith C^{\text{faith}} but none under C orig C^{\text{orig}} . This does not tell which criteria are right, which section 4.2.1 addresses, but it shows that the score of exposure does not carry between two criteria that score the same instruction.

Exposure makes self-improvement fit the criteria rather than learn the instructed task. A higher score from reading the criteria is commonly taken as faster learning of the task. A learner that reads the criteria, however, revises the library until it passes the verifier it reads, so the library learns the task only as far as the criteria agree with the instruction. Under instruction-faithful criteria the exposed library loses successes that the success-only library gains, and each exposed library scores best only under the criteria it read: on press_by_number it solves all 20 layouts under C orig C^{\text{orig}} and none under C faith C^{\text{faith}} , and the library that read C faith C^{\text{faith}} solves 65.0% of its test episodes under C faith C^{\text{faith}} but 13.5% under C orig C^{\text{orig}} . Self-improvement should therefore be measured without exposure by default, with the success rate under instruction-faithful criteria reported alongside: a robot in the real world has no criteria code, so the part of a gain that survives a change of criteria is the part to expect there.

Exposure changes what the learner writes down. A learner that reads the criteria can explain a failure by the condition it violated, so its experience is phrased in the terms of one verifier; a learner that sees only success has to find a physical cause, and its rules are closer to regularities of the robot. About a third of the exposed memory entries cite the criteria code, and none of the success-only ones do.

passages.section: 4.3 Reusing the Library: What Carries Over
passages.location: 4.3 Reusing the Library: What Carries Over
passages.text: Finally, we carry the libraries to new tasks in RoboDojo and to two further benchmarks.
We distill the libraries of ten learned tasks into one library per setting and apply it to ten target tasks that none of the source tasks covers, paired with the empty library on the same layouts.

Every row is paired with the empty library on the same layouts; parentheses give the change in successes against it.

Both settings help on the target tasks (first row of table 2 ): the empty library solves 65 of 200 episodes, the success-only library 80 and the exposed one 71. The 14.2-point lead of exposure on its own tasks does not reappear.

We apply the same libraries, translated to each target’s prompt and primitives, on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365, whose primitives we aligned with RoboDojo’s. On LIBERO-PRO the empty library already solves 34 of the 40 tasks on all five seeds, so we use the 6 others, with ten seeds each. On RoboCasa365 we also distill one library per setting from other RoboCasa365 tasks, as an in-benchmark reference.

The libraries from RoboDojo add little on either benchmark ( table 2 ): 48 and 46 of 60 episodes against 45 on LIBERO-PRO, and 24 and 24 of 100 against 22 on RoboCasa365. The libraries distilled within RoboCasa365 do better, 33 (w/o CE) and 29 (w/ CE) of 100.

What exposure adds is specific to the task it was learned on. One might expect the setting that scores higher on its own tasks to transfer better. It does not: the lead of exposure disappears on target tasks. Exposed experience carries the conditions and precision needed to pass one task’s criteria, which become noise or overhead elsewhere, whereas rules about the gripper hold across tasks.

Experience transfers where the bottleneck is shared. Within a benchmark the robot, the scenes and perception stay the same, and learned rules carry over. Across benchmarks the general part of the experience is already covered by the target’s prompt, while what the target lacks has no counterpart in the source, so the transferred skills go unused; experience gathered on the target benchmark, even on other tasks, addresses its own bottleneck and helps.

The instruction-faithful criteria are ours, and the feedback is simulated. C faith C^{\text{faith}} serves as our proxy for the success the instruction asks for, S τ S_{\tau} . Neither setting’s libraries saw the rewritten criteria when they were written; rules and types were fixed in advance; a second seed was judged independently and every flipped episode checked. Still, only RoboDojo’s criteria were rewritten, and success-only feedback in simulation is cleaner than the success a human or a VLM reports for a robot in the real world, which has no criteria code. Next steps are an independent review, released criteria code, rewritten criteria for a second benchmark, and VLM success detection in place of the simulator’s success [ 11 ] .

Exposure is studied at two levels, as current systems implement it. Most existing systems sit at intermediate levels (rule descriptions, published scoring tables, partial thresholds), which we did not study separately. A next step is to expose these levels one at a time and measure how the gain under C orig C^{\text{orig}} , and its loss under C faith C^{\text{faith}} , grow with what the learner reads.

Samples are small and the mechanisms are inferred. Each task has 20 test layouts, so quantitative claims use pooled results and single tasks are described only qualitatively; and distillation variance was not estimated. The accounts of what exposure writes into the library, of what carries over and of how the actor uses transferred libraries rest on entry text, skill calls and action statistics, not on ablations. Next steps are repeated distillations and ablations that remove or swap individual entries, such as the re-measuring entries of the distilled w/ CE library or the memory entries of a translated library.

In this paper, we studied what a self-improving embodied agent learns when it reads the success criteria, by comparing one self-improvement loop with and without Criteria Exposure, under the benchmark’s own and instruction-faithful criteria, and on new tasks and benchmarks. Our results show that self-improvement from success alone is real and survives a change of criteria, whereas the score that Criteria Exposure adds comes mainly from satisfying the criteria that were read: it appears only where the criteria and the instruction disagree, disappears under instruction-faithful criteria, and across benchmarks neither the exposed nor the success-only library gives a clear gain, while only in-benchmark experience helps. These findings provide a more careful reading of reported self-improvement gains on embodied benchmarks and practical guidance for measuring them: use the feedback a robot receives in the real world, and judge by criteria that verify what the instruction says. A robot in the real world never sees its verifier; the agent we measure should not either.
Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement

Benchmark. RoboDojo’s simulation track uses a dual-arm ARX-X5 with RGB observations only; its 42 tasks span five capability dimensions. The 20 tasks on which the zero-shot actor solves fewer than half of the episodes of the official evaluation seed, with five stronger ones, make the 25 compared tasks ( table 4 ). Every run uses one version of RoboDojo (Table 3 ); task source, criteria, leaderboard script and evaluation layouts are identical file by file across the checkouts we compare.

Conditions. The actor’s model, primitives and prompt are the same in every condition. The learner with Criteria Exposure reads the criteria code, each episode’s score and its passed stages; the one without sees full trajectories and success only. All conditions are compared over five rounds of improvement (rounds 0–5). The groups (Appendix B ) rest on reading the code, the learners’ diagnoses and the failed rollouts.
Layouts. Development reruns layouts 0–4 of official evaluation seed 1 every round; the test layouts are layouts 0–19 of seed 0 (500 episodes per condition), which no learner sees.

Statistics. Development batches are noisy: rerunning one library on one layout changes the verdict in 4% of cases, and the two round-0 batches of the same empty library differ in at least 13% of episodes. We therefore draw conclusions from the test layouts and pooled curves, and read single-task development curves only qualitatively.

Actor. GPT-6 Astra writes one code cell per MLLM call against PyRUA-Lean’s frozen robo API [ 29 ] : RGB perception (SAM 3 [ 7 ] and multi-view measurement) and motion primitives, with no VLA policy, depth or simulator state. The library is installed as a package library/: cells import its skills, and its live memory entries are appended to the prompt.

Library. A skill is a function of robo that imports only standard modules, numpy and other library modules, does no I/O and returns {"ok": …, "why": …, …}. A memory entry is ## {task}-<stage>-<nnn> followed by stage, symptom, applies, do, status and evidence. A task’s library holds at most 40,000 characters, all of which the actor reads.

Learner. Claude Code reads the session, the task’s dev runs, the API source and, with Criteria Exposure, the task’s criteria; it writes only the candidate library, its verification rollouts and its notes. Without Criteria Exposure, criteria, scores and stages are removed from the evidence.

Acceptance and rollback. A candidate may change only the task’s own directory, must keep every memory entry identifier, must cite a judged rollout or dev batch for each entry newly marked dev_verified, and must pass the static skill rules and the size limit; none of this looks at success, and no candidate was refused. The active revision rolls back to the best earlier complete batch when a complete batch has two or more fewer successes; ties go to the batch that passed more stages, and a batch with an episode lost to infrastructure neither triggers a rollback nor becomes the best.

analysis.overview: 本文将自改进循环的反馈暴露作为变量：无CE仅向learner给轨迹和二元成功，有CE还给判据代码、分数和阶段；actor固定，仅改技能/记忆库。16类判据与指令不一致任务的同一批轨迹，用原判据计CE优势23.8个百分点，用作者重写判据则约−2.2个百分点，差距收缩25.9个百分点。可复用的是同轨迹双判、互换学习判据和迁移评测，不是证明所有显式规格都无用。重写判据是作者代理，含主观阈值及两臂回位保留；CE反馈多因素捆绑，跨任务机制只有描述性证据，仍须独立规范审查与分项消融。
analysis.notice: 当前会话代理完整读完HTML证据85/85片段。提取包在附录C表头处结束，漏掉算法具体步骤、表6内容与附录D–J；已从固定PDF补读这些部分，含表7–10、蒸馏说明、记忆/技能调用案例和原语对齐，未将85/85本身冒充全文完整。PDF共22页、3182400字节，补读参考文献与实现，目视物理页4/6/7/8/16/17/18/20/22，核算法1、图2–5及7、表1/2/6–10。作者所有实验均为仿真，本轮未运行代码、模型、仿真或外部模型API，未复现；公开项目页浏览不可访问，curl TLS连接失败，未验证代码发布内容。

findings.title: 评分器与指令不一致时，得分可混入补全隐含规格的收益
findings.text: 研究问题是自改进所得增益在多大程度上来自阅读评测判据，而非新控制技能。作者将判据与reset时指令有冲突、额外隐含要求或遗漏要求的任务称criteria-limited，审查RoboDojo42任务后统计20类、26变体；只在RoboDojo重写判据。隐含顺序、阈值、一次性事件、缺陷、额外终态、过松判据与矛盾均可能改变得分。部分规则本就在官网公开，只是未出现在reset指令；所以CE不全是作弊，可能补足合法任务信息。作者称模仿数据通常已含这些细节，不等于本轮证明所有模仿策略评测都不受该错配影响。

findings.title: 暴露发生在learner，且代码、分数、阶段一起增加
findings.text: 固定actor为GPT-6 Astra高推理，通过PyRUA-Lean RGB感知/SAM3和运动原语写代码，不用VLA、深度或sim状态；作者的learner为Claude Code/Opus5.5高推理，只改每任务技能及记忆库，actor不直接读判据，但库可间接传递其内容。无CE给完整轨迹与成功，有CE同时加代码、分数、阶段，因而实验识别的是反馈包效应，不能独立归因于读代码。每任务5轮×5个开发layout，库最多40000字符，测试冻结只读；完整开发批次比历史最好少≥2次成功则回滚。附录还用阶段数为并列批次破同分，因此无CE是learner看不到阶段，不是整个选库控制器完全不使用阶段。各条件同轮数与上限，不代表实际调用token/验证次数或总费用相同；本轮未调用作者模型或API。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 同轨迹双判减少行为混杂，但新判据并非无主观性的真值
findings.text: 只改判据及内存中的资产标注，不改指令或原仓库；既放宽也收紧/纠错，并非原判据的简单超集。PDF表6：press_by_number由两组红键中间/末尾各蓝一次改为按每卡红键次数后蓝一次，另修按键释放阈值；倒液阈值97%→90%，fasten_screws拧紧由下沉9mm收紧为35mm，同时共轴容差放宽。作者还定义塔与笔记本可落边，保留所有两臂回位，尽管42任务有33要求回位、只有5条指令明说。因此C_faith是作者对意图的代理，不是独立测得的任务真值。离线单测、seed0/2双判及手查翻转增加可信度，但未报告盲评、多评审一致性。双判只有两者都得出结论才早停，确保判决未截断，也与单判立即停止协议有差别。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 原判据下CE增益集中在16类错配任务，不能说无CE不学习
findings.text: 表1：25任务×20测试布局，空库24.6%，无CE47.8%，CE62.0%；无CE自身已有+23.2个百分点，CE额外+14.2。16类criteria-limited中8.4→27.8→51.6，9类faithful中53.3→83.3→80.6。后者没有CE优势，但未作等效性验证，不能宣称两者严格一样。样本并非随机全42任务：选20个零样本成功不足半数的任务加5个较强任务；开发seed1 layouts0–4反复使用，测试seed0 layouts0–19未给learner。开发相同空库起点也能差约13%–14%，曲线只作描述，不能将某轮差距当稳健学习加速。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 同轨迹换判据使CE优势收缩25.9个百分点
findings.text: 图4及PDF表7，每库16任务×20布局=320轨迹，保持行为不变双判：CE原判据165/320=51.6%，新判据144/320=45.0%；无CE89/320=27.8%→151/320=47.2%。原CE仅胜93布局、无CE仅胜17；新判据对应47对54，差−7例。CE在重判时失27、得6；无CE失2、得64，说明不是统一加分或重新执行更好。两条件差距收缩25.9个百分点，95%按任务bootstrap区间4.7–54.4，区间宽但支持评价依赖；新判据下−2.2个百分点不能当无CE已显著优于CE。press_by_number CE原20/20而新0/20，无CE原0而新19；原库确实匹配另一套按钮协议，不等于证明读取任何明确规格都会损害物理能力。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 互换学习所读判据后，高分跟着所读规格走
findings.text: 图5与PDF附录E表8只比较10任务、每库200测试轨迹，不是上项16任务320轨迹。读原判据的库在原/新下57.0/45.0%；读新判据的库在新/原下130/200=65.0%和27/200=13.5%。pour_by_language读新规则后19/20通过新判据，原判据0，因不再把瓶摆正而原规则在该事件才验收。这支持跨规则稳健性不足，但新旧规格要求并不语义完全等价，方向不对称；分数跟规则也可能是对明示规格的正常优化，不能由此确定哪套规范正确或评价所有形式化目标。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 记忆条目内容提示规则拟合，机制尚无条目级因果消融
findings.text: 主文称约三分之一CE记忆引用判据。PDF附录F细数19/55条，占47%字符；无CE0/53。例子包括蓝键顺序、夹拉按键帽以满足释放阈值、按原判据不看扫帚而建议不用扫帚。无CE的空夹问题追到KEEP会再次闭指，形成空手移动显式OPEN规则；CE保留半开公式。附录H图7/表9空手移动OPEN比例为空库35%、无CE91%、CE3%；insert_tubes重测动作均值40/57/116、成功12/11/6（各20布局）。这些是条目/调用/动作统计的描述，不是已隔离的原因；表9行为统计仅取首跑，147/132可用episode且部分任务不足10，不能把它们当全部200任务执行的无偏机制估计。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 迁移比较包含单次蒸馏及CE专用过滤，优势未复现
findings.text: 表2同RoboDojo十目标任务200例，空库65、无CE80、CE71；十源任务与这十目标不重合，不等于目标均在全25学习任务之外。PDF附录G：每库只蒸馏一次，CE brief额外要求删掉仅描述判据的规则，实际删9条；这套蒸馏/翻译操作也是处理的一部分，不能把最终差异完全归给原始暴露。跨基准LIBERO-PRO为45/60、48/60、46/60；RoboCasa365为22/100、24/100、24/100；同RoboCasa其他源任务蒸馏后33/100、29/100。均是各自原生判据，不是C_faith。没有迁移差值置信区间或重复蒸馏方差，支持本协议下CE优势未复现，不能证明所有库跨任务必不泛化。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 原语对齐显著改变空库基线，不能混用官方分数
findings.text: 跨基准前先将原语及prompt与RoboDojo对齐。PDF附录J表10：对齐后空库LIBERO-PRO四suite成功41/50、47/50、50/50、50/50，共188/200；已发表PyRUA-Lean同任务种子为36/50、45/50、44/50、39/50。RoboCasa原子55/90对59/90，复合54/160对32/160，说明接口改动本身可改变基线，不能归因于库迁移。40任务中34任务五seed全成，迁移专挑其余6任务扩为10seed=60，不是整个LIBERO-PRO仅75%或更广泛泛化基准。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 技能未调用、目标瓶颈不同，尚未隔离迁移失效路径
findings.text: PDF附录I：来自RoboDojo的两库在200条RoboCasa目标episode都没调用skill，LIBERO-PRO各5和12/60调用；memory始终进prompt，因此没调用技能不等于库完全无影响。同RoboCasa源库合计158/200有技能调用，主要感知/关节余量；源库不含移动基座或铰接部件经验，目标正需要这些。该描述与迁移不足相符，但未做强制调用、去memory/去skills或瓶颈匹配消融；也只测试一种翻译。作者不能由调用相关性单独证明通用物理规则与判据规则各自的因果迁移价值。

additional_sources.note: 固定PDF补读或目视核对；这些细节未在HTML提取包中完整收录。

findings.title: 指令代理、二元干净反馈与单模型组合限制外推
findings.text: 全部为模拟、同一actor/learner与原语栈，只有RoboDojo重写判据；没有实机、真实人/VLM噪声反馈、中间暴露水平或代码/分数/阶段独立消融。每任务20测试布局，单任务案例是定性，蒸馏随机性未估；作者称分组/重写规则提前定好，本轮未独立审其时间线、原始库、轨迹或评审独立性。回位保留与拧紧35mm等规范需独立审核。项目页本轮浏览不可访问、curl TLS连接失败，不能声称代码已验证可获取；也不据此断言资源永久不存在。实际真实机器人可获得明确任务规格、规划约束或用户反馈，本文不证明一律隐藏形式规格最佳；应先保证指令/评分契约一致，再比较等信息和等成本的学习。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：补全指令后，原规则暴露的额外优势是否仍存在？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：先把独立评审认可的合法任务要求补全到指令，并保持反馈信息量与预算可比后，源码暴露相对仅分数/阶段反馈的额外收益会明显缩小，且更少依赖某一个判据实现。仅公开仿真实验草案：先用公开轨迹离线比较现有判据，不调用任何模型API；进一步实验在本地可执行的固定coding-agent组合上，将原简略/补全指令两组与四种learner反馈交叉：轨迹+二元成功、再加分数阶段、代码+二元成功、全包。相同轮次/布局/动作和上下文预算，记录token、验证调用与wall-clock，不将同轮数等同同成本；选库并列规则统一只用成功，避免阶段暗入控制器。至少3次独立库学习和蒸馏、每任务20以上独立测试布局，按任务分层bootstrap。开发前由未看策略输出的评审冻结完整任务规范和至少两套语义等价的判据实现，额外盲评视频，保留评审分歧，不把同团队重写判据当绝对真值。对全部轨迹双判且统一停止规则，分别报告原规则得分、规范一致任务完成、跨判据差距、原任务与匹配瓶颈的源外迁移、成本；技能/记忆的删除和互换另设因果消融。若补全规范后源码相对同等分数阶段反馈仍在两套判据及盲评上稳定显著提高完整完成与迁移，而非仅多用预算，则推翻假设；区间宽时保留无定论。草案未执行、未创建选题，未全面查新或声称研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: 把判据暴露做成实验变量：同轨迹换评分器，额外优势消失
frontier_brief.change_type: 自改进反馈与基准效度审计
frontier_brief.delta: 固定actor和原语，只让learner可选读取判据代码/分数/阶段；冻结技能记忆库后，对同轨迹用原判据与作者重写判据双评，再互换学习所读规则、测试库迁移。
frontier_brief.before: 只在learner见过的判据上报告自改进，隐含按钮协议、阈值、缺陷或遗漏动作可能把规格拟合计为通用能力增益。
frontier_brief.after: 16类错配任务各320轨迹，CE/无CE原判据51.6/27.8%，换判据45.0/47.2%；优势收缩25.9个百分点，95%按任务bootstrap4.7–54.4。无CE本身仍有学习收益。
frontier_brief.relevance: 适合设计具身自改进与编码代理的反馈和评测：区分读形式规格与改进控制，固定明确指令/评分契约，报告独立判据与迁移，保留真实调用成本。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者实验未复现、全为仿真；新判据是作者代理，保留两臂回位且含自定阈值。CE把代码/分数/阶段捆绑，未隔离源码效应；蒸馏单次且CE条目过滤不同。跨基准未重写判据，无实机或真实噪声反馈证据。
frontier_brief.question: 补全合法任务规格并等信息/等成本后，读取源码还能比仅分数阶段反馈更稳定地改善任务完成与迁移吗？

evidence.label: 原判据下的增益来源
evidence.context: 表1，空库→无CE→CE，每任务20测试布局。16错配任务27.8对51.6，9 faithful任务83.3对80.6；CE未在后组显示优势，但非严格等效性检验。

evidence.label: 同轨迹双判
evidence.context: 图4、PDF表7；原→作者新判据，同一行为无重跑混杂。CE失27得6，无CE失2得64；优势收缩25.9pp、任务bootstrap95%区间4.7–54.4。

evidence.label: 互换学习所读规则
evidence.context: 图5、PDF表8，10任务×20布局；130/200在新判据成功，27/200在原判据成功。两套规则并非简单宽松包含，不能以此裁定哪个规范客观正确。

evidence.label: 迁移优势未复现
evidence.context: 表2；十源库一次蒸馏，CE额外删除判据专用规则。跨RoboCasa目标仅22→24/100，同基准源库达33/29；无重复蒸馏区间，不是所有迁移必失败。

evidence.label: 评分代理有规范选择
evidence.value: 两臂回位保留；拧紧35mm；倒液90%
evidence.context: PDF表6及附录C；作者也收紧遗漏动作并修缺陷，非统一放宽。42任务33要求回位仅5指令明说；人工翻转核查未替代独立盲评。

mechanism.title: 反馈包驱动库修改
mechanism.text: actor不直接读判据；learner写技能与记忆后间接传递规则。CE全包与二元成功条件不同，源码/分数/阶段没有分别消融。

mechanism.title: 双判轨迹与互换所读规则
mechanism.text: 相同轨迹按两套判据判断，停止需两者均有结论；再让learner读另一规则，区分评分依赖与行为改变，但新判据仍为意图代理。

mechanism.title: 把迁移看成另一检验

passages.section: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model Thanks: ‡ Correspondence Author.
passages.location: Reinforcing End-to-End Autonomous Driving Safety via Negative-Aware Planning in a Unified World-Action Model Thanks: ‡ Correspondence Author.
passages.text: World-action models (WAMs) jointly model future traffic states and driving actions for end-to-end autonomous driving in intelligent transportation systems. However, their action learning remains dominated by expert-trajectory imitation, leaving unsafe alternatives close to expert trajectories insufficiently constrained. To improve WAM robustness in safety-critical scenarios, we propose NegWAM , a safety post-training framework for unified WAMs that learns explicit safety boundaries from near-expert failure trajectories. NegWAM constructs negative trajectories that are geometrically close to the expert trajectory yet carry safety risks, uses them as repulsive anchors to steer predictions away from dangerous behavior, and encodes them as scene-conditioned rider tokens to learn scene–trajectory compatibility. During training, NegWAM jointly optimizes the flow-matching and near-expert negative objectives, while the auxiliary rider branch is discarded at inference, incurring no additional overhead. On NAVSIM v2, NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard , a 4.1 % relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest . These results demonstrate that NegWAM achieves strong performance in safety-critical scenarios while preserving routine-driving performance. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM further demonstrates cross-benchmark generalization. The code is available at https://github.com/Zizizi-hao/NegWAM .

End-to-end autonomous driving systems typically learn driving policies from large-scale expert demonstrations and perform well in routine scenarios [ 1 , 2 ] . However, hazardous behaviors and failure cases are scarce in real-world driving data, making it difficult for imitation learning to acquire explicit safety boundaries [ 3 , 4 ] . World-action models (WAMs) introduce stronger priors over scene dynamics into end-to-end autonomous driving by predicting future world states and leveraging future representations to guide planning [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Yet their action branches are still trained primarily through flow matching on expert trajectories. This supervision tells the model what to imitate, but not which near-expert alternatives should be rejected as unsafe. Consequently, stronger world modeling alone does not establish explicit safety boundaries, motivating safety-oriented post-training for WAMs.

Fig. 1: Sources of supervision for post-training in end-to-end autonomous driving. (a) Environment-derived rewards from closed-loop interaction with a simulator or world model. (b) Trajectory scores from an external rule-based or learned scorer. (c) NegWAM uses offline-mined negative trajectories as repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens to introduce negative-aware losses into a unified world–action model.

Post-training offers a natural avenue beyond these limitations, but a central challenge is constructing learning signals that faithfully encode desired driving behavior [ 8 , 4 ] . Existing methods primarily rely on two sources of supervision. One line of work (Figure 1 a) explores policies in closed-loop environments built with a simulator [ 9 , 10 ] or a world model [ 11 , 12 ] , but is constrained by the sim-to-real gap, environment construction costs, and reconstruction artifacts [ 13 , 12 ] . Another line (Figure 1 b) scores candidate trajectories using rule-based evaluators or learned reward models, but the quality of its supervision is limited by handcrafted rules, privileged information, and evaluator bias [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . These limitations underscore the need for additional sources of effective supervision for autonomous driving post-training.

Unsafe driving behaviors provide critical cues for delineating safety boundaries and are often easier to characterize than the full range of desirable driving behavior [ 17 , 18 ] . Building on this insight, we propose NegWAM , a negative-aware safety post-training method that incorporates offline negative supervision into a unified WAM (Figure 1 c). Specifically, near-expert negatives serve as repulsive anchors that mark locally unsafe regions in trajectory space and as scene-conditioned rider tokens that enable shared attention layers to learn scene–trajectory compatibility. Together with the original imitation objective, these mechanisms enable the WAM to learn not only how experts drive but also which behaviors should be avoided in the current scene.

Unlike prior hard-negative learning that primarily regularizes planner outputs [ 17 ] , NegWAM post-trains both the single-rollout action flow and the shared world–action representation of a unified WAM. It mines near-expert trajectories that fail offline safety evaluation and jointly optimizes the original flow-matching objective with two hard-negative objectives. The evaluator is used only for offline mining, while the rider branch and compatibility head are removed at inference, adding no inference-time modules. On NAVSIM v2 [ 19 , 20 ] , NegWAM achieves 40.4 EPDMS on navhard , a 4.1 % relative improvement over the strongest compared scorer-free WAM baseline, and achieves 93.3 EPDMS on navtest , surpassing the strongest baseline score of 92.9 by 0.4 points and demonstrating stronger challenging-scenario performance without compromising routine driving. Zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM [ 21 ] further supports cross-benchmark transfer, with NegWAM achieving a higher HD-Score than DriveWAM (30.6 vs. 27.2).
In summary, our key contributions are as follows:

We revisit unified world–action models through safety post-training, showing that augmenting flow-matching imitation with near-expert negative supervision improves challenging-scenario performance without compromising routine driving.

We propose NegWAM, a near-expert negative safety post-training method for WAMs that jointly optimizes the original flow-matching objective and two complementary near-expert negative objectives without introducing additional inference-time overhead.

We introduce two complementary near-expert negative mechanisms. Repulsive anchors push predictions away from locally unsafe trajectories, while scene-conditioned rider tokens enable the unified WAM to determine whether a trajectory is compatible with the current scene.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on end-to-end autonomous driving, world–action models, and policy post-training. Section III introduces NegWAM, including its core components and training objective. Section IV evaluates its planning performance and zero-shot closed-loop generalization, with ablation studies and supporting analyses. Section V summarizes the main findings and discusses limitations and future directions.

Fig. 2: Architecture of our NegWAM. In Stage 1, we adapt a pretrained world-action DiT into a unified world–action model through flow matching. In Stage 2, scene-specific hard-negative trajectories are used as both repulsive anchors and trajectory riders for compatibility learning. The auxiliary rider branch is removed at inference, introducing no additional deployment cost.

End-to-end autonomous driving maps sensory observations to planned trajectories through a learned policy [ 2 , 22 ] . Joint optimization connects scene understanding with planning and reduces information loss across separately designed modules [ 1 ] . Scaling driving data further improves the coverage of learned behavior [ 23 ] , while generative future prediction introduces temporal structure and motion priors into policy learning [ 24 , 25 ] . These developments strengthen the policy’s ability to represent traffic scenes and reproduce expert decisions across diverse driving conditions.

Expert demonstrations nevertheless provide an uneven account of driving behavior: successful maneuvers are abundant, whereas safety-critical failures and recovery interactions are comparatively scarce [ 3 , 12 , 4 ] . Expert-trajectory supervision identifies a desirable action for the observed scene, but supplies few explicit comparisons with nearby unsafe alternatives. Such alternatives are informative because geometric similarity to an expert trajectory does not establish that an action is safe in the same traffic context [ 17 , 26 ] . Learning to distinguish these alternatives introduces a specific supervision requirement beyond reproducing the demonstrated trajectory.

Pretrained video generative models provide temporal and motion priors that can be transferred to action learning [ 27 , 5 , 7 ] . Their role in driving has expanded from supporting scene synthesis and simulation [ 11 , 28 ] to providing future representations for trajectory prediction [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] . Recent approaches further couple future visual modeling with action generation, bringing anticipated scene evolution into the policy’s prediction process [ 5 , 32 , 6 ] . This progression makes world modeling increasingly relevant to how driving actions are represented and generated.

Recent work [ 7 , 33 ] realizes this coupling through shared video–action transformers trained using flow matching. Such architectures allow action supervision to shape the shared world–action representations. Their training objectives, however, focus on fitting demonstrated video–action sequences without explicitly contrasting expert trajectories with undesirable alternatives. This raises the question of how negative trajectories can provide supervision for both action generation and scene–trajectory compatibility during safety post-training.

Driving policy post-training introduces feedback beyond expert matching through simulated rollouts, reward-based optimization, and trajectory preferences [ 3 , 4 ] . Closed-loop learning uses synthetic simulators such as CARLA [ 9 , 34 ] , reconstructed scenes, or learned environments to expose policies to the consequences of their actions [ 13 , 12 ] . These mechanisms often overlap: DreamerAD [ 14 ] combines latent-world rollouts with learned reward feedback, while WorldRFT [ 15 ] uses collision-aware rewards for reinforcement fine-tuning. Complementary to policy post-training, TOAD [ 16 ] uses a learned trajectory scorer to guide test-time search without retraining the policy.

Preference-based methods express the additional supervision through comparisons between trajectories. TakeAD [ 35 ] derives preferences from expert takeover data. DriveDPO [ 26 ] combines imitation similarity with rule-based safety scores for policy learning, then applies Safety DPO using human-like but unsafe rejected trajectories. Its preference construction thus retains explicit safety evaluation without requiring a separately trained reward model. BeyondDrive [ 17 ] develops this failure-based perspective through a flow-matching generator, expert-proximity and safety filtering, and a repulsive distance loss defined on predicted trajectories. These studies establish the value of near-expert failures as supervision, with distinct choices of policy objective and negative construction.

For a unified WAM, an unsafe alternative is both a trajectory to avoid and an example of incompatibility between the scene and an action. NegWAM learns these two aspects from the same offline-mined failures: repulsive anchors supervise the generated action trajectory, while rider tokens expose the expert and negative trajectories to the observed scene through shared attention for compatibility learning. The original flow-matching objective remains active throughout post-training. Safety evaluation supplies the offline negative labels; subsequent optimization internalizes this supervision in the WAM, and the auxiliary rider branch is removed at inference.

NegWAM post-trains a unified world–action model using scene-specific failures close to expert trajectories. Each retained failure supplies two related learning signals: a motion to avoid during action generation and a scene–trajectory pair to distinguish from the expert. Figure 2 illustrates how repulsive anchors and scene-conditioned rider tokens introduce these signals into the same backbone while retaining its flow-matching objective.

To couple future scene modeling with action generation in one backbone, we adopt a unified world–action architecture [ 27 , 7 ] built on a pretrained video backbone [ 36 ] as the base model. The same failures also define scene–trajectory comparisons. We encode the expert and each negative as a separate auxiliary rider group ℛ g \mathcal{R}_{g} , using the shared action embedding and the same rotary positional encoding grid. Each group contains a zero conditioning chunk and an eight-step trajectory chunk, giving 16 action tokens. Riders are clean, with no diffusion noise and a flow-time input t = 0 t=0 . The expert occupies group zero; the remaining groups represent the negatives. Figure 3 illustrates the shared attention and scoring pathway.

The riders access the scene through shared attention while remaining invisible to the original streams. Let 𝐱 c v , obs \mathbf{x}_{c}^{v,\mathrm{obs}} contain the clean visual conditioning tokens of the current observed frame. At every DiT block, the attention visibility is

Thus, each rider sees only the current observed visual tokens and its own trajectory group. Future target tokens are excluded from these keys, and the observed tokens retain their original causal visibility. The original sequence cannot attend to riders, so appending them preserves its forward attention path at fixed backbone weights. Matching the expert and negative groups’ tokenization, positions, and visibility reduces structural differences in their scoring inputs.

where τ s = 0.1 \tau_{s}=0.1 . The expectation denotes the mean over samples with valid negatives; we set ℒ compat = 0 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{compat}}=0 when ℬ + \mathcal{B}_{+} is empty. This objective ranks the expert above valid scene-specific negatives. Its gradients propagate through the shared attention projections, adding an explicit scene–trajectory ranking objective to the backbone. Rider groups and the compatibility head are used only during post-training.

Our training procedure consists of two consecutive stages. In the first stage, we initialize the model from the pretrained video generative model Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [ 36 ] and adapt it to autonomous driving by following the unified world–action flow-matching paradigm of DriveWAM [ 7 ] . This stage optimizes only the flow-matching objective defined in Section III-A , enabling the model to jointly learn future visual dynamics and expert trajectory prediction. The resulting model serves as the base WAM checkpoint shared by all subsequent experiments.

In the second stage, we initialize from this shared checkpoint and perform hard-negative safety post-training. We retain the original flow-matching objective as supervision for visual dynamics and expert actions, while introducing repulsive trajectory supervision and scene-conditioned compatibility learning. The overall post-training objective is

ℒ post = ℒ FM + λ rep ​ ℒ rep + λ compat ​ ℒ compat , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{post}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FM}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rep}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{compat}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{compat}}, (11)

where ℒ rep \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rep}} pushes predictions away from unsafe neighbors in trajectory space, and ℒ compat \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{compat}} learns scene–trajectory compatibility through rider tokens. λ rep \lambda_{\mathrm{rep}} and λ compat \lambda_{\mathrm{compat}} control the contributions of the two hard-negative objectives. All post-training variants start from the same first-stage checkpoint, controlling for differences in base-model initialization.

At inference, we discard the rider groups and compatibility head and use the original world–action generation pathway with the updated backbone. The model encodes the available observations, generates future visual latents with three Euler updates, and then generates the eight-step action chunk with ten Euler updates. These are integration-step counts rather than total backbone forward-call counts. The action decoder converts the generated tokens to the final trajectory; no hard-negative candidates or evaluator are used at this stage.
