passages.section: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.location: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.text: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

passages.section: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.location: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
passages.text: Keywords: Code-as-policy agents, Self-repair, Execution feedback, Test-time evaluation

Code-as-policy agents translate language instructions into executable robot programs [ 1 ] . Their failures often follow clear patterns: a program may skip the grasp, release an object after lifting, or place it away from the target. A common response is iterative self-reflection. The model reads its failed program and execution trace, writes a critique, and tries again [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Retry success can reflect additional sampling, concise task instructions, feedback about the current failure, or editing the previous program. We ask whether feedback after failure improves recovery over guidance available from the first attempt.

We study this question with frozen Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B models in a reset-and-retry setting. Each retry starts from the original scene. Our main conditions generate a fresh program with the failed program omitted from the prompt. We use template-based feedback to study which information improves retry success. A fixed lookup selects instructions using the failure label and API variant, such as “MUST grasp the object before lifting.” We call this condition Compiled . The lookup lets us replace matched feedback with another episode’s feedback, hold the guidance fixed, or remove it while keeping the retry loop unchanged (Figure 1 ). Separate editing conditions expose the previous program and request a revision. All conditions restart the original scene. We do not test recovery from the physical state left by failure.

Figure 1: Template-based feedback improves recovery over resampling. (a) Reset-and-retry loop and feedback methods. (b) Recovery on 252 initial failures, with similar outcomes for Compiled, Different-Label Feedback, and Fixed Task Template.

Compiled recovers 85.3% of the 252 initial failures within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The gain persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and one fixed template per task produce similar point estimates. We detect no benefit from matching the coarse failure label to the current episode. The confidence intervals still allow differences between conditions. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to Compiled’s, with fewer tokens per solved episode. That comparison changes initial guidance and the generation instruction together. Their individual contributions remain unresolved.

We compare feedback content and program-generation strategies under matched retry budgets to test how additional sampling, reusable task guidance, and failure-label matching affect recovery. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include static guidance as a baseline for adaptive feedback.

Language models for robot control. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt generate executable programs from grounded robot skills [ 1 , 5 ] . SayCan selects actions using language-model and affordance scores [ 6 ] . CaP-X evaluates code-generating agents across robot APIs and feedback modalities, including multi-turn interaction without scene resets [ 7 ] . Robot recovery systems often ask a model to interpret a failure. REFLECT summarizes robot experience to support failure explanation and correction [ 8 ] . DoReMi compares a plan with its execution [ 9 ] . TCoT adds trajectory-level reasoning to a vision-language-action model [ 10 ] . Our reset-based comparisons examine feedback content and program-generation strategies on paired episodes under matched retry budgets.

Evaluation of iterative self-repair. Reflexion and Self-Refine use model-written critiques to improve later outputs [ 2 , 3 ] . Self-Debugging conditions code generation on the previous program and its execution results [ 4 ] . On code benchmarks, Olausson et al. [11] found that self-repair often does not outperform independent sampling at matched compute. Self-correction of reasoning is also unreliable without external feedback, whereas critique grounded in external evidence can help [ 12 , 13 ] . We extend matched-sampling comparisons to embodied code execution and test whether guidance must match the current failure or follow a failure at all.

Execution feedback and interactive evaluation. CodeRL, RLEF, and MURPHY use compiler or test feedback to update model parameters [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . RLEF also tests random execution feedback from unrelated programming problems at inference time. This comparison tests the value of feedback specific to the current problem, although its training, tasks, and feedback construction differ from ours. Inference-time agents such as ReAct, Voyager, and LATS use feedback during search or interaction [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . InterCode, AppWorld, and AgentBoard evaluate execution outcomes and intermediate progress [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . With model weights fixed, we ask which information in a robot’s retry prompt accounts for recovery.

We evaluate frozen code models in robosuite simulation with a Panda arm [ 23 , 24 ] . Models receive state information and generate Python programs using a documented robot API, without images. The primary evaluation uses Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct [ 25 ] with the primitive API on cube lifting and stacking.

An episode comprises an initial program execution for a task and scene, followed by any retries under one method. The initial execution is attempt 0 . After an initial failure, the model is allowed up to five retries . Before each retry, the simulator resets to the original scene. Each retry produces a complete program, either generated from scratch or revised from the previous program.

We use 252 initial failures for evaluation and 40 for development. The sets contain distinct initial programs, identified by their hashes. The evaluation covers 159 combinations of task, API variant, and scene, including 24 also used in development. All methods are evaluated on the same stored initial failures. The end-to-end studies pair methods by scene seed.

Conditional recovery@ k k is the fraction of attempt-0 failures solved within k k retries. This metric measures sequential retries and differs from pass@ k k estimated from independent samples. For end-to-end studies, initial success is success on attempt 0 and overall success@6 is success in any of the six allowed executions. An attempt is valid if its program compiles, uses only documented API functions, and finishes before timeout.

The generalization study includes Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B and two additional pick-and-place tasks. We combine results across seven settings that meet the predefined eligibility criteria. Separate studies examine API variants with fewer high-level helper functions, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, and DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B [ 26 ] . Further details of the software, tasks, evaluation sets, and metrics are provided in Appendix A .

After an unsuccessful execution, a rule-based labeler assigns one primary label from a 14-label taxonomy. Compiled maps this label and the API variant to a fixed feedback template containing a diagnosis and short MUST/NEVER instructions (Table 1 ). This lookup requires no additional model call. The instructions guide code generation without imposing execution-time checks.

Compiled accumulates feedback from the initial failure and subsequent failed retries, retaining the labels and attempt indices. The feedback block presents the newest feedback first, omits duplicate instruction lines, and respects the feedback-length limit. The generation prompt contains the task, API documentation, and accumulated feedback, with the previous program omitted. An example from the earlier study shows an initial failure followed by a successful fresh retry (Figure 2 a). The prompts are provided in Appendix B , and the reset-and-retry algorithm is given in Algorithm 1 .
Table 1: Failure labels select fixed retry guidance. Example instruction excerpts for the primitive API. Full templates are provided in Appendix D .

Detected failure Guidance added to the retry prompt Grasp did not secure the object MUST: grasp at the object’s CENTRE: …, with the gripper empty Object grasped but not lifted MUST: … call lift(name, height=0.1) after the grasp Unsupported function call MUST: use ONLY the documented API functions … NEVER: import statements

We compare methods within each study using the same generator, task, API, decoding settings, and retry limit. Resample repeats the base retry prompt without feedback. Other-Episode Feedback replaces the current episode’s feedback with feedback from other failures, matched by task, API variant, and initial task-progress bin. The primary matching control, Different-Label Feedback , selects individual feedback records from other episodes of the same task, preferring the same initial task-progress bin and requiring a different failure label whenever available. Both add feedback as the evaluated episode accumulates failures and use the same feedback-length limit. These controls test the value of matching the coarse failure label while retaining useful task information. The matching and fallback rules are specified in Appendix B.3 .

We select a fixed template for each task from the development data, choosing the most frequent failure label with task-compatible guidance. Fixed Task Template reuses this template across retries after the initial failure. Static-from-Start uses the complete Fixed Task Template retry prompt from attempt 0, changing both the initial generation instruction and the presence of guidance.

Direct+Compiled shows the failed program and requests an edit, jointly changing code exposure and the generation instruction. Reflection uses an extra model call to critique the failed program and execution log. Its generation call receives the accumulated critiques and omits the previous code. Reflection was tested only in the earlier core evaluation with the original generation instruction.

The primary evaluation uses a condition-neutral generation instruction for regeneration methods. The original instruction referred to a repair plan even when feedback was absent. Both prompt versions are provided in Appendix B.4 .
Eligibility criteria, multiplicity corrections, decoding settings, and token accounting are specified in Appendix A .

Figure 2: Guidance improves recovery under fixed token budgets. (a) An initial failure followed by a successful retry after reset. (b) Recovery under total-token budgets. (c) Paired recovery@5 comparisons show an advantage over resampling, with no detected advantage over different-label or fixed-template guidance.

In the primary evaluation, Compiled recovers 85.3% of the 252 held-out failures within five retries. Resample, with the same retry cap, recovers 68.3%, a difference of + 17.1 +17.1 pp (95% CI [ + 9.9 , + 24.2 ] [+9.9,+24.2] ). 1 1 1 pp denotes percentage points. Bands and error bars show 95% CIs: Wilson for recovery proportions and paired bootstrap for differences. Compiled recovers more failures than Resample from the first retry (Figure 1 b) and uses fewer total model tokens, including prompts and completions.

Under fixed token budgets, Compiled improves recovery over Resample by + 15.9 +15.9 pp at 2,000 tokens and + 14.7 +14.7 pp at 5,000 (Figure 2 b). Fixed Task Template and Different-Label Feedback yield similar observed recovery rates to Compiled, while Direct+Compiled has lower recovery. Compiled also achieves higher overall success than Resample in the earlier 700-scene end-to-end study with the original generation instruction (Appendix C ).

Different-Label Feedback and Fixed Task Template each recover 86.1% in the primary evaluation, compared with 85.3% for Compiled. We detect no advantage from matching the coarse label to the current failure, although the paired confidence intervals do not establish equivalence (Table 2 ; Figure 2 c). In earlier studies, we also detected no advantage for Compiled over Other-Episode Feedback, Permuted Labels, or Initial-Label Only (Appendix C ).

In the primary evaluation, the exploratory Repeated API Rules control copies rules already in the prompt and does not reproduce Compiled’s improvement. Earlier comparisons using the original generation instruction likewise show lower recovery with content-free feedback and All-Template Union than with concise feedback templates (Appendix C ).
Table 2: Primary paired contrasts on 252 initial failures. Each entry is Compiled minus the comparator in recovery@5, with a 95% paired-bootstrap CI.

Comparator Question Δ \Delta (pp; 95% CI) Resample benefit beyond another sample? + 17.1 +17.1 [ + 9.9 , + 24.2 ] [+9.9,+24.2] Different-Label Feedback must the label match? − 0.8 -0.8 [ − 6.3 , + 4.8 ] [-6.3,+4.8] Fixed Task Template dynamic versus fixed guidance? − 0.8 -0.8 [ − 6.7 , + 5.2 ] [-6.7,+5.2] Direct+Compiled does editing improve recovery? + 63.9 +63.9 [ + 56.7 , + 70.6 ] [+56.7,+70.6]

On 700 new scenes, Static-from-Start increases initial success from 19.3% with the standard prompt to 36.9%. It uses the complete Fixed Task Template retry prompt from the first attempt, changing both task guidance and the generation instruction. Their individual contributions remain unresolved.

By the sixth execution, Static-from-Start reaches 92.4% overall success, compared with 89.6% for Compiled and 90.1% for Fixed Task Template (Figure 3 ). Its advantage over Compiled is not statistically significant after multiplicity correction ( + 2.9 +2.9 pp; Holm-adjusted p = 0.13 p{=}0.13 ). It also uses the fewest total model tokens per solved episode. Complete results and prompt differences are reported in Appendix C.2 .

Figure 3: A fixed guided prompt improves initial success. (a) Initial and overall success on 700 fresh scenes. (b) Total model tokens per solved episode. Static-from-Start changes both the initial instruction and guidance.
The matching controls and Static-from-Start results suggest that reusable task guidance accounts for the gain. These results do not establish that the model uses the current execution trace.

Direct+Compiled achieves 21.4% recovery in the primary evaluation. Earlier analyses show smaller program changes with editing than with fresh generation. Because Direct+Compiled changes code exposure and the generation instruction together, the cause of its lower recovery remains unresolved.

In the earlier core evaluation, Reflection achieves 56.0% recovery, below Resample, while using more completion tokens and wall-clock time. These findings concern the tested editing and reflection implementations. Further editing and critique results are summarized in Appendix C.1 .
Figure 4: Guidance benefits vary across tasks and models. Compiled–Resample recovery differences across evaluated settings. The diamond summarizes the seven eligible generalization settings.

Across seven Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B settings covering four tasks and 354 initial failures, Compiled improves recovery@5 over Resample by + 18.1 +18.1 pp (CI [ + 13.3 , + 22.9 ] [+13.3,+22.9] ). Its difference from Other-Episode Feedback is smaller, at + 2.3 +2.3 pp (CI [ − 1.1 , + 5.6 ] [-1.1,+5.6] ), with no detected advantage over this same-task feedback control (Figure 4 ; Appendix C.3 ).

The recovery advantage persists in most additional evaluations of API variants, pose noise, and generation seeds. At temperature 0.2 on lifting with pose shift, however, Compiled’s recovery is 19.6 pp lower than Resample’s.
With Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Compiled and Resample solve the same 52 of 55 initial stack failures (94.5% recovery@5). This high recovery rate leaves limited room for further improvement.

On nut insertion, the required rim grasp conflicts with the center-grasp instruction in the pick-and-place template for failed_grasp . Recovery@5 is 82.5% with Compiled and 97.5% with Resample, a difference of − 15.0 -15.0 pp (CI [ − 27.5 , − 2.5 ] [-27.5,-2.5] ). The decrease is consistent with the incompatible grasp instruction, while attempt validity remains similar. Guidance that helps within one task family can therefore be harmful in another.

Our results suggest that reusable task guidance explains the recovery advantage of template-based feedback over resampling in the tested tasks. Fixed guidance and feedback from other failures yield similar recovery point estimates to Compiled, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. Static-from-Start also achieves similar observed overall success to Compiled while using fewer tokens per solved episode. Evaluations should test fixed guidance from the first attempt alongside feedback selected after failure. The Static-from-Start comparison changes both guidance and the generation instruction, so their individual contributions remain unresolved.

Evaluations of self-repair should therefore distinguish the contributions of additional sampling, reusable guidance, and failure-specific information. Resampling provides a baseline for additional sampling, with retry and token budgets matched across methods. Static guidance tests whether instructions are useful before a failure occurs, while mismatched feedback tests the value of matching the coarse failure label to the current episode. These comparisons should check for instructions that conflict with a task’s requirements, such as center-grasp guidance on a task requiring a rim grasp.

Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, static guidance from the first attempt, and previous-program editing, with retry and token budgets matched across methods.

Our findings are limited to simulated manipulation with privileged state and coarse feedback. Some comparisons combine instruction and information changes. Future work should isolate these effects and examine larger models on harder tasks or under tighter budgets. Extending evaluation to visual feedback and physical recovery, including post-failure states and action costs, would clarify when adaptive feedback improves on static guidance.

passages.section: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: We evaluate text-only code generation with privileged state in robosuite 1.5.2 and MuJoCo 3.3.5 using a simulated Panda arm. Python programs run through a documented position-control API in isolated subprocesses with a 60 s timeout. The primitive API includes lift and place_on ; the position-only API omits them. The tasks are cube lifting, stacking, cube-to-zone, and place-in-bin, with additional evaluations on nut insertion and door opening.

passages.section: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: The evaluation sets, retry instructions, and outcome measures are summarized in Table A1 . The primary dataset contains 360 Qwen2.5-Coder-7B programs (18.9% initial success). Its 292 failures unrelated to infrastructure errors are divided into 40 development and 252 evaluation failures by initial-program hash.

passages.section: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: Within each study, eligibility requires initial success in the predefined range [ 10 % , 70 % ] [10\%,70\%] . The combined generalization estimate weights the 354 initial failures from seven eligible settings equally. Settings outside this range and separately designed studies are reported separately.

passages.section: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: Table A1: Evaluation sets and endpoints. Comparisons pair conditions within each study. Original and neutral instructions are reproduced in Appendix B.4 .

passages.section: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.location: A.1 Tasks, APIs, and evaluation sets
passages.text: Study Model and evaluation set Retry instruction Main endpoint Primary Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; 252 held-out failures, lifting and stacking Neutral Recovery within five retries Generalization Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B; 354 failures across seven eligible settings, four tasks Original Recovery within five retries Earlier end-to-end Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; 700 fresh scenes, lifting and stacking Original Overall success within six executions Static-from-Start Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; 700 separate fresh scenes, lifting and stacking Neutral Overall success within six executions

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: After an initial failure, each condition receives at most five retries from the original scene. Within a study, conditions share the model, task, API, decoding settings, and retry cap. Unless stated otherwise, generation uses temperature 0.7, top- p p 0.95, a 1,024-token completion limit, and a 768-whitespace-token feedback cap. Reflection calls allow 256 completion tokens.

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: Conditional recovery@ k k is the fraction of initial failures solved within k k sequential retries. Task success is checked by an independent final-state geometric predicate. Valid programs compile, call only documented functions, and finish before timeout. An execution counts as a safety violation if it leaves an object off the table.

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: Confidence intervals for paired differences use 10,000 bootstrap replicates. Exact McNemar tests assess significance at the final retry, with Holm correction within each predefined comparison group. Intervals are 95% unless an earlier secondary result is marked 90%. The primary analysis treats each stored initial failure as one observation. An exploratory bootstrap over the 159 task–API–scene clusters accounts for dependence within scene configurations and retains the + 17.1 +17.1 pp Compiled–Resample difference (95% CI [ + 10.1 , + 24.2 ] [+10.1,+24.2] ).

passages.section: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.location: A.2 Decoding, metrics, and statistical analysis
passages.text: Fixed-token analyses replay logged calls in order. Each call’s prompt and maximum completion allowance must fit within the remaining budget. Token use includes prompts, completions, and reflection calls. The budgets are 2,000, 5,000, and 9,500 tokens. No call fits within the original 1,000-token budget. In end-to-end studies, tokens per solved episode is total token use across all scenes, including attempt 0 and unsolved scenes, divided by the number of solved episodes.

Development and evaluation contain distinct initial programs but share 24 of the 159 evaluation scene configurations. The earliest core comparisons pair stored initial failures, though a placement-sampler seeding limitation allowed retry layouts to differ. Later studies seed every reset, and the subsequent evaluation with the original generation instruction uses rebuilt software. Each comparison uses a single software build. Seeding does not guarantee bitwise deterministic simulation.

The generalization question was revised after the core results, with settings and analysis fixed before generation for that study. The Static-from-Start study was also specified before generation. Fixed Task Template was selected on development data, so its first held-out comparison is exploratory. Later studies reused this fixed text. Direct+Compiled was selected in a separate 116-failure pilot.
Failure labels were audited on scripted faults, without human audits of natural failures. Oracle-hint performance and template-authoring cost were not measured.

passages.section: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.location: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.text: The labeler checks execution errors, safety events, absence of API calls, and task subgoals in a fixed priority order to assign one of 14 failure labels. The lookup Compile ​ ( 𝑙𝑎𝑏𝑒𝑙 , 𝑣𝑎𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑛𝑡 ) \textsc{Compile}(\mathit{label},\mathit{variant}) returns a diagnosis and MUST/NEVER instructions. Three templates vary across APIs, yielding 17 label-specific texts. All templates, API substitutions, and the generic fallback are reproduced in Appendix D .

passages.section: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.location: B.1 Failure labels and template selection
passages.text: Compiled adds one feedback record after each failure. Records are ordered newest first, with duplicate instruction lines removed and the shared feedback-length limit applied. Attempt indices remain in the headers, so repeated labels can appear under different attempt headers.

Regeneration with Compiled, mismatched feedback, and fixed guidance is described in Algorithm 1 , with selection rules in Appendix B.3 . Each failure record includes its label and the information used to match source episodes.
Algorithm 1 Reset-and-retry regeneration with condition-specific feedback
Regeneration prompts omit the previous program (Table A2 ). Direct+Compiled and Reflection Repair include it and request a revision, changing both code exposure and the generation instruction.
Table A2: Prompt inputs for each feedback and editing condition. Source-episode selection and prompt construction are specified below.

Condition Feedback supplied to program generation Resample / Compiled No feedback / accumulated templates for the observed labels. Other-Episode Feedback Accumulated feedback from a matched source episode. Different-Label Feedback Feedback from another failure, prioritizing a different label. Permuted Labels A fixed permutation replaces every observed label with a different label. Cross-Task Feedback A fixed assignment of source episodes from a different task. Fixed Task Template One fixed development-selected template per task, reused after failure. Static-from-Start The complete Fixed Task Template retry prompt from attempt 0 onward. Initial-Label Only The initial failure’s template, unchanged across retries. All-Template Union Goal-compatible templates ordered by development frequency. Static Prior One fixed task-independent text per model, without accumulation. Placebo / Repeated API Rules Length-matched generic instructions / existing API execution rules. Direct+Compiled Previous program and accumulated feedback templates. Reflection Accumulated model-written critiques; previous program hidden. Reflection Repair Previous program, latest critique, and truncated execution log.

Other-Episode Feedback selects feedback from another episode matched by task, API variant, and initial task-progress bin. Progress is the fraction of ordered subgoals completed before the first unmet subgoal, grouped into four equal-width bins over [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Source histories are limited to the evaluated episode’s failure count.

Different-Label Feedback selects one source record per observed label from the same task, preferring a different label in the same progress bin. If none is available, the progress-bin match is relaxed before allowing the same label; the task match is always retained. In the primary evaluation, all 627 selected records had a different failure label from the corresponding observed failure. Both controls use Compiled’s feedback ordering, deduplication, and length limit.

Fixed Task Template uses the most frequent failure label with task-compatible guidance for each task, selected from the fixed 40-failure development set. Static-from-Start also reuses the retry instruction and historical failure header (Appendix C.2 ).
Following Reflexion [ 2 ] , Reflection uses a separate critic call that receives the previous program and truncated log. Generation receives only the accumulated critique.
A generation prompt concatenates four blocks:
API documentation → \rightarrow task and objects → \rightarrow condition-specific feedback → \rightarrow generation instruction .
The API and task blocks below are the primitive-tier stacking example; only the feedback block varies across regeneration conditions.
For the primitive API tier, releasing a lifted object produces the following exact block:
The primary evaluation used the following instruction for regeneration conditions:

The position-only tier removes lift and place_on from the API block. Earlier runs used a suffix that referred to a “repair plan,” must_change items, and a verification checklist even when those fields were absent. We therefore repeated the core comparisons with the neutral instruction above; the main paper reports that evaluation. The original generation instruction was:
In the primary evaluation, Direct+Compiled uses the following editing instruction:

The previous program is included only in the editing prompt. Reflection uses a separate call with the instruction “In at most 6 sentences, reflect on why the program failed the task and what to do differently next time. Output only the reflection.” Serialized prompts and model revisions are recorded in the experiment artifacts.

passages.section: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.location: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.text: Figure A1: (a) Recovery with feedback and editing conditions in earlier evaluations. (b) A task-independent prompt improves recovery on stacking but reduces it on lifting.

passages.section: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.location: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.text: We detect no advantage from matching the coarse failure label in the primary evaluation. The paired recovery difference between Compiled and Different-Label Feedback is − 0.8 -0.8 pp (95% CI [ − 6.3 , + 4.8 ] [-6.3,+4.8] ). Earlier comparisons using the original generation instruction also show little benefit from updating the initial label or preserving the label mapping (Table A3 ). These intervals do not establish equivalence.

passages.section: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.location: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.text: In these earlier comparisons, recovery is lower with content-free instructions and All-Template Union than with concise, task-compatible feedback (Figure A1 ). The exploratory Repeated API Rules control also yields lower recovery than Resample in the primary evaluation (61.1% versus 68.3%).

passages.section: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.location: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.text: Table A3: Additional controls test feedback content and label matching. Comparisons using the original generation instruction on 252 held-out failures. p p -values are Holm-adjusted within predefined groups of secondary comparisons.

passages.section: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.location: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching

passages.section: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.location: C.1 Feedback content and failure matching
passages.text: Reflection achieves 56.0% recovery in the earlier core evaluation, compared with 70.6% for Resample, and uses more completion tokens and wall-clock time. In the subsequent evaluation using the original generation instruction, recovery is 25.0% for Reflection Repair and 21.4% for Direct+Compiled, compared with 89.7% for Compiled. Editing produces smaller program changes than fresh generation. Because the editing comparisons change code exposure and instruction together, the cause of the lower recovery remains unresolved.

passages.section: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.location: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.text: The Static-from-Start study compares overall success across 700 shared fresh scenes, using six executions per condition, neutral retry instructions, and fixed template text (Table A4 ). Resample, Compiled, and Fixed Task Template share attempt 0 and its 565 failures, whereas Static-from-Start has 442 initial failures. Conditional recovery is therefore reported descriptively.

passages.section: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.location: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.text: The standard initial prompt ends with “Write a Python program using ONLY the API above.” Static-from-Start instead uses the complete retry prompt, including the longer neutral instruction in Appendix B.4 and the historical “attempt 0 failed” header. It changes initial guidance and the generation instruction together. Their individual contributions remain unresolved.

passages.section: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.location: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.text: Table A4: Static-from-Start increases initial success and reduces tokens per solved episode. Results on 700 fresh scenes with neutral retry instructions. Success and recovery are percentages; recovery uses different initial-failure subsets.

passages.section: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.location: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.text: Condition Initial Overall@6 Recovery@5 Tok/solved Static-from-Start 36.9 92.4 88.0 2,087 Fixed Task Template 19.3 90.1 87.8 2,564 Compiled 19.3 89.6 87.1 2,578 Resample 19.3 73.1 66.7 3,623

passages.section: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.location: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.text: Static-from-Start achieves + 2.9 +2.9 pp higher overall success than Compiled (95% CI [ + 0.0 , + 5.7 ] [+0.0,+5.7] , Holm-adjusted p = 0.13 p{=}0.13 ). Its advantage over Fixed Task Template is + 2.3 +2.3 pp ( [ − 0.4 , + 5.0 ] [-0.4,+5.0] , unadjusted p = 0.13 p{=}0.13 ). An exploratory replay under fixed token budgets gives an advantage over Compiled of + 17.6 +17.6 pp at 2,000 tokens ( [ + 13.0 , + 22.1 ] [+13.0,+22.1] ) and + 4.6 +4.6 pp at 5,000 ( [ + 1.1 , + 8.0 ] [+1.1,+8.0] ).

passages.section: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.location: C.2 Static guidance from the first attempt
passages.text: The earlier end-to-end study uses 700 separate scenes and the original generation instruction. Attempt 0 succeeds on 147 scenes, leaving 553 shared failures. Compiled reaches 92.9% overall success, compared with 73.1% for Resample and 95.6% for Fixed Task Template. The template comparison is exploratory.

Across the seven eligible Qwen2.5-Coder-3B/7B settings, Compiled improves recovery over Resample by + 18.1 +18.1 pp (95% CI [ + 13.3 , + 22.9 ] [+13.3,+22.9] ). Its difference from Other-Episode Feedback is smaller, at + 2.3 +2.3 pp ( [ − 1.1 , + 5.6 ] [-1.1,+5.6] ). The additional studies below are excluded from this combined estimate.

Recovery gains vary across API and perturbation settings. With the position-only API, Compiled improves recovery over Resample by + 30.0 +30.0 pp on cube-to-zone. Both methods reach 93.3% recovery on place-in-bin. Across three generation seeds, Compiled exceeds Resample in all six tested seed–setting pairs ( + 10.7 +10.7 to + 26.7 +26.7 pp). With 5 mm pose noise, the difference is + 16.7 +16.7 pp on lift and + 10.0 +10.0 pp on stack, with only the lift interval excluding zero. At temperature 0.2 on lift with pose shift, Compiled’s recovery is 19.6 19.6 pp lower than Resample’s (90% CI [ − 28.6 , − 10.7 ] [-28.6,-10.7] ).

The model-specific results cover different levels of initial success (Figure A2 ). DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B falls below the minimum initial-success rate required for inclusion on both tasks. Its combined recovery is 50.8% for Compiled and 41.7% for Resample ( n = 120 n{=}120 ; difference + 9.2 +9.2 pp, [ − 1.7 , + 20.0 ] [-1.7,+20.0] ). The separate door-opening study has 1.3% initial success and also falls below the minimum required for inclusion.

With Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, all 80 lift scenes succeed initially. On stack, 105 of 160 initial attempts succeed, and Compiled and Resample solve the same 52 of the remaining 55 failures (94.5%). The paired interval has zero width because the methods produce identical outcomes on these 55 failures. Equivalence on other evaluation sets remains untested.
Figure A2: Recovery differences between Compiled and Resample across model-specific studies. Each point compares Compiled with Resample within a separately evaluated model and task set.

On nut insertion, Compiled recovers 82.5% of initial failures, compared with 97.5% for Resample ( n = 40 n{=}40 ; − 15.0 -15.0 pp, 95% CI [ − 27.5 , − 2.5 ] [-27.5,-2.5] ). The decrease is consistent with the center-grasp instruction conflicting with the required rim grasp. Other-Episode Feedback reaches 62.5% recovery. Attempt validity remains similar for Compiled and Resample (85.1% and 84.9%).

analysis.overview: 这篇提供的是自修复的评测拆解：恢复可能来自多一次采样、可复用任务指导，或真正针对当前失败的信息。固定代码模型与预算后，匹配粗粒度失败标签没有显示出优于同任务固定提示或不同标签反馈的额外收益。这个结果支持增加更强的对照，不能推广成所有自修复无效；任务不兼容的提示还会反向降低恢复率。
analysis.notice: 已阅读提取的96个文字片段，覆盖主文、实验、附录A–D；另读取同一缓存HTML中未进入段落索引的23个listing（API、任务、生成/编辑提示、14标签模板、通用回退和API变体替换），并查看PDF第12页算法。固定版本PDF共19页，目视核对第5、12、16、17页的图2、表2、算法1、表A3/A4及泛化/失败案例。没有逐图核查所有图片、重算原始实验、逐篇核查参考文献或执行代码。补充listing原文保存在本报告supplementary_reading中；页面段落引用仍按96个提取片段定位。所有实验来自作者，未独立复现。

findings.title: 研究增量：把自修复收益拆成三种来源
findings.text: 作者在冻结模型下分别控制额外采样、可复用任务指导和匹配当前粗粒度失败标签的信息。主实验用Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct、robosuite仿真Panda、特权状态和文本API，没有图像输入。每次重试重置到原始场景，主条件从头生成整段程序，隐藏上一份代码；这不是在失败遗留的物理状态下在线恢复，也不是对视觉VLA做新训练。
findings.quote: We do not test recovery from the physical state left by failure

findings.title: Compiled是标签查表提示，不是额外反思模型
findings.text: 规则labeler按优先级分配14类失败标签，结合API变体查表生成诊断和MUST/NEVER指导。累计反馈最新在前、指令去重，上限768个空白分词token；反馈查表无需额外模型调用，也不施加运行时约束检查。默认生成temperature0.7、top-p0.95、completion上限1024。附录D已读23个listing中的模板与API说明，不把这些论文提示当作本轮执行指令。
findings.quote: This lookup requires no additional model call

findings.title: 核心消融：标签匹配没有测出额外优势
findings.text: 同一批252个初始失败、最多5次重试：Compiled恢复85.3%，Different-Label Feedback和Fixed Task Template各86.1%。Compiled减不同标签对照为−0.8个百分点，95%配对bootstrap区间[−6.3,+4.8]；减固定模板为−0.8，[−6.7,+5.2]。区间仍允许条件间差异，不能宣称等效。不同标签仍保留同任务信息，主评测627条选中的记录全部来自不同失败标签；因此这不是完全随机、无关任务的反馈。
findings.quote: the paired confidence intervals do not establish equivalence

findings.title: 模板确实优于无指导重采样，但不能据此证明读懂失败
findings.text: 主实验Compiled对Resample的恢复率为85.3%/68.3%，作者按未舍入计数报告差+17.1个百分点，95%CI[+9.9,+24.2]。等上限重试仍未完全匹配token开销，因此另用日志重放的固定token预算：2000/5000 tokens时优势为+15.9/+14.7个百分点。该结果支持指导内容有用，结合固定与不同标签对照后，尚不能证明模型理解或利用了当前执行轨迹。

findings.title: Static-from-Start：有用的低成本基线，但有提示混杂
findings.text: 另一次700个共同新场景评测，Static-from-Start初次成功36.9%，标准提示19.3%；最多6次执行总体成功92.4%，Compiled89.6%、Fixed Task Template90.1%、Resample73.1%。Static与Compiled差+2.9个百分点在Holm校正后p=0.13，未显著。tokens/solved为2087/2578；这个成本口径包含全部场景、首轮和未解决场景。首轮静态方案同时改了指导、较长生成指令和历史“attempt 0 failed”头，不能把全部收益归因于静态指导一句话。

findings.title: 反例：把中心抓取模板搬到边缘抓取会伤害恢复
findings.text: 螺母插入需要rim grasp，却复用failed_grasp的中心抓取指导。40个初始失败中Compiled恢复82.5%，Resample97.5%，差−15.0个百分点，95%CI[−27.5,−2.5]；程序有效率仍相近85.1%/84.9%。结果与任务不兼容的指导一致，但没有通过单独替换抓取句子来隔离因果；不能把所有差距都确定归于这一句。它说明固定提示需先检查任务适配。

findings.title: 恢复率、整体成功与pass@k是不同指标
findings.text: 主实验85.3%以attempt0失败为分母，不是所有场景的总体成功率；顺序重试的recovery@k也不等于独立采样估计的pass@k。Static-from-Start改变首轮成功，初始失败442个，其他三组565个，不能把88.0%与87.1%的条件恢复率直接当同一失败集合上的配对胜负。公平的首轮指导比较应以共同场景上的overall@6为主。

findings.title: 开发与评测程序分离，不代表场景完全未见
findings.text: 252评测失败与40开发失败按初始程序hash分离，但159个评测task–API–scene组合中24个也用于开发。主要分析按初始失败计，作者还做159个场景簇的探索性bootstrap，Compiled对Resample仍为+17.1个百分点，CI[+10.1,+24.2]。较早核心比较曾有重置采样器seeding限制，后续实验修正；不应混用早期/中性指令/不同软件构建的数值。失败标签仅审计脚本故障，未人工审计自然失败；固定模板首个held-out比较是探索性的。
findings.quote: share 24 of the 159 evaluation scene configurations

findings.title: 小模型多任务结果不能自动推广到更强模型
findings.text: 泛化汇总是7个符合初始成功率10%–70%筛选条件的Qwen3B/7B设置、354个失败，Compiled对Resample+18.1个百分点，但对同任务Other-Episode Feedback仅+2.3，CI[−1.1,+5.6]。32B栈任务两方法都解决同样52/55个初始失败，恢复94.5%；不能把零宽配对区间推广为其他任务等效。温度0.2、lift pose shift另有−19.6个百分点反例，使用90%而非95%区间。
findings.quote: The additional studies below are excluded from this combined estimate

findings.title: 编辑/反思较差不等于这些范式普遍无效
findings.text: Direct+Compiled主实验恢复21.4%，但同时让模型看旧代码并改成编辑指令，无法单独归因于代码锚定。Reflection56.0%属于较早原指令评测，对照Resample70.6%，不能与主实验68.3%直接拼成同一消融。反思多用模型tokens与墙钟时间也是所测实现的结果，尚不足以否定更强模型、视觉反馈、真实失败状态或其他反思实现。

hypotheses.title: 最小实验：统一指令后，动态反馈还有多少独立收益？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：统一生成指令后，所测代码策略的主要恢复收益仍来自任务兼容的固定指导，而非当前粗粒度失败标签。先在一个lift和一个stack仿真任务上，用同一冻结模型、API版本、采样参数与共同场景种子比较5组：无反馈重采样、首轮即加固定任务提示、首败后固定提示、匹配当前标签提示、同任务不同标签提示。所有组统一中性生成指令，首轮不加入伪造的失败历史；固定文本仅用独立开发场景选择。每次重试重置原场景，最多6次总执行，同时按2000/5000总tokens重放计算预算，包含所有prompt/completion。主要报告共同场景的overall@6、配对差异区间、总tokens/solved和墙钟成本；后三个首败后指导组与无反馈组另在相同初始失败上比较recovery@5。先小规模检查，再增加场景与至少3个生成种子；用场景簇重采样，避免同景程序当独立样本。若匹配反馈相对两种固定指导均提升超过预先约定的5个百分点且差异区间下界大于0，则反对固定指导主导假设。另在需要边缘抓取的任务比较适配/不适配模板，检查负迁移；不把仿真重置恢复外推到真实失败状态。实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。
hypotheses.quote: changes initial guidance and the generation instruction together

frontier_brief.title: 代码策略自修复：先加固定提示与等预算重采样对照
frontier_brief.change_type: 自修复评测 · 配对消融
frontier_brief.delta: 把失败后的恢复拆成额外采样、可复用任务指导和当前失败信息三部分。固定模型与预算后，匹配粗粒度失败标签没有测出优于固定任务提示的额外收益；评估自修复时，这两种对照都该补上。
frontier_brief.before: 失败后加入反思或修复反馈，再与不重试或无指导的初始程序比较，容易把更多采样和任务提示的收益都算成自修复。
frontier_brief.after: 用同一批初始失败、同一重试上限与总token预算，对照重采样、固定任务提示、同任务不同失败标签反馈；首轮静态指导另按共同场景的总体成功率比较。
frontier_brief.relevance: 研究代码策略或机器人agent修复时，先实现简短、任务兼容的静态指导，再比较动态反馈是否还有增益。记录初始失败分母、场景重置和全部token成本；若关注真实失败后的恢复，需要另做不重置场景的实验。
frontier_brief.caveat: 仅在特权状态输入、文本API和重置仿真中评测。未检出差异不等于等效；首轮静态方案同时改了生成指令。中心抓取指导迁移到边缘抓取任务反而降低恢复。作者实验未复现。
frontier_brief.question: 统一生成指令后，动态失败反馈还能胜过固定任务提示吗？

evidence.label: 匹配失败标签，没有测出额外收益
evidence.context: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B，lift/stack同一批252个初始失败，最多5次重试。Compiled/固定任务模板恢复率为85.3%/86.1%；配对差−0.8个百分点，95%CI[−6.7,+5.2]，不证明等效。

evidence.label: 有指导优于纯重采样

mechanism.title: 固定重试条件
mechanism.text: 同一代码模型与原始场景，每次先重置再生成完整程序，主条件隐藏上一次代码。最多5次重试，另核对总token预算。

mechanism.title: 替换反馈内容
mechanism.text: 以同任务固定模板或其他失败标签反馈替换当前标签指导，保持生成指令中性，区分任务信息和真正的失败匹配。

mechanism.title: 报告正确的分母
mechanism.text: 同一批初始失败比较恢复；首轮加指导会改变失败集合，应按共同场景比较总体成功。再检查任务不兼容提示及更强模型的边界。

passages.section: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
passages.location: RAFT: Reasoning-Aligned Fine-Tuning Improves Robustness of VLA Post-Training
passages.text: Adapting a generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policy to a target task with limited demonstrations can improve nominal task success while reducing robustness to variations in appearance, objects, and instructions. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning (RAFT), a two-stage post-training procedure: RAFT first trains low-rank adapters on task-relevant reasoning annotations, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. On a physical DROID robot, RAFT achieves 75.0 % 75.0\% out-of-distribution success, compared with 27.9 % 27.9\% for plain fine-tuning; on a multi-stage bimanual YAM task, it reaches 70.0 % 70.0\% mean success, compared with 36.0 % 36.0\% for the strongest baseline. RAFT also improves success under visual, object, and instruction shifts in simulated pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. Compared with plain fine-tuning, RAFT policies place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity in later layers. A broader reasoning-data mixture further improves downstream success across demonstration budgets.

Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies, built on pretrained vision-language models and large robot datasets [ 1 , 7 , 22 , 24 , 3 , 2 ] , typically still require adaptation to reach the success rates needed to deploy the policy on a real-world target task [ 4 , 23 ] . Because collecting task-specific demonstrations is expensive, this post-training often relies on a small dataset collected in a narrow set of environments. Fine-tuning can improve nominal success while reducing robustness to visual and semantic variations absent from those demonstrations [ 12 , 43 , 35 , 37 , 21 , 38 ] . Existing approaches address this problem through parameter merging, as in RETAIN [ 39 ] , or regularization during adaptation [ 20 , 17 ] . We study a complementary approach, aligning a pretrained policy with task-relevant reasoning supervision before adapting it to the target actions.

Figure 1 : Reasoning-aligned fine-tuning for robust VLA adaptation. (a) Plain FT, fine-tuned only on actions, succeeds in the training layout but fails under small scene changes. (b) RAFT first learns task-relevant reasoning through LoRA adapters, then freezes them while fine-tuning the policy on action demonstrations. (c) With the same demonstrations, RAFT succeeds under these shifts. On physical robots, RAFT raises success over Plain FT from 34.7 % 34.7\% to 70.0 % 70.0\% on YAM and from 27.9 % 27.9\% to 75.0 % 75.0\% on out-of-distribution DROID trials.

Reasoning supervision can teach policies to identify task-relevant objects, spatial relations, and motion structure [ 41 , 10 , 42 , 26 ] . We study how reasoning capabilities in pretrained VLMs can support low-data adaptation of generalist VLAs to a target skill. We introduce reasoning-aligned fine-tuning ( RAFT ), a two-stage adaptation procedure. Stage I learns low-rank adapters in the language and vision modules from task-relevant reasoning annotations while keeping pretrained parameters fixed. Stage II freezes these adapters and fine-tunes the language model, action expert, and projection layers on action demonstrations. Action gradients therefore do not directly update the reasoning-adapter weights. We find that how reasoning supervision is incorporated matters: jointly co-training reasoning and actions underperforms plain fine-tuning ( 63.2 % 63.2\% vs. 79.6 % 79.6\% mean success on simulated pick and place), and updating the reasoning adapter during action learning falls below Plain FT ( 74.0 % 74.0\% vs. 79.6 % 79.6\% ) (Secs. 8.3 and 8.2 ). Staging the two, with the adapter frozen, yields these robustness gains. RAFT policies also place more attention on annotated task regions and yield higher linear-probe accuracy for object identity and episode-time position than plainly fine-tuned policies (Sec. 4.3 ).

We evaluate RAFT on two simulated tasks and two physical platforms: the single-arm DROID setup [ 22 ] and the bimanual YAM setup [ 10 ] . Evaluations test visual, object, instruction, and geometric variations of the adapted tasks. RAFT achieves the highest mean success on simulated pick and place and improves open-drawer success, with the largest gains on the physical robots: success on 75 % 75\% of out-of-distribution DROID trials versus 28 % 28\% for plain fine-tuning, and 70 % 70\% mean success on the multi-stage YAM task versus 36 % 36\% for the strongest baseline. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We propose RAFT a post training recipt that separates task relevant reasoning supervision from action fine tuning (2) We show improved downstream performace and robustness in simulation and on two physical robot platforms; and (3) We analyze why RAFT helps generalist policy adapt to a target by analyzing the features learned by RAFT.

Generalist robot policies have made substantial progress in learning transferable skills and supporting deployment through post-training [ 5 , 24 , 34 , 15 , 27 , 40 , 30 ] . Within this setting, work on VLA fine-tuning studies reliable task execution [ 23 , 43 ] , while FAST improves action tokenization for autoregressive VLAs [ 31 ] . ControlVLA uses object-centric conditioning for few-shot adaptation [ 28 ] . These advances make specialization more effective, but nominal task success can still mask failures under distribution shift [ 12 , 44 , 11 ] . This motivates studying robustness to variations absent from the target demonstrations.

Robust post-training methods seek to adapt generalist policies while retaining useful pretrained capabilities. Weight-space approaches interpolate or merge pretrained and adapted parameters [ 36 , 18 , 9 ] , while regularization and steerability-preserving adaptation constrain changes during fine-tuning [ 20 , 14 , 33 , 17 ] . RETAIN [ 39 ] interpolates pretrained and fine-tuned policy weights to improve generalization to variations of a new skill and retain broader capabilities. DeLock [ 17 ] regularizes visual-encoder weight drift during post-training and uses contrastive prompt guidance at inference. RAFT instead introduces task-relevant reasoning alignment before action fine-tuning, with complementary parameter freezing across the two stages.

Reasoning and grounding supervision provide a foundation for this approach. Embodied Chain-of-Thought interleaves sub-goal, spatial, and motion reasoning with action prediction [ 41 ] . Related work incorporates spatial representations, affordances, keypoints, and manipulable parts [ 10 , 42 , 26 ] , or object- and language-grounded supervision [ 3 ] . Steerable Policies use commands at multiple abstraction levels to control [ 6 ] , while VLS uses VLM-generated rewards to steer frozen policies at inference [ 29 ] . Reasoning supervision is used to prepare that policy for specialization, and the learned adapters are held fixed during subsequent action learning. To the best of our knowledge, reasoning supervision has not been studied for low-data post-training of a pretrained generalist VLA. We evaluate this adaptation schedule through downstream robustness, additional training controls, and analyses of task-relevant representations.

Figure 2 : Overview of RAFT . Stage I updates only the reasoning adapters, using reasoning annotations. Stage II freezes the adapters and updates the language model, action expert, and projection layers on action demonstrations, so action gradients do not reach the reasoning adapters.

We consider task adaptation from a pretrained generalist policy using a small demonstration dataset 𝒟 η = { ( s t , a t , T ) } \mathcal{D}_{\eta}=\{(s_{t},a_{t},T)\} collected in a narrow set of environments. Here s t s_{t} contains the policy observations, a t a_{t} is the demonstrated action, and T T is the task instruction. We denote the Stage-II trainable non-adapter parameters (the language model, action expert, and projection layers) by θ \theta , initialized from θ pre \theta_{\mathrm{pre}} , and the LoRA parameters by ϕ \phi [ 16 ] . In RAFT , the pretrained SigLIP weights remain frozen throughout adaptation, while LoRA modules in both the vision encoder and language model are trained in Stage I. Stage II freezes these learned adapters and updates θ \theta . Thus, vision adaptation in RAFT occurs through Stage-I LoRA rather than updates to the pretrained SigLIP weights. The resulting action policy is π θ , ϕ ​ ( a t ∣ s t , T ) \pi_{\theta,\phi}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},T) . Figure 2 summarizes the two stages; Sec. 6 gives the adapter placement and optimization settings.

Figure 3 : Example Stage-I reasoning annotation. In this YAM example, the left arm holds the lid open while the right arm reaches for the toy. The target combines language, object boxes, keypoints, motion traces, and per-arm state information. Blue and green mark the box and toy, yellow marks keypoints, and red marks the active arm’s trace.

Stage I trains the adapter to predict task-relevant reasoning annotations. A VLM annotator (Gemini 3.1 Pro) produces task-relevant reasoning targets from observations and instructions on 𝒟 η \mathcal{D}_{\eta} , yielding 𝒟 reason = { ( s , r , T ) } \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{reason}}=\{(s,r,T)\} . These annotations describe the objects and interactions relevant to the task. The annotation choices include bounding boxes, keypoints, traces, spatial descriptions, and visual question answering. Section 8.1 compares their effects. Each annotation is represented as a target token sequence r = ( r 1 , … , r | r | ) r=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{|r|}) . We train the LoRA adapter using standard autoregressive cross-entropy:

ℒ reason ( ϕ ) = − 𝔼 ( s , r , T ) ∼ 𝒟 reason ∑ j = 1 | r | log p θ pre , ϕ ( r j ∣ s , T , r < j ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{reason}}(\phi)=-\mathbb{E}_{(s,r,T)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{reason}}}\sum_{j=1}^{|r|}\log p_{\theta_{\mathrm{pre}},\phi}(r_{j}\mid s,T,r_{<j}). (1)
Only ϕ \phi is updated in this stage; all remaining parameters are frozen. This supervision encourages task-relevant grounding before action adaptation.

Stage II turns the reasoning-aligned initialization into an action policy for the target task. We retain the learned adapter ϕ ⋆ \phi^{\star} and freeze its parameters. The Stage-II parameter set θ \theta is then updated by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on the task demonstrations [ 24 , 23 ] :

θ ⋆ = arg ⁡ min θ ⁡ 𝔼 ( s , a , T ) ∼ 𝒟 η ​ [ ℓ SFT ​ ( π θ , ϕ ⋆ , s , a , T ) ] ⏟ ℒ BC ​ ( θ , 𝒟 η , ϕ ⋆ ) . \theta^{\star}=\arg\min_{\theta}\,\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{(s,a,T)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\eta}}[\ell_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\pi_{\theta,\phi^{\star}};s,a,T)]}_{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{BC}}(\theta;\mathcal{D}_{\eta},\phi^{\star})}. (2)

Here ℓ SFT \ell_{\mathrm{SFT}} is the underlying policy’s action-supervision objective. Stage II updates the language model, action expert, and projection layers while the adapter and SigLIP vision tower remain frozen. At deployment, the resulting policy is π θ ⋆ , ϕ ⋆ \pi_{\theta^{\star},\phi^{\star}} . The adapter ablation in the appendix (Sec. 8.2 ) evaluates the benefit of freezing the reasoning adapter during action learning. Attention and linear-probe analyses (Sec. 4.3 ) provide empirical evidence of retained task grounding in the resulting policy.

The goal of our experiments is to evaluate RAFT ’s ability to retain task-relevant information and improve downstream robustness. Concretely, we aim to answer: (1) does RAFT generalize better than baselines under distribution shift, in simulation and on physical robots? (2) do RAFT ’s representations retain more task-relevant information than a plainly fine-tuned policy, and does this track downstream success? (3) how does downstream performance scale with the amount of reasoning data used in Stage I? and (4) How freezing Stage-I adapted compares with common approaches like co-training simulatenously?

Figure 4 : Evaluation scenes. Representative in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) observations, left to right: simulated pick and place, simulated open drawer, physical DROID pick and place, and the physical YAM two-stage task. The OOD panels show texture changes in simulation and background changes on the physical robots. The full set of evaluated shifts is shown in Fig. 20 .

We compare RAFT with standard supervised fine-tuning ( Plain FT ), RETAIN [ 39 ] , which merges pretrained and fine-tuned weights, and DeLock [ 17 ] , which regularizes visual-encoder weight drift during fine-tuning and applies contrastive prompt guidance at inference. We additionally report Base , the pretrained generalist policy evaluated without post-training. All fine-tuned policies are evaluated after 5,000 action-training steps. Sec. 6.3 gives the baseline settings; Sec. 4.5 ablates the training design, with full adapter and co-training results in the appendix (Secs. 8.2 and 8.3 ).

Figure 5 : Simulation results under distribution shift. Success rates for pick and place (left) and open drawer (right), with 106 trials per split. RAFT uses full reasoning for pick and place and bounding-box supervision for open drawer (Sec. 8.1 ). RAFT has the highest mean success on both tasks: 83 % 83\% versus 80 % 80\% for Plain FT on pick and place, and 39 % 39\% versus 29 % 29\% on open drawer.

We evaluate RAFT on pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks in simulation and on two real-world platforms: the single-arm DROID setup [ 22 ] and the dexterous, dual-arm YAM setup [ 10 ] , under the visual, object, and instruction or geometric shifts described below.

We evaluate MolmoBot [ 8 ] in the MolmoSpaces simulator [ 25 ] on pick-and-place and open-drawer tasks. For each task, we use 106 successful demonstrations from one layout provided in the MolmoSpaces benchmark for post-training. We measure robustness using perturbations absent from the demonstrations. OOD-light changes the number, position, and intensity of light sources; OOD-texture replaces table and scene textures; OOD-object substitutes a semantically similar manipulation object unseen during post-training and is evaluated only for pick and place; and OOD-prompt paraphrases the instruction without changing its meaning. ID uses the demonstration layout. Each evaluation split contains n = 106 n=106 trials with matched seeds across methods.

passages.section: RAFT has the highest simulated success, with the largest margin on novel objects
passages.location: RAFT has the highest simulated success, with the largest margin on novel objects
passages.text: On pick and place, RAFT achieves 83 % 83\% mean success across the five evaluation splits, compared with 80 % 80\% for Plain FT, 79 % 79\% for RETAIN, and 74 % 74\% for DeLock (Fig. 5 ). The largest margin is under object shift: 43 % 43\% for RAFT versus 36 % 36\% for Plain FT and 37 % 37\% for RETAIN. On the open drawer task, RAFT reaches 44 % 44\% success in ID and 28 % 28\% under texture shift, versus 29 % 29\% and 15 % 15\% for Plain FT, and it also leads under lighting and instruction shifts.

We post-train MolmoBot [ 8 ] on 50 pick-and-place demonstrations and evaluate on a physical DROID robot under four axes: the demonstration setup (ID; blue, yellow, and brown toys), novel object colors (OOD-Object, e.g., a white toy in place of the brown one), added distractors (OOD-Distractor), and a changed tabletop surface (OOD-Background). On out-of-distribution DROID trials, RAFT succeeds in 75.0 % 75.0\% of trials versus 27.9 % 27.9\% for Plain FT (Fig. 6 ): 83 % 83\% versus 33 % 33\% with novel object colors, 75 % 75\% versus 25 % 25\% with distractors, and 65 % 65\% versus 25 % 25\% on the changed tabletop. In the demonstration setup, the two are close ( 63 % 63\% versus 60 % 60\% ).

Figure 6 : Real-robot results under distribution shift. Left: DROID pick and place. Right: YAM box opening and place inside box. RAFT has the highest success on both platforms: 75 % 75\% versus 28 % 28\% for Plain FT on out-of-distribution DROID trials, and 70 % 70\% versus 35 % 35\% on YAM.

For the dual-arm YAM platform, we post-train π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] on 100 demonstrations of a long-horizon task: open a hinged box, pick up an object, and place it inside. Because placement depends on the box being open, the task separates completing the first interaction from completing the whole sequence. We evaluate in the demonstration setup and under four shifts: clutter, box pose, object color, and background. On the bimanual YAM task, RAFT completes the full sequence in 70.0 % 70.0\% of trials pooled over the five axes, versus 36 % 36\% for DeLock, 35 % 35\% for Plain FT, and 29 % 29\% for RETAIN (Fig. 6 ), and it has the highest success on every axis ( 73 % 73\% in-distribution and 60 % 60\% – 80 % 80\% under the four shifts). Plain FT usually opens the box but then fails to place the object.

Figure 7 : Successful physical-robot rollouts. Ordered frames show DROID picking up the brown toy and placing it in the bowl (top) and YAM opening the box and placing the toy inside (bottom). Numbers indicate temporal order; circles and arrows mark the manipulated object and motion.

Figure 8 : Attention maps along one trajectory. Columns show successive observations; rows compare Base, Stage I, RAFT , and Plain FT. Overlays identify annotated task regions, and color scales are shared within each column. RAFT places more attention on the annotated regions than Plain FT; Fig. 10 quantifies this across layers.

Figure 9 : Layer-wise linear probes. Balanced accuracy for object identity (left; chance 1 / 7 1/7 ) and episode-time quartile (right; chance 1 / 4 1/4 ). Policies use the same 414 frames; episodes are held out from probe fitting, not policy training. Shading marks layers 14–17. In these layers, RAFT reaches 0.51–0.53 object-identity accuracy versus 0.45 for Plain FT, and 0.62–0.65 quartile accuracy versus 0.55.
We examine representation dimensionality, linearly decodable task information, and visual attention to assess what RAFT preserves during post-training. The measurement protocol is in Sec. 10 .

passages.section: Late-layer dimensionality correlates with downstream success
passages.location: Late-layer dimensionality correlates with downstream success
passages.text: We measure the effective dimensionality of the backbone’s hidden states with the participation ratio (PR) [ 13 , 32 , 19 ] :

passages.section: Late-layer dimensionality correlates with downstream success
passages.location: Late-layer dimensionality correlates with downstream success
passages.text: PR = ( ∑ i λ i ) 2 ∑ i λ i 2 , \mathrm{PR}\;=\;\frac{\left(\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\right)^{2}}{\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2}}, (3)

passages.section: Late-layer dimensionality correlates with downstream success
passages.location: Late-layer dimensionality correlates with downstream success
passages.text: where λ i \lambda_{i} are the eigenvalues of the covariance of mean-pooled hidden states across frames. Across six Stage-I reasoning variants, late-layer PR correlates with success on each task-matched evaluation axis; at layer 15, absolute PR has mean Spearman ρ = 0.76 \rho=0.76 (Fig. 19 ).

passages.section: Object identity and task progress are more linearly decodable from RAFT ’s late layers
passages.location: Object identity and task progress are more linearly decodable from RAFT ’s late layers
passages.text: We fit linear probes on the same late layers to predict object identity (seven classes, chance 1 / 7 1/7 ) and episode-time quartile (four bins, chance 1 / 4 1/4 ). In layers 14–17, probes on RAFT reach 0.51–0.53 balanced accuracy for object identity, against 0.45 for Plain FT and 0.40 for the base policy, and 0.62–0.65 for episode quartile, against 0.55 and 0.51 (Fig. 9 ). Object-identity decoding also rises sharply between layers 13 and 15 for RAFT , but barely changes for Plain FT or the base policy. The layers where PR tracks success are the same layers where this information becomes decodable.

passages.section: RAFT has higher attention enrichment on annotated task regions
passages.location: RAFT has higher attention enrichment on annotated task regions
passages.text: We measure how much of the policy’s visual attention falls on annotated task regions, such as the manipulated object, the target, and the gripper, relative to their share of the image (enrichment; values above one mean attention is concentrated there). At layer 11, RAFT gives these regions 3.2–3.4 times their uniform share of attention, against 1.9–2.1 for Plain FT, while attention to the background stays near uniform (Figs. 8 and 10 ); the separation narrows in later layers. The concentration persists through Stage-II action training and stays above that of plain fine-tuning. The size of these effects depends on the reasoning modality used in Stage I; Sec. 8.1 reports the full modality ablation.

passages.section: RAFT has higher attention enrichment on annotated task regions
passages.location: RAFT has higher attention enrichment on annotated task regions
passages.text: Figure 10 : Layer-wise attention enrichment. Enrichment for object boxes, keypoints, traces, and background; values above one indicate attention exceeding a region’s image-area share. Curves compare Base, Plain FT, Stage I, and RAFT ; shading marks layers 14–17. At layer 11, RAFT gives task regions 3.2–3.4 times their area share, versus 1.9–2.1 for Plain FT, while background attention stays near uniform.

passages.section: RAFT has higher attention enrichment on annotated task regions
passages.location: RAFT has higher attention enrichment on annotated task regions
passages.text: Figure 11 : Effect of reasoning data and demonstration budget. Left: held-out reasoning loss across corpus sizes and constructions. Middle: in-distribution pick-and-place success after 5,000 Stage-II steps from in-domain and broader-mixture Stage-I initializations. Right: RAFT versus Plain FT across demonstration budgets, with 106 evaluation episodes per budget. The broader mixture lowers held-out loss (0.29 versus 0.62) and improves this success by 0.9–3.8 points at every budget.

passages.section: More reasoning data lowers held-out loss
passages.location: More reasoning data lowers held-out loss
passages.text: On a common 560-record held-out split, cross-entropy on full-reasoning targets falls as the number of reasoning records grows, in both frame- and episode-subsampled series (Fig. 11 , left). Corpus composition also matters: 628 frame-subsampled records reach a loss of 0.77, while 680 episode-subsampled records reach only 1.48. The broader mixture, which adds roughly 60,000 records to the 5,000-record in-domain corpus, gives the lowest loss (0.29, versus 0.62 in-domain) and still reaches 0.39 with target-simulator records removed.

passages.section: Broader reasoning data also helps downstream
passages.location: Broader reasoning data also helps downstream
passages.text: Initializing Stage II from the broader-mixture adapter instead of the in-domain one improves in-distribution success by 0.9–3.8 points at each of the three demonstration budgets (Fig. 11 , middle). Against Plain FT at matched budgets (right panel), the two methods tie with 25 demonstrations ( 46.2 % 46.2\% success each), and RAFT leads modestly at intermediate budgets. With all demonstrations, RAFT reaches 95.3 % 95.3\% ID success against 90.6 % 90.6\% for Plain FT (Fig. 5 ).

We ablate two design choices of RAFT on simulated pick and place: how reasoning and action supervision are combined, and whether the reasoning adapter is updated during action learning (Fig. 12 ). Co-train trains on reasoning and action examples jointly, sampling them equally and weighting their losses 1:1. Adapter trainable runs both stages but keeps the Stage-I adapter trainable in Stage II, and Stage I only applies the adapter without action fine-tuning.

Figure 12 : Training-scheme ablation on simulated pick and place. Mean success over trials. Staged training with a frozen adapter achieves the highest success ( 83.2 % 83.2\% ), above Plain FT ( 79.6 % 79.6\% ), a trainable adapter ( 74.0 % 74.0\% ), and co-training ( 63.2 % 63.2\% ).

Across five matched splits with 106 episodes each, co-training reaches 63.21 % 63.21\% mean success, below both Plain FT ( 79.62 % 79.62\% ) and RAFT ( 83.21 % 83.21\% ). Updating the adapter in Stage II lowers success to 73.96 % 73.96\% , and Stage I alone reaches 48.30 % 48.30\% . Plain FT with a frozen vision encoder also stays at 79.62 % 79.62\% , so freezing the pretrained vision weights alone does not account for the gain. Split-level results are in Tables 3 and 4 .

We presented RAFT , which first trains a low-rank adapter on task-relevant reasoning annotations, freezes it, and only then fine-tunes the pretrained VLA on actions. Across two simulated tasks and two real robots, this staging improved success under distribution shift relative to plain fine-tuning, RETAIN, and DeLock. We also show how training reasoning adapter on different modalities can lead to varied performance gains and selection of optimal reasoning modality for a specific task remains an open question. Since, RAFT approaches post-training from a different perspective to current approaches, it makes RAFT compatible with these approaches and future work could explore utlizing a combination of RAFT and existing methods to do more robust post-training.

Section 8.1 varies the format of the Stage-I supervision target; Section 8.2 ablates how the Stage-I reasoning adapter is treated during Stage II; Section 8.3 compares staged training with co-training and with frozen-vision fine-tuning; and Section 8.4 tests whether RAFT composes with RETAIN weight merging.

We vary the Stage-I supervision target across six formats: full reasoning, visual question answering (VQA), spatial descriptions, bounding boxes, keypoints, and trajectory traces; Table 2 gives an example of each. Each variant changes only the format of the Stage-I target, while Stage-II action training and the evaluation protocol are held fixed. The main-text results use full reasoning for pick and place and bounding-box supervision for the open drawer task, with the modality fixed across evaluation perturbations within each task; the remaining modalities are reported here. Figure 19 summarizes success on both tasks together with a layer-wise participation-ratio analysis.

Figure 19 : Effect of reasoning modality on success and representation dimensionality. Left: ID and OOD-visual success on the open drawer task for six reasoning modalities. Center: ID and OOD-object success on pick and place for five modalities. Red crosses denote no-reasoning controls, and dashed lines mark Plain FT. Each policy is evaluated on 106 trials per axis. Right: Layer-wise mean Spearman correlation between participation ratio and success, pooled over three task-matched evaluation axes and six reasoning variants, for four participation-ratio measures. Filled markers denote significance after FDR correction; shading marks layers 14–17.

On the open drawer task, trajectory-trace supervision achieves the highest ID success ( 49.06 % 49.06\% vs. 29.25 % 29.25\% for Plain FT). Under the visual shift, spatial descriptions, bounding boxes, and trajectory traces reach 29.25 % 29.25\% , 28.30 % 28.30\% , and 23.58 % 23.58\% , respectively. On pick and place , full reasoning achieves the highest ID success ( 95.28 % 95.28\% ), whereas trajectory traces achieve the highest OOD-object success ( 45.28 % 45.28\% ), followed by VQA and full reasoning ( 43.40 % 43.40\% each). Bounding-box and keypoint supervision each reach 34.91 % 34.91\% , comparable to Plain FT ( 35.85 % 35.85\% ).

Figure 20 illustrates the in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions used in our simulated and physical-robot experiments; the evaluation protocol is described in Appendix 6.4 . Simulation task construction, resets, initial-state matching, and success criteria follow MolmoSpaces [ 25 ] . Within each perturbation, all methods are evaluated on identical episodes. On the physical robots, resets preserve the task configuration and initial state.

Figure 20 : Evaluation setup across the four robot tasks. Each row begins with an in-distribution observation, followed by its OOD variants. Pick and place varies lighting, target object, instruction, and scene texture; the open drawer task varies lighting, instruction, and scene texture; DROID varies background, clutter, and object appearance; and YAM varies box pose, object color, clutter, and background. Instruction shifts reuse the ID image because only the task prompt changes.

The participation-ratio (PR) analysis in Figure 19 uses the first 400 records of the held-out iTHOR FloorPlan13 validation split, spanning five episodes. The linear-probe results in Figure 9 use a capture of 414 frames: nine evenly spaced frames from each of 46 policy-training episodes.

For each frame and decoder layer ℓ \ell , we mean-pool hidden_states[ ℓ \ell ] over non-padding positions to obtain a 400 × 2048 400\times 2048 matrix X ℓ X_{\ell} . After centering the columns, we compute the covariance eigenvalues λ i \lambda_{i} from the squared singular values and define PR ℓ = ( ∑ i λ i ) 2 / ∑ i λ i 2 \mathrm{PR}_{\ell}=(\sum_{i}\lambda_{i})^{2}/\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}^{2} . PR thus measures the effective dimensionality of across-frame variance. Each evaluation axis pairs one downstream benchmark with one PR probe domain. Figure 19 pools the three task-matched axes. For each layer and axis, we compute the Spearman correlation across the same six Stage-I arms and assess significance with a two-sided exact permutation test over all 6 ! = 720 6!=720 assignments, applying Benjamini–Hochberg FDR correction across the 19 layers.

Episode-time labels are defined as min ⁡ ( 3 , ⌊ 4 ​ frame ​ _ ​ idx / total ​ _ ​ frames ⌋ ) \min(3,\lfloor 4\,\mathrm{frame\_idx}/\mathrm{total\_frames}\rfloor) , giving a chance balanced accuracy of 1 / 4 1/4 . The labels reach , grasp , transport , and place denote the four positional (timestep) quartiles of each episode. Within each leave-one-episode-out fold, we fit StandardScaler , PCA(64) , and LogisticRegression(C=0.5) . Layer-band uncertainty and differences from Plain FT are estimated with a paired bootstrap over episodes ( B = 1000 B=1000 ).

At each layer, we extract the attention from text queries to image keys, A [ : , 256 : , : 256 ] A[:,256:,:256] , average it uniformly over heads and text queries, and L 1 L_{1} -normalize it over the 256 image patches; no individual head or last-token readout is selected. Band-level maps average the normalized per-layer maps. Because this normalization removes the total attention mass on the image, we report that quantity separately as img_mass . For visualization, patch values are upsampled by nearest-neighbor tiling, and all arms share a color scale capped at the 99th percentile of interior-patch attention; the border ring is excluded from this scale because it exhibits attention-sink/register behavior. Bounding boxes are mapped to patches using floor/ceiling boundaries and may include up to one extra patch on each edge; each keypoint or trace point is mapped to the patch that contains it, and the background is the complement of all annotated patches. A frame enters a given region analysis only if it contains at least two bounding-box patches, one keypoint, or one trace point, as applicable. For a patch mask M M and normalized attention p j p_{j} , we define enrichment as ( 256 / | M | ) ​ ∑ j ∈ M p j (256/|M|)\sum_{j\in M}p_{j} , so that a value of 1 corresponds to uniform attention. Bounding-box, keypoint, and trace masks may overlap and therefore do not partition the image; only the background mask is defined by complementation.

Figure 21 expands the main-text probe comparison to all nine model arms. VQA and trace show the largest late-layer recovery in object-identity decoding and the strongest novel-object results; spatial, bounding-box, and keypoint variants show no comparable recovery and are the weakest on that shift.

analysis.overview: 值得关注的是“推理适配 → 冻结适配器 → 动作微调”这一训练配方。正文消融支持它优于所测联合训练和可训练适配器；收益依任务和扰动差别很大。优先理解训练顺序和控制实验，再决定是否复现。
analysis.notice: 已阅读提取出的91个文字片段（主文与附录），并目视核对PDF第6、7、10、15、19、20、21页关键图表；未逐一检查所有图片、公式、引用文献或执行代码。逐字引文匹配只验证出处，不证明语义判断正确；实验数值来自作者，未复现。

findings.title: 关键增量：冻结推理适配器，再学习动作
findings.text: RAFT 的增量是后训练的参数与顺序安排。先用任务相关推理训练视觉和语言 LoRA；动作训练阶段冻结它们，更新语言模型、动作专家与投影层。它不要求推理时先生成文字链再动作。作者的消融支持这一配方，但不能据此证明冻结对所有 VLA 都有效。

findings.title: 两阶段具体更新哪些参数？
findings.text: 第一阶段只更新 LoRA，预训练 SigLIP 与其余主干冻结；第二阶段 LoRA 与 SigLIP 仍冻结，语言主干、动作专家、投影层参与动作微调。仿真/DROID 配置的 LoRA rank=64、alpha=128，覆盖视觉和语言模块。YAM 使用 π0.5，不直接套用 MolmoBot 的全部配置。

findings.title: 新增数据：推理标注也有成本
findings.text: 作者用 Gemini 3.1 Pro 为观测和指令生成框、关键点、轨迹、空间描述或 VQA 标注。主实验抓放用 full reasoning，开抽屉用 bbox；同一任务内部固定模态。相同动作示范数不代表没有额外数据加工、模型标注和计算成本。

findings.title: DROID：75.0% 来自三类 OOD 的合并结果
findings.text: MolmoBot 用50条抓放示范适配。作者报告 RAFT/Plain FT 的 OOD 成功率75.0%/27.9%：换物体颜色83%/33%（24次）、干扰物75%/25%（24次）、背景65%/25%（20次），共68次 OOD 试验。ID另有30次，约63%/60%。75%不等于图6含ID的 Mean，后者约71%。

findings.title: YAM：70% 是完整任务，且包括 ID
findings.text: π0.5 用100条示范学习开箱、取物并放入箱内。70.0%是五个轴的整段任务合并成功率；DeLock36%、Plain FT约35%、RETAIN29%。它既不是仅开箱成功率，也不是仅OOD。附录明确每个OOD轴30次，但没有同样明确写出YAM的ID次数，因此本试跑不补写总样本数。

findings.title: 仿真：83.21% 对79.62%，需看分轴
findings.text: MolmoBot/MolmoSpaces 每任务106条单布局成功示范；抓放五个评测划分各106次，方法间使用匹配初始条件。表4均值83.21%/79.62%，差约3.59个百分点；纹理与指令轴与普通微调打平。真机的大幅提升不能替代仿真结论，本报告也不据此断言跨训练随机种子的显著性。

findings.title: 核心消融：冻结、继续更新与联合训练
findings.text: 仿真抓放中冻结适配器83.21%，动作阶段继续更新73.96%，仅推理阶段48.30%；推理与动作1:1联合训练63.21%，普通微调79.62%。这支持分阶段与冻结的重要性，但这一联合配方的失败不等于所有联合训练无效。

findings.title: 更强控制：冻结视觉已缩小部分差距
findings.text: 冻结视觉的Plain FT平均79.62%，但新物体成功率从35.85%升至40.57%；RAFT为43.40%，相对这个控制只高2.83个百分点。应同时看这个控制，避免把所有收益归因于推理内容。

findings.title: 复现条件：额外1,000步训练与外部标注
findings.text: 表1的仿真/DROID配置：推理阶段1,000步、有效batch48、单张46GB L40；动作阶段5,000步、有效batch512、四张46GB L40。基线统一动作训练5,000步，但总训练预算并不完全相等。已读文字未提供足够的标注美元成本、端到端工时和所有训练重复信息，暂不估算费用。

findings.title: 推理模态没有通吃的赢家
findings.text: 抓放新物体成功率：轨迹45.28%，VQA/full reasoning各43.40%，bbox/keypoint各34.91%，普通微调35.85%；开抽屉不同模态在ID和视觉扰动上各有优势。监督内容本身需要验证，不能认为任意推理标注都能改善结果。

findings.title: 表示分析提供相关证据，尚非因果证明
findings.text: 线性探针414帧来自46个策略训练episode；按episode留出探针拟合，不代表这些轨迹未进入策略训练。所谓任务进度标签是时间四分位，并非人工标定的实际子任务完成度。注意力集中与PR相关性支持表示变化，不单凭这些测量证明因果或通用推理能力。

findings.title: 口径核查：39%和38.05%不是同一均值

hypotheses.title: 最小实验：收益对标注噪声有多敏感？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：冻结适配器保留的既可能是任务信号，也可能是错误标注。先只做一个仿真抓放任务，固定动作示范、初始化、数据顺序、动作训练步数与评测episode。四组为冻结视觉Plain FT、标准RAFT、10%记录加入可控对象/坐标错误的RAFT、30%同类错误的RAFT。RAFT各组固定推理训练量，单独记录额外GPU时与标注量。先小规模检查，再以至少3个训练种子评测ID/新物体/纹理成功率及配对差异区间；另加总GPU时匹配的动作训练控制。若噪声不影响结果，或预算匹配控制达到相同收益，就反对“精确任务推理信号是主要来源”的解释；只在单一扰动退化则缩小假设。实验尚未运行，也未全面排查相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。
