passages.section: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
passages.location: When Does Test-Time Search Help World Action Models? An Empirical Audit of Candidate Selection and Simulator Integrity
passages.text: World-action models increasingly apply test-time scaling, spending extra inference computation on candidate selection and adaptive allocation to improve control. Such gains are credible only when candidates carry exploitable signal, nominal compute savings become real speedup, and evaluation stays reliable. We audit all three on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa with a premise-first, pre-registered methodology. On clean data, a learned value selector is 1.66 pp worse than random; a hindsight oracle gains only 1.40 pp, with an episode-level interval spanning zero; and 82% of states show identical candidate outcomes, leaving little selection headroom. Token pruning cuts per-forward FLOPs by up to 47% but yields at most a measured 1.15 × \times end-to-end speedup on the deployed path (1.25 × \times on a decode-excluded path), short of a 1.5 × \times target, and our adaptive-allocation experiment is inconclusive under a power gate. We further identify and fix a silent rendering corruption whose rate rises sharply along compute-heavy planning paths while leaving the official direct-policy result unaffected, and release a detector, fix, and scripts. These findings show why test-time scaling should be audited as a chain of premises (decision signal, realized efficiency, evaluation integrity) rather than by success rate alone. Conclusions are scoped to the tested configuration.

Figure 2 : A premise-first audit of test-time scaling in Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa. (1) Planning selection. Limited variation in candidate outcomes constrains the headroom for selection, and the deployable value selector underperforms random selection, while the hindsight oracle provides only modest evidence of improvement. (2) Adaptive allocation. Substantial nominal FLOPs reductions translate into modest end-to-end latency gains, while the joint allocation effect remains unresolved at the available noise and statistical power. (3) Evaluation reliability. Rendering corruption becomes much more frequent in the compute-intensive planning path than under direct-policy or best-of- N N evaluation, while the official direct-policy result remains essentially unaffected. All findings are scoped to the tested Cosmos Policy–RoboCasa configuration.

World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos Policy [ 14 ] adapt large pretrained video models into robot policies that jointly generate actions, future states, and values within a shared latent diffusion process. A central promise of this design is test-time scaling : by generating candidate actions, predicting their future consequences, and evaluating them with a value function, WAMs can allocate additional inference-time computation to identify promising actions. Related peer-reviewed work has explored complementary aspects of this problem, including model-based planning with action-conditioned video world models [ 27 ] and efficient diffusion-based robot policies through one-step distillation [ 22 ] , training-free adaptive caching [ 11 ] , and rollout-adaptive pruning and activation reuse [ 12 ] .

Yet whether extra inference-time computation improves control remains insufficiently examined. More computation helps only if it exposes decision-relevant candidate differences, produces practical end-to-end effects, and is evaluated reliably; success rates alone cannot distinguish a weak selection signal, unrealized compute savings, and simulator artifacts [ 17 ] . We therefore audit test-time scaling as a chain of premises rather than a single performance number: is useful signal present, do nominal savings translate into end-to-end gains, and does the evaluation path remain reliable under added computation?

We instantiate this audit on Cosmos Policy and RoboCasa [ 20 ] . Rather than proposing a planner, we combine paired candidate comparisons and a deployment-conditioned hindsight oracle, pre-registered decision criteria and a power gate, complete-query latency measurements, and a framebuffer-sentinel integrity check.
The audit yields three findings.

(1) Candidate selection is limited by the available signal, not just by the selector. On render-verified clean data, the deployable value selector performs 1.66 1.66 pp worse than random, and even a hindsight oracle (an upper bound) gains only 1.40 1.40 pp with an interval including zero, because in 82 % 82\% of query states all candidates share an outcome. This does not show selection is generally ineffective; it shows selector quality must be read alongside the separability of the candidates it receives.

(2) Nominal compute reduction is not a reliable proxy for practical acceleration. Directly timing the complete query, token pruning yields at most a measured 1.15 × 1.15\times end-to-end speedup on the deployed path ( 1.25 × 1.25\times with future-image decode excluded), below the pre-specified 1.5 × 1.5\times target, because the gain is bounded by the irreducible autoencoder encode and decode. A separate joint-allocation diagnostic falls below the measurement’s noise resolution and did not clear its power gate, so it is inconclusive rather than evidence of no effect.

(3) Evaluation integrity can depend on the inference path being evaluated. We identify and fix a silent rendering corruption in the RoboCasa/ robosuite stack whose frequency is small under the official direct-policy protocol but rises sharply in the compute-intensive planning path. It is more than a generic simulator bug: changing inference-time computation changes exposure to a measurement failure, so the compute-intensive paths that realize test-time scaling are the most exposed.
Together, these findings make the contribution a testable audit methodology and a configuration-specific case study, not a claim that test-time scaling fails for all WAMs.

World models for control. World models that predict action-conditioned futures have advanced rapidly, spanning diffusion-based video prediction [ 1 , 7 , 4 ] , 3D and persistent representations [ 26 , 19 ] , and manipulation-specific models [ 13 ] . The backbone we study, Cosmos Policy [ 14 ] , follows the joint action-video line in which actions, futures, and values are produced within a single denoising process [ 7 ] . We do not propose a new world model; we audit whether the inference-time computation layered on top of such a model improves control.

Efficient world-model inference. Because prediction and planning in these models are costly, a growing body of work reduces their inference cost, through sparse imagination of rollouts [ 4 ] , disentangled dynamics prediction [ 23 ] , efficient on-policy rollout in diffusion world models [ 5 ] , and warm-started prediction that reuses spatiotemporal consistency [ 15 ] . These methods report nominal compute reductions. We audit whether such reductions convert to end-to-end latency on a representative stack, and find that token-level savings are capped by an irreducible encoding fraction rather than realized as speedup, and that the joint allocation effect lies below the measurement noise floor. X-WAM [ 6 ] audit underscores why architectural avenues can be more fruitful than token pruning alone for practical speedups.

Test-time scaling and candidate selection. A parallel line scales inference by sampling and selecting candidate actions, through verifier-free scoring [ 9 ] , relative action critics [ 16 ] , and reward-ranked world-model rollouts [ 24 ] ; analogous strategies in text and digital-agent settings use self-verification, process reward models, and execution-free critics [ 25 , 2 , 8 , 21 , 9 ] . These works propose selectors and report positive scaling. We instead audit whether the selection signal exists, and find a learned value selector worse than random on a strong base policy where candidate outcomes rarely differ.

Reliability of policy evaluation. Recent work asks whether simulator- and world-model-based evaluation is trustworthy, training learned evaluators to match real rollouts [ 18 ] , testing robustness under real-to-sim translation [ 10 ] , and reducing evaluation cost while preserving rankings [ 3 ] . These address the fidelity of a learned evaluator or a synthesized scene. Our reliability finding is at the level of the evaluation stack itself: a silent rendering corruption in the standard RoboCasa and robosuite pipeline whose rate rises with per-query inference compute, for which we release a detector and a fix.

passages.section: 3 A Diagnostic Methodology for Test-Time Compute
passages.location: 3 A Diagnostic Methodology for Test-Time Compute
passages.text: Because extra inference compute can change outputs without improving control, success-rate movements alone are not evidence of scaling gains. Our pre-registered, falsification-first audit tests for usable candidate signal and reliable evaluation before interpreting success (Section 6 ).

passages.section: 3.1 Verify the Premise Before Measuring the Gain
passages.location: 3.1 Verify the Premise Before Measuring the Gain
passages.text: Before evaluating an inference-time mechanism, we test whether its required signal exists. For best-of- N N planning, candidate outcomes must differ in ways a selector can recover; we test this directly in Section 4 , rather than infer it from downstream success. Supplement Figure 5 summarizes the audit gates.

passages.section: 3.2 Causal Ablation and an Oracle Headroom Estimate
passages.location: 3.2 Causal Ablation and an Oracle Headroom Estimate
passages.text: For each query state, we replay all N N candidates under a fixed continuation policy and let a hindsight oracle select a successful one. This estimates outcome-level selection headroom in the current candidate pool; because it uses unavailable outcome information, it is not deployable. We also probe input importance by leave-one-out patch masking, trusting the probe only if irrelevant background ranks below relevant end-effector and contact regions in a pre-registered sanity check.

For the selection audit, we fix decision thresholds and the replicate-consistency gate before inspecting the corresponding data and report the gate’s verdict even when it fails. A power gate avoids launching experiments unlikely to yield a verdict: from a smoke sample, we estimate the paired-residual standard deviation σ ^ r \hat{\sigma}_{r} and project the two-sided confidence-interval half-width at the planned sample size,

launching the full run only if h ⁡ ( N full ) < Δ prereg h(N_{\text{full}})<\Delta_{\text{prereg}} , the separation between the pre-registered outcomes; otherwise the run is not launched. Every reported comparison states its bootstrap resampling unit and interval, so that an effect whose significance depends on that choice is presented as such rather than as a settled result. Closed-loop success is measured by snapshot replay, in which we restore a state, execute a candidate action chunk, and continue under a fixed dense base policy, rather than inferred from a single-step action deviation.

Our empirical findings are limited to Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa. The audit components—premise checks, oracle headroom, a power gate, and render-integrity verification—can also inform audits of other diffusion control policies. We release a framebuffer-sentinel detector, a fix for the identified OpenGL-context bug, and reproduction scripts; the detector principle may transfer across backends, but this fix is stack-specific.

Figure 3 : Auditing best-of- N N planning selection. (a) Success-rate difference against the random baseline for the deployable value selector and the hindsight oracle, under state-level and episode-level bootstrap, with 95% CIs. The value selector is below zero under both schemes; the oracle estimate crosses zero under episode-level resampling and is an upper bound, not a deployable selector. (b) Only a minority of query states show any outcome variation across candidates and repeated executions, leaving little for a selector to recover in the rest; a stricter decomposition (Supplement Section 13 ) further separates stable between-candidate differences from variation that is not stable across repeats.

passages.section: 4 Auditing Best-of- N N Planning Selection
passages.location: 4 Auditing Best-of- N N Planning Selection
passages.text: We apply the audit to best-of- N N planning, comparing the model’s value-based ordering with random selection and estimating outcome-level headroom using a hindsight oracle.

On render-verified clean data, we compare the value selector, random selection, and the deployment-conditioned hindsight oracle on paired sets of N = 8 N{=}8 candidates with common continuation seeds. Differences from random are reported with state-within-task and episode-within-task bootstrap intervals.

Continuation protocol. In snapshot replay, each candidate’s first 16 16 steps of a generated 32 32 -step chunk are executed, stopping on success; the episode then replans every 16 16 steps under a fixed base policy until success or the 500 500 -step task limit. The base policy uses one sample, all tokens, 10 10 denoising steps, and no value head; all selectors share the same outcome matrix and continuation seeds ( R = 2 R=2 ). This controls the candidate’s single-switch effect but does not reproduce the full deployment distribution. The selection audit’s 10 10 -step continuation is distinct from the 2 2 -versus- 5 5 -step allocation factorial, whose dense reference is D ⁡ ( 5 , F ) D(5,F) .

passages.section: 4.2 Weak Selection Signal and a Negative Value Selector
passages.location: 4.2 Weak Selection Signal and a Negative Value Selector
passages.text: The value selector is 1.66 1.66 pp worse than random (95% CIs: state bootstrap [ − 2.97 , − 0.31 ] [-2.97,-0.31] ; episode bootstrap [ − 2.49 , − 0.71 ] [-2.49,-0.71] ), driven largely by TurnOnStove ( − 3.87 -3.87 pp). Excluding that task, the state-weighted estimate remains negative ( − 0.77 -0.77 pp; episode CI [ − 1.27 , − 0.21 ] [-1.27,-0.21] ; state CI [ − 1.54 , − 0.03 ] [-1.54,-0.03] ). Thus, the result is not uniform across tasks, but no task reverses into a measured value-selector benefit.

passages.section: 4.2 Weak Selection Signal and a Negative Value Selector
passages.location: 4.2 Weak Selection Signal and a Negative Value Selector
passages.text: The hindsight oracle’s gain is + 1.40 +1.40 pp, with a state-bootstrap CI of [ + 0.31 , + 2.60 ] [+0.31,+2.60] pp and an episode-bootstrap CI of [ − 0.25 , + 3.40 ] [-0.25,+3.40] pp. Under the pre-registered rule, the missed replicate-consistency gate and episode-level interval make this weak, inconclusive evidence. With R = 2 R=2 , the reliability estimate is only about 0.33 0.33 (Supplement Section 10 ); we therefore do not infer a definitive ceiling from either the cross-fitted estimate or the in-sample + 7.1 +7.1 pp maximum. More structurally, outcomes vary across candidates and/or repeats in only 48 / 263 48/263 states ( 18 % 18\% ; Fig. 3 b). The within-state ICC is 0.20 0.20 , which indicates limited repeat agreement under this protocol; the decomposition below distinguishes stable separation from variation not stable across repeats.

passages.section: 4.2 Weak Selection Signal and a Negative Value Selector
passages.location: 4.2 Weak Selection Signal and a Negative Value Selector
passages.text: How much of this separability is real? Outcome uniformity is not explained simply by near-identical actions: states with no outcome variation have no smaller action-space dispersion (Supplement Section 13 ), though geometric diversity need not be task-relevant. Of the 48 48 varying states, 20 20 show stable separation (one candidate succeeds in both repeats and another fails in both); the other 28 28 do not meet this criterion. A label-shuffle null expects about 14.8 14.8 stable-separable states, so the observed 20 20 are not 20 20 confirmed opportunities. The descriptive oracle contribution is + 1.85 +1.85 pp for the first group and − 0.44 -0.44 pp for the second; the pooled oracle gain under the null is + 0.01 +0.01 pp. With only two repeats, reproducible selection headroom remains uncertain.

Under this configuration, the negative value-selector result is clear, whereas reproducible oracle headroom remains uncertain. The oracle measures outcome-level headroom only for the observed candidates and specified single-switch continuation, not general decision relevance. We therefore make no claim that planning is universally ineffective; alternative candidate-generation and continuation policies remain untested.

passages.section: 5 A Feasibility Audit of Adaptive Compute Allocation
passages.location: 5 A Feasibility Audit of Adaptive Compute Allocation
passages.text: We audit whether reducing denoising steps or processing fewer tokens can deliver practical efficiency on this stack. Because the preregistered criteria are end-to-end latency and a resolvable joint interaction effect, and the power gate was not cleared, this is a feasibility diagnostic rather than a confirmatory test of joint allocation.

passages.section: 5.1 Nominal FLOPs Savings Do Not Convert to Wall-Clock Savings
passages.location: 5.1 Nominal FLOPs Savings Do Not Convert to Wall-Clock Savings
passages.text: Dropping all future frames plus the value frame removes 47.9 % 47.9\% of per-forward FLOPs, but direct complete-query timing shows only 1.152 × 1.152\times speedup on the deployed eager path and 1.253 × 1.253\times when future-image decode is excluded; neither reaches the preregistered 1.5 × 1.5\times target (Table 1 ). This fixed whole-frame mask adds no per-token scoring. The five DiT forwards account for 530.7 530.7 ms of the 1241.8 1241.8 ms dense query, while VAE encode ( 238.0 238.0 ms) and future-image decode ( 434.4 434.4 ms) are not reduced by token pruning. This is a latency-only result (dropped frames receive zero output); full settings and per-level latency percentiles are in Supplement Section 9 and Table 3 .

passages.section: 5.2 The Preliminary Interaction Effect Is Below the Noise Resolution
passages.location: 5.2 The Preliminary Interaction Effect Is Below the Noise Resolution
passages.text: The decisive comparison is independent of any chosen threshold: the preliminary systematic component ( 0.0045 0.0045 ) is smaller than the mean noise floor ( 0.0066 0.0066 ) and comparable to the temporal main effect itself ( 0.0053 0.0053 ) in the same states. A joint effect that is smaller than the per-state noise it must be read against cannot be resolved from this measurement, whatever decision threshold is adopted. Figure 4 places these quantities on the same absolute scale. For completeness, under the currently locked threshold θ B \theta_{B} (Supplement Eq. 3 ) the minimum detectable interaction is 0.0265 0.0265 to 0.0583 0.0583 , that is 5 5 to 11 11 times the temporal main effect; we note that this range depends on the threshold calibration still pending sign-off, and it will be recomputed for the camera-ready version, but the threshold-free comparison above does not depend on it.

passages.section: 5.2 The Preliminary Interaction Effect Is Below the Noise Resolution
passages.location: 5.2 The Preliminary Interaction Effect Is Below the Noise Resolution
passages.text: This is inconclusive, not a null result: the full factorial was not launched because the power gate failed. The estimated sample requirement— hundreds to roughly two thousand states, is an extrapolation from the current detection limit (Supplement Section 10 ), not a verified power result. Whether joint allocation helps on this stack remains open.

Efficiency claims should pair FLOPs with complete-query latency, and allocation claims should be judged against a preregistered detection limit. Here, token-pruning savings miss the latency target and the smoke-scale joint effect is unresolved; this does not establish that adaptive allocation is ineffective in general.

passages.section: 6 Evaluation Reliability: A Silent Rendering Corruption
passages.location: 6 Evaluation Reliability: A Silent Rendering Corruption
passages.text: We identify a third threat to test-time-scaling evaluation: silent, compute-dependent rendering corruption in the RoboCasa/ robosuite stack, to which compute-intensive inference paths are more exposed.

The corruption originates in OpenGL context management during environment resets. On a hard reset the stack constructs a new simulation instance while an orphaned instance remains eligible for garbage collection; when the orphan is later collected, its GL context is freed while a different context is active, silently invalidating the framebuffer of the live environment. Subsequent renders return corrupted observations, frozen or noise-like frames, with no error raised. Figure contrasts a corrupted frame with the correct render of the same state. We confirm the mechanism with a framebuffer sentinel that pre-fills each render target with a marker and flags targets left substantially untouched after rendering. 1 1 1 We attribute this corruption to OpenGL context management during hard resets in the tested stack, confirmed by our framebuffer sentinel and eliminated by our fix. We have not sought maintainer confirmation of the root-cause attribution.

passages.section: 6.2 Effect on the Official Direct-Policy Benchmark
passages.location: 6.2 Effect on the Official Direct-Policy Benchmark
passages.text: We first ask whether this corruption materially affects the officially reported RoboCasa numbers. We run the unmodified official evaluation file in two arms, bug-present and render-fixed, paired episode by episode on the four tasks where our baseline run exhibited corruption, over 50 consecutive episodes each (200 paired episodes), with the framebuffer sentinel active throughout.

passages.text: Table 2: Paired bug-vs-fix comparison under the official direct-policy protocol. All three outcome flips are corrupted episodes moving from failure to success; none move the other way. Among the 192 uncorrupted episodes, success is identical in both arms.

passages.section: 6.2 Effect on the Official Direct-Policy Benchmark
passages.location: 6.2 Effect on the Official Direct-Policy Benchmark
passages.text: As Table 2 shows, under the direct-policy protocol the measured corruption rate is 8 / 1200 8/1200 ( 0.67 % 0.67\% per episode in the bug arm, and zero in the fixed arm), and the paired effect of fixing it is + 3 +3 successes over 200 episodes. All flips move corrupted episodes from failure to success, so the corruption understates success. Extrapolated to the full 24-task, 50-episode protocol, the effect is about + 0.25 +0.25 pp and never exceeds an upper bound of + 0.6 +0.6 pp. We conclude that the officially reported direct-policy figure of 67.1 % 67.1\% is not materially affected: the corruption is real and present in the official stack, but its direct-policy impact is small and in the direction of underreporting success.
The direct-policy result does not bound the risk for test-time scaling, because corruption frequency depends on how much computation each query allocates. We observe a sharp, monotone dependence:
Direct policy (one forward pass per query): 0.67 % 0.67\% of episodes corrupted, paired-verified in Table 2 .

Direct-mode best-of- N N ( N = 8 N{=}8 candidates, simple forward passes): 0 / 40 0/40 episodes corrupted, with identical success ( 29 / 40 29/40 ) in both arms. Additional sampling alone does not raise the rate.
Planning mode (separate future-state and value calls per query, substantially more allocation per query): up to 65 % 65\% of episodes corrupted.

The 65 % 65\% figure is observed under a compute-heavy planning configuration and should be read as an upper-bound illustration of the trend, not as the corruption rate of any standard benchmark. RoboCasa provides no native planning-mode evaluation, and this configuration is non-standard; the official repository exposes best-of- N N planning only for a real-robot platform that does not pass through robosuite , so the planning-path corruption touches no number the official benchmark reports. On the LIBERO stack, which on a hard reset explicitly destroys the prior simulation before constructing a new one and so leaves no orphan, the trigger condition is not met; we infer from the source that the reported LIBERO figure is unaffected, though we did not run that environment.

The official direct-policy result is largely unaffected, but compute-heavy planning is more exposed. Studies using this stack should verify render integrity before attributing gains to inference-time methods.

Our three audits are independent, but they point in the same direction: on the tested Cosmos Policy configuration, the computation added at inference time to realize test-time scaling does not buy what it is assumed to buy, and part of the apparent benefit reported in this setting can arise from evaluation artifacts rather than from the method.

What the findings do and do not say. None of the three results claims that planning, adaptive allocation, or test-time scaling is useless in general; each is stated at the scope of the tested configuration. The planning result is that the deployable selector is worse than random and that selection headroom is small, not that no selector can ever help. The allocation result is that nominal FLOPs savings do not convert to end-to-end speedup here, together with a detectability statement from a smoke-scale sample whose preregistered power gate was not cleared, not a confirmed null. The reliability result is that a real, compute-dependent corruption exists in the official stack while leaving the reported direct-policy number essentially intact.

A methodology, not only a set of negative results. The value of a negative audit depends on whether its measurements can be trusted, which is why the diagnostic methodology is our primary contribution. Premise-first verification keeps us from building on a signal that does not exist; the oracle bounds the achievable gain before any selector is tuned; the power gate stops an experiment that cannot yield a verdict before it consumes compute; and render-integrity checking protects every closed-loop number. These components are model-agnostic and transfer to any audit of test-time compute in a diffusion-based control policy, even though the specific render fix is tied to the stack we study. We release the detector, fix, scripts, and preregistered protocols so the audits can be repeated. Our strongest limitation is scope: whether these findings generalize to other models, simulators, or real hardware is an open question the methodology is designed to answer rather than presuppose, and we see the audits not as a verdict against inference-time computation but as checks that should precede any claim that test-time scaling improves control.

We presented an empirical audit of test-time scaling in a representative world-action model, Cosmos Policy on RoboCasa, built around a premise-first, pre-registered methodology with explicit statistical power control and render-integrity verification. The audit yields three independent reasons an apparent gain may not be real: best-of- N N candidate selection carries little usable signal and its deployable selector is worse than random; nominal compute savings from token-level allocation do not convert to practical speedup, and the joint allocation effect lies below the system’s noise resolution; and a silent, compute-dependent rendering corruption inflates the reliability risk of exactly the compute-intensive inference paths that test-time scaling relies on, while leaving the official direct-policy benchmark intact. We release the methodology and tools so that these checks can be applied before performance gains are attributed to test-time scaling rather than to unverified assumptions or evaluation artifacts.

This supplement documents the measurement setup behind Table 1 and the single-forward mechanism that explains why per-forward savings do not carry the whole query. All figures are directly measured; none are composed from component times.

NVIDIA RTX A6000, PyTorch 2.7.0 with CUDA 12.8 and cuDNN 90701, model nvidia/Cosmos-Policy-RoboCasa-Predict2-2B with weights in bf16, latent shape [ 1 , 16 , 11 , 28 , 28 ] [1,16,11,28,28] (11 latent frames × \times 196 tokens = = 2156), batch 1, and 5 denoising steps per action query (confirmed as exactly 5 DiT forwards per call). The only tracked code modification is a logging patch to run_robocasa_eval.py (commit 18a2acc ).

For each pruning level and each of the two paths (deployed, and decode-excluded), we time the complete action-inference query, dense against pruned, under the deployed eager backend. We discard warmup and then record N = 30 N=30 timed queries per cell, reporting the median with the 10 10 th and 90 90 th percentiles; the directory out_e2e_prune/raw.jsonl holds all 420 timed calls. Paired per-state speedups agree with the reported median ratios to within 0.001 0.001 . The decode-excluded dense baseline is directly measured at 812.7 812.7 ms (it is not the decode-subtracted estimate used before this run). The whole-frame prune is applied inside the real query path; because whole-frame pruning is a fixed structural mask, there is no per-token scoring step, and the frame slicing and scatter-back run inside the timed region, so the measured speedups carry full real overhead for this pruning type.

passages.text: The complete query contains host-side control flow, host-device copies and array post-processing that cannot be CUDA Graph captured without restructuring the code, so no graph-timed stage is mixed into the end-to-end numbers. Eager is in any case the deployed evaluation backend.

To locate the ceiling of the pruned stage, we separately time the DiT forward in isolation. Under CUDA Graph the single forward speeds up by at most 1.73 × 1.73\times (dense 102.75 102.75 ms to all-future-frames-plus-value 59.42 59.42 ms), with output bit-identical to eager. This is a single-forward, CUDA-Graph measurement and is not directly comparable to the eager end-to-end speedups in Table 1 b; we report it only to show that even a forward driven nearly to its floor cannot carry the query, because the five DiT forwards are under half of the end-to-end latency (Table 1 c) while VAE encode and future-image decode are not reducible by token pruning.
Per-forward FLOPs in Table 1 a are measured with FlopCounterMode (matmul + + SDPA).

With R R replicate rollouts per state, the reliability of the mean candidate estimate follows the Spearman–Brown form
Rel ⁡ ( R ) = R ​ ρ ICC 1 + ( R − 1 ) ​ ρ ICC . \mathrm{Rel}(R)=\frac{R\,\rho_{\text{ICC}}}{1+(R-1)\,\rho_{\text{ICC}}}. (4)

With the measured intraclass correlation ρ ICC = 0.20 \rho_{\text{ICC}}=0.20 and R = 2 R=2 , Rel = 0.33 \mathrm{Rel}=0.33 , so a single continuation ranks candidates with only about 20 % 20\% reliability and the cross-fitted oracle estimate is itself noisy.

Figure 5 : The premise-first methodology as a chain of gates. Each candidate test-time-scaling gain passes three checks in order before it is credited: verify that the decision signal exists (causal ablation and oracle ceiling); a statistical power gate that halts a run which cannot resolve the pre-registered outcome; and closed-loop measurement under framebuffer-sentinel render-integrity checking. A “no” at the first gate reports a negative result and at the second an inconclusive one, separating a genuine negative from an underpowered or invalid measurement.

Figure 5 shows the audit as a single procedure: three gates applied in order before any test-time-scaling gain is credited. Each gate corresponds to one of the three ways an apparent gain can fail, and to one of the paper’s three audits.

The first gate verifies the premise that the added computation exposes a usable decision signal, using the causal ablation and oracle-ceiling construction of Section 6 ; when no signal exists the result is reported as negative rather than pursued further, as in the planning audit of Section 4 . The second gate is statistical: from a smoke sample it projects the confidence-interval width at the full sample size and halts the run when the pre-registered outcome cannot be resolved, so compute is not spent on an experiment that cannot yield a verdict, and the outcome is reported as inconclusive rather than as evidence of absence, as in the allocation audit of Section 5 . The third gate measures closed-loop success under the framebuffer-sentinel render check and routes the verdict by pre-registered thresholds, the render-integrity guard whose necessity the reliability audit of Section 6 establishes.

The value of the procedure is in its two “no” branches: they separate a genuine negative from an underpowered or invalid measurement, a distinction that success rate alone cannot make. The gates are model-agnostic and apply to any audit of test-time compute in a diffusion-based control policy; only the render fix itself is specific to the stack we study.

Table 3 reports the full measurement behind Table 1 (b): both query paths at all six pruning levels, with the 10th and 90th percentiles over the N = 30 N=30 timed queries per cell. Three observations follow, all from directly measured values.

First, the end-to-end speedup grows monotonically but sublinearly with the nominal FLOPs reduction. Cutting 47.9 % 47.9\% of per-forward FLOPs (all future frames plus value) buys only 15.2 % 15.2\% of wall-clock on the deployed path and 25.3 % 25.3\% on the decode-excluded path; the remaining time is dominated by the autoencoder encode and future-image decode, which token pruning does not touch.

Second, the decode-excluded path scales better at every level, reaching 1.253 × 1.253\times against 1.152 × 1.152\times on the deployed path at the most aggressive prune. Removing the fixed future-image decode shrinks the denominator and enlarges the share of the query that pruning can act on, yet even this most-favorable configuration stops well short of the 1.5 × 1.5\times target.

Third, the percentile spread is tight: the 10th and 90th percentiles lie within about 1 % 1\% of the median at every cell, so the medians are stable and the sub- 1.5 × 1.5\times conclusion is not an artifact of run-to-run variance. No pruning level on either path reaches 1.5 × 1.5\times .

Table 3 : Full end-to-end query latency under whole-frame token pruning, both paths, all levels (Cosmos Policy, RoboCasa, batch 1, 5 denoising steps; NVIDIA RTX A6000, bf16, eager). Every value is directly measured over N = 30 N=30 timed queries per cell; median with the 10th and 90th percentiles. The deployed path is the query as the eval calls it (future-image decode and value extraction included); the decode-excluded path removes future-image decode on both sides. Speedup is dense median divided by pruned median. No pruning level on either path reaches the pre-registered 1.5 × 1.5\times target. This expands the medians and speedups of main-body Table 1 (b).

These diagnostics address whether the limited selection headroom in Section 4 is an artifact of near-identical candidates or of replicate noise. They are descriptive and read only saved files (candidate actions, per-candidate closed outcomes with two repeats, and value scores); they do not run inference, and they do not claim that greater diversity would improve success.

For each state we z-score the seven action dimensions across the dataset, flatten each candidate’s executed 16-step chunk to a 112-vector, and take the mean pairwise Euclidean distance among the eight candidates. No state has identical candidates (minimum dispersion 0.18 0.18 ). States without outcome variation show greater absolute dispersion than states with it (pooled median 0.78 0.78 vs 0.48 0.48 ; Mann–Whitney p = 5 × 10 − 5 p=5\times 10^{-5} ; Spearman ρ = − 0.25 \rho=-0.25 against outcome degree), a pattern driven mainly by TurnOnStove. Scale-free coefficient-of- variation metrics show no significant group difference ( p = 0.07 p=0.07 – 0.10 0.10 ), so the difference is largely one of absolute action magnitude. Value-score dispersion is uniformly tiny (median standard deviation ≈ 3 × 10 − 4 \approx 3\times 10^{-4} ) and unrelated to outcome variation in the pooled analysis ( p = 0.62 p=0.62 ), consistent with a value selector that carries little usable ranking signal; TurnOnStove, where the value selector is worst, is the only task with larger value dispersion on varying states.

The 48 48 of 263 263 states with any variation (across eight candidates and two repeats) split into those with a stable between-candidate difference and those without one. We call a state stably separable when some candidate succeeds in both repeats while another fails in both.

All 28 28 are graded ( 0.5 0.5 vs 0 0 or 0.5 0.5 vs 1 1 ); none is a full-repeat flip. passages.section: Even the stable states are near chance.
passages.location: Even the stable states are near chance.
passages.text: A within-state null that independently shuffles the candidate labels in each repeat (preserving each repeat’s success count but breaking candidate identity across repeats, 2000 2000 draws) expects ≈ 14.8 \approx 14.8 stably separable states by chance, against the observed 20 20 ; the excess is about 5 5 states, mostly PnPCounterToCab. The cross-fitted hindsight oracle (same estimator as the main text) gains + 1.40 +1.40 pp pooled, decomposing as + 1.85 +1.85 pp from the 20 20 stably separable states and − 0.44 -0.44 pp from the 28 28 states without stable separation (on which the cross-fitted oracle never beats random). Under this specific label-shuffle null the pooled cross-fitted oracle has a near-zero mean gain ( + 0.01 +0.01 pp), providing no indication of upward inflation under the null; with only two repeats per candidate, the amount of reproducible selection headroom remains uncertain. This contribution split is exploratory: the grouping is itself defined from the two repeats and is subject to sampling randomness.

Actions cover only the executed first 16 16 of the 32 32 generated steps. With two repeats per candidate we cannot adjudicate per state whether a stable separation is real or coincidental; the graded ( 0.5 0.5 -valued) states are indistinguishable from noise at this sample size. States within an episode are not independent and the reported p p -values are not corrected for multiple comparisons, so they are exploratory rather than confirmatory. The diagnostics cover four tasks and three episodes and do not speak to other candidate counts, sampling temperatures, or continuation policies. Full numbers and reproducible scripts are in probes/P5_oracle/ ( p5_diversity.py , p5_noise_decomp.py ).

analysis.overview: 本文把WAM测试时扩算拆为三个先决条件：候选是否存在可复现的结果差异、FLOPs节省能否转为完整查询加速、评测渲染是否可靠。Cosmos Policy/RoboCasa配置中，价值选择低于随机1.66个百分点，交叉拟合oracle仅+1.40个百分点且episode级区间跨零；两次重复不足以确定真实上限。整帧裁剪省47.9%单前向FLOPs，完整部署查询仅1.152倍加速且未测动作质量。16状态分配实验未过统计功效门槛，结论是无定论。另有与重置/GL上下文有关的静默渲染错误，重规划路径较易暴露，但官方直接策略结果只小幅低报。本轮核对还纠正加速倍数与耗时下降百分比的混用。

findings.title: 先验证扩算前提，分别记录负结果与统计无定论
findings.text: 本文提出的是诊断协议而非新规划器：在归因测试时扩算收益前，先检验可选择信号、实际端到端效率及渲染完整性。方法包括配对候选闭环回放、不可部署的事后oracle、统计功效门槛和帧缓冲哨兵。固定检验规则后再读数据是作者的预注册主张，本轮未独立核其事前时间戳。价值选择器表现差、达不到设定时延目标、未过功效门槛，是三种不同判断，不能统一写成规划或自适应分配无效。可迁移的是审计思路，经验结论限该Cosmos Policy/RoboCasa配置。

findings.title: 候选只切换一次，后续统一由稠密基础策略继续
findings.text: 在渲染核验后的状态上比较8个候选，执行生成32步chunk的前16步，成功即停；之后每16步重规划，使用1样本、全token、10去噪步、无价值头的固定基础策略，直到成功或500步。所有选择器共享结果矩阵和continuation seeds，每候选仅R=2重复。该协议控制首次候选选择的局部效应，并不等于整段episode不断用价值选择/规划的部署分布。分配诊断另用2与5去噪步，不能把10步continuation同其5步稠密参考D(5,F)混为一个实验。263是查询状态数，同episode状态相关，不能当263条独立完整任务。

findings.title: 价值选择器低于随机，且不是只由一个任务造成
findings.text: 图3：价值选择减随机为−1.66个百分点，95%状态bootstrap区间[−2.97,−0.31]、episode bootstrap[−2.49,−0.71]，两者均在零下。TurnOnStove贡献较大（−3.87个百分点）；去该任务后状态加权均差仍−0.77，episode区间[−1.27,−0.21]，状态区间[−1.54,−0.03]。支持该价值排序在本候选/续行配置下比随机差，不能扩展成所有critic或所有WAM无法选动作。没有呈现跨更多模型、候选生成方式或完整持续规划的等预算验证。

findings.title: oracle的1.40个百分点仍不确定，不能锁成确定天花板
findings.text: 事后交叉拟合oracle相对随机+1.40个百分点，状态bootstrap95%区间[+0.31,+2.60]，episode级[−0.25,+3.40]；未过重复一致性门槛。因此不能仅挑状态区间宣称显著可用收益，也不能把含噪点估计当所有选择器的硬上限。样本内取最大+7.1同样不是可部署或可复现收益。ICC0.20、两次重复的Spearman–Brown可靠性约0.33，说明oracle的排序基准本身不稳。48/263状态有候选/重复结果变化，215/263约82%均一；20个稳定可分状态中，两次重复都成功/都失败的结构在标签置乱null下也预期出现约14.8个，故20并非20个已证实可利用机会。

findings.title: 动作几何多样性不等于任务结果可分性
findings.text: 补充13节将执行的16步×7维动作按数据集z-score后展开112维，8候选两两距离最小离散度仍0.18，没有完全相同候选。无结果变化状态的绝对离散度中位数0.78，反而高于有变化的0.48，主要由TurnOnStove驱动；尺度无关变异系数无显著组差（p约0.07–0.10），不能把原始距离差当独立结构效应。价值分数标准差中位约3×10⁻⁴，与结果变化无明显关系。48变化状态中20稳定可分、28未达标准；0.5值来自重复结果的分级统计，不能当单次任务半完成。检验未作多重比较校正且同episode相关，均为探索性；不能据此宣称增加动作分散就提高成功率。

findings.title: 47.9%单前向FLOPs下降，部署查询耗时只下降约13.2%
findings.text: 核表1/3：RTX A6000、bf16、batch1、eager、每查询5次DiT，11帧×196=2156token；裁去全部未来帧和value剩1176token，单前向8.535→4.446TFLOP，省47.9%。完整部署查询中位1254.9→1088.9ms，加速1.152×；同时去未来图像解码的有利路径812.7→648.6ms，为1.253×，均未到作者预设1.5×。按毫秒值计算耗时分别降13.2%和20.2%，补充12节把15.2%/25.3%写成耗时节省混淆了speedup−1与1−1/speedup，本卡采用毫秒重算。稠密分解DiT五次合530.7ms，VAE编码238.0、解码434.4ms，后两项不随token裁剪减少。计时为完整真实查询，包含切片/scatter，但丢弃帧以零输出、只测延迟，未验证策略质量，不能当保持成功率的可用加速。独立CUDA Graph单forward1.73×不是eager完整查询结果。

findings.title: 分配交互的完整实验未启动，不能称已经验证无收益

findings.title: 渲染哨兵检测未写入目标，根因归属限作者的栈诊断
findings.text: 作者解释hard reset新建sim后，旧孤立实例延迟GC，在另一个GL context活跃时释放旧context，导致当前framebuffer失效；画面可冻结或噪声化且不抛异常。哨兵先用标记填充render target，再检查render后是否大面积仍未覆盖。PDF图1补充了提取包未列的画面：左右/腕三相机拼图被重复成马赛克，作者以修复重跑的同状态对照展示。作者称修复消除故障，但脚注明确尚未获维护者确认根因；本轮未运行复现器或修复、未独立检查源码。可以采用完整性检测原则，不可把栈特定GL修复当跨渲染后端通用安全保障，也不能认为哨兵覆盖所有视觉失真。

findings.title: 官方直接策略受影响很小，200配对子集与1200总体需区分
findings.text: 核表2：先选原基线出现损坏的四任务，各50条连续episode，共200对bug/fix，成功102→105，8条损坏，全3次翻转均从失败到成功，其余192条完全一致。该选中子集损坏8/200，而论文0.67%用整个24任务×50=1200条bug臂作分母8/1200，两者不同，不能混写。按全协议外推+3/1200=0.25个百分点，作者称官方67.1%结果基本不受影响，且方向是修复前低报；这不是官方分数被大幅虚增的证据。完整24任务两条件配对未展示，不能把子集外推说成全1200对都重跑验证。

findings.title: 至多65%属于非标准重规划路径，不是所有加算力都会损坏
findings.text: 直接策略总体约0.67%损坏；直接模式8候选简单forward的40例为0损坏且bug/fix都29/40成功；分开调用未来状态/value的某重计算规划配置至多65%。后者没有完整分母/配置扫描，且RoboCasa无原生规划模式，此为非标准风险示例，不能叫标准基准腐坏率，也不能仅凭配置相关性证明FLOPs是唯一因果变量。40例无损坏不等于风险为零。作者明确官方真实机器人规划不经robosuite，故这一路错误不影响该官方规划数字；LIBERO因其先销毁旧sim的代码路径推断无触发条件，但作者没有运行LIBERO，不能写成实测无故障。

findings.title: 优先复用审计设计，保留原始记录与统计校准缺口
findings.text: 实证仅一个模型/仿真栈：选择诊断四任务，附录称three episodes，逐任务episode分配需原始日志确认；仅R=2、执行前16步、固定continuation，未测其他候选数、温度、难度分布或实机。作者声明发布detector/fix/scripts并给相对脚本/结果路径，本轮未验证独立下载、原始矩阵和预注册时间戳；统计阈值尚待校准，不视作完整锁定认证。计时正文称每cell30，表有6档×2路径=360次，而附录又称420次计时，是否额外dense对照未说明，保留记录数映射缺口；不擅改原表。FLOPs与完整耗时、单步与整任务、oracle估计与硬上限、未过功效与真负结果都需分开。该方法学可影响研究预算判断，不能据单栈审计否定测试时搜索的普遍价值。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：增加独立episode与候选重复后，原配置仍无实用选择余量吗？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：保持原候选生成和single-switch续行协议时，增加独立episode与候选重复后，可复现oracle收益仍低于预设的2个百分点实用门槛，价值选择器也不会优于随机。仅公开仿真实验草案：固定Cosmos Policy权重、RoboCasa版本/任务、8候选和10去噪步续行，渲染固定版及哨兵在所有条件一致；每任务至少30个独立episode，从预设时间网格抽状态，不能因候选是否可分才挑样本。先用独立smoke估episode级方差/功效，在预算上限内预注册最终状态数及R=2/4/8重复设计，若功效不足则如实无定论。比较同一候选池上的随机、部署价值排序、样本内最大值和训练/评估重复分离的交叉拟合oracle，不把后两者当可部署算法。以episode为bootstrap重采样单位、按任务分层，报oracle/价值减随机95%区间、稳定可分比例、重复一致性及完整查询墙钟与总回放预算；预先定义连续规划为另一独立实验，不混入本single-switch效应。只有oracle区间上界低于2个百分点才支持缺少实用余量；若下界超过2个百分点或价值排序在独立评估上显著为正，则推翻假设；区间跨门槛时不能硬判无效。对任何渲染损坏用预注册规则整对重跑或留作失效，不按结果删样本。实验未执行，未创建选题，未全面查新；即使支持也只适用于所测试任务与候选数，仍不否定新候选生成器或其他WAM。

frontier_brief.title: 给WAM扩算先验信号、再测完整查询，并核渲染完整性
frontier_brief.change_type: 测试时搜索与评测审计
frontier_brief.delta: 对同状态候选做配对闭环续行，以随机和交叉拟合oracle分开检验排序质量与可选择余量；计完整查询时延，用功效门槛区分负结果和无定论，以framebuffer哨兵保护评测。
frontier_brief.before: 仅报规划成功率、动作差异或单前向FLOPs，难区分候选同质、排序无效、固定编解码开销和无报错的渲染失真。
frontier_brief.after: Cosmos Policy/RoboCasa该配置下，价值选择低于随机1.66个百分点；oracle+1.40但episode级区间跨零。裁剪省47.9%单前向FLOPs，完整部署查询仅1.152倍且未测动作质量；分配完整实验未过功效门槛。
frontier_brief.relevance: 在投入WAM best-of-N或自适应去噪/裁剪前，先估候选可复现结果差异、按真实调用路径核算延迟，再验证渲染与统计单位，避免把低可用信号或无定论当明确收益。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者实验未复现，仅一个模型/栈、四任务选择诊断、两次重复和一次候选切换；不是持续规划或所有WAM的判决。65%是非标准重规划风险示例，官方直接策略仅小幅低报。预注册/脚本未独立审计，计时次数映射与阈值校准仍有缺口。
frontier_brief.question: 更多独立episode与候选重复能否确认至少2个百分点可复现选择余量，还是只有当前噪声下的点估计？

evidence.label: 排序质量与选择余量
evidence.context: 图3，8候选、263查询状态、R=2，先执行16步后固定策略续行。价值episode95%区间[−2.49,−0.71]，oracle[−0.25,+3.40]；后者不能称确定收益上限。

evidence.label: 可分性与重复噪声
evidence.context: 表4，48状态有任意变化，20达双重复稳定分离，但置乱null预期约14.8；可靠性约0.33。动作多样不等于结果可选，20不是已证实可利用机会。

evidence.label: 真实延迟对FLOPs
evidence.context: 表1/3，A6000、bf16、batch1、eager、5去噪步；完整部署查询1.152×，耗时按表算降13.2%。不解码路径1.253×、降20.2%，均不到1.5×；裁剪只测时延未测动作质量。

evidence.label: 分配结果性质
evidence.context: 图4，初步系统项0.0045小于逐状态噪声均值0.0066；功效门槛失败，阈值校准仍待签核。不能称自适应分配已验证无效。

evidence.label: 渲染与官方结果
evidence.context: 表2，四个已出现故障任务，8/200损坏；全1200条协议损坏8/1200、外推修复约+0.25pp。非标准重规划至多65%仅风险示例，官方直接策略67.1%基本不受影响。

mechanism.title: 同候选池固定续行
mechanism.text: 8候选共享结果矩阵与continuation seeds，只切换首个16步动作，后续全token基础策略；比较排序质量，另估不可部署的事后余量。

mechanism.title: 按瓶颈测效率
mechanism.text: 整帧裁剪降低DiT计算，VAE编码/未来图像解码仍固定；分别直接计部署和不解码路径，CUDA Graph单forward不冒充端到端。

mechanism.title: 统计与渲染均有失效分支
mechanism.text: 功效不足报告无定论；渲染前填标记检查是否被覆盖。GL上下文修复是栈特定实现，图像完整性未证时不能将任务得分变化全归于搜索。

attention.reason: 配对续行、完整计时与模拟器哨兵可改善研究判断，但单模型少任务的负结果不能外推全部WAM；作为路线评测方法跟进。
attention.notice: 阅读优先级判断，不是科学质量定论。

impact.comparison: 配对续行、完整计时与模拟器哨兵可改善研究判断，但单模型少任务的负结果不能外推全部WAM；作为路线评测方法跟进。

passages.section: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
passages.location: Concertina: Embodying Manipulation and Cognition in One Diffusion Vision-Language Model
passages.text: Most vision-language-action (VLA) policies decouple manipulation from cognition by bolting an external action mechanism onto a vision-language model (VLM)—either quantizing actions into discrete tokens whose errors bear no stable correspondence to physical displacements, or delegating continuous trajectory generation to a separate action expert whose gradients compete with or are blocked from updating the VLM backbone. We argue that manipulation and cognition should instead be embodied in the same model, shifting from a decoupled VLA to an Embodied Vision-Language Model ( eVLM ). We introduce Concertina, an eVLM that places continuous trajectory representation, blockwise generation, and physical-coordinate supervision directly on the computation and parameter path of a shared diffusion VLM backbone. Each control timestep is encoded as one continuous latent action token in the backbone hidden space, and the shared Transformer reconstructs temporally ordered action blocks via the same corrupt-and-reconstruct operator used for multimodal pretraining. Active action projections account for only 0.21 % 0.21\% of parameters in the 4.46B model with zero separate action-generator layers, compared with 16.5 % 16.5\% – 35.1 % 35.1\% dedicated action-expert capacity in representative continuous VLAs. Using our proposed Action Interface Audit , we confirm that cross-time trajectory coupling emerges in the middle and late layers of the shared backbone rather than at the action interfaces. On standard benchmarks, Concertina achieves 98.15 % 98.15\% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9 % 85.9\% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC–D.

The premise of vision-language-action (VLA) policies is to transfer the visual perception, semantic grounding, and generalization of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to physical manipulation. Beneath specific design choices lies a foundational question: how can we enable a pretrained VLM to natively output precise continuous actions while preserving its visual-language generalization, its model architecture, and its native training paradigm? Existing VLAs largely compromise on at least one of these requirements by treating action as an external attachment to a VLM—dividing manipulation and cognition across separate representations, modules, or training objectives, where the VLM handles scene and instruction understanding while another mechanism handles action representation, trajectory generation, or coordinate supervision. Our thesis is that manipulation and cognition should not be decoupled across a bolted-on VLA pipeline; they should be embodied in a single Embodied Vision-Language Model ( eVLM ). Concretely, in an eVLM, actions are represented directly in the backbone’s continuous hidden space, generated across time by the same parameters and native generative operator that process vision and language, and supervised in physical coordinates end-to-end without degrading the shared VLM.

Three principles motivate this shift from decoupled VLAs to a unified eVLM. First, cognition should participate in manipulation at every layer. Grasping, placement, and obstacle avoidance rely on the same spatial and physical cues as scene understanding; when trajectory generation happens outside the VLM, cognition is reduced to a one-time conditioning handoff and cannot interact with evolving action states across depth. Second, manipulation should shape cognition in return. Robot trajectories are the primary source of physical and spatial grounding for a VLM; only when continuous action gradients directly update the vision-language parameters can manipulation experience consolidate into the backbone’s spatial cognition rather than remaining confined to an external head. Third, preserving the backbone’s architecture, training paradigm, and representation stability enables end-to-end scaling. When cognitive and motor modules rely on incompatible paradigms or objectives, their gradients compete and degrade pretrained representations, often forcing practitioners to insulate or freeze the backbone ( Driess et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2025 ) and permanently fixing the separation between perception and control.

From this perspective, conventional VLAs fail to form a unified eVLM in two primary ways (Table 1 ). The first is representational decoupling . Methods such as RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) and OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) quantize each action dimension into discrete bins and reuse the language vocabulary under cross-entropy loss, while FAST ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) compresses action chunks via a discrete cosine transform and byte-pair encoding. Although these methods preserve the VLM architecture and training paradigm, control is moved from physical space into symbol space: token-level cross-entropy penalizes adjacent-bin and far-bin errors equally, and compressed tokens entangle multiple timesteps and dimensions so that a single token error can corrupt an entire trajectory. The second is computational and parameter decoupling . Continuous policies such as π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) , GR00T N1 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , and X-VLA ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) preserve physical coordinates via flow matching or diffusion, but alter the model architecture and training paradigm by delegating trajectory generation to a dedicated action expert or 24-layer action Transformer outside the VLM. Because action supervision primarily updates the external expert and its competing gradients can degrade pretrained VLM features, Knowledge Insulation ( Driess et al., 2025 ) blocks expert gradients from entering the backbone—resolving training instability by hard-wiring architectural decoupling. Recent hybrids partially restore coupling along individual axes—sharing a backbone over discrete diffusion tokens ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , combining discrete and continuous branches ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , training a separate trajectory codec ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , or switching from discrete pretraining to downstream flow matching ( Ye et al., 2025 ) —yet none realizes a true eVLM that natively generates continuous physical trajectories while preserving its model architecture, its native pretraining paradigm, and its visual-language generalization.

Columns 1–2 reflect representational coupling (whether actions enter and are supervised in physical coordinates); columns 3–4 reflect computational and parameter coupling (whether the VLM backbone directly generates trajectories without a separate action Transformer, DiT, flow expert, or post-codec generator); the remaining columns summarize training and decoding structure. We instantiate this eVLM paradigm in Concertina through an end-to-end continuous latent action representation inside a diffusion VLM. Prior latent-action works (LAPA, IGOR, UniVLA, Moto, villa-X, CAT ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) ) show that mapping diverse robot controls into a shared latent space decouples embodiment-specific kinematics from sequence modeling, but they rely on separately pretrained VQ codebooks or trajectory codecs. We place this latent space directly inside the hidden space of a diffusion VLM (BARD-VL ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ): at each control timestep, a lightweight position-wise action encoder maps the complete D D -dimensional action vector into a single continuous latent action token in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} , so a horizon- H H trajectory occupies H H tokens rather than H ​ D HD scalar symbols. Vision, language, and latent action tokens are jointly contextualized across every layer of the shared Transformer, and a lightweight position-wise action decoder maps output hidden states back to physical coordinates under direct coordinate reconstruction loss.

Figure 1: Concertina (eVLM) reconstructs continuous action blocks inside a shared diffusion vision-language model. Multimodal inputs and continuous latent action tokens are jointly processed across all layers of the shared Transformer F θ F_{\theta} , combining position-wise continuous coordinate projections ( E ϕ , D ψ E_{\phi},D_{\psi} ), packed blockwise teacher forcing during training, and risk-guided blockwise reconstruction at inference. Amber tiles denote complete action vectors; dashed “M” tiles denote masked vectors.

Building on this principle, Concertina partitions the H H -step horizon into temporally ordered action blocks that are causal across blocks and bidirectional within each block, allowing contiguous action segments to be generated and refined jointly. During training, the multimodal conditioning prefix, corrupted action tokens, and teacher-forced clean action tokens are packed into a single sequence, supervising all block-conditional distributions in one forward pass and providing a compute-efficient, scalable end-to-end training path. Because the VLM backbone is already pretrained with masked block reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , Concertina reuses the exact same corrupt-and-reconstruct generative operator for continuous control without introducing a second training paradigm or external diffusion network.

To rigorously test whether a policy acts as a decoupled VLA or a true eVLM—and to localize where action representation and trajectory computation reside—we introduce the Action Interface Audit , a checkpoint-level methodology comprising three metrics aligned with the three decoupling axes: (i) Error-Geometry Consistency ( EGC = p 95 / p 05 \mathrm{EGC}=p_{95}/p_{05} ), measuring whether unit training errors map stably to physical action errors; (ii) Trajectory Coupling Attribution (TCA) via the non-local response ratio ( NLR \mathrm{NLR} ), using deterministic finite differences to localize where cross-time dependencies emerge; and (iii) Action-Specific Capacity Ratio ( ASCR \mathrm{ASCR} ), quantifying parameters dedicated solely to action generation. The audit reveals that uniform discrete bins induce a 25.14 × 25.14\times physical-error span per single-token error and FAST-style compressed tokens suffer 77.9 % 77.9\% – 82.2 % 82.2\% structural decoding failures under single-token edits; π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} derive all cross-time coupling from external action experts ( ASCR = 16.51 % \mathrm{ASCR}=16.51\% and 19.17 % 19.17\% , rising to 22.19 % 22.19\% in SmolVLA and 35.10 % 35.10\% in X-VLA); whereas Concertina’s active action interfaces occupy only 0.21 % 0.21\% of the 4.46B model, exhibit zero cross-time response on their own ( NLR = 0 \mathrm{NLR}=0 ), and delegate all temporal trajectory coupling to the middle and late layers of the shared VLM backbone ( NLR = 4.06 % \mathrm{NLR}=4.06\% in pretraining, 4.10 % 4.10\% on CALVIN, and 1.22 % 1.22\% on LIBERO). Furthermore, a matched counterfactual intervention shows that attaching a second coordinate objective to the shared hidden space induces opposing gradients (cosine − 0.891 -0.891 ) and collapses CALVIN chain length from 2.970 2.970 to 0.237 0.237 , confirming that enabling native action generation in an eVLM without degrading the shared VLM requires co-designing the action representation and its supervision objective as a unified whole. On standard closed-loop benchmarks, Concertina reaches 98.15 % 98.15\% average success on regular LIBERO, 85.9 % 85.9\% on the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, and 4.142 4.142 average completed chain length on CALVIN ABC–D (Table 2 ).
Our contributions are threefold:

Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM) Paradigm. We formulate the eVLM paradigm, embodying manipulation and cognition within a single VLM across representation, supervision, and generation so that a pretrained VLM natively generates continuous action trajectories while preserving its model architecture, native training paradigm, and visual-language generalization.

Continuous Blockwise eVLM Architecture (Concertina). We introduce Concertina, representing a horizon- H H trajectory as H H continuous latent action tokens with blockwise causal-bidirectional visibility and packed teacher forcing, requiring only 0.21 % 0.21\% active interface parameters and no external action expert, tokenizer, or codec.

Action Interface Audit and Empirical Validation. We introduce EGC, TCA ( NLR \mathrm{NLR} ), and ASCR to audit representative discrete VLAs, action-expert VLAs, and our eVLM, provide counterfactual evidence on shared-space objective design, and demonstrate state-of-the-art closed-loop performance on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus alongside strong zero-shot transfer on CALVIN ABC–D.

Several recent works learn compact latent action variables from video or robot demonstrations before policy learning. LAPA and IGOR extract discrete latent actions from action-free videos and image-goal pairs before grounding them into physical controls in a subsequent stage ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024a ) , while UniVLA ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , Moto ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , villa-X ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and CAT ( Yang et al., 2026b ) introduce task-centric codebooks, motion tokens, proprioceptive latent dynamics, or frozen trajectory codecs. Because these methods freeze the tokenizer or codec prior to policy optimization, the latent space is never shaped directly by closed-loop physical control gradients. By contrast, Concertina embeds continuous actions directly into the hidden space of the diffusion VLM through lightweight position-wise projections co-trained end-to-end with the backbone under physical-coordinate reconstruction loss.

passages.section: External action experts versus shared-backbone generation.
passages.location: External action experts versus shared-backbone generation.
passages.text: Building on diffusion and flow-matching policies ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , continuous VLA architectures such as π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) , GR00T N1 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , and X-VLA ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) preserve continuous control coordinates by pairing a VLM with a dedicated flow-matching action expert or a 24-layer external action Transformer, while OpenVLA-OFT attaches a continuous regression head ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Delegating trajectory generation to an external module separates motor computation from visual-language reasoning and introduces cross-module gradient tension; Knowledge Insulation ( Driess et al., 2025 ) addresses the resulting backbone degradation by blocking expert gradients from updating the VLM, permanently fixing the division between perception and control. Concertina eliminates the external action generator altogether, executing trajectory reconstruction inside the shared VLM Transformer so that manipulation and cognition co-adapt along a single parameter path.

A third paradigm represents robot controls as discrete symbols over the language vocabulary. RT-2 and OpenVLA quantize each action coordinate into uniform bins ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) ; FAST compresses action chunks via a discrete cosine transform and byte-pair encoding ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) ; OAT learns ordered discrete action tokens ( Liu et al., 2026 ) ; and Discrete Diffusion VLA, MMaDA-VLA, and LLaDA-VLA apply masked discrete diffusion over quantized action tokens ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Wen et al., 2025 ) . Operating in symbol space decouples the training loss from physical error geometry: cross-entropy penalizes near-miss and large-displacement bin errors equally, while frequency-compressed tokens entangle multiple timesteps so that a single token error can invalidate an entire action chunk. Concertina retains token-level sequence length 𝒪 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{O}(H) while supervising every token directly in normalized physical coordinates.

Figure 2: From decoupled VLAs to an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM). Comparison of four architectural routes to robot manipulation: (A) OpenVLA quantizes coordinates into discrete vocabulary tokens (language-objective VLA); (B) π 0 \pi_{0} delegates continuous trajectory generation to a separate flow-matching action expert (separate-objective VLA); (C) Dream-VLA retains a shared diffusion VLM backbone but switches to a flow-matching objective for continuous control (switched-objective VLA); (D) Concertina instantiates an eVLM that preserves both the shared diffusion VLM backbone and its native masked block reconstruction operator over continuous latent action tokens.

Blockwise diffusion models combine causal ordering across blocks with parallel bidirectional denoising within each block. BARD-VL bridges autoregressive and diffusion vision-language modeling via progressive block merging and stage-wise distillation over packed clean and corrupted sequences ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Recent VLA adaptations apply block diffusion to discretized action bins ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , combine autoregressive and continuous diffusion branches ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , or switch from discrete masked pretraining to downstream flow matching ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Concertina instead generalizes masked block reconstruction directly to continuous latent action vectors, turning the diffusion VLM itself into an eVLM that preserves both its shared backbone and its native pretraining operator (Figure 2 ).

Concertina instantiates an Embodied Vision-Language Model (eVLM) that embodies manipulation and cognition within a single diffusion vision-language model, enabling the pretrained backbone to natively generate continuous action trajectories without altering its model architecture or training paradigm. Its atomic generation unit is one complete continuous action vector at one control timestep, represented as a continuous latent action token: a lightweight position-wise encoder maps it into the VLM hidden space, and a position-wise decoder maps the contextualized hidden state back to physical control coordinates. All cross-time and cross-modal dependencies are modeled by the shared Transformer F θ F_{\theta} without an external action expert or discrete action tokenizer. This design establishes two direct coupling pathways between cognition and control: in the forward pass , action tokens attend to visual and linguistic representations at every Transformer layer rather than receiving a one-time conditioning summary; in the backward pass , physical-coordinate reconstruction gradients update the shared vision-language parameters end-to-end, consolidating manipulation experience into the backbone’s spatial representations.

We evaluate Concertina across three questions: (i) how a single shared diffusion VLM performs on standard closed-loop manipulation benchmarks (Section 4.2 ); (ii) how blockwise partition topology, pretraining coordinate weighting, and shared-space objective design govern closed-loop control (Sections 4.3 – 4.4 ); and (iii) where trajectory representation, temporal coupling, and parameter capacity reside across VLA families under our Action Interface Audit (Section 4.5 ). Appendix B provides complete training recipes, inference configurations, and additional evaluations on decoding budgets, replanning frequency, and representation stress tests.

Our main benchmark evaluation covers regular LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC–D ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Mees et al., 2021 ) . Regular LIBERO evaluates 50 episodes per task across four suites (LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, LIBERO-Goal, and LIBERO-10; 2,000 episodes total); LIBERO-Plus evaluates all 10,030 perturbed tasks across the four suites; CALVIN ABC–D evaluates all 1,000 official five-task instruction chains in the unseen environment D after training on environments A, B, and C. We report success rate (%) on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and average completed chain length (AvgLen) alongside task- k k chain success rates (SR@ k k ) on CALVIN.

Multi-embodiment pretraining (60,000 updates followed by a 30,000-update continuation on the 80.2M-frame mixture) and CALVIN finetuning (5,000 updates) use eight GPUs with global batch size 1,536 (192 per GPU), while regular-LIBERO finetuning uses eight GPUs with global batch size 448 (56 per GPU). Appendix B.1 documents the dataset mixture, training stages, and inference hyperparameters.

Table 2 compares Concertina against representative discrete, action-expert, and diffusion-based VLA policies across regular LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN ABC–D. On regular LIBERO, Concertina achieves 99.0 % 99.0\% on Spatial, 100.0 % 100.0\% on Object, 98.8 % 98.8\% on Goal, and 94.8 % 94.8\% on LIBERO-10, reaching an overall average of 98.15 % \mathbf{98.15\%} across 2,000 episodes—the highest average among all compared methods, outperforming continuous action-expert policies such as π 0 \pi_{0} ( 94.2 % 94.2\% ), π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( 97.5 % 97.5\% ), and X-VLA ( 98.1 % 98.1\% ), as well as discrete and hybrid diffusion policies including Discrete Diffusion VLA ( 96.4 % 96.4\% ) and Dream-VLA ( 97.2 % 97.2\% ). On the 10,030-task LIBERO-Plus benchmark, Concertina attains the highest score on every suite— 87.7 % 87.7\% on Spatial (2,106/2,402), 88.0 % 88.0\% on Object (2,216/2,518), 83.0 % 83.0\% on Goal (2,150/2,591), and 85.1 % 85.1\% on LIBERO-10 (2,143/2,519)—yielding 85.9 % \mathbf{85.9\%} (8,615/10,030) overall and surpassing EFFVLA ( 79.8 % 79.8\% ) by + 6.1 +6.1 percentage points and OpenVLA-OFT ( 69.6 % 69.6\% ) by + 16.3 +16.3 points. On the zero-shot environment-transfer benchmark CALVIN ABC–D, Concertina reaches an average completed chain length of 4.142 4.142 across 1,000 chains, achieving 98.6 % 98.6\% SR@1 and 93.8 % 93.8\% SR@2 (second-best overall and higher than X-VLA’s 97.1 % 97.1\% SR@1 and 92.6 % 92.6\% SR@2) while outperforming the shared-backbone diffusion policy LLaDA-VLA ( 4.01 4.01 AvgLen, 95.6 % 95.6\% SR@1) across all chain lengths.

passages.section: Block partition and physical action coherence.
passages.location: Block partition and physical action coherence.
passages.text: To examine how intra-block bidirectional context and inter-block causality affect policy learning, we first conduct a controlled ablation at a fixed horizon of H = 50 H=50 , varying the partition from ten blocks of five ( M = 10 , K = 5 M=10,K=5 ) to five blocks of ten ( M = 5 , K = 10 M=5,K=10 ) under identical pretraining and downstream finetuning budgets (2,400 finetuning updates on LIBERO and 2,600 on CALVIN), and evaluating on 200 regular-LIBERO episodes (40 tasks × \times 5 episodes) and all 1,000 official CALVIN ABC–D sequences. Enlarging each block from K = 5 K=5 to K = 10 K=10 substantially improves closed-loop control across every suite and chain depth (Figure 3 a,c). On regular LIBERO, the five-blocks-of-ten ( M = 5 , K = 10 M=5,K=10 ) layout reaches 73.0 % 73.0\% (146/200) compared with 38.5 % 38.5\% (77/200) for ten blocks of five ( M = 10 , K = 5 M=10,K=5 )—raising Spatial from 50 % 50\% to 82 % 82\% , Object from 62 % 62\% to 100 % 100\% , Goal from 24 % 24\% to 54 % 54\% , and LIBERO-10 from 18 % 18\% to 56 % 56\% ( + 34.5 +34.5 percentage points overall, with 32 of 40 tasks improving, seven tying, and only one declining). On CALVIN ABC–D, average completed chain length rises 35 × 35\times from 0.055 0.055 to 1.945 1.945 , SR@1 jumps from 5.1 % 5.1\% to 78.2 % 78.2\% , and SR@5 rises from 0 % 0\% to 11.7 % 11.7\% . Replacing uniform visible substitution with Gaussian corruption at M = 10 , K = 5 M=10,K=5 leaves LIBERO success unchanged at 38.5 % 38.5\% (CALVIN AvgLen 0.147 0.147 ), while extending the horizon to H = 100 H=100 with twenty blocks of five ( M = 20 , K = 5 M=20,K=5 ) reduces valid unpadded trajectory starts ( 12.5 % 12.5\% on LIBERO, 0.115 0.115 on CALVIN). Moreover, holding the M = 5 , K = 10 M=5,K=10 partition fixed on CALVIN (Figure 3 c), adding inverse- t t loss weighting (Equation 7 ) lifts three-state mixed corruption from 1.333 1.333 to 1.701 1.701 AvgLen ( + 13.6 ​ pp +13.6\text{ pp} SR@1), and switching to mask-only inverse- t t reconstruction further raises performance to 2.087 \mathbf{2.087} AvgLen ( 81.9 % 81.9\% SR@1, 12.5 % 12.5\% SR@5).

passages.section: Multi-block pretraining and receding-horizon closed-loop execution.
passages.location: Multi-block pretraining and receding-horizon closed-loop execution.
passages.text: Multi-block packed training ( M > 1 , K = 10 M>1,K=10 ) and receding-horizon closed-loop control play complementary roles across pretraining and deployment. During pretraining, supervising multiple consecutive blocks in a single packed forward pass requires the shared VLM backbone to model cross-block phase transitions and longer-horizon task progression. During closed-loop control, the robot executes one coherent K = 10 K=10 action block ( H exec = 10 H_{\mathrm{exec}}=10 , corresponding to 0.33 ​ s 0.33\text{\,s} at 30 ​ Hz 30\text{\,Hz} ) before incorporating fresh visual observations. As shown in Table 4 , aligning the downstream finetuning horizon directly with this executed K = 10 K=10 block concentrates gradient updates on the active control segment, raising CALVIN AvgLen from 3.535 3.535 ( H = 50 H=50 ) to 3.768 3.768 ( H = 20 , H exec = 20 H=20,H_{\mathrm{exec}}=20 ), 3.924 3.924 ( H = 20 , H exec = 10 H=20,H_{\mathrm{exec}}=10 ), and 4.135 \mathbf{4.135} at H = 10 , H exec = 10 H=10,H_{\mathrm{exec}}=10 ( 98.7 % 98.7\% SR@1, 64.2 % 64.2\% SR@5). At the same time, multi-block context remains vital during pretraining: continuing pretraining for 30,000 updates with two-block H = 20 ​ ( M = 2 , K = 10 ) H=20\ (M=2,K=10) reaches 4.142 \mathbf{4.142} AvgLen ( 64.9 % 64.9\% SR@5), outperforming a 40,000-update single-block H = 10 ​ ( M = 1 , K = 10 ) H=10\ (M=1,K=10) continuation ( 3.786 3.786 and 3.934 3.934 ) by + 0.208 \mathbf{+0.208} AvgLen (95% paired bootstrap CI [ + 0.119 , + 0.298 ] [+0.119,+0.298] , + 6.6 ​ pp +6.6\text{ pp} SR@5). Multi-block pretraining thus endows the shared backbone with multi-phase dynamical representations that directly strengthen single-block closed-loop execution.

passages.location: 4.4 Co-Design of Action Representation and Objective in the Shared Hidden Space
passages.text: Figure 4: Co-design of action representation and supervision objective in the shared hidden space. (a) Shared-hidden gradient cosine between the main relative-action objective and auxiliary absolute-action objective across eight fixed windows is − 0.891 -0.891 ( 99 % 99\% of action slots < 0 <0 ), reducing combined-vs-main alignment to + 0.474 +0.474 (auxiliary/main norm ratio 0.88 × 0.88\times ). (b) Layerwise parameter update divergence across all 26 active Transformer layers (L2–L27): while relative update norm Δ ​ W / W \Delta W/W rises from 4.6 % 4.6\% to 9.3 % 9.3\% with identical overall magnitude ( 1.003 × 1.003\times ), the parameter update direction cosine plunges from 0.604 0.604 at Layer 2 to 0.138 0.138 at Layer 22 (pooled cosine 0.225 0.225 ). (c) Resulting readout degradation ( 5.12 × 5.12\times teacher action loss, 2.47 × 2.47\times position error, 1.60 × 1.60\times normalized MAE) and 92.0 % 92.0\% closed-loop CALVIN collapse ( 2.970 → 0.237 2.970\rightarrow 0.237 ). (d) Complete 2 × 2 × 2 2\times 2\times 2 factorial co-design across 8,000 CALVIN chains on 4.46B BARD-VL-B4, showing consistent gains from probability-valued gripper BCE ( + 0.427 +0.427 AvgLen) and trainable action interfaces ( + 0.311 +0.311 ).

Enabling a VLM to natively output continuous actions without degrading its pretrained representations requires care: when manipulation and cognition share a single hidden space, that space is not a passive feature buffer onto which incompatible coordinate readouts can be attached in parallel. We test this principle via a matched counterfactual intervention on the 8.35B shared-backbone checkpoint ( H = 25 H=25 ) that holds every model and optimization setting identical except for the supervision target: the single-objective baseline supervises relative actions alone, whereas the dual-objective variant attaches a frozen auxiliary decoder supervising absolute actions at loss weight 0.5 0.5 , with all 21/21 main action-interface tensors initialized bitwise identically from pretraining.

Attaching the second coordinate target induces severe gradient conflict directly on the shared backbone hidden states (Figure 4 a–c). Across eight fixed CALVIN windows, the pooled cosine similarity between the relative main gradient and absolute auxiliary gradient on the shared hidden state is − 0.891 -0.891 , with 99 % 99\% of individual action-token gradients pointing in opposing directions. Even at weight 0.5 0.5 , the auxiliary gradient norm is 0.881 × 0.881\times the main gradient norm, reducing the cosine alignment between the combined gradient and the main objective to 0.474 0.474 . Inspecting the resulting parameter updates across all 26 trainable Transformer layers (Figure 4 b) reveals that while both runs make updates of virtually identical magnitude (relative L 2 L_{2} update norm rising from 4.6 % 4.6\% in shallow layers to 9.3 % 9.3\% in layers 17–22; overall norm ratio 1.003 × 1.003\times ), the parameter update direction cosine drops from 0.604 0.604 at Layer 2 down to 0.138 \mathbf{0.138} at Layer 22 (pooled cosine 0.225 0.225 )—precisely the middle and late layers where trajectory coupling resides. Consequently, teacher-forced main loss increases 5.12 × 5.12\times , one-pass position error increases 2.47 × 2.47\times , normalized MAE increases 1.60 × 1.60\times , and closed-loop CALVIN chain length drops by 92.0 % 92.0\% from 2.970 2.970 to 0.237 0.237 across 1,000 sequences (Figure 4 c). In a unified model, the action coordinate representation and its supervision objective jointly define the optimization geometry of the shared VLM backbone and must be co-designed as a single coherent interface.

passages.section: (i) Error-Geometry Consistency (EGC) and Latent Manifold Rank: Representational Coupling.
passages.location: (i) Error-Geometry Consistency (EGC) and Latent Manifold Rank: Representational Coupling.
passages.text: Fixing a unit training-event error (one token substitution for discrete tokenizers; a unit coordinate error for continuous heads), we measure the resulting physical action error distribution on 512 contiguous CALVIN windows ( H = 30 , D = 7 H=30,D=7 ) and define EGC = p 95 / p 05 \mathrm{EGC}=p_{95}/p_{05} . While continuous coordinate supervision guarantees EGC = 1 \mathrm{EGC}=1 by construction, 256-bin uniform quantization ( Kim et al., 2024 ) yields p 05 = 0.0549 p_{05}=0.0549 and p 95 = 1.3804 p_{95}=1.3804 , an error-geometry span of EGC = 25.14 × \mathrm{EGC}=25.14\times ( 25.57 × 25.57\times on an expanded 8,192-window sample) because cross-entropy penalizes adjacent and distant bin errors identically. For compressed frequency-domain tokenizers, single-token substitutions break sequence decodability in 82.23 % 82.23\% of windows for FAST+ ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) and 77.93 % 77.93\% for repaired MolmoAct2-FAST, and shape-valid edits perturb a median of 30 / 30 30/30 timesteps across the entire window (Figure 5 a). Conversely, auditing the local Jacobian ∂ E ϕ ​ ( a ) / ∂ a ∈ ℝ 2560 × 20 \partial E_{\phi}(a)/\partial a\in\mathbb{R}^{2560\times 20} of Concertina’s continuous action encoder across pretraining checkpoints confirms that E ϕ E_{\phi} embeds actions as a smooth, non-collapsed 20D chart inside the VLM hidden space (Figure 5 b): its entropy effective rank evolves from 19.78 / 20 19.78/20 at initialization to 19.30 19.30 , 18.90 18.90 , and 18.63 / 20 18.63/20 at 5 ​ k 5\text{k} , 10 ​ k 10\text{k} , and 15 ​ k 15\text{k} updates (median condition number 1.73 → 3.22 1.73\rightarrow 3.22 ), while retaining a 0.855 0.855 – 0.931 0.931 pairwise distance Spearman correlation with physical coordinates.
