(1)

Having pretrained the action prior from privileged RL rollouts, we next adapt it to downstream visual observations, where privileged task information is unavailable. We learn a visual conditioning module from limited demonstrations while keeping the pretrained action decoder fixed. Specifically, an image encoder E vis E_{\mathrm{vis}} , instantiated with DINOv2 ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , encodes the visual history as 𝑭 t = E vis ​ ( ℐ t ) {\bm{F}}_{t}=E_{\mathrm{vis}}(\mathcal{I}_{t}) . We keep the pretrained action decoder v θ v_{\theta} fixed and train the visual pathway on 𝒟 vis \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{vis}} using the same flow-matching objective in Equation 1 . The action loss provides the only supervision; no privileged-state labels or pretrained latent targets are required.

We consider two interfaces for conditioning the pretrained action prior from visual observations. In latent transfer , a visual Q-Former Q ϕ Q_{\phi} maps image features directly to the decoder context,
𝒁 t latent = Q ϕ ​ ( 𝑭 t ) ∈ ℝ M × d . {\bm{Z}}_{t}^{\mathrm{latent}}=Q_{\phi}({\bm{F}}_{t})\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d}.

This replaces the pretrained state tokenizer and state Q-Former, while preserving the action decoder and its proprioceptive conditioning pathway. We optimize E vis E_{\mathrm{vis}} and Q ϕ Q_{\phi} with 𝒁 t = 𝒁 t latent {\bm{Z}}_{t}={\bm{Z}}_{t}^{\mathrm{latent}} .

In explicit transfer , a bridge B ρ B_{\rho} first maps visual features to a privileged-shaped history, 𝒫 ^ t = B ρ ​ ( 𝑭 t ) \widehat{\mathcal{P}}_{t}=B_{\rho}({\bm{F}}_{t}) , which is then processed by the pretrained state encoder. The two interfaces are therefore

𝒁 t latent = Q ϕ ​ ( 𝑭 t ) , 𝒁 t explicit = Q ψ ​ ( T η ​ ( 𝒫 ^ t ) ) . {\bm{Z}}_{t}^{\mathrm{latent}}=Q_{\phi}({\bm{F}}_{t}),\qquad{\bm{Z}}_{t}^{\mathrm{explicit}}=Q_{\psi}\!\left(T_{\eta}(\widehat{\mathcal{P}}_{t})\right). (2)
For explicit transfer, we freeze T η T_{\eta} , Q ψ Q_{\psi} , and v θ v_{\theta} , and optimize only E vis E_{\mathrm{vis}} and B ρ B_{\rho} .

Many bimanual manipulation tasks build on dexterous skills that are already required at the single-arm level, which motivates reusing the pretrained single-arm RL prior for both arms, while learning the additional inter-arm coordination from bimanual demonstrations. Rather than introducing a separate bimanual action decoder, we retain the shared single-arm decoder and extend its visual conditioning to produce coordinated, arm-specific contexts.

Specifically, as shown in Figure 1 , we assign M M queries to each arm and process the two query groups jointly with the visual Q-Former. Self-attention between the groups allows each arm’s context to incorporate information from the other arm before action generation. The resulting contexts 𝒁 t L {\bm{Z}}_{t}^{L} and 𝒁 t R {\bm{Z}}_{t}^{R} are paired with the corresponding proprioceptive histories ℛ t L \mathcal{R}_{t}^{L} and ℛ t R \mathcal{R}_{t}^{R} . The same frozen decoder v θ v_{\theta} processes the two context–proprioception pairs separately to generate arm–hand actions for the left and right arms, respectively. Thus, both arms reuse the action-generation and proprioceptive processing learned during privileged pretraining, while cross-arm coordination is introduced through the jointly inferred visual contexts.

We first evaluate whether the pretrained action prior improves visual-demonstration efficiency across downstream dexterous manipulation tasks. We then compare latent transfer, which maps visual features directly to decoder context tokens, with explicit transfer, which conditions the decoder through the pretrained state encoder, in terms of adaptation performance and training stability. Next, we examine the effects of fine-tuning the image encoder E vis E_{\mathrm{vis}} and the action decoder v θ v_{\theta} . Finally, we investigate what control behaviors and physical information are retained from large-scale RL training after visual adaptation, using mass-variation tests and contact-force probes.

We conduct the experiments in MuJoCo Warp (MJWarp) ( Google DeepMind and NVIDIA, n.d. ) using KUKA iiwa arms equipped with SHARPA dexterous hands. Figure 2 shows the pretraining task (Section 3.2 ) and three downstream tasks.

Figure 2: Pretraining and downstream tasks. Left: the pretraining task of target pose alignment with varied procedural objects; the inset shows example object templates. Right: the downstream tasks of target pose alignment with a held-out brush, door lifting, and bimanual assembly (left to right). The same pretrained action decoder is reused for visual adaptation across all three downstream tasks.

Pretraining. Following the SimToolReal experimental setup ( Kedia et al., 2026 ) , a single arm–hand system reorients procedural object templates with randomized shapes, sizes, and densities to target poses. We measure translation and orientation error using four corresponding keypoints from the clean object and target poses: d max = max j ∈ { 1 , … , 4 } ⁡ ‖ 𝐤 j obj − 𝐤 j goal ‖ 2 d_{\max}=\max_{j\in\{1,\ldots,4\}}\|\mathbf{k}_{j}^{\mathrm{obj}}-\mathbf{k}_{j}^{\mathrm{goal}}\|_{2} . Success requires d max ≤ ϵ = 0.015 d_{\max}\leq\epsilon=0.015 m on 10 policy steps, not necessarily consecutive (Figure 3 ).

Downstream tasks. (1) In target pose alignment , the robot grasps a blue brush excluded from pretraining and aligns it with a target pose. We use the same keypoint criterion and report strict ( ϵ = 0.015 \epsilon=0.015 m) and relaxed ( ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 m) success rates. (2) In door lifting , the robot lifts a door to reveal a cube behind it. We randomize the cube’s height, color, and size, as well as the door’s position and orientation. Success requires lifting the door above the cube’s height. (3) In bimanual assembly , two arm–hand systems grasp separate objects from a tabletop, reorient them in hand, and insert a cubic protrusion on one object into a matching cavity in the other. We randomize the objects’ masses and sizes, as well as the cavity size. Success requires full insertion, measured by insertion depth relative to cavity depth. Blue-brush alignment evaluates transfer to an unseen object within the pretraining task, whereas door lifting and bimanual assembly evaluate transfer to different tasks.

We fine-tune the released SimToolReal teacher checkpoint ( Kedia et al., 2026 ) on procedural target pose alignment and collect 100,000 successful rollouts for 𝒟 RL \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RL}} . We train a separate SAPG policy ( Singla et al., 2024 ) for each downstream task and collect its a small amount rollouts for 𝒟 vis \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{vis}} . Table 3 shows the dataset details. Unless otherwise noted, we use latent transfer (Section 3.3 ) with DINOv2-Small (ViT-S/14) as E vis E_{\mathrm{vis}} and reuse the same pretrained action decoder across downstream tasks.
Figure 3: Target pose alignment success criterion.
Table 1: Datasets for privileged pretraining and visual adaptation. F: front; S: side; H: in-hand (L/R: left/right).

Dataset Episodes Arm–hand systems Images Privileged information Pretraining 100,000 single – Yes Target pose alignment 4,000 single F, S, H No Door lift 500 single F, S, H No Bimanual assembly 5,000 bimanual F, H L , H R No

We compare our method with (1) full-parameter fine-tuning of the vision-language-action models π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and GR00T N1.7 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) ; (2) a scratch baseline that uses the same visual policy architecture without the pretrained action prior; and (3) explicit transfer, as defined in Section 3.3 .

For the main comparisons, we fine-tune GR00T N1.7 and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} for 30,000 optimization steps using their officially recommended fine-tuning hyperparameters. We train our policy for 100,000 steps. For all methods, we save checkpoints every 5,000 steps and retain the final five for evaluation. We evaluate these checkpoints on held-out environment configurations, which means environment seeds distinct from those used for dataset generation. Each checkpoint is evaluated over 256 policy rollouts. Following prior work ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) , we report the highest success rate among the five evaluated checkpoints for each run. Unless otherwise noted, we use three training seeds and report the mean and standard deviation of these per-run maximum success rates. The training seeds control demonstration subsampling and the PyTorch random-number generator such as the initialization of newly introduced parameters.

passages.section: 4.2 Latent RL Prior Enables Data-Efficient Visual Adaptation
passages.location: 4.2 Latent RL Prior Enables Data-Efficient Visual Adaptation
passages.text: Figure 4: Comparison with full-parameter fine-tuning of GR00T N1.7 and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across demonstration budgets. (a) Target pose alignment at strict ( ϵ = 0.015 \epsilon=0.015 m) and relaxed ( ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 m) thresholds; (b) door lifting; (c) bimanual assembly. We report average success rate and standard deviation across three random seeds.

As shown in Figure 4 , our method achieves higher success rates than GR00T N1.7 and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with limited visual demonstrations across all three tasks. The advantage is particularly pronounced in the low-data regime. On door lifting, our method trained with only 50 demonstrations outperforms both VLA baselines trained on the full 500-demonstration dataset, using 10 × 10\times fewer demonstrations. On bimanual assembly, it likewise surpasses both full-data baselines with 1,000, a 5 × 5\times reduction. For target pose alignment, under the strict 0.015 0.015 -m criterion, our method maintains an advantage across demonstration budgets, consistent with the pretrained RL prior retaining control capabilities useful for precise alignment. Under the relaxed 0.05 0.05 -m criterion, the advantage remains clear in the low-data regime but narrows as more demonstrations become available, with performance becoming numerically comparable to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} at 4,000 demonstrations. Overall, these results indicate that the RL prior is most beneficial when visual demonstrations are scarce or when the task demands precise control.

Figure 5: Target pose-alignment ablations with the action decoder frozen for both latent-transfer variants. Results show mean success rates and standard deviations over three random seeds, except for explicit transfer, which uses five seeds.

passages.section: Contribution of the pretrained RL prior.
passages.location: Contribution of the pretrained RL prior.
passages.text: To isolate the contribution of the pretrained RL prior, we compare latent transfer with training from scratch using the same visual policy architecture and training setup. As shown in Figure 5 , latent transfer with the image encoder frozen consistently achieves higher success rates than the from-scratch baseline across the evaluated demonstration budgets and success thresholds. Since the visual encoder remains fixed, these gains cannot be explained by improved visual representation learning during adaptation. The results therefore support that reusing the pretrained RL action prior substantially improves learning from limited visual demonstrations, providing a key source of the data efficiency observed in our method.

passages.section: 4.3 Latent Transfer Is More Effective under Action-Only Supervision
passages.location: 4.3 Latent Transfer Is More Effective under Action-Only Supervision
passages.text: We compare latent and explicit transfer under action-only supervision, considering both adaptation performance and training stability.

As shown in Figure 5 , latent transfer achieves substantially higher target pose-alignment success than explicit transfer across the evaluated demonstration budgets under both the strict and relaxed success criteria (note that the image encoder is frozen). These results favor latent transfer for visual adaptation under action-only supervision. Interestingly, under the strict 0.015 0.015 -m criterion, explicit transfer still outperforms training from scratch across most demonstration budgets, suggesting that the pretrained RL prior retains useful capabilities for precise manipulation even when accessed through the explicit interface. Under the relaxed 0.05 0.05 -m criterion, however, explicit transfer performs similarly to the from-scratch baseline for much of the data range, with a clearer advantage only in the low-data regime. This pattern is consistent with the results in Section 4.2 , where the benefit of the RL prior is most pronounced with limited demonstrations and under stricter precision requirements. More importantly, the substantially stronger and more consistent performance of latent transfer indicates that effectively reusing the RL prior depends not only on its presence, but also on how visual observations interface with the pretrained controller.

As shown in Figure 6 , with the image encoder frozen, latent transfer exhibits rapid performance improvement together with relatively consistent learning trajectories across random seeds. In contrast, explicit transfer shows greater run-to-run variability, while training from scratch is comparatively stable but converges to lower performance. Thus, latent transfer combines consistent learning with stronger performance.

Figure 6: Training stability on target pose alignment at a relaxed ( ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 m) threshold. Dotted curves show individual runs for latent transfer, explicit transfer, and scratch training; shaded regions show the mean ± \pm one standard deviation. Explicit transfer uses five random seeds, while latent transfer and scratch training use three seeds each.

passages.section: 4.4 Ablations on Visual and Action Adaptation
passages.location: 4.4 Ablations on Visual and Action Adaptation
passages.text: To examine how visual adaptation should modify the pretrained policy, we independently sweep the learning rates of the image encoder E vis E_{\mathrm{vis}} and action decoder v θ v_{\theta} , while keeping the visual Q-Former Q ϕ Q_{\phi} trainable throughout.

As shown in Figure 7 (a), with the action decoder frozen, conservative updates to the image encoder improve strict pose-alignment success across demonstration budgets, whereas larger updates degrade performance. This effect is particularly pronounced in the low-data regime: with 500 demonstrations, increasing the learning-rate scale leads to both lower mean success and greater variation across seeds, while the 1,000- and 2,000-demonstration settings are comparatively less sensitive. Under the relaxed criterion, the benefit of image-encoder adaptation is less uniform. These results suggest that limited-data adaptation benefits from small, conservative updates to the visual representation, especially when precise alignment is required.

As shown in Figure 7 (b), fine-tuning the action decoder provides no benefit across the tested learning-rate scales and demonstration budgets. Keeping the pretrained decoder frozen performs best under the strict criterion, while larger updates reduce performance. We hypothesize that fine-tuning the decoder on a much smaller downstream dataset may lead to overfitting and reduce the benefit of the control prior learned from large-scale privileged pretraining with 𝒟 RL \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{RL}} in Table 3 . These results favor keeping the action decoder frozen during visual adaptation.

Figure 7: Learning-rate ablations for (a) the image encoder with the action decoder frozen and (b) the action decoder with the image encoder frozen. Panels report strict ( ϵ = 0.015 \epsilon=0.015 m) and relaxed ( ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 m) pose-alignment success. We report average success rate and standard deviation across three random seeds. Each scale multiplies the tested module’s original learning rate; zero freezes it.

Having shown that the pretrained RL prior enables data-efficient visual adaptation, we next investigate what control behaviors and physical information from large-scale RL pretraining remain after visual adaptation. These retained properties may help explain the observed data-efficiency gains.

Figure 8: Generalization to increased object mass. (a) Target pose alignment at a relaxed ( ϵ = 0.05 \epsilon=0.05 m) thresholds. (b) Door lift. The leftmost point in each plot corresponds to the reference mass used for downstream visual training, e.g., for 𝒟 vis \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{vis}} .

RL pretraining includes randomization over object density, whereas the visual demonstrations contain only a single object mass for each task. We therefore test whether generalization to mass variation learned during RL pretraining remains after visual adaptation by evaluating the policies on increasingly heavy objects without further training (see results in Figure 8 ). For door lifting, our policy uses only 50 demonstrations compared with 500 for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ; for pose alignment, the corresponding budgets are 1,000 and 2,000. At the reference mass, the two methods achieve similar performance. As mass increases, however, our policy degrades more gradually: for example, on door lifting, it retains 32.6% success at 5.0 kg compared with 12.9% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . These results provide evidence that robustness acquired during RL pretraining can remain useful after visual adaptation.

Contact forces are central to dexterous manipulation, and large-scale interaction during privileged RL pretraining may induce representations that capture contact-related physical information. To examine whether such information is retained after visual adaptation, we probe the hidden representations of the action decoder for contact forces. Specifically, for target pose alignment, we collect a separate force-annotated dataset 𝒟 probe \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{probe}} and fit linear ridge probes to the hidden state at each decoder layer, while keeping the adapted policy frozen. We compare the RL-prior policy with the same architecture trained from scratch. As shown in Figure 9 , contact-force information is substantially more linearly decodable from the RL-prior representations: the RL-prior model achieves lower probe RMSE than the scratch model across all evaluated layers and demonstration budgets. More notably, with only 200 visual demonstrations, the RL-prior model already matches or outperforms the scratch model trained with 4,000 demonstrations across the force targets, with substantial margins on most metrics. This result suggests that large-scale privileged RL pretraining implicitly learns structured contact-related physical representations that are retained after visual adaptation, but are difficult to acquire from limited visual demonstrations alone. Such retained physical knowledge may therefore contribute to the strong data efficiency provided by the RL prior.

Figure 9: Linear contact-force probes of the visual policies. Panels predict (a) total grasp normal force, (b) per-finger normal forces, (c) per-finger tangential forces, and (d) per-finger Cartesian force vectors from each layer of the action decoder. Colors denote visual-demonstration budgets; solid and dashed curves denote the frozen pretrained and trainable scratch action decoders. Both policies fine-tune the image encoder at 0.2 × 0.2\times its base learning rate for 100k steps. Curves average three policy seeds on the same IID probe test episodes.

Our results concern downstream visual-demonstration efficiency, not total data or compute efficiency: the method relies on a capable privileged teacher and substantial simulated experience. The frozen prior may inherit the teacher’s failure modes and restrict adaptation when new tasks require different control behaviors. All tasks use the same arm–hand system; bimanual transfer reuses the single-arm decoder and does not establish transfer to different robot morphologies. The evaluation is entirely in simulation, including visual demonstration collection, so physical-robot performance remains untested. Finally, mass robustness and force readout support the proposed interpretation but do not isolate a causal mechanism for the demonstration-efficiency gains.

We presented Latent RL Prior, a simple yet effective framework that transfers RL control behavior to visual dexterous manipulation by adapting latent conditioning around a frozen action decoder. This adaptation uses action supervision alone, without privileged information in the visual demonstrations, and sharing the decoder extends a single-arm prior to bimanual manipulation. Across three simulated tasks, the method improves visual-demonstration efficiency, surpassing the evaluated VLA baselines trained on the full task datasets with 10 × 10\times and 5 × 5\times fewer demonstrations on door lifting and bimanual assembly, respectively. Further investigations favor latent transfer over the tested explicit interface for performance and training stability, while separate adaptation studies favor conservative visual updates and a frozen decoder. Robustness to mass variation absent from visual demonstrations and greater linear accessibility of contact-force information than in policies trained from scratch provide evidence consistent with retained control knowledge. These findings support preserving RL control priors and adapting their visual interfaces for data-efficient dexterous manipulation.

We used generative AI tools to help draft and refine manuscript text based on author-provided drafts and an author-defined narrative, and to assist with coding and figure preparation. We did not use AI to propose research ideas, design experiments, or analyze or interpret results. The manuscript was reviewed by the authors, who take responsibility for the final content.
This work studies dexterous manipulation for robotics. No human data are used.

The experiment results are evaluated using at least three random seeds. The main text describes the method and experimental setup for reproducibility. We plan to publicly release the training and evaluation code and datasets.

analysis.overview: 可复用的选择是：先把特权RL教师轨迹蒸馏为动作解码器，再冻结动作与本体感觉通路，仅用动作损失训练图像到上下文的接口。直接接潜变量优于本文测试的显式状态形状接口；双臂只共享同构单臂解码器。证据支持降低下游视觉示范量，尚不支持总数据、总算力更省或真机迁移。

findings.title: 转移对象：控制先验与视觉接口分开学习
findings.text: 目标是将依赖物体和目标状态的仿真RL控制器用于图像观测任务。策略保留本体感觉历史的独立处理路径，让视觉适配主要承担任务上下文，而非重新学习全部动作生成。本文没有证明任意RL技能都可这样接入。

findings.title: 预训练：特权上下文交叉注意力，本体感觉经AdaLN输入
findings.text: 先微调已发布的SimToolReal教师，在形状、大小和密度随机化的位姿对齐任务收集100,000条成功轨迹。状态tokenizer与Q-Former生成上下文；Transformer动作token对它做交叉注意力，本体感觉历史与flow time经AdaLN进入各层。用条件flow matching拟合未来动作块，蒸馏后的解码器才是被复用的先验，不是直接冻结原始RL教师网络。

findings.title: 适配：动作损失直接训练图像到潜变量的通道
findings.text: DINOv2-Small ViT-S/14与视觉Q-Former替换特权状态编码通路，解码器和本体感觉通路冻结；视觉侧用与预训练相同的flow-matching动作目标更新。下游不需要特权状态标签、教师latent目标或与预训练配对的轨迹。显式对照先预测特权状态形状的中间历史，再穿过冻结的状态tokenizer/Q-Former；它同样仅用动作监督，不能当成有真值状态监督的感知器。

findings.title: 双臂：先联合推断上下文，再分别调用共享解码器
findings.text: 左右臂各分配M个query，两组在同一视觉Q-Former中通过自注意力交互。输出的两组上下文分别配各臂本体感觉，独立调用同一冻结单臂解码器。新增协调主要在视觉条件侧；实验是相同KUKA iiwa加SHARPA手的双臂扩展，不能写成跨形态或零样本双臂迁移。

findings.title: 主结果：10倍与5倍指下游示范预算
findings.text: 表1下游完整数据分别为对齐4,000、抬门500、双臂装配5,000条，均来自各任务单独训练的SAPG策略在仿真中采集。图4与正文对应：抬门50条超过π0.5和GR00T N1.7各500条的全参数微调；装配1,000条超过两者各5,000条。10倍/5倍只比较下游视觉示范数，不含10万条先验轨迹、教师训练或通用底座数据。

findings.title: 成功阈值：四个点全部达标，累计10个策略步
findings.text: 位姿对齐用清洁物体与目标姿态的四个对应关键点最大距离，严格阈值15mm、宽松阈值50mm，须有10个达标策略步且不要求连续。它不是平均平移误差15mm或持续保持成功。图4在4,000条数据时严格成功率本方法仅约31%（目视近似）；宽松约55%，与π0.5数值接近。抬门以超过立方体高度为成功，装配以完全插入及相对腔深衡量，三任务成功口径不同。

findings.title: 同架构控制：冻结视觉后仍能从先验获益
findings.text: 图5对齐任务中，冻结图像编码器的latent-transfer版本，在各示范预算和两种阈值下整体优于同视觉策略架构从零训练。此控制排除了视觉适配期间更新图像编码器作为该部分增益的解释；但预训练轨迹与算力并未等量消除，因此不能把它解释成无额外经验的架构改进。

findings.title: 接口消融：直连latent更好，但显式对照仅限动作监督
findings.text: 图5/6固定图像编码器后，直接latent接口比经冻结状态编码器的显式接口表现更强、训练轨迹更一致；latent和scratch为3个种子，显式为5个。图5同时画了可微调视觉的橙线，不能将橙线与显式线的全部差距归因于接口。显式在严格阈值多数预算仍优于scratch，宽松时差距较小。没有带真值状态辅助监督、参数量和优化难度完全对齐的更强显式接口控制，故不能推广成显式状态表征普遍无效。

findings.title: 适配消融：小幅动视觉，冻结动作解码器
findings.text: 图7独立扫描图像编码器和动作解码器学习率，视觉Q-Former始终训练。对齐任务上，视觉低学习率有益，0.5/1.0倍尺度在图7(a)两阈值下接近失效；冻结视觉时，解码器扫描中严格阈值以冻结最好，较大更新退化。横轴是相对各模块原始学习率的比例，正文未给绝对值，不能直接复用成某个绝对学习率。过拟合是作者解释，消融本身未隔离其机制。

findings.title: 质量外推：相似起点下退化更缓慢
findings.text: 图8下游抬门训练质量为2.5kg，视觉示范预算本方法50条、π0.5为500条；测试质量升至5.0kg时，正文报告成功率32.6%对12.9%，差19.7个百分点。对齐则用1,000对2,000条，宽松50mm阈值，从0.28kg向更大质量测试。基准质量表现接近；结果支持预训练随机化鲁棒性可保留，但示范量不同，且未比较关闭密度随机化的匹配先验，尚非机制因果证明。

findings.title: 接触力探针：可读出性提高，不等于控制时估力
findings.text: 图9从冻结视觉策略的解码器各层隐藏状态拟合线性岭回归，预测总法向力、逐指法向/切向力和笛卡尔力向量。先验版本200条视觉示范的探针结果已匹配或优于scratch 4,000条；两者视觉编码器均以基准学习率0.2倍训练100k步，三策略种子、相同IID探针测试episode。力标签只用于独立分析集，不是视觉适配监督；正文没有充分披露探针样本规模、正则选择和拆分细节。更低RMSE不能证明控制策略显式估力或该表示导致示范效率增益。

findings.title: 评估与预算：每种子末五个checkpoint取最好
findings.text: VLA基线训练30,000步，本方法100,000步；每5,000步存档，末五个checkpoint各用256次留出配置rollout评估，每个训练seed取五次中的最高成功率，再跨种子报告均值与标准差。它不是固定最终checkpoint成绩或置信区间，环境seed与数据采集不同也不能自动消除选checkpoint的乐观偏差。论文未充分报告GPU型号、总GPU时、教师训练成本、完整模型尺寸及绝对学习率；不能由下游示范减少推断总数据或计算效率提高。

findings.title: 迁移边界：全仿真、同形态、先验可能限制新技能
findings.text: 所有三任务、视觉示范采集与评测均在MuJoCo Warp；蓝刷是同类预训练对齐任务的未见物体，抬门和双臂装配才测试任务转移。全部使用同样的臂手配置，双臂共享单臂先验并未证明跨机器人形态。冻结先验可能继承教师失败、限制需要新控制行为的任务。本文声明计划公开代码和数据，本轮未运行实现或复现实验，也未验证真机部署。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：质量外推收益是否来自先验的密度随机化？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：冻结先验的质量外推优势主要来自RL预训练中的密度随机化。先只做抬门，在相同形状和尺寸随机化下分别训练有/无密度随机化的教师，匹配教师训练预算，并报告参考质量成功率；各收集相同数量成功轨迹，以同架构、蒸馏步数和动作目标训练先验。下游两组固定相同50条2.5kg视觉示范、冻结解码器，仅训练相同视觉接口；至少5个匹配训练种子。在独立验证集选checkpoint后锁定，在全新测试配置测2.5/3.5/4.0/4.5/5.0kg成功率、抓取滑移/掉落和训练GPU时，给出配对差异区间。另报告参考质量任务表现以识别教师能力混淆。若有随机化先验在重物上的收益消失，或优势完全由参考质量教师表现差异解释，就推翻或缩小密度随机化解释；若两者相当则寻找视觉适配或动作先验的其他来源。实验未运行，尚未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: Latent RL Prior：冻结动作解码器，用动作损失接通视觉潜变量
frontier_brief.change_type: 训练方法 · RL先验迁移
frontier_brief.delta: 先将特权RL教师的轨迹蒸馏为flow-matching动作解码器，再冻结动作和本体感觉通路。下游只用动作监督，让DINOv2与视觉Q-Former直接产出上下文token；双臂在视觉query侧学协调，共享同一单臂解码器。
frontier_brief.before: 所测对照包括：全参数微调π0.5/GR00T N1.7；或从图像先预测特权状态形状的中间量，再经过冻结状态编码器接入动作先验。
frontier_brief.after: 图像直接接入动作解码器的潜变量上下文，替换特权状态编码通路；动作损失穿过冻结解码器训练视觉侧，不需要下游状态标签或教师latent目标。
frontier_brief.relevance: 已有高质量特权RL教师、下游视觉示范有限且动作技能相近时，可优先验证“冻结控制、适配上下文”这一路线。复现应同时保留冻结视觉、scratch和显式接口控制，先检查先验是否覆盖目标技能。
frontier_brief.caveat: 全部为同一种臂手配置的仿真实验。先验依赖10万条成功轨迹与教师训练；本方法下游100k步，对照30k步，结果还按每seed末五个checkpoint取最好。减少的是下游视觉示范，真机、跨形态、总算力节省和机制因果关系均未证实。
frontier_brief.question: 关闭先验的密度随机化后，重物泛化优势还在吗？

passages.section: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
passages.location: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
passages.text: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans—points, bounding boxes, and trajectories—to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive’s type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model’s exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25 × 25\times faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

passages.section: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
passages.location: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
passages.text: Figure 1: VFlash is a generalist decoding framework for fast, accurate visual planning across Physical AI tasks such as robotics and autonomous driving. By aligning prediction blocks with the known structure of visual primitives, it enables parallel decoding of common structured outputs such as bounding boxes, variable-length 2D/3D trajectories, and dense point motion, while retaining verified speculative decoding for text and sub-task plans. Compared with autoregressive (AR) decoding, VFlash improves accuracy on 3D robot trajectory planning while substantially reducing decoding latency across NVIDIA platforms, including Jetson Thor, DGX Spark, and H100.

Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level brains for physical AI systems, interpreting visual observations and task instructions to guide behavior in robotics and autonomous driving ( Gemini Robotics Team, 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . Their reasoning need not be expressed solely in language. VLMs can formulate intermediate predictions as visual plans: points and bounding boxes identify relevant locations or objects ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) , while trajectories describe intended motion or forecast how a scene will evolve ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Recent work uses spatial traces and visual primitives to guide action generation ( Li et al., 2025a ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . These plans make spatial goals and anticipated motion explicit before action. Each visual primitive has identifiable boundaries and an organized coordinate layout.

Generating such plans efficiently becomes increasingly important as their spatial detail grows. Longer trajectories, additional objects, and joint 2D image and 3D predictions require more coordinate tokens, which autoregressive VLMs decode sequentially ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) . For physical agents that update their plans as new observations arrive, sequential decoding limits spatial detail and update frequency under a fixed latency budget. This motivates decoding methods that can generate complete visual plans with fewer sequential forward passes while preserving their spatial accuracy.

Parallel decoding offers a promising route to reducing this sequential cost, particularly for latency-sensitive physical AI systems operating at batch size one. Existing approaches include speculative decoding with parallel verification ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025b ) and diffusion language models (dLLMs) with parallel denoising ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Arriola et al., 2025 ) . However, dLLMs often exhibit a speed–quality trade-off relative to autoregressive models ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . DFlash combines these approaches using a lightweight block diffusion draft model to predict draft tokens in a single forward pass, followed by target verification that preserves the autoregressive model’s output distribution ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . For visual outputs, LocateAnything exploits spatial structure through parallel box decoding ( Wang et al., 2026 ) .

In this work, we introduce VFlash , a generalist decoding framework for physical AI (Figure 1 ) that accommodates both text (e.g., sub-task plans) and diverse visual primitives, such as bounding boxes, variable-length trajectories, and dense 3D motion predictions. Our study reveals an interesting observation: a lightweight diffusion drafter can even surpass its autoregressive target in spatial accuracy of the visual plans while decoding much faster. The structure of visual primitives helps explain this finding: once a primitive’s type, dimensionality, and length are specified, its boundaries and coordinate layout are known. Aligning draft blocks with these boundaries allows an entire geometric object to be predicted jointly, with tens to hundreds of tokens decoded in a single forward pass. These observations motivate aligning training and decoding with complete primitive boundaries and directly accepting structurally valid drafts without requiring token-level agreement with the target, while retaining verified decoding for text.

At the center of VFlash is Flash Primitive Decoding (FPD), which uses the requested output structure to organize both drafter training and inference. A tool call specifies the size of a variable-length prediction, while the primitive type determines its coordinate layout. Conditioned on features from a frozen target VLM, a lightweight diffusion drafter learns to predict complete primitives from annotated spatial data. At inference, the decoder applies layout-specific constraints ( Willard and Louf, 2023 ; Geng et al., 2023 ) and accepts valid primitives in full. The target VLM supplies context for subsequent predictions, and ordinary text retains speculative decoding with target verification.

We evaluate VFlash on 2D and 3D robot trajectories, bounding boxes, and dense 3D point motion forecasting, and study its use in downstream manipulation and driving. VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to its autoregressive target across the evaluated robot trajectory tasks. In the downstream robot manipulation pipeline shown in Figure 1 , it reduces inference latency by about 80% on both Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. These visual plans also provide useful conditioning for action models: on MolmoSpaces ( Kim et al., 2026b ) , a world action model ( Ye et al., 2026 ; NVIDIA, 2026c ) conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

Beyond acceleration, our work suggests a broader role for parallel decoding in multimodal systems. Lossless speculative decoding preserves the autoregressive target’s output distribution ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023a ) , whereas structured visual planning instead permits predictions to be judged by their spatial accuracy and usefulness for action, in the spirit of relaxed acceptance criteria ( Bachmann et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . VFlash enables a System-1 mode ( Kahneman, 2011 ) of visual planning in VLMs, producing fast, structured spatial predictions through joint coordinate decoding. This perspective interestingly connects to recent System-1 models such as Jev, which emphasize fast, typed decisions ( Almeida, 2026 ; Yu and Yao, 2026 ) . VFlash brings this perspective to complete geometric predictions, exploiting structure within each primitive. The resulting gains in both speed and spatial accuracy suggest that autoregressive decoding need not define the quality ceiling for visual outputs.
This section presents the generalist decoding framework of VFlash for physical AI, covering both the preliminaries of DFlash and the detailed design of Flash Primitive Decoding (Figure 2 ).
In speculative decoding, a draft model q ϕ q_{\phi} proposes γ \gamma tokens that the target model p θ p_{\theta} verifies in parallel, giving an average per-token latency of
L = T draft + T verify τ , L=\frac{T_{\mathrm{draft}}+T_{\mathrm{verify}}}{\tau}, (1)

where τ \tau is the expected number of tokens accepted per cycle ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . DFlash reduces the numerator with a lightweight block diffusion drafter. Features H θ ​ ( x ) H_{\theta}(x) from selected target layers are fused and injected as keys and values into each draft layer. Given a start token a 0 a_{0} , the drafter predicts γ \gamma masked tokens in one bidirectional forward pass, yielding T draft = t par ≪ γ ​ t step T_{\mathrm{draft}}=t_{\mathrm{par}}\ll\gamma\,t_{\mathrm{step}} , where t step t_{\mathrm{step}} is the sequential drafting cost per token. Longer drafts, however, need not increase τ \tau : greedy verification accepts tokens only up to the first mismatch with the target:

τ ver = 1 + max ⁡ { k ≤ γ : a j = arg ​ max v ⁡ p θ ​ ( v ∣ x , a < j ) ​ for all ​ j ≤ k } . \tau_{\mathrm{ver}}=1+\max\Big\{k\leq\gamma:\;a_{j}=\argmax_{v}\,p_{\theta}\!\left(v\mid x,a_{<j}\right)\ \text{for all}\ j\leq k\Big\}. (2)

τ ver \tau_{\mathrm{ver}} often saturates well below γ \gamma . Thus enlarging a block does not necessarily enlarge its final throughput. For text generation, the goal is to preserve the target distribution ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ) via verification. But token-level agreement need not reflect spatial accuracy. VFlash retains the drafting architecture and replaces Eq. 2 with direct acceptance of structurally valid visual primitives.

Given visual observations and a task instruction, the VLM predicts spatial objects such as boxes, robot trajectories, or future point positions. Each prediction is a visual primitive with a schema s s specifying its type, coordinate dimensions, and extent. This fixes each coordinate’s role while leaving its value to be inferred from the input. A trajectory’s 2D image coordinates and 3D spatial coordinates can form one primitive and be predicted jointly. For variable-length predictions, a tool call declares the extent, which together with the primitive type determines the layout; for fixed-size predictions such as boxes, the type alone suffices. The structure is thus known before coordinate prediction, and each decoding block covers a complete primitive.

The schema defines a block of length B ⁡ ( s ) B(s) : an observed start token a 0 a_{0} followed by B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 B(s)-1 masked tokens. An autoregressive target factorizes the blocks as ∏ j p θ ​ ( a j ∣ x , a < j ) \prod_{j}p_{\theta}(a_{j}\mid x,a_{<j}) and needs B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 B(s)-1 sequential passes. Given the layout and the target context, VFlash instead predicts all positions conditionally independently,

q ϕ ( a 1 : B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 ∣ H θ ( x ) , a 0 ) = ∏ j = 1 B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 q ϕ , j ( a j ∣ H θ ( x ) , a 0 , MASK B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 ) , q_{\phi}\!\left(a_{1:B(s)-1}\mid H_{\theta}(x),a_{0}\right)=\prod_{j=1}^{B(s)-1}q_{\phi,j}\!\left(a_{j}\mid H_{\theta}(x),a_{0},\mathrm{MASK}^{B(s)-1}\right), (3)

in a single forward pass. The complete primitive is thus the unit of parallel prediction, with a speculation budget γ = B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 \gamma=B(s)-1 set by the request rather than by a fixed window. The same principle covers targets that emit coordinates as ordinary text: we align their numeric fields in a fixed-width layout and render the predictions back into the target’s text format. Appendix A gives the coordinate conventions and serialization formats of each task.

Figure 2: FPD design. A primitive-start token triggers a prediction block layout determined by the primitive type and the preceding tool calling. By adapting the prediction block to each primitive’s structure, VFlash supports different spatial formats and lengths without requiring token-level agreement with the VLM.

Visual plans often require large, variable-length draft blocks. For example, NAVSIM requires eight waypoints over four seconds, while Waymo requires twenty over five seconds. Drafting such blocks introduces challenges in format following and spatial accuracy. We find that two design principles help address these challenges:

Boundary alignment decides what is predicted together: each draft block covers one complete primitive, avoiding the splits caused by fixed-length windows. The tool call declares the block length, from which the waypoint count P P follows, and a shared layout template accommodates different lengths, allowing the whole primitive to be drafted in one pass.

Position alignment decides what each position predicts: every slot has a known role—a waypoint, axis, or delimiter—before decoding. This supports parallel prediction with a consistent layout and per-position constraints at inference.

Table 1: Primitive layouts. Each block begins with the start token a 0 a_{0} . P P denotes the number of points; ( u , v ) (u,v) and ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) denote image-plane and metric coordinates in special tokens.

Primitive Layout B-box <box> u 1 ​ v 1 ​ u 2 ​ v 2 u_{1}\,v_{1}\,u_{2}\,v_{2} </> 2D+3D traj. <2D> ( u ​ v ) × P (u\,v)\!\!\times\!\!{P} </> <3D> ( x ​ y ​ z ) × P (x\,y\,z)\!\!\times\!\!{P} </> Dense motion <Dense> t 1 ​ t 2 t_{1}t_{2} [ k ( s d 1 ⋯ d 5 ) × 3 ] × P \big[\,k\;(s\,d_{1}{\cdots}d_{5})\!\!\times\!\!{3}\,\big]\!\!\times\!\!{P} </>

Maintaining this layout requires each coordinate to occupy a fixed number of positions. Recent VLMs normalize image coordinates to 0–1,000 and write them as ordinary text ( Bai et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) ; models built around visual primitives often use special tokens ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . A special coordinate token occupies one position, whereas text tokenization can vary with the value and shift subsequent coordinates. VFlash supports both representations.

For our base model (Section 3 ), typed start and end tokens mark primitive boundaries and transitions between text and primitive decoding. Each coordinate uses one of 1,001 special tokens, allowing prediction to be restricted to its legal vocabulary. For text-tokenized targets, VFlash gives each coordinate a sign and five digit positions, with unused high-order positions filled by the mask token. This fixed-width grid preserves position roles and is rendered back into the target’s text format, whose delimiters mark block boundaries. Table 1 and Appendix A give the formats details.

We adapt an autoregressive VLM to the spatial response format with next-token supervision, then freeze it and train a shallow, non-causal drafter on its features. For an annotated block a a , we minimize the weighted cross-entropy of Eq. 3 ,

ℒ prim = − ∑ j = 1 B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 w j log q ϕ , j ( a j ∣ H θ ( x ) , a 0 , MASK B ⁡ ( s ) − 1 ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{prim}}=-\sum_{j=1}^{B(s)-1}w_{j}\log q_{\phi,j}\!\left(a_{j}\mid H_{\theta}(x),a_{0},\mathrm{MASK}^{B(s)-1}\right), (4)

with all logits computed jointly in one forward pass. Primitive positions use uniform w j w_{j} , unlike the decaying weights that favor early positions under Eq. 2 . Crucially, labels a j a_{j} come from annotated coordinates or rendered grids rather than the target’s continuation, optimizing the drafter for spatial accuracy instead of token-level agreement.

Each annotated primitive contributes one complete block. Where the response also contains text, sampled short blocks train the ordinary drafting path, so one drafter serves both the verified text path and the direct primitive path. Packed attention keeps examples and independent blocks separate while preserving attention within each primitive. Backbones, data, validity weights, and adaptation recipes are given in Appendix B .

Decoding runs 16-position DFlash blocks until a primitive-start token is accepted; the decoder then resolves the declared schema and drafts the complete block of length B ⁡ ( s ) B(s) in one pass. Per-position constraints restrict coordinates and delimiters to their legal vocabularies, and cross-position rules pair out-of-frame coordinates; both act on logits already computed and add no neural evaluation.

Let a ^ \hat{a} be the resulting prediction and A s A_{s} its acceptance test: the schema validator, plus for boxes the spatial-confidence guard of LocateAnything ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . VFlash replaces Eq. 2 with
τ dir = { B ⁡ ( s ) , A s ​ ( a ^ ) = 1 , 1 + r , otherwise , \tau_{\mathrm{dir}}=\begin{cases}B(s),&A_{s}(\hat{a})=1,\\[2.0pt] 1+r,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (5)

where the first r r draft slots are retained ( r = 0 r=0 for trajectories; for boxes, those before the first uncertain coordinate) and the rest are regenerated by constrained target AR. An accepted primitive is committed without token-level agreement; one target pass updates the cache and context features and emits the next token. Text still follows Eq. 2 ; Appendix C gives both procedures.
Substituting Eq. 5 into Eq. 1 , a valid primitive costs
L dir = t par + t target B ⁡ ( s ) , L_{\mathrm{dir}}=\frac{t_{\mathrm{par}}+t_{\mathrm{target}}}{B(s)}, (6)

against one target forward t target t_{\mathrm{target}} per coordinate under autoregressive decoding, up to prefix and continuation overhead. Both passes grow mildly with B ⁡ ( s ) B(s) , but their number does not, so a more detailed plan adds no sequential decoding steps.

Base VLM. Most experiments use a customized embodied VLM combining Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , a native-resolution MoonViT encoder ( Kimi Team, 2025 ) , and an MLP connector. It is trained progressively on general vision-language tasks, grounding ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , embodied spatial understanding, and joint 2D/3D trajectory prediction. Coordinates for bounding box and trajectory use special tokens, with 2D image coordinates normalized to 0–1,000 and 3D coordinates uniformly quantized within predefined ranges. For dense motion prediction, we use the released MolmoMotion-AR model ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , retaining its text-based coordinate representation.

Per-task training. For clean ablation studies, we fine-tune the AR target on task-specific data, then freeze it and train a five-layer VFlash drafter on the same data. For MolmoMotion, we train only the drafter on the frozen released target. Detailed per-task datasets, training mixtures, and optimization settings are provided in Appendix B .

Visual-plan conditioning. Despite differences in DiT/WAM architectures and their interfaces with the VLM, a commonality is that the action models cross-attend to VLM features encoding the generated visual plans. These features are obtained by processing VFlash’s accepted primitives with the frozen target VLM. Appendix D details the architectures and conditioning mechanisms.

Table 2: Open-loop 2D trajectory prediction. DFD, HD, and RMSE in normalized image coordinates ( ↓ \downarrow ). Reference rows are taken from prior work; Baseline (AR) and VFlash share the same 4B target and differ only in the decoder. Bold and underline mark the best and second-best values.

Table 3: Category-conditioned box generation. F1 (%, ↑ \uparrow ) and boxes per second (BPS, ↑ \uparrow ). Direct accepts every schema-valid box without verification; AR fallback regenerates boxes rejected by the spatial-confidence guard with constrained AR (Appendix F.4 ). BPS is measured separately on each dataset.

Table 4: Open-loop 3D robot trajectory prediction. ADE and FDE in meters ( ↓ \downarrow ); SR@5 and SR@10 are the fraction of waypoints within 5 cm and 10 cm ( ↑ \uparrow ). The three variants differ in what the model generate (3D only, 2D+3D) and whether wrist-camera views were added in training. All groups are evaluated with the same single-view inputs. Bold marks the best value per column.

2D trajectory prediction. On ShareRobot-Bench ( Ji et al., 2025 ) and VABench-V ( Yuan et al., 2026a ) , VFlash lowers all six errors of its AR target (Table 3 ), by 7% on HD and 3–6% on DFD and RMSE across both benchmarks. On VABench-V, VFlash cuts every error by roughly 40% relative to the best prior model, LoHo-Manip ( Liu et al., 2026b ) , with our AR target already outperforming the listed baselines; on ShareRobot-Bench, VFlash is second only to RoboBrain-2.0 ( BAAI RoboBrain Team, 2025 ) .

2D bounding box prediction. On COCO ( Lin et al., 2014 ) and Dense200 ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) , VFlash with AR fallback matches AR on mean F1 while decoding 2.6–2.8 × \times faster (Table 3 ), with higher F1 at IoU 0.50, especially on the crowded Dense200 scenes, but lower F1 at IoU 0.95. Without fallback, mean F1 drops by about 20 points on Dense200.

3D trajectory prediction. On InternA1 ( Tian et al., 2026 ) , AgiBot ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , and MolmoBot ( Deshpande et al., 2026 ) , VFlash improves all four metrics for all three target variants (Table 4 ). ADE falls by 18–49% with the 3D-only target and by 28–61% with the 2D+3D target; waypoint accuracy at 5 cm on AgiBot rises from 50% to 73% and from 40% to 74%, respectively. With joint 2D+3D outputs, AR’s 3D ADE is 15–51% higher than with 3D-only outputs, while VFlash maintains similar accuracy by predicting both segments in one parallel pass. The wrist-camera training variant further reduces VFlash’s ADE by 3–12%, with evaluation still using only the primary camera.

Dense 3D motion prediction. On PointMotionBench ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , we freeze the backbone of MolmoMotion-AR and draft each future frame of query points as one block with a fixed-width digit layout (Appendix A ). As shown in Table 5 , VFlash reduces DAVIS ADE and FDE by 27% and 19%, respectively, and HOT3D FDE by 8%. Its ADE ranks second on HOT3D and WorldTrack, behind AR but ahead of the flow-matching variant, although WorldTrack FDE increases by 15% and PWT is 7–12% lower across the three datasets. These results extend VFlash to dense motion prediction with text-tokenized coordinates, with gains over AR on several error metrics and approximately 25 × 25\times faster single-rollout generation (Appendix F.3 ).

LIBERO family. On LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , and LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) , we train a PIv3 flow-matching action head in StarVLA ( StarVLA Community, 2026 ) , with per-layer cross-attention to a frozen VLM. As shown in Figure 3 , gains over the baseline increase from 0.8 percentage points on LIBERO to 1.9 on LIBERO-Plus and 6.8 on LIBERO-PRO, indicating greater benefits under perturbations. On LIBERO-PRO, visual plans improve Spatial, Object, and Goal by 11.1, 9.4, and 6.9 points over the baseline. Compared with subtask-only conditioning, they add 2.6 points on Spatial, 1.2 on Goal, and 2.0 on Long, showing that trajectories provide useful information beyond the generated subtask.

Autonomous driving. For NAVSIM ( Dauner et al., 2024 ) and Waymo ( Xu et al., 2026b ) the policy is a ReCogDrive-derived diffusion transformer ( Li et al., 2026 ) that reads the VLM’s final-layer states over the prompt and the generated plan through cross-attention, alongside ego history and vehicle state, and outputs a continuous trajectory. The VLM is frozen and generates a 2D+3D trajectory on each dataset’s native grid; separate heads are trained on Waymo, NAVSIM, and Alpamayo-derived data. RL then fine-tunes the head alone with PDMS and RFS as rewards, so the plans are identical in the SFT and RL rows.

As shown in Table 8 , VFlash achieves competitive driving performance with a frozen planning VLM and a small action head. With supervised training, it reaches 87.1 PDMS on NAVSIM, above ReCogDrive (86.8), and 7.79 RFS on Waymo, comparable to Qwen-Drive-1.0-SFT (7.78). RL on the action head raises these scores to 90.7 PDMS and 7.86 RFS, matching Qwen-Drive-1.0-RL on NAVSIM and coming within 0.05 RFS of the best listed Waymo result. These gains require no updates to the VLM or its generated plans. Together, the results show that VFlash supports competitive plan-conditioned driving while substantially reducing decoding latency (Section 3.3 ).

Figure 4 splits per-step latency into visual encoding, prefill, decoding, and the action model at batch size one on Jetson Thor, DGX Spark, and H100. Thor is an embedded platform for robots and vehicles and Spark a desktop-class system, typical on-device hardware for the System-1 visual planning of Section 1 ; H100 is the server reference. Appendix E gives the timing boundary and the full table. Across devices, VFlash cuts per-step latency 5.1–5.2 × \times on MolmoSpaces on Thor and Spark and 3.6 × \times on H100, and 3.4–3.6 × \times and 2.6 × \times on NAVSIM; on Waymo (Figure 5 ) the H100 reduction is 4.5 × \times . The gain comes almost entirely from decoding: under AR it takes 75–87% of each step on Thor, and VFlash cuts it 12–42 × \times while the other stages are unchanged.
Figure 4: VFlash latency across different downstream tasks on Jetson Thor, DGX Spark and H100.

AR decoding runs one 4B VLM pass per token (35–39 ms on Thor, 33–40 ms on Spark, 4.7–6.0 ms on H100), so decoding time grows roughly linearly with token count. Drafting predicts the remaining tokens of a 36–84-token primitive in one pass, taking 13–23 ms on Thor and 1–3 ms on H100. Verification still needs a target pass per block, so its benefit depends on the tokens committed per iteration. On MolmoSpaces, DFlash commits 5.5 tokens per iteration on subtask text but only 2.2 within trajectory blocks: a coordinate one bin off the target’s choice fails Eq. 2 even with small geometric error. DFlash thus only about halves decoding time. VFlash skips token-level verification for visual primitives, using one drafter pass and one target pass per primitive; the target pass updates the cache and extracts hidden states for the action head, amortized over the block. On Thor, decoding takes 72–78 ms as the driving primitive grows from 36 to 84 tokens, so denser plans add little latency over this range.

Embodied VLMs and visual plans. Embodied VLMs are increasingly used as high-level modules that turn visual observations and language instructions into plans, affordances, and trajectories ( Ji et al., 2025 ; BAAI RoboBrain Team, 2025 ; Gemini Robotics Team, 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026b ; Dang et al., 2026 ) . Spatial prediction is central to these models: points and boxes localize objects or affordances ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025a ; Deitke et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) , while traces describe intended or predicted motion ( Zhou et al., 2026a ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . These visual plans can condition manipulation policies ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Tan et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) or be fed back as prompts ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Other work reasons spatially before acting ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) , predicts future states ( Kim et al., 2026a ; Ye et al., 2026 ) , or plans driving trajectories from scene understanding ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . While this literature asks what embodied models should predict, we ask how fast such spatial predictions can be produced. Token-by-token coordinate generation makes every extra waypoint, object, or dimension an additional decoding step.

Parallel and speculative decoding. Speculative decoding accelerates LLM inference by verifying multiple drafted tokens in parallel ( Stern et al., 2018 ; Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023a ) . Medusa, EAGLE, TIDAR, and DFlash explore different ways to produce these drafts ( Cai et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Liu et al., 2026c ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . For visual outputs, LocateAnything decodes points and boxes as units, but is limited to fixed-size 2D primitives ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Closest to this work, Spec-VLA accelerates OpenVLA by accepting draft action tokens whose bins lie near the target’s ( Wang et al., 2025c ) . However, it still verifies each action token against the target and commits only 2.10 2.10 – 2.94 2.94 tokens per pass. Based on our finding that, for visual trajectory prediction, one-pass drafts are more accurate than the autoregressive target, VFlash instead drafts the entire visual primitive in one pass rather than by agreement with the target.

Embodied and System-1 models. In a deployed perception-action loop, VLM latency directly limits how quickly the agent can react. Prior efficiency works mainly accelerate the action execution pipeline, for example via action compression, parallel action chunks, or flow matching ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . Prior VLM-based planning, however, still often rely on highly autoregressive token decoding. System-1 models such as Jev make fast typed decisions that downstream applications can use directly ( Almeida, 2026 ) , and Visual Jev answers many independent visual questions in parallel after one image encoding ( Yu and Yao, 2026 ) . Our work can be seen as a relevant effort that enables System-1 VLM spatial prediction. Within this context, our work studies optimized token representation and decoding schemes systematically, supporting both dedicated special tokens ( Chen et al., 2022 ) and plain numbers ( Chen et al., 2023b ; Bai et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) .

In summary, VFlash uses DFlash-style drafting without target-token agreement, extending fast and accurate visual plan generation from LocateAnything’s parallel box decoding to richer and more general visual primitives that are useful for downstream embodied applications. It also enables more efficient decoding parallelism via systematic studies, in contrast to relevant or concurrent works.

We presented VFlash, which uses the known structure of visual primitives to replace sequential coordinate generation with parallel prediction. Our results show that useful spatial predictions need not reproduce an autoregressive model’s output: direct drafts reduce robot trajectory errors, while single-rollout timing estimates indicate approximately 25 × 25\times faster generation for 3D object point forecasting. Plan-conditioned manipulation further demonstrates how these predictions support downstream action generation. Future work will examine whether generating multiple complementary primitives from shared observations improves control within a fixed latency budget.

Validity rules. A block is accepted only if every delimiter is in its declared position, every coordinate position holds a number token, and the waypoint count matches the tool call. Boxes within a category are generated one block at a time, sorted lexicographically in training, and an empty category is answered with the text None . Decoding enforces the same rules by restricting each position to its legal tokens (Appendix C ).

Dense motion on a text-tokenized target. The MolmoMotion target keeps its own tokenizer and text format: coordinates are signed millimeter integers relative to the first query point at the current frame, and future frames are separated by a fixed separator. One block covers one future frame of P P query points and has 19 ​ P + 3 19P+3 positions: the frame separator serves as the start token, two positions hold the timestamp, and each point gets one position for its index followed by three coordinates of a sign and five digits. Unused high-order digits, and every position of a point the target would omit, are filled with the target’s mask token, so an omitted point is signaled by a masked index rather than by a shorter frame. The completed block is rendered back into the target’s text by inserting its fixed punctuation; the mask token never appears in the rendered answer. The target’s vocabulary is unchanged. Following MolmoMotion ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , we use P = 8 P=8 and five-digit coordinates in all experiments (Appendix B ).

Base VLM. The visual encoder is MoonViT-SO-400M ( Kimi Team, 2025 ) with 27 layers of width 1,152, 14-pixel patches, and 2 × 2 2\times 2 spatial merging; a two-layer MLP connects it to Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , whose decoder has 36 layers of width 2,560. It is trained on image and video question answering, grounding, pointing, and spatial reasoning data. Every task-specific AR target in Section 3 is fully fine-tuned from this checkpoint. The dense-motion experiment instead uses the released MolmoMotion-4B-H3-F30 ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) target without fine-tuning.

Drafter architecture. Following DFlash ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , the drafter has five full-width Qwen3 transformer layers with 32 query heads, eight key/value heads, 128-dimensional heads, and a 9,728-dimensional feed-forward layer. Target layers 1, 9, 17, 25, and 33 (zero-based) provide context features; their concatenated 12,800-dimensional states are projected to 2,560 dimensions and RMS-normalized. The drafter shares the frozen target’s input embedding and output projection and has 537M trainable parameters. Positions inside a block attend to each other and to the target context before the block; target features are computed online with gradients disabled.

Loss weights. We minimize Eq. 4 over the annotated sequence, with the target encoding the clean sequence and the drafter reconstructing the masked positions. Primitive positions have unit weight. Ordinary-text positions decay as w j = exp ( − ( j − 1 ) / 7 ) w_{j}=\exp(-(j-1)/7) with distance from the anchor, following DFlash. Out-of-frame labels are downweighted by 0.1 in both the target’s fine-tuning loss and the drafter loss. Anchors and padding are excluded. No soft-logit distillation or hidden-state regression is used.

Block sampling and packing. Each annotated primitive contributes one complete block. The 2D, 2D+3D, and wrist-camera drafters additionally sample up to 512 ordinary-text anchors per example, shared across assistant turns, so that one drafter serves both the text and the primitive path; text blocks stop at primitive boundaries. The 3D-only and box drafters train on primitive blocks only. Packed examples keep independent position indices and attention masks: each block sees only its own positions and the target positions of its own example before its anchor, so schemas and lengths mix freely in a batch without leaking labels across blocks or examples.

The 2D target uses ShareRobot ( Ji et al., 2025 ) trajectories and affordances plus FSD ( Yuan et al., 2026a ) direct and reasoning annotations: 69,129 source records, 152,346 repeat-weighted examples per pass, about two passes, two 8,192-token packs per update. Its drafter trains for three passes with 16 examples per GPU on four GPUs and a 1,700-token limit per example. The two primary-view robot targets share 5,215,780 repeat-weighted examples from MolmoBot ( Deshpande et al., 2026 ) , AgiBot ( Bu et al., 2025 ) , InternA1 ( Tian et al., 2026 ) , OXE-Trace ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024 ) , and DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , serialized as 3D-only or joint 2D+3D trajectories; each AR run covers about one pass with 16 packs of 32,768 tokens per update, and each drafter trains for three passes with a 4,096-token limit per example. The wrist-camera variant adds LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) two-camera observations and additional views of the same robot data, for 7,902,844 weighted examples; its target uses 32 packs of 16,384 tokens, its drafter an 8,192-token limit. All runs use AdamW, BF16, zero weight decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, and cosine decay to zero. Target warm-up is 200 updates for 2D trajectories and 500 for robot 3D and boxes; drafter warm-up is 4% of the budget. Each drafter is paired with its own target and evaluated at the final checkpoint.

Boxes. The box target is trained on COCO train2017 ( Lin et al., 2014 ) , CountAnything ( Lei et al., 2026 ) , and KubriCount ( Liu et al., 2026a ) multi-turn conversations. Each COCO image is queried for its present categories and up to ten sampled absent categories, with the image supplied in the first turn only; three COCO variants differ in their negative-category samples, and CountAnything and KubriCount use positive categories. Repeating each source twice gives 1,256,254 weighted conversations per pass, with category outputs capped at 900 boxes. Post-training image identifiers do not overlap the evaluation sets. The AR target trains for 3,000 updates with 16 packs of up to 32,768 tokens per update. The drafter trains for three passes with 16 conversations per GPU on 16 GPUs and a 262,144-token pack limit, supervising every six-token box block with uniform weights; a mixed text-and-box variant with up to 512 text anchors was also trained, but the reported results use the box-only drafter.
