Text and routing. After multimodal prefill, ordinary text is generated in DFlash blocks of 16 positions: one accepted anchor and up to 15 proposals. The target verifies the block in one pass and keeps the longest matching prefix plus its own next token. The tool call is generated on this path. When an accepted prefix reaches a primitive-start token, any speculative tokens after it are discarded and the declared schema and block length take over. A block whose length exceeds the remaining budget is rejected before drafting.

Primitive prediction and acceptance. The drafter processes the start token and all masked positions in one pass. Delimiter positions are fixed, coordinate positions are restricted to number tokens, and coupled rules such as the pairing of out-of-frame markers and the ordering of box corners are resolved by a small selection loop over the logits already computed, with no further network evaluation. The target then processes the completed block once to update its cache, supply context features for the next block, and predict the continuation. A schema-valid block is accepted in full without token-level agreement. If validation fails, the target cache is rolled back to the anchor and the block is regenerated by constrained target AR from the first invalid position ( r = 0 r=0 for trajectories); the drafter cache is reset afterwards. The DFlash baseline in Section 3.3 instead applies 16-position blocks and longest-prefix acceptance throughout the response, including inside primitives.

Dense motion continuation. For the MolmoMotion target the drafter fills the 19 ​ P + 2 19P+2 positions of one frame. The rendered frame receives one target pass, which supplies the next frame’s features and chooses between the frame separator and the closing delimiter; the target writes the answer’s opening and closing text autoregressively. Missing or non-increasing timestamps are set to the previous timestamp plus one, and a frame whose points are all masked keeps its highest-margin point. Malformed frames fall back to target AR. Generation continues for at most 30 frames, so parallelism is across the points and coordinates of one frame while frames remain sequential.

Plan conditioning. The manipulation policy is the world action model (WAM) of MolmoSpaces ( Kim et al., 2026b ) , obtained by post-training Cosmos-Predict2.5 ( NVIDIA, 2026c ) for robot control. Unless otherwise specified, MolmoSpaces uses the primary-view 2D+3D robot target–drafter pair described in Appendix B . We replace its text-encoder context with states from the frozen 4B planning VLM. For every retained position, each of the VLM’s 36 layer outputs is standardized along its 2,560 channels and the results are concatenated; a newly initialized linear projection followed by GELU maps this vector to the WAM’s context width. The resulting 512 context positions enter the WAM through its existing text cross-attention path. The trajectory reaches the WAM only through these states; there is no separate numeric trajectory encoder. The VLM stays frozen throughout.

Post-training. All five configurations start from the same pretrained WAM checkpoint and are evaluated after 100,000 post-training updates. Post-training uses AdamW with learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 0.01, gradient-norm clipping at 1.0, BF16, and global batch size 512 (32 GPUs, four examples per device, four accumulation steps); the schedule warms up for 15,000 steps and stays at its peak through the evaluated checkpoint, for 51.2 million samples per model. Training uses seed 24, and every configuration is evaluated at the same update count rather than at its own best checkpoint. The post-training data are 172.5 million frames of simulated Franka demonstrations in six task splits covering picking, placing, and opening

Execution and scoring. The WAM executes 20-action chunks. A new plan is generated synchronously every three chunks, or 60 control steps; the simulator pauses during inference. Evaluation uses seed 42 and all 3,915 benchmark episodes: 1,000 each for Pick, Pick & Place, and Open, and all 915 Close episodes. Horizons are 455 control steps for Pick, Open, and Close and 682 for Pick & Place. An episode succeeds if the goal is reached at any step; episodes run to the horizon. Suite success is aggregated before rounding, and the mean is the unweighted average of the four suites. Each row is one training seed and one evaluation seed.

Action head. The LIBERO policies use the PIv3 flow-matching action head of StarVLA ( StarVLA Community, 2026 ) . The LIBERO experiments use the wrist-camera-trained 2D+3D robot target–drafter pair described in Appendix B . A LayerNorm and linear projection map each of the frozen VLM’s 36 hidden-state layers from 2,560 to 1,024 dimensions, and action-transformer layer i i cross-attends to projected VLM layer i i . The 36-layer head and projections contain about 634 million trainable parameters. Both primary and wrist images are rotated by 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} , resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 , and included in the VLM sequence; no proprioceptive input is used. The head predicts eight seven-dimensional actions (end-effector increments and a gripper command) with four flow-matching steps. VFlash generates a fresh subtask and plan before every action chunk. The two context variants retain the prompt through the generated subtask, or the prompt through the full generated answer. The baseline is the same head on a frozen Qwen3-VL-4B that encodes only the images and the instruction.

Training and evaluation. All policies train on 273,463 demonstration steps from the same 1,693 episodes. The randomly initialized heads train for 80,000 AdamW updates with batch size 128, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , 5,000 warm-up steps, cosine decay to 10 − 6 10^{-6} , ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) , weight decay 10 − 8 10^{-8} , BF16, and seed 42. Evaluation uses seed 7. LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) covers four suites with ten tasks and 50 initial states each (2,000 episodes). LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) evaluates 10,030 perturbed task instances once each. LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) crosses the four base suites with object, swap, language, and task perturbations (8,000 episodes); environment perturbations are excluded. The policies train on the standard 40 LIBERO tasks and are evaluated unchanged on the two perturbation benchmarks. Success follows each environment’s goal predicate. We report the unweighted mean of the success rates across its four task suites.
Conditioning on the target VLM.

The action head conditions on selected 2,560-dimensional final-layer states of the frozen target VLM. States at generated trajectory positions are obtained by processing the accepted primitive with the target VLM. We define conditioning sequence as prompt and plan. Variable-length BF16 states are projected to 384 dimensions, with padding masked in pooling and cross-attention.

Ego motion inputs. The head uses 16 history entries, each containing position and heading ( x , y , ψ ) (x,y,\psi) , three availability indicators, and a relative timestamp. The resulting 112-dimensional vector is standardized using training-set statistics, with unavailable values zeroed and shorter histories left-padded. The 16-dimensional current-state vector contains four command indicators, four motion measurements, and eight availability indicators. Separate MLPs with 1,024 hidden units and LayerNorm map the history and current state to 384-dimensional embeddings.

Trajectory head. The ReCogDrive-derived head alternates eight self-attention and eight cross-attention blocks, with eight heads of width 48, adaptive normalization, and SwiGLU feed-forward layers. Each noisy waypoint is embedded with a learned index and a sinusoidal encoding of its physical future time; the index table supports up to 64 waypoints. Concatenating the waypoint embedding with the broadcast history embedding and masked mean VLM context yields 1,152 channels, which are projected to 384. The current-state and diffusion-timestep embeddings condition the transformer blocks. A 512-dimensional output projection followed by an MLP with 1,024 hidden units predicts three noise components per waypoint, for ( x , y , ψ ) (x,y,\psi) on NAVSIM and ( x , y ) (x,y) on Waymo, where the heading channel is masked. NAVSIM and Waymo use the same architecture with separately trained weights.
Diffusion objective and sampling. For normalized recorded future waypoints Y ~ \widetilde{Y} , the head ϵ θ \epsilon_{\theta} minimizes masked noise-prediction error:

Y s = α ¯ s ​ Y ~ + 1 − α ¯ s ​ ϵ , ℒ drive = 𝔼 ⁡ [ ∑ h , c m h ​ c ​ ( ϵ θ , h ​ c ​ ( Y s , s , Z , u , τ ) − ϵ h ​ c ) 2 ∑ h , c m h ​ c ] . Y_{s}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{s}}\,\widetilde{Y}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{s}}\,\epsilon,\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{drive}}=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{h,c}m_{hc}\bigl(\epsilon_{\theta,hc}(Y_{s},s;Z,u,\tau)-\epsilon_{hc}\bigr)^{2}}{\sum_{h,c}m_{hc}}\right]. (8)

Here ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) , s s is the diffusion timestep, α ¯ s \bar{\alpha}_{s} is the cumulative noise schedule, Z Z denotes VLM states, u u contains ego history and state, and τ \tau contains future timestamps. The mask m h ​ c m_{hc} is one for valid coordinates and zero otherwise; the heading channel is masked out on Waymo. The schedule has 100 training timesteps. Five deterministic DDIM steps ( Song et al., 2020 ) , at indices 80, 60, 40, 20, and 0, produce the continuous trajectory. During SFT, only the action head and its input projections receive gradients.

Normalization and training configuration. Each channel is mapped affinely to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , z norm = 2 ​ ( z − z min ) / ( z max − z min ) − 1 z_{\mathrm{norm}}=2(z-z_{\min})/(z_{\max}-z_{\min})-1 , with bounds set per dataset. The NAVSIM head inherits the fixed ReCogDrive bounds: X in [ − 1.57 , 65.17 ] [-1.57,65.17] m, Y in [ − 19.68 , 22.32 ] [-19.68,22.32] m, and ψ \psi in [ − 1.67 , 1.86 ] [-1.67,1.86] rad; targets are not clipped, while denoised predictions and the final normalized actions are clipped to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . The Waymo head uses X in [ − 46.98,138.77 ] [-46.98,138.77] m and Y in [ − 18.14 , 17.81 ] [-18.14,17.81] m, fitted on training trajectories as the smaller of zero and the minimum to the 99th percentile for X and the 0.5th to 99.5th percentiles for Y, with no clipping. Both heads are initialized from scratch and trained for 200 epochs with AdamW at learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} , ( β 1 , β 2 ) = ( 0.9 , 0.95 ) (\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.95) , and gradient-norm clipping at 1.0; three warmup epochs are followed by cosine decay to 10 − 6 10^{-6} . Training uses batch size 64 per GPU on eight GPUs with FP16 mixed precision.

Reinforcement learning. After SFT, each head is fine-tuned with DiffGRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) , which treats the five-step DDIM chain as a policy rollout. For every training scene, the head samples eight trajectories, scores them with a dataset-specific reward, and updates with group-standardized advantages. A behavior-cloning loss with weight 0.1 regularizes the update. It is the negative log-likelihood under the current head of denoising chains sampled from the frozen SFT head. No KL penalty is used. Both heads use an initial learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} with cosine decay and no warmup. On NAVSIM the reward is PDMS from the non-reactive simulator ( Dauner et al., 2024 ) on the training split, with ego progress, time-to-collision within bound (TTC), and comfort weighted 10/5/2 during training against the official 5/5/2 used for evaluation. Training runs 10 epochs (6,650 updates) at batch size 16 per GPU on eight GPUs. The checkpoint is selected by PDMS on an internal validation split held out from navtrain by log (18,179 clips, Appendix F.5 ). On Waymo the reward is RFS from the official implementation on the 479 validation scenes. Training runs 20 epochs (300 updates) at batch size 4 per GPU on eight GPUs, and the checkpoint is selected on the same 479 scenes, so the selection score is in-sample. These settings are shared by all layout and context configurations. The VLM, its plans, and the conditioning states stay fixed, so the SFT and RL rows of Table 8 consume identical plans and differ only in head weights. Reported scores use the held-out test splits, which take no part in SFT, RL, or checkpoint selection.

Figure 5: Waymo planning latency on H100 (ms, batch size one). AR, DFlash, and VFlash share the VLM, primitive, and action head and differ only in the decoder. Qwen-Drive-1.0 is measured on the same hardware; the Fast-dDrive value is from its paper and its AR baseline is not the AR bar shown here.

Hardware and runtime. All measurements use batch size one and one request at a time on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor (SM110), DGX Spark (GB10, SM121), and a single H100 80 GB (SM90). Our models run in a locally modified TensorRT-Edge-LLM ( NVIDIA, 2026b ) C++ runtime: vision encoder, target VLM, and drafter are exported through ONNX and compiled into TensorRT engines, TensorRT selects kernels for the exported operators, and Edge-LLM plugins supply attention (CuTe DSL FMHA for vision and prefill, XQA for decoding and speculative verification), cache updates, and positional encoding. Engines and kernel artifacts are built separately for each architecture. The stacks are CUDA 13.0 and TensorRT 10.15.2.7 on Thor, CUDA 13.0.88 and TensorRT 10.14.1.48 on Spark, and CUDA 12.9.86 and TensorRT 10.11.0.33 on H100. All Thor runs use a modified Edge-LLM 0.9.0 tree; all Spark runs and the H100 MolmoSpaces runs use Edge-LLM 0.10.1; the H100 driving runs use the 0.9.0 tree with an SM90 attention bridge. Vision, target, and draft engines run in FP16 with FP16 KV caches; no weight or KV quantization is used.

Decoders. AR performs target-only single-token decoding. DFlash drafts 16-token blocks and accepts the longest prefix that matches the target’s greedy choice exactly, plus the correction token; numeric coordinates receive no tolerance. VFlash decodes text with the same verified blocks, then drafts the whole primitive in one unverified block (54 tokens for MolmoSpaces, 36 for NAVSIM, 84 for Waymo) and runs one cached target prefill over the accepted block, the EOS token, and end-of-text padding to produce the hidden states the action model consumes. This prefill is counted as decoding. For MolmoSpaces the prefill retains 512 non-image positions from all 36 target layers; for driving it exports the final layer only, padded to 2,200 positions on NAVSIM. In both pipelines the fixed tool-call JSON is supplied rather than generated; on MolmoSpaces it is committed inside the text verification pass, and on driving the think-and-tool prefix precedes generation, so decoding covers exactly the primitive. All decoders use the same supplied tool-call JSON and the same primitive length. AR and DFlash reuse the target states computed during generation and need no separate feature pass.

Action models. The MolmoSpaces WAM runs one WAN encoder call and four DiT calls (joint, action, joint, action) inside a CUDA graph, with BF16 DiT weights and FP16 attention through a custom head-dimension-128 CuTe DSL kernel on Thor and Spark; the H100 baseline uses native TensorRT attention. The ReCogDrive head is a BF16 TensorRT engine containing feature encoding and the DDIM sampler. Latency profiles unroll ten DDIM steps to match the ten-step Qwen-Drive planner; the quality results of Table 8 use five steps (Appendix F.5 ).

Qwen-Drive-1.0. We run the released checkpoint in its reasoning planning mode with greedy decoding. On Thor and Spark it uses a customized Edge-LLM 0.9.0 runtime with CuTe DSL Gated DeltaNet kernels for its 24 linear-attention layers and FMHA/XQA for its eight full-attention layers; on H100 it uses the TensorRT-LLM backend with FlashInfer kernels. Its 1.04B flow-matching planner is a separate TensorRT engine with BF16 weights, FP16 attention, and ten Euler steps in a CUDA graph. Inputs are one 1600 × \times 896 front image on NAVSIM (1,400 visual tokens; 1600 × \times 800 in the Thor runs) and three 800 × \times 896 images on Waymo (2,100 tokens). The Fast-dDrive value in Figure 5 is taken from its paper and was not measured here.

Timing protocol. Each request starts from fresh vision computation and model state. CUDA events bracket each stage (preprocessing and vision encoding, prefill, decoding, action model) and are summed over all calls within a request; these intervals include host launch gaps and are not kernel-only durations. Model loading, engine construction, graph capture, warmup, image loading and CPU preprocessing outside the instrumented modules, and output detokenization are excluded. Repeat counts differ by run: the Thor MolmoSpaces pipeline uses 24 records and ten passes after five warmups; the Spark and H100 robotics runs one pass over the same 24 records after five warmups; driving runs five records and ten passes after five warmups; the Qwen-Drive H100 run five scenes twice after five warmups. Reported per-step latency is the sum of stage means. Within each device and task, the vision, prefill, and action-model means are shared across decoders; decoding is profiled separately. The MolmoSpaces AR decoding time comes from an earlier standalone profile with an output-only target engine, whereas the VFlash decoding time includes the all-layer feature completion described above; the driving decoders share one target-engine configuration.
Table 12 lists the stage means behind Figures 4 and 5 , and Table 12 the decoding statistics behind the per-pass numbers of Section 3.3 .

Table 11: Per-step latency by stage (ms). Batch size one, FP16 VLM engines. Action is WAN encoder plus DiT for MolmoSpaces and the ReCogDrive DiT (ten DDIM steps) or the Qwen-Drive planner for driving. Within each task and device, vision, prefill, and action means are shared across AR, DFlash, and VFlash and shown once; decoding is profiled separately and for VFlash includes the target prefill over the accepted primitive. Total is the sum of stage means. Qwen-Drive-1.0 is measured end to end on its own stack (Appendix E.1 ); Fast-dDrive is reported by its paper without a stage split.

Table 12: Decoding statistics on MolmoSpaces (Thor). Tokens committed per target pass, passes per request, and per-pass cost of the drafter and target. The output is 88.75 tokens on average: about 36 of text and tool call, then the 54-token primitive. VFlash’s text stage uses the same verified blocks as DFlash; the fused tool-call JSON is excluded from its committed count. DFlash’s decoding time in Table 12 additionally includes a final padding forward that completes the feature sequence (58.5 ms on Thor, 54.5 on Spark, 11.2 on H100); for VFlash this work is folded into the target prefill over the primitive.
Decoder Segment Tokens/pass Passes Drafter ms Target ms AR all 1.0 88.75 – 35.0 DFlash all 3.0 29.5 9.1 35.7 text 5.5 trajectory 2.2 VFlash text 5.5 3.25 11.8 42.5 primitive 53 1 12.9 68.4

We evaluate 200 ShareRobot-Bench queries and 300 VABench-V queries with the same 4B target and its drafter. Coordinates are on the 0–1,000 image scale. Predictions are linearly interpolated by waypoint index to the reference point count before computing discrete Fréchet distance, symmetric Hausdorff distance, and RMSE, the square root of the mean squared Euclidean waypoint error; Table 3 divides each distance by 1,000. All AR and VFlash outputs parse and enter the means.

Inputs and references. Every decoder is evaluated on the same 1,000 InternA1, 999 AgiBot, and 4,221 MolmoBot records. InternA1 uses the current image; AgiBot contains 499 image and 500 video records, MolmoBot 2,757 and 1,464. Video records sample six frames from the preceding three seconds and exclude the current frame. Each record supplies only the primary camera, including for the model trained with wrist-camera views. References contain ten waypoints per gripper, uniformly resampled by 3D arc length over a nominal five-second window that may end early at an episode or action boundary; they describe path geometry rather than fixed-time control samples. Coordinates are in meters in the current primary camera frame and lie on a 1 cm grid inherited from the annotation export.

Metrics. The scorer requires the expected arm identities and exactly ten points per arm, without interpolation or repair; all reported configurations return valid trajectories for every record. ADE averages Euclidean waypoint error and FDE the final-waypoint error over the evaluated arms. SR@ τ \tau is the fraction of waypoints with error below τ \tau , averaged within a record and then across records, for τ = 5 \tau=5 and 10 cm. An arm is active when the sum of its XYZ standard deviations is at least 5 mm; if any reference arm is active, only active arms are scored. InternA1 evaluation episodes are absent from training; MolmoBot uses five held-out validation configurations covering pick, place, and opening tasks.

Inputs and selection. Each record gives three observed frames, the caption, and the observed XYZ coordinates of eight query points, and asks for up to 30 future frames. We use PointMotionBench with one fixed point selection shared by all local evaluations: points must be visible with finite coordinates in all three observed frames; at most 24 are sampled per clip with seed zero and split into groups of eight, discarding incomplete groups; HOT3D uses one fifth of its clips. This gives 491/144/88 clips and 1,473/412/257 records for HOT3D/WorldTrack/DAVIS. Frames are consecutive at the source rate, so the horizon is 1.0 s for HOT3D and WorldTrack and 1.25 s for DAVIS; shorter clips keep their available frames. WorldTrack uses the provided world coordinates.

Speed annotation. The 25 × 25\times in Table 5 compares one VFlash rollout with the target’s AR rollout on the same selections, both on one H100 at batch size one: 3.21/3.86/3.78 s against 79.8/90.6/99.6 s on HOT3D/WorldTrack/DAVIS, or 24.8/23.5/26.4 × \times .

Queries and generation. Evaluation uses 4,952 COCO val2017 images and 200 Dense200 images. The prompt asks for every instance of a given category in the primitive format. COCO queries each ground-truth-present category as one turn of a multi-turn conversation over the image; Dense200 has one category per image. AR and VFlash share the image, query, and reference records, decode greedily with neutral repetition penalty, and apply no resizing before the model’s image processor. The output budget is 512 new tokens per COCO turn and 4,096 per Dense200 query; only complete boxes are returned when the budget runs out. Boxes are mapped back to pixels and merged per image.

Direct and AR fallback. Direct accepts every schema-valid box. AR fallback adds the spatial-confidence criterion of LocateAnything ( Wang et al., 2026 ) : for each coordinate, the numeric tokens among the five most probable full-vocabulary predictions are examined, and the box is regenerated by constrained target AR if this set is empty, or if the top numeric token has probability below 0.9 and at least two numeric candidates span more than 60 bins. Boxes before the first uncertain coordinate are kept (Eq. 5 ). On COCO a third consecutive identical box ends the list, keeping the first two copies; Dense200 uses the guard without this rule.

Metrics. COCO F1 follows the inherited evaluator: every prediction receives confidence 0.2, and per-category precision and recall are aggregated into F1 at each IoU threshold; this is distinct from COCO AP. Dense200 greedily matches ground-truth boxes to unused predictions at each τ ∈ { 0.50 , 0.55 , … , 0.95 } \tau\in\{0.50,0.55,\ldots,0.95\} , averages per-image precision and recall, and computes F 1 , τ = 2 ​ P ¯ τ ​ R ¯ τ / ( P ¯ τ + R ¯ τ ) F_{1,\tau}=2\overline{P}_{\tau}\overline{R}_{\tau}/(\overline{P}_{\tau}+\overline{R}_{\tau}) ; mean F1 averages the ten thresholds. Boxes per second (BPS) divides the number of returned boxes by generation time on one H100 at batch size one, where generation time covers all queries of an image including prefill, target passes, and fallback, and excludes model loading.

Splits and data separation. NAVSIM training uses navtrain, divided by log into 85,109 training and 18,179 internal validation clips; SFT and RL fit on the former, and checkpoints are selected on the latter by PDMS. Test scores use all 12,146 navtest scenes. Waymo SFT uses the official training split. The 479 validation scenes provide the RL reward and are used to select both SFT and RL checkpoints by RFS. Test scores come from the official test split. Neither test split enters SFT, RL, or checkpoint selection. The upstream VLM was fine-tuned on all of navtrain and on the Waymo training split. The NAVSIM internal validation clips are therefore held out from action-head fitting but not from VLM fine-tuning. The Waymo validation scenes and both test splits are excluded from VLM fine-tuning.

Scoring. Each scene is evaluated once: the initial Gaussian noise is seeded from the clip identifier, and five deterministic DDIM steps produce the trajectory. On NAVSIM the head’s eight ( x , y , ψ ) (x,y,\psi) waypoints at 2 Hz are scored by the official non-reactive PDM simulator ( Dauner et al., 2024 ) with the standard 5/5/2 weights for ego progress, time-to-collision within bound, and comfort. On Waymo the head’s twenty ( x , y ) (x,y) waypoints at 4 Hz are scored by the official RFS implementation, and ADE at 3 s and 5 s averages Euclidean position error over the horizon; both require a complete prediction through the horizon.

Compared methods. DiffusionLTF is the DiffusionDrive-based policy released with Open X-AV ( Nguyen et al., 2025 ) ; its scores are taken from the WOD-E2E leaderboard. Qwen-Drive-1.0 ( Zhou et al., 2026b ) couples Qwen3.5-4B with a flow-matching planner conditioned on VLM representations of the scene and an autoregressively generated text reasoning trace; its RL stage, like ours, optimizes only the planner with PDMS and RFS rewards. Fast-dDrive ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) is a block-diffusion dLLM that generates reasoning and trajectory as structured text and reports Waymo results only. Both reason in text where VFlash uses a visual plan. Latency measurement conditions for these methods, including our own measurement of Qwen-Drive-1.0, are given in Appendix E .

analysis.overview: VFlash将投机解码的接受目标从“逐token符合AR目标”改为“整块视觉基元结构有效”，用额外训练的537M drafter一次预测完整轨迹，文字仍验证。该选择在同target的机器人轨迹上有受控精度提升，并显著降低所测推理阶段耗时，值得优先核查。它同时改变学习目标和额外训练量，不是无损且免费的解码插件；框检测需置信回退，密集运动部分指标更差。MolmoSpaces70.2%来自重训动作头及仿真暂停条件，25倍只是单rollout密集运动计时，不能直接写为真机闭环收益。
analysis.notice: 完整阅读139个提取片段，覆盖正文与附录A–F；另读取原PDF算法1及相关实验协议文本。固定版本PDF28页，目视核对物理页4/6/7/8/10/21/25/26的图2/3/4、表2–7和11/12、算法与计时边界。其他图像、参考文献所引各论文、源码与运行结果未独立复核，作者实验未复现。摘要初筛仅为排序，全文后的attention判断基于本报告方法与实验；无真机闭环或多训练seed置信保证。

findings.title: 改变接受标准：空间预测不再以AR逐token一致为质量上限
findings.text: DFlash在首个不同token处停止接受，即便坐标只差一个bin也会打断整块。VFlash保留target特征和drafter架构，对视觉基元直接接受结构有效的整块预测，普通文字仍用最长一致前缀验证。因此它主动放弃视觉输出的AR分布保持保证，以标注几何与下游效果评价；不是无损投机解码。一次并行预测只针对一个已知schema的基元，后续target上下文仍需更新。

findings.title: 块边界与坐标槽位同时对齐，长度由schema决定
findings.text: 工具调用声明block_size（含起始和分隔token），类型决定轴、点数和分隔符位置：单臂联合2D+3D长度5P+4，P10即54。专用坐标token有1001档；机器人XYZ范围[-5,5]/[-5,5]/[0,10]m、1cm栅格，摄像机OpenCV坐标。普通文字数值target则固定sign+5digit并填mask，再还原原格式。固定布局减少可变分词错位，不等于连续坐标精度无限或自动满足2D/3D重投影几何一致。

findings.title: 冻结target后另训537M草稿器，标签来自标注而非target续写
findings.text: 主要target是MoonViT-SO400M+Qwen3-4B，先按任务完整微调，再冻结，五层非因果drafter融合target第1/9/17/25/33层特征，537M可训参数，共享冻结embedding/output。对完整primitive做均匀CE，文字位置权重衰减，没有soft-logit蒸馏或hidden regression。机器人target约521.6万repeat-weighted样本，drafter再训3遍；腕视角变体约790.3万weighted样本且预算更高。Dense target用已发布MolmoMotion不再微调，但drafter在32 H100上以1270万采样窗口训练。因而准确度优势同时涉及标注目标、全块建模和新增训练，不能单归为推理时并行。

findings.title: 有效性检查管格式，失败才回退；target仍做特征完成
findings.text: 约束覆盖delimiters、数值词表、点数、成对oof标记，box另要求角点顺序和空间置信guard；未含碰撞、动力学或通用空间误差验证。有效块提交后还要一次target forward更新KV并提取动作头特征，非完全跳过target。轨迹失败r=0、整段约束AR重生；box保留不确定坐标前缀。Dense每未来帧一个块、帧间仍顺序，最多30帧；时间戳修复和全mask帧保留最高margin点是额外规则。不能把schema通过率等同预测准确度。

findings.title: 2D同target小幅改善，40%跨模型差距多已来自更强target
findings.text: 表2对同4B AR：ShareRobot DFD/HD/RMSE0.202/0.175/0.142→0.194/0.162/0.133；VABench0.130/0.125/0.093→0.126/0.116/0.089。200与300条query，按waypoint index插值到参考点数后评分，距离除1000归一化。相对LoHo-Manip约40%的跨模型差距不能全算解码收益，因为AR target本来已更好；ShareRobot上RoboBrain-2.0仍优于VFlash。所有本地输出均可解析，未用格式失败筛掉差例，但没有多run差值区间。

findings.title: 3D最清楚的对照：联合2D+3D时AR更易退化，整块预测缓解
findings.text: 表4联合2D+3D：InternA1 ADE0.153→0.062m、AgiBot0.105→0.041、MolmoBot0.076→0.055；对应3D-only AR0.101/0.083/0.066，VFlash0.065/0.042/0.054，说明AR加2D段后3D误差增大而VFlash保持接近。评估1000/999/4221 records，所有配置只看primary view；腕相机仅训练增强，另有更多数据/更新，不能当测试时多相机收益。SR@5/10是waypoint误差阈值比例，不是机器人成功率。十点参考按3D弧长重采样，是路径几何而非等时间控制命令。

findings.title: 框检测反例：只验格式掉约21点，回退仍损高IoU
findings.text: 表3 Dense200 mean F1：AR60.10、直接39.09、带AR fallback61.78；IoU0.95则16.95→6.59/12.11，回退也未恢复精定位。COCO mean48.68→41.32/47.79；fallback boxes/s3.15→8.76，Dense6.73→17.46。Guard检查每坐标全词表top5的numeric candidates：空集或top数值概率<0.9且候选跨度>60bins则回退。两数据集F1协议不同，COCO每预测置信固定0.2，不能称COCO AP；BPS还受输出box数量影响，非单query延迟。

findings.title: 密集运动25倍只是单rollout，质量收益并非全面
findings.text: 表5 DAVIS ADE/FDE1.227/2.108→0.893/1.716m，但HOT3D ADE0.109→0.122更差，WorldTrack FDE0.261→0.300更差；PWT三集0.444/0.445/0.153→0.391/0.408/0.143均下降。固定8点/3历史帧/最多30未来帧，采样限制为三帧皆可见，HOT3D仅1/5clips；三集491/144/88clips、1473/412/257records。F.3单H100 batch1的一次VFlash/AR rollout耗时3.21/79.8、3.86/90.6、3.78/99.6s，约23.5–26.4倍；不是全数据重复profile均值、p95或实时机器人速度。

findings.title: MolmoSpaces先看AR计划61.0对VFlash70.2，原生62.6对照还改编码器
findings.text: 表6原生WAM62.6→70.2%同时把Cosmos-Reason换成自建VLM，并输入Q+subtask+trajectory，因此非纯解码对照。表7更接近：同规划VLM与同WAM架构，AR2D+3D61.0、VFlash70.2；VFlash image-context63.7、3D-only69.3。五组从同预训练WAM起点各自训练100k更新，51.2M样本/模型，不能称动作权重完全相同。3915仿真episode，四suite等权平均，单训练seed24/评测42；20动作chunk、每三chunk同步重规划，推理时simulator暂停。成功提升支持计划条件化，但不能证明低延迟在不停表闭环中带来该提升。

findings.title: LIBERO-PRO总+6.8点，单独加入轨迹只贡献额外1.7点
findings.text: 目视图3：baseline/自建VLM仅subtask/完整计划为LIBERO93.4/93.4/94.2%，Plus60.7/62.6/62.6%，PRO40.2/45.3/47.0%。因此PRO相对Qwen3-VL底座的6.8点中，subtask-only配置已高5.1点，轨迹额外1.7点；Plus完整与subtask均62.6，不应称所有扰动均因轨迹而改善。PIv3+projection约634M可训参数、同1693episode/273463步训练80k updates，无proprio；两图像+每8动作重规划。评估标准LIBERO2000、Plus10030、PRO8000次且排除environment扰动，单训练/评测seed，不含真机。

findings.title: 驾驶RL只更新动作头，不能归因于更好的VFlash计划
findings.text: 表8 NAVSIM PDMS87.1→90.7、Waymo RFS7.79→7.86来自head-only DiffGRPO，VLM与生成plans完全固定；这是动作头优化效果，不是FPD精度又提高。测试NAVSIM12146场景用non-reactive PDM、Waymo官方test，每scene一次固定噪声；各外部模型非同底座训练预算。NAVSIM action-head内部验证按log留出，但这些clip曾用于上游VLM微调；Waymo479validation既供RL reward又选checkpoint，选择分数in-sample，最终test未用于训练/选择。不能把公开test成绩称真实道路安全验证。

findings.title: 实际加速取决于target调用数：Thor Molmo请求3.55→0.70秒
findings.text: 表11 batch1，MolmoSpaces Thor total3552.7→703.3ms约5.05倍、Spark3356.5→649.9约5.16倍、H100516.1→142.3约3.63倍；均含表列视觉/prefill/解码/动作阶段均值。Thor纯解码3107.6→258.2ms约12倍，不是25倍。NAVSIM Thor1842.5→534.4ms，Waymo H100617.3→136.6ms。表12 DFlash轨迹平均仅2.2tokens/target-pass、文字5.5；VFlash一次提交53预测位置，drafter12.9ms仍需target68.4ms完成特征。target没有消失，收益来自摊薄其调用，长块也有长度成本。

findings.title: 计时是阶段均值相加，排除系统外输入输出并依赖定制部署
findings.text: 测量用CUDA events含host launch gap，total=sum(stage means)，其他阶段均值在decoders间共享，解码分别profile；非整请求wall-clock尾分布。排除model load/build/capture/warmup、图像载入、仪表模块外CPU预处理及detokenization；Molmo AR来自早期output-only engine profile而VFlash含all-layer feature completion。Thor/Spark/H100各有不同定制TensorRT-Edge-LLM版本与kernel，FP16权重/KV无量化，跨硬件不代表通用开箱性能。Thor robotics24records×10passes、Spark/H100仅24records一遍、driving5records×10，均未给p95/p99或功耗。

findings.title: 性能协议预先提供工具调用，质量用五步动作头、计时用十步
findings.text: 方法支持AR文字生成schema工具调用；但E.1所有计时decoder共用预给JSON、已知primitive长度，驾驶只profile primitive，未测自主选schema/长度的全部代价。Driving latency把head展开10DDIM步以对齐Qwen-Drive，而表8质量用5步，不能把速度和质量拼成同一未经说明的运行配置。Fast-dDrive665ms取自其论文、未在本栈实测。论文所有控制/驾驶结果为仿真或数据benchmark，无真实机器人闭环、持续传感-执行延迟与schema失配外推验证；“一遍草稿”不等于整个感知到动作只一遍网络。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：轨迹的低置信回退能否改善格式正确但空间错误的尾部？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：少量schema有效但几何错误的轨迹可由校准后的草稿置信度识别，并在保留大部分速度收益时降低空间长尾误差。先冻结同一robot target–drafter和全部训练权重，在按episode隔离的开发集校准每primitive的置信分数及回退阈值；测试比较全直接FPD、原DFlash、校准后按整块回退AR、以及随机同回退比例对照。固定schema、点数、上下文和精度；先用InternA1/AgiBot同记录做配对，记录ADE/FDE均值与p95/p99、SR@5、schema通过率、回退比例、请求wall-clock p50/p95/p99和target总调用数，再冻结同一动作策略做仿真计划替换诊断，单列分布变化。计时包含工具调用、特征完成与detokenization，驾驶若扩展则速度/质量采用相同DDIM步数。至少3搜索/运行seed，置信阈值不看test。若置信回退不比随机相同比例更改善长尾，或其调用开销吃掉主要延迟收益，则推翻这种选择性回退可用的假设；若仅框有效而轨迹无效，结论限于基元类型。实验未执行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白或保证正确性的验证器。

frontier_brief.title: VFlash：视觉基元整块预测，跳过坐标逐token一致性验证
frontier_brief.change_type: 推理与训练 · 结构化视觉规划
frontier_brief.delta: 用标注空间目标训练五层drafter，按schema一次预测整条视觉轨迹；格式有效就整块接受，target仅完成特征/缓存，普通文字仍投机验证。
frontier_brief.before: DFlash对每个坐标要求与AR目标逐token一致，微小bin差异也截断接受；Thor轨迹段仅平均提交2.2tokens/target-pass。
frontier_brief.after: VFlash整块提交十点2D+3D计划；同target在AgiBot联合轨迹ADE0.105→0.041m，Thor Molmo推理阶段总均值3552.7→703.3ms。
frontier_brief.relevance: 空间预测若可按几何误差评价，应考虑直接训练并行基元解码器，而非把AR token一致当质量上限；先按基元类型验证尾部精度和回退成本，再决定采用。
frontier_brief.caveat: 额外537M drafter需训练，视觉路径非无损分布保持。Dense200直接接受mean F1掉约21点；密集运动有指标退化。Molmo成功率在暂停仿真下测得，计时工具JSON预给、部分阶段均值共享；无真机闭环。
frontier_brief.question: 对schema正确但空间误差大的轨迹做校准置信回退，能否保留速度同时改善长尾？

passages.section: Scale : Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
passages.location: Scale : Real-Time Latent Communication for Cyber-Physical Agents
passages.text: Latent communication enables agents to collaborate efficiently by directly exchanging intermediate model representations rather than raw sensor data or text messages. Existing approaches, however, are primarily designed for LLM agents and do not consider the bandwidth constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines faced by cyber-physical agents. In this work, we propose Scale , a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Motivated by the spatio-temporal continuity of the physical world, Scale matches tokens across consecutive latent messages using similarity scores to identify reusable information and avoid redundant transmission. It then profiles the semantic gain and communication cost of transmitting different amounts of latent information. Based on these profiles, Scale employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which pending messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send, subject to available bandwidth and task deadlines. We evaluate Scale across three cyber-physical benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions and heterogeneous task deadlines. Our results show that Scale significantly improves both task performance and on-time delivery in bandwidth-constrained networks. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SCALE-4E80/ .

Communication is fundamental to cyber-physical agents. Individual agents often possess only partial observations or complementary capabilities, and therefore must exchange information with one another to accomplish diverse cyber-physical tasks ( Patel et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) . However, transmitting raw sensor observations incurs substantial communication overhead, while natural-language communication introduces additional computational overhead from generating text at the sender and interpreting it at the receiver. These limitations make conventional communication inefficient for real-time multi-agent systems.

Latent communication has emerged as a potential “AI language”, allowing agents to directly exchange hidden states or intermediate representations to improve efficiency ( Du et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . However, existing methods are primarily designed for LLM-based agents and focus on reducing model-side computation, with limited consideration of communication bandwidth and task deadlines. Meanwhile, communication-efficient collaborative-perception methods consider bandwidth and delay ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) , but primarily focus on task-specific perception rather than multiple concurrent CPS tasks sharing a bandwidth-constrained link. Thus, latent communication for CPS agents under practical network constraints and heterogeneous task deadlines remains largely underexplored.

We propose Scale , a real-time latent communication method tailored for cyber-physical agents. Scale exploits the spatiotemporal continuity of the physical world to reuse latent information already available at the receiver, reducing redundant transmission. It employs a real-time scheduler that jointly determines which messages to transmit and how many latent tokens to send based on semantic gain, available bandwidth, and task deadlines, thereby improving both task utility and message on-time delivery. In addition, Scale is lightweight and operates on latent tokens produced by existing modality encoders without modifying the underlying models, supporting different sensory modalities and downstream CPS tasks.

Designing Scale addresses three technical challenges. First, spatiotemporal variation makes it difficult to determine what information has actually changed. Physical observations often evolve continuously, but object, agent, or viewpoint motion can make fixed-position latent comparisons overestimate motion for semantic change. Scale therefore performs semantic change evaluation by matching current latent tokens against the receiver’s acknowledged latent state and measuring change relative to their best correspondences. Second, the amount of latent information to transmit must adapt to each message. The semantic gain from transmitting additional latent tokens varies across messages, making a fixed transmission size inefficient. Scale therefore performs utility–cost profiling for each message, ranking latent tokens by semantic change and characterizing the cumulative semantic gain and communication cost at different transmission sizes to guide real-time scheduling. Third, limited and time-varying bandwidth must be allocated across messages with heterogeneous deadlines. Allocating more latent tokens to one message increases its semantic gain but may delay other messages beyond their deadlines. Scale therefore employs a real-time scheduler that greedily allocates latent tokens based on marginal semantic gain per communication cost, while maintaining deadline feasibility for all selected messages under earliest-deadline-first (EDF) ordering.

We implement and evaluate Scale on CooperScene Wu et al. (2026) , OPV2V Xu et al. (2022c) , and LIBERO Liu et al. (2023a) , covering autonomous driving and robotic manipulation benchmarks. We further conduct a physical spider robot case study. Our evaluation considers constrained bandwidth, time-varying link capacity, and background traffic, with heterogeneous task deadlines. We compare Scale against full latent transmission, uniform compression, and four state-of-the-art methods Xu et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2022b) ; Hu et al. (2022) ; Mukhopadhyay et al. (2026) . Our results show that Scale achieves the highest task performance in almost all settings while significantly improving on-time delivery rates (see Fig. 1 for an example).
We make the following contributions:

We identify and formulate the problem of real-time latent communication for CPS agents, where latent messages from multiple downstream tasks with heterogeneous deadlines share a bandwidth-constrained communication link, a setting not adequately addressed by existing methods.

We propose Scale , a real-time latent communication method that combines spatiotemporal latent reuse, utility–cost profiling, and deadline-aware scheduling to improve both task utility and message on-time delivery under bandwidth constraints.

We implement and evaluate Scale across three CPS benchmarks and a physical spider robot case study under diverse network conditions, demonstrating its effectiveness in both benchmark evaluations and a physical robotic system.
Figure 1: Comparison between Scale and other latent communication baselines on the OPV2V benchmark at 15 Mbps. Scale achieves the best mIoU scores and message on-time rates.

Recent LLM-based latent communication methods enable multi-agent systems to exchange latent representations, such as hidden states or KV caches, to reduce model inference and computation overhead ( Du et al., 2026 ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . These approaches primarily focus on efficient latent interaction and reducing model-side computation, with limited consideration of the underlying communication network. Scale instead studies latent communication over resource-constrained networks, a practical setting for cyber-physical agents.

Communication-efficient collaborative perception has been extensively studied in cyber-physical systems, where agents exchange intermediate features to improve shared perception ( Wang et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2021 ) . Existing methods explore when, where, and how agents should communicate through communication triggering ( Liu et al., 2020 ) , spatial feature selection ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , and feature sparsification ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . Other work improves robustness to communication delay and asynchrony ( Lei et al., 2022 ; Wei et al., 2023 ) or exploits temporal redundancy to reduce repeated transmission ( Mukhopadhyay et al., 2026 ) . Recent methods further improve the perception–communication tradeoff through adaptive feature selection ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . In the semantic communication literature, existing task-oriented methods tailor transmitted representations according to downstream task utility ( Xie et al., 2021 ; Gündüz et al., 2022 ) , jointly allocate communication resources under bandwidth constraints ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Cai et al., 2025 ) , and account for communication latency ( Sagduyu and Erpek, 2026 ) . However, these methods are primarily designed for individual perception or communication tasks, rather than the broader CPS setting where multiple downstream tasks with heterogeneous deadlines coexist and share a bandwidth-constrained communication link.

Following common settings in prior works ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) , we consider cyber-physical agents that locally encode their observations and exchange latent representations over a communication link. For an observation x i x_{i} , a local encoder produces a latent representation:

where each h i , j ∈ ℝ d h_{i,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a fixed-dimensional latent token, and N i N_{i} is the token length. Encoders may be modality-specific, e.g., for image, audio, or text inputs. Within each agent, multiple downstream tasks may coexist and generate latent messages that share the same communication link.

We denote the available rate of the communication link by R ⁡ ( t ) R(t) , which may vary over time. Within each agent, multiple latent messages from different tasks compete for the same communication resources. Scale consists of three stages: semantic change evaluation , utility–cost profiling , and real-time scheduling . In the first two stages, it identifies latent information that is new relative to the receiver’s acknowledged state, and characterizes the semantic benefit and communication cost of different transmission lengths. The scheduler then combines these profiles with available bandwidth and task deadlines to determine which message to transmit and how many latent tokens to send. We demonstrate the system flow of Scale in Fig. 2

Figure 2: Scale system design. Semantic change evaluation and utility–cost profiling guide the real-time scheduler in jointly selecting messages and transmission sizes under bandwidth and deadline constraints.

Physical observations often evolve continuously, creating substantial redundancy between consecutive observations. In this stage, we aim to measure such semantic redundancy and identify the nonredundant information to transmit. A key challenge is that directly comparing two latent messages token by token can be unreliable because their corresponding observations may be misaligned due to object or viewpoint motion. Scale therefore first establishes token-level correspondences between the current latent message and the receiver’s acknowledged latent state before quantifying their semantic changes.
Therefore, for each current token h i , j h_{i,j} , we first find the most similar token in the receiver’s acknowledged latent state:

Let c i , j c_{i,j} denote the corresponding maximum cosine similarity. We then quantify the semantic change of token h i , j h_{i,j} as:

Consequently, highly similar tokens receive small change scores, while tokens with low similarity receive larger scores. We further use a similarity threshold τ \tau to determine whether the matched receiver-side token can be reused: a match is reusable only when c i , j ≥ τ c_{i,j}\geq\tau . Matching is performed against the receiver’s acknowledged state to ensure that only information confirmed to be available at the receiver is reused.

The semantic change scores obtained above capture the amount of new information carried by individual latent tokens. In this stage, we further characterize the trade-off between semantic gain and communication cost at different transmission sizes K K , where K ≤ N i K\leq N_{i} denotes the number of latent tokens transmitted for message i i .

Specifically, we prioritize tokens with larger semantic change scores by sorting them in descending order according to s i , j s_{i,j} . We define the cumulative semantic gain and communication cost as:

U i ​ ( K ) \displaystyle U_{i}(K) = ∑ k = 1 K s i , ( k ) , \displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{K}s_{i,(k)}, (5) B i ​ ( K ) \displaystyle B_{i}(K) = K ​ b tok + B i meta ​ ( K ) , \displaystyle=Kb_{\mathrm{tok}}+B_{i}^{\mathrm{meta}}(K),

where s i , ( k ) s_{i,(k)} denotes the k k -th largest semantic change score, b tok b_{\mathrm{tok}} is the serialized size of one latent token, and B i meta ​ ( K ) B_{i}^{\mathrm{meta}}(K) accounts for the metadata required to interpret the transmission, including token indices, correspondence mappings, and the reference-state version. The resulting pairs ( U i ​ ( K ) , B i ​ ( K ) ) (U_{i}(K),B_{i}(K)) characterize the available transmission choices for message i i . As a result, a larger K K generally preserves more new semantic information but incurs greater communication cost.

In the final stage, the scheduler takes as input the utility–cost profiles { ( U i ​ ( K ) , B i ​ ( K ) ) } \{(U_{i}(K),B_{i}(K))\} and task deadlines of all messages in 𝒬 ⁡ ( t ) \mathcal{Q}(t) , together with the current link rate R ⁡ ( t ) R(t) . Based on this information, it determines the transmission size K i K_{i} for each message and their transmission order.

Scale first determines the transmission size K i K_{i} for each pending message. Following the scheduling objective in Section 3 , we employ a greedy algorithm to maximize semantic gain under the deadline constraints. Specifically, we initialize K i = 0 K_{i}=0 for each pending message and iteratively allocate tokens one at a time. Suppose message i i has already been allocated K i K_{i} tokens. The marginal semantic gain per communication cost of adding its next token k = K i + 1 k=K_{i}+1 is:

At each step, the scheduler considers the next token of every pending message and prioritizes the one with the largest ρ i , k \rho_{i,k} , subject to the message deadlines. To check deadline feasibility, let π 1 , … , π m \pi_{1},\ldots,\pi_{m} denote the currently selected messages ordered by earliest deadline first (EDF). The completion time of message π q \pi_{q} is estimated as:
C π q = t + ∑ ℓ = 1 q 8 ​ B π ℓ ​ ( K π ℓ ) R ⁡ ( t ) . C_{\pi_{q}}=t+\sum_{\ell=1}^{q}\frac{8B_{\pi_{\ell}}(K_{\pi_{\ell}})}{R(t)}. (7)

An allocation is feasible only if C π q ≤ d π q C_{\pi_{q}}\leq d_{\pi_{q}} for all q = 1 , … , m q=1,\ldots,m . Among all feasible token increments, the scheduler selects the one with the largest ρ i , k \rho_{i,k} , updates K i ← K i + 1 K_{i}\leftarrow K_{i}+1 , and repeats this process until no additional token can be allocated without violating a deadline.

The resulting K i K_{i} values determine the transmission size of each message, where K i = 0 K_{i}=0 indicates that the message is not selected. Messages with K i > 0 K_{i}>0 are transmitted in EDF order. In this way, Scale prioritizes semantic gain relative to communication cost while using task deadlines as feasibility constraints on both message selection and transmission size. After transmission, the receiver updates its latent state with the received tokens and reuses matched tokens from its previous state according to the correspondences established in the semantic change evaluation stage. The receiver then acknowledges the updated state, allowing the sender to maintain an accurate view of the receiver’s state for subsequent communication. The detailed scheduling algorithm can be found in Appendix 1 .

We evaluate Scale on three cyber-physical benchmarks: CooperScene Wu et al. (2026) , OPV2V Xu et al. (2022c) , and LIBERO Liu et al. (2023a) . CooperScene is a real-world cooperative autonomous-driving benchmark with LiDAR and camera observations from vehicles and roadside infrastructure. OPV2V is a simulated cooperative-perception benchmark with LiDAR and camera observations from multiple vehicles. LIBERO provides language-conditioned robotic manipulation tasks with visual observations and robot states. These benchmarks cover different CPS use cases, and their detailed descriptions are provided in Appendix B .

On CooperScene, we evaluate concurrent 3D object detection and 5-sec trajectory prediction tasks, with deadlines of 100 ms and 200 ms. We use CoBEVT Xu et al. (2022a) for detection and a frozen, pretrained Motion Transformer (MTR) Shi et al. (2022) for prediction. On OPV2V, we evaluate concurrent 3D object detection and BEV semantic segmentation using the LiDAR-based detection and camera-based segmentation variants of CoBEVT, each with its own pretrained weights. Their deadlines are 100 ms and 200 ms, respectively. On LIBERO, we evaluate object manipulation using SmolVLA Shukor et al. (2025) , with the deadline determined by the time remaining before the robot exhausts its buffered actions, plus reserving 100 ms for inference and 10 ms for returning actions. Across all benchmarks, a sensing agent sends latent features to another agent or remote server for inference.

For each benchmark, we evaluate four fixed-bandwidth settings and one time-varying setting. The fixed rates correspond to different fractions (e.g., 20%, 50%) of the average bandwidth required for full latent transmission in each benchmark. In the time-varying setting, the link alternates between low and high rates every 2 seconds. In all settings, we account for both queueing and transmission time when computing communication delay. More detailed network settings, including the bandwidth values for each benchmark, are provided in Table 5 in the Appendix.

Table 2: OPV2V results on 528 detection jobs and 265 segmentation jobs. AP denotes average precision, mIoU denotes mean IoU score, and OT denotes on-time rate (%).

We compare Scale with Full-send , which transmits the complete latent message, and Uniform compression , which uniformly selects a fraction of latent features for transmission based on the available bandwidth. On CooperScene, we additionally compare with CoSDH ( Xu et al., 2025 ) and V2X-ViT ( Xu et al., 2022b ) . On OPV2V, we additionally compare with CooperTrim ( Mukhopadhyay et al., 2026 ) and Where2comm ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . All baseline methods use earliest-deadline-first (EDF) transmission ordering.

We evaluate Scale in terms of task utility and message on-time rate. Task utility measures downstream task performance, while on-time rate is the percentage of messages received before their deadlines.

We use task-specific performance metrics to evaluate the two tasks on CooperScene. For the 3D object detection task, we report average precision (AP) and the message on-time rate, where AP is computed using an intersection-over-union (IoU) threshold of 0.5 to match predicted boxes to ground-truth boxes. For the trajectory prediction task, we report task success and the message on-time rate, where task success is the percentage of prediction targets for which at least one of six predicted trajectories is within 2 m of the ground-truth position.

Table 1 presents the results. The results show that Scale achieves the highest detection AP and prediction task success across all settings. In particular, for 3D object detection at 20 Mbps, Scale achieves 51.53 AP, exceeding the strongest baseline, CoSDH, by 20.19 points. It also delivers 80.36% of detection messages on time, compared with 48.02% for CoSDH. For trajectory prediction under fixed bandwidth, Scale maintains task success between 60.82% and 60.85%, while delivering at least 99.82% of prediction messages on time. Under varying bandwidth, Scale achieves 56.09 detection AP and 60.81% prediction task success, with detection and prediction on-time rates of 94.52% and 99.71%, respectively.

Similarly, we use task-specific performance metrics to evaluate the two tasks on OPV2V. For the 3D object detection task, we report AP and the message on-time rate. We evaluate BEV semantic segmentation using mean intersection-over-union (mIoU) and also report its message on-time rate, where mIoU averages the IoU between predicted and ground-truth regions across semantic classes.

Table 2 presents the results. The results show that Scale achieves the highest segmentation mIoU and segmentation on-time rate across all settings, and the highest detection AP except at 8 Mbps. In this setting, Scale achieves 83.41 AP, slightly below CooperTrim’s 84.25 AP, while delivering 37.74% of detection messages on time, compared with 0.73% for CooperTrim. For BEV semantic segmentation, the largest mIoU improvement over the strongest baseline occurs at 15 Mbps, where Scale achieves 47.14 mIoU, exceeding Where2comm by 9.97 points. It also delivers 97.09% of segmentation messages on time, compared with 7.82% for Where2comm.

Our LIBERO evaluation focuses on a single language-conditioned robotic manipulation task. We report task success, defined as the percentage of episodes completed within 280 steps, and the communication on-time rate.

Table 3 presents the results. The results show that Scale achieves the highest task success and on-time rate across all settings. At the lowest tested bandwidth of 3.4 Mbps, Scale completes 44.44% of episodes, while both baselines fail all episodes. In particular, Uniform compression achieves a similar on-time rate (74.47% versus 77.76% for Scale ), showing that timely delivery alone does not ensure task success. The largest task success improvement over the strongest baseline occurs at 5.0 Mbps, where Scale achieves 86.67% task success, compared with 24.44% for Full-send and 0.00% for Uniform compression. Its communication on-time rate also reaches 84.57%, exceeding both baselines.

We measure message lateness as L i = C i − d i L_{i}=C_{i}-d_{i} , where C i C_{i} and d i d_{i} are the completion time and deadline of message i i , respectively. On-time messages have L i ≤ 0 L_{i}\leq 0 , while delayed messages have L i > 0 L_{i}>0 . To better illustrate real-time performance, Fig. 3 shows the lateness distributions for CooperScene at 20 Mbps for both object detection and trajectory prediction tasks. In the figure, the cumulative percentage at zero gives the on-time rate, which is computed over all generated messages, including undelivered ones.

The results show that Scale delivers 80.36% of detection messages and 100.00% of prediction messages on time, compared with 68.64% and 94.44% for Uniform compression. Uniform compression achieves the highest on-time rates among the baselines at this bandwidth, but its task utility is significantly lower than that of Scale . We also observe a steep rise in the detection CDF just before the deadline for the object detection task, indicating that many messages complete shortly before their deadlines. This behavior is consistent with Scale ’s greedy allocation of available bandwidth to maximize semantic gain under deadline constraints. The complete distributions for all three benchmarks and bandwidth settings appear in Appendix C (Figures 8 , 9 , and 10 ). Across these results, Scale improves on-time delivery in every tested setting and achieves the highest on-time rate among all methods in most settings.

We conduct a hardware-in-the-loop case study using a Raspberry Pi-based spider robot, as shown in Fig. 4 . The robot is equipped with a camera and an ultrasonic sensor and performs two tasks: object detection and distance measurement on a fixed robot patrolling route. The patrolling route is a 55.4-second walk through a miniature city containing objects such as small road signs, pedestrian figures, and buildings. Among the two tasks, object detection is time-sensitive, with a communication deadline of 1,000 ms, while ultrasonic distance measurements generate background traffic over the shared link. We compare Scale against two baselines: Raw RGB, which transmits uncompressed images, and Full-send, which transmits complete intermediate latent features. We evaluate the system in three bandwidth settings, including 1, 2, and 8 Mbps.

We report task success and message on-time rates. Table 4 presents the results. We observe that Scale substantially outperforms both baselines under constrained bandwidth. Specifically, at 1 and 2 Mbps, both baselines achieve zero detection success, whereas Scale achieves success rates of 77.62% and 91.67%, respectively, with on-time rates of 100% and 96.43%. At 8 Mbps, all methods achieve 100% detection success and on-time delivery. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of Scale in preserving timely detection performance on a physical robotic platform under limited bandwidth.

In this work, we present Scale , a real-time latent communication method for cyber-physical agents. By exploiting spatiotemporal continuity, Scale avoids retransmitting latent information already available at the receiver. To support timely communication, we design a real-time scheduler that jointly selects messages and transmission sizes based on semantic gain, available bandwidth, and task deadlines. We evaluate Scale on three benchmarks and conduct a physical robot case study. The results demonstrate improved task performance and high message on-time rates under constrained and varying network conditions. These findings highlight Scale as an effective and efficient method for meeting the communication and timing requirements of CPS agents.

While Scale significantly improves bandwidth efficiency and supports real-time scheduling for CPS agents, it has two limitations. First, the communication savings of Scale depend on spatiotemporal redundancy in latent representations. However, observations in the physical world can change abruptly, which may reduce the amount of reusable information and increase the communication required to maintain task performance. Second, the scheduling algorithm assesses deadline feasibility using the current link rate. However, this design cannot handle unexpected bandwidth decreases that occur on timescales shorter than the minimum scheduling interval, which may affect message timeliness before the scheduler can adapt.
Algorithm 1 Greedy Deadline-Feasible Semantic Allocation

We provide the detailed scheduling procedure used by Scale in Algorithm 1 . We define U i ​ ( 0 ) = B i ​ ( 0 ) = 0 U_{i}(0)=B_{i}(0)=0 for all messages i i . Our design separates semantic prioritization from deadline feasibility. At each iteration, it considers one additional token for every pending message and admits only increments for which all currently selected messages remain deadline-feasible under EDF ordering. Among these feasible increments, it selects the one with the largest marginal semantic gain per communication cost. The procedure terminates when no additional token can be admitted without causing a deadline violation.

CooperScene Wu et al. (2026) is a real-world cooperative autonomy benchmark collected using three connected vehicles and one roadside unit. It provides synchronized LiDAR, camera, and GNSS/IMU observations, together with C-V2X communication measurements. The dataset contains approximately 59,000 LiDAR frames, 53,000 image frames, and 344,000 annotated 3D bounding boxes. Its scenes cover intersections, freeway ramps, local streets, and parking lots, supporting cooperative 3D object detection and motion prediction.

OPV2V Xu et al. (2022c) is a simulated cooperative perception benchmark generated using OpenCDA and CARLA. It contains 73 scenes across eight CARLA towns and a digital replica of Culver City, with 11,464 frames and 232,913 annotated 3D vehicle bounding boxes. Each frame includes observations from two to seven connected vehicles, each equipped with a 64-channel LiDAR, four RGB cameras providing a combined 360-degree view, and GPS/IMU sensors. The dataset supports cooperative 3D object detection, BEV semantic segmentation, tracking, and prediction.

LIBERO Liu et al. (2023a) is a benchmark for knowledge transfer in language-conditioned robotic manipulation. It contains 130 tasks organized into four suites: LIBERO-Spatial, LIBERO-Object, and LIBERO-Goal, each containing 10 tasks, and LIBERO-100, containing 100 tasks. The suites vary spatial relationships, object identities, and manipulation goals to evaluate different forms of knowledge transfer. The benchmark provides language instructions, RGB observations from workspace and wrist cameras, and robot proprioceptive states.
Table 5 presents the detailed experimental settings for our evaluations on these benchmarks, including the evaluated tasks, test set sizes, task rates, deadlines, and bandwidth configurations.

Figures 6 and 7 compare the detection results of Full-send and Scale against ground-truth annotations on CooperScene and OPV2V, respectively. Figure 5 illustrates a successful LIBERO manipulation episode with Scale . Figures 8 , 9 , and 10 present the message lateness CDFs for CooperScene, OPV2V, and LIBERO, respectively, under fixed and varying bandwidth settings.

Table 6 reports the computational overhead of Scale on CooperScene across five bandwidth settings. We measure runtime on an Intel Core i9-13900K using four CPU cores and four OpenBLAS threads. We report the overhead of the three design stages: semantic change evaluation, utility–cost profiling, and real-time scheduling, with the last stage also accounting for message preparation and state updates. Averaged over all generated detection and prediction messages, the total overhead remains below 1 ms per message across all settings, ranging from 0.813 to 0.884 ms. These results highlight the low computational overhead of Scale .

analysis.overview: SCALE在已有模型编码器与接收端推理之间加入通信层：按余弦近邻复用接收端已确认token，把变化分数转成不同消息长度的收益/字节曲线，再按边际收益与EDF可行性联合选消息和长度。它把通信时效与任务质量一起评估，比单独压缩比例更贴近共享链路决策。作者在协同感知、单任务LIBERO闭环和固定路线蜘蛛机器人上给出收益；但没有模块消融或多seed误差，变化分数未验证等于下游价值，低于1ms开销仅桌面CPU平均。适合跟进通信系统设计，尚不足以推出任意边端或突发网络下的硬实时保证。

findings.title: 从固定压缩量改成共享链路上的消息与长度联合选择
findings.text: 多任务潜在消息共享变化带宽链路；每条消息有截止期，超过期限按firm-deadline目标不贡献效用。优化变量既包含选哪条消息，也包含各自传多少token，而非只统一截短编码器输出。SCALE运行于已有模态编码器之上，作者声明无需修改底层模型；本轮实际评测是感知/操控模型的中间特征，不应外推成任意异构LLM隐藏状态互通。

findings.title: 先对齐接收端已确认状态，再决定哪些token可复用
findings.text: 对当前每个token，找接收端已确认潜在状态中余弦相似度最大的token；变化分数为1−最大余弦，相似度达到tau才可复用。这样允许物体或视角移动时跨位置对应，避免仅同位置比较把移动都当新信息。它是逐token最近邻，不是文中已证明的几何对齐或一一匹配；余弦变化也不是任务敏感性或幅值差异的直接度量。后两点是依据公式的解释边界，作者未以专门实验量化。

findings.title: 收益是变化分数的前缀和，成本需包含映射与版本元数据
findings.text: 把token按变化降序排列，U_i(K)为前K个变化分数之和，B_i(K)=K×序列化token字节数+元数据；元数据包括token索引、对应映射和参考状态版本。这里所谓语义收益是余弦变化代理，没有用下游任务损失或成功概率拟合效用，也没有证明不同任务特征的变化分数可直接公平比较。方法公式纳入元数据是重要设计，但正文未给逐基准实测元数据/ACK占比或不同长度的字节分布，不能凭图示KB数字推算真实压缩比。

findings.title: 逐token贪心分配，并检查所有已选消息的EDF可行性
findings.text: 所有K从0开始，每轮考察各消息的下一个token，以增加的U除以增加的B排序；试加后按EDF重排已选消息，使用当前R(t)计算每个前缀完成时间t+sum(8B/R)。只有所有已选消息都在deadline内的增量才可选，直到再无可行增量，随后按EDF传输。附录算法1确认为每轮重新形成可行候选集合，而非只检查被加token的那条消息。此为贪心启发式，文中无全局最优性或近似比证明；基于当前速率的可行性也不是未来链路的保证。

findings.title: 复用依赖接收确认，协议正确性与链路预测仍有边界
findings.text: 接收端用新token更新状态，未更新部分按已建立对应复用旧token，随后确认新状态；发送端仅以已确认状态作为后续参考，减少把未收到内容当缓存的风险。论文成本项包含参考版本，但未详细说明丢包、ACK丢失/乱序、重连、首次无参考时初始化、以及预算不足而未发送且不满足复用阈值的token如何处理；本轮未审计实现，不能声称这些条件已解决或一定有bug。当前速率估算来不及应对短于调度间隔的骤降，是作者明确承认的限制。

findings.title: CooperScene有任务–时效联合收益，也有非最优准时率

findings.text: SmolVLA执行一个语言条件任务，每法每带宽45回合，280步内完成计成功；图5展示拿汤罐放入篮子的单回合。机器人20Hz，上传期限由动作缓冲剩余时间决定，并预留100ms推理与10ms动作返回。3.4Mbps下SCALE成功44.44%、准时77.76%，Uniform成功0%、准时74.47%，支持按时到达不等于保留有效信息；5Mbps成功86.67%，Full-send24.44%、Uniform0%，约为39/45对11/45和0/45。变带宽3.4/20Mbps时SCALE100%成功、89.28%准时，但这不是LIBERO全套或多任务泛化统计，亦无重复训练seed/置信区间。

findings.title: 蜘蛛机器人验证受限链路检测，不是导航能力或碰撞率测试
findings.text: 树莓派蜘蛛机器人沿55.4秒固定路线走过微缩城市，相机检测与超声背景流量共用链路；检测通信期限1000ms。表4在1/2Mbps时SCALE检测成功77.62/91.67%、准时100/96.43%，原始RGB和全潜在发送两基线都是0；8Mbps全部100%。这说明受限链路感知在硬件在环场景可工作，但没有给检测成功的严格匹配阈值、评测消息/事件分母、重复路线次数或误差范围，也没有闭环自主导航、避碰或控制稳定性结果。不能把此检测百分比描述成路线任务完成率。

findings.title: 通信层平均开销低于1ms，仅针对指定桌面配置
findings.text: 表6在CooperScene测SCALE三阶段每消息平均开销0.813–0.884ms，Intel i9-13900K用4CPU核与4个OpenBLAS线程；最后一阶段包含消息准备和状态更新。20Mbps分项0.355/0.130/0.374ms，总0.859ms。它不是编码器、下游推理、排队、网络和ACK整个链路的总延迟，也不是树莓派实测或尾延迟/最坏执行时间上界。论文网络延迟明确含排队与传输，但没有完整拆账证明所有控制路径开销均进入deadline核算，故部署前仍需端到端计时。

findings.title: 收益依赖时空冗余，骤变与消息淘汰会削弱硬实时解释
findings.text: 作者承认场景突变降低可复用信息，短于最小调度间隔的带宽骤降会使当前速率可行分配失效。主实验只给固定率及每2秒切换的链路，不是任意突发拥塞保证。准时率分母包括所有生成消息及未送达消息，CDF在deadline处的值才是OT，不能只按收到者统计；CDF未到100%可能包含未送达，不代表观测截断后必会交付。结果中大量消息在期限前集中完成说明余量很小，也提示需额外测试速率估计误差和计算抖动。

findings.title: 整系统对照尚未隔离复用、评分与调度各自贡献
findings.text: 全文实验包含完整方案对全发、均匀压缩及任务专用基线，没有关掉匹配、改同位置匹配、固定K、随机选token或只换调度器的组件消融。已有基线统一EDF有助于控制传输次序，却不能单独证明余弦变化评分或贪心长度分配各自是收益原因。正文/附录未给tau数值及敏感性、各模型token数量/维度/精度、缓存启动和替代规则的完整参数，基线自身模型/训练差异也未被统一消除。45回合仅LIBERO单任务，感知job/目标数量不是独立重复实验数量；表中无多seed波动或显著性检验。本轮未审计公开匿名代码，以上为论文正文证据边界，非断言代码一定缺失。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：收益来自跨位置复用还是联合长度调度？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在保留相同模型与EDF次序后，跨位置token匹配和按边际收益分配长度各自对任务质量–准时率前沿有独立贡献，而非仅仅少发送字节。仅做公开数据回放与LIBERO仿真，固定编码器/下游权重、token序列化、截止期、初始ACK状态和同一链路轨迹，采用2×2对照：余弦跨位置匹配或同位置匹配，贪心可行长度或校准固定长度；另加同字节随机token、无复用对照。每种条件匹配实际总字节（含索引、映射、版本和ACK），在低带宽及每2秒切换之外加入预先定义的100ms短时骤降与场景切换，至少5组随机消息/网络seed，LIBERO扩展多个任务且每任务至少45同初始状态回合。记录各任务AP/mIoU/闭环成功、所有生成消息OT、信息年龄、缓存重建误差、CPU/GPU耗时与p99端到端延迟；同时独立测余弦变化与真实任务损失增量相关性。若匹配字节后跨位置匹配或贪心长度的收益消失、低变化但关键token引发任务失败，或计算/ACK开销吞噬deadline余量，则推翻独立收益假设。实验未执行，不调用外部付费服务，不创建选题；未全面查新，不宣称研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: SCALE：复用已确认潜在token，联合选择消息与传输长度
frontier_brief.change_type: 推理系统 · 通信预算与截止期
frontier_brief.delta: 对当前token与接收端确认缓存做余弦匹配，用变化分数/字节建立不同长度选项；逐token贪心分配并检查所有已选消息的EDF完成期限，避免统一压缩比例。
frontier_brief.before: 全发或按带宽统一截短后再EDF，未同时利用跨位置缓存复用与每条消息不同的变化收益；准时到达也可能只送到不足以完成任务的信息。
frontier_brief.after: 无需修改底层模型的通信层，在协同感知与单任务LIBERO低带宽测试改善质量和多数准时率；桌面CPU测得0.813–0.884ms平均通信层计算开销，未证明边端最坏延迟。
frontier_brief.relevance: 多个感知/控制消息竞争同一链路时，可把“发谁、发多少、接收端已有多少”一起决策；评测应保留任务质量与所有生成消息准时率两个轴。
frontier_brief.caveat: 缺少组件消融/多seed误差，变化分数非真实任务效用；低带宽检测并非所有指标最优。LIBERO仅1任务，蜘蛛机器人固定路线检测，短时带宽骤降与缓存协议细节仍待核查。
frontier_brief.question: 匹配总字节和EDF次序后，跨位置复用与可变长度调度各能保留多少独立收益？

evidence.label: 协同感知对照
evidence.context: CoSDH→SCALE，CooperScene3936检测job，100ms期限；全部基线亦EDF。15Mbps时SCALE检测准时率反低于Uniform。

evidence.label: 质量与时效分开
evidence.context: Uniform→SCALE，SmolVLA、LIBERO单任务、每法45闭环回合；不能外推全套LIBERO。

evidence.label: 低带宽反例
evidence.context: OPV2V528检测job；SCALE准时37.74%，亦低于Uniform46.49%，并非所有任务指标都最高。

evidence.label: 有限开销证据
evidence.context: CooperScene，i9-13900K四核/四OpenBLAS线程，三阶段含状态更新；非树莓派、端到端或尾延迟。

mechanism.title: 以接收确认状态作匹配参考
mechanism.text: 每个当前token找缓存余弦近邻，相似度过阈值才能复用；发送对应映射/版本并由接收端确认更新。

mechanism.title: 按变化代理建立长度选项
mechanism.text: 变化=1−最大余弦，按降序前缀累计收益，成本包含token字节与元数据；不等同于直接优化任务成功概率。

mechanism.title: 逐次加token并检查全队列
mechanism.text: 选择边际变化收益/字节最大的可行增量，每次核所有已选消息EDF前缀deadline；仅当前速率模型可行，无全局最优或未来网络保证。

passages.section: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World
passages.location: PyRUA-REAL: Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning through RSI in the Real World
passages.text: Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra connect spatial reasoning with executable robot behavior, raising the question of how such agents can produce lasting improvements in robot capabilities from physical interaction. In this work, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) through real-world exploration, code refinement, and deployment using PyRUA-REAL, a framework in which coding agents retain interaction experience as persistent memory and reusable executable skills that inform subsequent exploration and improvement. Our empirical study places physical manipulation at the center of the improvement process, examining how agents collaborate, what kinds of execution feedback support effective code refinement, and how task specifications and previously acquired skills influence robustness and task transfer. We further investigate the efficiency and capability of the resulting programs when deployed without involving an online agent for decision-making. Across eight real-world tasks, PyRUA-REAL achieves an average success rate of 91.1%. In complementary evaluation on 42 tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark, it achieves an average success rate of 84.4%. This study provides empirical guidance for turning physical exploration into reusable robot skills that support continued improvement and robust, efficient deployment.

Figure 1 : PyRUA-REAL: Python-based Robot-Use Agents for Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning. (a) Coding agents iteratively explore, execute, diagnose, and revise robot programs, retaining rollout experience as persistent memory and reusable skills. (b) Development-stage improvements in success rate and cycle time, including reset, for stacking, tic-tac-toe, and Hanoi. (c) Real-world success rates aggregated over development attempts for seven agent-free skills. (d) RoboDojo performance compared with eight baselines, measured by success rate averaged equally over five capability groups. (e) The eight real-world tasks include semantic reasoning, precise manipulation, contact-rich manipulation, deformable object manipulation and long-horizon tasks.

Large language models can translate task instructions into robot programs that combine perception, spatial reasoning, and feedback control [ 11 , 6 ] . Coding agents powered by models such as GPT-6-Astra extend this interaction by executing code, inspecting observations, and adapting subsequent actions through execution feedback [ 16 ] . These capabilities make code a practical interface between high-level reasoning and physical behavior. They also raise a question beyond completing an individual task: How can coding agents turn physical interaction experience into robot capabilities that persist and improve across successive attempts?

Experience-based adaptation and iterative code modification offer ways to improve agents while keeping foundation model parameters fixed [ 15 , 24 ] . In robotics, recent work has explored skill and agent-harness evolution in simulation [ 18 ] , simulation-based practice followed by physical deployment [ 20 ] , and policy improvement through direct robot interaction [ 22 , 19 ] . Building on these developments, we study embodied recursive self-improvement (RSI) as a process in which execution experience informs code revisions and is retained as memory and reusable skills for subsequent exploration. Our focus is an empirical account of this process in real-world manipulation, tracing how capabilities are acquired, refined beyond first success, and converted into programs for deployment.

Physical exploration presents challenges at several levels. Agents must decide which experiments to run, which implementation details to revise, and when to reconsider the underlying approach. Repeated local changes may leave an unsuitable perception or control strategy intact. Execution feedback is also ambiguous: an apparent task failure can originate in motion, perception, or the procedure used to verify success. Moreover, success under one configuration does not establish robustness to changes in object positions, orientations, or task requirements. Retaining a successful implementation therefore raises further questions about its reuse on new tasks and its ability to operate without repeated online agent decisions. Understanding embodied RSI requires examining these aspects of the improvement process alongside task success.

We present PyRUA-REAL (Python-based Robot-Use Agent for Robot Exploration and Adaptive Learning) as an embodied RSI framework for this study (Figure 1 ). A researcher agent selects experimental objectives and technical approaches, while an engineer agent implements programs, executes robot trials, and diagnoses failures. Their interaction connects local code improvement with task-level reassessment. A persistent repository records environmental facts, attempted approaches, execution outcomes, and reusable implementations, allowing later experiments to build on earlier experience while model parameters remain fixed. For deployment, the resulting code can be frozen and executed without runtime language-model calls, while still responding to live observations through its perception, control, and recovery routines. This separation enables us to study both the process of developing robot capabilities and the behavior of the programs that retain them.

Our experiments cover eight manipulation tasks on a dual-arm Franka platform, spanning reasoning, long-horizon execution, precise contact, deformable objects, and bimanual coordination. Recorded development success averages 91.1% across tasks. These rates aggregate attempts across code revisions; frozen-program performance is evaluated separately. Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo tasks yields 84.82% success, averaged equally over five capability groups, compared with reported results of 50.35% for PyRUA-Lean and 22.48% for GPT-6-Astra. Our main contributions can be summarized as:

An empirical study of skill acquisition and continued improvement through real-world interaction. Across eight physical manipulation tasks, we trace how coding agents turn exploration experience into executable robot skills and improve them beyond first successful rollout, documenting gains and trade-offs in task completion, execution time, and placement precision across program revisions.

Case studies on the factors shaping embodied RSI. Through comparative experiments and diagnostic case studies, we examine how agent coordination, execution feedback, explicit task requirements, and previously acquired skills affect revision efficiency, robustness, and transfer to new tasks.

An evaluation of the resulting robot capabilities and their deployment costs. Real-world evaluations compare frozen programs with online agent execution, quantifying execution-time benefits and identifying situations that still require online assistance. Complementary evaluation on 42 RoboDojo tasks measures performance across five capability groups against reported baselines.

Our work lies at the intersection of programmatic robotic control and agent-driven self-improvement, aiming to enable robots to continuously improve their capabilities through real-world interaction. We review related research in LLM for robotic control, agentic RSI, and embodied RSI.

LLM for Robotic Control. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled robot control by composing perception, planning, and control primitives into executable programs [ 11 , 6 , 5 ] . Recent advances further explore direct agent-driven control [ 7 , 27 , 14 ] , as well as code-based approaches that improve action abstraction, execution feedback, and runtime efficiency [ 2 , 16 , 1 ] . Complementary approaches integrate programmatic skill representations with learned world and action models [ 12 ] . Agents can also propose structural priors that shape skill policy training and inform skill composition [ 8 ] . While online agent control offers flexible reasoning and adaptation, frequent model inference introduces computational overhead and latency. In contrast, executable programs enable efficient closed-loop control without continuous LLM intervention. Building on this paradigm, we employ coding agents to construct and progressively refine both reusable robot primitives and task-specific policies, while delegating high-frequency control to independently executable robot programs.

Agentic RSI. Recent research has explored improving LLM-based agents through accumulated experience and autonomous modification, without necessarily updating model parameters. Experience-driven approaches retain reflections, interaction histories, and reusable knowledge to improve subsequent decisions [ 15 , 28 ] . Beyond memory-based adaptation, agentic RSI methods optimize the agents’ underlying scaffolds, execution logic, and search procedures through iterative code modification and evaluation [ 24 , 4 , 23 , 26 ] . These approaches demonstrate how improvements can persist beyond individual attempts and benefit future problem-solving. Inspired by these developments, our work extends agentic self-improvement to physical interaction, where coding agents continuously accumulate execution-grounded knowledge and reusable control capabilities to improve subsequent robot policy generation and refinement.

Embodied Recursive Self-Improvement. Recent embodied RSI research leverages environmental feedback to autonomously improve robot policies, reusable skills, and agent capabilities. Simulation-centered approaches evolve skills and agent harnesses in virtual environments, sometimes followed by real-world transfer [ 18 , 20 , 17 ] . Other works investigate autonomous policy improvement through direct physical experimentation [ 22 , 19 ] , as well as reusable program libraries, hierarchical skill refinement, and persistent experience accumulation [ 13 , 21 , 3 , 10 ] . Building on these advances, our work emphasizes the complete process of exploration, improvement, and deployment in the real world, rather than treating physical robots merely as a final validation platform.

We study how executable robot policies improve through environment interaction while foundation model parameters remain fixed. Improvements persist as reusable skills and experience.
