passages.section: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
passages.location: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
passages.text: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

passages.section: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
passages.location: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
passages.text: Fig. 1 : Overview. Inspired by industrial applications, VABAR includes six manipulation task classes: (1) Tool Sorting, (2) Tool Hanging, (3) Gear Meshing, (4) Syringe Packing, (5) Cable Insertion, and (6) Cable Routing. The benchmark includes both single-arm and bimanual robot embodiments and evaluates manipulation under specific tiers of geometric and physical variations. VABAR is open access and runs on GPU workstations and on Isaac Lab Arena.

For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must solve Variational Automation (VA) tasks, where operational objectives and workspace persist with structured variations in objects, layouts, task parameters, and execution conditions across instances. In fixed automation , robots repeatedly execute carefully engineered programs in highly structured environments, often achieving high reliability and throughput but requiring substantial human effort to design, deploy, and retune when conditions change [ 1 ] . In comparison, generalist robotics aims to perform a broad range of open-ended tasks, but current model-free end-to-end approaches struggle to achieve the speed and reliability required for commercial and industrial adoption. VA tasks lie between fixed automation and fully generalist robotics.

Recent advances in agentic robotics provide a promising approach to implementing VA by combining the reliability and interpretability of classical robot programming with the adaptability of learned policies. Rather than directly mapping observations to low-level actions through a monolithic model-free policy, agentic robotic systems use multiple LLM agents to reason about task instances, generate and modify executable robot programs, and invoke perception, planning, and control modules named skills.

Existing robot manipulation benchmarks (e.g., LIBERO [ 2 ] , ManiSkill [ 3 ] , and SimplerEnv [ 4 ] ) evaluate the robustness and generalization of language-conditioned deep visuomotor policies by offering simulation environments, human-teleoperated training episodes, and success metrics across new scene configurations. Many of these have recently been saturated by systems that achieve very high success rates and they primarily focus on household pick-and-place tasks.

We introduce VABAR , a Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics . VABAR provides six application-oriented manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure settings: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. Each task is defined with a set of instances with explicit variation axes, difficulty levels, and success conditions. For each task, we provide a physics and photorealistic simulation environment, a set of generalizable skills to facilitate execution, and a human-authored reference solution expressed as a computation graph over the same skill library. The reference solution is executed with the same perception, planning, and execution stack available to coding agents.

We evaluate VABAR using GaP, an open agentic manipulation baseline [ 5 ] , and with Isaac Lab Arena to establish baselines and to study how performance scales with task difficulty and structured variation.
This paper makes 5 contributions:

Variational Automation task formulation. We introduce and formalize Variational Automation , a manipulation class between fixed automation and unconstrained general-purpose manipulation, in which persistent operational objectives must be achieved across a structured distribution of task instances.

Design principles for agentic robotics benchmarks. We define practical criteria for evaluating agentic systems, emphasizing accessibility, repeatability, controlled diversity, application relevance, physical realizability, resistance to saturation, and computational efficiency.

VABAR task definition We instantiate these principles in six application-oriented manipulation task classes—(1) tool sorting, (2) tool hanging, (3) gear meshing, (4) syringe packing, (5) cable insertion, and (6) cable routing—with standardized task variations, difficulty levels, success metrics, and support for single-arm Franka and bimanual YAM embodiments.

VABAR simulation, Agentic Skills and Human-authored solutions For each task, we provide a photorealistic simulation environment, 33 generalizable skills that facilitate solving the tasks, and a human-authored code solution.

Initial agentic manipulation baselines. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic robotic system and characterize performance as task complexity and instance variation increase, establishing reference results and identifying remaining challenges for agentic manipulation.

Robot manipulation benchmarking has roots in early efforts to evaluate robotic assembly. In its discussion of benchmark tests for comparing manipulators, the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology defines benchmark for robotics such as the Robot Characterization Testing report [ 6 ] references Nof and Paul’s work on planning robotic assembly [ 7 ] . The Cranfield Assembly Benchmark [ 8 ] provided a standardized physical assembly test, while YCB [ 9 ] later broadened evaluation through shared object sets and protocols. NIST assembly task boards [ 10 ] further standardized tests of insertion, fastening, and gear meshing. Alongside these physical benchmarks, reusable simulation suites emerged to evaluate manipulation algorithms and learned policies. Meta-World [ 11 ] and RLBench [ 12 ] provide diverse manipulation task suites, while ManiSkill [ 13 , 3 ] emphasizes generalization across manipulation skills and object geometries. CALVIN [ 14 ] studies long-horizon language-conditioned manipulation, and LIBERO [ 2 ] focuses on knowledge transfer and lifelong robot learning. VIMA-Bench [ 15 ] , ARNOLD [ 16 ] , and VLABench [ 17 ] further evaluate multimodal prompting, language grounding, and generalization. Beyond tabletop manipulation, BEHAVIOR [ 18 , 19 ] , RoboCasa [ 20 ] , and ManiSkill-HAB [ 21 ] consider household and mobile manipulation, while FurnitureBench [ 22 ] and RoboTwin [ 23 , 24 ] emphasize contact-rich, assembly, and bimanual tasks. RoboLab [ 25 ] provides language-guided scene and variation generation and can perform sensitivity analysis of robot policies, and RoboDojo [ 26 ] provides a comprehensive simulation and real evaluation to robot Vision-Language-Action policies. These benchmarks enable systematic evaluation across increasingly diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments, but are primarily organized around general-purpose manipulation, household activities, individual skills, or generalization across distinct tasks. VABAR focuses on application-oriented automation, where a persistent operational objective must be achieved across structured variations of the same task class over time.

passages.section: II-B Robustness and Variation in Manipulation Evaluation
passages.location: II-B Robustness and Variation in Manipulation Evaluation
passages.text: A growing class of benchmarks explicitly evaluates robustness under controlled variation and distribution shift. LIBERO-Plus [ 27 ] introduces perturbations across object layouts, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, language instructions, lighting, textures, and sensor noise; LIBERO-PRO [ 28 ] varies manipulated objects, initial states, task instructions, and environments; and LIBERO-X [ 29 ] evaluates increasingly challenging spatial, object, and instruction-level shifts. Rather than treating variation as a perturbation around a nominal task, VABAR defines structured variation as an intrinsic part of a Variational Automation task: a persistent operational objective is paired with an expected distribution of variation in objects, geometry, layout, task parameters, and execution conditions. Success therefore requires reliable performance across the intended operating range of an automation application, where variation is expected rather than anomalous.

passages.section: II-C Agentic Robotics and Executable Robot Policies
passages.location: II-C Agentic Robotics and Executable Robot Policies
passages.text: Recent work has explored robotic systems in which foundation models reason over task instances, invoke external tools, and generate executable robot behaviors. Code-as-Policies [ 30 ] demonstrated that language models can compose perception and control APIs into executable programs, while subsequent agentic approaches extend this paradigm toward task decomposition, planning, tool use, execution feedback, and iterative refinement. CaP-X [ 31 ] extends this paradigm by systematically evaluating and improving coding agents for robot manipulation, emphasizing executable policy generation across diverse manipulation tasks. Recent approaches iteratively improve robot programs through feasibility checking and execution feedback. GaP [ 5 ] operates offline; it explicitly represents policies as computation graphs and refines their structure and parameters through parallel simulation rehearsal and generates ROS2-like graph for repeated online execution. ENPIRE [ 32 ] extends agentic policy improvement to repeated real-world trials, and ASPIRE [ 33 ] accumulates reusable skills through iterative program repair and exploration.

passages.section: II-C Agentic Robotics and Executable Robot Policies
passages.location: II-C Agentic Robotics and Executable Robot Policies
passages.text: Agentic robotics is particularly relevant to Variational Automation because agentic systems can retain the interpretability and modularity of classical robot programming while adapting behavior across task instances. However, comparing such systems is difficult because they may differ substantially in internal representations, tools, perception interfaces, planning methods, and controllers. VABAR evaluates externally measurable task objectives and structured variation distributions rather than prescribing a particular agent architecture, enabling generated-code, computation-graph, tool-use, learned-policy, and hybrid systems to be compared under common conditions.

passages.section: II-C Agentic Robotics and Executable Robot Policies
passages.location: II-C Agentic Robotics and Executable Robot Policies
passages.text: Fig. 2 : Overview of the VABAR evaluation framework. Left: Tasks are specified by initial and goal configurations, an asset library, and robot definitions. Top right: Admissible task variations span objects, arrangements, and positions, with examples at two levels. Bottom right: Robot policies are evaluated across diverse manipulation tasks, including object sorting, tool hanging, gear assembly, insertion, and cable routing.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 1. Relevance to agentic robotics. The benchmark should support evaluating agents that construct, test, and revise robot programs from task specifications. It should provide documented robot and tool interfaces for composing perception, planning, and manipulation capabilities, together with execution feedback for program and skill refinement during development. Evaluation should assess reliable task completion across variations without prescribing a particular program representation or agent architecture.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 2. Application relevance. Tasks and variations should reflect realistic operating requirements, with benchmark results predictive of real-world success, cycle time, and intervention needs.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 3. Accessibility and clarity. Benchmark environments, task specifications, assets, evaluation metrics, and variation parameters should be publicly available and clearly documented so that independent researchers can reproduce and extend the evaluation.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 4. Controlled diversity. Each task should specify explicit variation axes and difficulty levels rather than rely solely on unconstrained randomization.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 5. Repeatability. Task generation and evaluation should use controlled random seeds and standardized success criteria to support repeatable experiments and meaningful comparisons between methods.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 6. Computational efficiency. Evaluation should be computationally efficient enough to support repeated experimentation, sensitivity analysis, and large-scale benchmarking.

passages.section: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.location: III-A Agentic Robotics Benchmark Design Criteria
passages.text: 7. Durability. The benchmark should support systematic extensions of variation ranges and task complexity to remain informative as robotic systems improve. Extensions should be versioned to preserve comparability with previously reported results.

We define a Variational Automation (VA) task class as 𝒯 = ( ℰ , ℛ , 𝒜 , 𝒪 , p 𝒪 , 𝒮 ) , \mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{R},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{O},p_{\mathcal{O}},\mathcal{S}), where ℰ \mathcal{E} defines environmental coordinate frames, ℛ \mathcal{R} denotes the robot and gripper specification, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} denotes the set of admissible initial assets, each with physical properties and collision mesh, and 𝒪 \mathcal{O} denotes the space of admissible object configurations. p 𝒪 p_{\mathcal{O}} defines a distribution over admissible object configurations, and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} denotes the measurable success condition. Each task instance configuration τ i = { ( a j , 𝐱 j ) } j = 1 N i ∈ 𝒪 , \tau_{i}=\left\{(a_{j},\,\mathbf{x}_{j})\right\}_{j=1}^{N_{i}}\in\mathcal{O}, specifies each instantiated a j ∈ 𝒜 a_{j}\in\mathcal{A} and its initial pose 𝐱 j ∈ S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) \mathbf{x}_{j}\in SE(3) for each of the N i N_{i} objects and fixtures in the scene.

Importantly, 𝒪 \mathcal{O} is not defined by unconstrained scene randomization. Instead, the variation space and its sampling distribution are designed to represent meaningful changes in the operating conditions of an automation task.

We use the following principles to define admissible variations: a. Task invariance. All generated instances remain instances of the same VA task. b. Physical feasibility. Generated configurations satisfy physical constraints on object support, collision, and geometric consistency, preventing inadmissible initial scene configurations. c. Robot feasibility. Variations are bounded by the operational workspace of the specified robot ℛ \mathcal{R} . Object and fixture configurations are restricted to reachable regions, to avoid failures caused solely by physically inaccessible configurations. d. Controlled difficulty. Each task has levels of difficulty variation regimes. Increasing difficulty progressively broadens difficulty for the robot to solve. e. Skill preservation. Variations are designed such that instances across the same difficulty levels can be solved using the same underlying set of manipulation skills or extensions.
These principles define the admissible configuration space 𝒪 \mathcal{O} and constrain the support of p 𝒪 p_{\mathcal{O}} . An individual task instance is τ i ∼ p 𝒪 . \tau_{i}\sim p_{\mathcal{O}}.

Task-level success indicates whether an execution achieves its objective, but does not explain where or why it fails. This is particularly important for agentic robotics, where execution feedback may be used to diagnose failures, revise programs, and introduce recovery behaviors. VABAR therefore records the execution evidence needed to relate task outcomes to both the program’s decisions and the resulting physical interaction. For agentic robotics, we define the task execution record as decomposition mapping between components.

Fig. 3 : Diagnostic execution flow. VABAR records observations and estimated state, system actions, resulting physics states and contacts, and verification outcomes. Dashed boxes denote privileged simulator state and dotted box denote the physics object contact information used for diagnosis.

Here, we define 𝐬 t \mathbf{s}_{t} as the true physical state of the robot and scene, available only to a “privileged” observer; 𝐨 t \mathbf{o}_{t} is the sensor observation; 𝐬 ^ t \hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t} is the system’s estimated task state; 𝐚 t \mathbf{a}_{t} is the action produced by the policy, program, or execution graph; 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} records physical contacts generated during execution; and 𝐞 t + 1 \mathbf{e}_{t+1} denotes the resulting verification or execution event. We define the following mapping that forms the diagnostic flow, as shown in Fig. 3 :
𝐨 t → 𝐬 ^ t \mathbf{o}_{t}\rightarrow\hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t} : perception or state-estimation failures;
𝐬 ^ t → 𝐚 t \hat{\mathbf{s}}_{t}\rightarrow\mathbf{a}_{t} : program-generation, planning, skill-selection, or decision failures;
𝐚 t → ( 𝐬 t + 1 , 𝒞 t ) \mathbf{a}_{t}\rightarrow(\mathbf{s}_{t+1},\mathcal{C}_{t}) : grasping, motion-execution, collision, contact, or other physical-interaction failures;
( 𝐬 t + 1 , 𝒞 t ) → 𝐞 t + 1 (\mathbf{s}_{t+1},\mathcal{C}_{t})\rightarrow\mathbf{e}_{t+1} : task verification, failure detection, and recovery triggering.

The distinction between physical state and contact is important. Object poses and velocities describe the resulting scene configuration, whereas contact records describe how that configuration arose through physical interaction. For example, a failed placement may leave an object in an incorrect pose, while its contact history can reveal whether it collided with a fixture, was supported by another object, or became jammed. VABAR records both forms of evidence so that failure attribution can be grounded in the resulting physical execution rather than only in task-level success or software error messages.

VABAR spans six tasks across rigid-object manipulation, contact-rich assembly, and deformable-object manipulation, covering challenges in semantic perception, geometric reasoning, precision contact, and deformable-object interaction. To support these tasks with a consistent and reproducible benchmark, VABAR integrates four key components: a standardized asset library, representative single- and dual-arm robot embodiments, a unified task specification, and multi-physics simulation support.

Asset Library. VABAR provides a library of over 55 assets, spanning industrial tools, mechanical components, medical supplies, fixtures, connectors, and deformable objects. Assets are normalized in format, scale, appearance, and collision geometry to support controlled object and geometric variation across task instances.

Robot Embodiment. VABAR supports the single-arm Franka and bimanual YAM platforms, covering two representative manipulation settings. Franka provides a widely adopted platform for reproducible tabletop manipulation, while YAM enables tasks requiring coordinated bimanual interaction, particularly deformable-object manipulation.
Task Specification. VABAR represents tasks declaratively to specify task objects, initial configurations, variations, and success conditions.

Unified Multi-physics Support. VABAR provides unified support for rigid-body and deformable-body simulation and their interactions, with NVIDIA Newton enabling multi-physics dynamics. This allows the benchmark to span rigid manipulation, contact-rich assembly and insertion, and deformable-object tasks such as cable routing.

Fig. 4 : VABAR skill library. The 33 skills span perception, grasping, motion planning and execution, and verification. Colored cards marked “+” identify 25 added skill bundles relative to the May Graph-as-Policy library; white cards denote eight retained counterparts. Additions support functional-feature manipulation, constrained placement, cable handling, and execution checks.
(1) Tool Sorting The robot must place industrial tools into corresponding bins. Instance variation is introduced by changing the tools, their poses, and tool density.

(2) Tool Hanging The robot must pick up one or more industrial tools and hang or insert them into designated hooks, clips, or slots on a pegboard. Tools may include wrenches, screwdrivers, hammers, scissors. Task instance variation is based on tool type, the number of tools, initial tool pose, and holder pose.
TABLE I : Task difficulty levels. 1. TS: Tool Sorting; 2. TH: Tool Hanging; 3. GM: Gear Meshing; 4. SP: Syringe Packing; 5. CI: Cable Insertion; 6. CR: Cable Routing.

Task Level 1 Level 2 1 TS Singulated tools; no distractors Cluttered tools 2 TH One tool; known fixture pose Multiple tools and fixture types; randomized poses 3 GM Assemble two gears Assemble three gears 4 SP Singulated targets Cluttered scenes 5 CI Fixed, visible port; nearby connector with small misalignment Randomized port pose; moderate connector misalignment 6 CR 2–3 widely spaced pegs; short route; low turning angle 4–6 moderately spaced pegs; multiple turns; moderate initial cable variation

(3) Gear Meshing The task input is gears and axles. The single-arm robot must pick up multiple gears, assemble them onto a axles, such that they properly mesh, and press a button to activate the mechanism. The task varies the number of gears, gear size, and initial gear poses. To ensure physically valid instances, scenes can be initialized from a valid assembled configuration before selected gears are removed and repositioned.
(4) Syringe Packing The robot must place syringes into a disposal container while avoiding distractor objects. Instance variation includes the number object and disposal box type.

(5) Cable Insertion The YAM robot must pick up a connector, align it with its a USB-C port, and fully insert it. Instance variation includes the position and orientation of the connector and the port.

(6) Cable Routing The bimanual YAM robot must route a flexible cable around a specified ordered sequence of cylindrical fixtures mounted on a planar routing board. The task varies the number, position, and spacing of pegs; the ordered target sequence; cable length; initial cable configuration; cable slack and curvature; endpoint position; and the 3D pose of the routing board.
TABLE II : Task performance comparison across VABAR tasks and difficulty levels.
Metrics: Succ. : success rate (%); Cyc. : median cycle time (s) among successful trials.

To support the evaluation of agentic robotics systems in the VABAR task sandbox, we extend the Modular Open Robot Skill Library(MORSL) [ 5 ] with reusable procedures for functional-feature manipulation, constrained placement, and deformable cable handling (Fig. 4 ). Building on existing perception, grasp generation, and collision-aware planning primitives, the extensions provide metric feature localization, source–destination correspondence, in-hand registration, and staged feature mating. Cable-related skills estimate and track ordered 3D centerlines and support anchoring, routing, and terminal placement.

We focus on three questions: (1) how does agentic robotics success rate and cycle time change as the magnitude and dimensionality of task variation increase? (2) what are failure modes: perception, grasping, and motion? (3) can agentic systems reuse skills as task difficulty changes?
We provide two implementations of VABAR: on Newton and on Isaac Lab-Arena (ILA). The implementations have different texture, lighting, asset and robot implementations.

Newton: We develop VABAR with Newton Physics engine. To determine the success conditions, we extend Behavior Domain Definition Language (BDDL) [ 18 ] to represent both rigid and deformable objects as a common specification across the full task suite.

Isaac Lab-Arena (ILA): We provide an implementation of VABAR on top of NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena, a framework for composing, executing and analyzing policy evaluation benchmarks with GPU-acceleration. Isaac Lab-Arena provides tools for environment composition, including object placement based on semantic spatial relationships, multiple physics backends including Newton. It also enables running parallel evaluation on GPUs and analysis of policy robustness across environment and task variations. We execute VABAR on a cluster of NVIDIA L40 GPU nodes.

We report the success rate, cycle time, and failure mode rates. Success is determined by the dependency structure of each task. For tasks composed of repeated manipulation attempts that are independent by construction, such as sorting or hanging independently sampled objects, each object-level attempt is treated as a trial and success rate is the fraction of objects successfully manipulated. This avoids assigning zero success to an otherwise largely successful multi-object execution.

In tasks such as Gear Meshing, later insertions are conditioned on the states produced by earlier insertions: inserting one gear changes the geometry and contact configuration encountered by subsequent gears. Similarly, multiple cable insertions are treated as separate trials only when each insertion is independently initialized or reset; otherwise, their outcomes remain coupled through the evolving task state. We retain the complete task instance as the evaluation unit for sequential, state-dependent tasks, while optionally reporting subgoal-level success (e.g., success for each gear position) as a diagnostic measure. Cycle time is the simulated time elapsed from policy start until success, failure, or timeout.

For each unsuccessful execution, we record the observed failure outcome and assign a primary failure source when supported by execution evidence. For cascading failures, we attribute the execution to the earliest supported failure that explains the subsequent outcome. Failure-source percentages are conditioned on unsuccessful executions.

We integrate VABAR with GaP baselines. GaP is a multi-agent harness that represents a robot policy as a computation graph whose nodes are skills from MORSL [ 5 ] . We evaluate the following systems, labeled as in Table II : (a) GaP (Human) , a manually specified computation graph connecting MORSL skills, executed on both the Newton and ILA implementations (Human–Newton and Human–ILA); (b) Claude Code , a general-purpose coding agent (Claude Code with Claude Opus 5 [ 34 ] ) without a robotics-specific harness or skill library; (c) GaP , where the computation graph is autonomously generated by the same model and connected to MORSL. Systems (a) and (c) share the same perception, skill, planning, and execution modules, so their gap reflects graph composition and parameterization alone. Each task–difficulty combination contains N = 30 N=30 independently generated instances per evaluation condition.
TABLE III : Failure modes across VABAR difficulty levels.

Task Difficulty Perception Grasp Motion (%) (%) (%) Tool Sorting Level 1 37.8 51.4 10.8 Level 2 56.4 28.7 14.9 Tool Hanging Level 1 0.0 0.0 100.0 Level 2 21.4 28.6 50.0 Gear Meshing Level 1 N/A N/A N/A Level 2 7.1 21.4 71.4 Syringe Packing Level 1 0.0 0.0 100.0 Level 2 57.9 0.0 42.1 Cable Insertion Level 1 50.0 0.0 50.0 Level 2 0.0 4.0 96.0 Cable Routing Level 1 27.3 45.5 27.3 Level 2 5.3 31.6 63.2

Failure modes: Perc. : perception; Grasp : grasp generation or execution; Motion : motion planning or trajectory execution, including insertion, placement, and routing. Percentages are conditioned on failures.

Table II summarizes performance. Across all evaluated tasks, system performance exhibits a consistent inverse relationship with task difficulty: transitioning from low-variation regimes to multi-object, cluttered environments induces notable performance degradation alongside increased execution cycle times. This drop is particular in precision alignment and deformable object tasks, such as USB-C insertion and cable routing, where introducing geometric variation and tight physical constraints significantly decreases overall task completion. In contrast, discrete item-level manipulation tasks like tool hanging maintain relatively stable per-object success rates across difficulty tiers, though total episode times scale with object count. Overall, execution duration closely reflects task geometry and physical complexity, with single-object hanging tasks completing rapidly while multi-stage routing and cluttered tray operations require substantially longer execution windows. In addition, the same graph running in two different framework (Newton and ILA) has different object texture, scene configuration and lighting.

(a) Agentic harness and skill library enabling better performance. Using the same underlying language model, GaP achieves higher success rates than Claude Code in 11 of 12 task–difficulty conditions, supporting the value of a robotics-specific harness coupled with reusable manipulation skills. For example, GaP achieves 70.0% and 60.0% success on Level 1 and Level 2 Gear Meshing, respectively, whereas Claude Code achieves no successful trials. However, GaP remains below the human-authored graphs on Newton across all conditions, despite sharing the same perception, skill, planning, and execution stack. This gap suggests that reliable skill composition and parameterization remain important challenges for autonomous policy generation. These comparisons evaluate the combined system; they do not isolate the contributions of the harness and skill library.

(b) Most errors are due to motion planning. We decompose unsuccessful GaP executions into perception, grasp, and motion-planning failures. Table III reports failure sources across tasks and difficulty levels. In low-variation settings, perception and grasp generation operate with high reliability across most tasks, leaving motion planning and trajectory execution as the primary source of failure. However, as task variation increases, the dominant failure modes branch based on physical task characteristics. In cluttered scenes and deformable-object manipulation—such as syringe packing and cable routing—perception and grasping degrade significantly due to visual occlusions and unmodeled cable mechanics. Conversely, in precision contact tasks like USB-C insertion, state estimation remains robust under variation, but motion planning and fine insertion alignment overwhelmingly account for nearly all observed failures.

Fig. 5 : Example: Agent inspects Newton physics model to diagnose and fix failure due to syringes jamming inside disposal box . Left: simulated syringe-disposal scene with a top-down inset. Right: Netwon ground-truth front and side internal views of jammed episodes t01 and t29 . Red segments highlight syringes straddling the lid plane; blue segments show other syringes.

(c) Detailed physics model supports failure diagnosis. By pairing task-level verification with simulator-ground-truth inspection, VABAR helps identify the physical conditions associated with execution failures. Fig. 5 illustrates two jammed syringe-disposal episodes, t01 and t29 , which terminate with final verification reporting blocked and 7/8 and 6/8 syringes recorded as posted, respectively. In both examples, a syringe straddles the lid plane, with its needle end inside the cavity and its opposite end above the opening, consistent with incomplete passage into the container. The surrounding syringes occupy different configurations, highlighting execution-induced variation: earlier placements alter the geometry encountered by later insertions.

(d) Skill reuse is extensive across diverse task classes. Despite spanning rigid-object manipulation, contact-rich assembly, precision insertion, and deformable-object manipulation, VABAR policies exhibit substantial reuse of underlying skills and tools. Core robot and perception capabilities, including end-effector pose retrieval and SAM3 [ 35 ] -based segmentation, are shared across all six task classes. Higher-level semantic skills are also reused across tasks with different objects and applications but similar manipulation structure. For example, Tool Hanging and Syringe Packing both rely on skills for held-object motion, functional-feature perception, object registration, and feature mating. This reuse suggests that increasing task diversity does not necessarily require an entirely new set of skills. Instead, VABAR exposes a central challenge for agentic robotics on selecting appropriate skills, parameterizing them for the current geometry and task state, and composing them into effective task-specific behaviors. We hope VABAR will be used by others to facilitate and compare research progress worldwide.

analysis.overview: VABAR的新意是把工业操作的预期变化定义为可采样、可分级的任务空间，并在同一技能与执行栈下提供人工执行图和自动生成图作为对照。对研究最有用的不是另一个总分，而是区分技能能力、图组合及几何参数化的缺口。作者只提供仿真初始基线，尚不能证明工业可靠性或某个单独模块的因果收益。
analysis.notice: 已阅读HTML提取的72个文字片段，涵盖正文、方法、实验、讨论及表格；固定版本PDF共9页，无附录，另查看了第8、9页的提取文字和参考文献列表。目视核对PDF第5、6、7页的图3/4/5及表I/II/III。未逐图核查前四页图片、逐篇核查参考文献、运行代码或独立复现实验。项目页经HTTP读取可访问并提供仓库链接；仓库浏览请求超时，本轮未核查实现。逐字引文匹配验证出处，不保证判断正确。

findings.title: 技术增量：预期变化成为任务定义的一部分
findings.text: VABAR不是新控制器，而是面向agentic robotics的评测方法与环境。任务类显式定义环境坐标、机器人、资产、配置空间、采样分布及成功条件；变化需保持任务不变、物理与机器人可行、难度可控，并保留底层技能结构。它把固定自动化与无约束通用操作之间的“持续任务、结构化变化”变成可比较对象。
findings.quote: not defined by unconstrained scene randomization

findings.title: 把图组合与技能能力放在同一个对照里
findings.text: 人工编写GaP执行图与同一底层语言模型自动生成的GaP图，共享感知、MORSL技能、规划和执行模块；另有不带机器人专用harness和技能库的Claude Code。前两者的差距可定位到图组合/参数化这个组合层面。后两者同时改变harness与技能库，无法分离两项贡献。论文每个任务×难度×条件生成30个独立实例，但没有给出足够信息据此宣称训练随机性显著性或严格配对差异区间。
findings.quote: Systems (a) and (c) share the same perception, skill, planning, and execution modules

findings.title: 可复用技能扩展：功能特征、对接与线缆
findings.text: 技能库在MORSL上扩展到33个bundle：相对五月GaP库保留8个、增加25个，覆盖感知、抓取、运动/执行和验证。具体扩展包括度量功能特征定位、源目标对应、手中物体配准、分阶段特征对接，以及有序3D线缆中心线、锚定、绕线和端点放置。33是复用技能bundle数，不是33种机器人任务；不能把所有能力算成agent自己学会的。

findings.title: 关键对照：同样技能，齿轮任务仍相差30个百分点
findings.text: 表II的Newton齿轮啮合任务：人工GaP图在Level1/2成功率100.0%/90.0%，自动GaP图70.0%/60.0%，普通Claude Code均0。Level1装两个齿轮，Level2三个；该任务以完整依赖序列为评测单元，每任务难度条件30个生成实例。共享执行栈仍有30个百分点差距，提示应继续研究组合和参数化；这不是更换底层LLM带来的提升，也没有把组合与参数化分别消融。

findings.title: 不要把harness基线差距写成单模块增益
findings.text: 同一底层模型下，作者报告GaP优于普通Claude Code的条件为11/12；Tool Hanging Level2同为10.0%。但GaP同时获得机器人专用harness和技能库，而普通代码agent两者均无。因此该结果支持组合系统更有效，不能宣称“图表示单独提升11项任务”或“33技能库单独产生全部增益”。
findings.quote: they do not isolate the contributions of the harness and skill library

findings.title: 评测单元与时间口径不能混算
findings.text: 相互独立的分拣/悬挂尝试按物体统计，齿轮等有前后依赖的任务按完整实例统计；因此六任务的百分比不能无条件平均成统一整段成功率。表II的Cyc.是成功trial中的仿真周期中位数，不是全trial的平均耗时，也不是包含LLM生成、调试和仿真计算的墙钟延迟。GaP较快的成功子集不证明整体吞吐更好。
findings.quote: median cycle time (s) among successful trials

findings.title: 难度增加不保证每行数字都单调下降
findings.text: 难度表给出明确变化，例如绕线从2–3个宽间距peg变为4–6个并增加转弯。总体更难，但人工Newton绕线两级均46.7%，人工Newton插线时间78.8降到74.2秒（只看成功子集）。讨论里的概括不能改写成所有系统、任务和周期时间都单调退化，也不能把不同难度同时改变的因素当成单变量消融。

findings.title: 失败归因有未解释的表格缺口
findings.text: 协议把失败归到证据支持的最早原因，比例条件于失败trial。正文称表III分解GaP失败，但齿轮Level1在表II中GaP成功70.0%，表III同项三列却均N/A，未解释为何未统计。这一缺口尚未解决，不能由N/A推导没有失败；也不把其中某项96% motion解释为全部试验96%动作失败。
findings.quote: Gear Meshing Level 1 N/A N/A N/A

findings.title: Newton与ILA差异不是纯物理引擎消融
findings.text: 两实现的纹理、光照、资产、机器人配置均有差别。人工图插线Level1在Newton/ILA为86.7%/97.5%，绕线Level2为46.7%/5.0%。不能把差距全部归因于物理后端，或据此证明sim-to-real效果。作者在L40 GPU节点集群执行评测，已读文字未给每方法完整模型调用预算、墙钟成本和置信区间，本报告不估算费用。
findings.quote: different texture, lighting, asset and robot implementations

findings.title: 诊断真值与真实部署观测需要分开
findings.text: 记录链区分观测、估计、决策、物理状态/接触和验证；图3虚线框为特权仿真状态，可辅助诊断。图5通过内部视图识别针筒跨在盒盖平面上的卡住状态，示例分别有7/8和6/8已投入记录。它展示诊断信息，并没有报告修复前后受控成功率；不能说真值在线提供给部署策略，或说诊断已证明提升真实机器人可靠性。本篇基线均为仿真。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：图结构还是几何参数更限制齿轮装配？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在固定技能与执行栈后，几何参数化比执行图结构更限制GaP齿轮装配成功率。选择Newton齿轮Level1/2，固定感知/规划/技能版本、同一模型、生成与修复调用预算。四组为人工结构+人工参数、生成结构+生成参数、生成结构+人工校准参数、人工结构+模型参数；结构与参数的接口需预先约定，人工校准只用独立开发实例，不查看测试真值。先做小规模接口验证，再至少用30个全新共同测试配置并重复生成图，按完整任务统计成功率、配对差异区间、首次失败位置、仿真周期分布及全部运行的模型调用和墙钟成本。诊断真值离线标注，评测时所有策略只接收相同观测。若替换为人工校准参数不能稳定缩小差距，或仅更换图结构就带来更大改善，就反对参数化主导假设；若结果依难度而异，则按条件报告。该实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: VABAR：用同一套技能，对照人工与生成的执行图
frontier_brief.change_type: 评测方法 · 技能组合
frontier_brief.delta: 在预先规定变化范围的任务中，让人工执行图与模型生成图调用同一套感知、技能和规划模块，再比较表现。这样能把注意力转向技能如何组合、几何参数如何设定，而不只看换了哪个大模型。
frontier_brief.before: 只比较不同完整agent的成功率，或把场景变化当随机扰动；图生成、技能库和执行器的差异容易混在一起。
frontier_brief.after: 把对象、布局和几何变化定义为有约束的采样空间与难度层级，并提供共享执行栈的人工图参考；记录观测、决策、接触和验证链来诊断失败。
frontier_brief.relevance: 做代码策略或技能组合选题时，先复用一个同栈人工图作为参照，再区分结构生成、几何参数化和执行模块的瓶颈。齿轮任务适合按整段成功率做对照；不要把按物体统计的分拣与之直接平均。
frontier_brief.caveat: 仅有仿真初始基线；普通代码agent与GaP同时差在harness和技能库。表II周期只统计成功trial，表III的齿轮Level1失败归因有未解释的N/A。作者实验未复现。
frontier_brief.question: 固定技能栈后，应该先改执行图结构，还是几何参数？

evidence.label: 相同执行栈，生成图仍落后人工图
evidence.context: Newton齿轮啮合Level1：自动GaP图70.0%，人工GaP图100.0%；同感知、技能、规划和执行模块。两齿轮完整任务，每条件30个生成实例。表II；未提供配对差异区间。

evidence.label: 更难的装配仍保留30个百分点差距
evidence.context: Newton齿轮Level2改装三个齿轮：自动GaP图60.0%，人工图90.0%，普通Claude Code为0。后一个对照同时改变harness和技能库，不能归因于单独一个模块。

evidence.label: 时间口径会改变对快慢的理解
evidence.context: 同一Level1齿轮对照中，自动图/人工图的成功trial仿真周期中位数为156.6/165.9秒。但成功率不同，数字不含所有失败trial、LLM生成或调试墙钟成本，不能据此断言整体更快。

mechanism.title: 先规定变化
mechanism.text: 明确任务不变的目标、对象配置分布和可行性，再用难度层级逐步增加变化。六类任务涵盖刚体、精密接触与线缆操作。

mechanism.title: 共享底层技能
mechanism.text: 33个技能bundle包括功能特征定位、手中配准、特征对接和线缆处理。人工与生成图使用相同执行栈来比较组合和参数化。

mechanism.title: 保留失败链
mechanism.text: 将观测估计、图决策、物理状态/接触和验证结果关联。仿真真值用于诊断时单独标识，避免与策略可用观测混淆。

Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
Muhammad Danish Waseem * 1 Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan * 1

Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis on what are the real bottlenecks for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimization would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required saving and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are multimodal models that enable robots to translate visual observations and natural-language instructions into executable actions, such as moving an arm or opening a gripper. They typically build on pretrained vision-language models that are trained on robot demonstrations, connecting visual and semantic knowledge with the physical skills needed to perform tasks Zitkovich and others (2023) .
VLAs aim to support general-purpose robots that can follow diverse instructions and generalize to unfamiliar objects and environments Kim et al. (2024) ; Intelligence et al. (2025) .

Internally, VLAs typically run a VLM with millions or billions of parameters to generate the robot’s control steps. This limits the reaction time of a robot by the inference latency of the VLA. At each policy inference step, a typical VLA receives a natural-language instruction, represented as text, and image observations from one or more cameras. In a common architecture, a vision encoder converts camera images into visual embeddings, which are projected into the language model’s embedding space and processed jointly with the instruction tokens by a transformer backbone. The resulting representations condition the prediction of a robot action or a short sequence of actions with the action generations performed using an action-head.

VLAs need to be real-time, providing a robot with a sufficient number of actions such that the robot does not stall. Robots typically operate with strictly bounded latencies to maintain a continuous, closed-loop feedback cycle. In addition, if a VLA is too slow, it acts on stale visual data, i.e., by the time the model computes and outputs a command, the physical world has already changed leading to dropped objects, collisions, or unstable movement. This is challenging, especially when the VLA is running on the limited on-robot hardware. One approach to reduce the computational time of VLAs is to use optimization methods such as, token pruning, quantization, compilation, or CUDA graphs. However, our study of 25 published paper (Appendix E ) reveals that most of these approaches do not consider the intricacies of the different VLA architectures and the hardware they run on.

VLAs today vary in architecture, backbone size, visual token count and action path. These choices decide which stage dominates latency and therefore which optimization can help. The backbone size sets how many weight bytes every pass must read, so a large model could spend most of its time reading the model weights, whereas a smaller model could spend its time in the denoising loop of action head. In addition, previous work on VLA optimizations does not consider the inherent bottlenecks of the underlying hardware platform projecting generality of the results while only evaluating the work on a limited set of hardware. For example, many previous works evaluate the optimizations on GPUs such as NVIDIA RTX 4090s, a GPU that has a heavy weight and high power draw—it is neither designed for running on a robot platform nor is available on most clouds, hence, not supporting a cloud-robotic deployment.

In this work, we provide a comprehensive study of VLA optimization performance. We start by analyzing seven families of inference optimization methods, namely; CUDA graphs, compilation, fused attention, batching, reducing the denoising steps, token pruning and quantization. We evaluate these optimizations on seven VLAs, namely; OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, LLaVA-VLA, CogACT, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , GR00T, and SmolVLA, with four kinds of action head (token decoding, parallel decoding, diffusion, flow matching). These combinations are then tested on four different GPU families; a datacenter grade H100, a cloud A10G, a consumer RTX 4090, and an embedded Jetson Thor.
Our evaluations focus on the latency gains of these optimizations, showing that the optimization results are non-uniform. Gains differ between GPUs in magnitude, in sign and in rank.

For example, compiling GR00T with CUDA graphs makes it faster on the H100 and slower on the Thor, and storing CogACT’s weights in 8 bits makes it faster on the A10G and slower on the H100. In addition, we find that the choice of baseline to compare an optimization method to can be misleading, e.g., FastV Chen et al. (2024) and several other token pruning methods (Appendix E ) select the visual tokens to prune by their attention weights, so it is typically evaluated and compared to running with unfused attention. However, VLAs in production are often deployed with fused attention kernels such as FlashAttention-2 Dao (2024) , which never write attention weights to memory. Measured against unfused attention, FastV at 50 50 % pruning saves 21.4 21.4 % of OpenVLA-OFT’s inference time on an H100. Measured against FlashAttention-2, the same run saves 6.9 6.9 %, because the selector reads attention weights and forces the slower kernel (Table 5 ).

Our analysis also shows that each stage of inference is limited by either the GPU compute power, its memory bandwidth, or the CPU that launches the GPU kernels. This means that the same stage can be subject to a different bottleneck on different GPUs. Therefore, a proposed optimization method’s benefit may not extend beyond the platform it is tested on.

In addition, optimization methods can be combined, or stacked. Hence, running multiple optimizations in sequence means that later VLA optimizations act on the inference stages that are left by previous optimizations. Hence, the total gains from a later method depends on the methods applied before it. Based on the above observations, we formalize VLA-Triage , a systematic approach for evaluating the expected gains of multiple VLA optimization methods on a given hardware. To summarize, our paper has three connected contributions:

Characterisation : paired measurements of inference-stage costs and optimization benefits across seven VLAs and four GPU-host platforms, including cases where a method helps on one platform and hurts on another.
Interactions : We show how graphs, compilation and pruning change the gains for later applied methods, and how reusing standalone gains can change latency-budget decisions.
Guidelines : A measurement-based workflow for choosing an execution mode, checking feasibility under stated assumptions, and validating method combinations to be used in deployment.

VLA inference has three main stages. First, a vision encoder converts images into visual tokens. After that, the language backbone processes these tokens together with the task instructions; this stage is called prefill. Finally, an action-generation stage produces the robot’s commands. A chunk is a sequence of actions produced by one inference, so the robot can execute several control steps before requesting another prediction. One of the main differences between VLA models is in how they generate actions. This can be categorized in three main model categories:

Autoregressive decoding models , e.g., OpenVLA Kim et al. (2024) and LLaVA-VLA Song et al. (2026) : Represent actions as a sequence of tokens, generated one per forward pass. Repeated passes read the language-model weights, making memory transfers, CPU kernel launches, and kernel performance important.

Prefill-heavy models , e.g., OpenVLA-OFT Kim et al. (2025) and CogACT Li et al. (2024) : Run the language backbone once during prefill. OpenVLA-OFT predicts a chunk using action placeholder tokens processed in parallel. CogACT feeds prefill embeddings into a small diffusion transformer sampled with DDIM, a diffusion sampling method Song et al. (2020) .

Iterative flow models , e.g., π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. (2025) , GR00T Bjorck et al. (2025) , SmolVLA Shukor et al. (2025) : Refine an action chunk through multiple flow-matching steps Lipman et al. (2022) , using a small action network. We measured with four steps for GR00T and ten for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and SmolVLA.

The inference deadline depends on how the robot consumes its actions. A single-action policy must finish inference within one control period Δ \Delta , which is set by the robot motor frequencies. With asynchronous execution, a chunked policy computes the next chunk while the robot executes actions already in an action queue Black et al. (2026) . This can lead to the VLA acting on stale video data. Hence the number of actions should not be too large such that the robot will fail due to working on stale video data, or too few such that the robot movements are sluggish due to the VLA inference time.

We model the chunking policy through the asynchronous scheduler of LeRobot Cadene et al. (2026) , which initiates inference when A r A_{r} actions remain in the robot’s execution queue. For comparison, in our experiments, we request the next chunk when roughly half the current chunk remains: A r = ⌊ ( A − 1 ) / 2 ⌋ A_{r}=\lfloor(A-1)/2\rfloor for chunk length A A . The minus one accounts for discarding the action aligned with the observation time. The queued actions provide time for the next inference. With control period Δ = \Delta= 50 50 ms ( 20 20 Hz), used in all our experiments, this window is
B = { Δ , single-action policy , A r ​ Δ , asynchronous chunked policy . B=\begin{cases}\Delta,&\text{single-action policy},\\ A_{r}\Delta,&\text{asynchronous chunked policy}.\end{cases} (1)

Budgets range from 50 ms to 1200 ms (Table 1 ), based on the number of actions generated simultaneously by the VLA. We compare measured inference time T T with B B . Serial preprocessing of duration t preproc t_{\rm preproc} leaves B − t preproc B-t_{\rm preproc} for the model. If inference exceeds this window, the robot exhausts queued actions and spends a fraction q idle q_{\rm idle} of control steps idle. Figure 1 plots the resulting inferred slowdown 1 / ( 1 − q idle ) 1/(1-q_{\rm idle}) for executing the same action trajectory.

(2026b) ; Akbari et al. (2026) . The hatched band marks autoregressive decoding, which runs the language model.

Figure 2 maps the methods to the work they change. For interpreting performance, we distinguish methods that remove repeated work from those that change the GPU kernels used. Work-removing methods eliminate repeated operations. CUDA graphs NVIDIA (2026a) reduce repeated CPU launches by replaying recorded kernel sequences. Visual token pruning Chen et al. (2024) removes image tokens after early layers. Step reduction Tang et al. (2026) ; Luan et al. (2026) removes denoising passes in the action head. Kernel-replacing methods change how the GPU executes the computation. torch.compile Ansel et al. () fuses operations and generates kernels. Fused attention avoids writing large attention matrices to memory. Quantization Park et al. (2024) compresses weights (int8, int4) or uses lower-precision arithmetic (FP8, int8). A quantization scheme specifies weight and activation precision, together with a scaling rule. Weight-only quantization retains bf16 (16-bit floating-point) activations; int8 compute uses int8 weights and activations for matrix multiplication. FP8 and NVFP4 use 8-bit and 4-bit floating-point values, respectively. Different quantization schemes can use different kernel libraries. Batching processes requests together, sharing weight reads to improve throughput.

We call graphs, compilation and fused attention accuracy-neutral because they preserve the intended computation up to numerical rounding. We call pruning, step reduction, and quantization accuracy-risking , as they change the computation and require task-specific accuracy evaluation.

We evaluate the inference optimization methods shown in Figure 2 , with seven VLA models listed in Table 1 . Table 7 in Appendix lists the four GPU-host systems we tested with, along with their software versions, measured throughput, bandwidth and CPU launch costs.
We measure the time starting after CPU image preprocessing and ending when the model returns its actions.
We validate that the model’s input and output remain valid during measurements (details in Appendix A).

We compare three execution modes. 1) In eager execution, PyTorch launches operations as they run. 2) CUDA graphs replay recorded GPU work with a single CPU launch. 3) torch.compile is used with its reduce-overhead option, which also uses CUDA graphs where supported, and its max-autotune option, which also benchmarks alternative matrix-multiplication kernels. The Llama-family VLA stages are compiled separately so that CUDA events can still time them, with decode served by one graph over a fixed-size masked cache. OpenPi ships π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with the whole call compiled, and we keep that scope. For GR00T we compile the DiT action loop, which takes most of the inference time, and leave the Qwen3-VL backbone eager. For SmolVLA, compiling the whole call has no effect. Its vision embedding selects tokens with a mask computed from the image, so the resulting shape is only known at runtime. The compiler cannot trace such an operation, and torch.compile would then run the entire function eagerly. We therefore compile only the denoising step, which runs ten times per inference.

We keep each VLA’s attention backend as released. The Llama models use FlashAttention-2 Dao (2024) , GR00T and SmolVLA use scaled dot-product attention (SDPA), and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} uses unfused attention with OpenPi’s explicit prefix-LM mask, which the fused kernels do not accept. Accuracy-neutral modes are compared against eager execution. Token pruning and step reduction are evaluated against the unpruned and full-step baseline, respectively, in the same execution mode.

Quantization is compared in two execution modes. The main comparison (Table 8 ) uses reduce-overhead compilation, with the bf16 baseline measured in the same mode as the quantised runs. A separate comparison measures the same schemes under CUDA graphs without compilation, to separate the gain of the quantised kernels from the gain the compiler adds by fusing their scaling and casting. Only language-backbone linear layers are quantised. For each quantization scheme and platform, we time the available library implementations and use the fastest one whose output error stays within 1.25 times the smallest error among them (Table 9 ).

Short GPU kernels make latency sensitive to CPU launch delays. We pin the issuing process to an idle CPU core near the GPU and warm up before timing. Each measurement round repeats the job’s selected configurations. We report medians of at least 200 inferences per configuration, or 100 batches for batching. Across repeated jobs, the median latency difference is 0.2% under CUDA graphs and 1.4% in eager execution (Appendix B ). The largest eager baseline change we observed, when remeasuring the RTX 4090 baselines, is 5.3% (Appendix B ).

We test whether a saving measured before an optimization remains applicable after it. We call this measurement reuse. We ask whether the earlier optimization changes the GPU work. We call a change execution-preserving if it mainly removes CPU launches while retaining GPU kernels and their input dimensions, otherwise it is execution-altering . Compilation, pruning and quantization fall in the latter group. The distinctions serve different purposes. Accuracy-neutral or risking indicates whether task validation is needed. Work-removing or kernel-replacing describes what the method changes. Execution-preserving or altering indicates whether eager measurements may remain informative.

If an optimization changes only the stage it targets, accelerating a fraction σ \sigma of baseline latency by a factor s s saves an overall fraction g = σ ⁡ ( 1 − 1 / s ) g=\sigma(1-1/s) of baseline time. Here the stage share σ \sigma is the fraction of inference time spent in the affected stage, and s s is its speed-up. We use the identity to explain measured changes. An earlier optimization can change the stage share σ \sigma , the speed-up s s , or both. For instance, once compilation shortens the action loop, it lowers action head share σ \sigma , leaving fewer denoising steps less time to save. Similarly, pruning lowers the share of prefill layers and also changes their matrix sizes, and with them the speed-up s s of the quantised kernels applied to them. Section 5 examines these effects.

passages.location: 3.3 Stage Timings and Hardware Reference Costs
passages.text: The roofline reference Williams et al. (2009) (Figure 3 ) compares arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) with the ridge point C / B ​ W C/BW , where the idealised memory and compute references cross. For a bf16 linear layer with n n parameters and M M tokens, 2 ​ M ​ n 2Mn operations and 2 ​ n 2n weight bytes give an intensity near M M when weight reads dominate; long prefills can approach the compute limit, while single-token decoding ( M = 1 M=1 ) lies on the memory side .

Figure 3: Stage throughput against each platform’s roofline reference, unpruned bf16 at batch one. Colour denotes the model and shape denotes the stage. Arithmetic intensity uses the operator traffic of Equation ( 2 ).

Figure 3 shows the roofline model for the different stages of the seven VLAs on the four GPUs. Autoregressive decoding approaches the memory reference on A10G and Thor. H100 leaves more headroom. On the H100, a decoded Llama-2-7B token takes 9.6 ms under graphs (Table 4 ) against a 3.7 ms weight-read reference at the measured bandwidth. Each pass issues well over a thousand kernels. Compilation with max-autotune reduces kernel counts and brings the time per decoded token to 5.7 ms. Many of these kernels are short elementwise and normalisation operations that move little data and leave DRAM bandwidth underused, so fusing them closes part of the gap. The measurements do not isolate how much of the remaining gap each kernel accounts for. All Thor stages lie left of the ridge point under this traffic estimate, where memory cost exceeds compute cost in the reference.

The gap to measured performance can include kernel inefficiency, CPU launches and differences in actual traffic, so position in Figure 3 alone does not establish the bottleneck. Appendix Figure 8 helps interpret stage costs using measured graph savings, estimated overhead for flow models, compute and memory reference costs, and the unexplained remainder. The flow-model estimates do not isolate CPU waiting. Graphs can reduce launch delays, pruning can reduce token-dependent work, and quantization can reduce weight traffic or change arithmetic costs. Their opportunities therefore depend on which costs remain.

For the Llama-based models, CUDA graphs save more where the estimated idle share I / T I/T is larger (Appendix Figure 9 ). The idle share is the fraction of eager inference time in which no GPU kernel is running. On the A10G and Thor, decode loops spend more time reading weights and gain little from graphs. The saving depends on whether the CPU can launch the next kernel before the GPU finishes its current work.

Figure 4: Latency benefits and memory costs of accuracy-neutral methods. (a) Speed-up of reduce-overhead compilation over CUDA graphs alone for the four Llama-based models. The RTX 4090 shows compilation without graphs. Bar labels give the eager kernel count divided by the compiled count. (b) GPU memory beyond the model weights at batch sizes one and eight, medians over the GPUs where the configuration fits. The CUDA-graphs bars hold one graph. The four-level bars hold one graph per pruning level, each with its own memory pool, and at batch eight OpenVLA-OFT and LLaVA-VLA then exceed the 24GB of an RTX 4090 or A10G.

Compilation fuses elementwise and normalisation operations, reducing kernel counts by 1.9 × 1.9\times to 2.8 × 2.8\times in our experiments, and providing additional speed-ups after CUDA graphs reduce time outside kernels. Figure 4 a shows both effects. Its bar heights give the speed-up over graphs alone, and its bar labels the ratio of eager to compiled kernel counts. Fewer kernels also means fewer launches, so the speed-up may come from launch and scheduling savings as much as from reduced DRAM traffic. Compilation also changes the preferred quantization scheme. For OpenVLA-OFT on H100, static FP8 is fastest under compilation, speeding up whole inference by 1.43 × 1.43\times over compiled bf16 and prefill alone by 1.68 × 1.68\times (Table 8 ). Under graphs without compilation it is instead the slowest of the three, at 33.5 ms against 31.5 ms for dynamic FP8 and 31.0 ms for int8 compute. Compilation changes two things at once. It fuses the scaling and casting of activations into neighbouring kernels, and it can select different matrix-multiplication kernels.

Compilation can also slow inference. For GR00T on Thor, compiler-generated copy and conversion kernels increase GPU kernel duration despite shorter gaps between kernels (“GR00T compiled on the Thor” in Appendix D ). Execution modes also require memory and setup time. Each captured graph uses fixed tensor dimensions and reserved GPU memory pools, while compilation can take minutes (Appendix Table 6 ). Figure 4 b shows the memory each execution mode needs beyond the model weights. A CUDA graph is captured for fixed tensor shapes, so a deployment that varies its batch size or pruning level at run time must keep one graph per shape resident. Each graph reserves a memory pool roughly as large as the activation memory of eager inference at that batch size. At batch eight, four pruning-level graphs held at once reserve 11 to 13 GB of pools on top of 13 to 14 GB of weights for OpenVLA-OFT or LLaVA-VLA, which exceeds the 24 GB of an RTX 4090 or A10G.
Pruning reduces token-dependent work in the language-model layers. We use random token selection to measure the latency effect of token count.

These timings measure performance at each token count. They do not determine which token-selection method preserves task accuracy. Under CUDA graphs, prefill latency generally shortens with token count (Appendix Figure 10 ). Pruning reduces token-dependent computation but does not eliminate the weight reads of layers that still run.

Fewer tokens do not always reduce latency. Matrix-multiplication (GEMM) kernels process tokens in fixed-size blocks called tiles, so removing tokens that do not empty a whole tile saves little. Some measured points even become slower as the token count falls (Appendix Figure 10 ), likely because the library selects a different kernel at the new shape. In eager execution, pruning can also stop helping once CPU launches, rather than GPU work, set the latency.
Token selection adds its own cost. FastV Chen et al. (2024) ranks visual tokens by attention weights. Obtaining those weights requires a slower, unfused attention implementation.
Table 5 compares these variants with random selection, showing that selection overhead and the attention backend directly affect the realised latency saving.

In flow and diffusion heads, each denoising step repeats a forward pass over identical action-head weights. Fewer steps shorten this loop while leaving vision and prefill unchanged. Appendix Table 4 separates the cost of one denoising step from the time outside the denoising loop. In eager execution, small action heads issue many short kernels, leaving the GPU waiting for CPU launches. Compilation accelerates individual steps in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and SmolVLA by over 2 × 2\times , whereas GR00T’s generated kernels on Thor lengthen step time.

Quantization stores weights at lower precision. Quantization schemes that also quantize activations use lower-precision inputs for matrix multiplication. As shown in Table 8 , weight-only quantization schemes (int8, int4) accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound stages, cutting decode loop latency on the A10G and Thor. During prefill, dequantization and kernel overhead can outweigh the time saved by reading fewer weight bytes. Activation quantization schemes (FP8, int8 compute) use lower-precision tensor cores to accelerate dense prefill GEMMs. They need enough tokens for this saving to outweigh quantization and scaling overhead. A weight-only quantization scheme can therefore shorten decode while lengthening prefill in the same inference.

Zero means the percentage saving is unchanged. Positive values mean less saving than assumed, and negative values mean more. Appendix Tables 14 – 15 give the counts and millisecond-reuse results.

passages.section: 5 How One optimization Changes the Next
passages.location: 5 How One optimization Changes the Next
passages.text: A deployment may combine methods whose benefits were measured separately. We ask whether a method’s saving still holds once another optimization has been applied. We use the distinction between execution-preserving and execution-altering from Section 3.2 to interpret the results.

On a fixed model, platform and software version, we measure the baseline T 0 T_{0} , the earlier optimization alone T 1 T_{1} , the later method alone T 2 T_{2} , and both together T 12 T_{12} . The later method saves T 0 − T 2 T_{0}-T_{2} without the earlier optimization and T 1 − T 12 T_{1}-T_{12} with it. We test two assumptions about whether that saving remains unchanged. Percentage reuse assumes the later method saves the same percentage of time, giving T reuse = T 1 ​ ( T 2 / T 0 ) T_{\rm reuse}=T_{1}(T_{2}/T_{0}) . Millisecond reuse assumes it saves the same number of milliseconds, giving T reuse = T 1 − ( T 0 − T 2 ) T_{\rm reuse}=T_{1}-(T_{0}-T_{2}) . We compare the latency implied by each assumption with the measured T 12 T_{12} . An assumption is optimistic when the implied latency is lower than measured, and pessimistic when it is higher. We report cases where measured latency exceeds the implied value by more than 5.3%, the largest eager baseline change observed during remeasurement (Section 3 ).
We perfrom a case-study on three example and likely optimization sequences (summarized in Figure 5 ). These cases examine the selected sequences, not all possible optimization combinations.

CUDA graphs leave the GPU kernels unchanged. Pruning therefore removes the same token-dependent work as in eager execution. Graphs also remove launch overhead, so total inference is shorter. The kernel time that pruning removes is then a larger share of that shorter total. In eager execution part of that kernel time was hidden behind CPU launches, so the milliseconds saved change as well. The eager percentage therefore does not carry over exactly. In the recorded comparisons, measured latency under CUDA graphs ranges from 23 23 % below to less than 1 1 % above the value implied by applying pruning’s eager percentage saving unchanged. Profiles show that the small excesses involve changes in both kernel time and time outside kernels. Appendix F splits each excess into a kernel-time term and a time-outside-kernels term from the traces, and shows that both stay within about 1 ms on the H100 and A10G and largely cancel on the Thor.

LLaVA-VLA needs separate treatment because CUDA graphs change its decoding cache. Its decoding attends over a fixed-size masked cache, changing kernel timing (Section 3.2 ). LLaVA-VLA’s pruning savings must therefore be measured under CUDA graphs rather than carried over from eager execution. Figure 5 plots LLaVA-VLA in the “Graphs with cache change” row. OpenVLA uses the same cache layout, but its recorded timing changes are small, so we treat it as approximately execution-preserving.

passages.section: Case 2: Compilation, then pruning or fewer denoising steps.
passages.location: Case 2: Compilation, then pruning or fewer denoising steps.
passages.text: Compilation changes kernel execution times. This changes how much time pruning or fewer steps can save. For CogACT, 75% pruning saves 3.9 ms on H100 in eager execution and 4.1 ms after max-autotune compilation. Prefill is a small share of CogACT’s time on H100 in both modes, so pruning has little to remove either way. However, on A10G, CogACT’s saving falls from 74.2 to 33.5 ms as compilation already shortens prefill (Appendix Table 13 ). Compiler mode also matters: switching unpruned CogACT from reduce-overhead to max-autotune on A10G saves 42.7 ms, more than the subsequent pruning saves.
