passages.text: In 29 of 32 flow-model comparisons, latency is more than 5.3% higher than the percentage reuse implies, reaching up to 227% higher. For SmolVLA on RTX 4090, the assumption gives 17.4 ms versus 56.9 ms measured. Carrying over the eager millisecond saving gives zero or negative latency in 21 comparisons. Pruning and step-reduction savings therefore need measurement in the chosen compiler mode.

passages.section: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.location: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.text: Pruning is work-removing because it reduces token-dependent computation. The smaller matrices can nevertheless change kernel selection and efficiency. Quantization’s benefit can change in two ways. Pruning can reduce the share of inference spent in the layers quantization accelerates, while the changed matrix sizes can raise or lower the speed-up of quantised kernels. For example, on A10G with reduce-overhead compilation, 75% pruning reduces the prefill speed-up from int8 compute for CogACT but increases it for OpenVLA-OFT (Appendix Figure 11 , Table 2 ).

passages.section: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.location: Case 3: Pruning, then quantization, with execution mode fixed.
passages.text: In the 194 compiled pruning–quantization configurations, measured latency exceeds the value implied by unchanged quantization percentage savings by more than 5.3% in 52, including 24 for OpenVLA-OFT on Thor. The largest discrepancy is 49%. Other configurations have lower measured latency than the assumption implies. In comparisons retaining individual token selectors, updating the affected-stage share while assuming the unpruned quantization speed-up still leaves measured latency up to about 39% above the implied value. Both the affected-stage share and quantization speed-up therefore matter (Appendix G ). quantization should be evaluated at the retained token count and in the deployed execution mode.

A change in saving can determine whether a combination meets its inference-time budget. For CogACT with 75% pruning after max-autotune compilation on A10G, assuming unchanged eager millisecond savings gives 23.3 ms, below the 50 ms budget. The measured combination takes 64.1 ms and misses it. Assuming unchanged percentage savings gives 61.4 ms, also above the budget. On H100, compilation alone takes 21.5 ms and meets the budget without pruning.

Pruning and quantization can change budget decisions too. For CogACT on A10G with int4 weights and 75% pruning in reduce-overhead mode, assuming unchanged quantization percentage savings gives 48.5 ms, within the 50 ms budget. The combination measures 59.3 ms and misses it. With 87.5% pruning in max-autotune mode, the same assumption gives 59.2 ms, above the budget, while the combination meets it at 49.2 ms. Using the same assumption would therefore lead to the wrong budget decision in both examples. Appendix Table 3 gives further examples from earlier measurements, and Appendix Table 15 gives the full budget comparison. These checks concern inference time. Section 6 adds reserves for preprocessing, communication, and scheduling.

We also examine whether a method’s measured speed-up persists across platforms. Among the selected model–method settings, none of the 14 work-removing comparisons changes from a speed-up to a slowdown across platforms, while 6 of the 21 kernel-replacing comparisons do. With matching PyTorch versions on H100 and A10G, the counts are 0 of 14 work-removing comparisons and 3 of 13 kernel-replacing comparisons. Host CPUs and other software components still differ, so these comparisons do not isolate GPU architecture. At 25% pruning, compiled π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} becomes faster on the other tested platforms but slower on Thor. The Thor slowdown appears in two separate measurement jobs.
These cases show that a later method’s benefit depends on how much of inference it can shorten and how efficiently the remaining work executes.

Figure 6: Measured model latency relative to the nominal budget, on a logarithmic axis. Circles show eager execution and squares the selected execution mode. Orange diamonds show one further pruning or quantization setting from Appendix Table 17 , choosing pruning when both would qualify. Points are alternatives, not successive steps. Orange points are omitted when none is needed or none qualifies. All comparisons exclude deployment reserves.
VLA-Triage is a set of guidelines based on the findings of Sections 4 and 5 that can be used by practitioners for deploying (or evaluating) their VLA optimizations.
1. Set the budget. For deployment, reserve time for preprocessing, communication and scheduling delays within B B :
B model = B − t preproc − t comm − t margin . B_{\rm model}=B-t_{\rm preproc}-t_{\rm comm}-t_{\rm margin}. (3)

Here B model B_{\rm model} is the time left for model execution, and t margin t_{\rm margin} reserves time for scheduling delays and latency variation. The examples below set t comm = 0 t_{\rm comm}=0 and t margin = 0.05 ​ B t_{\rm margin}=0.05B . Tables that compare measured inference T T with B B rather than B model B_{\rm model} exclude these reserves.

2. Choose execution mode. Benchmark the supported execution modes (eager, CUDA graphs, and compilation) and attention backends on the physical target. The attention backend belongs here because it is accuracy-neutral. In the recorded comparisons the best fused backend was never slower than unfused attention on any platform, whether the gain was marginal or substantial, and it lowers attention-heavy prefill, so step 2 selects a fused backend together with the execution mode. Select the fastest mode that satisfies platform memory and setup constraints (Section 4.1 ). Use its total latency T T and stage timings for the checks in step 3, because eager stage shares need not remain valid after compilation. If the selected mode alone meets B model B_{\rm model} , skip steps 3 and 4 and go to step 5.
3. Screen unviable candidates.

Weight-read screen. If reading mandatory weights alone takes longer than B model B_{\rm model} , no faster kernel can make the candidate meet the budget under the same memory traffic. Let W p 4 W_{p}^{4} be the bytes of the vision-language-model weights read in forward pass p p , counted at four bits, the lowest weight precision among the evaluated quantization schemes. This gives quantization an optimistic reference, since higher-precision weights require at least as many bytes. These weights must be streamed from DRAM on every pass. Dividing their volume by datasheet memory bandwidth B ​ W data BW_{\rm data} gives a lower bound on latency:
L w = ∑ p W p 4 B ​ W data . L_{\rm w}=\frac{\sum_{p}W_{p}^{4}}{BW_{\rm data}}. (4)

If L w > B model L_{\rm w}>B_{\rm model} , no pruning or quantization setting can meet the budget, since all of them still read these weights. Only candidates that remove reads, by caching weights or dropping layers or passes, remain, and they need their own bound.

Affected-stage screen. Each method can only shorten the stages it acts on. Pruning acts on prefill. Quantization acts on the vision-language-model layers. Step reduction acts on the action loop of the flow models. Let L m L_{m} be the latency of method m m at its strongest setting. For pruning this is inference with all visual tokens removed, which still runs the vision encoder, the text tokens and decoding. For step reduction it is inference with one denoising step, which still runs vision and prefill. No milder setting is faster, so L m L_{m} is a lower bound for method m m alone. If L m > B model L_{m}>B_{\rm model} , skip m m as a standalone candidate. A pair of methods acts on more stages than either method alone, so this screen does not exclude pairs.
4. Test supported combinations.

A pruning level is the percentage of visual tokens removed. Mild levels are tested first because they risk less accuracy. If the mode selected in step 2 is CUDA graphs, which largely preserve GPU work, eager pruning timings estimate which levels can meet the budget, through the percentage-saving assumption of Case 1 in Section 5.1 . Select initial levels whose implied latency, T 1 ​ T 2 / T 0 T_{1}T_{2}/T_{0} , is at most ( 1 + δ ) ​ B model (1+\delta)B_{\rm model} . In the recorded comparisons this estimate was usually above the measured latency under CUDA graphs, so a level whose estimate slightly exceeds the budget may still meet it. The allowance δ \delta keeps such levels in the initial set. We use δ = 5.3 % \delta=5.3\% , the largest eager baseline change observed during remeasurement (Section 3 ), and Appendix H tests other values.

If the selected mode is compilation, eager timings cannot be used to skip evaluations, because Case 2 shows that their savings need not carry over. Measure pruning and step-reduction settings in the compiled mode, from the smallest change upwards.

Quantization schemes are chosen based on hardware support and task accuracy requirements. Measure them in the deployed mode at the retained token count, because pruning can increase or decrease their benefit (Case 3). If neither pruning nor quantization meets the budget alone, test pairs.

5. Validate task performance. For each candidate meeting the latency budget, check success on the chosen benchmark and control stability in deployment. If either fails, return to step 4 to test further candidates, including further levels or pairs.

Meeting the budget with headroom. For OpenVLA-OFT on the Thor, the budget is 150 ms. Reserving recorded serial preprocessing (7.1 ms) and 5% of B B leaves 135.4 ms for model execution. Step 2 selects compilation, with a model latency of 152.6 ms (Figure 6 ). Removing 50% of visual tokens drops model time to 97.6 ms. Pruning alone therefore meets the latency budget, so the next step is task validation rather than adding quantization.

A combination that fails once reserves are included. For CogACT on A10G, the 50 ms budget leaves only 40.5 ms for inference after 7.0 ms of serial preprocessing and a 5% reserve. Max-autotune takes 97.5 ms. Prefill accounts for 72.3% of that time, enough that the affected-stage screen does not rule out pruning alone. Removing 75% of visual tokens takes 64.1 ms, and int8 compute alone takes 67.0 ms. Together they take 49.6 ms. Although the pair meets the inference-only 50 ms comparison, it exceeds the time available in deployment. The fastest recorded setting, 87.5% pruning with int8 compute, still takes 46.4 ms. None of the recorded settings meets this deployment budget, so using one would require a longer control period. Appendix Table 17 reports the other cases with and without reserves.
Spare latency can support batching or a higher control rate, subject to renewed latency and control checks (Appendix Table 10 ).

Latency predictors and tensor compilers already account for operator fusion and shape-dependent kernel selection Zhang et al. (2021) ; Wang et al. (2020) ; Chen et al. (2018) ; Zheng et al. (2020) , so a saving measured in one execution mode is known not to transfer to another. VLA acceleration papers usually do not report the mode. We audit 25 VLA acceleration papers (Appendix E ). Only one states the execution mode of both baseline and the method. None of the token-pruning, reuse, merging, or sparsification entries do, and only one of them identifies its attention backend. Readers therefore cannot check whether a reported saving applies to their execution mode.

VLA-Perf Jiang et al. (2026b) models architectural and deployment choices with an analytical roofline to estimate ideal compute and memory bounds. The XPU study Zhou et al. (2026) benchmarks VLAs across GPUs, an Intel XPU and Ascend NPUs, measuring compilation and a few method pairs, without testing methods against latency budgets. Jung et al. (2026) characterise stage balance on an RTX 4090 and two Jetson SoCs and compare per-stage compilation with eager execution, but compilation is the only model-level optimization they measure.

Our paired measurements track how a method’s benefit varies across models and GPU-host systems, and how an earlier optimization changes a later method’s saving. We examine graphs before pruning, compilation before pruning or step reduction, and pruning before quantization, then test how the differences affect latency-budget decisions.

A VLA optimization’s benefit depends on the model, GPU-host platform and methods already applied. Across seven VLAs and four platforms, our measurements show how CPU launch costs, memory costs and kernel efficiency change the opportunity for optimization. Compilation changes pruning and step-reduction savings, while pruning changes quantization benefits. VLA-Triage formalizes these findings into guidelines for selecting an execution mode, checking feasibility, and validating combinations under a deployment latency budget. The resulting guidance identifies when standalone measurements remain informative and when the combined execution must be measured.

The released DDIM sampler constructs its step schedule on the CPU during each step, preventing this loop from being recorded as a CUDA graph. Our replacement precomputes the same schedule. Across five seeds, the maximum absolute difference between its actions and those of the released loop is 1.2 × 10 − 6 1.2\times 10^{-6} in fp32 on CPU, using identical weights, noise and conditioning inputs.

We check that the expected input sequence for each model: 291 tokens for OpenVLA, 605 for OpenVLA-OFT (including 56 action slots), 276 for CogACT (including the cognition token), and 633 for LLaVA-VLA. We also check LLaVA-VLA’s token IDs against its released server using the same instruction.

We simulate LeRobot’s asynchronous action queue, which the robot drains at the control rate while the policy refills it with each inference, to compute how often a given inference time leaves the robot with no action to execute.

passages.text: Timing begins with preprocessed camera frames and ends with actions, excluding CPU image preprocessing. CUDA events placed between modules divide inference into stages: host-to-device copy, vision encoder, projector, token selection where pruning is enabled, language-model prefill, then decoding for OpenVLA and LLaVA-VLA, the action head for OpenVLA-OFT and CogACT, or the denoising loop for the flow models, and postprocessing. Each stage time is the elapsed time between its two events on the GPU stream. Compilation uses torch.compile Ansel et al. () , and quantisation uses torchao torchao maintainers and contributors (2024) . Only the language-model linear layers of the Llama-based models are quantised. For each quantisation scheme and platform, we time the available library implementations and select the fastest one whose output error is within 1.25 times the smallest error measured for that quantisation scheme (Table 9 ).

passages.text: On x86 platforms, the Llama-based models and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} generally use PyTorch 2.7.1. The exceptions are quantised runs and compilation variants of the Llama-based models on the H100 and A10G, which use PyTorch 2.10 with torchao 0.13. The Thor uses this stack throughout. GR00T and SmolVLA use PyTorch 2.11 on x86 platforms and 2.10 on the Thor (Table 7 ). We do not report quantisation schemes on the RTX 4090.

When processing one request at a time, latency can depend on which CPU core launches GPU work. The protocol therefore pins the issuing thread to one core (Section 3 ). With pinning, OpenVLA’s eager rounds agree within 2.1%. Across identical configurations measured in separate jobs days apart, the median relative latency difference is 0.2% under CUDA graphs and 1.4% in eager execution. The 5.3% reporting cutoff is the largest eager baseline change observed when remeasuring the RTX 4090 at the end of its campaign. CUDA-graph latencies measured under the two software stacks in Table 7 agree within 4 ms. Recalculating each interaction example in Section 5 using every pairing of recorded baseline and optimized round medians preserves the reported direction. OpenVLA-OFT’s increase in pruning saving under CUDA graphs on the Thor remains positive in every pairing.

We compare kernel busy time from our CUPTI profiler with Nsight Systems, expressing differences relative to the CUPTI value. The differences are at most 0.12% on A10G and 2.1% under compilation and CUDA graphs on H100. For eager H100 runs, Nsight reports 4.7–12.2% more busy time and longer durations for short kernels. On Thor, the differences range from 0.8% to 2.1%, and both profilers give the same ordering for all 12 checked configurations.

Figure 7 shows that decoding dominates OpenVLA and LLaVA-VLA. CogACT shifts from a larger action-head share on H100 to a larger prefill share on A10G, changing how much time pruning can remove. Vision includes projection; other includes input transfer, postprocessing and unassigned time.

After finding a combination that meets the budget, a server can test whether the remaining time permits processing more requests together. Figure 14 first checks whether the entire batch finishes within the nominal inference budget. CogACT and OpenVLA-OFT use CUDA graphs; the flow models use reduce-overhead compilation with graphs. Each curve uses one mode per model, with no pruning. This batch-latency check does not determine robot capacity, because serving also depends on request arrival times and queue scheduling. Table 10 therefore estimates serving capacity by combining the measured batch latencies with the asynchronous scheduler replay. The bf16 serving replay dynamically batches waiting observations from robots with fixed random phase offsets. The reported robot counts apply to this request pattern and the replay’s scheduling assumptions, and its 5 ms server ticks make results close to the budget sensitive to scheduling. On the Thor, over-current protection events were observed during OpenVLA-OFT graph runs at batches 2, 4 and 8 and during compiled π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} runs at batches 4 and 16 but not 8. Repeated OpenVLA-OFT runs agreed within 2%, so the counts are reported.

Power-mode measurements vary CPU and GPU resources on one device (Table 11 ). On the Thor, both 90 and 70 W modes disable 8 of 20 streaming multiprocessors. Of the lower modes only 70 W lowers the CPU clock, from 2601 to 1998 MHz, according to recorded clocks. The other modes reduce GPU resources without lowering the CPU clock. Disabling streaming multiprocessors mainly slows prefill-heavy models, while leaving the decoding models almost unchanged, consistent with their weight-read costs. In these measurements, lowering the CPU clock mainly slows cases where the GPU waits for CPU launches. The compiled GR00T and SmolVLA entries at MAXN come from the denoising-step sweep, which was measured only without pruning. The π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} graph mode includes compilation.

Compiled GR00T and SmolVLA at MAXN use the full-step denoising runs, available only without pruning.

Compilation slows GR00T on the Thor. Between the eager and compiled profiles, gaps between kernels shrink from 42.1 to 18.7 ms, while the time covered by kernels grows from 134.8 to 178.8 ms. Among the most frequent kernels in each trace, those whose names identify them as copies or data-type conversions take 70.4 ms per inference in eager execution and 136.8 ms when compiled, and 93.9 ms of the compiled figure is in compiler-generated Triton kernels. These are profiler-session measurements, not an additive decomposition of the separate unprofiled latencies in Table 11 . The slowdown also appears with pruning and in every measured power mode (Table 11 ).

We audited 25 VLA acceleration papers that report inference speed-ups, token pruning, caching, or quantization (Table 12 ). The entries are the papers we identified that report a latency or speed-up for one of these methods on a named VLA, checked against each paper’s arXiv text. The list is not the result of a systematic database search and is not claimed to be exhaustive. Of the 13 entries listing token pruning, reuse, merging or sparsification, none specifies the baseline and method execution modes. One names only its attention backend. Among the step-reduction papers, Tang et al. (2026) report inference without compilation, using SDPA attention. For papers omitting execution-mode information, readers cannot check whether a reported saving applies to compiled execution or CUDA graphs.

Here we examine changes in pruning’s millisecond saving under CUDA graphs, which separate exactly into changes in kernel time and time outside kernels. Here Δ ​ X \Delta X means the value of X X before pruning minus its value afterwards. The difference between measured latency under CUDA graphs and the latency implied by unchanged millisecond savings is:

Positive excess means fewer milliseconds saved than assumed; negative excess means more. Only the change in time outside kernels under CUDA graphs enters the identity; its unpruned value alone does not determine the excess.

The contribution from time outside kernels under CUDA graphs, − Δ ​ I graph -\Delta I_{\rm graph} , ranges from − 0.56 -0.56 to + 0.76 +0.76 ms. The kernel-time contribution, Δ ​ K eager − Δ ​ K graph \Delta K_{\rm eager}-\Delta K_{\rm graph} , ranges from − 2.0 -2.0 to + 0.08 +0.08 ms.

passages.text: The largest positive excess for an individual selector is 1.04 ms (3.5%, OpenVLA-OFT H100 at 25% pruning). Its contributions include a 0.33 ms reduction in eager time outside kernels and a 0.76 ms increase in time outside kernels under CUDA graphs. After averaging paired selectors, the maximum millisecond-reuse error is 3.1% of measured whole-inference latency (Table 14 ).

passages.section: Appendix F CUDA Graphs: Changes in Kernel Time and Time Outside Kernels

passages.text: On the Thor, kernels keep the GPU busy for almost the whole inference. The kernel-time contribution ranges from − 10.7 -10.7 to + 11.1 +11.1 ms. The contributions largely cancel, leaving a maximum positive excess of 2.5 ms. Estimated time outside kernels is 5.6% to 6.9% of unpruned latency under CUDA graphs on the H100 (1.6 to 5.2 ms for OpenVLA-OFT, CogACT and OpenVLA; 25.7 ms for LLaVA-VLA), compared with 0.1% to 0.6% on the A10G, whose longer kernels more easily hide CPU launches. LLaVA-VLA’s kernel term is − 21 -21 ms and its excess − 28 -28 ms on the H100, and − 19 -19 and − 35 -35 ms on the Thor, because decoding under CUDA graphs attends over a fixed-size, masked key-value cache (Section 3.2 ).

We call the full set of four-latency comparisons the reuse census. Each method-pair comparison records four times: the baseline T 0 T_{0} , each method alone ( T 1 T_{1} , T 2 T_{2} ), and both together ( T 12 T_{12} ). The 714 comparisons comprise 682 for graphs, compilation and quantization on the four Llama-based models and 32 for step reduction on the flow models. A configuration fixes the model, platform, execution mode and optimization setting. Comparisons retain individual token selectors. Configuration-level results average paired selectors’ four latencies before applying the reuse assumptions. Software and power variants count separately.

The change in quantization saving is split into a contribution from the affected-stage share, ( σ 1 − σ 0 ) ​ ( 1 − 1 / s 0 ) (\sigma_{1}-\sigma_{0})(1-1/s_{0}) , and one from the stage speed-up, σ 1 ​ ( 1 / s 0 − 1 / s 1 ) \sigma_{1}(1/s_{0}-1/s_{1}) . In the 103 individual-selector comparisons from the H100, A10G and Thor campaigns above the 5.3% threshold of Section 5 , the affected-stage share falls in all 103 and the stage speed-up also falls in 99. The largest ratio of measured latency to latency implied by the updated assumption is 1.385.

The share and speed-up decomposition omits changes outside the affected prefill/decode stages. The absolute difference between attributed and measured whole-inference saving has a median of 0.4 percentage points and a maximum of 4.1 points. The attribution is therefore approximate.

passages.section: Appendix H Preference Order and Screening Consistency
passages.location: Appendix H Preference Order and Screening Consistency
passages.text: Table 17 lists the recorded settings that meet the inference-time budget for each over-budget model–platform case, using a fixed preference order. For pruning, select the lowest percentage of tokens removed that meets the budget. For quantization, consider groups in this order: int8 weights, int4 weights, 8-bit compute (int8, dynamic FP8 or static FP8), then NVFP4. Select the fastest scheme in the first group containing a budget-meeting option. Consider pairs only when neither method meets the budget alone, ordered by pruning level, then quantization group, then latency. This order is fixed solely to make the comparison on the recorded grid reproducible. It does not rank task accuracy or prescribe a quantization order for deployment. Each case uses one execution mode and only the settings recorded in it. Pruning uses random token selection; recorded levels vary by platform, with 6.25% increments on RTX 4090. H100 and A10G cases use the PyTorch 2.10 and torchao 0.13 campaign, while LLaVA-VLA compilation and the other platforms retain earlier records.

passages.section: Appendix H Preference Order and Screening Consistency
passages.location: Appendix H Preference Order and Screening Consistency
passages.text: Checking the screens of Section 6 against the recorded measurements confirms that neither excludes a budget-meeting candidate. The all-tokens-removed latency used by the affected-stage screen is recorded only in eager execution and under CUDA graphs. On the three cases whose selected mode is CUDA graphs, it excludes pruning alone in two, and neither has a pruning level meeting the budget. Because the compiled cases lack this measurement, Table 16 instead removes each affected stage entirely, counting prefill plus decode for autoregressive pruning. This weaker form excludes nothing on the grid. The weight-read screen excludes candidates in four cases, and each excluded candidate’s own measured latency, after its pruning or quantization, is at least 2.67 ​ B 2.67B (median 6.67 ​ B 6.67B ). This audit does not test how well the screens distinguish candidates close to the budget. The weight-read bound assumes unchanged layer counts, at least 4-bit weights, and mandatory weight streaming from DRAM on each pass without inter-pass cache reuse. These assumptions must be checked before using the bound to exclude a deployment candidate. Table 16 gives the counts for each search strategy.

analysis.overview: 这篇的增量是如何选择和组合 VLA 推理优化：先在目标机器确定执行模式，再重测剪枝、减步和量化的组合收益；用扣除预处理与调度余量后的预算判断能否部署。跨模型、跨平台配对测量支持这个流程，但没有证明相应剪枝或量化仍保留任务成功率。
analysis.notice: 已阅读提取出的185个文字片段（主文、附录及提取出的表格），目视核对固定版本PDF第8、10、24、26页的组合误差图、预算示例及表13/17；未逐图核查全部图片、重推全部公式、逐篇核查参考文献或运行代码。前四个片段为排版警告，不是研究结果。引文匹配只验证出处；作者测得的延迟未独立复现。

findings.title: 增量：在部署模式下重测优化组合
findings.text: 研究覆盖7种VLA、7类优化和H100/A10G/RTX 4090/Jetson Thor四组GPU及主机。VLA-Triage先扣除预处理、通信和调度余量，再选执行模式与注意力后端，筛查不可行候选，然后测组合并验证任务表现。它是测量与筛选流程，并非一种新剪枝器或新VLA模型。
findings.quote: Measure pruning and step-reduction settings in the compiled mode

findings.title: 最小配对测量：基线、A、B、A+B四个延迟
findings.text: 固定模型、机器及软件，分别测T0、T1、T2、T12。保持单项百分比收益会预测T1×T2/T0；保持节省毫秒数会预测T1−(T0−T2)。用实测T12检查两种预测。编译会改阶段占比和kernel效率，剪枝又会改变矩阵尺寸，因此两种外推都可能失准。
findings.quote: Millisecond reuse assumes it saves the same number of milliseconds

findings.title: CogACT：编译后剪枝仅再省33.5 ms
findings.text: 表13同一软件栈、A10G、CogACT、75%视觉token剪枝：eager从200.1降至125.9 ms，省74.2 ms；max-autotune从97.5降至64.1 ms，省33.5 ms。若直接减去原先74.2 ms，会错误预测23.3 ms。H100同一对照中编译后只需21.5 ms，进一步剪枝17.4 ms；两台主机的收益不能互相套用。剪枝后的计时平均两个token选择器。

findings.title: 49.6 ms不等于满足50 ms部署预算
findings.text: 第6节的CogACT/A10G/max-autotune例子：单用75%剪枝64.1 ms，单用int8 compute 67.0 ms，组合49.6 ms。50 ms控制预算扣7.0 ms预处理和2.5 ms余量，只剩40.5 ms，组合仍超时。所测87.5%剪枝+int8最快46.4 ms，也未过线。这里通信预留为0；增加通信开销只会进一步收紧预算。
findings.quote: the 50 ms budget leaves only 40.5 ms for inference

findings.title: 组合误差不是只出现在一个例子
findings.text: 在194个已编译的剪枝—量化配置中，52个的实测延迟比沿用单项百分比节省所预测的延迟高出5.3%以上，最大约49%。在32个编译—减步配置中有29个超过这个门槛，SmolVLA/4090例为预测17.4而实测56.9 ms。但这些流模型例子都满足所测试预算，不能把预测误差直接说成控制失败；配置数也不是独立重复试验数。5.3%来自作者观察到的最大eager基线漂移，不是统计置信界。
findings.quote: The 32 flow combinations meet all three tested budgets

findings.title: 编译与注意力后端是实验条件
findings.text: 编译不一定加速：Thor上的GR00T有kernel间隙减少、kernel总时长反增的profile，作者归因分析涉及拷贝和类型转换；不能把这些profile项直接加减到独立计时。FastV读取注意力权重会改变所用后端，比较时必须计入选择开销并使用对应的融合注意力基线。论文引言50%剪枝示例与附录表5的75%剪枝不是同一条件，本报告不将两组数拼成一个消融。
findings.quote: the standard fused kernel does not write to memory

findings.title: 实测边界：不是完整机器人闭环实验
findings.text: 计时从CPU图像预处理之后开始，到模型返回动作结束；作者另用动作队列回放推导空闲和服务能力，不是真机闭环任务成功率。表17明确未评任务准确率，剪枝用随机token选择研究token数量的延迟影响。因此无法从更快推导抓取更准、控制更稳或剪枝精度可接受。

findings.title: 预算依赖动作消费方式
findings.text: 作者统一20 Hz（50 ms控制周期），单动作预算50 ms；分块异步策略在约半块动作剩余时请求下一块，预算为剩余动作数×50 ms。长chunk获得更宽计算窗口，同时可能面对观测陈旧。不能拿不同chunk模型的绝对推理延迟直接排名，也不能把这些预算当所有机器人默认要求。

findings.title: 跨平台结果含主机与软件差异
findings.text: H100和A10G部分编译/量化对照匹配PyTorch 2.10与torchao 0.13，但整个矩阵的软件版本、CPU和GPU并不全相同；Thor功耗模式也影响结论。跨平台的反转是整套GPU—主机部署的观察，不是隔离GPU架构的因果实验。本文未报告4090量化方案，不能补写该平台量化结论。
findings.quote: We do not report quantisation schemes on the RTX 4090

findings.title: 显存、启动时间和筛查假设也要算
findings.text: 每种固定shape的CUDA graph需要自己的内存池；batch8同时保留4档剪枝graph时，OFT/LLaVA-VLA会超24GB。编译启动可达分钟级。4bit权重读取筛查以每pass从DRAM读取、层数不变且不跨pass缓存为前提，不能排除通过缓存或删层改变这些前提的方案；筛查一致性来自记录网格，不代表对未见部署有保证。
findings.quote: These assumptions must be checked before using the bound

hypotheses.title: 待验证：eager上有效的token选择器，编译后还值得吗？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：编译后，token选择器自身的开销及其注意力后端代价，可能抵消它相对随机剪枝的质量优势。选一个可运行的OFT抓放任务，在同一GPU/主机、精度、图像输入、batch1、75%保留比例设置（即剪掉25%）下，比较无剪枝、随机选择、基于注意力的FastV；在eager与选定编译模式分别实测。为避免歧义，统一记录实际token数；再用50%与75%剪除率复测。每组热身后至少200次，记录中位数/p95/p99、选择器耗时、端到端含预处理延迟、峰值显存、编译/graph回退及失败率；任务用相同场景/种子评估成功率并报告差异区间。基线使用各模式支持的最佳融合注意力后端，FastV若需退回unfused则显式标记；另加支持时的融合评分实现。若在匹配任务成功率时FastV编译版仍稳定优于融合基线且没有模式回退，就反对“后端与选择开销吞掉收益”的假设；若只在某一token档失效，结论缩小到该shape。实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现空白。
hypotheses.quote: A fused scoring implementation (fastv_fa) retains the fused path

frontier_brief.title: VLA-Triage：先选执行模式，再测剪枝与量化的组合
frontier_brief.change_type: 推理部署 · 新测量方法
frontier_brief.delta: 先在目标机器选好编译模式与注意力后端，再重测剪枝、减步、量化的组合。编译会改变各阶段的耗时占比，剪枝会改变矩阵形状；单项加速比不能直接相乘，用它判断能否满足控制时限会出错。
frontier_brief.before: 分别在eager基线上测剪枝、减步、量化，再沿用各自节省比例或毫秒数，估计组合能否满足时限。
frontier_brief.after: 先确定真实部署模式，配对测基线、A、B与A+B四个延迟；按预处理、通信和调度余量扣减后的预算筛选，再检查任务成功率与控制稳定性。
frontier_brief.relevance: 做VLA加速选题或复现时，把eager和编译后的结果分别报告，保留完整的四组测量。优先在你实际用的GPU、注意力后端与token数上判断方案是否值得采用，再投入大规模任务评测。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者用随机token选择研究延迟，没有证明剪枝或量化保留任务成功率。计时不含CPU图像预处理；控制表现来自队列回放。跨平台还涉及主机和软件差异，数字不能直接搬到你的机器人。
frontier_brief.question: 注意力选token在编译之后，还能赢过融合注意力基线吗？

evidence.label: 编译改变了剪枝可节省的时间
evidence.context: CogACT / A10G，剪掉75%视觉token。eager为200.1→125.9 ms；max-autotune为97.5→64.1 ms。编译后再剪枝，节省时间已明显变小。表13，匹配软件栈。

evidence.label: 推理过线，部署仍超时
evidence.context: CogACT / A10G / max-autotune，75%剪枝+int8 compute测得49.6 ms。50 ms预算扣7.0 ms图像预处理和2.5 ms调度余量，模型仅剩40.5 ms。通信开销预设为0，第6节。

evidence.label: 百分比外推低估了组合延迟
evidence.context: 已编译的剪枝—量化配置中，52个比沿用单项百分比收益的预测慢5.3%以上，最大约49%。配置不是独立试验；5.3%是作者观测到的基线漂移门槛。

mechanism.title: 先建立部署基线
mechanism.text: 在目标机器实测eager、CUDA graphs和可用编译模式，连同注意力后端、显存与冷启动成本一起选择。

mechanism.title: 重测组合而非相乘
mechanism.text: 在选定模式和实际保留token数下，测基线、两种单项及组合。编译后的阶段占比和kernel效率可能已经不同。

mechanism.title: 把节省转成可用性
mechanism.text: 从控制预算扣除预处理、通信和调度余量。延迟过线后再测任务成功率；若已经满足，不继续盲目叠加有精度风险的优化。

passages.section: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
passages.location: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
passages.text: Online 3D bin packing with a processing buffer requires choosing which box to pack, its orientation, and its placement while keeping the stack stable under unknown future arrivals. A collapse ends the episode and forfeits the remaining volume. Existing methods use geometric rules or hard stability masks, limiting how risk can influence the joint choice of box, orientation, and placement. We propose Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning (SHORE), which combines a learned stability probability of a placement with an on-policy estimate of its return conditional on stability. A 3D U-Net learns stability from executed outcomes and simulated alternatives, revealing outcomes of actions underrepresented in early rollouts. A discrete on-policy actor–critic uses stability predictions in both its action values and policy prior, with gates that limit the effect of an untrained or changing model. In deployment, SHORE does not require additional search or simulation overhead. In Isaac Gym, SHORE reaches 73% space utilization by 0.4M environment steps, while the same learner without stability modeling reaches that level at about 1M. On the expanded 60-box set, SHORE achieves 0.734 space utilization versus 0.588 for the GOPT state-of-the-art baseline, with a higher placement-failure frequency (1.03% vs. 0.63%), trading more risk for greater packed volume. The results show faster learning and higher utilization on the more demanding realistic box arrival set. Ablations suggest that simulated alternatives provide useful early supervision, while executed outcomes alone sustain later performance. We also demonstrate the method on a real robot to verify the simplicity of integrating the method to real bin packing pipelines.

passages.section: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
passages.location: SHORE: Stability-Hybrid On-Policy Reinforcement Learning for Online Bin Packing
passages.text: Fig. 1 : Illustration of the online bin packing setting with a finite processing buffer. The packing agent selects a box from the buffer, its orientation, and its placement while future arrivals remain unknown.

Online 3D bin packing requires selecting and placing boxes as they arrive, without knowing the complete arrival sequence. In warehouse settings, a small processing buffer allows for limited reordering prior to placement (Fig. 1 ). The objective is to pack densely while keeping the stack stable, which depends on the box dimensions, physics, and the order, orientation, and location of placement.

Physical stability depends on more than the visible top surface. Supporting material properties and the arrangement of multiple supporting boxes can affect a placement’s outcome. One box collapse can leave the bin disorganized and hurt the long-term packing compactness. Therefore, there have been works trying to integrate physics-aware stability information into packing decision making.

Reinforcement learning (RL) packers usually handle stability with an action mask. Most masks are computed using geometric or physics-based rules on the height map or the stacking structure [ 1 , 2 ] . Instead, [ 3 ] and [ 4 ] learn the stability mask through simulation outcomes together with a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy [ 5 ] , but apply the masks as hard filters on the placement of a box the policy has already chosen. Stability therefore cannot influence which box to pack, leading to a policy that is not jointly optimal. Moreover, a placement is either allowed or forbidden, with no trade-off between its risk and the volume it adds. This motivates designing a more advanced joint policy in which stability awareness can directly affect selection among boxes, orientations, and placements in the long run.

We propose SHORE, which separates the prediction of the outcome of the current placement from the value of the subsequent packing, but intelligently fuses the stability information back to guide the long-term joint policy learning. A 3D U-Net reads bin occupancy and the oriented box properties to estimate whether the whole stack satisfies the stability test after the placement. A separate action-conditioned critic learns the return if the current placement holds, including its immediate reward and subsequent packing, from on-policy rollouts. The stability estimate modulates this value and provides a soft prior to the joint actions of the actor (Fig. 2 ). In this on-policy actor–critic method, the critic scores every valid (box, orientation, placement) triple, and the actor follows the exact expected gradient over all of them, so the stability estimate shapes which box is packed and how it is turned, not only where it goes. At inference, SHORE chooses each placement with one pass of the actor and of the stability network.
In short, our contributions are:

A physics-aware RL strategy that uses learned placement-stability probabilities as continuous weights on action values for policy improvement over joint box–orientation–placement actions, so that the packing agent can trade the risk of an unstable placement against the volume it adds.
A highly parallel, Isaac Gym-based bin packing environment that enables fast, large-scale on-policy RL training.
An empirical study of the efficiency of this method on a realistic box distribution, together with an initial real-robot deployment test.

Online 3D Bin Packing. This problem setting involves making packing decisions without knowledge of incoming items, leading to unique challenges in achieving optimality and efficiency. The early efforts on this problem are mostly studies about developing adaptive heuristics and algorithms that can handle the sequential nature of item arrivals. For example, [ 6 ] and [ 7 ] utilize deepest-bottom-left (DBL) heuristics, while [ 8 ] introduces Heightmap-Minimization heuristics.

Recent work in this area has moved beyond classical heuristics to incorporate deep learning, physics constraints, and more generalizable models. [ 9 ] use DRL to solve the specific setting with an arbitrary number of bins and any bin size, and show RL + search heuristics outperform traditional online heuristics across a range of instances. [ 10 ] tackle the problem with constrained DRL, framing the problem as a constrained Markov decision process under limited lookahead and enforcing physical stability, and show strong improvements over previous heuristics. [ 11 ] designs a complete robot pipeline to narrow the gap of heuristic DRL framework between simulation and real world. More recently, [ 2 ] introduces a DRL model that not only places items but also generalizes to bins of varying sizes via a transformer architecture that fuses item and bin subspace features. [ 12 ] integrate a physics heuristic with object rearrangement and stable placement into a DRL framework to reduce wasted space and improve utilization. However, the design of good heuristics remains a challenge, which leads to the emergence of learning-based action masking models.

Action masking models. Action masking has emerged as a practical strategy to tackle the enormous, state-dependent action space in the online 3D bin packing setting. [ 13 ] propose a feasibility-prediction module that learns a binary “feasibility mask” over placement choices and uses that mask to modulate actor probabilities during training, which substantially speeds learning and enforces collision/stability constraints. Building on the same idea, [ 14 ] allows custom action-mask definitions including reorientation and empty maximal spaces (EMSs), and compares masking strategies with search-based planners. [ 1 ] instead compute the feasibility mask for the placement actions based on the stacking tree analysis. [ 4 ] incorporate physics properties into the mask calculation to improve sample efficiency and reduce unsafe actions during exploration. [ 2 ] uses pairwise action-masking between EMSs and orientations to guarantee that the policy only samples pairs, further improving generalization in the online setting. [ 3 ] learn the mask online from physics simulations, jointly with the policy. All of these masks are hard filters on placements. SHORE instead keeps a geometric mask only for fit and support, and uses a learned stability probability inside the action value, where it can be traded against packed volume and affects which box is packed.

We consider online 3D single-bin packing with a processing buffer of size N N . Only the first N N unplaced boxes are visible, and placing one admits the next arrival. The full simulator state ξ t \xi_{t} includes the physical configuration and the entire arrival queue. It evolves as an MDP ℳ = ( 𝒳 , 𝒜 , P , r ¯ , γ ) \mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{A},P,\bar{r},\gamma) , where 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is the full state space, 𝒜 \mathcal{A} the joint action space, P P the transition kernel, and r ¯ ( ξ , a ) = 𝔼 [ r t ∣ ξ t = ξ , a t = a ] \bar{r}(\xi,a)=\mathbb{E}[r_{t}\mid\xi_{t}=\xi,a_{t}=a] the expected reward. We use γ = 1 \gamma=1 and maximize J ⁡ ( θ ) = 𝔼 π ​ [ ∑ t γ t ​ r t ] J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[\sum_{t}\gamma^{t}r_{t}] , the expected packed-volume fraction. The policy receives only the observation s t s_{t} defined below, so its decision problem is partially observable. Arrival order is exogenous; the agent controls only the reordering allowed by the buffer.

The policy observation is s t = ( C t , d t ) s_{t}=(C_{t},d_{t}) : the voxelized bin configuration and the properties of the visible boxes. The unseen arrival queue and unresolved contact details belong to ξ t \xi_{t} , not s t s_{t} . We use s s as shorthand for this observation in the policy, critic and stability model. The bin has physical dimensions ( L p , W p , H p ) (L_{p},W_{p},H_{p}) and is discretized into ( l p , w p , h p ) (l_{p},w_{p},h_{p}) cells. C t C_{t} records voxel densities, and its height map η t ∈ { 0 , … , h p } l p × w p \eta_{t}\in\{0,\dots,h_{p}\}^{l_{p}\times w_{p}} gives the top occupied cell of each column. The buffer d t d_{t} contains each visible box’s dimensions and density. Following GOPT [ 2 ] , these observations are encoded as two token sets (Fig. 2 ):

Item tokens. There is one token for each pair u = ( b , j ) u=(b,j) of a visible box b b and an orientation j ∈ 𝒪 j\in\mathcal{O} , where 𝒪 \mathcal{O} contains the six axis-aligned orientations. Token 𝐱 u \mathbf{x}_{u} contains the oriented extents, expressed in voxel units and normalized by ( l p , w p , h p ) (l_{p},w_{p},h_{p}) , the similarly normalized unrotated extents, a heavy flag derived from density, a presence flag and a selectability flag. Duplicate tokens remain in the observation but are not selectable.

Placement tokens. There are at most K K empty maximal spaces (EMSs), each extending to the bin’s maximum height. For EMS k k , let ( x 1 , y 1 , z 1 ) (x_{1},y_{1},z_{1}) and ( x 2 , y 2 , h p ) (x_{2},y_{2},h_{p}) be its corners in voxel coordinates. Its token 𝐲 k \mathbf{y}_{k} contains these first five coordinates normalized by the corresponding grid dimensions, followed by support fractions ρ k flat \rho_{k}^{\mathrm{flat}} and ρ k rigid \rho_{k}^{\mathrm{rigid}} . These measure the part of its base supported at height z 1 z_{1} , and the part supported there by the bin floor or a heavy box, respectively. They are the only density-layout information provided to the actor and critic. EMSs are sorted by ( z 1 , y 1 , x 1 ) (z_{1},y_{1},x_{1}) and truncated to K K ; unused slots are zero-padded and cannot be selected.

An action a = ( u , k ) a=(u,k) pairs an item token u = ( b , j ) u=(b,j) with an EMS k k . Box b b is rotated to orientation j j and placed with its minimum corner at ( x 1 , y 1 ) (x_{1},y_{1}) of EMS k k , resting on the highest column under its footprint. Placements are therefore limited to EMS corners rather than every grid cell, and box order, orientation and placement are chosen jointly at every step. A rule-based mask m ⁡ ( s , a ) ∈ { 0 , 1 } m(s,a)\in\{0,1\} admits a pair if and only if u u is selectable, the oriented box fits inside the EMS (and hence inside the bin and below H p H_{p} ), and the placement passes GOPT’s geometric support test [ 2 ] . The test requires that more than half of the footprint rests at the placement height, or that the footprint center lies within the convex hull of the supported cells. The valid action set is 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) = { a : m ⁡ ( s , a ) = 1 } \mathcal{A}(s)=\{a:m(s,a)=1\} , with | 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) | ≤ 6 ​ N ​ K |\mathcal{A}(s)|\leq 6NK .
The goal is to maximize space utilization while every placement stays stable. The reward at each step is the placed box’s share of the bin volume:
r t = χ t ​ V b t V bin , r_{t}=\chi_{t}\,\frac{V_{b_{t}}}{V_{\mathrm{bin}}}, (1)

where b t b_{t} is the selected box, V b t V_{b_{t}} its volume, V bin = L p ​ W p ​ H p V_{\mathrm{bin}}=L_{p}W_{p}H_{p} , and χ t ∈ { 0 , 1 } \chi_{t}\in\{0,1\} is the observed stability outcome: it is one exactly when Eq. ( 2 ) holds. An unstable placement earns zero and ends the episode (Sec. III-E ). With γ = 1 \gamma=1 , the undiscounted reward sum is the stably packed volume fraction at termination, bounded by the total sequence volume ( 0.691 0.691 for the base set and 0.866 0.866 for the expanded set). The reward of a successful placement depends only on its box volume; order, orientation and placement affect subsequent rewards through future fit and stability. Learners use the scaled reward c r ​ r t c_{r}r_{t} , with c r = 10 c_{r}=10 .

Near the end of an episode the buffer can hold fewer than N N boxes. Empty slots are marked absent and masked, so the policy cannot select them. No invalid-selection penalty is needed, unlike the penalty used in [ 3 ] .

We make the two criteria used throughout the paper explicit. Stability (evaluated after placement). A placement is executed by releasing the box 2 2 mm above its target position in the chosen orientation and simulating the scene forward for τ = 80 \tau=80 ms. Let 𝐩 i tgt , 𝐩 i settled ∈ ℝ 3 \mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}},\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{settled}}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} denote box i i ’s target and settled positions, and let ℐ t \mathcal{I}_{t} contain all boxes in the stack, including the new box. Stability requires
max i ∈ ℐ t ⁡ ‖ 𝐩 i settled − 𝐩 i tgt ‖ 2 ≤ ϵ s . \max_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{t}}\left\|\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{settled}}-\mathbf{p}_{i}^{\mathrm{tgt}}\right\|_{2}\leq\epsilon_{s}. (2)

The threshold ϵ s \epsilon_{s} is a positional displacement tolerance; the test checks movement of both the new box and previously placed boxes. Feasibility (evaluated before placement). Feasibility is the geometric mask m ⁡ ( s , a ) m(s,a) of the action definition. Apart from excluding duplicate tokens, it encodes only fit and GOPT’s support test, both computed from the height map, so it does not predict Eq. ( 2 ), which depends on box densities and on the response of the whole stack. Stability is learned instead: SHORE trains a separate model of the probability that a placement satisfies Eq. ( 2 ) (Sec. IV-C ) and uses it in both the critic and the policy.

An episode ends in one of three ways: (i) completion , when every box in the sequence has been placed; (ii) infeasibility , when the method’s feasibility filter admits no placement for the next decision; and (iii) instability , when an executed placement violates Eq. ( 2 ). For SHORE, GOPT+ and GOPT, the feasibility filter is purely geometric: it is the rule-based mask m ⁡ ( s , a ) m(s,a) of Sec. III-B , which admits a placement only if the oriented box fits inside the EMS and passes GOPT’s support test, both computed from the height map. SHORE and GOPT+ apply it to every visible box in every orientation, so an infeasible ending means that no visible box fits anywhere with enough support; GOPT applies it only to the buffer head in its stored orientation. For OL Mask, the filter of the selected box also includes the learned stability mask, so its episodes can also end when the mask rejects every placement as unstable. An infeasible ending can therefore mean that no box fits in the remaining space, or that the filter rejects placements that would in fact be stable, and the evaluation does not separate the two.

Fig. 2 : SHORE framework. The bin configuration C t C_{t} and the buffer d t d_{t} are encoded as EMS tokens and (box, orientation) item tokens, and the rule-based mask m m keeps the geometrically valid pairs. The actor, a Packing Transformer, scores every valid pair and samples the action a = ( u , k ) a=(u,k) , which Isaac Gym executes and adjudicates by Eq. ( 2 ). A second Packing Transformer, the critic, values every pair in one pass, and a discretized REPPO learner updates both from on-policy rollouts (Sec. IV-B ).

SHORE trains an actor–critic over the joint action a = ( u , k ) a=(u,k) with a discretized version of REPPO [ 15 ] (Secs. IV-A – IV-B ) and adds a learned estimate S ⁡ ( s , a ) S(s,a) of the probability that placement a a holds, i.e., satisfies Eq. ( 2 ) (Secs. IV-C – IV-D ). S S enters learning in two places: it weights the critic’s value ( critic weighting , Sec. IV-E ) and it acts as a prior on the actor ( actor prior , Sec. IV-F ). Two safeguards keep an untrained or changing S S from disturbing the learner (Sec. IV-G ). Fig. 2 gives an overview, and Algorithm 1 lists one training iteration.

The stability model addresses a specific weakness of the plain learner. A collapse pays 0 and ends the episode, so a plain critic must learn, for every action, the product of two different quantities: the chance that the placement holds, which depends on the densities and support under the footprint, and the value of the packing that follows. The token observation shows EMS rectangles and two support fractions but not the interior of the stack, and collapses are rare, so the critic learns this product slowly and only for the actions the policy executes.

The actor and the critic each have their own Packing Transformer backbone [ 2 ] . MLPs embed the item tokens 𝐱 u \mathbf{x}_{u} and EMS tokens 𝐲 k \mathbf{y}_{k} into 𝐡 u , 𝐞 k ∈ ℝ 128 \mathbf{h}_{u},\mathbf{e}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{128} , and three encoder blocks apply self-attention within each token type and cross-attention between items and EMSs. Actor and critic parameters are denoted θ \theta and ϕ \phi . A label is the binary outcome of a placement, y = 1 y=1 if it held and y = 0 y=0 if it collapsed, stored with its state in a buffer 𝒟 S \mathcal{D}_{S} . Recorded physical outcomes can be reused across policy updates; predictive accuracy is checked on recent held-out placements as the visited states change. They come from two sources, collected during the rollout phase of Algorithm 1 :

Executed placements. Every placement executed in a rollout is labeled by its real outcome, with label weight ζ = 2 \zeta=2 . A random 10% of executed outcomes go to a holdout set, excluded from supervised training and used to assess the learning copy S ψ S_{\psi} before activation (Sec. IV-G ).

Simulated placements. At every step, up to B = B s + B r B=B_{s}+B_{r} other valid placements per environment are tested in a copy of the environment and labeled by their simulated outcome, with label weight ζ = 1 \zeta=1 . passages.text: Algorithm 1 SHORE: one training iteration

The critic, the label buffer and the simulator are used only during training. At deployment, SHORE computes the geometric mask, one actor pass and the stability network’s passes for the visible items. It then executes arg ⁡ max a ∈ 𝒜 ⁡ ( s ) ​ [ ℓ θ ​ ( s , a ) + w π ​ log ⁡ S ~ ​ ( s , a ) ] \arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{A}(s)}[\ell_{\theta}(s,a)+w_{\pi}\log\widetilde{S}(s,a)] , the mode of Eq. ( 9 ). No search is run and no placement is simulated.
The experiments answer three questions:
Does explicit stability modeling accelerate policy learning and improve the trade-off between packed volume and collapse risk, beyond the benefit of buffer selection and rotation?
Where must the stability estimate act: in the critic, in the policy, or in both?
Do simulated stability labels help beyond the labels of executed placements, and is choosing them by uncertainty better than choosing them at random?

All methods share the simulator, box sets, stability criterion (Eq. ( 2 )) and evaluation protocol (Sec. V-C ). The baselines keep their own action spaces and rewards. Except where stated, they place every box in its stored orientation, as in their original implementations, while SHORE and GOPT+ choose among six orientations.

Masked-PPO variants. OL Mask [ 3 ] learns a stability mask online from physics simulations, jointly with a PPO policy. It is the strongest prior method in this setting and the closest to ours, since it also learns stability from physics. Nomask removes masking entirely. Random Selection randomly picks the box from the buffer with only the placement decided by the policy network; Random Placement places at random positions with only box selection determined by the policy.

Learning-based state of the art. GOPT [ 2 ] is a transformer-based DRL packer using Empty Maximal Spaces (EMSs — the maximal axis-aligned empty boxes remaining in the bin) as placement candidates. We use the official implementation (Packing Transformer, EMS placement generator, and masked PPO) and swap only its geometric environment for ours, so that placements are executed and adjudicated by the same physics: unstable placements terminate episodes exactly as for the other methods. Since GOPT is a strict online packer without buffer selection, it packs the buffer head at each step. GOPT+ extends GOPT to the action space of SHORE. The same Packing Transformer chooses any visible box in any of its six orientations, i.e., a joint (box, orientation, EMS) action, and is trained with GOPT’s masked PPO [ 5 ] , with the clipped ratio applied separately to the (box, orientation) choice and to the EMS choice. Its rollout size, learning rate and number of updates are matched to SHORE − - actor prior − - critic weighting, so GOPT+ has the actor network and the action space of SHORE − - actor prior − - critic weighting and differs from it in the learner.
TABLE I : Box specifications in the simulation environment.

To assess sensitivity to box geometry, the expanded evaluation uses the 12 geometries in Tab. II , with five boxes per geometry (60 arrivals per episode), alongside the four-type base set. Density is assigned independently of geometry: each odd-numbered geometry contributes three light and two heavy boxes and each even-numbered geometry two light and three heavy, giving 30 light and 30 heavy boxes per episode. Light and heavy boxes use the two materials of the base set (100 kg/m 3 with rigidity 0.5, and 5000 kg/m 3 with rigidity 3; Tab. I ). The 60 boxes fill 86.6% of the bin volume, against 69.1% for the base set, so the expanded set is both more heterogeneous and tighter. Every learned method is retrained from scratch on the expanded set with unchanged hyperparameters, and no policy is transferred between box sets. We run all training and evaluation in Isaac Gym [ 20 ] with the GPU-accelerated PhysX backend. A placement is executed as a release 2 2 mm above the target position in the selected orientation, without a full arm trajectory or added Gaussian position or rotation perturbations. This deliberate simplification keeps the property that matters for the decision problem, whether the stack holds, while abstracting away manipulator dynamics. A single box released on the bin settles onto its target with zero measurable drift.

For sim-to-sim transfer, we calibrated Isaac Gym’s PhysX contact behavior against high-fidelity MuJoCo using paired placement replays (Appendix A ). This aligns the faster simulator with MuJoCo’s placement outcomes while retaining Isaac Gym’s GPU-parallel capacity for large-scale RL training. Agreement is high but imperfect, so reported results remain specific to the calibrated Isaac Gym model.

In implementation, the bin is 25 × 25 25\times 25 cm with a maximum stacking height of 20 20 cm, discretized into 25 × 25 × 20 25\times 25\times 20 voxels of 1 1 cm for placement choice. The length of the processing buffer is set to 5. Our box configuration uses light and heavy densities of 100 100 and 5000 5000 kg/m 3 , respectively, following the released implementation of [ 3 ] . This density contrast makes density-aware ordering important. The experimental settings used for our comparisons are listed here rather than assumed to match all settings reported in the original paper. All remaining hyperparameters are listed in Tab. VII (Appendix A ).

With N = 5 N=5 and K = 80 K=80 , each state has at most 6 ​ N ​ K = 2,400 6NK=2{,}400 joint actions, against 6 ​ N ​ l p ​ w p = 18,750 6Nl_{p}w_{p}=18{,}750 if every cell of the 25 × 25 25\times 25 grid were a placement choice. This action space is still large enough to make learning challenging.

Four types of boxes with different dimensions (length, width, and height), densities, and rigidities are used. While the density parameter controls how heavy the box is, the rigidity parameter controls the deformation degree of the box under contact forces; both impact placement stability. The detailed box specification is listed in Tab. I . The mixture of light deformable and heavy rigid boxes is what makes stability depend on more than geometry: for example, packing the light 6 × 6 × 4 6\times 6\times 4 boxes first produces a soft top surface, and any heavy 8 × 6 × 6 8\times 6\times 6 box arriving later must either be placed on that yielding surface (typically unstable) or terminate the episode. A policy that knows which surfaces will hold can choose its boxes and placements to keep rigid support available.

The total volume of all boxes in the base set is 0.691 0.691 of the bin volume, which caps utilization even if every box is packed successfully. This near-saturation ceiling makes the base set a weak test of further packing gains. We therefore also evaluate on the expanded FBA set, whose broader range of 12 carton dimensions better represents varied fulfillment-box sizes and raises the all-boxes-packed ceiling to 0.866 0.866 . The expanded set offers more headroom for comparing packing strategies and makes box choice and orientation more consequential. The base set remains useful for checking whether the method’s behavior transfers to a simpler, nearly saturated inventory.
Space utilization is the total stably packed box volume divided by bin volume. Mean episode length counts boxes successfully placed before termination.

Completion rate and unstable rate report the fractions of episodes that end with every box placed and with a collapse (Sec. III-E ). We do not report the share of infeasible endings as a metric: what it measures depends on each method’s feasibility filter (Sec. III-E ), so it is not comparable across methods. Collapses per placement is the number of collapses divided by the number of placement attempts (placed boxes plus collapses) over a method’s 50 evaluation episodes, in percent. An episode has at most one collapse. Thus, within a training seed, if f col f_{\mathrm{col}} is the fraction of episodes ending in collapse and L ¯ \bar{L} is the mean number of successfully placed boxes, collapses per attempt is f col / ( L ¯ + f col ) f_{\mathrm{col}}/(\bar{L}+f_{\mathrm{col}}) before conversion to percent. This normalizes failures by the number of executed attempts; it is not an independent outcome from episode length and unstable rate. It estimates the observed failure frequency under each policy’s visited states, rather than risk on a common set of stacks. A low per-attempt frequency can still accompany frequent episode failures when many placements must succeed in succession.

Stability-model metrics. The ablations (Sec. V-E ) evaluate the learning copy S ψ S_{\psi} on held-out executed outcomes. These outcomes are excluded from supervised training, but simulated labels can cover the same state–action pairs (Sec. IV-D ); the evaluation therefore does not establish generalization to entirely unseen placements. It also does not directly assess the acting copy S ψ ¯ S_{\bar{\psi}} .

AUROC , the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 1 − S ψ 1-S_{\psi} detecting collapses, measures ranking: the probability that a collapsed placement receives a lower prediction than a successful one, with half credit for ties. A score of 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect ranking. This metric opens the activation gate. Expected calibration error (ECE) groups predictions into ten equal-width bins and averages the absolute difference between each bin’s mean prediction and observed success frequency, weighted by bin size. Zero means perfect agreement at this bin resolution. Probability accuracy matters because the critic uses S ψ ¯ S_{\bar{\psi}} multiplicatively, but low ECE does not prove the pointwise accuracy required by Eq. ( 8 ). The metrics are complementary: with rare collapses, a constant high prediction can have low ECE while ranking at chance; good ranking can coexist with pessimistic probabilities. Both metrics use the most recent held-out outcomes after each training iteration: about 4,000, including 37–66 collapses at the reported ablation checkpoint.

Although the box type distribution is shared between training and evaluation (a realistic assumption for a warehouse with standardized box sizes), the arrival order is independently randomized in every evaluation episode, so evaluation sequences are almost surely never seen during training; the combinatorial space of arrival orders is ( 40 10 , 10 , 10 , 10 ) ≈ 4.7 × 10 21 \binom{40}{10,10,10,10}\approx 4.7\times 10^{21} . All metrics are averaged over 50 evaluation episodes with the same fixed episode seeds across all methods, using deterministic (argmax) actions and no search for the learned policies.

Separating action flexibility from stability awareness. The base-set comparison is close to its packing ceiling, while the expanded set tests the method in a more demanding regime: varied geometries constrain future fit, and material properties are independent of shape, so geometry alone cannot identify reliable support. At the base-set checkpoint, GOPT+ has higher utilization and completion than the single-seed SHORE run, despite SHORE’s earlier rise in training reward. The curves therefore suggest faster early learning in this run, not a base-set evaluation advantage or a seed-robust difference. The expanded set provides the stronger test of whether modeling stability helps when box choice, orientation, and future fit interact.

Fig. 3 : Training curves on the base box set for the methods of Table III , up to 1M environment steps, computed from training episodes as in Fig. 4 . (a) Mean reward of training episodes (packed volume fraction). (b) Fraction of training episodes that end in a collapse. (c) Collapses per placement attempt (log scale). The original GOPT runs did not log how training episodes end, so GOPT appears only in (a).

The comparison between GOPT and GOPT+ tests the value of broadening decisions beyond the buffer head and its fixed orientation. GOPT+ is our extension of the official GOPT baseline: it can choose a visible box, its orientation, and an EMS placement, so order, orientation, and location all affect the next packing state. Its stronger performance indicates that exposing these choices can improve packing on the expanded set and supports the importance of flexible, coordinated decisions. This is evidence for the value of the expanded decision space, though the comparison does not isolate action flexibility alone: GOPT+ also uses a different PPO update, with clipped ratios applied separately to item-orientation and placement choices.

Against this stronger diagnostic baseline, SHORE attains higher mean utilization while experiencing fewer collapses both per episode and per placement attempt, despite sharing its action space and actor backbone. The comparison therefore tests what stability-aware valuation and policy guidance add after the joint choices are available. To isolate stability modeling, the relevant control is REPPO-D, which shares the learner but removes both SHORE components. Its eventual utilization matches SHORE within training-seed variation. The evidence thus points to earlier acquisition and a better packing–risk balance, rather than a higher final utilization ceiling.

Why stability supervision helps learning. Figure 4 (a) and the intermediate deterministic checkpoint evaluations show that SHORE reaches its high-utilization regime earlier than the learner without S S . The advantage persists across intermediate checkpoints and appears under both sampled training actions and deterministic evaluation, so it is not merely a consequence of exploration noise in training returns. This pattern supports the hypothesis that separating immediate physical survival from continuation value makes learning easier. Without S S , the critic must infer both effects from returns; a failed placement also removes the opportunity to observe later packing decisions. In SHORE, supervised placement outcomes train a dedicated model with access to the internal density layout, and that information immediately affects the values and probabilities of joint box–orientation–placement choices. The later catch-up of the base learner is consistent with S S supplying useful information sooner, while both ultimately optimize the same packed-volume objective. This learning advantage is measured in rollout environment steps.

Stability without sacrificing useful packing. Table IV shows that SHORE packs more volume than GOPT+ with fewer failures per attempt, while their episode lengths are comparable. Its lower episode-collapse share thus accompanies a lower observed placement failure frequency, rather than simply fewer opportunities to fail. This supports using S S to guide productive joint actions. The two collapse metrics summarize the same failures at different scales; their agreement clarifies the packing–risk trade-off rather than providing independent statistical evidence.

Figure 4 (c) shows how this trade-off develops during learning. After the initial improvement, SHORE sustains fewer collapses per attempt than the learner without S S , alongside higher packed-volume reward in panel (a). GOPT+ approaches its placement-level failure frequency later, consistent with explicit stability supervision accelerating the acquisition of useful physical constraints. OL Mask reveals why both collapse metrics are needed: its failures per attempt decline while its episode-collapse share stays near saturation. It sustains more successful placements before failure, but still fails before completion. Panel (c) therefore reveals progress that panel (b) obscures. These sampled training trajectories complement the deterministic evaluation comparison; they do not measure deployment-policy performance directly.

Balancing stability against packed volume. The expanded set shows two ways to get this trade-off wrong. GOPT is the conservative extreme. It has the lowest observed collapse frequency, yet packs much less volume than the methods that choose from the whole buffer. Its low collapse share is partly a consequence of stopping early: it places only the buffer head in its stored orientation, so most of its episodes end once that box has no admissible placement, after about 41 boxes, and each episode contains fewer placements that could fail. Its restricted actions also make each placement more conservative: it never turns a box onto a smaller face and never packs the last, tightest part of the bin. The training curves show the same regime throughout learning (Fig. 4 ): about 30% of GOPT’s training episodes end in a collapse, the fewest of any method, while its training reward stays near 0.5. GOPT+ is the aggressive counterpart. With buffer selection and rotation it packs more volume, but incurs a higher collapse rate. Because a collapse ends the episode and forfeits every box not yet packed, neither extreme is optimal: avoiding risk leaves space unused, and ignoring risk lets a single failed placement discard the volume the remaining boxes would have added. SHORE’s action value prices this trade-off directly, as the probability that a placement holds times the return if it holds. With the same action space and backbone as GOPT+, it attains higher utilization while experiencing fewer episode collapses and fewer failures per placement. The aim is thus not the lowest collapse rate, which GOPT shows can be bought by stopping early, but the most packed volume for the risk taken. OL Mask fails on both counts: its hard mask admits placements that do not hold, and 99% of its episodes end in a collapse after about 16 boxes, although its different architecture, orientation restriction and training procedure prevent isolating soft versus hard masking as the cause.

No method completes the expanded sequences. For SHORE, fewer collapse endings accompany more geometrically infeasible endings, identifying preservation of usable space and support as a remaining challenge. Its soft prior does not remove geometrically valid actions; earlier choices can nevertheless leave no admissible placement. Infrequent placement failures can still interrupt a long sequence, while avoiding collapse alone does not preserve room for the remaining boxes. Normalization accounts for the number of attempts but not differences in the states visited; establishing lower risk on the same candidate placements would require a separate controlled comparison.

The ablations change one part of SHORE at a time on the expanded set, with all other settings fixed, and fall into two groups. For the component ablation (Table V ), AP (actor prior only) sets w Q = 0 w_{Q}=0 , CW (critic weighting only) sets w π = 0 w_{\pi}=0 , and REPPO-D switches off both SHORE components ( w π = w Q = 0 w_{\pi}=w_{Q}=0 ), leaving the discretized REPPO backbone of Sec. IV-B . The second group tests where the stability labels come from (Table VI ), with both components in place: executed placements only ( B s = B r = 0 B_{s}=B_{r}=0 , no simulator calls beyond the rollout), one simulated label per step ( B s = 1 B_{s}=1 , B r = 0 B_{r}=0 ), eight uniformly random simulated labels ( B s = 0 B_{s}=0 , B r = 8 B_{r}=8 ), or the default eight, six chosen by π γ π ​ ν \pi^{\gamma_{\pi}}\nu and two at random ( B s = 6 B_{s}=6 , B r = 2 B_{r}=2 ). All variants are compared at the same checkpoint, 901,120 environment steps. Every run that trains a stability model was resumed from this checkpoint, and a resume empties the label buffer, so a later checkpoint would compare variants at different distances from a reset. Each variant is scored with the protocol of Sec. V-C , and its stability model is also scored by AUROC (how well S S separates placements that collapse from placements that hold) and ECE (how closely S S matches the observed rate of holding), both defined in Sec. V-C .

The component and label-source variants are exploratory single-seed comparisons, whereas SHORE and SHORE − - actor prior − - critic weighting average multiple training seeds. Their small differences in packing or collapse share should therefore be treated as directional evidence. The reported metrics describe the learning copy, whereas decisions use the interpolated acting copy. Stability-model metrics also fluctuate across training iterations and are measured on each policy’s own held-out executed outcomes, rather than a common candidate set. They diagnose behavior on the actions each policy encounters; they do not establish uniform accuracy across the joint action space.

Complementary roles of value weighting and the action prior. Table V supports complementary roles for the actor prior and critic weighting: retaining either alone does not recover the full method’s packing performance. Critic weighting makes the value reflect the chance of losing both the current reward and the continuation, but its influence on action selection must pass through actor learning. The prior changes relative action probabilities directly, using voxel information unavailable to the actor, but by itself does not separate survival probability from the critic’s return estimate conditional on survival. Their combination supplies both a physically informed action value and an immediate bias toward actions likely to hold. The observed ordering is consistent with this division of labor, although repeated seeds are needed to establish the interaction reliably.

The CW variant is especially informative: its stability model ranks outcomes at least as well as the full model at the reported checkpoint, yet its packing performance is lower. Prediction quality alone therefore does not explain the full method’s advantage; how the estimate enters decision making matters. This is empirical support for the integration of S S into both modules, rather than evidence that a more accurate classifier automatically yields a better packer. The value factorization in Sec. IV-E supplies the mathematical justification under pointwise accurate stability probabilities and exact mean fitting; these ablations test its practical usefulness with an imperfect learned model. They do not independently validate the stability activation gate or stability trust region, which are retained in the tested variants.

What additional simulated labels contribute. Table VI shows that executed outcomes alone suffice to reach comparable packing performance at the ablation checkpoint. Together with the earlier checkpoint advantage of the default label scheme, this suggests that simulated alternatives mainly help acquire useful stability information before the rollout has supplied enough examples. They are not required to sustain the observed late-stage packing quality. Uncertainty-directed sampling also gives no demonstrated packing advantage over uniform sampling at this budget. The evidence therefore supports the stability model more strongly than it supports a particular acquisition rule or the necessity of extra simulator calls.

The ranking and calibration results explain why more labels need not improve control. The default simulated-label scheme yields stronger outcome ranking but poorer probability calibration than learning from executed outcomes alone. The recorded copy bias provides a plausible mechanism: simulated copies sometimes report collapse where the executed placement holds, pushing S S toward pessimistic probabilities. A ranking metric can improve despite this shift, while the multiplicative critic weighting depends on the probabilities themselves. Conversely, low ECE on mostly successful executed placements need not imply good discrimination of rare failures (Sec. V-C ). These findings support assessing both properties and caution against using either as a surrogate for packing performance. They also identify a concrete improvement path: reduce copy bias and assess label acquisition at matched simulation budgets, while retaining executed outcomes as the calibration reference.

We demonstrate the packing policy on a UFactory Lite6 arm with a vacuum gripper. The system uses a ZED 2i stereo camera and a hand-mounted camera. Fig. 6 shows one illustrated placement sequence. The yellow area serves as the packing bin. The sequence of cubes arrives in the order from right to left. This demonstration shows that our policy can be easily integrated into a robot packing pipeline.

We presented SHORE, an on-policy reinforcement learning method for physics-aware online 3D bin packing, which incorporates learned stability information through a policy prior and continuous weighting of action-conditioned critic values. The experiments support faster acquisition of high-utilization policies than learning without explicit stability modeling. Against GOPT+, which shares the joint action space and actor backbone, SHORE achieves higher mean utilization with fewer collapses per episode and per placement attempt. The training curves further show that the stability model reduces failures per attempt relative to the same learner without it. These findings support using stability information in both action valuation and selection to improve the packing–risk trade-off; the eventual catch-up of the base learner limits claims of a higher final performance ceiling.

Meanwhile, the method is limited by its observation and candidate representations, approximate stability probabilities, and simulator fidelity. A collapse is attributed to the triggering placement even when earlier choices created the fragile structure; those earlier choices receive information only through returns, and the value network cannot see the raw voxel grid of the bin. Collapses per placement account for the number of attempts, but remain specific to the states each policy visits; earlier infeasible termination can prevent exposure to difficult late-stage placements. Stability metrics must therefore be interpreted together with utilization and termination modes. Besides, there are more sim-to-real factors that we did not take into account, such as contact-parameter mismatch, bin wall collisions, and robot reachability.

For future work, it is better to specifically distinguish exogenous factors like incoming box distribution from endogenous factors, and tackle the problem from the exogenous MDP perspective [ 21 ] . Techniques can include, but are not limited to, exogenous state decomposition [ 22 ] or training a predictive model of the exogenous factors.

We used a system-identification-style paired-replay method: identical placement sequences were run in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym, and PhysX parameters were tuned to match per-placement stability verdicts. This increased agreement from 67.0% before calibration to 94.8% after calibration. MuJoCo served as the high-fidelity reference for sim-to-sim transfer; large-scale training and evaluation use Isaac Gym.
