findings.title: 目标仍是稳定装入体积：失败通过终止损失未来机会
findings.text: 任务只见接下来5个箱子，选择其中一个后才补入新到货。稳定放置得到箱体积/箱容积，失败当前奖励为0且回合结束，gamma=1；既往成功体积不因本次失败而清零。因此学习目标不是显式约束失败概率，也没有单独的坍塌惩罚；风险经未来装箱机会损失进入回报。方法要解决的是几何可放与物理可稳不同，以及单个回报同时混合即时失败和后续空间价值的问题。

findings.title: 联合箱子、朝向与EMS位置，同时保留几何硬掩码
findings.text: 每步联合选可见箱子、6种朝向和最多80个EMS角点，最多2400对候选；只在EMS角点放置，不搜索所有网格格点。尺寸合适、可选token与支撑条件仍是硬掩码，SHORE取消的是学习稳定性硬拒绝，并非所有掩码。actor和逐动作critic各用Packing Transformer，输入箱子与EMS token；只有表面支撑/重物比例，不能直接读取整个密度体素。GOPT只放队首固定朝向，故两者总差距不能归因于稳定机制。

findings.title: 额外体素模型与标签副本带来信息，也带来成本
findings.text: 稳定网络读取占据、密度体素和当前朝向箱子的尺寸/密度，3D U-Net共享主干接5个bootstrap头；均值给稳定概率，BALD分歧只用于选标签，不等于5个独立网络。相同尺寸与密度token共享前向，每次前向覆盖该token的所有EMS，每状态最多30次稳定网络前向。默认每环境步最多另试8个动作：6个按策略概率平方根乘分歧选择，2个随机；每8步再复制已执行动作诊断偏差。执行标签权重2、模拟标签权重1，40k状态缓冲，每rollout后64次监督更新。执行副本出现偏向失败的标签差异，不能把更多标签等同于更准。额外模型还获得actor/critic缺失的信息，纯学习算法归因需保留此差别。

findings.title: 条件价值乘稳定概率：等式有明确假设
findings.text: 对固定策略和回报目标，立即失败时G为0，所以Q_G=S_true×E[G|本步稳定]。SHORE用Q=U×(1−w_Q+w_Q S)，对成功样本赋权1、失败样本赋权1−w_Q；w_Q=1时U只用本步成功样本训练，但仍包含以后失败的风险。S不接critic梯度。论文式8表明，精确拟合加权均值时仍有(1−w+wS)/(1−w+wS_true)偏差因子；仅S逐点等于真实概率或w=0时恢复原Q。低总体ECE不能证明此逐点条件，有限数据、分布值编码、辅助损失也会引入误差；S_true=0且w=1时条件目标未定义。

findings.title: 策略用稳定性软先验，熵正则也须同步修改
findings.text: 联合策略概率正比于几何mask×exp(actor logit)×max(S,1e−6)^w_pi。预测不稳的几何合法动作仍有非零概率，可从真实执行结果纠偏；这是一种风险偏置，不是安全约束。熵项改为相对于稳定性先验的log(pi/S^w)，软价值使用同一正则，避免普通熵目标在理想解中抵消先验；目标熵取先验熵的一半。部署为几何掩码、一次actor和各可见item的稳定网络前向，按logit+w log S取argmax，不用critic、搜索或放置仿真；未报告端到端推理延迟。

findings.title: 启用门槛与双重KL控制限制策略漂移，不保证物理安全
findings.text: 学习副本在留出执行标签上AUROC至少0.8且至少观察50个失败，才打开一次性门槛，随后10万环境步把两个强度从0拉到1。执行副本在rollout和actor/critic更新期间冻结；actor沿用逐状态KL≤0.1的REPPO-D门控，模型副本另在256个近期状态上用参数插值二分限制平均策略KL≤0.02。后者只限制模型插值造成的漂移，不覆盖强度爬坡单独造成的改变。AUROC门槛检查排序而非概率校准；消融未独立检验这些保护机制的必要性。

findings.title: 扩展集有更好的装箱–风险点，但同学习器后期能追上
findings.text: 表IV固定1M训练checkpoint、12种几何60箱、每法50个相同随机到货seed的argmax评测，报告3个训练seed均值±标准差。SHORE利用率0.734±0.006，GOPT+为0.715±0.007，增加0.019；每次尝试失败1.03±0.10%对1.20±0.17%，回合失败0.53±0.05对0.61±0.08。GOPT为0.588±0.017且尝试失败更低0.63±0.15%。GOPT+虽共享联合动作与actor骨干，仍用不同PPO更新；真正隔离稳定机制的控制是两强度设0的REPPO-D，其最终利用率在seed波动内追上SHORE。图4支持更早获得高回报与风险权衡改善，不证明更高最终上限；摘要0.4M对1M只计rollout环境步。基准4类40箱反例：SHORE单seed利用率0.657、完成率0.84，低于GOPT+的0.683、0.95。两套箱集各自训练，不是对新几何零样本泛化。

findings.title: 双通路消融有方向性，分类排序更好并不自动装得更好
findings.text: 表V在901120环境步比较：SHORE利用率0.734、回合失败0.53；仅critic weighting为0.708/0.60，仅actor prior为0.699/0.58，两者都关的REPPO-D为0.699/0.62。仅critic的AUROC0.86还高于完整方法0.85，说明如何接入策略与价值比分类排序单一指标更能解释该checkpoint差异。组件变体是探索性单seed，SHORE和无两组件控制跨seed平均；不能把单点差值当显著性或独立验证门控/信任域。所有训练稳定模型的run均在该checkpoint恢复且清空标签缓冲，作者以同一恢复点避免不同重置距离混淆。

findings.title: 后期额外标签的增益未成立，总成本仍需公平对照
findings.text: 同一901120步的表VI：默认6+2模拟标签利用率0.734、回合失败0.54；只用执行标签为0.731/0.52，8个随机标签为0.732/0.52；1模拟标签为0.716/0.52。默认AUROC0.85/ECE0.040，只执行为0.77/0.009，排序与校准出现相反变化。作者把额外标签主要解释为早期获知稳定性的帮助；这里没有证明不确定性采样优于等数量随机，也没有证明后期必须增加仿真。只执行且关闭周期复制时，无rollout之外模拟调用。环境步预算未覆盖每步额外查询、3D网络训练与最多30次前向，288环境池/64次监督更新也不是实测算力；论文无匹配总模拟步、GPU时间和墙钟的端到端成本结论。相关小差异多为单seed，只能形成待验证成本假设。

findings.title: 1.03%按次失败率并非长序列可靠性，稳定判定也很短
findings.text: 扩展集SHORE每次尝试失败约1.03%同时有53%回合以失败结束，全部方法60箱完成率为0；其余回合无可行放置。按次失败率由回合失败比例/(成功箱数均值+失败比例)汇总得来，不是与回合失败独立的第二份统计证据，也未在共同候选堆叠上比较条件风险。仿真从目标上方2mm释放、只等待80ms，判定整堆所有箱子的三维位置位移不超过2cm，没有单独角度或长时稳定阈值；不模拟完整机械臂轨迹，也不加高斯位置/旋转噪声。图5的SHORE例子未整堆倒塌仍触发稳定失败，故不能把所有失败都理解为肉眼可见坍塌。

findings.title: 留出执行结果不等于未见状态动作泛化
findings.text: 10%执行结果不参与监督训练，但同一(s,a)可能通过模拟副本进入训练，尤其每8步执行动作复制；因此留出评价不是完全隔离状态动作的泛化测试。AUROC与10等宽箱ECE评的是学习副本，不是决策实际用的插值执行副本，约4000个近期点仅含37–66次失败。各变体还在自身策略访问的分布上测，不能据此断言共同候选动作上的风险更低。低ECE可由多数成功样本主导；排序好不能证明式8所需逐点概率准确。

findings.title: 真机四次放置与模拟器对齐，尚不构成真实部署成功率
findings.text: 图6只给Lite6真空夹爪、ZED2i和手端相机的一段示例，空箱后连续4次放置；没有跨场景试验数、成功率、吞吐或误差统计。附录将PhysX与MuJoCo配对回放一致率从67.0%调至94.8%，是sim-to-sim接触参数校准，不是真实机器人验证；文中未给该校准的样本数及独立留出拆分。正文承认接触失配、箱壁碰撞和可达性尚未纳入；actor缺失原始体素、EMS候选限制和早期动作只经回报承担后续失败，也限制外推。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：门槛启用后停止额外仿真，能否保留学习优势并减少总成本？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：额外模拟标签主要帮助稳定模型的早期启用，达到启用门槛后停止副本查询，可保留默认SHORE的学习与装箱–风险水平，同时减少总模拟和墙钟成本。先仅在同一公开装箱仿真任务做预算对照：始终6+2查询、启用门槛后切换执行标签、从头只执行、始终8随机；同一REPPO-D、联合动作、体素网络、训练更新规则及至少5个训练seed，使用相同50个以上固定评测到货序列。分别按rollout环境步、含副本的总模拟步与相同墙钟预算比较达目标利用率所需成本、回报曲线面积、完整回合成功率、每次尝试失败与不可行终止；另测GPU时间、峰值显存、稳定网络前向及端到端推理延迟。建立状态动作严格隔离的共同重放评价集，分别评学习和执行副本的稀有失败排序及校准，记录复制偏差，避免执行留出与模拟训练重叠。若停查询使多seed早期优势或回合可靠性持续下降、相同总成本下不优于只执行/随机，或省下查询却不减少墙钟，则推翻假设。实验未执行；匹配模拟预算亦为作者提出的未来方向，未全面查新，不宣称新研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: SHORE：稳定概率乘入条件价值，并作为联合装箱策略的软先验
frontier_brief.change_type: 训练方法 · 物理风险建模
frontier_brief.delta: 在联合箱子–朝向–EMS策略之外训练体素稳定网络：Q用条件回报乘稳定概率，actor概率再乘稳定性先验，并修改相对熵正则；用执行/副本标签监督而非学习稳定性硬拒绝。
frontier_brief.before: 无稳定模型的同款REPPO-D需从回报共同学习即时失败与后续空间价值；原GOPT另受队首、固定朝向限制，不能把其全部差距归给稳定机制。
frontier_brief.after: 扩展集1M步SHORE利用率0.734，GOPT+为0.715；同学习器最终能追上，主要证据是更早获得高回报及较好的装箱–风险点。部署免搜索/仿真，但仍需额外稳定网络前向。
frontier_brief.relevance: 为逐步物理操作选择失败模型的接入位置：可比较价值分解与策略先验的组合；先核查概率校准、模型额外观测与总模拟成本，再决定是否引入副本查询。
frontier_brief.caveat: 扩展集每次尝试失败1.03%仍对应53%回合失败，60箱全部未完成；同学习器无更高最终上限。组件/标签小消融多为单seed，未报告总算力收益，真机仅一段四次放置。
frontier_brief.question: 稳定模型启用后停止额外副本查询，能否以更少总模拟与墙钟保留早期优势和回合可靠性？

evidence.label: 同动作空间对照
evidence.context: GOPT+→SHORE，12几何/60箱，1M步，50回合，3训练seed；学习器仍不同，非稳定机制纯隔离。

evidence.label: 更能区分解释的控制
evidence.value: 去掉两项稳定机制的同款REPPO-D，后期利用率追上
evidence.context: 图4及正文：优势在早期获取和风险权衡，不能声称更高最终上限；基础集SHORE0.657还低于GOPT+0.683。

evidence.label: 标签成本反例
evidence.context: 表VI，901120步，标签变体探索性单seed；不确定性采样无确定后期优势，未匹配总模拟或墙钟预算。

evidence.label: 可靠性边界
evidence.context: 表IV，稳定检查仅释放后80ms、全堆位置位移≤2cm；1.03%按次失败不能替代长序列完成率。

mechanism.title: 按本步存活分解动作价值
mechanism.text: Q=U(1−w_Q+w_QS)，失败样本权重随w_Q下降；w_Q=1时U学条件回报，仍含未来失败风险，准确恢复Q依赖逐点稳定概率与精确均值拟合。

mechanism.title: 软先验与相对熵同步
mechanism.text: pi∝几何mask×exp(logit)×S^w，保留合法动作探索概率；熵正则相对于稳定先验，避免理想更新抵消该先验。

mechanism.title: 监督概率模型受控更新
mechanism.text: 密度体素3D U-Net五头，默认每步6个定向+2个随机副本；AUROC门槛后渐进启用，执行副本冻结并限制诱发策略KL，非物理安全保证。

attention.reason: 稳定先验的组合有明确增量，但学习器差异、单seed组件与仅四次真机放置限制机制证据；不按整体利用率提升判为路线变化。
attention.notice: 阅读优先级判断，不是科学质量定论。

impact.comparison: 稳定先验的组合有明确增量，但学习器差异、单seed组件与仅四次真机放置限制机制证据；不按整体利用率提升判为路线变化。

passages.text: We investigate a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach for UAV autopilots. The proposed approach exploits geometric symmetries between flight missions by transforming obstacle configurations into a shared canonical coordinate frame. This enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across arbitrary missions, reducing the amount of high-fidelity simulation data required for training. The surrogate model is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles and is used to guide test generation towards safety-critical scenarios. We evaluate this approach using the Aerialist UAV test bench and benchmark its performance against techniques from the 2024 to 2026 UAV Testing Competitions. Results show that the approach achieves an average critical-test-case hit rate of 42% across the evaluated missions, compared with approximately 10% for the constrained-random baseline used to generate the training data. This approach also achieves high input diversity and competitive benchmark performance. However, our findings reveal limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with differing flight-path characteristics, highlighting the boundaries of geometric canonicalization. To support reproducibility and future research, we provide the trained surrogate model and a dataset comprising more than 2,500 high-fidelity simulations.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly employed in applications that require autonomous navigation in complex environments, such as indoor facilities [ 1 ] , urban areas [ 2 ] , and disaster sites [ 3 ] . In such environments, failures in obstacle avoidance can lead to collisions, making the safety and reliability of autonomous navigation systems a critical concern.

To address these concerns, verification and validation methods, such as simulation-based testing, play an important role in establishing confidence in the trustworthiness of these systems. Simulation-based testing uses high-fidelity simulators to evaluate autonomous UAVs under a diverse range of environmental conditions while reducing the time, cost, and safety risks associated with physical flight testing. However, the input space makes exhaustive testing impractical. Search-based testing offers a systematic approach to this challenge by guiding test generation towards scenarios that are more likely to reveal system failures [ 4 ] . This process, however, requires evaluating numerous candidate scenarios, making the computational cost of high-fidelity simulations a significant bottleneck.

Surrogate-assisted testing offers an approach to mitigating this bottleneck by using computationally inexpensive surrogate models to estimate test outcomes without executing the high-fidelity simulator [ 5 ] . These models learn an approximation of the relationship between test inputs and simulation outcomes using data from previously executed high-fidelity simulations. Since evaluating a surrogate model is generally much less expensive than executing a high-fidelity simulation, a large number of candidate test scenarios can be assessed before selecting a smaller subset for simulation.

In UAV obstacle-avoidance testing, test scenarios can be constructed by placing obstacles along a flight mission, with the objective of identifying configurations that cause the UAV to approach obstacles closely or exhibit unsafe behaviour. A flight mission may consist of multiple segments with different positions and orientations, each requiring its own obstacle configurations. Developing an accurate surrogate model for such scenarios requires training data representative of the configurations encountered across these segments. However, obtaining sufficient training data through high-fidelity simulations can be prohibitively expensive, especially when separate training data must be collected for different flight segments or missions.

An opportunity to address this challenge arises from the geometric symmetries between flight segments. Obstacle configurations associated with different flight segments may have identical relative geometries despite differing in their global positions and orientations. Such geometrically equivalent configurations can be represented relative to a reference flight segment in a canonical coordinate frame, which we refer to as the canonical flight frame.

In this work, we investigate a surrogate-assisted test-generation approach that exploits these geometric symmetries to reuse a neural-network surrogate across different flight missions. During training, the surrogate is trained to predict the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and surrounding obstacles for a reference flight mission. This reference flight mission defines the canonical flight frame. During test generation, candidate obstacle configurations for a target flight mission are transformed into the canonical flight frame and evaluated using the trained surrogate. Promising configurations are then transformed back into the target mission’s coordinate system and evaluated using the high-fidelity simulator.

Geometric equivalence does not necessarily imply equivalent UAV behaviour. The response of an autonomous UAV may also depend on factors such as its incoming velocity, heading, controller state, preceding flight segments, and the surrounding environment. Consequently, the extent to which a surrogate trained in a canonical frame can provide accurate predictions for different missions must be established empirically.

This work investigates the efficiency and effectiveness of canonical surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing, as well as its limitations. Specifically, we address the following research questions:
RQ1: How does surrogate prediction accuracy vary across different flight missions?
RQ2: To what extent does an NN-based surrogate improve the efficiency of test generation?
RQ3: How does filtering based on a canonical surrogate affect test-suite diversity?

To answer these questions and evaluate our approach, we apply it to efficiently create effective test cases for PX4-Avoidance, a vision-based autonomous obstacle avoidance system developed on top of PX4-Autopilot [ 6 ] . We benchmark our approach against the test case generators that participated in the UAV Testing Competition 2024, 2025 and 2026 versions [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
By addressing these research questions, this work makes the following main contributions:
A neural network surrogate model that approximates the PX-4 obstacle avoidance system and estimates the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and an obstacle.
An extensive empirical evaluation comparing the efficiency and effectiveness of the surrogate-guided test-case generator with those of state-of-the-art test-case generators.
The limitations of canonical surrogate reuse for simulation-based UAV testing.
A dataset of simulation results for over 2500 different obstacle configurations for a flight mission, which can be used to develop other types of surrogate models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work and Section III introduces the UAV case study. Section IV describes the symmetry-aware testing approach, while Section V reports the empirical evaluation. Section VI discusses the findings, assumptions, and limitations. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper and outlines future work.

The UAV testing competition has motivated several strategies for exploring the test-input space. In particular, DeepHyperion-UAV [ 12 ] uses illumination search, CAMBA [ 13 ] employs cost-aware mutation, and TUMB [ 14 ] uses Monte Carlo Tree Search to generate obstacle configurations. These approaches employ different search strategies to identify critical test cases, but evaluating candidate configurations through high-fidelity simulation remains computationally expensive.

To address the cost of simulation-based testing, researchers have explored alternative approaches to test evaluation and generation. Shrinah and Eder [ 15 ] employed a manually constructed low-fidelity path simulator to approximate UAV behaviour at a lower computational cost.

Other approaches have investigated learning-based techniques. Zhu et al. [ 16 ] proposed SaFliTe, which uses a large language model to predict test interestingness from textual safety objectives and the current system state. Peltomäki and Porres [ 17 ] proposed WOGAN, which iteratively trains a Wasserstein generative adversarial network to learn a distribution over counterexamples from which failure-inducing inputs can be sampled.

The use of surrogate models to reduce the cost of search-based testing is well established. Nejati et al. [ 4 ] provide a taxonomy of surrogate-assisted search-based testing. Beglerovic et al. [ 5 ] combined surrogate modelling with stochastic optimisation to search for fault-revealing regions when testing autonomous vehicles. Similarly, Haq et al. [ 18 ] employed surrogate-assisted many-objective optimisation to improve the efficiency of online testing of DNN-enabled systems. These approaches establish that learned approximations can reduce the cost of evaluating candidate tests during search. In contrast, our work is concerned with the representation used to train such an approximation: rather than learning separately over mission-dependent spatial coordinates, geometrically equivalent local flight configurations are mapped to a common reference frame.

Menghi et al. [ 19 ] proposed ARIsTEO for testing compute-intensive cyber-physical models. ARIsTEO constructs a cheaper surrogate of the model under test, searches this approximation for failure-revealing inputs, validates candidate failures on the original model, and refines the approximation when a candidate is spurious. This approximation–refinement strategy addresses errors in the surrogate dynamically.

Neural-network-based guidance has also been investigated in evolutionary testing. Zhong et al. [ 20 ] proposed AutoFuzz, which combines neural-network guidance with evolutionary fuzzing to identify traffic-violation scenarios for autonomous vehicles. Similarly, Zohdinasab et al. [ 21 ] proposed DeepAtash-LR, which integrates a surrogate model into an evolutionary focused-testing process for autonomous driving, directing test generation towards specified combinations of structural and behavioural features. While these approaches demonstrate different ways of using learned models to guide test generation, they do not investigate the reuse of a single surrogate across geometrically related test scenarios through canonical representation.

Geometric symmetry has been widely investigated as a means of reducing redundant variation in machine learning. Cohen and Welling [ 22 ] introduced group-equivariant convolutional networks, which incorporate transformations such as rotations and translations into the network architecture. Bietti et al. [ 23 ] studied the sample-complexity benefits of learning under invariance. These works motivate the exploitation of geometric symmetry, but do not address surrogate reuse in simulation-based testing.

Kaba et al. [ 24 ] proposed learning canonicalisation functions that transform inputs into a canonical representation before prediction. Our approach follows the same general principle, but determines the transformation directly from the geometry of a UAV flight segment rather than learning it. The objective is to reuse simulation data collected for one reference configuration when testing different mission segments, while ensuring that the generated obstacle configurations remain feasible.

Wang et al. [ 25 ] investigated approximately equivariant networks for dynamical systems in which geometric symmetry is imperfect. This limitation is also relevant to our work: geometrically equivalent obstacle configurations may produce different UAV behaviour because of controller state, preceding flight segments, or environmental constraints. We therefore evaluate cross-mission surrogate accuracy empirically rather than assuming that geometric equivalence guarantees identical simulation outcomes.

Existing research has established surrogate-assisted testing as a means of reducing expensive simulations [ 4 , 5 , 19 , 21 ] and canonicalisation as a means of exploiting geometric symmetry [ 22 , 24 , 23 ] . Our work combines these established ideas to investigate whether a safety surrogate trained on a single canonical UAV flight configuration can be reused across different mission segments without retraining.

We use the UAV Testing Competition as a case study for evaluating our symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted testing approach. The competition was introduced at SBFT in 2024 and subsequently organized at both SBFT and ICST in 2025 and 2026. The competition provides a benchmark for comparing automated test-case generation techniques for autonomous UAVs.

The system under test is PX4-Avoidance, an obstacle-avoidance system built on PX4-Autopilot. Test cases specify the geometry and placement of cuboid obstacles for a given flight mission. According to the competition constraints, valid test cases must have non-overlapping obstacles that lie entirely within the designated obstacle-placement area, defined as a 70 , m × 40 , m 70,\mathrm{m}\times 40,\mathrm{m} rectangle.

Test cases are used to expose unsafe behaviours by executing the given flight mission in the presence of the obstacles defined by the test case using Aerialist, a simulation-based UAV testing framework for PX4-Autopilot [ 26 ] .

The competition scores test generators based on the criticality and diversity of their test suites. Criticality is measured by the minimum clearance distance between the UAV and the obstacles, while diversity is assessed by comparing test-case similarities within the suite. We use the competition missions and evaluation criteria to assess the efficiency and effectiveness of our approach.

Our approach generates a set of tests that are predicted to cause a UAV to fly close to an obstacle for a given flight mission. Each test case consists of two obstacles, each parameterised by five values: width, height, centre coordinates, and rotation. Together, the two obstacles form a ten-element test vector.

The approach uses a neural network surrogate model to estimate the minimum clearance distance between a UAV and an obstacle during a mission. The model is trained using randomly generated tests from a single canonical mission, which serves as the reference mission during training and inference.

A transformation is found between any arbitrary mission and the canonical mission. This transformation enables tests to be generated within the surrogate model’s training domain, where prediction accuracy is expected to be highest.

During test generation, batches of tests are first produced using a constrained-random generator. The surrogate model is then used in a filtering mechanism to select tests that are both critical and diverse. Critical tests are defined as those for which the minimum clearance distance is below 1.5m. Diverse tests are defined as those that increase the structural variability of non-overlapping geometries in the test suite’s input space (Equation 9 ). Finally, the selected test cases are executed in the high-fidelity simulator to obtain their actual minimum clearance distances and verify the surrogate’s predictions.

passages.text: To ensure the surrogate model is always used within its training domain, each arbitrary mission is transformed into a canonical mission. The canonical mission is a single vertical flight path, centred horizontally within the designated obstacle-placement area, as illustrated in Figure 1 .

passages.text: The transformed segment-placement zone defines the geometric constraints used during random obstacle generation. Depending on the mission geometry, this zone may occupy only a subregion of the obstacle placement zone used to train the surrogate model. Consequently, all generated obstacles remain within the surrogate model’s training domain.

passages.section: IV-B Canonical Representation of Flight Segments

passages.text: After test generation, the inverse transformation is applied, mapping the generated obstacles from the canonical representation back to the original mission frame. Tests expressed in the original mission frame are then evaluated using the Aerialist simulator.

The surrogate model is a neural-network regression model that predicts the minimum clearance distance between the UAV and any obstacle during the mission. The model takes the geometry of two obstacles as input and outputs an estimated minimum clearance. Its architecture, depicted in Figure 2 , comprises two parallel subnetworks, one for each obstacle, with sizes of 5 input, 10 hidden and 20 output layer neurons.
Fig. 2 : The architecture of the surrogate model.

The outputs of the subnetworks are concatenated and passed to a fully connected network with 40 input, 20 hidden and 1 output neuron. ReLU activations are used for all hidden layers, while the output layer uses a linear activation. This architecture was selected empirically using validation performance.

The surrogate model’s dataset is created from 2716 random test cases of two obstacles within the designated obstacle-placement area. Eighty percent of the random test cases were used for training, and the remaining twenty percent were used for validation.

The dataset was sampled from the space of all possible obstacle configurations by a specialist constrained-random generator that employs semantic sampling rather than direct geometric sampling. Scenario features such as obstacle intrusion into the flight path, size, aspect ratio, rotation, relative neighbour direction, and passage width were discretised into a set of categories. For example, obstacle rotation was classified into low ( 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} to 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} ) and high ( 45 ∘ 45^{\circ} to 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} ) categories, while relative obstacle placement was classified into one of eight neighbouring sectors. Data generation first uniformly sampled a combination of these categories, one from each feature, and subsequently randomly sampled geometric values from the corresponding parameter ranges. This approach ensured balanced coverage of distinct scenario types and avoided over-representation of geometrically similar configurations.

This sampling process was observed to produce highly skewed distributions for the obstacle widths and the x x coordinate of obstacle one. Hence, to reduce the effect of skewness, a log transformation was applied to these features prior to standardisation. All ten geometry features were then normalised using feature-wise mean and standard deviation statistics calculated from the training set. Each obstacle configuration was evaluated using Aerialist to obtain the ground-truth minimum clearance distance used in training.
The network was trained for 200 epochs using the Adam optimiser, a batch size of 128, and mean absolute error (MAE) as the loss function.

The trained surrogate model is used with a constrained-random generator that generates obstacle geometries (tests). The constraints for this random generator are derived from the segment-placement zone for each mission, transformed into the canonical representation. These constraints are applied to the generation of the ten obstacle parameters to ensure that each obstacle pair do not overlap and remain entirely within the placement zone.
Test generation is split into two phases. In both phases, a fixed-size leaderboard is maintained to store the most critical and diverse tests discovered so far.

Phase one focuses on identifying tests with low predicted obstacle clearances. A batch of tests is repeatedly generated by the constrained-random generator. For each test, the surrogate model predicts the minimum obstacle clearance distance. The leaderboard is then updated to retain the tests with the smallest predicted clearances seen so far, while tests with larger predicted clearances are discarded. This process of generation and selection is repeated 100 times. At the end of phase one, the leaderboard contains tests with small clearances, but potentially poor diversity.

Phase two shifts the emphasis to improving leaderboard diversity while retaining only critical tests. The constrained-random generator generates new batches of tests to improve test suite diversity, and the surrogate model filters out any non-critical tests (predicted minimum clearance distance > > 1.5m), leaving a set of candidate tests. For each candidate set, a series of alternative leaderboards are created by replacing one existing test with a candidate test, and evaluating the diversity of the resulting leaderboard using Equation 9 , described in Section V . The leaderboard with the highest diversity is retained for the next iteration. The process of candidate generation, selection and diversity evaluation is repeated for 100 rounds, producing a leaderboard that balances both test criticality and diversity.

Phase three verifies the predicted criticality of test cases in the leaderboard. Each test in the final leaderboard is evaluated using the high-fidelity simulator to obtain a more accurate estimate of minimum clearance. Our approach balances computational efficiency and prediction accuracy. In the first two phases, the approach rapidly explores a large space of potential tests, while the computationally expensive simulator is reserved for the relatively small set of tests selected for the final leaderboard in phase three. Consequently, simulation effort is concentrated on the most promising tests, improving confidence in the final ranking without requiring exhaustive simulation of all considered tests.

The performance of our approach was benchmarked against submissions from the 2024, 2025 and 2026 editions of the ICST/SBFT UAV testing competitions. The benchmark comprises the flight mission set, simulation budget and scoring criteria. We aligned our evaluation with these components to enable a direct comparison between our proposed approach and the prior competition entrants. We also recalculated the scores of the benchmarks using the publicly available simulation artifacts and scoring criteria. All experiments were conducted on a machine equipped with an Intel Core i7-10870H processor (8 cores, 16 threads) and 32 GB of RAM, running Ubuntu 20.04.6 LTS. UAV simulations were executed in Docker containers using Aerialist version 0.2.02 (Git revision f44ea6a ) with Ubuntu 18.04.5 LTS as the container operating system. The datasets, source code, and experimental artifacts supporting this study are available on Zenodo [ 27 ] .
Each component of the benchmark is summarised in this section, with complete details of the format and scoring for each competition year found in [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
Fig. 3 : The flight missions, path segments, and segment-placement zones for transformation to the canonical mission.

The three flight missions common to all competitions, namely CS2, CS4 and CS5, were selected for evaluating our approach. Each mission varies in the number and layout of waypoints, and the extent to which the flight-path segments overlap the valid obstacle-placement area. See Figure 3 .

The simulation budget defines the maximum number of test cases that can be evaluated using Aerialist during test generation, prior to submission and scoring. In accordance with the competition requirements, we use simulation budgets of 200 for 2024 and 100 for 2025 and 2026. Consequently, we execute our approach twice: once with a budget of 200 to generate a test suite for comparison against the 2024 entrants, and once with a budget of 100 for comparison against the 2025 and 2026 entrants. In both runs, the leaderboard size is set equal to the corresponding simulation budget.

The scoring is based on simulations of the submitted test suite using Aerialist. Each test case is simulated three times, and averages are calculated for the minimum clearance distance, flight path, and execution time. Each simulation run was limited to 500 seconds. Runs that exceeded this limit before completing the required flight mission were terminated and recorded as timed out. Different scoring criteria is used for each year, reflecting changes made by the competition organisers intended to improve the assessment criteria.

The proposed approach demonstrated strong performance across the three competition editions as shown in Table III , Table IV , and Table V . Under the 2024 evaluation criteria, it achieved the highest score for all three missions. In 2025, it obtained the best overall ranking, achieving the highest failure scores for CS2 and CS5 and the second-highest for CS4. In 2026, the approach ranked second overall.

A noteworthy observation is that our approach achieved the highest precision in all three benchmark evaluations. We define precision as the proportion of test cases identified as critical by a generator that are subsequently confirmed as critical by the high-fidelity simulator. To account for non-determinism in the simulation environment, criticality is confirmed by taking the average minimum clearance distance from three high-fidelity simulations.

In 2024, our approach submitted 228 test cases across the three missions. Of the 60 cases selected for evaluation, 53 were confirmed critical, yielding a precision of 88.3%. This exceeded the 79.2% precision achieved by the next-best competitor in terms of precision, TAIist, which submitted 24 test cases, 19 of which were confirmed critical. In 2025, our approach submitted 146 test cases and achieved a precision of 96.7% (58 out of 60 evaluated cases), compared with 66.7% (40 out of 60) for PALM, which submitted 216 test cases. In 2026, the same 146 test cases and their evaluation from 2025 were reused for benchmarking the precision of our approach. Thus, the 96.7% (58/60) precision from the total of 146 submitted test cases exceeded the 76.8% precision (43 out of 56 evaluated cases) achieved by Intelligent-UAV-Gen, which submitted 159 test cases.

Overall, the results show that our approach consistently achieved higher precision than the strongest competing generators across all three benchmarks. Its high precision, together with the large number of generated test cases, indicates that our approach has high repeatability.

Another particularly interesting observation concerns the relationship between input and output diversity. In 2026, our approach achieved the highest input-diversity score for all three missions. This is consistent with the design of the second test-generation phase, which explicitly maximises input diversity. With regard to output diversity, our approach ranked third for CS2 and fourth for CS4 and CS5. The relatively low output diversity of our approach is explained in the discussion of RQ3 in Section VI-C . These contrasting results indicate that generating geometrically diverse obstacle configurations does not necessarily produce diverse UAV flight trajectories.

Another observation is that output diversity varies across missions. In 2026, three of the four approaches achieved their lowest output-diversity scores on CS4. One potential explanation is that among the three missions, CS4 has the largest proportion of its planned flight path outside the obstacle placement zone (56.84%, compared with 44.51% for CS2 and 51.84% for CS5). Consequently, a smaller proportion of its route lies within the region where obstacles can be placed, potentially limiting opportunities for obstacle-induced behavioural variation.

passages.text: Prediction accuracy is quantified using the root mean squared error (RMSE) between the NN surrogate’s predicted minimum clearance distance and the ground-truth clearance obtained from Aerialist. The assessment is made using 300 tests, which are the combined set of tests generated by the proposed approach for the 2024 and 2025/2026 benchmarks. None of these tests were included in either the training or validation sets, ensuring the evaluation measures the model’s performance on previously unseen test cases.

Comparing these results enables the accuracy of the surrogate model on generated tests to be contrasted with its accuracy on tests drawn from the same distribution as the training process.

passages.location: VI-A RQ1: How does the Surrogate Prediction Accuracy vary for different flight missions?
passages.text: The validation data were generated for the canonical mission, which contains only a single flight-path segment. However, the benchmark missions may feature multiple flight path segments that pass through the obstacle placement zone. These additional segments can interact with the obstacles and influence the minimum observed clearance during simulation. Such interactions are not represented in the surrogate model’s training data and therefore are a source of error for its predictions.

passages.location: VI-A RQ1: How does the Surrogate Prediction Accuracy vary for different flight missions?
passages.text: The characteristics of the three benchmark missions support this explanation. Of the three missions, only mission four has a single flight path segment through the obstacle placement zone (See Figure 3 -b). In contrast, mission two crosses its respective obstacle placement zone twice and mission five passes through it three times. As the number of flight-path crossings through the obstacle placement zone increases, so does the opportunity for obstacle interactions that are not represented in the canonical mission training data.
The efficiency of a test generation method can be measured by how many critical test cases are generated from a given testing budget. We call this ratio a hit rate.

We compare the hit rate of our approach with the constrained-random generator used to create the surrogate model’s training and validation datasets. During dataset generation, the constrained-random generator produced 2716 test cases for the canonical flight mission of which 265 are critical, i.e. it has approximately a 10% hit rate. This dataset does not exclude tests that cause the UAV to exceed the allowed time limit of 500 seconds as specified in the competition scoring criteria. Consequently, the constrained-random generator’s hit rate is an upper limit.

In contrast, the surrogate-assisted pseudo-random generator used a total simulation budget of 900 to identify 375 critical test cases across the benchmark missions, corresponding to a hit rate of approximately 42%. The overall hit rate of our approach is calculated as the number of critical test cases identified by our approach divided by the sum of the simulation budgets for all missions for 2024 and 2025/26 benchmarks. The surrogate-assisted approach achieved a critical-test-case hit rate approximately four times that of the constrained-random generator.

It is also noticeable from Table II that the hit rate for our approach varied by mission. Taking the average hit rate across the 300 simulations for each mission (200 from 2024 and 100 from 2025/26), produced hit rates of 34%, 49% and 42% for missions CS2, CS4 and CS5, respectively. Each of these average hit rates is higher than the hit rate achieved by the constrained-random generator.

Note that we compared the efficiency of our approach against a constrained-random generator rather than a purely random generator, as the latter would have produced far fewer critical test cases. The constrained-random generator is more efficient than a purely random generator that does not embed domain knowledge into the generation process.

passages.section: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.location: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.text: This research question investigates whether surrogate-based filtering restricts the behavioural diversity of resulting test suites, given that the model is trained on pseudo-randomly generated test cases for a single canonical flight mission.

passages.section: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.location: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.text: As discussed in RQ1, the surrogate may produce more accurate predictions for flight missions whose characteristics resemble those of the canonical mission used during training. However, differences in prediction accuracy across missions do not necessarily imply that the filtering process systematically favours particular types of test cases. Prediction accuracy and selection bias are distinct concerns. Nevertheless, our approach achieved one of the lowest behavioural diversity scores among the participants in the 2026 competition.

passages.section: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.location: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.text: One possible explanation for the low behavioural diversity is the restricted range of obstacle configurations produced by the constrained-random generator in the first phase of our approach. To remain within the surrogate’s training domain, obstacle configurations are restricted to a predefined region relative to the flight path. These constraints limit the variety of configurations that can be generated and may reduce interactions with other flight segments, potentially resulting in less diverse UAV trajectories.

passages.section: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.location: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.text: Another possible explanation concerns obstacle size. Our approach generated comparatively small obstacles, which may cause relatively minor deviations from the intended flight path and reduce the likelihood of interactions with other flight segments.

passages.section: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.location: VI-C RQ3: How Does Canonical Surrogate-Based Filtering Affect Test-Suite Diversity?
passages.text: Overall, the relatively low behavioural diversity achieved by our approach may be associated more strongly with the restrictions imposed during initial test-case generation than with surrogate-based filtering. However, confirming the effect of these restrictions on diversity would require comparing the output diversity of two test suites, one generated by a purely random test generator and the other using the constrained-random generator under otherwise identical conditions.

This paper investigated a symmetry-aware surrogate-assisted approach for simulation-based testing of autonomous UAVs. By transforming obstacle configurations into a canonical flight frame, the approach enables a neural-network surrogate trained on a single reference mission to be reused across different flight missions without retraining. The surrogate estimates the minimum clearance distance between the UAV and surrounding obstacles, allowing potentially critical test cases to be identified before executing computationally expensive high-fidelity simulations.

The empirical evaluation demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach in generating critical test cases. Compared with the constrained-random generator used to produce the training data, the surrogate-assisted approach increased the critical test-case hit rate from approximately 10% to 42%. It also achieved competitive results against participants in the 2024–2026 UAV Testing Competitions, ranking first overall in 2024 and 2025 and second in 2026. However, the results also revealed limitations in transferring surrogate predictions across missions with different flight-path characteristics. Furthermore, although the approach achieved high input diversity, this did not consistently translate into high diversity in the resulting UAV trajectories.

Future work will investigate integrating the trained surrogate into search-based and evolutionary test-generation techniques. Since the surrogate can estimate obstacle clearance distance at a fraction of the computational cost of high-fidelity simulation, it offers the potential to evaluate large populations of candidate test cases efficiently and guide the search towards critical scenarios. Another direction is to investigate neural-network-based generative approaches, including generative adversarial networks, for learning to produce critical obstacle configurations. The trained surrogate could serve as a computationally inexpensive evaluator to guide these generators towards failure-revealing scenarios. Finally, we plan to explore combining large language models with the surrogate to generate and evaluate critical test cases, exploiting the complementary capabilities of language models for scenario generation and neural-network surrogates for rapid prediction of test outcomes. Future work will also investigate improving surrogate generalisation across missions by incorporating flight-context information and accounting for interactions with multiple flight-path segments.

analysis.overview: 把目标任务的一个航段及障碍可放置区，用二维平移/旋转映射到单直线参考任务，在共享坐标中用小型神经网络预测最小间隙，筛选危险且输入几何多样的双障碍测试，再反变换并作高保真验证。值得复用的是任务相对表示和两级筛选流程；几何对齐并未消除控制器状态、多航段交互或生成限制。作者给出375/900约42%的生成命中率，但约10%对照来自参考任务训练数据，且2716例前置采集未计入900预算，不能直接称全成本四倍加速。高输入多样性伴随较低轨迹多样性，是测试覆盖决策的重要边界。
analysis.notice: 本轮由当前会话代理读完固定HTML证据128/128片段，涵盖相关工作、方法、公式、全部实验与结论；该版本无附录。固定PDF10页、272979字节；目视物理页3–10，核图1–3、公式1–13与表I–V，额外补读PDF方法、评测及资源引用。未运行模型、仿真或代码，作者实验未复现；原始逐例日志、预算映射及筛选种子未独立审计。论文资源DOI本轮HTTP404，未验证数据/权重/代码实际内容。

findings.title: 重用的是任务相对表示，不是无人机行为的严格对称定理
findings.text: 昂贵步骤是PX4-Avoidance在Aerialist中的障碍场景验证。本文把单参考任务收集的最小间隙回归器复用于CS2/CS4/CS5，不在每个任务重新训练。改变的是代理输入的坐标表示与测试筛选流程；既有代理测试和规范化各有先例，不能把两者本身称全新。作者明确指出来向速度、航向、控制器状态、先前航段和环境均可破坏行为等价，因此局部几何重合不是完整动态系统不变性或安全保证。

findings.title: 选最大可放置区航段，再作二维刚体坐标变换
findings.text: 测试每例有两个不重叠长方体，每障碍五个几何参数，总计十维。对每个相邻航点段构造关于该段对称、且完全位于70m×40m测试区内的最大矩形，选择矩形面积最大的那一段；以二维平移和旋转将航段及矩形变到图1单直线参考系，生成障碍后反变换回原任务验证。这里图中竖直是平面坐标上的航线方向，不是垂直起降。约束保证几何合法和坐标范围，并不证明生成分布等于训练分布，也没有把所有航段/历史状态都编码进网络。正文称宽/高，图2标签为L/W/X/Y/R；复现时应核资源参数语义，不能由这五维宣称支持任意三维障碍变化。

findings.title: 2716例语义约束采样训练小回归器
findings.text: 2716例参考任务双障碍测试按80/20训练/验证划分。基础生成器先均匀抽侵入程度、大小、长宽比、旋转、邻域方向和通道宽度等离散语义类别组合，再在相应范围抽几何量，不是纯几何均匀随机。对障碍宽度及第一个障碍x坐标等偏斜特征作对数变换，再用训练集均值/标准差归一化十维输入。网络图2是两支5→10→20，拼接后40→20→1，隐藏ReLU、输出线性，Adam、batch128、200epoch、MAE训练；结构由验证表现选择。未说明两支共享权重，不能因有两个分支就断言障碍置换不变或群等变。RMSE评估与训练MAE也不可混用。

findings.title: 先挑低预测间隙，再提高几何多样性，最后仿真确认
findings.text: 维持定长候选榜：第一阶段反复生成批次并保留预测最小间隙较低的测试，共100轮；第二阶段以预测间隙≤1.5m为候选门槛，逐个替换榜中测试并保留输入多样性最大的榜，再100轮；最终榜作高保真验证。正文先称两阶段，随后列第三个验证阶段，应理解为两阶段代理选择加仿真确认，而非仅有两个操作。输入多样性采用公式9的几何并集覆盖与面积变异系数组合，未直接优化飞行轨迹。验证不等于在线校正：论文没有展示将伪阳性反馈后重新训练代理的闭环。批次大小/候选总量与端到端生成耗时未充分报告。

findings.title: 生成预算、提交集合、复评样本三种分母必须区分
findings.text: 每任务2024生成仿真预算200，2025/2026预算100，榜大小等于预算；三任务两次生成合计900例。评分复评每例三次，单次上限500s。2024从提交集随机取20例/任务作直接评分，并给剩余例分配折算分、用轨迹DTW相似惩罚；2025/2026则依据第三阶段已有仿真分数选择每任务20例复评，未选例不计分。2025总排名按失败0.75/几何多样0.25；2026按失败0.50/输入多样0.25/输出多样0.25。因分数还依赖障碍数平方和飞行时间，不能把跨年分数当统一成功率，更不能将900预算、提交374例和复评120例混为一组独立样本。2026复用2025本方法数据，并非又一次独立生成。

findings.title: 375/900支持筛选富集，约四倍不等于端到端省算四倍
findings.text: 核表II：2024三个任务预算各200，危险例62/88/79；2025/2026各100，危险例40/59/47，合计375/900=41.7%。超时合计73例也占预算；三任务合并各300例命中约34%/49%/42%。对照265/2716=9.8%来自参考任务的语义约束随机训练数据，且未剔除500s超时，所以作者称其为该口径上界。此为跨任务/采样条件的参考比较，不能认定同任务、同几何分布、同总成本下的受控四倍收益。900未含2716例前置收集、训练、代理筛选及复评分数开销，未给墙钟加速或摊销拐点；更没有危险例召回率或全空间覆盖证明。表II的2024 CS5危险79与表III提交78相差一例，未有日志解释，保留两表各自口径不擅改。

findings.title: 跨任务RMSE增大，几何范围内仍可能行为分布外
findings.text: 核表I：参考任务验证RMSE0.50m；CS2/CS4/CS5为1.35/0.71/1.46m。作者称在300个未参与训练/验证的生成测试上评估，但未清楚交代其与900生成预算逐例映射，不能冒称独立随机测试集。图3中CS4只有一个穿越放置区的航段，CS2有两次、CS5三次；额外航段可成为全任务最小间隙的来源，却不在单段回归输入中，结果与该解释一致，但无隔离航段/来向状态的消融，不能据相关模式证明唯一成因。几何对齐保证的坐标约束不能解决遗漏动态上下文，较低全局RMSE也不直接证明危险阈值附近分类校准。

findings.title: 96.7%是已筛选并复评的60例，不是所有候选的命中率
findings.text: 2024提交228例，随机选60例复评、53例危险，precision88.3%；2025提交146例，依阶段三分数选60例复评，58例危险，96.7%；2026原样复用这146例及复评数据。危险以三次高保真最小间隙的平均值确认，阈值1.5m，不等同真实碰撞。2025 PALM为40/60、2026 Intelligent-UAV-Gen为43/56，其条件下本方法精确率较高，但挑选集合与年份协议各异。该数不能替代所有100例/任务预算上的命中率、模型阈值分类指标或危险情景召回；三次仿真复评也不等于多个独立生成seed的稳定性试验。

findings.title: 最高输入多样性同时伴随较低轨迹多样性
findings.text: 核表III–V：按作者复算的三届协议，本方法2024/2025总排名第一，2026第二。2026输入多样性CS2/CS4/CS5为39.11/16.85/32.76，均第一；输出最近邻DTW平均为2.72/1.37/2.41，排名3/4/4。TLQD输出23.31/14.44/39.62，三项第一，但危险复评数7/4/10，低于本方法20/19/19；这是覆盖与危险富集的取舍，不是全面占优。作者推测放置区限制或较小障碍使轨迹变化不足，并承认需要同条件生成器对照。现有结果不能区分约束生成与代理过滤的因果贡献，几何多样性不能代替机器人行为覆盖。

findings.title: 尚未隔离规范化本身的收益，也没有安全认证或实机迁移
findings.text: 全部为一个PX4-Avoidance/Aerialist配置的三个竞争任务、双障碍仿真。几何规范化、语义生成、代理过滤和多样性替换共同变化，未给相同训练量下原坐标模型、规范化模型与逐任务重训的直接消融，不能把整个管线的危险富集归因于坐标变换一项。无代表性多控制器、环境动力学、风场或实机验证，无统计区间和独立生成重复足以证实一般稳定性；未发现危险不表示系统安全。未来加入多航段/飞行上下文是作者方向，本轮不将其写成已实现方法或未经查新的研究空白。

findings.title: 公开资源声明尚未转成已验证可复用资产
findings.text: 作者在实验设置及参考文献27声明Zenodo提供数据、代码、模型与实验产物，运行环境为i7-10870H/32GB、Ubuntu20.04.6、Aerialist0.2.02（f44ea6a）Docker。固定PDF引用DOI为10.5281/zenodo.23876845；本轮浏览工具无法访问，随后curl只读检查该DOI返回HTTP404。因此仅保留作者资源声明与版本线索，不声称已成功下载或审计2716例数据、权重、分割/预处理、预算日志或评分代码；也不据一次404断言资源永久不存在。复现还需澄清2024 CS5生成/提交一例差异、RMSE300例映射和输入L/W语义。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：加入其余航段和来向状态，能否改善迁移且保留轨迹覆盖？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：固定几何生成器与高保真总预算后，加入多航段及来向速度/航向上下文，可降低跨任务最小间隙误差，并在危险例富集不明显下降时扩大轨迹覆盖。仅公开仿真实验草案：使用Aerialist/PX4的固定版本，先确认公开数据可获取，再比较原坐标单任务模型、论文规范化几何模型、规范化加多航段/来向状态模型，以及逐任务重训参考；每模型相同网络容量或报告容量差异、相同训练仿真总量及调参预算，数据按整任务/路线划分，禁用测试标签选模型。构造局部几何相同而1/2/3次穿越放置区、来向速度/转弯历史不同的配对场景。第二组用同一候选流做无过滤/纯间隙过滤/几何多样替换/轨迹表征多样替换消融，隔离生成范围与选择偏置；任何行为代理均计训练成本。至少10个独立生成seed、每条件100例高保真验证，三次复评另计；同时报未筛选留出集RMSE、1.5m阈值precision/recall、含超时命中率、输入多样性与输出DTW、独特危险行为簇、总仿真与墙钟成本，训练采集成本随任务数摊销。不得将按先验仿真选出的top20精确率替代全预算指标。若改善只出现在调参任务、阈值召回下降，或相同危险数下轨迹覆盖无改善且全成本更高，则推翻该上下文扩展足以改善迁移与覆盖取舍的假设。实验未执行、未创建选题、未全面查新；无实机或安全认证结论。

frontier_brief.title: 把航段对齐到同一参考系复用间隙代理，几何多样仍不保证轨迹覆盖
frontier_brief.change_type: 仿真测试表示与候选筛选
frontier_brief.delta: 选择障碍可放置区最大的航段，用二维平移/旋转映射到单直线参考系；复用小型间隙回归器，先筛低间隙、再优化几何多样性，最后反变换作高保真验证。
frontier_brief.before: 逐任务采集高保真数据训练代理成本高；本文参考任务的语义约束随机2716例中265例危险，约9.8%，并非同目标任务的均匀随机对照。
frontier_brief.after: 单参考任务代理不重训，跨CS2/CS4/CS5两组生成预算共900例确认375例危险，41.7%；参考验证RMSE0.50m，跨任务0.71–1.46m，几何对齐未消除行为分布差异。
frontier_brief.relevance: 适合大量复用相似航段的仿真测试筛选；研究决策应同时看训练成本摊销、全预算危险命中和轨迹覆盖，不能按最高几何多样性或top20精确率选测试器。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者结果未复现，仅PX4-Avoidance三任务双障碍仿真；约四倍命中对照跨任务且未计2716例前置采集，无规范化单项消融。2026复用2025数据；2024生成/提交相差一例。资源DOI本轮404，尚未验证可下载。
frontier_brief.question: 匹配训练与仿真总预算后，加入其余航段和来向状态能否同时改善危险阈值召回与轨迹覆盖？

evidence.label: 生成预算命中
evidence.context: 表II；每任务2024预算200、2025/2026预算100，三个PX4/Aerialist任务。对照来自单参考任务数据，超时口径不同；900未含2716例预采集和复评，不是全成本四倍加速。

evidence.label: 代理迁移边界
evidence.context: 表I，参考验证对CS2/CS4/CS5；作者称300个未训练生成测试，非完整无偏目标分布。多航段可改变全任务最小间隙，未作来向/历史状态隔离消融。

evidence.label: 选中集精确率
evidence.context: 146例提交中按阶段三已有仿真分数，每任务选20例作三次复评；2026复用2025数据。这不是900预算命中率、全体候选召回或无人机安全率。

evidence.label: 输入与轨迹覆盖相反
evidence.context: 2026表V，本方法CS2/CS4/CS5输入39.11/16.85/32.76，输出最近邻DTW2.72/1.37/2.41；总排名第二。限制生成区域/障碍大小与过滤的贡献尚未隔离。

mechanism.title: 选段并对齐坐标
mechanism.text: 最大对称矩形限制障碍在合法区内，变到平面参考航段后生成，再反变换；是几何可行性约束，不是完整飞行动力学的对称性保证。

mechanism.title: 代理选择与验证分开
mechanism.text: 两支5→10→20网络拼接40→20→1预测间隙，100轮低间隙保留加100轮几何多样替换，最终榜经高保真验证；未展示用验证误差在线重训。

mechanism.title: 覆盖应看行为
mechanism.text: 几何并集和障碍面积变异系数直接用于选择；输出多样性按轨迹最近邻DTW计算。高几何分数仍可能只覆盖相似轨迹，不能代替危险行为覆盖。

passages.section: Energy-Aware Open-Vocabulary Detection Scheduling for Low-Power Robotic Autonomy
passages.location: Energy-Aware Open-Vocabulary Detection Scheduling for Low-Power Robotic Autonomy
passages.text: Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets robots search for run-time object queries, but fixed-rate inference spends embedded compute on low-value frames during idle motion, map revisits, or stable viewpoints. This paper presents an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. The scheduler uses odometry, map change, and detector confidence to switch among low-, mid-, and high-power YOLO-World-S modes on a Jetson Orin Nano. We evaluate the energy-quality trade-off on an AgileX LIMO using 40 real navigation trials: two target objects, five placements per target-policy pair, and four perception policies. Across bottle and cup trials, the scheduler records 8/10 mission success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline, while reducing mean Jetson input power (a Jetson-side power-draw metric) by 5.2% relative to an 8 Hz high-rate baseline and lowering achieved OVD call rate by 34.0%. It does not minimize mission-window Jetson input energy because longer missions can erase instantaneous power savings. A separate 60 s stationary microbenchmark isolates the perception workload: the scheduler lowers mean power from 8.045 W to 7.301 W and energy from 484.7 J to 438.1 J relative to the 8 Hz baseline. These results support robot-state-aware OVD scheduling as a promising power-management mechanism with competitive task reliability, while showing that mission-window Jetson input energy must be read together with task progress and runtime.

Open-vocabulary object detection (OVD) lets mobile robots ground run-time object queries, such as “find the bottle near the doorway,” in their camera stream instead of searching only fixed trained labels. This capability is enabled by vision-language models and open-vocabulary detection/grounding systems, including CLIP [ 1 ] , OWL-ViT [ 2 ] , GLIP [ 3 ] , Grounding DINO [ 4 ] , Detic [ 5 ] , and YOLO-World [ 6 ] . In robotics, similar representations support language-grounded maps, open-vocabulary scene graphs, and object-centric navigation [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

The deployment problem is that OVD is expensive on embedded robots. A low-power robot must share a small battery across the embedded GPU, RGB-D camera, LiDAR, wireless stack, controller, and drive base. Mean Jetson input power is therefore a practical Jetson-side power-draw metric, especially for robots that keep monitoring or waiting after a target event. A fixed high detector rate gives fast response but wastes power during idle motion, map revisits, or low-information views. A fixed low-rate or quantized detector saves power but can delay target acceptance or miss short visual opportunities. The right operating point changes during the mission.

This motivates mission-level perception scheduling: each inference should be worth its energy at the current robot state. We ask whether an embedded robot can reduce Jetson input power for OVD while maintaining mission completion by scheduling detector rate from robot state. Our hypothesis is that low-value frames can be sampled sparsely, while candidate-target phases need high-rate response. A stationary frame in a stable map has lower marginal value than a frame near a plausible target; once a target appears, aggressive throttling is risky.

Existing work covers pieces of the problem but not the full intersection. OVD papers emphasize zero-shot recognition, language-grounded navigation emphasizes semantic goal reaching, and adaptive video analytics emphasizes throughput or resource budgets for passive streams. Our focus is more targeted: deciding when an embedded robot should spend OVD compute during search. As summarized in Table I , prior works generally do not combine OVD, robot-state-aware adaptation, Jetson input-power/energy accounting, and task-level metrics such as success rate and time-to-detect (TTD).

We present an energy-aware OVD scheduler that treats detector invocations as mission-level computational resources. The scheduler uses odometry, map changes, and detector confidence to adaptively switch among low-, mid-, and high-power operating modes. We evaluate YOLO-World-S on a Jetson Orin Nano mobile robot against fixed-rate 8 Hz, 5 Hz, and 2 Hz baselines across bottle and cup search tasks. Fig. 1 illustrates the overall runtime flow.

We formulate energy-aware OVD as a mission-level scheduling problem that trades Jetson input power and detector invocation rate against search success and TTD, rather than only reducing per-frame inference cost.
We design a finite-state runtime that switches OVD rate from robot-native signals with explicit thresholds and hysteresis, including a low-power configuration for low-value frames.
We implement the scheduler with YOLO-World-S on an AgileX LIMO equipped with a Jetson Orin Nano and compare it against fixed-rate high-, medium-, and low-rate baselines.
We report a real-robot evaluation with 40 navigation trials across two queried objects and a separate stationary microbenchmark that isolates perception power.
We show empirically that lower mean power does not necessarily imply lower mission-window Jetson input energy, because slower or less reliable perception can increase navigation time.

The main finding is that lower instantaneous detector power is only one part of the robot objective. The scheduler reduces mean Jetson input power relative to the high-rate baseline and shows slightly higher aggregate success in the evaluation logs, but mission-window Jetson input energy still depends strongly on runtime. We therefore report power, energy, success, TTD, and time-domain traces rather than optimizing energy in isolation.

Table I positions representative prior work by this paper’s evaluation axes. The comparison is qualitative: the proposed scheduler builds on OVD models but studies their coupling with robot-state-aware scheduling, Jetson input-power/energy accounting, and task-quality metrics.

Modern OVD systems inherit generalization from image-text pretraining. CLIP [ 1 ] introduced transferable vision-language representations, and OWL-ViT [ 2 ] , GLIP [ 3 ] , RegionCLIP [ 17 ] , Detic [ 5 ] , Grounding DINO [ 4 ] , and YOLO-World [ 6 ] adapt them to region-level localization. These works emphasize recognition accuracy, vocabulary generalization, and frame latency, but rarely ask how often an embedded robot should invoke OVD during a mission.

Open-vocabulary perception also supports semantic robot behavior. VLMaps [ 7 ] , LM-Nav [ 10 ] , open-vocabulary scene graphs [ 8 ] , ConceptGraphs [ 9 ] , ROVER [ 11 ] , and RoboAuditor [ 18 ] use language-grounded perception for navigation, mapping, planning, object search, or inspection. These systems show the utility of open vocabularies for robots, but not the scheduling and energy cost of the detector.

Efficient inference and adaptive perception provide the closest systems context. Approximate video analytics adapts resolution, model size, or sampling rate for passive camera workloads [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] ; edge systems partition or accelerate neural computation [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] ; continual-learning surveys highlight deployment adaptation challenges in autonomous systems [ 22 ] ; and active/NBV perception decides where or when to sense using task state or information gain [ 12 , 13 ] . In contrast, a mobile OVD robot has mission-native signals such as odometry, map change, and target confidence, and a missed target can change task outcome. These systems are complementary but optimize frame-level or edge-cloud decisions, whereas our evaluation couples OVD scheduling to closed-loop success, TTD, and mission-window power. This paper targets that intersection by treating OVD calls as mission resources and evaluating robot-state-aware scheduling with Jetson input energy, success, and TTD.

We consider a differential-drive mobile robot performing language-guided object search using an embedded open-vocabulary detector (OVD). For each mission, the robot is provided with a target query q q and autonomously searches the environment until either the task is completed or a mission duration 𝒯 max \mathcal{T}_{\max} is reached. Perception and navigation operate continuously throughout the mission, while detector execution is governed by the proposed energy-aware scheduling policy. We define TTD as the elapsed time from mission start to the first detection of the queried object; this event is used as an evaluation metric and does not terminate the mission. where t first ​ conf t_{\mathrm{first\;conf}} is the first target detection above τ conf \tau_{\mathrm{conf}} . TTD is a perception-timing metric, not the success label. Aggregate TTD is reported over successful runs only; failures remain in success counts, runtime, and mission-window Jetson input energy.

The design objective is to reduce Jetson input power and detector workload while maintaining success and acceptable TTD relative to a high-rate detector baseline. We also report E m E_{\mathrm{m}} to capture the effect of mission duration. Unlike offline detector compression, the scheduler is conditioned on robot state and spends computation unevenly across the mission.

The tri-state scheduler maps these signals to LOW/MID/HIGH detector modes, while the logging pipeline records Jetson input power, mission-window energy, inference count, success, TTD, and mode occupancy.

Fig. 1 shows the runtime. The robot runs ROS Noetic with GMapping and move_base . The OVD node receives RGB frames from an Astra/Dabai U3 RGB-D camera and evaluates YOLO-World-S for the queried class. Requested rates are upper bounds: the camera continues streaming, but frames reach the detector only when the scheduler permits a new OVD call. A state monitor subscribes to odometry, the occupancy grid, and detector outputs. A logger records scheduler events, poses, detector calls, mission outcomes, and Jetson power from tegrastats .

The proposed scheduler uses a finite-state policy with hysteresis. Each state has a fixed target rate and preferred inference mode:

LOW : requested INT8. Used after sustained evidence that the robot is nearly idle and the local map is stable. This state samples frames sparsely to retain target awareness without continuous high-rate detection.
MID : FP16. Used during normal navigation and mapping, where new viewpoints arrive but there is no confident target.
HIGH : FP16. Used when a target candidate is detected or the robot is near a recent target estimate, prioritizing high-rate response over energy.

HIGH denotes a high-power candidate-response state rather than a distinct long-term tracking mode. The scheduler operates deterministically: transitions to HIGH are triggered by moderate evidence of the target, whereas entry into LOW is permitted only after sustained inactivity and persistent evidence of map stability.

The perception runtime maintains both the high-rate YOLO-World-S inference path and the INT8 TensorRT engine in memory, selecting the appropriate execution mode according to the scheduler state. INT8 inference is used exclusively in LOW mode, where frames are processed at reduced precision to support coarse target awareness with lower computational cost. MID and HIGH modes use the FP16 inference path to provide higher-fidelity localization and response. The INT8 decision threshold, τ int8 \tau_{\mathrm{int8}} , is applied only within the LOW-mode detector, whereas mission-level detection decisions and time-to-detection (TTD) are evaluated using the common confidence threshold τ conf \tau_{\mathrm{conf}} . All reported experiments were conducted with the INT8 engine available and without precision fallback.

For mission runs we log success, TTD, runtime, path length, OVD invocations N inf N_{\mathrm{inf}} , average OVD rate N inf / 𝒯 N_{\mathrm{inf}}/\mathcal{T} , state occupancy, mean Jetson input power, and mission-window energy. State occupancy is the realized time fraction in LOW/MID/HIGH using the corresponding raw labels. Power is scoped to the Jetson module, not the full robot battery: the analysis uses tegrastats VDD_IN total_W at a 50 ms requested sampling interval, with GPU and SoC rails used only as diagnostics. For every reported trial, the power trace is aligned to mission start/end wall time and energy is integrated by a trapezoidal sum over valid in-window samples. Failed missions remain in all-run averages because they consume real time and power.
Fig. 2: Real-robot arena with fixed LIMO start pose and bottle/cup target placements reused across policies.

Experiments use an AgileX LIMO differential-drive robot with an Astra/Dabai U3 RGB-D camera, 2D LiDAR, and NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano 8 GB. The robot runs ROS Noetic, GMapping, and move_base . The OVD node runs YOLO-World-S with one queried target class. Final navigation trials use “bottle” and “cup” queries to test scheduling across two targets.
We compare four perception policies:
Base-8Hz : fixed 8 Hz high-power mode (TRACK).
Base-5Hz : fixed 5 Hz mid-power mode (EXPLORE).
Base-2Hz : fixed 2 Hz low-power INT8 mode (SLEEP).
Proposed : tri-state low-/mid-/high-power scheduling.

The paper reports LOW/MID/HIGH as conceptual modes and keeps SLEEP/EXPLORE/TRACK as labels where needed. Achieved rates can be below requested values because detector latency and gating limit calls, so results report measured invocation rates.

The real-robot evaluation comprises 40 trials spanning two target objects, four perception policies, and five repetitions for each object–policy combination. As shown in Fig. 2 , all trials begin from a fixed robot pose, with each target placed at one of five predefined locations. The same placements are reused across policies to support controlled comparison. Bottle and cup trials are conducted in separate batches; between trials, the target is moved to the next location and the navigation stack is reinitialized.

Each trial has a maximum duration of 180 s. Experiments are executed in policy-specific blocks rather than randomized order, so gradual changes in battery state, illumination, or system temperature may introduce temporal drift. Each policy is therefore evaluated across all five placements, and aggregate statistics are reported to reduce sensitivity to individual trial conditions. For every trial, the navigation stack is restarted, system power is monitored externally using tegrastats , and mission outcomes are recorded by the energy-aware navigation framework. The mission-level success field in the corresponding mission_summary record is used for evaluation.

In addition to the navigation trials, we perform a 60 s stationary microbenchmark for each policy to characterize perception-related power consumption independently of robot motion and navigation workload. During this benchmark, the camera, detector or scheduler, and power logger remain active, while navigation, SLAM, move_base , and velocity-command execution are disabled. For the proposed policy, scripted inputs exercise the scheduler across low-, mid-, and high-response phases, whereas each fixed-rate baseline remains in its assigned operating mode. This benchmark isolates the contribution of detector execution rate and scheduler state composition from variability introduced by the navigation stack.

We use the metrics in Section III-E . Navigation results cover all 40 trials, with aggregate summaries over bottle and cup. TTD is averaged over successful runs only, while Jetson energy and runtime are averaged over all runs because failures consume real time and power. The stationary benchmark is reported separately as a mechanism check. With five placements per object-policy pair, we report descriptive rather than inferential statistics.

Note: E m E_{\mathrm{m}} is mission-window Jetson input energy; TTD is conditional on success. L/M/H maps raw log labels to low-/mid-/high-power modes.

Fig. 3: Policy dashboard over the 40 navigation trials. The proposed scheduler has the highest aggregate success count and lower mean Jetson input power than Base-8Hz, while Jetson input energy is dominated by runtime.
Fig. 4: Mission runtime versus Jetson input energy for all 40 trials. Circles are successes, crosses failures, and open diamonds condition means; dashed lines show constant-power contours.

Table III summarizes the 40 real-robot navigation trials. The proposed scheduler has the highest aggregate success count, 8/10, while each fixed-rate baseline succeeds in 7/10 trials. It reduces mean Jetson input power from 9.35 W for Base-8Hz to 8.86 W, a 5.2% reduction, and lowers achieved OVD rate from 4.74 Hz to 3.12 Hz. Runtime is the mission-window duration over all runs; TTD succ measures only first accepted detection on successful runs. Base-2Hz has the lowest mean power, 8.38 W, but the longest mean runtime and largest mean Jetson input energy. Accordingly, the navigation result is best read as power/workload reduction at competitive task reliability, not as a statistically large reliability improvement.

Fig. 3 visualizes the same summary. The main claim is a power-management trade-off, not guaranteed E m E_{\mathrm{m}} minimization. Relative to Base-8Hz, the scheduler reduces mean power and detector calls, yet mean E m E_{\mathrm{m}} is higher because missions last 35.8% longer on average. Base-2Hz is clearer: it cuts mean power by 10.3%, but runtime rises by 51.4%, producing the largest mean E m E_{\mathrm{m}} . Its low TTD succ reflects successful easy cases, not generally faster search. Fig. 4 shows why energy-aware OVD must be evaluated as a closed-loop workload.

Fig. 5: Compact proposed-scheduler trace from the 60 s scripted stationary run. Colored regions show state, orange ticks show detector calls, the blue curve is Jetson input power, and the red dashed line is mean power.
Fig. 6: Representative adaptive navigation trace showing Jetson input power/energy, scheduler state and detector calls, detector confidence with the 0.25 threshold, and path length.

Fig. 7: Qualitative video-frame progression for representative bottle and cup searches. Blue R marks the robot and red T marks the target; LOW/MID/HIGH labels are qualitative stage estimates, not synchronized scheduler labels.

Fig. 5 shows the proposed scheduler in the 60 s scripted stationary run. This is not a navigation trial: it isolates detector/scheduler power from path length, obstacle avoidance, and mission duration. The run has 7.30 W mean Jetson input power, consumes 438.1 J, executes 202 detector calls, and spends 50/38/13% of the horizon in LOW/MID/HIGH modes. The power step between LOW and MID/HIGH makes the mechanism behind Table IV visible in time.

Fig. 6 complements the stationary trace with a closed-loop run. It shows the same scheduler while the robot moves, accumulates path length, and receives intermittent target-confidence events. The run is illustrative, exposing timing relationships among power, state, confidence, and path progress. Fig. 7 adds visual context from two run videos. Early frames show stable or low-value viewpoints where LOW is appropriate, middle frames show obstacle-aware navigation where MID maintains periodic OVD, and late frames show target-adjacent candidate response where HIGH is appropriate. The figure is qualitative; quantitative occupancy and timing come from synchronized logs in Tables III and IV and Fig. 6 .
TABLE IV: Stationary microbenchmark over the power-integration window.
Note: OVD Hz is computed as #Inf./mission-window duration.

The stationary microbenchmark isolates detector and scheduler power from navigation-related variability. OVD frequency is computed from detector invocations within the same time window used for power and energy integration. The fixed-rate baselines exhibit the expected monotonic reduction in power as the detector rate decreases from Base-8Hz to Base-5Hz and Base-2Hz.

The proposed scheduler operates between the Base-5Hz and Base-2Hz baselines, reflecting its mixed operating profile: approximately 50% of the benchmark is spent in LOW, 37.6% in MID, and 12.5% in HIGH. Relative to Base-8Hz, the proposed policy reduces mean power by 9.2% and energy consumption over the 60 s benchmark by 9.6%.
Fig. 8: Object-level success and state occupancy, mapped to LOW/MID/HIGH power modes. In the top plot, solid bars denote bottle and hatched bars denote cup.

The combined result hides object-level variation. On bottle trials, Base-8Hz succeeds in 5/5 runs, the proposed scheduler in 4/5, and the 5 Hz and 2 Hz baselines in 3/5 each. On cup trials, the proposed scheduler, Base-5Hz, and Base-2Hz each succeed in 4/5, while Base-8Hz succeeds in 2/5. Fig. 8 shows this split and state mix. Thus, the adaptive policy has the highest aggregate success count here, but the sample is too small to claim universal dominance.

This paper presented an energy-aware OVD scheduler for low-power mobile robots. It treats detector frames as mission resources: low-value frames can be sampled slowly, while candidate-target phases benefit from high-rate response. In 40 real AgileX LIMO navigation trials across bottle and cup searches, the scheduler shows 8/10 success compared with 7/10 for each fixed-rate baseline and reduces mean Jetson input power by 5.2% relative to Base-8Hz. The same trials show the key caution: lower mean power does not guarantee lower mission-window Jetson energy, because longer runtime can dominate the integral. A stationary microbenchmark confirms the mechanism, with 9.6% lower 60 s energy than Base-8Hz. Future work will broaden objects and environments, add external labels, randomize trials, measure whole-robot energy, and study motion-predictive scheduling.

analysis.overview: 将YOLO-World-S调用时机与精度绑定到机器人状态：根据运动、局部占据图熵变化、目标置信度与距离，在LOW/MID/HIGH之间切换。可复用的是带滞回的部署调度机制，以及必须联合报告功率、运行时长、能量与任务质量的评测口径。40次实机搜索中，相对固定8Hz高精度策略，平均Jetson输入功率下降5.2%、实际调用率下降34.0%，但平均任务窗口能量从866.9J增至1114.0J。成功次数8/10对7/10且存在对象间反向结果，不能确证可靠性提升。静止脚本实验支持感知负载省电，不足以证明完整导航更省能。
analysis.notice: 当前会话代理完整阅读固定HTML证据78/78片段，涵盖方法、全部实验、讨论和结论；该版本无附录。额外读取固定PDF（6页、1451273字节），目视物理页3/4/5/6，核架构图1、参数表II、实机照片图2、主表III、静止表IV及图3–8；补读PDF方法与实验口径。全部实验为作者结果，未复现，未运行论文代码或机器人试验，未独立审计原始逐次日志、INT8校准或成功标签。图7的阶段文字为定性估计，不当作同步状态日志。

findings.title: 把检测帧当作任务资源，但必须检验闭环能量
findings.text: 本文改变推理调用策略，而非重新训练检测器：ROS导航持续运行，摄像头持续送流，状态调度器决定何时允许YOLO-World-S执行及用何精度。固定高调用率可能把边端计算花在稳定视角；作者目标是降低Jetson功率与检测负载并保持任务表现。任务能量是从开始到结束的Jetson功率积分，低功率若拖长搜索可增加总能量；首次过阈检测时间TTD不终止任务，也不等于任务成功。该取舍是本文值得复用的评测认识，不能改写为整机续航已提高。

findings.title: 用占据图变化与新鲜目标信号驱动调度
findings.text: 局部信息代理是机器人中心4m×4m窗口内二元占据熵的归一化均值变化，不是图像语义信息增益；未知栅格取0.5，不同地图范围采用重叠索引单元。调度20Hz，比较相邻0.05s的绝对熵差。运动信号来自线速度；置信度只在检测调用后更新，MID进入HIGH的置信度分支必须使用新输出。距离分支采用未过期目标估计：RGB-D框中心反投影、0.3m范围LiDAR吸附、α=0.3指数滤波，30s未更新则距离置无穷。这些时效规则避免把过期置信度直接当作新的目标证据，但占据熵仍只是新空间的代理。

findings.title: 三态规则带滞回，设定频率不能当作实际吞吐
findings.text: 参数表II与公式4–7：LOW/MID/HIGH请求1.5/4/8Hz；LOW在速度>0.03m/s或熵差>0.02时进入MID；MID在新鲜置信度≥0.25或目标距离≤2m时进入HIGH；连续5次检测评估置信度<0.20才从HIGH退到MID；低速且熵差<0.02持续2s再降LOW。5次指检测评估，不是5个20Hz调度tick；所有轨迹参数固定。摄像头流速不随之降低，请求频率只是检测门控上限，实际受延迟限制。主表中固定8Hz实际4.74Hz，调度策略3.12Hz，其LOW/MID/HIGH驻留25/60/15%。正式转移规则未列出静止LOW状态下仅凭新目标置信度直接升档的路径，现有汇总不能独立判断该边界的实现行为。

findings.title: 频率与量化同时变化，尚未隔离状态选择的独立收益
findings.text: 运行时将高精度路径和INT8 TensorRT引擎同时常驻内存；仅LOW使用INT8，MID/HIGH使用FP16。LOW检测内部阈值0.20，但任务检测/TTD统一采用0.25。全部报告实验INT8可用，没有回退，因此不能把这批数据解释为含精度回退的部署验证。共同数值阈值也不证明两种精度的置信度经过等效校准；未给出可核验的INT8校准数据与精度损失分析。固定8/5Hz是FP16，固定2Hz是INT8，主比较同时改变调用率、时机与精度，没有等实际调用预算、固定精度的消融来单独证明状态感知调度优于均匀降频。

findings.title: 能耗边界是Jetson模块，失败任务也纳入积分
findings.text: 功率来自tegrastats的VDD_IN total_W，采样请求间隔50ms，GPU/SoC子轨仅诊断。按任务开始/结束墙钟对齐，对窗口内有效样本作梯形积分；失败任务纳入时长与能量平均。该测量不含完整电池侧的电机、相机、LiDAR等所有负载，且不是独立外接功率计审计。表中功率是试验平均功率再汇总，不能用平均功率×平均时长替代逐次积分能量，特别是时长与负载相关时。主张低功率、低任务能量和整机续航需要分开验证。

findings.title: 40次实机试验复用位置，但顺序与成功标签存在边界
findings.text: 平台为AgileX LIMO、Orin Nano 8GB、RGB-D和2D LiDAR，ROS Noetic/GMapping/move_base，YOLO-World-S每次只查询一个类别。瓶/杯两对象×四策略×五位置共40次，每策略10次；固定起点，各策略复用五个目标位置，单次上限180s，试验间重启导航。对象分批、策略按块执行而未随机化，电池、温度和光照漂移可能影响对照。成功取框架mission_summary字段；论文未给独立外部成功标签或足够可复核的操作定义，不能由TTD替代。作者仅报描述统计，无置信区间或显著性检验；这些约束限制从8/10推断稳定可靠性增益。

findings.title: 降低平均功率，却增加任务窗口能量
findings.text: 目视核对表III、图3/4：固定8Hz与调度策略平均功率9.35→8.86W（下降5.2%）、实际调用4.74→3.12Hz（下降34.0%），但平均时长92.8→125.9s，任务窗口Jetson能量866.9→1114.0J。由表中四舍五入数计算，能量增加约28.5%；作者按其原始汇总给时长增35.8%，舍入表值约35.7%。调度成功8/10、固定8Hz 7/10。与固定5Hz比，功率8.92→8.86W差距很小，能量1019.8→1114.0J亦更高；固定2Hz功率最低8.38W，却因140.4s时长达到最高1155.0J。该组实机数据支持功率/工作量取舍，提供低功率不等于低任务能量的明确反例。

findings.title: 成功条件下的TTD不能代表全体搜索速度
findings.text: 表III成功试验TTD为固定8/5/2Hz的25.9/53.6/0.9s，调度10.9s。TTD是首次共同阈值0.25检测事件，既不终止任务，也不是成功标签；失败试验被排除出TTD而保留在其余全体指标。固定2Hz的0.9s反映成功的容易案例，不能据此称最慢调用策略普遍搜索更快；同理，调度10.9对25.9s不直接证明所有任务的达标速度提升。应共同看超时、成功与全任务时长，未来评估可纳入失败截尾的时间到事件分析。

findings.title: 合并成功次数掩盖瓶类回退
findings.text: 图8及对应正文：瓶类固定8Hz成功5/5、调度4/5、固定5/2Hz各3/5；杯类调度和固定5/2Hz各4/5、固定8Hz 2/5。调度的8/10对7/10来自跨对象合并，瓶类并未优于高频策略；每对象仅5次且没有随机顺序/统计区间，不能宣称普遍占优或将单次成功差异转成稳健可靠性提升。对象仅瓶/杯，也未覆盖多类别同时查询与新环境泛化。

findings.title: 静止脚本隔离出感知功率取舍，不能替代导航收益
findings.text: 核表IV、图5：名义60s静止测试保留相机、检测/调度与记录器，但关闭导航、SLAM、move_base与速度命令执行；调度使用预设输入经过三态，基线保持固定模式。固定8Hz实际6.67Hz、402次，8.045W/484.7J；调度3.37Hz、202次，7.301W/438.1J，功率下降9.2%、能量下降9.6%。频率由调用数除以实际同一积分窗口，不必强行按恰好60.000s反算。调度驻留约50/37.6/12.5%，表内50/38/13%有舍入；不能据101%判数据错误。固定2Hz仍更低，6.847W/410.8J；调度位于固定2与5Hz之间。该脚本机制检验没有任务质量对照，且驻留由脚本决定，不能外推完整搜索节能或证明最优调度。

findings.title: 图像阶段标注与同步日志的证据强度不同
findings.text: 目视图6为一个导航运行的功率、置信度、路径进展与状态时序示例，不能与图5静止60s或主表平均值混用。图7瓶/杯视频帧上的LOW/MID/HIGH仅为定性阶段估计，不是同步调度标签；量化驻留与时序依据表III/IV及图6，不能用选取的画面独立核证触发规则。原始逐次日志、功率轨迹与成功外标未在本轮独立核查，INT8校准与精度/时机分离消融也不足。作者提出扩展对象环境、随机化、外部标签与整机能量测量；当前仅支持小样本平台部署结果，尚不能确认整机续航或多环境可靠性收益。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：相同调用预算下，状态选择时机能否改善任务能量与质量？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在精度和实际检测调用预算匹配时，状态感知调用时机仍能比均匀调用降低达到相同任务质量所需的Jetson任务能量。实验草案先在公开导航仿真中做状态/均匀时机×固定FP16/LOW使用INT8的二乘二对照，统一检测模型、导航器、目标位置、种子与超时；均匀策略的实际调用预算应由独立开发集确定，不能使用测试任务结束后的调度次数作在线先验。记录预设预算误差并作预算扫描，而非将请求Hz当匹配依据。按对象与场景分层随机区组，至少30个配对种子/条件；增加静止LOW时目标新出现的事件，核实升档路径与漏检。先用开放图像/回放核精度和置信度校准，再做闭环仿真，回放结果不代替闭环收益。能量结论另需在相同Jetson平台的实机验证：记录有效功率采样覆盖、逐任务Jetson积分及独立电池侧整机能量；由预定义距离/可见性标准或外部标签确认成功，区分首次检测与达成目标，失败超时也计成本。报告成功率配对区间、含失败截尾的达标时间、全体/成功/失败能量与时长、实际调用数、各对象回退，以及固定时限负载实验；在成功率非劣界和预算容差预注册后比较能量。若固定FP16且预算相当时优势消失、只依赖INT8，或功率降低但时间/失败代价使等质量能量不降，则推翻状态选择本身足以带来任务节能的假设。此为未执行的可编辑实验草案，未创建选题，未全面查新，不宣称研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: 按运动与目标证据切换OVD频率和精度：功率下降，导航能量反升
frontier_brief.change_type: 推理调度与评测反例
frontier_brief.delta: 在YOLO-World-S前加入20Hz三态调度，以线速度、局部占据熵变化、新鲜置信度和目标距离，选择1.5Hz INT8或4/8Hz FP16调用；使用滞回抑制频繁切换。
frontier_brief.before: Orin Nano上固定8Hz FP16检测，导航实际4.74Hz；固定5Hz FP16、2Hz INT8提供降载对照，摄像头与导航仍持续运行。
frontier_brief.after: 40次瓶/杯搜索中，调度实际3.12Hz、平均Jetson功率8.86W，相对固定8Hz的9.35W下降5.2%；平均任务时长125.9s、能量1114.0J，高于92.8s、866.9J。
frontier_brief.relevance: 适用于Orin级移动平台的感知负载/散热预算决策；若目标是任务续航，必须把达到目标、超时及运行时长纳入功率积分，不能按瓦数或静止省电率选方案。
frontier_brief.caveat: 作者实验未复现；每策略仅10次、两对象，策略顺序未随机化，成功为框架字段。8/10对7/10不确证可靠性提升，瓶类还从5/5退到4/5。量化与频率同时变化，未隔离状态选择的独立收益；测量仅Jetson模块，非整机电池。
frontier_brief.question: 固定精度并匹配实际调用预算后，状态感知选择帧的时机能否在成功率不降时减少闭环任务能量？

evidence.label: 导航主对照
evidence.context: 表III；LIMO/Orin Nano 8GB，瓶/杯各5位置、每策略10次，固定8Hz FP16对三态调度；实际调用4.74→3.12Hz，时长92.8→125.9s。能量增28.5%由舍入表值计算，失败亦计入。

evidence.label: 任务质量与条件TTD
evidence.context: TTD只在成功试验上平均，首次检测不终止任务。瓶类固定8Hz 5/5而调度4/5；杯类2/5→4/5。小样本、非随机顺序，不能断言普遍更可靠或整体更快。

evidence.label: 静止机制检验
evidence.context: 表IV/图5，名义60s，导航/SLAM/运动执行关闭；固定8Hz对脚本三态，实际6.67→3.37Hz、402→202次。固定2Hz仍最低410.8J；该节能率不能外推闭环搜索。

evidence.label: 更接近的降频基线
evidence.context: 导航表III，均7/10成功；平均功率8.92/8.38W、时长114.2/140.4s。调度不是最低能量策略，固定2Hz虽最低功率却能量最高。

mechanism.title: 用机器人信号分配检测帧
mechanism.text: LOW因运动/地图变化进入MID；新鲜目标置信度或近目标触发HIGH。20Hz监测与检测调用解耦，摄像头持续送流；熵变化仅为新空间代理。

mechanism.title: 滞回与精度绑定
mechanism.text: 静稳2s后降LOW；HIGH连续5次检测低置信度才回MID。LOW 1.5Hz INT8，MID/HIGH 4/8Hz FP16，双路径常驻；所有报告运行INT8可用、无回退。

mechanism.title: 按闭环任务积分验证收益
mechanism.text: tegrastats VDD_IN按任务窗口积分，失败也纳入；降低调用可能延长任务，实机主表出现平均功率下降却能量增加。成功条件TTD与脚本静止结果分别解释。
