passages.section: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
passages.location: T3R: Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement Towards Efficient and Robust VLA Models
passages.text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable end-to-end robot control, but inference is increasingly expensive: each decision processes hundreds of visual tokens, often across multiple cameras, leading to substantial computation while allowing irrelevant background content to distract action prediction under distribution shift. We argue that these issues stem from two complementary forms of redundancy: many visual tokens are spatially irrelevant, while attention over the remaining tokens is often misallocated. Based on this observation, we propose T3R, a Training-Free Two-Stage Token Refinement framework. In the first stage, segmentation-guided token pruning removes irrelevant visual patches to reduce computation and eliminate distracting context. In the second stage, saliency-guided attention biasing reallocates attention toward action-critical visual regions and language instructions within the retained tokens. Together, pruning produces a cleaner candidate set, while attention biasing further emphasizes the most decision-relevant evidence, yielding a better accuracy-efficiency frontier than either stage alone. On LIBERO-Spatial, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while essentially matching the unpruned success rate, and improves success by up to 7 percentage points under out-of-distribution object-placement perturbations. The timing comparison attributes 7.8 ms per inference call to pruning and attention-bias application. As input resolution increases, LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3 × 3.3\times speedup over the unpruned baseline. Evaluations across LIBERO, SIMPLER, and RoboTwin with three VLA backbones show the strongest accuracy-efficiency benefits in multi-camera settings. These results demonstrate that training-free token refinement is a practical approach to efficient and robust VLA inference.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Brohan et al., 2023a ; Black et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) provide a unified interface from pixels and language to robot actions, but this generality carries a substantial inference burden. At every decision step, the model propagates a long visual sequence through a large language backbone. In a typical OpenVLA-style setup, a 224 × 224 224\times 224 image produces 256 256 visual patches ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) , and multi-camera inputs multiply this token load before any action token is predicted. Attending over such long sequences at every control step is expensive and increases latency, which is detrimental to real-time control and can further induce observation–action distribution shift through stale observations and delayed actuation ( Arachchige et al., 2025 ) .

Figure 1. Two-stage T3R pipeline. Stage 1 (pruning): POS-weighted SigLIP text–patch similarity localizes the target; the top-scoring patch positions (with SigLIP/DINOv2 features) prompt EfficientTAM to produce an object mask, which is converted to a patch-level pruning decision while preserving original RoPE positions, so only the “interested tokens” enter the LLM. Stage 2 (biasing): Integrated Gradients over the instruction identifies salient words; an additive attention bias ( β = 2.0 \beta{=}2.0 ) is injected into the middle decoder layers for action-token queries, steering attention toward salient text tokens and retained visual patches before the action chunk is decoded. A closed-loop robot-control diagram. Camera observations and the instruction feed image and text encoders. In the first stage, similarity-selected image patches and DINOv2 features guide EfficientTAM to generate a mask; only selected visual tokens enter the language model. In the second stage, Integrated Gradients assigns importance to instruction words, illustrated by bowl and plate, and attention biases emphasize those words and selected visual tokens. The model outputs action tokens, the robot executes the actions, and a new observation starts the next iteration.

Many visual tokens are weakly coupled to the language instruction ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Shang et al., 2024 ) . These tokens can diffuse attention and distract action prediction, especially under viewpoint or object-placement shifts. Effective refinement must both remove irrelevant tokens and reinforce instruction-relevant evidence among those retained.

Redundancy acts at two coupled stages: token-set construction and attention allocation . Pruning can discard critical cues, while attention steering retains the full token cost and noisy input. We therefore prune first and refine attention only over the retained sequence.

Building on this view, we introduce T3R, a training-free two-stage token refinement framework. Stage 1 performs segmentation-guided token pruning with position preservation, so compression happens before the VLA decoder and every transformer layer benefits from a shorter input. Stage 2 compensates for pruning-induced information loss by injecting task relevance into the retained sequence: saliency-guided attention biasing in intermediate layers steers action-token queries toward instruction-salient words and retained task-relevant regions.

We evaluate T3R on OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , CogACT ( Li et al., 2024b ) , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) across LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , SIMPLER ( Li et al., 2024a ) , and RoboTwin ( Mu et al., 2025 ) . Across these systems, multi-camera settings show greater pruning headroom than the single-camera zero-shot setting. This trend suggests that overlapping visual evidence creates opportunities for token reduction.

We propose T3R, a training-free two-stage framework that couples segmentation-guided, position-preserving token pruning with saliency-guided attention biasing, jointly optimizing token selection and attention allocation in a single inference pass.

On LIBERO-Spatial with OpenVLA-OFT, T3R removes 85% of scene-camera tokens while retaining 96% success, reduces VLA inference latency by 14%, and improves OOD success by up to 7 pp. Resolution-scaling profiling shows up to a 3.3 × 3.3\times LLM-forward speedup over the unpruned baseline.
We evaluate T3R across VLA backbones and camera setups. The observed accuracy-efficiency trends are consistent with greater sensor redundancy providing more headroom for token pruning.

Vision-Language-Action models. VLA methods cast robot control as conditional sequence modeling over observations, instructions, and actions. RT-1/RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023b ; Brohan et al., 2023a ) established large-scale vision-language pretraining for manipulation, while OpenVLA and OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) improved openness and adaptation efficiency. Parallel efforts including π 0 \pi_{0} / π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , CogACT ( Li et al., 2024b ) , and GR00T ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) scale model capacity and control fidelity. Inference still relies on propagating long visual token sequences through heavy backbones, leaving efficiency and robustness under perturbation as open bottlenecks.

Token-efficient inference. Token reduction has been studied in vision transformers and multimodal LLMs via pruning, merging, and routing ( Bolya et al., 2023 ; Rao et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Shang et al., 2024 ) . In embodied settings, EfficientVLA, LightVLA, and TeamVLA ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) adapt these ideas with task-aware scoring and runtime compression; FastV ( Chen et al., 2024 ) prunes visual tokens after an early decoder layer; ADP ( Pei et al., 2025 ) performs action-aware dynamic pruning; and VLA-Cache ( Xu et al., 2025 ) reuses KV-cache entries across frames. T3R targets the harder decoder-entry regime: tokens are removed before any decoder layer, benefiting all layers, but selection is irreversible and lacks internal attention guidance. T3R addresses this by coupling external vision-language grounding with post-pruning attention repair. T3R and VLA-Cache are complementary (spatial vs. temporal redundancy).

Segmentation priors and attribution steering. Promptable segmentation models such as SAM/SAM2 and efficient variants ( Kirillov et al., 2023 ; Ravi et al., 2024 ; Xiong et al., 2024 ) provide a strong prior for locating instruction-relevant regions; we use segmentation as an intermediate computational prior rather than a perception output. Attribution methods, especially Integrated Gradients ( Sundararajan et al., 2017 ) , estimate token contribution without parameter updates; since raw attention is not always a faithful importance indicator ( Jain and Wallace, 2019 ; Patro et al., 2022 ) , we use external relevance signals to bias middle-layer action-token attention, following the spirit of inference-time intervention ( Nguyen and Le, 2026 ) .

Positioning. To our knowledge, T3R is the first training-free approach to prune 85% of scene-camera tokens before decoder entry while retaining success within 1 pp of the unpruned baseline on LIBERO-Spatial. External grounding and attention repair benefit every decoder layer without retraining.

T3R follows a two-stage pipeline (Fig. 1 ): segmentation-guided token pruning (Sec. 3.1 ) removes spatially redundant tokens, then saliency-guided attention biasing (Sec. 3.2 ) sharpens attention on the most important tokens that remain.

We remove visually irrelevant patches before they reach the VLA backbone, reducing effective sequence length while preserving tokens that carry task-relevant evidence. We first estimate patch-level relevance with the SigLIP vision-language encoder, which yields a text–patch similarity map, then refine it into an object mask with a SAM-based segmenter.

Task-guided patch scoring. Given an instruction ℓ \ell and an image I ∈ ℝ 224 × 224 × 3 I\in\mathbb{R}^{224\times 224\times 3} , SigLIP partitions the image into N = 256 N{=}256 patches with features V ∈ ℝ N × d V\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and tokenizes the instruction into T ∈ ℝ M × d T\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d} . Natural-language instructions mix nouns, spatial relations, and function words that are not equally informative for grounding. We therefore compute a part-of-speech (POS)-weighted patch-relevance score
(1) s i = ∑ j = 1 M w j cos ( v i , t j ) ∑ j = 1 M w j , s_{i}=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{M}w_{j}\,\cos(v_{i},t_{j})}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}w_{j}},

where t j t_{j} is the embedding of token j j , w j w_{j} its POS-dependent weight, and cos ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) \cos(\cdot,\cdot) cosine similarity. This softly emphasizes object nouns and descriptive adjectives while down-weighting verbs and prepositions, without supervision or architectural changes.

Segmentation-based mask generation. Relevance scores localize the target coarsely but lack precise boundaries. We refine them with EfficientTAM-S ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) , which generates masks from sparse point prompts. Because nearly uniform similarity scores make top- K K prompt selection unstable, we adopt an oversample-cluster-refine strategy: select the K init = 50 K_{\text{init}}{=}50 highest-scoring patches, apply DBSCAN ( ϵ = 2.0 \epsilon{=}2.0 in patch units) on their 2D grid coordinates, retain the largest spatial cluster, and take its K = 8 K{=}8 top-scoring patches as positive prompts plus K neg = 3 K_{\text{neg}}{=}3 lowest-scoring patches as negative prompts. This spatial coherence reduces mask flicker across frames. A patch is retained if the mask covers more than 30% of its pixels ( τ = 0.3 \tau{=}0.3 ). SigLIP text embeddings are cached per instruction; masks are updated asynchronously every five VLA calls.

Figure 2. Qualitative pruning on a sparse LIBERO-Spatial scene (“pick up the bowl between the plate and the ramekin”). Top: input, POS-weighted SigLIP similarity, and the EfficientTAM mask with its point prompts. Middle: T3R keeps only 13/256 patches (95% pruned), tightly localized on the target. Bottom: TeamVLA’s similarity+expansion+merge retains 226/256 (12% pruned), leaving most of the background in the sequence through the early decoder layers. A three-by-three panel comparison of patch selection in a tabletop scene containing a robot gripper, bowls, a plate, and a ramekin. The top row shows the original image, a colored similarity heatmap, and a green segmentation mask with positive and negative point prompts. The middle row shows a small retained region around the target, the image with discarded regions darkened, and the original image for comparison. The bottom row shows TeamVLA's similarity, expansion, and final merging masks, which retain much more background. Green patches are retained and red patches are discarded.
Position-preserving pruning. The input layout is
[ bos , v 1 : 256 , v 1 : 256 ′ , q proprio , t 1 : L ] [\textsc{bos},\,v_{1:256},\,v^{\prime}_{1:256},\,q_{\text{proprio}},\,t_{1:L}]

with sequential RoPE positions ( Su et al., 2024 ) . Naively re-indexing after pruning shifts downstream tokens to positions never seen in pretraining and collapses success to near zero in our tests. We instead assign each retained patch its original position ID: for the retained index set S S the sequence becomes
preserving the pretrained positional structure and visual–language relationships.

Scheduling. Segmentation runs asynchronously , with updates scheduled every five VLA inference calls. Action inference reuses the latest completed mask without waiting for an update. On suites where segmentation is ambiguous, an optional similarity-union rule additionally retains patches above the 75th percentile of the similarity scores, trading a little compression for recall.

Pruning inevitably removes scene information. To mitigate the loss of task-relevant signal, we steer attention toward salient instruction tokens and retained task-relevant patches within the reduced sequence.

Attribution via Integrated Gradients. We adopt Integrated Gradients (IG) ( Sundararajan et al., 2017 ) , which attributes a prediction to input tokens by integrating gradients along a straight-line path from a neutral baseline to the actual input and satisfies the completeness axiom. At the start of each task we compute token-level IG on the embedding layer, interpolating between a pad-token baseline and the input in n steps = 5 n_{\text{steps}}{=}5 steps; the normalized attribution α ∈ ℝ L \alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{L} designates the top 30% of tokens as salient. The attributions are cached and reused across all evaluation episodes of that task.
Attention-bias injection. We add the attribution as an additive bias to the attention logits of the middle decoder layers:
(2) a i ​ j = q i ⋅ k j d + β w j 1 [ j ∈ S bias ] 1 [ i ∈ Q action ] , a_{ij}=\frac{q_{i}\!\cdot\!k_{j}}{\sqrt{d}}+\beta\,w_{j}\,\mathbf{1}[j\in S_{\text{bias}}]\,\mathbf{1}[i\in Q_{\text{action}}],

where β \beta is a scalar strength, w j w_{j} the bias weight at key position j j , S bias S_{\text{bias}} the union of salient text positions and retained visual patch positions, and Q action Q_{\text{action}} the action-prediction queries. The bias is applied only to action-token queries and restricted to middle layers (8–23), preserving early feature extraction and late output formatting. Biased positions are drawn from (i) salient text tokens weighted by their IG scores and (ii) retained visual patches weighted by SigLIP similarity scaled by 0.5 0.5 . This forms a two-level funnel: pruning removes clearly irrelevant tokens; biasing further differentiates among those that remain.

Figure 3. Most visual tokens are near-inert. (a) Across all 32 decoder layers, 93.9% of visual tokens receive < < 0.2% of the action queries’ attention each. (b) Per-patch action-query attention concentrates on a few task-relevant patches (here the gripper and target bowls), while the background receives negligible weight. Two panels summarize visual-token attention. The left bar chart shows that 30.7 percent of tokens receive less than 0.1 percent attention each, 63.2 percent receive 0.1 to 0.2 percent, and 6.1 percent receive more than 0.2 percent. The right panel overlays a patch-grid heatmap on the scene. Most patches have low attention, with a few high-attention regions near the gripper and target bowls. The color scale runs from blue for low attention to red for high attention.

We test three hypotheses: (H1) segmentation-guided pruning substantially reduces scene-camera tokens while maintaining success; (H2) fewer tokens lower inference cost; and (H3) the full T3R pipeline improves robustness under out-of-distribution object-placement shifts. We then examine cross-backbone generalization and sensor redundancy.

Setup. Our primary study uses OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025 ) (SigLIP ViT-SO400M + LLaMA-2-7B, LoRA rank 32, chunk size 8, dual camera ⇒ \Rightarrow 512 visual tokens/call) on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , a MuJoCo tabletop-manipulation suite of four task families (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long). Spatial uses a 220-step horizon. Saliency uses IG with n steps = 5 n_{\text{steps}}{=}5 , top- k k ratio 0.3 0.3 , β = 2.0 \beta{=}2.0 , layers 8–23, and a 0.5 0.5 visual scaling. Unless noted we evaluate 10 episodes/task (seed 7 nominal, seed 42 OOD) on a single NVIDIA L40S (48 GB). For generalization we additionally port T3R to CogACT ( Li et al., 2024b ) on SIMPLER ( Li et al., 2024a ) (single third-person camera) and to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) on RoboTwin ( Mu et al., 2025 ) (three cameras), covering a 1 × 1\times / 2 × 2\times / 3 × 3\times spread in camera count. Baselines are the unpruned model, TeamVLA ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , ADP ( Pei et al., 2025 ) , and FastV ( Chen et al., 2024 ) ; each baseline runs at its native operating point, and we additionally force ADP/FastV into T3R’s high-reduction regime where noted. Reported reductions refer to scene-camera tokens removed before decoder entry.

passages.text: Table 1 shows that T3R achieves approximately 5.7 × 5.7\times the scene-camera token-reduction rate of TeamVLA (85% vs. ∼ \sim 15%), while achieving a higher success rate (96% vs. 94%). At the same 85% reduction, ADP and FastV fall to 66% and 14%; native ADP preserves accuracy at only 33.5% reduction. The retained budget adapts to task difficulty: T3R keeps 9–15 patches in sparse scenes and up to 121 in clutter, versus TeamVLA’s fixed ∼ \sim 203–233, avoiding a worst-case token count.

passages.section: 4.1. T3R Prunes Aggressively While Maintaining Success (H1)
passages.location: 4.1. T3R Prunes Aggressively While Maintaining Success (H1)
passages.text: Across all four LIBERO suites (10 tasks × \times 10 episodes each), T3R matches or beats TeamVLA on latency everywhere and on success on 3/4 suites, matching the unpruned baseline within 1 pp on Spatial (96 vs. 97) and Goal (98 vs. 99) at roughly 88–93 ms/call vs. the baseline’s 105–108 ms. The Object suite is the exception (82% vs. TeamVLA’s 86%), reflecting segmentation failures discussed in the failure analysis.

For each decoder layer we sum attention mass from every action-token query to every visual key and express each token’s share as a percentage of the total, averaging over 32 layers, 10 LIBERO-Spatial tasks, and 3 timesteps/task. 93.9% of visual tokens receive less than 0.2% of action-query attention each . In late layers (24–31), 50–75% of tokens fall below 0.1%. This shows most tokens are near-inert, but safe pre-decoder removal still depends on selecting the retained set well.

Profiling on an L40S across 11 token counts (8–256 patches) reveals an approximately linear trend, 0.040 ​ ms/token + 53.3 ​ ms 0.040\,\text{ms/token}+53.3\,\text{ms} ( r = 0.97 r{=}0.97 ). At 224 224 px, 85% scene-camera token reduction lowers VLA inference latency from 107.5 to 92.5 ms per call: a 14% reduction or 1.16 × 1.16\times speedup. Each call produces an eight-action chunk, not one environment step.

Comparing LLM-only savings ( 58.9 − 36.1 58.9-36.1 ms) with reported VLA-call savings ( 107.5 − 92.5 107.5-92.5 ms) yields a 7.8 ms residual per call, attributed to pruning and attention-bias application and already included in 92.5 ms. This accounting assumes comparable timing conditions; it does not isolate individual components. Segmentation (54 ms per update, every five VLA calls) runs asynchronously. IG is computed once per task and reused across its episodes; a 1 s cost corresponds to approximately 0.45 ms per environment step over ten full 220-step episodes.

Resolution scaling and hardware implications. The effective per-token marginal cost rises from 0.040 0.040 ms at sequence length ∼ \sim 200 to 0.064 0.064 ms at ∼ \sim 500, marking the transition from a bandwidth-bound to a compute-bound attention regime. Because T3R fixes the pruning ratio rather than an absolute token count, its retained sequence stays in the cheaper bandwidth-bound regime as resolution grows, while the unpruned baseline enters the quadratic compute-bound regime. LLM-forward profiling shows up to a 3.3 × 3.3\times speedup at 768 px. For accelerator co-design the implication is concrete: pre-decoder pruning shifts the operating point back toward the memory-bound regime that current LLM inference hardware handles most efficiently. Using the measured LLM cost on an L40S and adding a fixed 48.6 ms non-LLM cost, we project end-to-end inference latencies of 100 / 115 / 132 100/115/132 ms at 384 / 512 / 768 384/512/768 px for T3R, versus the baseline’s 144 / 182 / 327 144/182/327 ms and ADP’s 109 / 145 / 238 109/145/238 ms, a 2.47 × 2.47\times projected speedup over baseline at 768 px, versus ADP’s 1.37 × 1.37\times . These projections do not independently measure refinement overhead at each resolution.

We apply Gaussian positional noise to object placements (0–5 cm; 21 levels, 10 ep/task). T3R tracks the baseline within 1–2 pp for small perturbations, matches or exceeds it at ≥ 2 {\geq}2 cm, and leads by up to 7 pp at 4 cm ( + 4.8 +4.8 pp average at ≥ 4 {\geq}4 cm); TeamVLA degrades fastest (35% at 5 cm vs. our 48%). These full-pipeline gains are consistent with pruning reducing misleading background context and attention refinement emphasizing task-relevant evidence.

To test whether T3R’s benefit transfers across backbones and sensor suites, we port it to CogACT on SIMPLER (single third-person camera) and to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on RoboTwin (three cameras). Both evaluations are zero-shot with no fine-tuned checkpoint, so absolute success is low; we focus on relative behavior versus the unpruned base and competing pruners at matched budgets.

Single-camera (CogACT / SIMPLER). Table 2 (left) reports CogACT on the SIMPLER Google-Robot (11 tasks, 189 episodes per method) and WidowX/Bridge (4 tasks, 96 episodes per method) suites, each using one third-person view. Here T3R with a 60% keep ratio matches base on Bridge and trails by 5.5 pp on Google-Robot, while methods retaining more tokens (ADP, FastV) fare better. With one view, little cross-sensor redundancy remains, so aggressive pruning removes tokens the policy still needs.

Multi-camera ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} / RoboTwin). For π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on RoboTwin (three cameras), we evaluate each method/budget on five tasks with 12 episodes each (60 total; Table 2 , right). Success rates are computed from pooled counts and rounded once. T3R achieves the highest or joint-highest success among the evaluated pruners across the reported budgets. At a 50% keep ratio it matches baseline (both 33.3%); at 62.5% it reaches 38.3%, exceeding baseline by 5.0 pp and the best competing pruner by 10 pp. ADP, FastV, and TeamVLA remain below baseline at these two budgets.

Takeaway. Across the evaluated backbones and benchmarks, T3R shows greater pruning headroom in multi-camera settings. This cross-system trend suggests that overlapping visual evidence provides opportunities for token reduction.

We isolate each component on LIBERO-Spatial (10 tasks × \times 10 episodes). Prune-only reaches 90% at 85% scene-camera token reduction, bias-only 98%, and full T3R 96%, versus a 97% baseline. Biasing recovers 6 pp of pruning loss; bias-only exceeding baseline indicates diffuse unpruned attention. In the bias-only layer sweep (no pruning), middle-layer biasing (8–23) reaches 98%, versus 95% for early, 92% for late, and 93% for all layers, consistent with early feature distortion and late output disruption.

Why T3R outperforms prior pruners. T3R prunes before all 32 decoder layers ( ∼ \sim 37 scene tokens retained), while TeamVLA carries 512 tokens through layers 0–15, allowing irrelevant context into representations before merging. Segmentation preserves coherent object regions and RoPE geometry rather than disjoint similarity samples; IG-guided attention repair then offsets pruning loss.

Hyperparameter robustness. One hyperparameter set served all 10 LIBERO-Spatial tasks and all four suites, without per-task tuning. Sweeping bias strength, active layers, saliency top- k k , and pruning threshold changed SR by 1–6 pp; DBSCAN ϵ \epsilon and SAM point counts follow the fixed patch-grid geometry.

passages.section: 4.7. Design Study: When and How to Steer Attention
passages.location: 4.7. Design Study: When and How to Steer Attention
passages.text: A pilot on ECoT-OpenVLA-7B ( Zawalski et al., 2025 ) (30 offline LIBERO-Spatial demos, L2 action error) crossed text-token IG with image-token Grad-CAM ( Selvaraju et al., 2017 ) , reasoning with action phases, and positive with negative biasing. Action-phase biasing cuts error by 5.4% ( p = 0.062 p{=}0.062 ), while reasoning-phase biasing raises it by 9.3% ( p = 0.018 p{=}0.018 ). Text IG outperforms image Grad-CAM, and negative biasing never helps. These results support positive text-IG steering during action generation: the policy under-attends relevant tokens, so biasing can recover pruning loss.

T3R underperforms TeamVLA on LIBERO-Object (82% vs. 86%). These tasks place a source object into a visually dominant destination (e.g., a basket), so SigLIP similarity splits between the two and EfficientTAM segments the wrong region or produces an overly narrow mask. Multi-phase LIBERO-Long tasks (e.g., “put the bowl in the drawer and close it”) pose a related issue: the relevant region shifts mid-episode, but similarity is computed from the full instruction and does not adapt to the current phase, so pruning may mask regions that become critical later. More broadly, (i) Stage 1 depends on promptable segmentation as an intermediate prior and inherits its failure modes on merged or coarse boundaries; (ii) IG adds a one-time per-task cost that may not amortize over short task runs or meet strict initialization deadlines; and (iii) our single-camera zero-shot results (Sec. 4.5 ) show the method offers little benefit when the sensor suite carries little redundancy. Phase-aware re-prompting and camera-adaptive budgets are natural extensions.

All evaluations use simulation; physical-robot control and asynchronous execution with real sensor and actuation delays remain unvalidated. Hardware profiling uses only an NVIDIA L40S, with no energy measurements or edge-device tests. Latency improvements alone therefore do not establish energy savings or edge performance. Occlusion and lighting changes may degrade segmentation and discard task-relevant patches. We have not isolated these effects on task success or compared alternative segmenters.

We presented T3R, a training-free two-stage framework that couples segmentation-guided token pruning with saliency-guided attention biasing. On LIBERO-Spatial with OpenVLA-OFT, it removes 85% of scene-camera visual tokens while retaining success within 1 pp of baseline, reduces VLA inference latency, and improves OOD robustness by up to 7 pp. Evaluations on CogACT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across SIMPLER and RoboTwin suggest that overlapping multi-camera evidence provides more headroom for token pruning. From a design perspective, the value of T3R lies in where it acts. By discarding irrelevant tokens before decoder entry, every transformer layer operates on the shorter sequence, so the retained tokens stay in the cheaper bandwidth-bound regime even as resolution grows, yielding a projected speedup of up to 2.47 × 2.47\times at 768 768 px. Mask updates run asynchronously, while IG computation is amortized across each task’s episodes. Because the pipeline is training-free and leaves the underlying VLA weights unchanged, it applies directly to existing pretrained policies. Together, these properties make task-conditioned, pre-decoder sparsification a practical, first-class knob for co-designing efficient embodied inference systems. Across scenes, its adaptive budget retains 9–15 patches in sparse cases and up to 121 in clutter, while middle-layer biasing recovers 6 pp of the prune-only accuracy loss. Together with the 93.9% attention-sparsity result, these measurements explain why aggressive pruning remains viable and when additional evidence must be retained.

findings.title: 增量在剪枝位置与后续修复，不是重新训练底座
findings.text: T3R在进入decoder之前确定保留集合，使全部32层使用更短序列；代价是删掉的线索后续无法找回，因此又对保留token做注意力偏置。training-free指不更新既有VLA权重，不是无需预训练分割器、额外梯度计算或初始化成本。主研究为OpenVLA-OFT双相机；所有任务与控制验证均为仿真。

findings.title: 掩码选择：先聚类相似度种子，再做对象分割
findings.text: SigLIP图文patch余弦相似度按词性加权，强调名词/形容词、弱化动词/介词。取最高50个patch，在patch坐标上DBSCAN（epsilon=2.0），保留最大簇的8个高分点为正提示，另取最低3点为负提示交给EfficientTAM-S。掩码覆盖patch超过30%才保留。模糊suite可额外并入相似度75分位以上patch。该外部先验不是VLA自己的因果重要性判别；POS具体数值、部分实现与失败回退配置仍需代码确认。

findings.title: RoPE：删token但不把后面的索引重新压紧
findings.text: 主布局是BOS、256个scene token、256个另一视角token、proprio与文本。剪后保留scene patch原位置ID，第二视角仍在257–512，状态/文本继续原位置；作者称直接连续重编号在其测试中成功近零，但未给完整数值消融。表1的85%是场景相机删减比例，另一相机仍保留；若两视角各256且只删一侧85%，总视觉token删减约42.5%，再计状态/文本后总输入比例更低，不能称整模型删掉85%输入。

findings.title: 注意力修复：任务开始算一次IG，只偏置动作query
findings.text: 任务开始在embedding层从pad-token基线到输入做5步Integrated Gradients，归一化后取最高30%文本token，并跨该任务所有评测episode缓存。对8–23中间层的action-token query加logit偏置，beta=2.0；文本key按IG权重，保留视觉key按SigLIP相似度再乘0.5。不改早层/末层，也不是每帧重新做完整归因。正文未明确到可完全复现程度的IG标量目标、初始化观测选择与全部后端细节，不假定无需反向计算。

findings.title: 异步调度：每五次VLA调用刷新，控制复用最近完成掩码
findings.text: 分割每5次VLA inference call异步更新，动作推理不等它完成，直接用最新完成mask；文本embedding按指令缓存。分割一次54ms不直接等于每次调用阻塞54ms，也不能把其GPU资源需求当成零。物体移动或操作阶段切换时，mask可能陈旧；论文没有在真机传感/驱动延迟下验证这一调度。

findings.title: 组件消融：偏置补回6点，但单独偏置精度反而更高
findings.text: LIBERO-Spatial共10任务×10episode：baseline97%、85%场景剪枝的prune-only90%、bias-only98%、full96%。偏置在已剪枝集合上补回6个百分点，full仍比baseline少1点；不能说full在纯成功率上超过两种单阶段方法。无剪枝时，中层偏置98%，早层95%、晚层92%、全层93%。这些点来自有限任务/episode，未给配对差值或多运行区间，也未报告足够单组件延迟来证明所有精度/速度组合都严格Pareto占优。

findings.title: 主表：96%对97%，107.5→92.5ms是每个八动作调用
findings.text: 表1同OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Spatial，T3R删85%场景token，成功96%，未剪枝97%；L40S上VLA-call107.5→92.5ms，省15ms、约14%，即1.16倍。每次产生8动作块，不能写成每环境步节省15ms。TeamVLA约15%删减、94%、102.6ms；所谓5.7倍是85/15的删减率比，不是运行加速。ADP原生33.5%删减可维持97%，强压到85%则66%；FastV在高删减点14%，且剪枝发生在早层之后，比例相同不代表所有方法都从decoder入口获得同样计算收益。

findings.title: 7.8ms是差额归因，IG摊销以完整220步episode为前提
findings.text: 文中用LLM-only节省58.9−36.1=22.8ms，减去VLA-call节省107.5−92.5=15ms，得到7.8ms残差，归因于pruning/bias应用且已计在92.5ms里；不是逐模块独立计时，也不应再加一次。IG约1秒/任务，按10条完整220环境步episode摊得约0.45ms/环境步；短运行、提前结束或每次新指令都初始化时不能沿用。每5调用的54ms分割还会占资源并影响mask年龄，本文未给完整异步时间线、尾延迟和编译/融合注意力后端的对照。

findings.title: 高分辨率3.3倍与端到端2.47倍是不同证据等级
findings.text: 768px最高3.3倍来自LLM-forward profiling；端到端327→132ms、2.47倍则是给测得LLM耗时加固定48.6ms非LLM成本的投影。384/512/768px投影T3R为100/115/132ms，baseline144/182/327ms；各分辨率refinement开销未独立实测，不能把132ms当完整实测系统延迟。0.040ms/token等拟合也只适用于所测L40S/shape范围；没有功耗或边缘设备数据，不能据此宣称省电或可直接部署端侧。

findings.title: OOD提升：4cm最多+7点，来自整套管线
findings.text: 图4在物体位置高斯扰动0–5cm的21档、每任务10episode，seed42：小扰动基本贴近baseline，4cm处最多高7个百分点，≥4cm平均+4.8点；5cm时T3R48%、TeamVLA35%。名义测试用seed7，不能把不同seed曲线拼成同一训练重复统计。未有OOD下prune-only/bias-only和背景因果控制，结果与降低背景干扰的解释一致，但不证明仅剪背景或仅注意力修复导致了提升；摆位噪声也不覆盖真实遮挡/照明变化。

findings.title: 跨系统有反例：单相机Google Robot掉5.5点
findings.text: 表2单相机CogACT/SIMPLER，T3R保留60%token时Google Robot67.7%对baseline73.2%（11任务189episode/方法），Bridge10.4%对10.4%（4任务96episode）；ADP/FastV使用各自原生不同预算，不能当全部严格匹配。三相机π0.5/RoboTwin是零样本5任务×12=60episode，每相机保留128/256时T3R33.3%与baseline相同，160/256时38.3%，高5点。相机数、底座、任务、checkpoint适配状态一起变化，所以“多相机冗余更大”是跨系统趋势，不是只改变相机数量的因果消融。

findings.title: 注意力稀疏统计：0.2%阈值不能直接证明可删93.9%
findings.text: 图3/4.2按action-query到visual-key的注意力份额，跨32层、10任务、每任务3时刻平均，称93.9%视觉token各低于0.2%。作为数量级参照，512视觉token的均匀份额为100/512≈0.195%，已接近该阈值；这是本轮计算，不是作者新实验。因此单token阈值占比不等于这批token的累计权重很小，也不等于反事实删掉它们不会改变行为。需要看保留策略的实际成功率与消融，而非把注意力图当“93.9%输入因果无用”的证明。

findings.title: 失效与外推：对象/阶段切换和短时任务仍会破坏收益
findings.text: LIBERO-Object本方法82%低于TeamVLA86%；源物体/目的容器竞争相似度会让分割选错或过窄。LIBERO-Long多阶段指令不随当前阶段改写，后续关键区域可能提前被删。30条ECoT离线设计研究中，action-phase L2误差降低5.4%但p=0.062，不能写为通常0.05阈值下已显著；reasoning-phase反而升9.3%（p=0.018）。当前所有控制评估为仿真、仅L40S profile，没验证实际传感和执行延迟、替代分割器、能量或真机安全效果；训练自由不等于调参和初始化都免费。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：五次调用复用mask是否导致阶段切换后的失效？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在相同保留token预算下，阶段切换后的部分失败来自mask陈旧，而不是注意力偏置本身。先选一个LIBERO-Long多阶段任务，冻结同一checkpoint、IG缓存、beta、层范围和分割器；比较每次调用刷新、每五次刷新、阶段切换时额外刷新三组，阶段切换触发器只在开发集制定并另报其开销。每组将保留数限制到相同档位，保留相同RoPE策略与评测场景seed；另做同步oracle当前mask作为仅诊断上界，不把它写成可部署方法。在显式模拟传感/分割/动作调度的闭环中测整任务与逐阶段成功率、关键区域保留率、mask年龄、端到端p50/p95/p99、截止期错失和GPU时；IG冷启动单列，不跨任务隐式摊销。至少3次独立运行，用配对episode差值区间评估。若更鲜mask在预算匹配后不改善阶段切换失败，或刷新资源竞争使实时闭环表现反而更差，就推翻其主要来自缓存陈旧的解释；若只有oracle有效则结论转向分割/触发质量。实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: T3R：解码器前分割剪枝，再用中层注意力偏置补回精度
frontier_brief.change_type: 推理方法 · 剪枝与注意力修复
frontier_brief.delta: 先用SigLIP相关性与EfficientTAM掩码在decoder入口剪场景相机token，并保留原RoPE位置；再对8–23层的动作query添加文本IG和视觉相似度偏置。底座权重不更新，归因按任务缓存，mask每五次调用异步刷新。
frontier_brief.before: 仅剪token可能删掉任务线索；仅调注意力仍保留全序列成本。早层之后再剪，也不能让所有decoder层都受益。
frontier_brief.after: 先压缩候选集合再修复保留集合内的注意力分配。LIBERO-Spatial的85%只针对一个场景视角，另一相机及状态/文本保留；IG与分割计算另需调度。
frontier_brief.relevance: 双/多视角存在冗余且已有OpenVLA-OFT部署时，可把入口剪枝与动作query偏置分别验证。先保留位置ID并实测完整调用、冷启动和mask年龄，再决定是否值得比原生剪枝器更激进。
frontier_brief.caveat: 224px实际VLA调用仅107.5→92.5ms（14%）；3.3倍是高分辨率LLM前向，2.47倍端到端是投影。全部控制验证为仿真，单相机会退化；分割错误和阶段变化会不可逆地删线索，作者结果未复现。
frontier_brief.question: token预算相同时，更新更鲜的mask能否减少多阶段任务的后半段失败？

evidence.label: 同模型组件消融
evidence.context: LIBERO-Spatial 10任务×10episode，baseline97%，剪枝率为85%场景相机token。偏置补回6点损失，full并非最高成功率；单组件延迟披露不足。

evidence.label: 实测调用收益
evidence.context: 表1/L40S/224px，每次VLA调用给8动作。96%对baseline97%；7.8ms为两种计时节省的差额，已计入92.5，不是额外再加。

evidence.label: OOD整套管线表现
evidence.context: 图4，21个0–5cm位置噪声档、10episode/任务；seed42。尚无OOD逐组件对照，不能将全部提升单归因于剪背景或注意力。

evidence.label: 跨系统反例
evidence.context: CogACT/SIMPLER，T3R保留60%；三相机π0.5/RoboTwin在50%保留时33.3%匹配baseline。相机数与底座/任务同时变，不能据此给冗余作独立因果结论。

mechanism.title: 先把相似度变成连贯对象掩码
mechanism.text: 词性加权SigLIP得分取50个候选，DBSCAN后8正/3负点提示分割器；覆盖超过30%的patch保留，原始位置ID不重排。

mechanism.title: 只偏置中层动作查询
mechanism.text: 每任务5步IG标出最高30%文本token；动作query在8–23层对这些文本及保留视觉key加偏置，视觉权重缩0.5、beta2.0。

mechanism.title: 把异步成本和缓存失效分开测
mechanism.text: 控制读取最近完成mask，每五调用刷新；IG跨episode重用。延迟、初始化和mask新鲜度是不同指标，不能以异步为由忽略GPU资源与物体运动。

attention.reason: 存在组件对照，但实际调用节省有限、无真机且附加掩码会失效；目前作为特定多视角条件的备选。

impact.comparison: 存在组件对照，但实际调用节省有限、无真机且附加掩码会失效；目前作为特定多视角条件的备选。

attention.headline: T3R：入口剪枝后用中层注意力补偿
attention.summary: 先用SigLIP相关性与EfficientTAM掩码在decoder入口剪场景相机token，并保留原RoPE位置；再对8–23层的动作query添加文本IG和视觉相似度偏置。底座权重不更新，归因按任务缓存，mask每五次调用异步刷新。

passages.section: MoMaSplat : Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
passages.location: MoMaSplat : Dynamic Novel-View Demonstration Augmentation for Mobile Manipulation
passages.text: Visuomotor policies trained through imitation learning are highly sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint. This is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa), where robots rarely execute manipulation from the exact same base pose used during demonstration collection due to navigation uncertainty, localization drift, and environmental constraints. Recent approaches use novel-view synthesis (NVS) to augment demonstrations with unseen viewpoints, but they assume static scenes and therefore fail to re-render the manipulated object during the post-contact interaction phase, leaving the most critical parts of the demonstration unaugmented. We present MoMaSplat , a novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes full manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions. Our key insight is that standard MoMa data collection naturally provides the multi-view observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. MoMaSplat combines 3D Gaussian Splatting, feed-forward 3D foundation models, and kinematics-based action retargeting to separately reconstruct the scene and manipulated object, render them from novel viewpoints, and generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations paired with transformed actions. We evaluate MoMaSplat on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. MoMaSplat substantially improves robustness to unseen base poses, more than doubling the average success rate of the strongest baseline and maintaining non-trivial success at large base displacements where all baselines fail, while reducing the need for large-scale real-world data collection. More information at: https://robin-lab.cs.utexas.edu/momasplat/

Imitation learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for training visuomotor policies that perform complex manipulation tasks directly from image observations [ 1 , 2 ] . However, these policies are notoriously sensitive to changes in camera viewpoint [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Even small deviations in camera pose can significantly degrade performance, since the policy learns a narrow visual distribution tied to the demonstrations used during training.

This sensitivity is particularly problematic for mobile manipulation (MoMa). Unlike tabletop manipulation setups, where demonstrations are often collected from a fixed robot camera pose, mobile manipulators rarely execute tasks from the exact same location at deployment time. Navigation uncertainty, localization drift, obstacle avoidance, and imperfect planning routinely place the robot at different base poses relative to the workspace. As a result, the robot observes the manipulation scene from viewpoints that may differ substantially from those seen during demonstration collection. Robust deployment therefore requires visuomotor policies that generalize across a distribution of robot base poses rather than a single viewpoint.

A straightforward solution would be to collect demonstrations from many different robot locations. However, large-scale real-world teleoperation is expensive and difficult to scale [ 6 , 2 , 7 ] . Recent work has therefore explored synthesizing additional demonstrations through novel-view synthesis (NVS), generating virtual observations from unseen viewpoints using real-world captures [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . While promising, existing approaches assume a static scene and therefore fail during the most important part of manipulation: object interaction. Since the manipulated object moves throughout the demonstration, prior NVS methods cannot consistently re-render the object from novel viewpoints during the post-contact interaction phase, restricting augmentation primarily to pre-contact motions or introducing geometrically inconsistent generations.

Fig. 1 : MoMaSplat . Starting from mobile-manipulation data collected at the original base pose (white and red robot), MoMaSplat synthesizes demonstrations from sampled novel base poses ( yellow -outlined gray robot). The top-right sequence shows the source manipulation demonstration, while the bottom-right shows the corresponding synthesized trajectory, including the dynamic object as it is moved by the robot. Augmenting the source manipulation dataset with these demonstrations enables execution from unseen deployment-time base poses ( blue -outlined gray robot).

In this work, we present MoMaSplat , a demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete manipulation trajectories from unseen robot base poses, including dynamic object interactions (Fig. 1 ). Our key insight is that standard mobile-manipulation data collection naturally provides the multi-view observations needed to reconstruct both the static scene and the manipulated object in 3D. During navigation, the robot observes the scene from diverse viewpoints that enable scene reconstruction, while the manipulation demonstrations themselves provide object-centric observations that enable reconstructing the manipulated object and its motion.

Building on this observation, MoMaSplat separately reconstructs the static scene and manipulated objects using 3D Gaussian Splatting [ 11 ] and feed-forward 3D foundation models [ 12 ] . Given a novel robot base pose, MoMaSplat re-renders the scene, manipulated object, and robot from the new viewpoint and retargets the original actions through kinematics-based transformations to generate geometrically consistent synthetic demonstrations.

We evaluate MoMaSplat on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks involving both rigid and articulated objects across three scenes, and validate the fidelity of its synthesized demonstrations against ground truth in simulation. Our experiments show that MoMaSplat substantially improves robustness to unseen deployment-time base poses, outperforming prior augmentation approaches across 12 12 unseen base poses ( 3 3 rollouts per pose) per task as the robot moves farther away from the source demonstration locations.
Our contributions are threefold:
A novel-view demonstration augmentation framework for mobile manipulation that synthesizes complete trajectories, including dynamic object interactions.
A geometry-consistent generation pipeline that separately reconstructs scenes and manipulated objects and retargets actions to unseen base poses.
Substantial improvements in robustness to deployment-time viewpoint variation across multiple real-world mobile manipulation tasks.
Our method proposes a solution to train imitation learning visuomotor policies for mobile manipulators via data augmentation. Here, we review the most relevant related work in those areas.

Demonstration Synthesis in Simulation. A prominent line of work synthesizes new demonstrations by replaying source actions in randomized simulated scenes. The X-Gen family [ 7 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] procedurally generates data by transforming and sequencing object-centric trajectory segments, with extensions such as MoMaGen [ 15 ] addressing mobile-manipulation constraints like base reachability and visibility. However, because the generated plans are purely kinematic, they typically rely on open-loop on-robot rollouts to verify feasibility and capture visual observations, at a cost that rivals manual data collection [ 17 , 8 ] . A parallel line of work uses simulators to generate data from multiple viewpoints [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] , but requires modeling the full environment and task dynamics in simulation, suffering from the visual and physical sim-to-real gap. Our work avoids on-robot rollouts and full-scene simulation by reconstructing the real scene and manipulated object via novel-view synthesis, using simulation only to render the known robot embodiment.

Demonstration Augmentation from Real-World Captures. Beyond 2D image augmentation [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] , recent methods synthesize observations from real-world captures. Neural simulators [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] use generative video models but can suffer from hallucinations and geometric inconsistencies. Alternatively, novel-view synthesis (NVS) enables viewpoint augmentation [ 9 , 10 , 17 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] . VISTA [ 27 ] uses ZeroNVS [ 32 ] , while Yang et al. [ 9 ] employ 3D Gaussian Splatting [ 11 ] ; however, both focus on third-person tabletop settings requiring multi-camera pre-scans. Closer to our setting, One-Thousand Trajectories [ 8 ] supports moving eye-in-hand cameras, while EgoDemoGen [ 33 ] generates paired egocentric observations and actions using a generative model. However, these methods do not explicitly reconstruct dynamic objects and restrict augmentation to pre-contact motion. In contrast, MoMaSplat jointly models the static scene and manipulated objects, enabling kinematically consistent augmentation across both pre-contact and post-contact interaction phases for mobile robots with egocentric cameras.

Mobile Manipulation. Mobile manipulation remains a key challenge in robot learning [ 34 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] , particularly in selecting robot base poses. Traditional methods use geometric heuristics such as Inverse Reachability Maps [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] , while learning-based navigation [ 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] often overlooks downstream policy sensitivity to viewpoint changes. Mobi- π \pi [ 3 ] selects base poses matching the training distribution but requires pre-scanning and test-time optimization. In contrast, we train policies robust to diverse base poses, reducing the need for precise base placement at deployment.

We aim to augment a mobile-manipulation dataset with synthetic demonstrations from unseen robot base poses. From source demonstrations at a few robot locations, MoMaSplat synthesizes observations and actions for nearby deployment-time poses never physically demonstrated.

To achieve this, MoMaSplat decomposes the environment into three components: i) a static scene model, ii) a dynamic object model for the manipulated object, and iii) the robot embodiment itself. The scene and object models are reconstructed independently and aligned into a shared metric frame. A key observation is that the navigation trajectories naturally provide the bridge between both reconstructions: during navigation, the manipulated objects remain static, allowing the object-centric and scene-centric trajectories to be consistently registered.

For augmentation, given a sampled robot base pose, MoMaSplat renders the scene, manipulated object, and robot from the corresponding viewpoint and retargets the demonstrated actions through kinematic transformations. The resulting observations and transformed actions form synthetic demonstrations that augment the dataset for policy training. Fig. 2 provides an overview of the full process.

Fig. 2 : Overview of MoMaSplat . 3D Reconstruction: We build 3D models of the environment from the navigation and manipulation data. We estimate camera poses via structure-from-motion and fit a 3D Gaussian Splatting model of the static scene, 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} . For the dynamic objects, we segment each manipulated object and estimate its per-frame pose trajectory with a feed-forward 3D foundation model; since the scene and object poses lie in separate reference frames, we align them with a Sim(3) transformation and fit a separate object model 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} . Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses: Given a robot base pose, T ~ \tilde{T} , sampled around the original demonstration poses (left), we render the scene and object from the new viewpoint, transform the source end-effector trajectory into the new base frame to render the robot from a simulator, and composite the three streams into a photorealistic novel observation. Paired with the transformed actions a ~ 1 : L j \tilde{a}_{1:L_{j}} , this forms a synthetic demonstration; repeating across sampled poses yields the generated dataset. Imitation Learning: the policy is trained on the union of source and generated demonstrations.

Problem Formulation. We consider an imitation learning setting on a mobile manipulator operating in a scene. The robot alternates between two modes of operation: navigation, which changes the robot base pose, and manipulation, which executes arm actions from a fixed base location. We represent the robot base pose as a transform T w b ∈ S ​ E ​ ( 2 ) {}^{b}_{w}T\in SE(2) with respect to a stationary world frame w w , parameterized by a planar position ( x b , y b ) (x_{b},y_{b}) and heading θ b \theta_{b} . The robot observes the scene through an egocentric RGB camera mounted on the robot body (e.g., head or torso). The camera pose relative to the robot base is determined by the robot configuration through forward kinematics, such that both changes in base pose and articulation of the robot body induce changes in viewpoint.
During data collection, the robot navigates to a predefined set of N N target base poses:

from which manipulation demonstrations are collected. The robot executes N nav N_{\text{nav}} navigation trajectories from different starting locations toward the target base poses, either teleoperated or autonomously, and performs M M manipulation demonstrations from each fixed base pose without further base motion.

This process produces two complementary datasets. First, we collect a navigation dataset 𝒟 nav = { d nav 1 , … , d nav N nav } \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}}=\{d^{1}_{\text{nav}},\dots,d^{N_{\text{nav}}}_{\text{nav}}\} , where N nav N_{\text{nav}} denotes the number of navigation trajectories and each trajectory d nav k = ( ( I 1 , q 1 ) , … , ( I L k , q L k ) ) d^{k}_{\text{nav}}=\big((I_{1},q_{1}),\dots,(I_{L_{k}},q_{L_{k}})\big) contains RGB observations and robot states recorded while navigating toward one of the target base poses. These trajectories provide diverse multi-view observations of the environment and manipulated objects before interaction. Second, we collect a source manipulation dataset 𝒟 src = { d src 1 , … , d src N src } \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}}=\{d^{1}_{\text{src}},\dots,d^{N_{\text{src}}}_{\text{src}}\} of N src = N × M N_{\text{src}}=N\times M demonstrations, where each trajectory d src j = ( ( I 1 , q 1 , a 1 ) , … , ( I L j , q L j , a L j ) ) d^{j}_{\text{src}}=\big((I_{1},q_{1},a_{1}),\dots,(I_{L_{j}},q_{L_{j}},a_{L_{j}})\big) contains manipulation observations and actions recorded during task execution from one of the N N base locations. We represent actions as 7-D commands a t = ( p t , o t , g t ) a_{t}=(p_{t},o_{t},g_{t}) , consisting of desired end-effector translation and rotation deltas p t ∈ ℝ 3 p_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} and o t ∈ S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) o_{t}\in SO(3) applied in the robot base frame, together with the gripper command g t ∈ ℝ g_{t}\in\mathbb{R} .

Our goal is to augment the source manipulation dataset 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} with a synthetic dataset 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} of demonstrations generated at unseen base poses to obtain a base-pose robust policy trained on 𝒟 = 𝒟 src ∪ 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{src}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} . To achieve this, MoMaSplat first reconstructs the scene and manipulated objects in 3D and aligns them into a shared metric frame (Sec. III-A ). It then synthesizes demonstrations from sampled base poses by rendering the scene, object, and robot from the corresponding viewpoint and retargeting the actions and proprioception to remain geometrically consistent (Sec. III-B ). The synthesized demonstrations are combined with the source dataset for policy training (Sec. III-C ).

To synthesize demonstrations from unseen robot base poses, MoMaSplat requires a 3D representation that can be rendered from arbitrary viewpoints. A central challenge is that manipulation involves dynamic objects whose pose changes throughout the demonstration. Unlike prior novel-view synthesis approaches that model the environment as a single static scene, MoMaSplat reconstructs the static scene and manipulated objects separately, leveraging observations naturally produced during mobile-manipulation data collection. Navigation trajectories cover the environment while the objects are static, and manipulation trajectories capture the objects in motion.

3D Scene Model Reconstruction. As the robot moves through the workspace, its camera naturally captures diverse viewpoints, providing the multi-view coverage needed for 3D reconstruction without external cameras or scanning. We therefore use 𝒟 nav \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} to build a photorealistic 3D scene model: we recover per-image camera poses with structure-from-motion via COLMAP [ 46 ] , which also produces a sparse point cloud that initializes a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 11 ] reconstruction.

We optimize the Gaussians by minimizing a photometric loss between rendered and observed images. Since the scene is not perfectly static across navigation trajectories, transient content may appear between demonstrations; we adopt the uncertainty-aware formulation of WildGaussians [ 47 ] , which down-weights inconsistent regions during optimization to yield a robust model 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} . We additionally mask out pixels belonging to the manipulated object and the robot during scene reconstruction, preventing the object from being baked into 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} and avoiding a static “ghost” when the independently reconstructed dynamic object is later composited into the scene.

Structure-from-motion reconstructs the scene only up to an unknown global scale, while our framework transforms metric actions and therefore requires a metric reconstruction. We recover the scale using the robot’s onboard depth sensor: for the frames in 𝒟 nav \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} , we compare the measured depth maps to depth maps rendered from 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} and take the median per-pixel ratio of measured to rendered depth as the scale factor.

3D Object Model Reconstruction. Since the object of interest moves independently from the scene, we build a separate 3DGS model for it. Conceptually, the steps mirror those for the scene: we estimate the object’s pose in each frame and use these poses to optimize a 3D Gaussian reconstruction. However, the challenges here are different. Correspondence-based methods [ 46 ] are poorly suited to small, weakly-textured objects, while instance-level pose trackers [ 48 ] require an existing 3D model of the object, which is not available to us. Instead, we find that our setting is amenable to recent feed-forward 3D foundation models, like VGGT [ 49 , 12 ] , which estimate camera poses directly from an unposed RGB sequence.

Specifically, for each trajectory d nav k ∈ 𝒟 nav d^{k}_{\text{nav}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} and source demonstration d src j ∈ 𝒟 src d^{j}_{\text{src}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} , we extract the RGB frames { I t k } t = 1 L k \{I_{t}^{k}\}_{t=1}^{L_{k}} and { I t j } t = 1 L j \{I_{t}^{j}\}_{t=1}^{L_{j}} , respectively, and obtain per-frame segmentation masks ℳ t k \mathcal{M}_{t}^{k} and ℳ t j \mathcal{M}_{t}^{j} for the object using an open-world segmentation pipeline [ 50 , 51 ] , which masks out the background and the robot.

Then, we apply FastVGGT [ 49 ] to the object-masked frames { I t k ⊙ ℳ t k } \{I_{t}^{k}\odot\mathcal{M}_{t}^{k}\} and { I t j ⊙ ℳ t j } \{I_{t}^{j}\odot\mathcal{M}_{t}^{j}\} , respectively. With everything else masked out, the model predicts a camera pose at each frame that is expressed relative to the object itself. These object-relative camera poses T ^ o , t ∈ S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) \hat{T}_{o,t}\in SE(3) act as the initial pose estimates in the model’s internal coordinate frame v v .

Frame Alignment. The estimates T ^ o , t \hat{T}_{o,t} lie in v v , with arbitrary scale, orientation, and origin relative to the metric world frame w w established by the Scene Reconstruction. To align the two frames, we use a set of frames from the navigation demonstrations 𝒟 nav \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} as a bridge. During navigation the object remains static, so the only motion comes from the robot itself, i.e., the pose trajectory recovered by the object model is purely due to camera motion. This is not true for the manipulation frames: the object moves, so the recovered trajectory conflates camera and object motion. On the selected navigation frames, the same cameras are posed twice, by the feed-forward model in v v and by structure-from-motion in w w . The two trajectories must describe the same motion up to an unknown Sim(3) transformation. We recover this transformation 𝐒 : v → w \mathbf{S}:v\to w in closed form via the Umeyama algorithm [ 52 ] . Applying 𝐒 \mathbf{S} to the estimated poses yields the aligned pose trajectory in the world frame, T o , t = 𝐒 ⋅ T ^ o , t T_{o,t}=\mathbf{S}\cdot\hat{T}_{o,t} .

Object 3DGS Optimization. Finally, we jointly optimize these aligned poses T o , t T_{o,t} alongside the Gaussian parameters of 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} , backpropagating the photometric loss through both. This yields a pose-disentangled representation 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} that can be rendered at arbitrary 6-DoF poses for compositing into novel-pose observations. For articulated objects, we model the moving rigid link separately from the static remainder of the object. For example, a laptop lid or the basket of an air fryer is represented by 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} , while the keyboard base or the air fryer’s surrounding body remains part of the static scene. The component represented by 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} therefore undergoes a rigid 6-DoF motion over the demonstrated trajectory, and we do not estimate articulation parameters or extrapolate beyond the demonstrated motion.

passages.section: III-B Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses
passages.location: III-B Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses
passages.text: Given the scene and object models, our framework synthesizes new demonstrations at unseen base poses in three stages. For each original robot base pose, T i w b {}^{\mathit{b}}_{\mathit{w}}{T}_{i} , we first sample a set of target base poses that cover possible deployment-time locations while remaining kinematically feasible (e.g., reachable for the arm). We then synthesize each source demonstration from each sampled pose by composing three separately rendered streams: the static scene (from the 3D scene model), the manipulated objects (from the 3D object model), and the robot body as seen from the new base location. Finally, we retarget the source action to be defined with respect to the virtual sampled base location to obtain a new pair of virtual image and action label.

passages.section: III-B Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses
passages.location: III-B Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses
passages.text: Sampling Base Poses. To generate synthetic demonstrations, we sample a set of target base poses 𝒯 i sampled = { T ~ 1 , … , T ~ K } \mathcal{T}^{\text{sampled}}_{i}=\{\tilde{T}_{1},\ldots,\tilde{T}_{K}\} (here, we omit the superindex b b and subindex w w from T ~ w b {}^{\mathit{b}}_{\mathit{w}}\tilde{T} for simplicity) that the policy should learn to handle around each of the original base locations, T i {T}_{i} . We sample the planar position ( x ~ j , y ~ j ) (\tilde{x}_{j},\tilde{y}_{j}) uniformly within a region surrounding the original base pose, chosen to cover the range of deployment-time poses the robot may reach. For each sampled position, we set the base heading θ ~ j \tilde{\theta}_{j} so that the object of interest is centered in the egocentric camera’s field of view, then perturb it with uniform noise to expose the policy to a range of object-in-frame configurations. We then apply the transformation Δ j i ​ T = ( T ~ j ) − 1 ⋅ T i \Delta^{i}_{j}T=(\tilde{T}_{j})^{-1}\cdot{T}_{i} that transforms the original base frame, T i {T}_{i} , to the sampled base frame, T ~ j \tilde{T}_{j} (where we lift Δ j i ​ T \Delta^{i}_{j}T from S ​ E ​ ( 2 ) SE(2) into S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) with zero vertical translation and zero roll/pitch when transforming 3D poses and vectors). We retain a sampled base pose, T ~ j \tilde{T}_{j} , only if the source arm trajectory, where the end-effector remains at the same pose with respect to the manipulated object, admits a valid inverse-kinematics solution at several probe timesteps spanning the demonstration; infeasible poses are rejected and resampled. To obtain the end-effector pose in the sampled base frame, we apply Δ j i ​ T \Delta_{j}^{i}T to the source end-effector pose T i b e ​ e {}^{ee}_{b}T_{i} , obtained from q q through forward kinematics. The resulting pose, T ~ j b e ​ e = Δ j i ​ T ⋅ T i b e ​ e {}^{ee}_{b}\tilde{T}_{j}=\Delta_{j}^{i}T\cdot{}^{ee}_{b}T_{i} , preserves the end-effector pose in the world frame.

passages.location: III-B Synthesizing Demonstrations from Unseen Base Poses
passages.text: Novel View Synthesis. We virtually place the egocentric camera at its mounted offset relative to T ~ j \tilde{T}_{j} using forward kinematics and the robot’s recorded configuration, q q , and matching the physical camera’s intrinsics. We then render three elements from the new view: i) the scene, ii) the manipulated object, and iii) the robot. From the scene model, 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} , we obtain a virtual RGB image I ~ scene \tilde{I}_{\text{scene}} , the depth map D ~ scene \tilde{D}_{\text{scene}} and the accumulated opacity α ~ scene \tilde{\alpha}_{\text{scene}} . For the manipulated object, we transform 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} to its source-demonstration pose T o , t T_{o,t} and rasterize it from the same camera, yielding per-timestep renders I ~ obj \tilde{I}_{\text{obj}} , depth maps D ~ obj \tilde{D}_{\text{obj}} and opacity image α ~ obj \tilde{\alpha}_{\text{obj}} . For the robot, we use inverse kinematics on the end-effector pose for the sampled base location, T ~ j b e ​ e {}^{ee}_{b}\tilde{T}_{j} , to recover a joint configuration, q ~ t j \tilde{q}^{j}_{t} , that would place the end-effector at the same location with respect to the object. Then, we apply the joint configuration to the robot and render it using OmniGibson [ 53 ] to obtain a robot-only RGB image I ~ robot \tilde{I}_{\text{robot}} , depth map D ~ robot \tilde{D}_{\text{robot}} and opacity mask α ~ robot \tilde{\alpha}_{\text{robot}} .

passages.text: To get a single RGB observation from the three virtual images, we need to combine them together, while respecting the depths and the opacities at each pixel. To achieve this, we use per-pixel alpha compositing. Specifically, at each pixel, we sort the three layers by depth, letting ( c i , α i ) (c_{i},\alpha_{i}) denote the color and opacity of the i i -th layer, with i = 1 i=1 being the nearest. Then, we combine them in a front-to-back manner: c = ∑ i = 1 3 c i ​ α i ​ ∏ j = 1 i − 1 ( 1 − α j ) c=\sum_{i=1}^{3}c_{i}\alpha_{i}\prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha_{j}) , so that nearer surfaces occlude farther ones. This generates virtual RGB images as would be seen from a physical camera at sampled location T ~ j \tilde{T}_{j} .

passages.text: Robot Action and Proprioception Retargeting. A change in base pose moves the coordinate frame in which both the robot’s end-effector proprioception and actions are expressed, so both must be retargeted to the sampled base frame T ~ j w b {}^{\mathit{b}}_{\mathit{w}}\tilde{T}_{j} . Because the policy conditions on end-effector proprioception in the robot base frame (consisting of the end-effector pose T i b e ​ e {}^{ee}_{b}T_{i} and gripper state), we transform the end-effector pose into the sampled base frame via T ~ j b e ​ e = Δ j i ​ T ⋅ T i b e ​ e {}^{ee}_{b}\tilde{T}_{j}=\Delta^{i}_{j}T\cdot{}^{ee}_{b}T_{i} (as above) while keeping the gripper state unchanged. Robot actions a t = ( p t , o t , g t ) a_{t}=(p_{t},o_{t},g_{t}) consist of desired end-effector translation deltas p t ∈ ℝ 3 p_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3} , rotation deltas o t ∈ S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) o_{t}\in SO(3) , and gripper commands g t ∈ ℝ g_{t}\in\mathbb{R} , where both translation and rotation deltas are defined and applied in the robot base frame (i.e., R t + 1 b e ​ e = R ⁡ ( o t ) ​ R t b e ​ e {}^{ee}_{b}R_{t+1}=R(o_{t})\,{}^{ee}_{b}R_{t} ). To retarget the desired end-effector translation delta, we apply the rotation component of Δ j i ​ T \Delta^{i}_{j}T so that p ~ t = R Δ j i ​ T ⋅ p t \tilde{p}_{t}=R_{\Delta^{i}_{j}T}\cdot p_{t} expresses the same world-frame displacement in the sampled base frame. Because rotation deltas are applied in the base frame, conjugating R ⁡ ( o t ) R(o_{t}) by R Δ j i ​ T R_{\Delta^{i}_{j}T} rotates its axis of rotation by R Δ j i ​ T R_{\Delta^{i}_{j}T} while preserving the rotation angle; in axis-angle format o t = ( u ^ t , ϕ t ) o_{t}=(\hat{u}_{t},\phi_{t}) , the retargeted rotation delta is therefore o ~ t = ( R Δ j i ​ T ⋅ u ^ t , ϕ t ) \tilde{o}_{t}=(R_{\Delta^{i}_{j}T}\cdot\hat{u}_{t},\phi_{t}) . The gripper command remains unchanged ( g ~ t = g t \tilde{g}_{t}=g_{t} ), yielding the retargeted action a ~ t = ( p ~ t , o ~ t , g t ) \tilde{a}_{t}=(\tilde{p}_{t},\tilde{o}_{t},g_{t}) . Pairing the virtual RGB images with the retargeted proprioception and actions a ~ t j \tilde{a}^{j}_{t} across the trajectory provides a synthetic demonstration at T ~ j w b {}^{\mathit{b}}_{\mathit{w}}\tilde{T}_{j} .

passages.text: Constructing the Augmented Dataset. For each of the N src = N × M N_{\text{src}}=N\times M source manipulation demonstrations in 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} , we generate K K synthetic demonstrations from K K sampled novel base poses, producing a synthetic dataset 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} of K ⋅ N src K\cdot N_{\text{src}} demonstrations that we combine with 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} to form 𝒟 = 𝒟 src ∪ 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}=\mathcal{D}_{\text{src}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} for policy training (Sec. III-C ).

We train a visuomotor policy on the union of source demonstrations 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} and synthetic demonstrations 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} using Diffusion Policy [ 1 ] , which models the conditional action distribution as a denoising diffusion process and is trained by minimizing the standard noise prediction loss:
ℒ = 𝔼 k , ϵ , ( o , a ) ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ ‖ ϵ − ϵ θ ​ ( o , a k , k ) ‖ 2 ] , \mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}_{k,\epsilon,(o,a)\sim\mathcal{D}}\left[\|\epsilon-\epsilon_{\theta}(o,a^{k},k)\|^{2}\right], (1)

where a k a^{k} is the ground-truth action sequence noised at denoising step k k with Gaussian noise ϵ \epsilon . The policy conditions on the RGB observation and end-effector proprioception, and outputs an action sequence of end-effector pose deltas. To balance the two datasets during training, we co-train with a sampling ratio of 0.25 0.25 for 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} and 0.75 0.75 for 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} , anchoring the policy to the source data while leveraging the broader pose coverage of the synthetic data.

We evaluate MoMaSplat on five real-world mobile manipulation tasks across three scenes, comparing against four baselines: no augmentation and three augmentation methods. Our experiments focus on a) whether MoMaSplat improves policy success at unseen base poses, b) how performance varies with the distance between the deployment-time base pose and the closest demonstration pose, and c) how policy success changes with the number of source demonstrations available for augmentation. Additionally, we evaluate the quality of the generated data itself. This requires ground truth observations at poses where no demonstration was collected, which is impractical in the real world. A human teleoperator produces a different motion on every attempt, so even a re-collected trajectory cannot serve as ground-truth for the generated demonstration. Therefore, we develop one task in simulation , where camera and object poses are known and source trajectories can be replayed from arbitrary base poses.

((b)) Tasks: placing a bottle, opening a drawer, closing a laptop, picking up a remote, and opening an air fryer in the real world; placing a bottle in simulation.

Fig. 3 : Tasks and scenes used in our experiments. We evaluate MoMaSplat on five real-world manipulation tasks across three scenes (top: scenes; bottom: per-task close-ups), covering manipulation of both rigid and articulated objects. The simulated scene and its task, Sim Pick-Place Bottle (right of the dashed lines), are used to measure the fidelity of MoMaSplat ’s generated demonstrations against ground truth.

Fig. 4 : Policy success across base poses. For each task, we evaluate 12 unseen base locations distributed across categorical distance bins that vary per task, with 3 trials per pose, and report success rate by distance to the nearest demonstration pose. The shaded gray region denotes the original base poses; locations 5–50 cm away are unseen deployment poses. MoMaSplat maintains substantially higher success as the base pose shifts away from the source demonstrations (where Source Only is labeled “Original data only”).

Fig. 5 : Spatial distribution of policy evaluation poses. Original demonstration poses are marked with circles, while evaluation poses are marked with squares; arrows indicate the robot heading at each pose. Evaluation poses are colored by MoMaSplat policy success rate, providing spatial context for the distance-based results in Fig. 4 .

Tasks. The robot performs (i) Pick-Place Bottle and (ii) Open Drawer in the desk scene; (iii) Pick-Place Remote and (iv) Close Laptop in the living room ; and (v) Open Air-fryer in the kitchen (Fig. 3 ). We additionally build (vi) Sim Pick-Place Bottle in OmniGibson [ 53 ] , a simulated scene modeled after the desk environment that follows the same task structure as (i) without replicating its exact geometry. The tasks span rigid pick-place and single-DoF articulated manipulation. We collect 75 75 manipulation demonstrations for Close Laptop and 90 90 for each other task across three base poses, forming 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} . We additionally collect nine navigation trajectories 𝒟 nav \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} from different starting poses to the target base poses.
Evaluation Protocol. For each task, we deploy the trained policy at 12 12 unseen base poses across the scene, with heading centered on the object, and perform 3 3 rollouts per pose.

Baselines. We compare against four baselines. Source Only (labeled “Original data only” in Fig. 4 ) trains Diffusion Policy [ 1 ] without augmentation. Action Augmentation [ 54 ] adds noise to proprioceptive states and actions while preserving observations. VISTA [ 27 ] generates novel-view images without transforming actions. One-Thousand Trajectories [ 8 ] reconstructs the static scene using 3DGS; we additionally provide our action transformation to account for changes in the robot base frame. All methods train on the same source demonstrations. For Pick-Place Bottle , we restrict synthetic generation for One-Thousand Trajectories to demonstrations whose initial object pose matches the reconstructed scene, since its static reconstruction cannot represent variation in this pose.

Data Augmentation Setup. Each method generates 10 synthetic demonstrations per source demonstration, yielding 750–900 synthetic demonstrations per task except One-Thousand Trajectories on Pick-Place Bottle , which generates 400. For MoMaSplat and One-Thousand Trajectories , we sample base poses within a 1.2 × 1.2 1.2\times 1.2 m region around each source pose (Sec. III-B ). Frame alignment uses 50 frames from one navigation demonstration.

Performance at Unseen Base Poses. Our main experimental results for policy success using MoMaSplat are summarized in Fig. 4 , where success rates are binned by their minimum distance to the nearest demonstration pose. We additionally evaluate the 3 original demonstration base poses with 15 rollouts per pose. At the original base poses, all methods perform comparably. The picture changes sharply at unseen poses. When we average the results over all five tasks, MoMaSplat succeeds on 37% of unseen evaluations, more than twice the rate of the strongest baseline ( One-Thousand Trajectories at 17%) and four to six times that of the remaining baselines ( Source Only 6%, VISTA 8%, Action Augmentation 6%). Critically, Source Only and Action Augmentation collapse to near-zero success beyond 10 cm on most tasks, confirming that perturbing actions without changing the observation gives little robustness to base-pose shifts. VISTA performs poorly throughout; since it is designed for static-base settings, it does not transform actions to match the synthesized viewpoints. Moreover, its lack of temporal consistency produces jittery camera trajectories that further degrade the augmented data. One-Thousand Trajectories degrades more gracefully but still falls off at large distances, since it augments only the free-space approach motion. MoMaSplat achieves the highest overall unseen-pose success rate on every task, outperforming or matching all baselines across every unseen distance bin while sustaining substantial performance at the largest evaluated distances. For example, MoMaSplat achieves 33% on Pick-Place Bottle at 30 cm and 50% on Close Laptop at 40 cm, where every baseline has dropped to zero success rates. Finally, to better contextualize the geometry of our tasks and scenes, Fig. 5 shows the spatial layout of these evaluation locations across each workspace.

Effect of Number of Source Demonstrations. To evaluate how the number of source demonstrations affects MoMaSplat , we use the Pick-Place Bottle task and train policies using 10, 50, and 90 source demonstrations. For each source demonstration, we generate 10 synthetic demonstrations. Across four test locations at a distance of 10 10 – 20 20 cm from the demonstration poses, we observe that success degrades gracefully with fewer source demonstrations. Specifically, we achieve success rates of 33 % 33\% , 42 % 42\% , and 50 % 50\% for 10, 50, and 90 source demonstrations, respectively. For reference, training on the full set of 90 source demonstrations without augmentation yields only an 8 % 8\% success rate at the same test poses. These results show that MoMaSplat substantially improves base-pose robustness even with a limited number of source demonstrations.

Generation Quality. We first evaluate generation quality in simulation, where the ground-truth counterpart of a generated demonstration is obtained by executing its transformed actions in the simulator and rendering the on-board camera at every timestep. We use the Sim Pick-Place Bottle task and evaluate 75 75 generated demonstrations, taking every tenth frame for a total of 2,486 2{,}486 frames. Unlike the policy evaluations above, which measure distance between base poses, here we measure how far each generated view is from the views that were used to build the reconstruction. For the 75 75 demonstrations, we find this distance to be between 0.4 0.4 and 27.3 27.3 cm. Since the static reconstruction does not change over a demonstration, we score the scene separately by rendering the scene splat and the empty simulated scene from the same camera pose once per demonstration, rather than considering every frame. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS over the full image, the scene, and over the robot and object regions using the simulator’s segmentation masks. Table I reports the detailed results. The reconstructed scene achieves the highest fidelity at 26.40 26.40 dB, followed by the manipulated object at 18.18 18.18 dB and the robot at 17.43 17.43 dB. For reference, the original 3DGS work [ 11 ] reports roughly 23 23 dB PSNR on Tanks & Temples [ 55 ] . This places our scene reconstruction in the range of standard novel-view synthesis, while the lower object PSNR reflects the harder setting of reconstructing a moving object with limited viewpoint coverage. The robot error is mainly caused by lighting and shadow differences introduced during compositing. We also evaluate object-pose accuracy to measure how well our estimated object trajectory matches the true object motion of the observations. On 30 30 source demonstrations, including poses directly registered by VGGT and interpolated poses, the predicted object pose has a mean translation error of 1.46 ± 0.71 1.46\pm 0.71 cm and rotation error of 4.01 ∘ ± 4.66 ∘ 4.01^{\circ}\pm 4.66^{\circ} relative to the simulator ground truth.

On real data, we evaluate scene reconstruction by masking out the robot and the manipulated object, and we obtain 24.00 24.00 dB PSNR on 110 110 held-out frames. For the manipulated object, we use its bounding-box crop and we mask out the background. At poses directly registered by VGGT, we obtain 23.63 23.63 dB, while at interpolated poses we obtain 22.59 22.59 dB. We do not report full-image view-synthesis metrics on real data because the simulated robot differs in appearance from the real robot and this appearance mismatch dominates the pixel-wise error that the view synthesis metrics evaluate.

Overall, the simulation results show that MoMaSplat produces observations that closely match the ground truth, while the real-world results show high-fidelity scene reconstruction and consistent object reconstruction across both directly estimated and interpolated poses.

Conclusion. We propose MoMaSplat , a framework for novel-view augmentation of mobile manipulation demonstrations that reconstructs the static scene and manipulated object in 3D, then re-renders full demonstrations, including the post-contact interaction phase, from unseen base poses. Unlike prior NVS augmentation methods that model only the static scene, MoMaSplat produces geometrically consistent observations across the entire trajectory. Across five real-world tasks in three scenes, this improves policy robustness, outperforming prior augmentation methods and maintaining performance beyond the distances where baselines fail. We will publicly release our code to support further research.

Limitations. MoMaSplat assumes mostly static scenes and rigid, visible objects, making deformable objects, heavy occlusions, and texture-poor surfaces challenging. Furthermore, because 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} is reconstructed from pre-interaction navigation views with object masks excluded, regions occluded by the object in its initial state (such as the surface beneath a lifted bottle or the interior of an opened drawer or air-fryer basket) are never observed during scene reconstruction and remain unmodeled when disoccluded. It also depends on consistent open-world segmentation and produces non-physical demonstrations by replaying source object trajectories without modeling contact forces or dynamics. Finally, view quality depends on navigation-data coverage. Addressing dynamic backgrounds, deformable objects, physical contact, and cluttered scenes remains future work.
