In this section, we provide more details about the baselines we are using in our evaluation.

Source Only. This baseline trains the same Diffusion Policy [ 1 ] as we do, but using only the source demonstrations 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} , without any augmentation. This allows us to quantify how well a policy trained only on the original base poses generalizes to unseen poses.

Action Augmentation. Following [ 54 ] , we augment each demonstration by perturbing the proprioceptive state and the action labels with zero-mean Gaussian noise while leaving the image observations unchanged. This exposes the policy to small action variations, but because the images remain the same, this augmentation provides no information about how the scene looks from a different base pose. We use this data to train the same Diffusion Policy and use the same training schedule as we do with all other baselines.

VISTA. VISTA [ 27 ] augments a demonstration by re-rendering its observations from perturbed camera viewpoints with ZeroNVS [ 32 ] , a zero-shot single-image novel-view-synthesis diffusion model, while leaving the actions unchanged. We run the publicly released ZeroNVS model and checkpoint. 1 1 1 https://github.com/s-tian/ZeroNVS For each source demonstration, we sample a small set of viewpoint perturbations: a planar camera offset ( d ​ x , d ​ y ) (dx,dy) drawn uniformly within ± 10 \pm 10 cm on each axis (the first sample is the unperturbed view), together with a single per-demonstration yaw that re-aims the camera at the object centroid, clipped to ± 0.5 \pm 0.5 rad; beyond this perturbation range, we observe large artifacts in image generation and worse imitation learning results. We then process each frame independently: conditioning on the original egocentric RGB image (center-cropped and resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 ) and the relative perturbation, ZeroNVS synthesizes the frame from the novel viewpoint. We sample with DDIM ( 50 50 steps, η = 0 \eta=0 ), a classifier-free guidance scale of 7.5 7.5 , and a 70 ∘ 70^{\circ} field of view matching our camera. Because ZeroNVS is a single-image model applied frame by frame, the synthesized views are not temporally consistent across a trajectory. The generated frames are paired with the original, unmodified actions and are used to train the same Diffusion Policy as all other methods.

One-Thousand Trajectories. One-Thousand Trajectories [ 8 ] reconstructs the static scene as a 3D Gaussian Splatting model and re-renders observations from novel viewpoints. In our implementation, we reconstruct the static scene using the same pipeline and navigation data 𝒟 nav \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} as 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} in MoMaSplat, but without masking out the manipulated object, so that the static scene model contains the manipulated object at its initial pose.

We use its novel-view augmentation component without the additional trajectory augmentation proposed in [ 8 ] . To account for changes in the robot base frame, we apply the same delta-based action retargeting used by MoMaSplat (Sec. III-B ). This baseline relies on a static scene reconstruction rather than explicitly reconstructing the dynamic manipulated object. For Pick-Place Bottle , we restrict synthetic generation to the 40 demonstrations whose initial object pose matches the reconstructed scene, producing 400 synthetic demonstrations. All 90 source demonstrations remain in the policy-training set. For the other tasks, the initial object pose is fixed, so all source demonstrations are used for synthetic generation.

Structure from motion and Gaussian Splatting. We reconstruct the static scene from the navigation frames 𝒟 nav \mathcal{D}_{\text{nav}} . We run structure-from-motion using COLMAP [ 46 ] with a sequential matcher over the navigation frames, together with a small set of context frames sampled just before each manipulation. This step returns per-image camera poses and a sparse point cloud. The sparse points are used to initialize a 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstruction that we train with WildGaussians [ 47 ] 2 2 2 https://github.com/jkulhanek/wild-gaussians . We use the nerfbaselines framework and train for 30,000 30{,}000 iterations. WildGaussians augments 3DGS with per-image appearance and exposure embeddings and a DINOv2-based uncertainty head that down-weights transient or inconsistent regions, such as the robot or moving objects, during optimization. We use a DSSIM weight of 0.2 0.2 in the photometric loss and hold out every eighth frame for evaluation.

Metric scaling. Structure-from-motion recovers the scene only up to an unknown global scale. However, our action retargeting is metric, so we rescale the reconstruction using the robot’s onboard depth sensor measurements. For each navigation frame we render a depth map from the scene model and compare it to the measured depth from the head-mounted RGB-D camera (stored in millimeters and converted to meters). We consider only pixels with valid measured depth (in ( 0 , 9 ] (0,9] m, at least 1000 1000 per frame) and for each frame, we take the median of the per-pixel ratios of measured to rendered depth. Eventually, the scale factor is set as the median of these per-frame median values, making it robust to outliers. This factor allows us to convert rendered depth and Gaussian coordinates into meters.

Scene pose interpolation. For the navigation frames that have not been registered by COLMAP, we estimate their scene camera poses using the same strategy as we do with objects (see Sec. -B-2 ). This includes SLERP-based interpolation, smoothness filtering, and cyclic-outlier rejection, applied per demonstration.

Segmentation. To obtain the per-frame object masks ℳ t j \mathcal{M}_{t}^{j} , we use Grounded-SAM [ 50 ] , prompting an open-world detector, GroundingDINO [ 56 ] , with a per-object text label to localize the manipulated object, and propagating the detected box through the clip using SAM 2 [ 51 ] 3 3 3 Grounded-SAM 2: https://github.com/IDEA-Research/Grounded-SAM-2 . We use a forward and a reverse pass from a per-object seed frame. When multiple objects are tracked, pixels claimed by more than one object are removed from all of them (exclusive masks). Object reconstruction uses the per-object masks to exclude the background and robot. For scene reconstruction, we additionally obtain a robot mask by rendering the robot in the simulator at the recorded configuration and camera pose. We exclude the union of the object masks and this robot mask when training 𝒢 scene \mathcal{G}_{\text{scene}} .

Frame Selection Strategy. A source manipulation demonstration d src j ∈ 𝒟 src d^{j}_{\text{src}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} contains several hundred RGB frames recorded at video rate, far more than the feed-forward model can process. Simultaneously, near-duplicate frames add little to the pose estimate while inflating compute. We therefore subsample each demonstration to a compact, motion-diverse set of roughly 10 10 – 20 20 frames before passing it to the model, using the per-frame object masks ℳ t j \mathcal{M}_{t}^{j} .

We first discard frames whose object mask is small or poorly segmented, removing views where the object is distant or occluded. From the remaining frames we drop near-duplicate, stationary views: scanning in temporal order, we keep a frame only when its mask bounding-box IoU with the previously kept frame falls below 0.8 0.8 (the same threshold for all tasks), or when more than 20 20 frames have elapsed since the last kept frame. The first and last frame of every demonstration are always retained to anchor the reconstruction to the endpoints of the clip. Additionally, 50 50 frames from one navigation demonstration are included for frame alignment, and the combined set is capped at the feed-forward model’s 400 400 -frame input budget.

Bundle Adjustment. For our feed-forward model, we use VGGT [ 12 ] 4 4 4 https://github.com/facebookresearch/vggt , as implemented by the training-free FastVGGT [ 49 ] acceleration 5 5 5 https://github.com/mystorm16/FastVGGT . For each selected frame, it predicts an object-relative camera pose T ^ o , t \hat{T}_{o,t} together with a per-frame intrinsics matrix and a dense depth map. These predictions are accurate but not multi-view consistent, so we refine them with a bundle-adjustment step. We first unproject the predicted depth into a set of 3D points and predict dense 2D feature tracks across the selected frames. Initializing a reconstruction with the predicted poses, intrinsics, and points, we filter tracks by reprojection error, using an adaptive threshold that grows until a sufficient fraction of frames retain enough inliers, and by track visibility, requiring every 3D point to be observed in at least two frames. We then run bundle adjustment, jointly optimizing the camera poses and 3D points (and, when intrinsics are not supplied, the focal length and principal point) to minimize reprojection error. The refined, multi-view-consistent poses replace T ^ o , t \hat{T}_{o,t} as the input to the Sim ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{Sim}(3) alignment.

Frame Alignment. The poses estimated above lie in the object model’s internal frame v v with arbitrary scale, orientation, and origin, whereas the scene lives in the world frame w w . We align them using the navigation frames, where the object is static so its recovered trajectory is explained purely by the camera motion. Effectively, the same cameras are posed twice: by the object model in v v and by structure-from-motion in w w . Matching the navigation cameras by frame, we fit the similarity transform S : v → w S:v\rightarrow w from their camera centers with the Umeyama algorithm [ 52 ] , solving for scale, rotation, and translation in closed form. To be robust to mis-registered frames, we wrap Umeyama in RANSAC: we repeatedly fit S S from minimal 5 5 -camera subsets, reject hypotheses whose scale leaves a plausible range, score each by the number of camera centers whose residual is below 0.2 0.2 m, keep the highest-consensus hypothesis, and refit on its inliers followed by a Huber-robust nonlinear refinement restricted to those inliers. We report the alignment quality as the camera-center residual (mean and median) and the RMS of the aligned sparse-point residuals. Applying S S maps the object poses into the world frame, T o , t = S ⋅ T ^ o , t T_{o,t}=S\cdot\hat{T}_{o,t} .

Object Gaussian Optimization. Given the registered frames and their aligned poses T o , t T_{o,t} , we fit a 3D Gaussian Splatting model [ 11 ] 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} of the object with the gsplat [ 57 ] trainer 6 6 6 https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/gsplat for 60,000 60{,}000 steps, supervising only the segmented object through its RGBA images, where the alpha channel is the object mask composited over a white background. We minimize an L 1 L_{1} plus SSIM photometric loss (SSIM weight 0.2 0.2 ) together with an L 1 L_{1} term on the rendered opacity against the mask. The per-frame poses are optimized jointly with the Gaussian parameters at a small learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , so the photometric loss is backpropagated through both appearance and pose, yielding the pose-disentangled model 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} that can be rendered at arbitrary 6-DoF poses.

Pose Interpolation. Because of frame selection, the feed-forward model only returns camera poses at the selected keyframes. In contrast to that, synthesizing a demonstration requires an object pose T o , t T_{o,t} at every timestep of the source trajectory. We therefore densify the keyframe poses by interpolation: rotations are interpolated with spherical linear interpolation (SLERP) and translations are interpolated linearly, between consecutive keyframes. To suppress residual estimation noise we add three refinements before interpolating. (i) A smoothness filter drops keyframes whose translation and rotation relative to the previous keyframe both fall below small thresholds, removing jitter from near-stationary stretches. (ii) A cyclic-outlier filter removes backtracking A → B → A A\!\rightarrow\!B\!\rightarrow\!A keyframes, where an excursion to B B is large enough to be meaningful yet the trajectory returns close to A A , a signature of transient pose-estimation errors. (iii) An ease-in parameterization places interpolated samples so that pose changes are concentrated toward the end of each keyframe interval, better matching the observed motion profile than uniform piecewise-linear filling. The densified trajectory { T o , t } \{T_{o,t}\} is what we rasterize 𝒢 obj \mathcal{G}_{\text{obj}} along when compositing novel-view observations.

Here, we expand on the procedure used to draw the sampled base poses 𝒯 i sampled = { T ~ 1 , … , T ~ K } \mathcal{T}_{i}^{\text{sampled}}=\{\tilde{T}_{1},\dots,\tilde{T}_{K}\} around each original base pose T i T_{i} (Sec. III-B ). Sampling operates per source demonstration about an anchor pose recovered for that demonstration, i.e., the original base position and heading expressed in the world frame, as it is established by the scene reconstruction.

Planar position. We draw the planar offset ( x ~ j , y ~ j ) (\tilde{x}_{j},\tilde{y}_{j}) from a distribution centered at the anchor. By default this is uniform over a square region around the original base pose (the region size used in our experiments is reported in Sec. IV-A ); we also support an isotropic Gaussian with magnitude bounds for annulus-shaped coverage.

Heading. For each sampled position we set the base heading θ ~ j \tilde{\theta}_{j} so that the egocentric camera points at the object’s 3D centroid (accounting for the camera’s fixed offset from the base), then perturb it with uniform noise (default ± 20 ∘ \pm 20^{\circ} ) so the policy sees the object at a range of positions in the camera view. The robot head is fixed, so the object is kept in view through the base pose alone; we discard samples that would place the object near the image edge or out of view before running the costlier IK check.

IK feasibility. Following Sec. III-B , a sampled base pose is retained only if the source arm trajectory, with the end effector held at the same pose relative to the manipulated object, admits a valid inverse-kinematics solution. We verify reachability at several probe timesteps spanning the demonstration and accept the sample only if all of them are reachable, querying the curobo inverse-kinematics solver for the TIAGo robot inside the OmniGibson simulator [ 53 ] 7 7 7 OmniGibson: https://github.com/StanfordVL/OmniGibson ; cuRobo: https://github.com/NVlabs/curobo . Infeasible candidates are rejected and resampled, up to a fixed draw budget per demonstration, and the first K K accepted samples are kept.

We provide implementation details for the policy trained with Diffusion Policy [ 1 ] on the union of source and generated demonstrations (Sec. III-C ).

Architecture. The policy is a conditional 1D U-Net denoiser. The egocentric head-camera RGB image is encoded by a ResNet-18 trained from scratch followed by a spatial-softmax pooling layer ( 32 32 keypoints), and the resulting visual features are concatenated with the low-dimensional proprioception to form the conditioning vector.

Observations and actions. At each step the policy conditions on the egocentric head-camera RGB image (resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 ) and the end-effector proprioception, stacked over the most recent n obs = 2 n_{\text{obs}}=2 steps. It predicts a chunk of n act = 8 n_{\text{act}}=8 future actions, each a 7 7 -dimensional command consisting of an end-effector translation delta, a rotation delta, and a gripper command expressed in the robot base frame, normalized to zero mean and unit variance. During training we apply random crop and translation together with color-jitter augmentation to the RGB input.

Diffusion process. We use a DDIM noise scheduler with 50 50 training timesteps, a cosine-based β \beta schedule, and ϵ \epsilon (noise) prediction, optimizing the mean-squared denoising loss of Eq. (1). At inference, actions are produced by running the reverse process for the same number of denoising steps.

Optimization. We optimize with AdamW (learning rate 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , weight decay 10 − 4 10^{-4} ) under a cosine schedule with 1000 1000 warm-up steps and a batch size of 32 32 for 100,000 100{,}000 gradient steps.

Source and synthetic co-training. We train on the union of the source demonstrations 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} and the generated demonstrations 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} using a weighted sampler that draws each training sequence from 𝒟 src \mathcal{D}_{\text{src}} with probability 0.25 0.25 and from 𝒟 gen \mathcal{D}_{\text{gen}} with probability 0.75 0.75 . This anchors the policy to the source data while exploiting the broader base-pose coverage of the synthetic data.

Hardware and data. We use a TIAGo mobile manipulator with a head-mounted RGB-D camera ( 70 ∘ 70^{\circ} field of view). We collect 75 source demonstrations for Close Laptop and 90 for each other task across three base poses, and generate 10 10 synthetic demonstrations per source demonstration within a 120 × 120 120\times 120 cm region around each source base pose. We evaluate each policy at 12 12 unseen base poses with 3 3 rollouts per pose. Table II summarizes the main hyperparameters across the pipeline.

analysis.overview: 可复用的增量是把静态背景、运动刚体和机器人拆开渲染，并同步变换动作与本体感觉，让新底座视角覆盖接触后的物体运动。导航时物体静止，提供场景与物体重建的共同标尺；这不等于学习了新接触动力学。真机未见位姿平均37%对最强静态重建基线17%，但没有等数量、逐组件的动态物体消融，且底座在操作期间固定。

findings.title: 问题范围：改变起始底座位姿，不是在操作中连续移动
findings.text: 目标是让同一操作策略容忍导航后的底座偏差，并补足静态NVS只覆盖接触前轨迹的问题。机器人先导航、再在固定底座上操作；实验只涉及三场景的五种刚体或单自由度关节任务，不是边走边操作、跨房间任务迁移或未知物体策略。测试朝向对准目标，未验证任意导航朝向。

findings.title: 场景重建：导航RGB建外观，RGB-D给米制尺度
findings.text: 导航记录经COLMAP恢复相机与稀疏点，再用WildGaussians拟合背景；屏蔽物体和机器人，避免物体运动后留下静态重影。静态场景30k迭代，DSSIM权重0.2，隔8帧留出。SfM任意尺度用机载深度恢复：每帧有效深度与渲染深度取像素比值中位，再跨帧取中位。方法离线需要深度、相机与运动学信息，不能描述成任意现成RGB示范都可直接增广；部署策略本身只读RGB与EEF状态。

findings.title: 动态物体：分割、前馈姿态、静止导航对齐，再联合优化
findings.text: GroundingDINO加SAM2按物体文字和种子帧提取mask；每轨迹约10–20帧，加一条导航的50帧，总输入上限400。FastVGGT预测相对物体的相机姿态、深度和内参，先bundle adjustment；导航时物体静止，让场景SfM和物体模型得到的同一批相机可用Sim(3)配准。附录是5相机子集、8000次RANSAC、0.2m相机中心内点阈值，再Huber细化；0.2m是配准筛选阈值，不是最终物体精度。物体3DGS训练60k步并以1e-5学习率优化姿态；SLERP/平移插值、平滑与回环异常过滤补齐中间帧。关节物体只重建运动刚性link并重放示范路径，不识别或外推关节动力学。

findings.title: 合成标签必须一起变：绝对姿态做刚变换，动作增量只旋转
findings.text: 每条示范在原底座周围1.2×1.2m采样，朝目标加±20°噪声，剔除越出视野或若干探测时刻IK不可达的样本。用Δ=(T_new)^−1 T_source将EEF状态变到新基座；保持世界中的末端轨迹不变。平移增量乘R_Δ，不加平移；基座坐标系左作用的旋转增量做共轭，等价于转轴乘R_Δ、角度不变，夹爪指令不变。新视角下分别渲染背景、运动物体、IK后的模拟机器人，按深度/alpha合成；不是只换图像保留动作标签。多时刻IK可达不构成全轨迹碰撞或接触可行证明。

findings.title: 训练：真实/合成25:75采样，策略仍是普通Diffusion Policy
findings.text: 每条源示范生成10条新基座轨迹；真实序列以0.25、合成以0.75概率采样，不能把文件数量10:1当成实际采样比例。策略为从零训练ResNet18加32关键点spatial-softmax、1D U-Net；输入最近2步224×224 RGB与EEF状态，输出8步7维动作。训练100k梯度步、batch32、AdamW3e-4，DDIM训练与推理均50步；没有换成VLA底座来解释增益。

findings.title: 真机主结果：37%对17%，仍有多数未见位姿试验失败
findings.text: 每任务12个未见底座×每位姿3次，五任务每方法合计180次未见位姿试验。另评三个原始位姿各15次，37%不含这组。作者报告未见位姿平均MoMaSplat37%、静态One-Thousand Trajectories17%、Source Only6%、VISTA8%、动作增广6%；约+20个百分点、2.18倍，均为取整汇总，不能还原精确成功计数。图4瓶子30cm处33%、关笔记本40cm处50%，对应基线均0；距离是到最近原始示范底座位置，不含朝向差。平均37%仍远非可靠全覆盖，且没有跨训练seed方差或配对显著性。

findings.title: 基线边界：静态方法被适配，但瓶子增广量不相同
findings.text: One-Thousand Trajectories复用相同导航与静态重建，并额外使用本方法动作变换；只采用其NVS部分，未采用原工作额外轨迹增广。瓶子任务因初始物体位置限制，只能从40条源轨迹生成400条，而本方法由90条生成900条；双方策略训练仍含全部90真实示范。VISTA只在±10cm范围逐帧生成、动作不变且时序不一致，与本方法1.2m区域及标签重定向不匹配。主比较支持整套增广管线，但没有在相同姿态/数量/渲染设置下只开关动态物体，不能把37对17的全部差距都归因于接触后动态重建。

findings.title: 少示范证据：10条加合成33%，90条不增广8%
findings.text: 瓶子任务用10/50/90条真实源示范，各自每条合成10条，在离示范10–20cm的四个测试位置，成功率分别33/42/50%；90条真实但不增广为8%。这是单任务和四位置子实验，不能替代五任务12位姿主评测。源轨迹减少也同时减少合成数量，且未量化导航、重建与模型处理总成本，不能直接称完整研究流程的数据/计算效率提高了9倍。

findings.title: 生成质量：只在一个仿真任务有同步真值
findings.text: OmniGibson瓶子任务75条生成轨迹，每10帧取样共2486帧；表I按75条示范汇总均值±标准差。全图PSNR21.27±1.12dB、对象18.18±2.15、机器人17.43±1.30；场景26.40±2.18只每示范一次、共75张。30条源轨迹（含直接估计和插值）物体位姿相对仿真真值：平移误差1.46±0.71cm、旋转4.01±4.66°，不是基座或末端控制误差。渲染视角距离0.4–27.3cm指到重建输入视角，不能与主评测到示范底座的30/40cm直接对齐。帧并非2486个独立任务，单仿真场景也未证明真实接触动力学正确。

findings.title: 真实图像质量：背景24dB不能当作完整动态合成质量
findings.text: 真机场景在110张留出帧屏蔽机器人/物体后PSNR24.00dB；对象用去背景bbox crop，直接注册姿态23.63dB、插值22.59dB。没有报告真机完整图像NVS指标，原因是模拟机器人与实机外观不同会主导像素误差；也没有真实物体运动真值的同类误差评估。不能用背景分数代替接触时的机器人遮挡、对象边界和全图时序质量。

findings.title: 物理与可见性边界：重放物体运动，不模拟新的接触
findings.text: 背景主要静态，物体须刚性、可见且可可靠分割；导航视图中被初始物体遮住的桌面、抽屉/炸锅内部等区域从未被背景重建，物体移开后会缺失。合成重放源物体轨迹，不建接触力或动力学，不能保证新IK姿态下抓握/碰撞一致。形变、强遮挡、弱纹理和动态背景仍是困难；view变化质量依赖导航覆盖。改变的是已演示轨迹的观察与机器人配置，没有生成新交互策略。

findings.title: 复现资源缺口：模块步数明确，端到端工时未披露
findings.text: TIAGo单平台、头部RGB-D，关笔记本75条操作示范、其他任务各90条，均来自三底座；论文另报告9条导航轨迹。每任务750–900条合成，但生成能力依赖多视角覆盖、分割、已知相机/机器人几何、COLMAP、VGGT/BA、场景30k和物体60k优化及策略100k步。未充分披露GPU型号/总GPU时、导航/重建工时、IK拒绝率、全部平滑阈值和跨训练重复，因此“减少额外实机示范”不等于免费、任意数据可用或端到端算力更省。本轮未运行任何依赖或外部付费API。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：匹配位姿和数据量后，接触后动态渲染还有独立贡献吗？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：MoMaSplat的关键额外收益来自接触后正确的物体运动渲染，而不是只扩大新位姿/训练样本覆盖。先用初始物体位置固定的Close Laptop任务，保持75条源示范、同一750个合成底座和IK结果、相同背景/机器人图层、动作与本体重定向、25:75采样及100k训练步。两组为完整动态物体、将物体固定在初始姿态；两组均渲染完整轨迹，并分别报告各阶段样本数与算力。以至少3个训练seed，在相同未见底座和朝向分箱做匹配评测；记录接触前到达率、闭合阶段条件成功率、全任务成功率、碰撞/抓握失效及按底座聚类的区间，不能把重建PSNR当成功率。若动态组在匹配位姿数量后不提高闭合阶段条件成功率，或静态组获得相同提升，就反对动态交互覆盖是主要来源的解释；若差距只在少量位置出现则缩小适用范围。实验未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: MoMaSplat：分离运动物体，连同动作重定向增广接触后视角
frontier_brief.change_type: 数据增广 · 动态新视角
frontier_brief.delta: 将导航和操作记录拆成背景3DGS、运动刚体3DGS和模拟机器人三层，用静止导航帧对齐物体与场景坐标。在新底座渲染整条轨迹，同时重定向EEF状态与动作，让接触后运动也进入视角增广。
frontier_brief.before: 静态场景NVS把物体固定在初始姿态，主要增广接触前；只换图像或加动作噪声还可能让图像、动作与新基座坐标不一致。
frontier_brief.after: 从真实示范恢复物体运动，在每个源时刻分别渲染背景/物体/机器人、按深度合成；在1.2×1.2m区域采样可达基座，合成标签与本体感觉一起变换，按真实/合成25:75训练同一个Diffusion Policy。
frontier_brief.relevance: 移动机器人导航后落点与示范不同、已有导航RGB-D及运动学记录时，可考虑复用轨迹重建并补足接触后视角。先核对覆盖、米制配准和动作坐标变换，再用等数量静态/动态组确认重建是否值得投入。
frontier_brief.caveat: 五任务未见位姿平均仍只有37%；每位姿仅3次。瓶子静态基线400条合成对本方法900条，缺少单独动态物体消融；物体运动是示范重放、无新接触动力学，操作时底座固定。作者结果未复现。
frontier_brief.question: 合成位姿与数量匹配后，接触后动态物体渲染还提高闭合阶段成功率吗？

evidence.label: 真机未见底座，整套管线比较
evidence.context: 五任务、三场景、每任务12未见底座×3次；MoMaSplat对适配后的One-Thousand Trajectories。作者取整平均，约+20个百分点，不能恢复精确成功次数。

evidence.label: 较远底座仍有部分成功
evidence.context: 图4/正文，同距离分箱的全部基线均0。距离到最近示范底座，分箱每任务不同，不能当任意朝向或连续作业半径保证。

evidence.label: 少示范的单任务子实验
evidence.context: 瓶子任务，四个距示范10–20cm的位置；每源轨迹生成10条。50/90条加合成为42/50%，不是五任务主评测或端到端成本对照。

evidence.label: 动态重建的真实边界
evidence.context: 30条源轨迹相对模拟器真值，含直接估计/插值；分别±0.71cm/±4.66°。是物体位姿估计误差，非实机末端精度，不能代替动力学可行性。

mechanism.title: 用静止导航解开相机与物体运动
mechanism.text: 导航时物体静止，同一批相机可分别由场景SfM与物体前馈模型定位，再经鲁棒Sim(3)对齐，给操作阶段的物体模型统一坐标与尺度。

mechanism.title: 把移动物体从背景中移除再重放
mechanism.text: 背景重建屏蔽物体/机器人，物体单独拟合并按源轨迹运动；新视角合成时由深度和alpha决定遮挡，避免静态物体重影。

mechanism.title: 同时变换标签与本体感觉
mechanism.text: EEF绝对状态做坐标刚变换；平移增量只旋转，旋转增量做共轭、夹爪保持。多时刻IK筛选用于可达性，尚不验证全程物理接触。

attention.reason: 有真机未见位姿结果，但合成数量不匹配、缺动态单项消融且最终成功率有限，先核成本与坐标配准。
attention.notice: 阅读优先级判断，不是科学质量定论。

impact.comparison: 有真机未见位姿结果，但合成数量不匹配、缺动态单项消融且最终成功率有限，先核成本与坐标配准。

passages.section: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human–Humanoid Social Interaction
passages.location: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human–Humanoid Social Interaction
passages.text: Figure 1. AffectiveVLA enables intent-aware and contact-safe execution of three social interactions: (a) handshake, (b) fist bump, and (c) hug. Arrows indicate the direction of interaction motion, and red regions highlight physical contact. A sequence of photographs showing a humanoid robot interacting with people through a handshake, a fist bump, and a hug. Red highlights mark contact regions and arrows indicate motion.

passages.section: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human–Humanoid Social Interaction
passages.location: AffectiveVLA: Safe and Intent-Aware VLA Control for Human–Humanoid Social Interaction
passages.text: Social touch interactions, such as handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs, require humanoid robots to infer human intent, generate contact-rich motions, and maintain safe physical contact. We present AffectiveVLA, an intent-gated Vision-Language-Action (VLA) pipeline deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. A lightweight RGB-based model recognizes interaction intent from two onboard cameras and converts it into a language prompt for the VLA policy. Low-confidence predictions suppress motion execution, reducing unintended activations. During physical contact, interaction-specific compliance profiles adjust arm impedance, while an independent voice-triggered mechanism initiates a latched safe-stop procedure. Using VR teleoperation, we collected approximately 1,300 multimodal interaction episodes and fine-tuned four VLA models: GR00T, RLDX-1, Being-H0.5, and UnifoLM-VLA-0. On-robot evaluation identifies GR00T as the best-performing standalone model. Integrating intent recognition increases its macro-F1 score from 0.75 to 0.90, while the intent model achieves a p95 inference latency of 6.27 ms. These results demonstrate that explicit intent gating improves the reliability of VLA-based social interaction without compromising real-time operation.

As humanoid robots enter human environments, they must participate in social rituals like handshakes, hugs, and fist bumps (Fig. 1 ). Unlike object manipulation, these interactions involve an active human partner whose intent must be inferred, requiring the robot to meet a moving target while ensuring safe, comfortable contact ( Block et al., 2021 ; Block et al., 2023 ) .

Existing approaches address this only partially: learned whole-body policies rely on explicit operator commands ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , compliance controllers typically use fixed settings ( Lu et al., 2025 ) , and vision-language pipelines infer intent with high latency, lacking physical execution ( Bao et al., 2025 ) . While end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can generate contact-rich motions, they risk unsafe false activations when human intent is uncertain.

To address this, we propose a four-component pipeline: (1) RGB-based intent recognition to gate and prompt the VLA, (2) VLA-based whole-body motion generation, (3) task-specific compliance adaptation, and (4) an independent voice-triggered safe stop.
This work investigates the following research questions:
RQ1: Which VLA model best performs contact-rich HRI actions after fine-tuning on the same dataset?
RQ2: Does the preferred arm compliance depend on the type of social interaction?
RQ3: Does intent gating improve the selection of the correct interaction, and can ongoing contact be safely interrupted?
A comparative evaluation of four fine-tuned VLA models (Being-H0.5, GR00T, RLDX-1, UnifoLM-VLA-0) on social touch tasks .
An intent-gated VLA pipeline with task-conditioned compliance and voice-triggered safe stopping, validated via ablation and user studies.

Social touch in HRI has focused on single, pre-selected interactions: HuggieBot established design guidelines for hugging robots ( Block et al., 2021 ; Block et al., 2023 ) , and tactile sensing has been used to time handshake phases ( Pequeno-Zurro et al., 2024 ) . Reinforcement learning now scales to general-purpose whole-body controllers ( Luo et al., 2025 ) , with systems like ECHO ( Mascaro et al., 2024 ) , RHINO ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and D-STAR ( Huang et al., 2026 ) learning hug and handshake policies. However, these systems rely on fixed skill sets and operator-selected interaction types rather than inferring intent from the partner. For safe contact, impedance control allows the robot to yield ( Lu et al., 2025 ) , but most systems use fixed compliance settings. For intent inference, foundation models can reason about social cues ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , but VLM-based approaches like HIAER ( Bao et al., 2025 ) suffer from multi-second latency and cannot execute contact-rich gestures.

VLA models map images and language to robot actions ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , extending to humanoid control ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , cross-embodiment learning ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , and dexterous manipulation ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Unitree, 2026 ) . These models target manipulation rather than social contact, though GIVE ( Liu et al., 2026 ) shows that textual gesture descriptions improve intent grounding. We use GR00T N1.6 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , RLDX-1 ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , Being-H0.5 ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , and UnifoLM-VLA-0 ( Unitree, 2026 ) as interchangeable action backbones.

Unlike skill-specific policies ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , we infer interaction from dual RGB views and verbalize it as a VLA prompt, enabling new gestures through data rather than reward design. Unlike HIAER ( Bao et al., 2025 ) , intent is recognized in ∼ \sim 6 ms by a lightweight video model, and the robot performs physical contact. Unlike fixed-compliance controllers ( Lu et al., 2025 ) , impedance adapts to each interaction. To our knowledge, this is the first system combining RGB-based intent recognition with VLA execution and interaction-specific impedance for social touch on a humanoid.

The platform used is a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo dexterous hands, controlled by the SONIC whole-body controller, which retargets operator motion into joint commands with per-joint impe-dance gains ( k p k_{p} , k d k_{d} ) for 17 upper-body motors. Teleoperation uses a PICO 4 Ultra headset running XRoboToolkit ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , streaming head/controller poses and 26-joint hand tracking at 90 Hz with stereoscopic passthrough feedback. Upper-body commands are forwarded to SONIC and finger trajectories to the BrainCo hands at 50 Hz, with grip presses serving as the episode-control interface. Each episode records three synchronized RGB views — ego-centric ( 1280 × 720 1280{\times}720 ) and head-mounted ( 1600 × 896 1600{\times}896 ) on the robot at 15 FPS, plus an external scene view ( 1280 × 960 1280{\times}960 ) on the host — and upper-body telemetry (joint states, velocities, torques, commands) at 50 Hz.

Demonstrations were collected by teleoperating the robot with a human partner in four interaction classes: handshake , fist bump , hug , and no interaction . Each episode stores participant profile, multimodal observations, robot states, action commands, and interaction labels in LeRobot format. Retained episodes were annotated with four temporal markers — approach start , contact start , release start , and idle start — used to train the interaction-intent model (Sec. 4.1 ). Episodes with tracking loss, safety stops, unintended contacts, or anomalous duration were discarded. The final dataset contains 1,270 episodes from 19 participants (13 male, 6 female; age 24.4 ± 3.7 24.4\pm 3.7 years; height 175.4 ± 8.6 175.4\pm 8.6 cm), with no participant overlap between the extended set (982 episodes, 15 participants) and test set (288 episodes, 4 unseen participants).

We evaluate four VLA models: Being-H0.5 ( Luo et al., 2026 ) , GR00T N1.6 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , RLDX-1 ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , and UnifoLM-VLA-0 ( Unitree, 2026 ) . All follow the same architecture — a ViT-based VLM backbone, a projector aligning visual and language features, and an action expert predicting chunked actions — operating in a unified 76-dimensional action space: 64-dimensional SONIC motion tokens for the upper body plus 6-DoF finger commands for each BrainCo hand, chunked over 40 steps. All models are fine-tuned using model-specific recipes. For Being-H0.5, RLDX-1, and UnifoLM-VLA-0, the language backbone is frozen while the ViT encoder, projector, and action expert are trained. For GR00T N1.6, only the action expert and projector are updated. Fine-tuning runs on a single A100 80GB GPU for 30k steps; UnifoLM additionally requires converting the dataset to HDF5/RLDS format.

Figure 2 presents the proposed pipeline. Camera observations are used to recognize interaction intent. A confirmed intent is converted into a task prompt for the VLA model, while task-specific compliance and an independent voice-triggered safe-stop mechanism supervise physical execution.

Figure 2. Overview of the proposed human-aware VLA pipeline. (a) The perception module estimates the human partner’s interaction intent from two RGB camera views, filters uncertain predictions, and independently detects voice commands for safe stopping. (b) The on-robot VLA bridge converts a confirmed intent into a task prompt, predicts whole-body action chunks, and applies playback smoothing and finger-contact safeguards. (c) During deployment, task-conditioned arm-compliance profiles and the latched safe-stop mechanism supervise the SONIC whole-body controller, enabling safe and compliant handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs. A three-part system diagram. Human intent is estimated from two robot camera views, while a separate voice module detects stop commands. Confirmed intent is converted into a prompt for the VLA policy, which generates smoothed whole-body and finger actions. During deployment, interaction-specific arm compliance and a latched safe stop supervise execution of handshakes, fist bumps, and hugs.

The human-intent module recognizes the interaction initiated by the human from two synchronized onboard RGB views: one for full-body motion and one for the hand-contact area. At each inference step, it processes the 16 most recent frame pairs sampled at 15 Hz, corresponding to about one second of motion history. Frames are resized to 224 × 224 224\times 224 using letterboxing.

A shared TinyViT encoder extracts frame-level features from both views. Separate causal VideoLightFormer modules aggregate temporal information, and attention-based fusion combines the two representations. The model classifies each observation window as handshake , hug , fist_bump , or no_interaction .

The recognized interaction is converted into the task prompt for the VLA policy. An intent is committed only when its probability exceeds 0.6 for three consecutive inference steps. Until then, motion execution remains disabled, reducing unintended activations from uncertain predictions.

Once an intent is accepted, it is mapped to a task prompt such as hug , handshake , or fist bump . The corresponding compliance profile is activated, and the prompt is passed to the VLA together with two camera views, the robot state, and measured BrainCo hand states.

The VLA runs at 5 ​ Hz 5\,\mathrm{Hz} and outputs action chunks with 64-dimensional motion tokens and normalized commands for the six actuators of each BrainCo hand. Actions are executed at 50 ​ Hz 50\,\mathrm{Hz} . Motion tokens are passed to GEAR-SONIC for whole-body joint targets and balance control, while finger commands are sent directly to the BrainCo controllers.

Per-actuator rate limiting prevents abrupt changes between chunks. Contact is detected from the difference between commanded and measured finger positions; after contact, further closing is blocked while opening remains enabled. If the prompt changes, queued actions are discarded and execution is held until a matching chunk is received. The compliance profile is maintained by a 10 ​ Hz 10\,\mathrm{Hz} heartbeat; if it stops, the last gains are held.
The compliance layer scales the impedance gains of the 14 arm joints, leaving torso and leg gains unchanged:
(1) K p , i = α i ​ K p , i 0 , K d , i = β i ​ K d , i 0 , K_{p,i}=\alpha_{i}K^{0}_{p,i},\qquad K_{d,i}=\beta_{i}K^{0}_{d,i},

with β i ≥ α i \beta_{i}\geq\sqrt{\alpha_{i}} . The recognized intent selects the profile; see Table 1 . Profiles change along minimum-jerk ramps (0.3 s softening, 1.0 s stiffening) that keep damping high during each transition.

Table 1. Implemented compliance profiles, shown as ( K p K_{p} scale, K d K_{d} scale). Interaction profiles are provisional, chosen from pilot sessions; final values will be set by the user study (Sec. 5.4 ).

An offline Vosk recognizer ( Alpha Cephei, 2026 ) with a restricted vocabulary (“stop”, “hold on”) triggers a deterministic, latched stop: operator and VLA commands are ignored, locomotion is set to idle, the arms soften to SOFT and are then lowered to the rest pose (first outward if a hug is detected), and the BrainCo fingers open. Only a manual release resumes control.

Each model (30k fine-tuning steps) predicts 40-step action chunks along the 288 held-out test episodes, and the predictions are compared with the teleoperated ground truth (Table 2 ). Being-H0.5, GR00T, and RLDX-1 are within 2% of each other in overall RMSE, while UnifoLM-VLA-0 is worse on all metrics. GR00T is the most accurate at the first and last chunk steps. Since the VLA is queried at 5 Hz and executed at 50 Hz, mainly the beginning of each chunk is executed, so first-step accuracy matters most on the robot.

Table 2. Offline open-loop action error (RMSE, lower is better) on 288 test episodes with 40-step action chunks. Body : 64-D SONIC motion token; Hand : BrainCo finger commands; First / Last : error at the first and last step of the chunk. Best in bold.

Five participants performed each interaction ten times ( 5 × 3 × 10 = 150 5{\times}3{\times}10=150 trials per policy) with each VLA alone and with our system (GR00T + intent recognition). Without the intent module, the VLA must infer the interaction from its visual observations alone. A trial is counted as correct if the robot performs the interaction the partner initiated (Table 3 ). All participants were informed about the experimental procedure and the laboratory’s internal regulations, which they acknowledged in writing prior to participation. Participation was voluntary, and participants were informed that they could withdraw from the experiment at any time.

GR00T is the best stand-alone VLA (macro-F1 0.75), but it often confuses the fist bump. Adding intent recognition raises macro-F1 to 0.90, improves every interaction (first bump: 0.50 → \rightarrow 0.78), and eliminates errors on hugs (RQ3). The online ranking differs from the offline one: Being-H0.5 is competitive offline but almost never performs the requested interaction, while UnifoLM ranks second online. Open-loop error is thus a poor proxy for interaction performance, and on-robot testing is needed to select a VLA (RQ1). Both stop phrases were detected in 10/10 trials through the robot’s onboard microphone at close range, with no false triggers during conversation (RQ3).
Table 3. Online evaluation on the robot: F1 score per interaction (higher is better), 150 trials per policy. Mean : macro-F1 over the three interactions. Best in bold.

Interaction Model Handshake Fist bump Hug Mean Being-H0.5 0.09 0.00 0.26 0.12 UnifoLM-VLA-0 0.57 0.38 0.94 0.63 RLDX-1 0.68 0.38 0.54 0.53 GR00T 0.86 0.50 0.89 0.75 GR00T + intent (ours) 0.92 0.78 1.00 0.90

We evaluated six causal video classifiers formed by combining three lightweight visual encoders—TinyViT, MobileViT, and EfficientFormer — with two temporal architectures, VTN and VideoLightFormer. All configurations used the same dual-view input, image resolution, and 16-frame history. The visual encoders were frozen during training, while the temporal modules, view-fusion layer, and classification head were optimized. The development data were derived from an approximately 1,000-episode dataset. This dataset was cleaned specifically for the interaction-phase prediction task by excluding episodes that were unsuitable for reliable phase prediction. After cleaning, 790 episodes remained, of which 632 were used for training and 158 for validation. A separate test dataset containing 288 episodes was used for the final model comparison. Because the test dataset contained no no_interaction episodes, its macro-F1 was computed over the three available interaction classes: handshake , hug , and fist_bump . Across the six configurations, test macro-F1 ranged from 0.51 to 0.76, with p95 inference latency ranging from 5.31 to 6.73 ms. TinyViT with VideoLightFormer achieved the highest test macro-F1 of 0.76 and an accuracy of 0.736, while maintaining a p95 latency of 6.27 ms. This configuration was therefore selected for integration with the VLA policy. On the validation set, the temporal commit rule produced no false activations across 54 no_interaction episodes. Moreover, 77% of interaction intents were committed before physical contact, with a median lead time of 2.1 s. Full per-model results are provided in the supplementary material.

To answer RQ2, a within-subject study varies shoulder, elbow, and wrist stiffness between rigid and soft ( 2 × 2 × 2 2\times 2\times 2 ; soft: K p × 0.6 K_{p}\times 0.6 , K d × 0.83 K_{d}\times 0.83 ), ordered by a balanced Latin square after an unrated rigid practice round. After each handshake, fist bump, and hug, participants rate safety, comfort, and naturalness on a 7-point scale. Two pilot sessions refined the protocol; data collection is ongoing.

The offline results were similar for Being-H0.5, GR00T, and RLDX-1, with an overall RMSE between 0.133 and 0.135. However, their online performance was very different. GR00T achieved the highest stand-alone macro-F1 of 0.75, whereas Being-H0.5 reached only 0.12 despite its competitive offline error. Thus, offline RMSE is not a reliable measure of real-robot interaction performance, and VLA models should also be evaluated online. For intent recognition, TinyViT with VideoLightFormer achieved the best results, with a test macro-F1 of 0.76 and a p95 latency of 6.27 ms. It was therefore selected for integration with GR00T. The combined system improved GR00T’s macro-F1 from 0.75 to 0.90. The largest gain was observed for fist bumps, where F1 increased from 0.50 to 0.78. The scores for handshakes and hugs also increased to 0.92 and 1.00, respectively. These results show that the intent module helps GR00T distinguish between similar interactions while maintaining real-time performance.

This study is limited by the number of participants, the use of only three predefined interaction types, limited environmental and user diversity, and evaluation on a single robot platform and whole-body controller. Although the intent dataset includes a no-interaction class, evaluation on labeled episodes does not fully represent continuous robot operation. Therefore, false activations during long periods without interaction require further study. The intent model may generalize poorly to unseen participants, especially for fist bumps. Speech recognition may also fail in noisy environments. Lowering K p K_{p} gives no formal bound on contact forces and, without gravity compensation, lets the arms sag slightly; this was acceptable for these gestures but would limit precise low-stiffness tasks. Future work will expand the dataset, evaluate false activations during continuous operation, include more diverse users and environments, improve contact-aware perception, and investigate stronger physical safety guarantees.

analysis.overview: 具体改动是把“选择哪一种互动”和动作执行分开：双视角视频先分类并经过置信度/连续帧确认，再产生语言提示和放行VLA；关节顺应及语音锁存停止独立于生成策略。小规模真机比较支持互动选择F1提高，尚不能将其解释为接触力有界、舒适度已验证或连续运行误触发已经解决。
analysis.notice: 完整阅读42个提取片段与固定版本5页PDF的技术内容，目视核对物理页2–5的数据划分、公式1、表1–3、图2和限制。PDF无附录；正文提及的意图分类器逐模型补充结果未在此版本PDF/HTML或公开TeX源包中找到，未宣称已读。未逐篇核查参考文献、执行代码、观看视频、接触机器人或复现实验。图2动作块50与正文/表2的40步不一致，已保留证据缺口。

findings.title: 研究范围：三类互动选择，不是开放式情感理解
findings.text: 系统处理握手、碰拳、拥抱三种预定义互动，并以no_interaction作为第四类。增量是让独立识别器确认动作类型后再提示VLA，而不是训练一个更大的端到端底座。主在线评测要求完成参与者发起的正确类型，不量化开放式意图、情感状态、长期无互动误触发或接触力，因此名称中的Affective不能直接读成通用情感理解。

findings.title: 门控：16帧双视角视频，加0.6阈值与三次确认
findings.text: 两路机载RGB分别覆盖身体和手部，15Hz采样最近16帧对、约1秒历史，letterbox到224×224。共享TinyViT提取特征，两个因果VideoLightFormer聚合，再attention融合分类。只有类别概率超过0.6连续三次推理才commit为语言提示，在此之前禁用运动。它是显式阈值与时间确认，未给概率校准或误触发统计保证；6.27ms网络计算也不等于完整意图确认延迟。

findings.title: 动作桥：提示换代清空旧块，手指闭合另有保护
findings.text: 接受意图后选择提示及顺应profile。VLA以5Hz输出76维动作：64维SONIC上身motion token，加每手6个BrainCo驱动命令；执行以50Hz交给全身控制器和手部控制器。按驱动器限速；命令与实测手指位置的差异用于接触判定，接触后阻止继续闭合但保留张开。提示变化时丢弃排队动作，等待匹配新提示的块。顺应profile以10Hz心跳维护，失联保持最后增益，而不是本文已证明的故障停机保证。

findings.title: 顺应：按互动切换14臂关节增益，数值仍是pilot配置
findings.text: 公式1按α/β缩放14个臂关节的Kp/Kd，躯干与腿不变，约束β≥sqrt(α)。表1握手只将肘缩为(0.60,0.83)，拥抱肩/肘/腕均用该缩放，碰拳肩/肘同样变软而腕保持(1,1)；SOFT为(0.25,0.50)。用minimum-jerk在0.3秒变软、1.0秒变硬。表注明确这些是pilot选的暂定值，不能当已通过偏好实验的最终最优参数，也不构成完整接触稳定性/力上界证明。

findings.title: 停止通路：语音触发锁存，需人工解除
findings.text: 离线Vosk用受限词表识别stop/hold on，触发后忽略操作者及VLA命令，步行置idle，手臂转SOFT并下放；拥抱先向外释放，手指张开，仅人工解除才恢复。它独立于VLA生成结果，但仍是本文软件系统内的确定性处理；不能据此宣称存在独立硬件安全认证或已测得最坏机械停止时间。

findings.title: 主在线证据：macro-F1 0.75→0.90，碰拳提升最大
findings.text: 表3每策略5名参与者×3互动×10次=150次，正确的定义是机器人执行人发起的互动类型。GR00T N1.6单独运行的握手/碰拳/拥抱F1为0.86/0.50/0.89；接意图模块后0.92/0.78/1.00，macro-F1从0.75到0.90，绝对+0.15，碰拳+0.28。这不是90%任务成功率、接触安全率或力降低15%。对照把外部分类、语言提示和门控一起加上，未拆开“正确提示”与“三次确认”的独立效果，未给参与者配对区间/混淆矩阵及拒绝率。

findings.title: 离线低误差不能直接给在线互动选型
findings.text: 表2在288条留出episode评40步开环动作误差：Being-H0.5/GR00T/RLDX-1总体RMSE0.135/0.135/0.133，但表3在线macro-F1为0.12/0.75/0.53；UnifoLM离线0.148最差、在线0.63却第二。GR00T首/末步RMSE0.085/0.156最好，且5Hz查询/50Hz执行主要消耗块前部。RMSE描述的是SONIC潜token和手指命令的开环匹配，不是毫米、角度或接触力精度；四底座的不同冻结策略也限制因果解释。

findings.title: 意图模型：0.76是三类测试F1，6.27ms只是模块p95
findings.text: 六种分类器由TinyViT/MobileViT/EfficientFormer与VTN/VideoLightFormer组合，冻结图像编码器、训练时间模块/融合/分类头。意图开发集另行清洗后790条，632训练/158验证，测试288条无no_interaction，只算三类macro-F1。最佳TinyViT+VideoLightFormer测试F1=0.76、accuracy0.736、p95=6.27ms；其余只给F1 0.51–0.76与p95 5.31–6.73ms范围，缺少可获取逐项补充表。论文按最高测试成绩选集成模型，未报告选择后独立锁定测试；也未充分披露计时硬件、端到端感知/确认/执行延迟，不能等同一次互动响应6.27ms。

findings.title: 误触发证据只来自验证集54条无互动
findings.text: 验证集54条no_interaction中观察到0次假激活，77%的互动意图在接触前commit，中位提前量2.1秒；这些不是未见长时连续部署的误报率或保证。测试集无no_interaction，未提供每小时假激活、连续等待总时长、置信区间及拒绝/延迟权衡。不能从0/54写成无意外动作，三个连续置信度判断也不是统计独立试验。

findings.title: 数据和训练：清洗与底座recipe要算入比较
findings.text: 最终1270条、19名参与者；extended982条/15人，test288条/4未见人，二者无人重叠。丢弃跟踪丢失、安全停止、非预期接触和异常时长episode，不能用清洗后的分布估计真实部署的异常/安全事件发生率。意图开发集另清洗为790条，不应和982条VLA扩展集混为一数；在线5参与者是否与训练人重叠未明确。四VLA均单张A10080GB训练30k步，但GR00T仅更新projector/动作专家，其他还更新ViT；相同步数不是相同可训练参数或总计算量，batch/总工时等复现信息未充分给出。

findings.title: 舒适度研究仍在收集，尚未回答各互动的最佳顺应
findings.text: 5.4节设计肩/肘/腕2×2×2刚软组合、balanced Latin square和7点安全/舒适/自然评分；只完成两次pilot，明确数据收集ongoing。因而RQ2尚无正式偏好结果。不能将贡献段的user studies措辞或表1profile理解为已证实某一互动更舒适、风险更低；相关数值应当作初步实现配置。

findings.title: 物理停止与力界：10/10口令不是系统安全率
findings.text: 两词在近距离机载麦克风测试被报告10/10检出，正文未明确是每词各10次还是合计，也未给噪声条件、对话暴露时长、声学检出到机械释放时间。没有接触力/压力峰值或伤害指标；作者明确降低Kp不提供形式接触力界，且无重力补偿会下垂。现有证据支持停止流程能触发的有限案例，不支持普遍安全、无漏检或舒适度已验证。

findings.title: 配置与材料缺口：图2的50步和正文40步未统一
findings.text: 正文3.3、5.1和表2为40步动作块；目视固定PDF页4图2，Action Chunk框标成50×[motion token R64,finger joints]。两者不一致，本轮以正文和表2解释离线评测，并保留实现配置待核对，未擅改图片或用50Hz执行频率代替块长。正文称六分类器逐模型结果在supplement，但固定版本5页PDF/HTML和只读源包均未发现附加材料；因此只报告正文明确给出的最佳值与范围，未编造补充结果。

hypotheses.title: 待验证：三次确认在同样提示下是否真正改善连续无互动误触发？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在保持意图分类器与提示相同的前提下，三次置信确认能降低连续无互动场景的假动作放行，同时保留足够的接触前提前量。先做离线双视角视频回放：使用同一冻结分类器，比较直接argmax提示、仅概率大于0.6、概率大于0.6连续三次三组；均明确no_interaction映射为空动作，其他VLA/控制配置相同，不进行人体接触实验。阈值及确认长度只在开发参与者上选择，最终测试使用独立未见参与者的长时无互动、相似抬手/转身及三类真实互动视频；记录累计时长、每小时假放行、每参与者事件率、拒绝/漏检、相对approach/contact标注的确认延迟与提前量分位数，报告按参与者聚类的区间。另以oracle类别提示估计分类错误上限，避免把提示纠正全部算作门控效果。若三次确认相对同提示单阈值不降低假放行，或多数接受事件已晚于可干预时刻，就推翻其能兼顾误触发与及时性的假设；若仅验证人群有效则缩小适用范围。实验未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。

frontier_brief.title: AffectiveVLA：先确认互动意图，再发语言提示并放行VLA动作
frontier_brief.change_type: 控制集成 · 意图门控
frontier_brief.delta: 把握手/碰拳/拥抱类型交给独立双视角视频分类器；概率超过0.6连续三次才转换为提示并放行VLA。提示切换清空旧动作块，顺应profile与语音锁存停止另走执行通路。
frontier_brief.before: 同一VLA直接依赖视觉观测判断人发起的是哪一种互动；开环动作误差接近，也可能在真机选错动作。
frontier_brief.after: 用TinyViT与因果VideoLightFormer处理16帧双视角历史，显式做置信度/时间确认再提示GR00T N1.6；执行层另管块更新、手指接触、14臂关节顺应与锁存停止。
frontier_brief.relevance: 在有限已知互动类别中，值得先区分“选对技能”和“动作拟合得准”。复现应固定同样类别提示，再消融阈值与连续确认，并增加长时无互动回放；把互动F1、误放行和接触物理量分开评估。
frontier_brief.caveat: 在线仅5人、每策略150次三类互动；0.90是macro-F1，非安全或成功率。0/54假激活来自验证集，测试无no_interaction；舒适度用户研究仍在收集，接触力无形式界，图2块长与正文不一致。作者结果未复现。
frontier_brief.question: 在同样预测提示下，连续三次确认还会降低长时无互动的假动作放行吗？

evidence.label: 真机互动选择的整模块收益
evidence.context: 表3，5人×3互动×10次=150次/策略；握手0.86→0.92、碰拳0.50→0.78、拥抱0.89→1.00。外部分类/提示/门控一起加入，未分离三次确认的贡献。

evidence.label: 低开环误差没有选出所有在线好模型
evidence.context: 表2/3，离线288条留出episode、40步块；误差是潜动作/手部命令量，不是接触力或末端毫米精度。底座微调recipe也不同。

evidence.label: 确认误触发证据的真实范围
evidence.value: 验证集0/54假激活；77%在接触前确认
evidence.context: 5.3节，no_interaction验证episode为54条，中位提前2.1秒；独立测试无no_interaction，因此不能据此推算连续运行每小时误触发。

evidence.label: 意图网络计算成本
evidence.context: TinyViT+VideoLightFormer，16帧/约1秒历史与三次确认另计；未提供充分硬件和完整响应延迟，也未找到正文所称逐模型supplement。

mechanism.title: 分类与放行分成两步
mechanism.text: 双机载RGB的历史先被编码、因果聚合与融合；只有满足概率和连续确认规则，才生成类别提示及允许运动，未确认时保持禁止执行。

mechanism.title: 语义更新约束动作缓存
mechanism.text: VLA5Hz预测、50Hz执行；提示变化清掉旧块，等待相同提示的新版结果，手指接触用命令/实测差异阻止继续闭合。

mechanism.title: 物理执行单独受限
mechanism.text: 14臂关节采用互动相关的暂定顺应profile；语音停止锁存并要求人工解除。这是实现机制，力界、长期误触发与舒适度仍需独立证据。

attention.reason: 有限互动类别的整模块收益不等同安全提升；缺少门控单项消融，不能作为广泛人机安全路线结论。
attention.notice: 阅读优先级判断，不是科学质量定论。

impact.comparison: 有限互动类别的整模块收益不等同安全提升；缺少门控单项消融，不能作为广泛人机安全路线结论。

passages.text: Compounding Physical RSI: Turning Execution Failure into Inherited Capability
Yixuan Yang 1 , Qiang Chen 1 , Run Shao 1 , Shuwei Dong 1 , Wenhao Li 1 , Yunpeng Wang 1
Wenhan Fang 1 , Haomiao Wu 1 , Xingyu Wang 1 , Lichen Man, Rong Zhang
Xuezhi Cui, Yuan Liu, Bingyan Lu, Jiawei Ma, Xiaoyang Ma, Zhemin Sun
Zhuorui Yao, Yutong Dong, Yuxuan Zhao, Yichong Mu, Jiabao Jiang
Wenxuan Deng, Junling Zhou, Yi Chen 2 , Deyu Zhang 3 , Yiming Yan 3
Yige Yuan 3 , Shan You, Fei Wang 2 , Haifeng Li 4 , Hongyan Xu 2 , Yichao Cao 5 , Xiu Su 6,∗
1 Core Algorithm Development & Implementation 2 Principal Contributor 3 Resource Contributor 4 Project Leader 5 Execution Leader & Principal Contributor 6 Technical Leader & Principal Contributor
ECCV 2026 RoboDojo Safe World Models Challenge | Champion | CSU-AI-07

Vision-language-action (VLA) models have substantially advanced generalist robot manipulation by unifying visual perception, language grounding, and action generation within a single policy [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Recent efforts have extended this paradigm across diverse embodiments [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , refined spatial representations and fine-tuning efficiency [ 9 , 10 ] , and scaled pre-training to over 100K hours of real-world trajectories [ 11 ] . Yet despite these advances in pre-training scale, a generalist policy still encounters many of its fundamental capability limits only after static training has ended and closed-loop physical execution begins.

This limitation stems from the sequential, stage-gated nature of manipulation. A robot must approach an object before grasping it, and must establish a stable grasp before transporting or placing it. Consequently, a deficiency in a downstream stage remains masked until the policy reliably passes all preceding stages: a policy that fails during grasping never reveals how it would fail during transport, because its rollouts never reach that state. Moreover, the failure modes encountered during transport depend directly on the contact configuration produced by the grasp, as each policy induces its own closed-loop state distribution [ 12 ] . We define the earliest task stage that a policy cannot yet pass reliably as its capability frontier . Because behavior beyond this frontier remains unobserved during execution, a fixed dataset cannot anticipate how the evolving policy will fail once it crosses the current barrier. Each successful fix advances the capability frontier and exposes the next latent failure mode.

A moving capability frontier naturally motivates Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) for embodied intelligence. Rooted in classical formulations of self-referential learning [ 13 , 14 ] and renewed in modern foundation-model research [ 15 ] , RSI recognizes that when a policy’s next bottleneck becomes visible only after the current one is resolved, improvement cannot be reduced to a single static training run. Instead, the robot must iteratively execute, diagnose its own failures, learn from them, and execute again so that each generation uncovers the empirical evidence required by the next. Physical RSI formalizes this paradigm for embodied systems, where contact-rich physical experience drives persistent policy evolution [ 16 , 17 ] . Recent studies have explored key facets of embodied self-improvement, including inference-time self-correction and subtask backtracking [ 18 ] , deployment-time adaptation and memory consolidation [ 19 , 20 ] , and iterative policy updates via autonomous data collection or residual reinforcement learning [ 8 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] .

While these efforts show that a robot policy can improve over a single update or within narrow task settings, the central open question is whether such improvements can compound across generations. The potential for compounding follows directly from the staged structure of manipulation. Because a task succeeds only when every constituent stage succeeds, overall task completion behaves like a product of stage-level pass rates. In such a product, stage-level gains multiply: stabilizing a grasp not only lifts the completion rate of every subsequent stage, but also sends a larger fraction of rollouts across the capability frontier, generating richer downstream evidence for the next generation. A recursive loop can therefore achieve super-additive progress across rounds, provided that each generation builds reliably upon the verified gains of its predecessor.

However, making Physical RSI compound in practice is hindered by three fundamental bottlenecks that mirror the lifecycle of a policy update. First, execution feedback suffers from opaque temporal credit assignment [ 24 ] : a terminal failure flag indicates that a trial failed, but rarely localizes which stage broke, as visible failure often manifests long after the erroneous action that caused it. Second, failed rollouts lack corrective supervision: even a precisely localized failure shows what went wrong without specifying the counterfactual action the policy should have executed. Third, multi-task gains are fragile under shared weights: because a generalist policy encodes all skills in one parameter set, an unconstrained update that repairs one failure stage can silently degrade previously mastered tasks [ 25 ] . Under the same multiplicative structure that amplifies stage-level gains, such cross-task regressions multiply losses, causing naive recursive loops to accumulate policy churn rather than lasting capability.

We argue that the core challenge of Physical RSI is therefore achieving compounding —ensuring that every generation diagnoses its active frontier, resolves it effectively, and inherits verified capabilities without regression. To this end, we propose Compounding Physical RSI , a three-stage self-evolving policy framework, and evaluate the resulting generalist policy, CSU-AI-07 , across all 42 tasks of RoboDojo-Sim. Our main contributions are:

Formulating compounding as the central problem of Physical RSI. We show how the stage-gated structure of manipulation necessitates recursive improvement and establish a formal structural definition of compounding across policy generations.

A closed-loop Diagnosis–Remedy–Retention framework. We couple stage-level capability-gap diagnosis with objective-conditioned offline reinforcement learning (remedy) and evaluation-guided weight-space consolidation (retention), ensuring that targeted frontier fixes are absorbed without eroding prior skills.

State-of-the-art generalist benchmark performance. Across the 42 tasks of RoboDojo-Sim, CSU-AI-07 ranks first on the overall leaderboard in both Overall Score (26.15) and Success Rate (20.70%), outperforming thirteen public generalist policies by substantial margins.

The stage-gated structure of manipulation imposes three strict requirements on a recursive improvement loop. First, because downstream weaknesses remain hidden behind earlier bottlenecks, improvement is most consequential where execution currently stalls; the loop must therefore accurately localize the active capability frontier. Second, because failed rollouts carry no explicit corrective labels, the loop must synthesize targeted supervision to cross that frontier. Third, because stage-level regressions multiply just as readily as stage-level gains, the loop must preserve previously mastered capabilities when absorbing new updates. Checking these three requirements across successive generations yields a structural definition of compounding:

The three clauses of this definition map one-to-one to the three stages of our framework: Diagnosis (Section 3 ), Remedy (Section 4 ), and Retention (Section 5 ). Consistent with recent formulations of Physical RSI [ 16 ] , the term physical denotes that the loop is driven by closed-loop, contact-rich execution governed by physical dynamics—whether in physics simulation or on physical hardware. In our instantiation, closed-loop execution in RoboDojo-Sim supplies the empirical failure evidence, and full-benchmark behavioral outcomes determine which candidate policy survives into the next generation.

For capability to accumulate across generations, the handover from one generation to the next must be governed by explicit operators. We formalize generation k k as a structured policy transition in which each intermediate product fulfills a distinct functional role. Let π k \pi_{k} denote the inherited reference policy at generation k k . Rolling out π k \pi_{k} across the task suite yields execution evidence E k = { ( o t , s t , a t , r t , τ t ) } t = 1 T E_{k}=\{(o_{t},s_{t},a_{t},r_{t},\tau_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T} , recording observations o t o_{t} , robot and object states s t s_{t} , actions a t a_{t} , rewards r t r_{t} , and task-stage annotations τ t \tau_{t} .
One recursive generation then proceeds as:

g k \displaystyle g_{k} = 𝒜 ⁡ ( E k ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{A}(E_{k}), ℬ k + 1 \displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{k+1} = ℬ k ∪ ℱ ⁡ ( E k ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{B}_{k}\cup\mathcal{F}(E_{k}), 𝒟 k + 1 \displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{k+1} = 𝒞 ⁡ ( ℬ k + 1 , g k ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{B}_{k+1},g_{k}), (1) π k ′ \displaystyle\pi^{\prime}_{k} = 𝒰 off ​ ( π k , 𝒟 k + 1 , g k ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{off}}(\pi_{k},\mathcal{D}_{k+1},g_{k}), π k + 1 \displaystyle\pi_{k+1} = 𝒮 ⁡ ( { π k ( i ) } , 𝒱 k + 1 ) , \displaystyle=\mathcal{S}\!\left(\{\pi_{k}^{(i)}\},\mathcal{V}_{k+1}\right),

where 𝒜 \mathcal{A} performs stage-level capability-gap assessment to extract the structured improvement objective g k g_{k} ; ℱ \mathcal{F} validates and normalizes new execution traces before integrating them into the accumulated experience base ℬ k \mathcal{B}_{k} ; 𝒞 \mathcal{C} curates the objective-relevant experience subset 𝒟 k + 1 \mathcal{D}_{k+1} ; 𝒰 off \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{off}} conducts behavior-regularized offline policy refinement to produce the evolved endpoint π k ′ \pi^{\prime}_{k} ; and 𝒮 \mathcal{S} selects the next generation’s reference policy π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} from weight-consolidated candidates { π k ( i ) } \{\pi_{k}^{(i)}\} via automated full-benchmark evaluation 𝒱 k + 1 \mathcal{V}_{k+1} . As shown in Figure 1 , the upper pathway executes this within-generation progression from rollout diagnosis to candidate promotion, while the lower pathway transfers the promoted policy π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} forward as the inherited reference state of generation k + 1 k+1 .

This transition architecture directly addresses the practical constraints of learning from physical interaction. Because physical rollouts are costly, execution is reserved for gathering diagnostic evidence and verifying candidate policies, whereas policy optimization is performed offline over accumulated experience without requiring new environment interactions at each gradient step [ 26 ] . Equally important, because proxy training losses correlate poorly with closed-loop success in contact-rich manipulation, the recursive loop is closed by empirical task evaluation 𝒱 k + 1 \mathcal{V}_{k+1} , ensuring that a candidate advances only when its complete behavioral profile justifies promotion.

Figure 1: Architecture of Compounding Physical RSI. Closed-loop execution in RoboDojo-Sim feeds automated stage-level capability-gap assessment (Diagnosis), which produces a structured objective g k g_{k} to guide experience curation and offline reinforcement learning (Remedy). Retention interpolates candidates between the inherited reference policy and the refined policy, promotes the best-performing candidate via full-benchmark evaluation, and passes it forward as the reference state for the next generation.

Diagnosis initiates each generation of the RSI loop by translating raw execution traces into an explicit specification of what the policy must improve next—fulfilling the first prerequisite for compounding.

A binary terminal reward reports only whether an entire chain of manipulation stages succeeded, obscuring where a failed rollout broke down. Two policies with identical overall success rates may stall at entirely different stages and require fundamentally different updates. To preserve the temporal structure of every trial, we execute the current policy π k \pi_{k} across diverse task configurations in RoboDojo-Sim, which provides a repeatable testbed for behavioral probing. Each rollout is logged as a time-indexed trajectory capturing task-stage boundaries, action transitions, robot and object state changes, terminal conditions, and behavioral responses to environmental variation.

Because manipulation progress is stage-gated, the most informative diagnostic signal in a failed rollout is the exact stage where progression halts. Downstream stages beyond that point remain unvisited—leaving little empirical basis for optimizing them—whereas resolving the bottleneck at the active capability frontier immediately benefits every subsequent stage. Our capability-gap assessment operator 𝒜 \mathcal{A} therefore evaluates each rollout against the expected stage progression of the task (e.g., approach , grasp , manipulate , place , and verify ). By detecting where closed-loop execution diverges from the expected progression and characterizing the conditions accompanying that divergence, the assessment isolates recurring failure patterns such as target misselection, unstable grasp formation, incomplete manipulation stages, inconsistent action transitions, and sensitivity to scene variations. Operating at the granularity of task stages allows 𝒜 \mathcal{A} to pinpoint the exact interaction segment associated with the bottleneck.

passages.location: 3.3 From capability gap to improvement objective
passages.text: For diagnostic findings to steer downstream learning, they must be represented in a form that directly parameterizes data curation and policy optimization. We therefore compile the identified capability gap into a structured improvement objective g k g_{k} that specifies the failing task context, the bottleneck stage, and the affected capability dimension—such as target selection, grasp stability, stage transition, or contact persistence. This structured objective g k g_{k} formally marks the capability frontier of generation k k , conditioning both experience selection ( 𝒞 \mathcal{C} ) and offline policy optimization ( 𝒰 off \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{off}} ) in the Remedy stage.

passages.section: 3.3 From capability gap to improvement objective
passages.location: 3.3 From capability gap to improvement objective
passages.text: Figure 2: Diagnosis and remedy across two representative manipulation failure modes. (a) Contact-to-transition failure on a desk object, where physical contact fails to advance the task stage. (b) In-hand transport instability, where an object is lifted successfully but slips during transport. In both cases, Diagnosis traces execution evidence to the specific failing stage, conditioning the selection of validated corrective experience in Remedy.

passages.section: 3.3 From capability gap to improvement objective
passages.location: 3.3 From capability gap to improvement objective
passages.text: Figure 2 illustrates this diagnostic-to-remedy linkage on two representative cases. In Case (a), initial contact with a desk object fails to trigger the intended task progression, localizing the limitation to the boundary between contact establishment and stage transition. In Case (b), the object is grasped and lifted but loses stability during transport, localizing the limitation to grasp maintenance and in-hand state transition. Case (b) also exemplifies how the capability frontier shifts across updates: the transport instability becomes observable only after the policy has acquired a reliable lifting capability.

While Diagnosis identifies where a policy fails, failed rollouts alone do not specify what the robot should do instead. The Remedy stage bridges this gap by curating validated, stage-targeted experience conditioned on g k g_{k} and converting it into a policy update.

Retrieving experience that directly addresses an improvement objective g k g_{k} requires a data representation that is jointly queryable by task, stage, and outcome. We standardize all robot experience into a unified, source-aware Episode schema that serves as the common unit for representing, validating, and releasing trajectories. Each Episode contains the task identity, language instruction, time-synchronized observation–state–action tuples, source provenance, task-stage boundaries, terminal outcome flags, quality status, and dataset version. Aligning observations, states, actions, and stage transitions along a shared time axis enables the same unit to support diagnostic analysis, stage-level experience selection, and offline policy optimization.

Because a failed rollout lacks the optimal counterfactual action, no single form of experience can supply all that is missing. A geometrically feasible path does not guarantee semantic instruction completion, whereas clean expert demonstrations rarely cover recovery from the specific off-nominal states visited by an imperfect policy. We therefore organize the experience base ℬ k \mathcal{B}_{k} around three complementary sources: (i) task exemplars , which express instruction-conditioned behavior and feasible multi-stage action sequences; (ii) geometric exemplars , which encode target-conditioned spatial structure; and (iii) on-policy execution evidence , which captures the actual state distribution induced by π k \pi_{k} , including successful progressions, incomplete actions, and near-frontier recovery behaviors. Incorporating on-policy execution evidence is vital because offline updates are most effective when supported by experience near the states the policy actually visits [ 12 , 22 ] .

Because offline learning optimizes directly against its dataset, even a small fraction of misaligned Episodes can teach erroneous behavior. Raw execution rollouts require particular care: failed trajectories are indispensable as diagnostic evidence, yet unsuitable as direct action targets. Our automated validation operator ℱ \mathcal{F} resolves this tension through a five-stage pipeline: normalization, temporal alignment, task-stage association, consistency assessment, and versioned release. Normalization standardizes observation and state fields; temporal alignment verifies correspondence between observations and control actions; task-stage association maps each trajectory segment to its manipulation phase; and consistency assessment checks coherence among the language instruction, scene state, robot configuration, and action sequence. Incomplete or unstable rollouts are flagged and retained strictly for capability-gap diagnosis ( 𝒜 \mathcal{A} ), whereas only validated, coherent segments join the experience base ℬ k + 1 \mathcal{B}_{k+1} as actionable supervision.

As the experience base ℬ k + 1 \mathcal{B}_{k+1} grows across generations, trajectories relevant to the active capability frontier occupy only a small fraction of the repository, so uniform sampling would dilute the corrective signal needed at generation k k . Instead, our curation operator 𝒞 \mathcal{C} actively selects a targeted subset 𝒟 k + 1 = 𝒞 ⁡ ( ℬ k + 1 , g k ) \mathcal{D}_{k+1}=\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{B}_{k+1},g_{k}) guided by g k g_{k} . Specifically, 𝒞 \mathcal{C} retrieves validated Episodes sharing the bottleneck task stage, object-interaction pattern, or state-transition boundary identified in g k g_{k} , prioritizing trajectories that demonstrate successful progression across the diagnosed limitation. The curated set 𝒟 k + 1 \mathcal{D}_{k+1} is versioned and linked to the objective g k g_{k} and reference policy π k \pi_{k} , ensuring that every policy update is traceable to the failure mode that motivated it.

To turn the curated dataset 𝒟 k + 1 \mathcal{D}_{k+1} into improved closed-loop behavior, the update must evaluate actions by their long-horizon consequences across stages [ 24 ] while learning strictly from a fixed offline experience distribution [ 26 ] . We formulate each remedy update 𝒰 off \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{off}} as an objective-conditioned offline reinforcement learning problem over 𝒟 k + 1 \mathcal{D}_{k+1} , where the improvement objective g k g_{k} acts as a goal in the sense of universal value functions [ 27 ] . Specifically, the update seeks a policy that maximizes objective-conditioned value while remaining anchored to the inherited reference policy π k \pi_{k} :

π k ′ = arg max π 𝔼 s ∼ 𝒟 k + 1 , a ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ s , g k ) [ Q ( s , a ∣ g k ) ] − λ D ( π , π k ) , \pi^{\prime}_{k}=\arg\max_{\pi}\;\mathbb{E}_{s\sim\mathcal{D}_{k+1},\,a\sim\pi(\cdot\mid s,g_{k})}\!\left[Q(s,a\mid g_{k})\right]-\lambda\,\mathrm{D}(\pi,\pi_{k}), (2)

where Q ⁡ ( s , a ∣ g k ) Q(s,a\mid g_{k}) is the learned value estimate on 𝒟 k + 1 \mathcal{D}_{k+1} , D ⁡ ( π , π k ) \mathrm{D}(\pi,\pi_{k}) measures divergence from the reference policy, and λ > 0 \lambda>0 controls anchor strength. While this formulation follows behavior-regularized and conservative offline reinforcement learning [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] to mitigate out-of-distribution value extrapolation, the divergence anchor serves a crucial second role in our framework: it constrains unnecessary parameter drift on states and tasks outside the current objective g k g_{k} . Rather than serving as a final deployment checkpoint, the refined candidate π k ′ \pi^{\prime}_{k} is passed to the Retention stage for verification.

Although Remedy produces an evolved policy π k ′ \pi^{\prime}_{k} with stronger performance on the targeted capability frontier, updating shared weights inevitably risks degrading previously mastered skills [ 25 ] . Because overall task success is a product of stage pass rates, even small cross-task regressions can erase net progress. The Retention stage governs what the next generation actually inherits, separating a compounding loop from a sequence of isolated fine-tuning runs.

Capability inheritance requires an explicit predecessor against which behavioral changes can be measured. The framework therefore maintains a shared reference policy π k \pi_{k} that can be evaluated as a complete controller at the start of each generation. Compatible policy checkpoints provide its parameter-space basis—with compatibility established by matching model architectures, parameter representations, and execution interfaces—and are integrated via model-soup weight averaging and interference-aware merging [ 31 , 32 ] . The resulting reference state gives offline learning ( 𝒰 off \mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{off}} ) a coherent initialization that preserves the capabilities verified prior to generation k k .

Directly adopting the evolved endpoint π k ′ \pi^{\prime}_{k} rarely achieves the optimal balance between new frontier gains and existing skills: full adoption ( π k ′ \pi^{\prime}_{k} ) risks cross-task regression, whereas full rejection ( π k \pi_{k} ) discards the newly acquired capability. Consolidation exposes the Pareto frontier between these extremes by constructing candidates along the linear weight-space trajectory from the inherited reference parameters θ k \theta_{k} to the evolved parameters θ k ′ \theta^{\prime}_{k} :
θ k ( i ) = ( 1 − α i ) ​ θ k + α i ​ θ k ′ , α i ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] , \theta_{k}^{(i)}=(1-\alpha_{i})\,\theta_{k}+\alpha_{i}\,\theta^{\prime}_{k},\qquad\alpha_{i}\in[0,1], (3)

where the consolidation coefficient α i \alpha_{i} sets how strongly each candidate π k ( i ) \pi_{k}^{(i)} incorporates the update. Searching this linear path is grounded in linear mode connectivity [ 33 ] : because θ k \theta_{k} and θ k ′ \theta^{\prime}_{k} share a common ancestor, weight-space interpolation retains functional coherence across the loss landscape. Moreover, because interpolation acts directly on weights rather than ensembling action distributions, each candidate π k ( i ) \pi_{k}^{(i)} remains a single standalone policy with zero additional inference overhead.

Because parameter-space proximity alone cannot guarantee skill survival in contact-rich control, retention must be adjudicated on closed-loop behavior across the full task set. Each consolidated candidate π k ( i ) \pi_{k}^{(i)} is evaluated under a standardized RoboDojo-Sim protocol ( 𝒱 k + 1 \mathcal{V}_{k+1} ) using Overall Score, Success Rate, and task-completion validity, weighing frontier gains on targeted tasks against any loss on others. The selection operator 𝒮 \mathcal{S} promotes the best-performing candidate to π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} and excludes all unpromoted variants.

Promotion is the point at which the loop compounds: the promoted state π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} becomes the inherited reference policy of generation k + 1 k+1 , which then executes π k + 1 \pi_{k+1} to diagnose the newly exposed frontier. Model identity, reference lineage, experience version, and evaluation logs are archived together, endowing the policy with a traceable evolutionary history.

Validating whether a recursive framework compounds calls for a broad benchmark where narrow overfitting or cross-task forgetting is immediately penalized in aggregate metrics. We evaluate on RoboDojo-Sim , part of the unified RoboDojo benchmark for generalist robot manipulation [ 34 ] . Its 42 tasks span five capability dimensions— generalization , memory , long-horizon execution , precision , and open task specification —ensuring that a fix that breaks another skill lowers the aggregate result. Overall Score captures continuous stage-level task progress, while Success Rate (SR) measures binary full-task completion. Reading the two metrics together separates policies that merely advance through early stages from those that cross the final frontier to finish the task, matching the diagnostic interpretation emphasized by the benchmark authors [ 34 ] . A shared protocol and public leaderboard via XPolicyLab place all policies on equal terms [ 35 ] , and the benchmark is highly demanding: the highest Success Rate among the thirteen public baselines in Table 2 is 14.88%.

Both the promoted policy checkpoint ( CSU-AI-07 ) and the benchmark configuration are fixed before evaluation, and performance is reported as the arithmetic mean over three independent evaluation seeds. As shown in Table 1 , CSU-AI-07 achieves a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 and a mean Success Rate of 20.70% , with seed-level results spanning a narrow range of 1.07 points and 0.74 percentage points. Notably, while Seed 0 was used for candidate selection during iteration, held-out evaluations on Seeds 1 and 2 remain closely aligned with Seed 0, confirming that evaluation-guided promotion yields stable cross-seed generalization.

Table 2 presents the overall RoboDojo-Sim leaderboard, where CSU-AI-07 ranks first on both metrics. It surpasses the next-best Overall Score (20.23) by 5.92 points and the next-best Success Rate (14.88%) by 5.82 percentage points —relative margins of 29.3% and 39.1% , respectively. Compared with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} (6.93% SR), a widely adopted open generalist policy, CSU-AI-07 achieves nearly three times the task completion rate. At the same time, a 20.70% Success Rate leaves substantial room for further progress across the 42 tasks; within our framework, these remaining failed trials constitute the empirical evidence that subsequent generations will diagnose and consolidate into inherited capability.

Compounding Physical RSI reframes generalist robot policy development: the central question shifts from how much static experience a policy consumes to how effectively each generation converts its own closed-loop failures into capabilities that its successors inherit. Crucially, the three stages of our framework are mutually indispensable in this loop: without stage-level Diagnosis , policy updates lack directional focus at the capability frontier; without targeted Remedy , localized failure modes do not translate into corrective supervision; and without evaluation-guided Retention , unconstrained updates risk silently erasing the accumulated gains of earlier generations.

The present scope also defines clear next steps. First, while our benchmark results evaluate the integrated system across 42 tasks, fine-grained ablations isolating the individual contributions of diagnosis, experience selection, and weight consolidation will further clarify the mechanics of compounding. Second, compounding here operates on policy capability while the improvement operators ( 𝒜 , 𝒞 , 𝒰 off \mathcal{A},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{U}_{\mathrm{off}} ) remain fixed; extending RSI to evolve the improvement procedure itself is the higher bar set by recent formulations of Physical RSI [ 16 , 17 ] . Finally, carrying this closed-loop framework from physics simulation to physical hardware—where each trial is far costlier—will make verified capability inheritance even more valuable.

Because behavior beyond the current capability frontier remains unobserved during execution, a generalist manipulation policy learns what it needs next by executing, failing, and improving. This report has argued that the central challenge of Physical RSI is ensuring that such iterative improvements compound across generations. Compounding Physical RSI addresses this challenge by diagnosing failure at the granularity of task stages, remedying it via objective-conditioned offline reinforcement learning over curated experience, and retaining verified gains through evaluation-guided weight consolidation. The resulting policy, CSU-AI-07 , ranks first on the overall RoboDojo-Sim leaderboard across 42 tasks with a three-seed mean Overall Score of 26.15 and Success Rate of 20.70%, demonstrating that execution failure can be systematically transformed into inherited capability.

hypotheses.title: 验证：插值真能兼顾新阶段与旧任务吗？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：在同一个离线更新终点上筛选权重插值候选，能比直接继承终点更好地兼顾新阶段通过率与旧任务保持。先选一个可运行的仿真抓放任务和已掌握的放置任务，固定同一祖先策略、离线轨迹、模型结构、价值学习器、行为约束和训练预算。对照A不更新，B直接采用更新终点，C在A/B之间取α=0、0.25、0.5、0.75、1；只用独立验证布局筛选，事先约定旧任务最大允许退化，再在完全留出的布局和随机种子上测试，不能用测试集挑α。报告新阶段的条件通过率、整体成功率、每个旧任务的成功变化、最差退化和全部候选rollout成本。先检查一轮，再跨至少3个训练种子及多轮更新比较。若C不能稳定优于B的保留—改进权衡，或旧技能仍持续退化，则反对该继承机制能保住旧技能的解释；另用较小更新范数的训练控制检查是否只是减弱更新。实验尚未运行，未全面检索相关工作，不能称为已发现研究空白。
