passages.section: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
passages.location: Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
passages.text: A robot action can satisfy shape and range constraints yet carry the wrong semantics: axes may be permuted, signs inverted, rotations rescaled, or gripper polarity reversed. We study learned state–action–effect relations as offline contracts for detecting these mismatches and ranking their likely fields. Clean held-out transitions calibrate alarms; a fixed inverse vocabulary supports closed-set localization. On ten LIBERO Spatial tasks comprising 432 source episodes, a capacity-controlled comparison at 2.5% empirical clean false-positive rate gives 46.1% recall for a ridge forward residual, 61.0% for a four-component joint Gaussian mixture, and 65.7% for the exact conditional of that same mixture. The joint score retains a 14.9 percentage-point advantage over ridge, while conditioning improves recall by a further 4.7 points. Joint scoring instead has higher localization: 95.8% versus 94.6%. These matched-rate comparisons are retrospective diagnostics, not deployment calibration guarantees. Earlier Object/Goal results broaden tasks within the LIBERO convention; DROID, all three HYDRA tasks, short temporal faults, small offsets, exact repair, and simulated mitigation fail their respective gates, while xArm contributes one task only. The evidence supports a bounded offline diagnostic and a detection–localization tradeoff, rather than joint-density superiority or cross-robot safety.

World models usually predict dynamics or support planning. At a controller boundary, they can also ask whether an action’s semantics agree with the observed transition. A seven-dimensional action vector may mix normalized translation, axis-angle rotation and gripper commands. Components can agree on shape and bounds while disagreeing about scale, axes, signs, rotation units or polarity. Such a command is numerically legal but inconsistent with the recorded state change.

We study whether recorded state–action–next-state tuples can supply an executable contract for this failure class. A detector is trained on clean transitions, a disjoint clean split fixes its alarm threshold, and in-range semantic mutations are applied only after that calibration is frozen. After an alarm, the system evaluates a declared set of inverse transformations and reports the one that best restores relational consistency. This separates two questions that aggregate anomaly scores often conflate: whether the transition should be inspected and which contract field is the most plausible explanation.

The diagnostic addresses interface semantics, not perception, planning, contact or task progress. Replay supplies the factual next state of the original action, not the physical outcome of executing a corrupted action. We evaluate offline alarms and closed-set localization; they do not measure task success or safe correction.

The study separates three sources of apparent advantage: using the observed transition, representing multimodal clean behavior, and choosing an alarm operating point. The original joint-mixture comparison outperformed a ridge forward residual, but those methods had different achieved false-positive rates. A post-decision capacity-controlled analysis addresses both confounds. At matched empirical clean FPR, the exact conditional of the fitted mixture has higher detection recall than the joint score; the joint score retains better closed-set localization. We report that reversal alongside episode-level uncertainty and the external and closed-loop failures that bound the method’s use.

World models learn compact predictive representations for control ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) ; here prediction is used as evidence about an interface, not as a rollout planner. Learned runtime monitors instead anticipate broad policy failures. Model-based monitoring uses interactive imitation learning ( Liu et al., 2023b ) ; Sentinel combines temporal action consistency with task progress ( Agia et al., 2024 ) ; and RAPT uses calibrated predictive deviation for deployment-time detection and diagnosis ( Munn et al., 2026 ) . These systems address general failure or distribution shift. Our scope is a declared vocabulary of controller-semantics transformations and attribution to a contract field.

Model-security work supplies a scope boundary. Backdoor detectability depends on nominal/hidden-task relation and detector assumptions ( Tang et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ) ; TrojAI distinguishes detection, diagnosis and mitigation ( Reese et al., 2026 ) . Backdoor suppression ( Zhu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) and model-lifecycle risks ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) concern different interventions. They provide no evidence for this fixed-weight interface diagnostic, and inverse ranking is neither model purification nor adaptive-attack robustness.

Action Mahalanobis distance is a natural cheap out-of-distribution baseline ( Lee et al., 2018 ) . It cannot, by construction, use the observed state change: a transformed action may remain marginally plausible while becoming inconsistent with the transition. A field-aligned static comparator can couple translation, rotation, and gripper coordinates to measured displacement, but public benchmark metadata omit the controller gains and absolute-versus-delta semantics needed for a faithful executable specification. We include both checks so that improvement is not measured only against range validation.

Robot-testing work explores a complementary axis. VLATest generates diverse manipulation scenes ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , FATE-VLA searches for failure-prone scenes ( Kanwal et al., 2026 ) , and metamorphic testing compares related executions without a task-specific oracle ( Valle et al., 2026 ) . ContractFuzz mutates action semantics rather than observations or scenes. The motivating deployment observation is that weights alone do not specify normalization and controller conventions ( Tai, 2026 ) ; our experiments test when a learned state–action relation can expose that missing contract.

Let s t ∈ ℝ d s s_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{s}} , a t ∈ ℝ d a a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} , and s t + 1 s_{t+1} be a clean recorded transition. A fault k k applies a transform T k : ℝ d a → ℝ d a T_{k}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} . We evaluate only changed rows whose transformed action remains inside clean training bounds,
𝒱 k = { t : T k ( a t ) ≠ a t , ℓ ≤ T k ( a t ) ≤ u } . \mathcal{V}_{k}=\{t:T_{k}(a_{t})\neq a_{t},\;\ell\leq T_{k}(a_{t})\leq u\}. (1)

The supported set contains halving the six motion coordinates, swapping the X and Y axes, reversing the X-axis sign, shrinking rotation units, and reversing gripper polarity. A fixed X-offset is retained as an unsupported stress test. Temporal delay, half-frequency hold, and chunk reversal are evaluated separately and fail the main detector gate.

This is a controlled counterfactual on recorded data: the detector receives ( s t , T k ​ ( a t ) , s t + 1 ) (s_{t},T_{k}(a_{t}),s_{t+1}) , but s t + 1 s_{t+1} is the recorded outcome of a t a_{t} . That design isolates relational inconsistency and supplies a known mutation label. It does not simulate contact dynamics, policy adaptation, or the task outcome of executing T k ​ ( a t ) T_{k}(a_{t}) .
From clean training transitions, we fit a ridge forward model
f θ ​ ( s t , a t ) ≈ s t + 1 − s t f_{\theta}(s_{t},a_{t})\approx s_{t+1}-s_{t} (2)
and normalize each residual dimension by its training root-mean-square error. The conditional score is

R f ​ ( s t , a , s t + 1 ) = mean ⁡ [ ( f θ ​ ( s t , a ) − ( s t + 1 − s t ) σ f ) 2 ] . R_{f}(s_{t},a,s_{t+1})=\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}\left[\left(\frac{f_{\theta}(s_{t},a)-(s_{t+1}-s_{t})}{\sigma_{f}}\right)^{2}\right]}. (3)

The original selected score is the negative log likelihood of a full-covariance mixture,
R G ( z ) = − log ∑ m = 1 M π m 𝒩 ( z ; μ m , Σ m + 10 − 3 I ) , R_{G}(z)=-\log\sum_{m=1}^{M}\pi_{m}\mathcal{N}(z;\mu_{m},\Sigma_{m}+10^{-3}I), (5)

with M = 4 M=4 and deterministic split-seed initialization. To control model capacity, we also evaluate the exact conditional of this fitted mixture. With x = [ s t , a ] x=[s_{t},a] and y = s t + 1 − s t y=s_{t+1}-s_{t} ,
R C ​ ( y ∣ x ) = R G ​ ( x , y ) + log ⁡ p G ​ ( x ) . R_{C}(y\mid x)=R_{G}(x,y)+\log p_{G}(x). (6)

The marginal p G ​ ( x ) p_{G}(x) uses the same weights, component input means and covariance blocks as p G ​ ( x , y ) p_{G}(x,y) . The conditional mixture therefore has input-dependent component weights and conditional means, without adding parameters or fitting a separate model. Its comparison with R G R_{G} isolates the contribution of the input marginal to the score; it does not compare independently optimized model classes. A disjoint clean calibration split sets each detector’s threshold to an empirical upper quantile targeting 2.5% false positives. No mutation outcome enters model selection or threshold fitting.

For attribution, each inverse hypothesis U j U_{j} , including identity, maps the observed action back into a candidate convention. The reported candidate is the one with the lowest relational score on ( s t , U j ​ ( a ) , s t + 1 ) (s_{t},U_{j}(a),s_{t+1}) . We call Top-1 agreement with the injected field localization ; earlier logs use repair_top1 , but a correct ranking does not demonstrate executable repair.

The primary benchmark is public LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023a ) , pinned to data revision e5907374380b8f96511957e6ba5582be52a1e179 . Episodes, not transitions, are partitioned 60/20/20 into training, calibration, and test sets for each deterministic split seed; at most 2,000 transitions are sampled per seed. The audit contains 1,243 task–episode clusters and 160,414 transitions across 30 retained Spatial, Object, and Goal tasks. Repeated split seeds reduce algorithmic Monte Carlo variation but do not create new trajectories.

External-convention screens use low-dimensional data only. DROID-100 ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) contributes 100 episodes and 32,112 transitions, but 46/47 task labels are singletons, so its frozen screen is pooled and episode-disjoint. The FOWM xArm Lift conversion ( Feng et al., 2023 ) contains 800 repeated episodes and 19,200 source-semantic XYZ-plus-gripper transitions from one task. Stanford HYDRA ( Belkhale et al., 2023 ) contains 570 episodes, three tasks, and 357,664 valid transitions with source-defined 7D end-effector-delta and gripper actions. Video and simulator assets are excluded. Conflicting HYDRA mirror metadata are handled conservatively by retaining the source-specific CC-BY-4.0 notice rather than interpreting license terms.

We report clean false-positive rate (FPR), mutation recall, recall gain over the named comparator, and closed-set localization Top-1. The cheap baseline is the better of a full-covariance action Mahalanobis detector and static range legality. A structured field-aligned displacement model independently fits clean affine maps from the named action coordinates to next-frame translation, relative axis-angle, and gripper aperture. The ridge forward score R f R_{f} is the original conditional baseline; the capacity-controlled conditional mixture R C R_{C} is added in the post-decision validation.

The original task gate requires FPR at most 0.05, recall gain at least 0.10 over action/static checks, and localization at least 0.70. Later mixture confirmation requires a task-median recall gain of 0.10 over ridge, wins on at least eight tasks, and both methods below 0.05 FPR. These are historical study gates, not matched-FPR comparisons. The supplement retains the aggregate gates, multiplicity correction, sensitivity results, and a run whose FPR of 0.0500375 exceeds the limit. Repeated split seeds are collapsed within source episode before paired task/episode inference; they do not create new trajectories.

A fixed protocol evaluates all ten Spatial tasks and five supported families on 100 episode-disjoint partitions per task (seeds 33001–33100), retaining the original fitting, preprocessing, transition cap and valid-row rule. No new source episodes are introduced. Each method is first evaluated at clean-calibration quantiles targeting 1%, 2.5%, and 5% FPR, with achieved test FPR reported separately. A second, retrospective diagnostic derives thresholds from held-out clean scores and interpolates adjacent clean-score cutoffs to match empirical FPR exactly. Mutation labels do not select those cutoffs. This curve compares scores; it cannot supply a test-free deployment threshold.

The primary endpoint is recall at 2.5% matched FPR, with two paired comparisons: joint minus ridge and joint minus conditional GMM. Repeated test appearances are averaged within episode–fault cells, then faults within episode, episodes within task, and ten tasks with equal weights. A paired hierarchical bootstrap uses 20,000 task/episode resamples. The reported 95% intervals are conditional on fitted scores and clean-reference thresholds; they exclude refitting and threshold-estimation uncertainty. Bonferroni 97.5% intervals for the two primary comparisons are retained in the supplement. Other FPRs and localization are descriptive endpoints.

Table 1 and Figure 1 compare the three scores without changing model capacity or empirical clean alarm rate. At 2.5% FPR, joint GMM recall is 0.6096 versus 0.4608 for ridge: the paired advantage is 0.1488, with 95% interval [ 0.1207 , 0.1798 ] [0.1207,0.1798] . The exact conditional GMM instead reaches 0.6566, exceeding joint recall on all ten tasks. Joint-minus-conditional recall is − 0.0470 -0.0470 with interval [ − 0.0632 , − 0.0350 ] [-0.0632,-0.0350] ; its two-comparison 97.5% interval [ − 0.0658 , − 0.0339 ] [-0.0658,-0.0339] also excludes zero. The conditional advantage is 0.0422 at 1% FPR and 0.0422 at 5%. The result supports multimodal relational modeling over the ridge residual, but rejects the claim that joint scoring has the best detection recall among the tested scores.

Localization includes all valid fault rows, not just alarms.

passages.section: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.location: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.text: At calibration-only thresholds targeting 2.5% FPR, the achieved equal-episode clean rates are 0.0263 for ridge, 0.0322 for joint GMM and 0.0285 for conditional GMM; corresponding recalls are 0.4413, 0.6086 and 0.6504. Sharing a nominal quantile or satisfying the same 5% cap therefore does not establish a matched operating point. The matched analysis removes that confound for this finite reference set while leaving clean-only deployment calibration as a separate task.

passages.section: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.location: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.text: Detection and attribution also rank the models differently. Closed-set localization is 0.9581 for joint GMM, 0.9462 for conditional GMM and 0.9270 for ridge. These accuracies use all valid mutated rows under the fixed inverse vocabulary. The joint score’s higher localization does not establish an end-to-end benefit after alarm selection, and its extra input-marginal term does not improve recall here.

passages.section: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.location: 5.2 Calibration and localization answer different questions
passages.text: All 1,000 GMM fits converge. Each episode–fault cell has at least 12 held-out appearances, averaged before inference. The supplement reports independent conditional-density and exact-FPR interpolation checks.

The original calibration-only comparison reports a task-median joint-minus-ridge recall difference of 0.15663. A previous 432-episode analysis estimates 0.16753 [ 0.13642 , 0.20297 ] [0.13642,0.20297] . Those values remain in the supplement with their original operating points; the matched-FPR estimate of 0.1488 above is the appropriate comparison for the present detection claim. Its different seeds and estimand mean that subtracting the two estimates does not identify a causal “FPR contribution.”

Earlier joint-GMM advantages over ridge also recur within LIBERO Object and Goal, with recall differences 0.21183 and 0.17956 under their original calibration protocols. They share LIBERO’s action convention. The new conditional and matched-FPR comparisons are restricted to Spatial; they have not been repeated on those suites. A field-aligned static displacement comparator has median recall 0.32020 and localization 0.84245, below the historical joint-GMM result, but absent controller gains prevent a faithful manufacturer-specification interpretation. Complete earlier operating-point, ablation and sensitivity values remain in the supplement as historical evidence.

passages.section: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.location: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.text: Fault families vary materially. Supported transformations have median recall gains 0.300–0.452 and localization 0.878–0.966. The fixed X-offset stress test has only 0.0047 gain and 0.555 localization under the original score; the GMM also passes 0/10 offset gates with median recall 0.0340. Yet seven-candidate localization is 0.7340. In a task/episode-clustered mechanism analysis, alarm recall is 0.0328, localization is 0.7304, and localization among non-alarmed rows is 0.7388; AUROC is only 0.5475. Relative candidate evidence can therefore be informative even when the absolute clean-versus-fault distributions overlap too strongly for a high-precision alarm.

passages.section: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.location: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.text: A selection-frozen descriptive reuse of the same 432 episodes places 74.01% of offset episodes in an explanation-only false-negative stratum. For supported families, 75.51% of episode–fault cells are detected and localized, 1.05% are localized without detection, none are joint failures, and 23.43% lie in a mixed boundary region. These values explain an existing result; they are not an independent confirmation.

passages.section: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.location: 6.1 Detection, explanation, and abstention are different decisions
passages.text: An omitted-family audit cross-fits confidence thresholds between fixed task halves using only the other four supported families. Aggregate rejection of a deliberately hidden family is 0.7411, but omitted X-sign rejection is only 0.3720 and 64.67% of those rows are forced into the XY-swap label. This rejects a universal open-set guarantee. The operational rule is consequently asymmetric: an alarm can request inspection for a represented family, but no alarm cannot certify a correct interface, and a high relative score cannot safely remap an unknown fault.

passages.section: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.location: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.text: DROID-100 passes low-dimensional schema checks, yet pooled scale, swap, and sign recalls are only 0.0193, 0.0777, and 0.0865. Its sparse task identity also prevents a multi-task replication. One xArm Lift task passes a separately frozen screen: GMM recall is 0.6016 versus 0.5046 for forward, with 0.0245 mean FPR. Because all 800 episodes repeat one task, it supports only a bounded one-task offline sanity check.

passages.section: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.location: 6.2 External conventions do not validate transfer
passages.text: HYDRA is the decisive negative external screen. It passes compatibility gates and provides three repeated tasks with auditable action semantics, but coffee, dish-rack, and toast GMM recalls are only 0.1063, 0.1097, and 0.1213; zero tasks pass. Three bounded rescues do not reverse that outcome. The final SAGE-R sequence-aware redesign also passes 0/3 and underperforms the strongest sequence baseline on every task. These failures are immutable evidence: the workshop rewrite neither tunes on the HYDRA test set nor turns the one xArm result into cross-robot validation.

passages.section: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.location: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.text: Replay uses the factual next state produced by the clean action. A deterministic clean-trained response proxy lowers median task GMM recall from 0.6379 to 0.2381 on LIBERO and mean recall from 0.6105 to 0.0972 on xArm, but factual-minus-proxy recall on HYDRA is − 0.0978 / + 0.0604 / − 0.0440 -0.0978/+0.0604/-0.0440 . These learned-response diagnostics are not environment rollouts or causal effects.

passages.section: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.location: 6.3 Replay evidence does not establish consequence or repair
passages.text: A small controlled simulator connects the detector to reject/hold/fallback under a fixed fault and delay budget. GMM fallback can recover success relative to no monitor, but it ties a ridge monitor and misses the GMM clean-FPR gate. It therefore does not demonstrate ContractFuzz-specific closed-loop success improvement. A separate continuous-offset repair sweep passes 0/10 gates, and linear, shrunk, quadratic, random-feature, and disjoint-task selectors all fail. Candidate ranking is useful diagnostic evidence; it is not a license to modify commands online.

Earlier ablations reject a universal best score. Forward-only and inverse-plus-forward scores both pass the original action/static gate, but their paired recall difference includes zero and forward-only localizes better. Four and eight GMM components pass the historical recall gate while two fail; calibration budgets of 100, 200 and 400 clean transitions pass. Family rankings differ, and small-offset or temporal severity sweeps cannot rescue the failed short-fault gates. The supplement retains the full numerical ablations and the distinction between predeclared comparisons and explanatory reuse.

The new conditional score is an analytic normalization of the same joint mixture. Its advantage does not establish superiority of every conditional architecture, and a separately optimized conditional mixture could behave differently. The post-decision analysis reuses the same 432 episodes, conditions uncertainty on the fitted scores and reference thresholds, and adds no robot, policy, or controller convention. Matched empirical FPR describes this finite offline reference set; production calibration and natural fault prevalence remain outside the evidence.

A multimodal state–action–effect relation can expose declared interface faults that remain numerically legal. The new comparison changes the interpretation of that result: a joint-mixture advantage over linear prediction error does not imply that modeling the joint density is better than conditioning. Here conditioning the same mixture improves recall, while the joint score ranks inverse candidates more accurately. Score choice should therefore follow the diagnostic decision and its alarm budget rather than an aggregate claim of model dominance.

A practical offline audit can pair clean calibration transitions with a declared inverse vocabulary and request inspection when an alarm occurs. It must report achieved clean FPR, detection recall and localization separately. Meeting a common FPR ceiling constrains the operating point but cannot replace a matched-rate comparison. No alarm cannot certify a correct interface, and candidate ranking cannot justify automatic command remapping. Independent robot conventions and actual counterfactual rollouts remain necessary to support broader deployment or safety claims.

The artifact records pinned data, splits, calibration rules, commands, checksums and CPU resources. The supplement retains all historical runtime and portability evidence, including the inconclusive exact-CPython-3.12.4 cross-host replay. The post-decision analysis adds no source data: 1,000 GMM fits and the conditional/ matched-FPR analysis take 40.40 seconds on one local CPU process with one BLAS/OpenMP thread (Python 3.11.2, NumPy 1.26.4, SciPy 1.13.1, scikit-learn 1.4.2). Its protocol, score arrays, episode metrics, hashes and independent aggregation audit are preserved separately from the original results.

This diagnostic could be misread as a safety certificate. We publish failures, restrict the claim to recorded replay, and do not recommend automatic correction. The evaluation uses public low-dimensional robot demonstrations. Physical deployment would require independent safety controls and oversight. Dataset license metadata are provenance facts, not legal conclusions.

Generative AI assisted research planning, software development, analysis and manuscript drafting. This revision used AI assistance for the post-decision code, mathematical checks, result interpretation, prose and figures. Authors remain responsible for verifying the evidence, citations and final text.

On locked LIBERO replay, calibrated relational scores detect and localize five numerically legal action-interface transformations. At matched empirical clean FPR, a joint GMM retains its recall advantage over ridge prediction error, but the exact conditional of that same mixture has still higher recall. Joint scoring instead has higher closed-set localization. The resulting detection–localization tradeoff, finite-episode uncertainty and negative external results support an auditable offline diagnostic for a declared vocabulary. They do not establish cross-robot generalization, closed-loop success improvement, causal safety or automatic repair.
Detecting Silent Action-Interface Mismatch with Calibrated Relational World Models
Evidence and Reproducibility Supplement
Rui Zhu 1 , Xurui Li 2 , Haixu Tang 3
1 Yale University 2 Ant Group 3 Indiana University
rui.zhu.rz399@yale.edu , xurui.lxr@antgroup.com , hatang@iu.edu

This supplement separates the retained original study from the post-decision matched-FPR and conditional-score validation in Section 9 . The latter reuses existing source episodes and introduces new scoring/operating-point results; all other reported values retain their original evaluation contracts and are linked to project-local commands and machine-readable results in Section 7 . The positive claim remains restricted to offline replay of five declared, numerically legal action-interface transformations within the LIBERO convention . DROID and HYDRA remain negative; xArm remains a one-task sanity check; simulator mitigation, exact repair, open-set rejection, small offsets, and short temporal faults remain unsupported.

Table 1 defines how each evidence level may affect the paper. Repeated split seeds characterize an algorithm under different episode-disjoint partitions; they are not independent robot executions. The episode-clustered analysis is the inferential anchor. Analyses that reuse those episodes after inspecting earlier outcomes are explicitly descriptive. External screens probe convention transfer but do not become positive replications unless their predeclared gate passes.
Table 1: Evidence hierarchy. “May support” is deliberately narrower than what the underlying metric could be used to suggest.

Level Statistical unit May support Fresh locked replay task summaries over unseen split seeds Detector ordering and clean-FPR compliance on recorded tasks Clustered confirmation task, then immutable source episode Finite-source Spatial effect and paired uncertainty Selection-frozen reuse previously used task–episodes Mechanism, heterogeneity, and failure description only Post-hoc severity task summaries at fixed severities Explanatory sensitivity, not rescue of a failed family External convention source-defined episodes and tasks Transfer only when the independently frozen gate passes Simulator proxy simulator episodes under matched budgets Only the specified mitigation comparison, never physical safety

An alarm is a thresholded clean-versus-mutated decision. Localization is Top-1 ranking among a fixed inverse-candidate set after an alarm score has been computed. Open-set rejection asks whether a held-out family should be rejected rather than forced into a known label. Repair asks whether an inferred continuous magnitude is accurate enough to modify an action. These are four different estimands. The paper supports the first two for represented LIBERO families and does not collapse them into a claim about open-set coverage, action correction, or task success.

LIBERO is pinned to revision e5907374380b8f96511957e6ba5582be52a1e179 . Table 2 reports the source units before any repeated split generation. Each deterministic split assigns whole episodes 60/20/20 to train, clean calibration, and test. At most 2,000 transitions are sampled per seed. Calibration uses an empirical upper quantile with method=higher ; mutation labels and outcomes are unavailable to fitting, model selection, and threshold choice.

The predeclared estimand first averages repeated test appearances for each episode–fault cell, then averages faults within episode and episodes within task, and finally assigns equal weight to each of ten Spatial tasks. The paired hierarchical bootstrap resamples tasks and then source episodes within task for 100,000 draws. Split-randomization replicates are collapsed and are never counted as independent clusters.

The family contains exactly three directional comparisons: GMM-minus-forward recall, GMM-minus-forward localization, and GMM-minus-joint localization. The earlier forward OFAT audit shows the same need to bind claims to an operating point. The locked baseline has gain 0.3763, localization 0.9297, and FPR 0.0314. Budgets of 500 and 1,000 preserve the ordering (gains 0.3639 and 0.3678). A 1% target lowers gain to 0.2858 and FPR to 0.0162. A nominal 5% target raises gain to 0.4389 but produces FPR 0.0601 and fails. Ridge values 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 2 10^{-2} are identical at reported precision. Mild versus severe transformations yield gains 0.2790 and 0.4362. Threshold and severity are therefore experimental factors, not post-hoc knobs.

In the fresh episode-clustered audit, alarm recall is 0.03282, localization 0.73042, localization among non-alarmed rows is 0.73881, and alarm AUROC is 0.54746. Thus a relative candidate can rank correctly even when the absolute score cannot separate clean from corrupted rows. A selection-frozen reuse places 74.01% of episodes in an explanation-only false-negative stratum. This mechanism result is descriptive , not independent confirmation.

A post-hoc delay severity curve rises sharply at four, eight, and sixteen frames (gains 0.2926/0.7179/0.9209), but it explains rather than rescues the frozen short-delay failure.

passages.text: In replay, the next state is the factual outcome of the original clean action, not the outcome that the transformed command would have produced. A deterministic clean-trained response proxy reduces median GMM recall from 0.6379 to 0.2381 on LIBERO and mean recall from 0.6105 to 0.0972 on xArm, but HYDRA factual-minus-proxy effects are − 0.0978 / + 0.0604 / − 0.0440 -0.0978/+0.0604/-0.0440 . This inconsistency prevents a causal reading.

passages.section: 6.3 Factual replay is not counterfactual consequence
passages.location: 6.3 Factual replay is not counterfactual consequence
passages.text: The smallest controlled simulator compares no monitor, ridge, GMM, and oracle under the same injected faults and response-delay budget. Ridge and GMM both improve success from 0.333 to 1.000, so the ContractFuzz-specific difference is exactly zero; GMM clean FPR is 0.08 and misses the 0.05 gate. Continuous-offset repair also passes 0/10 gates (median within-0.01 accuracy 0.4930). These results support neither a detector-specific closed-loop benefit nor automatic action correction.

passages.location: What would change the scientific conclusion.
passages.text: Widening requires new evidence: multiple independent tasks under a second auditable action convention, predeclared advantage over the strongest sequence baseline, and a real counterfactual environment where mitigation improves task success under the same fault and delay budget. These nontrivial extensions are outside this rewrite; more split seeds, post-failure threshold changes, or descriptive trajectory selection cannot substitute for them.

Each task uses 100 episode-disjoint 60/20/20 partitions with seeds 33001–33100 and the original 2,000-transition cap. All 1,000 GMM fits converge; each episode–fault cell has at least 12 held-out appearances. No mutation outcome selects a seed, component count, threshold or reported family.

Separately, each fitted score is evaluated against its held-out clean reference: adjacent clean-score cutoffs are interpolated to give exact empirical FPR at the specified targets. These weighting choices are explicit: a 2.5% matched clean-reference rate is not a claim that each episode individually has a 2.5% alarm rate. Because that restriction followed a family audit, we retain the six-family result and describe the five-family result as evidence-driven claim narrowing, not a replacement of the predeclared aggregate.

The forward model has median recall 0.4504 versus 0.3560 for the joint Gaussian and wins recall on all ten tasks, but it has lower localization on all ten: medians are 0.9285 and 0.9420. Maximum FPR is 0.0282 for forward and 0.0439 for joint. Thus the joint comparison rejects the original notion that a conditional residual dominates on both metrics; it reveals a calibrated recall–localization Pareto tradeoff.

Under this original ridge comparison, a deterministic four-component GMM is stronger. On 1,000 fresh split seeds, it beats forward recall on all ten tasks by 0.15663 in the task median while keeping maximum FPR at 0.03994. A separate localization confirmation reaches 0.95926 and beats forward by 0.02932, with paired-task 95% interval [ 0.02472 , 0.03553 ] [0.02472,0.03553] ; it beats joint Gaussian by 0.01728 [ 0.01398 , 0.01971 ] [0.01398,0.01971] . Component sensitivity is not uniform. Four and eight components pass with median recall advantages 0.16093 and 0.16341, but two components reach only 0.07252 with interval [ 0.04073 , 0.11486 ] [0.04073,0.11486] and fail the frozen gate. Localization remains above 0.956. By contrast, nested calibration caps of 100, 200, and 400 clean transitions all pass: recall advantages are 0.14526–0.15400, localization is 0.96069, and the largest FPR is 0.04123. The evidence supports a multimodal density under modest calibration budgets, not mixture-count invariance.

The equal-task/equal-episode GMM-minus-forward recall effect is 0.16753 with paired 95% interval [ 0.13642 , 0.20297 ] [0.13642,0.20297] . Localization effects are 0.03089 over forward and 0.01837 over joint Gaussian. Exact task-sign-flip p = 1 / 1024 p=1/1024 for each direction; Holm-adjusted p = 0.00293 p=0.00293 across the frozen three-comparison family. All 1,000 GMM fits converge, maximum task FPR is 0.0444, and every episode appears in at least 11 test splits. This analysis supports the Spatial ordering without treating split runs as independent trajectories. An unchanged Object/Goal extension crashes because one Object task has no valid gripper-polarity rows; we make no clustered claim for those suites.

passages.section: 10.3 Episode-clustered effect and matched static comparator
passages.location: 10.3 Episode-clustered effect and matched static comparator
passages.text: The field-aligned displacement contract is non-degenerate: task-median recall is 0.32020, localization 0.84245, and maximum FPR 0.02983. Nevertheless, it passes 0/10 GMM-noninferiority gates. Metadata-minus-GMM recall is − 0.31196 -0.31196 [ − 0.33328 , − 0.24729 ] [-0.33328,-0.24729] , and localization is − 0.10914 -0.10914 [ − 0.12655 , − 0.09866 ] [-0.12655,-0.09866] . This comparison rejects a range-check-only explanation, while its missing controller specification prevents us from presenting it as a faithful third-party implementation.

The earliest detector combined a forward residual with an inverse model that predicts a t a_{t} from ( s t , s t + 1 ) (s_{t},s_{t+1}) . On 500 unseen split seeds per Spatial task, forward-only, inverse-only, and combined variants all pass the action/static gate. The combined score raises paired median recall by only 0.0065 over forward, with a task-bootstrap 95% interval [ − 0.0042 , 0.0282 ] [-0.0042,0.0282] that includes zero. Forward-only localization is higher on all ten tasks: combined-minus-forward has paired median − 0.0053 -0.0053 , interval [ − 0.0094 , − 0.0026 ] [-0.0094,-0.0026] . The original study therefore retained forward-only as its parsimonious ridge conditional baseline. This ablation does not privilege a deterministic mechanism, because the later GMM comparison shows an advantage over ridge under the original calibration contract. The post-decision conditional comparison does not support joint-density superiority.

The original methods share a calibration quantile and a 5% test-FPR ceiling, but their achieved operating points differ. Forward and joint-Gaussian maximum clean FPRs are 0.0282 and 0.0439; forward and mixture maxima in the passing confirmation are 0.02763 and 0.03994. These ceilings do not establish a matched-FPR advantage. Section 9 supplies that comparison and the capacity-controlled conditional baseline. The earlier 200-split mixture screen reaches 0.0500375 and remains inconclusive under its frozen gate.

The forward-versus-joint tradeoff is transformation-dependent. Forward is better on both recall and localization for scale, with +0.2620 recall and +0.0098 localization; joint is better on both for X-sign, with +0.0242 recall and +0.0277 localization. Only rotation shrink satisfies the frozen material Pareto gate. A paired task bootstrap makes the limits sharper: scale recall remains directional at [ 0.2263 , 0.3125 ] [0.2263,0.3125] , but its localization interval [ − 0.0181 , 0.0019 ] [-0.0181,0.0019] crosses zero; for X-sign, joint localization remains directional at [ 0.0207 , 0.0319 ] [0.0207,0.0319] , while the recall interval crosses zero. Aggregate detector rankings therefore should not be read as uniform family dominance.

Fault magnitude changes explanation before it changes detection. For X offsets of 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.10, and 0.20, GMM recall is 0.0305/0.0314/0.0330/0.0424/0.1518 while exact-magnitude localization rises from 0.4710 to 0.9490. The curve is monotone but was run after the failed offset screen, so it is mechanism evidence rather than a rescued supported family. Temporal severity behaves similarly: forward-minus-action recall gain rises from 0.0049/0.0359 at one/two frames to 0.2926/0.7179/0.9209 at four/eight/sixteen frames. Severe misalignment becomes detectable, while the short, smoother latency most relevant to deployment remains unsupported. A learned temporal baseline using ( s t , a t − 1 ) (s_{t},a_{t-1}) also passes 0/10 short-temporal gates, which rules out only that simple feature omission, not richer sequence monitoring.

Task-held-out triplets pass 3/3 with median recall gain 0.1740, localization 0.7760, and maximum FPR 0.0143. Object and Goal repeats strengthen within-LIBERO task breadth. They do not change the action representation or data-collection convention. For the same reason, 4,000 deterministic split seeds cannot substitute for 4,000 new episodes. The 432-episode clustered estimand was the original headline interval because it makes that dependency explicit. The attempted all-task clustered extension is retained as a protocol failure rather than silently changing its fault vocabulary when one Object task has no valid gripper-polarity rows.

We use an evidence hierarchy to prevent reuse from widening the claim. Fresh splits under the frozen evaluator establish algorithmic ordering on recorded tasks. Episode-clustered analyses change the inferential unit and support only the Spatial effect for which the gate is well-defined. Selection-frozen reuses diagnose heterogeneity, false negatives, and candidate confusion. Post-hoc severity curves explain a failed family. External screens test whether the same contract survives a new convention. These levels answer different questions; none converts a descriptive mechanism audit into an independent robot or task replication.

analysis.overview: 可复用的改动是异常分数：同一联合GMM改算条件似然，在匹配误报率下提升接口故障召回；联合分数反而更会定位。适合离线审计选型，尚不能用于自动修复。
analysis.notice: 已完整阅读162个提取片段，覆盖主文、方法公式、实验、补充材料、负结果和资源记录。PDF共20页；目视核对物理页4、5、16、17的表1/2/11/12/13/14、图1与条件分数公式，补充材料内部页码与PDF物理页码不同。缓存HTML没有额外listing块。未逐图核查其他图片、逐篇核查参考文献或执行论文中的代码/命令；所引代码和结果路径未验证为可公开取得，作者实验未复现。

findings.title: 问题：数值合法，动作含义仍可能错
findings.text: 审计的是轴、符号、单位和夹爪极性等接口语义。仅检查形状与范围会漏掉这类错误；本文用状态、动作和实际状态变化的关系做离线一致性检查。

findings.title: 改动：同一个GMM，改算条件分数
findings.text: 先拟合标准化的x=(s,a)、y=s_next−s的四分量全协方差联合GMM，再算R_C=−log p(x,y)+log p(x)。复用同一组参数和协方差块，无需增加容量或另训模型；隔离的是输入边缘密度对分数的贡献。

findings.title: 校准：用干净轨迹定阈值，另做匹配误报率诊断
findings.text: 按完整episode分60/20/20训练、校准与测试，每个划分最多2000个transition；只用干净校准集取上分位阈值。匹配实际误报率的另一分析使用留出干净测试分数并插值，仅供回顾性比较，不能直接当部署阈值。

findings.title: 定位：在预先声明的逆变换里排序
findings.text: 对含identity在内的固定逆变换候选逐个重算关系分数，选择最低者。Top-1衡量已知故障字段的闭集定位，不是连续动作修复；它与是否报警是两个决策。

findings.title: 结果：条件分数多检出4.70个百分点
findings.text: 10个LIBERO Spatial任务、432个源episode、5类变换，实际干净误报率匹配为2.5%时，ridge/联合GMM/条件GMM召回为46.08/60.96/65.66%。条件相对联合提高4.70个百分点，配对95%区间[3.50,6.32]；十个任务均提高。
findings.quote: exceeding joint recall on all ten tasks

findings.title: 权衡：更会检出，不代表更会定位
findings.text: 联合GMM定位95.81%，条件GMM为94.62%，ridge为92.70%。分母是全部有效故障行，不限于已报警样本；不能把这组数读成端到端“检出且定位”成功率，或安全修复率。

findings.title: 误报率：同一个名义目标，不是同一个工作点
findings.text: 校准目标同为2.5%时，测试误报率实际为ridge 2.63%、联合3.22%、条件2.85%；对应召回44.13/60.86/65.04%。这些是独立于匹配分析的校准结果。匹配误报率按划分内transition计，校准测试指标按episode等权，不能混用分母。
findings.quote: does not establish a matched operating point

findings.title: 统计边界：重划分不等于新增机器人经验
findings.text: 每任务100次划分复用同432个episode，1000次GMM拟合不是独立新轨迹。先合并重复episode—故障观测，再做2万次任务/episode分层bootstrap；区间条件于已拟合分数与参考阈值，未传播重新训练和阈值估计的不确定性。新条件分数比较仅限Spatial。

findings.title: 故障边界：偏移、短时序和未知类仍会漏
findings.text: 小X偏移GMM召回仅3.40%，0/10任务过门槛；短延迟、保持与分块倒序也0/10。留一故障族时，隐藏X反号的拒识仅37.20%，64.67%被强归为XY交换。无报警不能证明接口正确，候选排名也不能支持自动改写未知动作。
findings.quote: no alarm cannot certify a correct interface

findings.title: 外部边界：尚无跨机器人可靠性证据
findings.text: DROID-100三类召回1.93–8.65%；HYDRA三个任务10.63–12.13%，0/3过门槛，序列改造也未挽回。xArm Lift召回60.16%、误报2.45%，但800个episode都来自一个任务。Object/Goal扩展仍沿用LIBERO动作约定，不能替代独立接口复验。

findings.title: 因果边界：改动作字段，没有执行错误动作
findings.text: 评测把动作替换成T(a)，下一状态仍保留干净动作a的事实结果；这是有标签的关系不一致测试，不是错误命令的真实后果。连续偏移修复0/10过门槛；小仿真fallback与ridge打平且GMM误报超门槛，未证明闭环任务收益。
findings.quote: not environment rollouts or causal effects

findings.title: 成本：CPU可做的分数消融，复现仍待完成
findings.text: 作者报告新一轮1000次GMM拟合及条件/匹配分析共40.40秒，单CPU进程、单BLAS/OpenMP线程、无GPU。该数字是整次离线工作负载，不是机器人单步时延。本轮核对原文与表格，未运行源码、验证私有路径工件或复现实验。

hypotheses.title: 验证：条件分数的收益能否跨动作约定保留？
hypotheses.text: 待验证假设：同一GMM改用条件分数后，在另一套明确动作约定的多任务数据上，仍能在可接受误报下提高故障召回。选择至少3个具有多个独立episode的公开任务，先核对源动作语义；各任务以整episode隔离训练、干净校准和最终测试。固定相同预处理、训练样本、四分量全协方差GMM和训练预算，比较ridge、联合分数与该GMM解析条件分数；这不是零样本迁移。预先声明与源语义相符的五类变换，只计真正改变且仍在训练范围内的行，逐类报告有效行数，不能删除零有效样本任务来抬分。主结果只用干净校准集按名义2.5%定阈值，报告最终测试实际误报率与召回，并预先设5%误报上限；超限不算有效提升。将测试干净分数匹配2.5%误报率的曲线另列为回顾性分数诊断，不回填部署阈值。以任务和源episode做配对不确定性分析，合并重复划分而非把随机种子当新数据；分别统计全部故障行的定位、报警后的定位及检出且定位。若条件分数不能在多任务中稳定改善召回，或实际误报反复超限，则反对该收益可跨接口保留的假设。只对公开离线记录做合成字段审计，不执行错误机器人命令；未知故障拒识与真实闭环修复另设实验。本实验未运行，未宣称研究空白。
hypotheses.quote: multiple independent tasks under a second auditable action convention

passages.section: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
passages.location: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
passages.text: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present SoccerBot , a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, SoccerBot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.

passages.section: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
passages.location: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
passages.text: Figure 1: Real-world soccer skill execution on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. SoccerBot learns a single unified policy that covers the full soccer behavioral spectrum, including moving, trapping, dribbling, and kicking, with agile and human-like whole-body coordination.

passages.section: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
passages.location: Playing Soccer Like Humans Do: Learning Versatile and Agile Humanoid Soccer via Latent Motion Priors
passages.text: Keywords: Humanoid Soccer, Latent Motion Priors

Soccer stands apart from sports such as table tennis [ 19 , 17 ] and tennis [ 28 ] as a uniquely demanding benchmark for humanoid robots: rather than isolating upper-body dexterity, it demands the inseparable coupling of agile whole-body locomotion and non-prehensile ball manipulation across a rich, continuous behavioral spectrum. Humans master this spectrum with remarkable fluency: sprinting, trapping, dribbling, and kicking compose seamlessly into a continuous, expressive behavioral repertoire. This fluency emerges from decades of motor learning that endows human motion with natural coordination, dynamic stability, and graceful skill transitions. Replicating such fluency on a humanoid robot is far from trivial: the robot must not only master a diverse set of highly dynamic skills, but also execute smooth, natural transitions across the full behavioral spectrum. Humanoid soccer thus emerges as a compelling platform for studying unified whole-body control, simultaneously demanding agile locomotion, non-prehensile object manipulation, impact-rich contact dynamics, and human-like motion quality within a single, coherent control problem.

Despite recent progress in reinforcement learning for humanoid locomotion [ 16 , 14 , 15 ] and motor skill acquisition [ 13 , 12 , 8 , 4 , 7 , 26 , 21 , 3 ] , existing approaches to humanoid soccer remain fundamentally limited along two orthogonal axes. On one axis, existing methods lack a unified skill repertoire: most prior works address only a narrow subset of soccer behaviors [ 6 , 22 , 23 ] , such as directed kicking, dribbling, or locomotion-only control, and even multi-skill systems rely on decoupled, independently trained controllers that cannot naturally bridge the dynamics between different actions [ 5 ] . Multi-skill soccer built on human motion priors has so far been demonstrated only for simulated characters [ 9 , 5 ] . The result is a fragmented behavioral space where inter-skill transitions are inherently discontinuous and unnatural, as evidenced by the jarring switches between running and trapping, or dribbling and kicking. On the other axis, many existing methods rely solely on task-reward-driven reinforcement learning without any motion prior [ 3 ] , leaving motion naturalness entirely unaddressed. Without structural regularization grounded in human motion, such policies produce erratic, mechanically unnatural behaviors that are both visually implausible and brittle under the contact-rich dynamics of real soccer interaction. Together, these two axes define a clear gap in the literature: the combination of human-like coordination and a complete, unified soccer skill set has never been simultaneously achieved in a single humanoid soccer system.

To close this gap, we propose SoccerBot , a hierarchical learning framework that addresses both limitations through a unified mechanism: a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. Building on recent advances in physics-based motion imitation [ 10 ] , we first distill a motion tracking policy into a compact latent action space that encodes a rich, dynamically plausible manifold of human-like whole-body motion. A unified skill-conditioned policy then operates within this latent space via residual control, learning to perform dribbling, trapping, kicking, and moving under a shared control formulation. By grounding all skills within the same motion prior, SoccerBot inherently produces natural, human-like motion across the full behavioral spectrum, and produces fluid, natural inter-skill transitions during commanded skill switching. To further support reliable real-world deployment, we incorporate robustness-oriented simulation design including ball dynamics modeling, domain randomization, and observation perturbation, enabling zero-shot sim-to-real transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot.

We evaluate SoccerBot in both simulation and real-world settings, demonstrating that a single unified policy can execute the full spectrum of soccer skills with agility and naturalness under real-world conditions. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We present SoccerBot , to our knowledge the first real-world humanoid soccer system that jointly achieves a complete skill repertoire and human-like motion quality, learning moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking within a single unified policy.

We propose a hierarchical latent motion prior framework with transition state initialization (TSI), grounding unified soccer skill learning within a structured motion manifold and enabling agile, human-like behaviors, fluid inter-skill transitions, and robust cross-skill composition without explicit state machines or separate controllers.

We conduct extensive simulation benchmarks and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1, demonstrating strong task performance across all four skills, structured latent skill-space organization, and reliable zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with minimal performance degradation.
Videos are available at https://soccerbot-humanoid.github.io .

Reinforcement learning has driven rapid progress in humanoid robot control, enabling robust locomotion [ 15 , 16 , 14 ] and whole-body motion tracking [ 8 , 4 , 2 , 27 , 21 , 7 ] from large-scale human motion capture data [ 11 ] . Beyond locomotion and motion tracking, RL has enabled humanoid robots to master a growing range of athletic skills, including tennis [ 28 ] , table tennis [ 19 , 17 ] , and parkour [ 24 , 26 ] . Among these, humanoid soccer stands out as uniquely demanding: it requires the tight coupling of agile locomotion and non-prehensile ball manipulation through the feet, sustained across a continuous and dynamic behavioral spectrum. Early learning-based soccer systems demonstrated agile ball interaction on simulated avatars [ 9 ] and small real bipedal robots [ 3 ] , while more recent work has explored soccer motion generation from human demonstrations [ 20 , 25 ] . On real humanoid robots, Dribble Master [ 23 ] learns agile dribbling through a two-stage curriculum with virtual-camera perception, and other works study perception-driven kicking and reactive soccer skills [ 6 , 22 ] . Most closely related to our work, PhysicsFC [ 5 ] learns dribbling, trapping, moving, and kicking with smooth transitions, but relies on skill-specific policies with an explicit finite-state machine and remains confined to simulation. In contrast, our work learns a single unified policy across the full soccer skill repertoire and deploys it on a real humanoid robot.

A prominent approach to regularizing humanoid reinforcement learning uses adversarial motion priors. AMP [ 13 ] learns a discriminator from unstructured motion clips to provide a style reward that guides task policies toward natural behaviors, and ASE [ 12 ] extends this by learning reusable adversarial skill embeddings for downstream task policies. While effective, adversarial approaches require careful balancing between task reward and motion realism, and can struggle to discover precise contact-rich strategies such as ball trapping. An alternative line of work constructs structured latent action spaces by distilling motion tracking controllers into compact motor representations. PULSE [ 10 ] distills a universal humanoid motion tracker into a VAE-style latent action space with a learned state-conditioned prior, enabling downstream policies to generate coherent human-like motions without adversarial rewards. Inspired by this framework, recent work has extended latent motion priors to athletic humanoid skills, demonstrating their effectiveness for contact-rich tasks such as tennis [ 28 ] . We adapt the latent motion prior framework to unified humanoid soccer, training a single residual latent policy conditioned on skill commands across moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking, which extends beyond single-skill athletic tasks to a complete soccer skill repertoire deployed on a real robot.

Figure 2: Overview of SoccerBot . The framework consists of three stages: (1) a motion tracking expert is trained on retargeted human soccer motion data; (2) the tracking expert is distilled into a structured latent motion prior via a variational encoder-decoder framework; (3) a unified skill-conditioned policy learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking via residual latent control over the frozen prior, with transition state initialization enabling robust cross-skill composition. Real-world deployment uses an external motion capture system for ball state estimation.

We present SoccerBot , a staged framework for learning a unified whole-body policy for humanoid soccer skills. The key idea is to separate low-level motor competence from high-level soccer task optimization. As shown in Fig. 2 , our pipeline has three stages: Stage I trains a motion tracking teacher from curated soccer demonstrations; Stage II distills this teacher into a compact latent motion prior; and Stage III trains a skill-conditioned soccer policy within this frozen latent action space. The final policy receives a skill command and task observation, predicts a latent residual, and decodes it into joint position targets through the pretrained motion decoder.

The first stage constructs a physically feasible motion corpus and trains a whole-body tracking policy π trk \pi_{\mathrm{trk}} . We source human soccer demonstrations from Soccer-X [ 25 ] and retarget them to the humanoid robot using GMR [ 1 ] . Since raw retargeted motions may contain kinematic artifacts such as foot skating, discontinuous contacts, and dynamically infeasible poses, we apply a filtering pipeline: a pretrained tracker rolls out each sequence in simulation, and segments that cannot be tracked under hardware torque limits are discarded. This yields approximately 2.5 2.5 hours of curated reference motions 𝒟 motion \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{motion}} .

We train π trk ​ ( a t ∣ s t , s ^ ref ) \pi_{\mathrm{trk}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t},\hat{s}_{\mathrm{ref}}) with reinforcement learning to imitate the filtered trajectories. The state is s t = ( s t prop , s t priv ) s_{t}=(s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{priv}}) , where s t prop s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}} contains proprioceptive observations such as joint positions and velocities, projected gravity, base angular velocity, and previous action, while s t priv s_{t}^{\mathrm{priv}} denotes privileged information available only in simulation, such as the base linear velocity. The reference s ^ ref ∈ 𝒟 motion \hat{s}_{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{motion}} specifies target full-body poses and velocities. The policy outputs joint position targets tracked by a low-level PD controller, and the reward combines pose and velocity imitation with balance and control regularization. After convergence, π trk \pi_{\mathrm{trk}} is executed on 𝒟 motion \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{motion}} and provides the teacher actions for distillation.

passages.section: 3.2 Latent Motion Prior Construction via Distillation
passages.location: 3.2 Latent Motion Prior Construction via Distillation
passages.text: The second stage distills the tracking teacher into a structured latent motion prior. The student consists of a posterior encoder q ϕ ​ ( z t ∣ s t prop , s t ref ) q_{\phi}(z_{t}\mid s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{ref}}) , a state-conditioned prior p ψ ​ ( z t ∣ s t prop ) p_{\psi}(z_{t}\mid s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}}) , and a decoder D θ ​ ( z t , s t prop ) D_{\theta}(z_{t},s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}}) . The posterior observes both proprioception and reference motion, while the prior observes only proprioception. This asymmetry lets the encoder infer the latent that best explains the teacher motion, while forcing the prior to model the motions that are feasible from the current body state alone, which is exactly the information available to the downstream soccer policy.

passages.text: The first term trains the decoder to reproduce the teacher’s joint targets. The second term regularizes the full information posterior toward the learned prior, so that the information carried by the reference motion is transferred into a distribution that can be queried without it. The third term penalizes abrupt changes of the posterior mean and yields temporally smooth latent trajectories, which improves the continuity of the decoded joint targets. After distillation, the posterior is discarded, while p ψ p_{\psi} and D θ D_{\theta} are frozen for downstream soccer learning.

The third stage trains a unified skill-conditioned policy π η \pi_{\eta} for the soccer skills. A single policy handles four primitives: dribbling , kicking , moving , and trapping . Its observation contains the velocity command, ball position and velocity in the robot frame, skill one-hot vector, and proprioceptive state. For moving , ball observations are masked, so the same interface supports both ball-centric and robot-centric behaviors without skill-specific observation spaces.

To preserve the stability and naturalness of the motion prior during dynamic ball interaction, the soccer policy does not act directly in joint space. Instead, it learns a residual in the pretrained latent motion space while the prior and decoder stay frozen. Given proprioception s t prop s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}} , task observation s t task s_{t}^{\mathrm{task}} , and skill command e t e_{t} , the frozen prior produces z t p = μ ψ ​ ( s t prop ) z_{t}^{p}=\mu_{\psi}(s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}}) . The policy samples a residual z t s ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( μ η ​ ( s t prop , s t task , e t ) , diag ⁡ ( σ η 2 ) ) z_{t}^{s}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\eta}(s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{task}},e_{t}),\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{\eta}^{2})) and decodes
z t = z t p + α ​ z t s , a t = D θ ​ ( z t , s t prop ) . z_{t}=z_{t}^{p}+\alpha z_{t}^{s},\qquad a_{t}=D_{\theta}(z_{t},s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}}). (2)

Here α \alpha scales the residual and σ η \sigma_{\eta} is a learnable state-independent standard deviation. PPO optimizes this latent residual distribution rather than the 29 29 -dimensional joint action: likelihood ratios, entropy, and KL terms are computed only in latent space. This restricts stochastic exploration to the neighborhood of the motion prior while still allowing the policy to adapt to dynamic ball interactions.
We regularize the residual mean by

ℒ bound = 𝔼 t ​ ∑ i [ max ⁡ ( | μ η , i ​ ( s t prop , s t task , e t ) | − 1 , 0 ) ] 2 . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bound}}=\mathbb{E}_{t}\sum_{i}\left[\max\left(|\mu_{\eta,i}(s_{t}^{\mathrm{prop}},s_{t}^{\mathrm{task}},e_{t})|-1,0\right)\right]^{2}. (3)
This keeps the task policy close to the motion prior while preserving the expressivity needed for ball interaction.

Each episode samples an active skill and interprets the command accordingly. For moving , the command specifies the desired robot velocity. For the ball-centric skills, it specifies the desired ball motion: dribbling samples low-speed target ball velocities, kicking samples high-speed target velocities together with strikeable initial ball states, and trapping launches incoming ground passes that the robot must intercept and damp. Rewards are routed by skill: only the terms of the active skill are enabled at each timestep, while a shared set of regularizers encourages consistent whole-body behavior.

We use transition state initialization (TSI) to train robust skill switching. For each skill, we keep a circular buffer of terminal robot and ball states from episodes that ended without failure. At reset, an episode of the target skill can be initialized from the terminal state of a preceding skill. This exposes the policy to the postures, momentum, and ball configurations resulting from the preceding skill, rather than relying solely on canonical initial states.
We train with lightweight randomization and observation corruption that target the two main sources of sim-to-real mismatch in soccer: contact-rich robot–ball dynamics and imperfect state estimation.

We randomize robot–ground and ball–ground friction and restitution and the ball mass, and we apply angular damping to the ball with a coefficient c a c_{a} sampled uniformly from [ 0.3 , 0.6 ] [0.3,0.6] for each environment at initialization. This encourages repeated interaction with the ball to maintain the commanded speed during dribbling. We further randomize the torso center of mass, default joint positions, and actuator latency. External velocity pushes during rollouts improve recovery from contact-induced disturbances.

Policy observations are corrupted with bounded noise on ball position, ball velocity, base angular velocity, projected gravity, joint positions, and joint velocities, which makes the controller less dependent on exact simulator states.

The multi-skill policy is trained within the NVIDIA Isaac Lab simulation environment tailored to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot. For real-world hardware deployment, exteroceptive states are captured via an external optical motion capture system. The tracked ball states are transformed into the local robot base coordinate frame before being fed into the control policy.

passages.section: 4.1 Main Simulation Results on Soccer Skills
passages.location: 4.1 Main Simulation Results on Soccer Skills
passages.text: We evaluate the proposed framework on four humanoid soccer skills: kicking, dribbling, trapping, and moving. These skills require not only task completion, but also stable whole-body dynamic balancing and human-like motion quality. Each method is evaluated on 2,500 2{,}500 episodes per skill with randomized simulation settings.

passages.section: 4.1 Main Simulation Results on Soccer Skills
passages.location: 4.1 Main Simulation Results on Soccer Skills
passages.text: We compare our method with the following baselines: 1) PPO : vanilla PPO trained with our task reward without human motions. 2) AMP : PPO with an adversarial motion prior reward computed from human motions. 3) ASE : an adversarial skill embedding baseline that pre-trains a latent-conditioned low-level controller on the human motions and then trains a high-level task policy that selects skill latents. 4) LATENT : a task policy trained in a learned latent action space with Latent Action Barrier [ 28 ] . We compare our method with the following ablations: 1) Ours w/o prior : removes the learned state-conditioned prior and predicts task latents directly. 2) Ours w/o TSI : trains without TSI.

passages.section: 4.1 Main Simulation Results on Soccer Skills
passages.location: 4.1 Main Simulation Results on Soccer Skills
passages.text: We use a compact set of task and motion metrics. SR is the percentage of trials that satisfy the skill-specific success condition without a fall or task failure. VelErr measures the speed tracking error of the task object: the ball for kicking and dribbling, and the robot base for moving. DirErr is the heading error between the realized motion and the commanded direction in the horizontal plane. For dribbling, ResT is the response time after a command switch. For trapping, StopT is the time from first ball contact to a stable stop, and DistErr is the ball displacement during stopping. Train ref. and Post-train ref. measure how closely a policy moves like a human: each is the squared maximum mean discrepancy, MMD 2 , between motion features of the policy’s rollouts and those of a human reference set. Train ref. uses the training motions 𝒟 motion \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{motion}} , and Post-train ref. consists of motion capture clips that were not used to train any of the evaluated methods.

Ours achieves the highest kicking ( 97.04 % 97.04\% ) and dribbling ( 89.88 % 89.88\% ) SR of all methods and completes every moving command. AMP, which directly rewards matching the motion distribution, is closest to both reference sets, and ASE, whose low-level controller imitates the reference motions, is second on the post-training clips. However, AMP traps only 23.08 % 23.08\% of passes and dribbles in 46.36 % 46.36\% of episodes, and ASE learns neither kicking nor dribbling. Among the methods that complete all four skills, Ours is closest to both reference sets.

passages.text: The components serve distinct roles: the frozen decoder, distilled from human soccer motions, carries the motion representation in every latent variant; the state-conditioned prior supplies a feasible latent anchor around which the residual explores; and TSI broadens the distribution of switching states. Because the w/o prior variant keeps the same decoder, it isolates the anchor. Both ablations trap more reliably than Ours. Ours tends to block fast passes with an extended leg, and the ball then rebounds beyond the displacement gate. Removing the prior lowers kicking and dribbling SR, and removing TSI lowers dribbling SR. The prior shows instead in how the policy moves: with the same decoder, removing it moves the policy further from both human reference sets, raising the mean MMD 2 to 0.234 0.234 and 0.582 0.582 . The benefit of TSI appears mainly when skills start from non-canonical states ( Sections 4.2 and 4.3 ).

In simulation, our full method achieves strong performance on near and mid-range static balls, with success rates of 98.6 % 98.6\% and 87.0 % 87.0\% , respectively. The policy also remains robust under more challenging incoming ball and wide yaw settings, achieving 72.9 % 72.9\% and 83.9 % 83.9\% success rates. passages.text: The real-world results further demonstrate the sim-to-real transferability of the learned policy in controlling kicking direction, with success evaluated solely based on directional accuracy. Despite the hardware and perception uncertainties in real deployment, the real-robot success rates remain close to the simulation results, with only a small average performance drop of about 3.1 3.1 percentage points. This suggests that the learned kicking strategy is not only effective in simulation but also transfers well to the real robot across different ball and command conditions.

We analyze how the latent action is constructed from the motion prior and the task residual. During evaluation rollouts, we record the prior latent z prior z_{\mathrm{prior}} , the task residual latent z task z_{\mathrm{task}} , and the final latent z z for kicking, dribbling, moving, and trapping. Samples from all three latent types are concatenated and embedded with a single joint t-SNE projection, then shown as three separate panels in Fig. 3 . Since the three panels share the same embedding space, we compare local neighborhoods and skill clusters, rather than interpreting the t-SNE axes directly.

Fig. 3 shows a transition from a shared motion prior to a skill-aware latent space. In z prior z_{\mathrm{prior}} , the four skills largely overlap, suggesting that the prior captures state-conditioned feasible motor modes rather than explicit skill identity. The residual latent z task z_{\mathrm{task}} introduces clearer skill-dependent separation. The final latent z z preserves the shared support of the prior while forming structured regions for dribbling, kicking, moving, and trapping. Moving and dribbling remain partially close because both rely on locomotion dynamics, while kicking and trapping occupy more specialized regions associated with striking and stopping the ball. This visualization indicates that the policy builds a structured skill space by adapting a shared motion prior with skill-conditioned residuals, rather than learning four isolated controllers.

We deploy the policy zero-shot on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Ball and robot states are tracked by an external optical motion capture system and transformed into the robot base frame. We evaluate each of the four skills with 20 20 trials: moving and dribbling vary the commanded speed and heading, trapping varies the incoming ball velocity, and kicking varies the target ball speed and heading. Table 4 compares it with its sibling simulation policy.

Table 4 shows the sim-to-real gap. Moving transfers most closely in speed: its speed error rises only from 19.14 % 19.14\% in simulation to 21.53 % 21.53\% on hardware. Dribbling and trapping degrade more across their continuous metrics. For dribbling, the speed error grows from 8.55 % 8.55\% to 30.17 % 30.17\% and the response time from 1.21 1.21 s to 2.37 2.37 s. For trapping, the stopping time grows from 0.78 0.78 s to 1.84 1.84 s, and the ball travels 1.07 1.07 m after contact instead of 0.31 0.31 m. Both skills depend on sustained robot–ball contact and rolling dynamics. Kicking retains substantially better directional than speed control: DirErr increases from 4.09 ∘ 4.09^{\circ} to 10.41 ∘ 10.41^{\circ} , whereas VelErr increases from 8.12 % 8.12\% to 47.38 % 47.38\% .

To diagnose the remaining gap, we conducted two ball dynamics identification experiments on the deployment surface. Twenty passive drop trials yield a ball–ground restitution of e = 0.654 e=0.654 , which falls within the randomized range of [ 0.45 , 0.85 ] [0.45,0.85] . Free rolling trials measure an effective rolling deceleration of 0.100 0.100 m/s 2 . Reproducing these trials in simulation over the randomized angular damping range yields mean decelerations of 0.097 0.097 to 0.167 0.167 m/s 2 , so both measurements fall within the corresponding domain randomization ranges, supporting coverage of the observed real-world ball dynamics. The higher outgoing ball speed on hardware points to stronger effective foot–ball impulse transfer: the simulated ball is rigid, whereas the real inflated ball deforms during impact, altering the contact duration, force profile, and effective restitution.

We presented SoccerBot , a hierarchical learning framework for unified humanoid soccer control. By decoupling whole-body motor competence from task-level optimization, our approach distills human motion data into a reusable latent motion prior, upon which a single skill-conditioned policy learns moving, dribbling, kicking, and trapping within a shared latent action space. Simulation and real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate robust skill execution, natural whole-body motion, and stable sim-to-real transfer. Beyond individual skills, the unified command interface enables higher-level planners to compose learned primitives into longer-horizon behaviors, suggesting a practical path toward autonomous planning and potentially multi-robot coordination.

Despite promising results, several limitations remain. First, the gap between simulation and real deployment varies across skills. On hardware, kicks overshoot the commanded speed, while dribbling and trapping exhibit the largest increases in continuous error metrics. These discrepancies may partly stem from the rigid ball contact model. Future work could explore compliant contact modeling and policy fine-tuning on the real robot. Second, the system relies on an external motion capture system for state estimation, restricting deployment to instrumented indoor environments. Integrating onboard perception would enable deployment in less structured settings. Third, the skill set is limited to four fundamental soccer behaviors; extending it with broader motion data and task curricula would make the policy more expressive. Fourth, our experiments focus on single-robot control, leaving multi-agent coordination and game-level decision making for future work. A natural direction is to use the learned skill-conditioned policy as a reusable low-level interface for autonomous planning and multi-agent humanoid soccer.

passages.section: Appendix C Training, Transition State Initialization, and Robustness
passages.location: Appendix C Training, Transition State Initialization, and Robustness
passages.text: We train the soccer actor with PPO in Isaac Lab/Isaac Sim using 8192 8192 parallel environments. The actor samples residual latents, and the frozen decoder maps them to joint position targets tracked by the robot low-level controller. The critic can use privileged simulation information during training, whereas the deployed actor only requires the policy observation terms in Table A.1 .

Transition state initialization (TSI) improves cross-skill recovery and skill switching. For each skill c c , we maintain a circular buffer ℬ c \mathcal{B}_{c} of terminal states. A stored state contains the robot root state, joint positions and velocities, and the ball state. At reset, an episode starts either from the canonical task initialization or from a sampled terminal state:

s 0 ∼ { p init ​ ( s 0 ∣ c ) , with probability ​ 1 − p TSI , ℬ c ′ , with probability ​ p TSI . s_{0}\sim\begin{cases}p_{\mathrm{init}}(s_{0}\mid c),&\text{with probability }1-p_{\mathrm{TSI}},\\ \mathcal{B}_{c^{\prime}},&\text{with probability }p_{\mathrm{TSI}}.\end{cases} (A.3)

Here c ′ c^{\prime} is a predecessor skill of the sampled target skill c c : dribbling can follow trapping; kicking can follow trapping and dribbling; moving can follow dribbling and kicking; and trapping can follow dribbling. The target command is then sampled and executed from the inherited robot and ball state. We use p TSI = 0.3 p_{\mathrm{TSI}}=0.3 and a buffer of 256 256 states per skill. The buffer stores only terminal states of episodes that end without failure. This expands the reset distribution without injecting falls or physically invalid configurations.

passages.section: C.2 Domain Randomization and Observation Corruption
passages.location: C.2 Domain Randomization and Observation Corruption
passages.text: The robustness design targets two deployment gaps: contact-rich robot–ball dynamics and noisy state estimation. Observation corruption is included directly in the Corruption column of Table A.1 . The implementation also supports a perception-stress setting that holds the previous ball observation and injects larger ball velocity noise for ball-interaction skills.

passages.section: C.2 Domain Randomization and Observation Corruption
